question: Frédéric Bastiat, a Paris journalist and deputy, spent the late 1840s fighting the heavy tariffs France laid on iron, cloth and grain from abroad. The tariffs let French makers raise their prices and still keep their buyers. Who paid the hidden cost?
answer: French households, through higher prices
choices: French households, through higher prices
Foreign makers, out of their own profits
The state, through the cost of customs posts
French makers, through higher wages
context: A tariff is a tax on imports. The July Monarchy laid heavy tariffs on iron, textiles and grain to protect French producers. Bastiat's point was that the shelter was paid for by every French buyer, who paid more for the protected goods, while the gain went to a few producers everyone could see. His Economic Sophisms (1845, 1848) is the classic satirical field guide to the protectionist arguments of the day. Source: http://davidmhart.com/liberty/Papers/Bastiat/EconomicSophisms/Hart_BastiatsSophismsAug2011.html.

question: Against Louis Blanc's National Workshops of 1848, which promised a wage to any jobless man who asked, Frédéric Bastiat kept pointing to a cost that nobody saw. What is the hidden cost of a scheme like that?
answer: The government has to tax everyone else a lot to pay them all
choices: The government has to tax everyone else a lot to pay them all
The jobless people refuse to accept any work
Foreign countries buy fewer of the country's goods
Interest rates automatically drop to zero
context: Louis Blanc (1811-1882) had published L'Organisation du travail (The Organization of Labor) serially in 1839, arguing that only the state could remedy unemployment through 'social workshops' organized craft by craft. In February 1848 he joined the Provisional Government and pushed the decree that created the National Workshops. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Blanc.

question: Louis Blanc saw his National Workshops open to every jobless man in February 1848, and by May more than 100,000 had enrolled, their wages paid out of taxes. Digging holes and filling them in again would not count as work. What is the built-in trouble with a guaranteed-job scheme on that scale?
answer: Too little real work, so most are paid to do almost nothing
choices: Too little real work, so most are paid to do almost nothing
The workshops make so many goods that prices fall
So many enroll that the city runs out of tools
Private firms match the wage, and prices soar
context: The National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) opened in late February 1848 and grew past 100,000 enrollees by May. The treasury could not pay them for real work, and wages became a straight welfare payment. Louis Blanc had originally wanted them run as producer cooperatives; the actual implementation, under minister Marie, was mostly digging and hauling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Workshops.

question: A man rakes leaves on a city payroll, one of 100,000 people hired for busywork like raking, filing and painting benches, all paid from the city budget. After a few years the money runs out, and one morning the whole scheme shuts at once. What usually happens in the streets right after?
answer: The suddenly unpaid workers riot over their lost income
choices: The suddenly unpaid workers riot over their lost income
The streets go quiet as the men head home to the villages
Crowds line up quietly at private hiring halls
The workers march peacefully and petition the city
context: The June Days (Journees de Juin, June 23-26, 1848) followed the closure of the National Workshops and were suppressed by General Louis-Eugene Cavaignac with heavy casualties. Louis Blanc, tainted by his association with the workshops, fled to England, where he lived in exile for 22 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Workshops.

question: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and Frédéric Bastiat argued in open letters from October 1849 until the following March, in Proudhon's own paper, La Voix du Peuple. Proudhon wanted his Bank of the People to lend money at no charge at all. What was Bastiat defending against the scheme?
answer: That interest is the market price of time-preference and cannot be legislated to zero
choices: That interest is the market price of time-preference and cannot be legislated to zero
That the state should replace private banks with a single central bank of issue
That labor unions should set wages by industry-wide bargaining
That gold coinage should be replaced with government paper money
context: Proudhon pushed his Banque du Peuple as an issuer of interest-free credit ('credit gratuit'). Bastiat defended interest as the real market price paid for the use of savings over time. Proudhon collected the letters as Interet et principal; Bastiat published his version, augmented by a fourteenth reply, as Gratuite du credit (1850). Source: https://praxeology.net/FB-PJP-DOI-IV-2b.htm.

question: Étienne Cabet imagined a perfect communist republic, Icaria, in a novel where everyone shared everything and no one owned private property. In 1848 he took several hundred followers across the Atlantic to build it on American soil, first in Texas and then at Nauvoo, Illinois. Dozens of small communist colonies rose in nineteenth-century America. What became of most of them?
answer: They fell apart within a few years from fighting and shortages
choices: They fell apart within a few years from fighting and shortages
They grew into huge successful cities within twenty years
They were shut down by the US government for being illegal
They were bought out by railroads building lines across the West
context: Etienne Cabet (1788-1856) published Voyage en Icarie in 1839, then led the Icarian emigration in 1848; the settlement eventually landed at Nauvoo, Illinois after the Mormons had abandoned it. Fourier (phalansteres) and Saint-Simon (industrial technocracy) were the earlier utopian-socialist generation whose ideas fed into the 1848 moment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Cabet.

question: Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq and their neighbors pump much of the world's oil. Suppose they stop selling it to certain nations, a cut-off called an embargo. Those nations still need oil to run their cars, trucks and factories. What happens to the prices they pay?
answer: They shoot way up
choices: They shoot way up
They stay the same
They drop
They double, then quickly return to normal
context: The 1973 Oil Crisis saw world oil prices roughly quadruple in a matter of months. The embargo formally ended March 1974 but prices remained substantially elevated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis.

question: A hurricane is on its way and gasoline is already running short. The government orders every station to keep its prices where they are, no matter what. Drivers hurry over, hoping to fill up at the normal price. What usually happens at the pumps next?
answer: Long lines form and pumps run empty faster
choices: Long lines form and pumps run empty faster
Drivers buy less, so the fuel lasts longer
Stations ship in extra fuel to meet the rush
Everyone gets a fair share, so no one waits
context: Odd-even license-plate rationing rules meant drivers with odd-ending plates could only buy on odd-numbered dates; even-ending plates on even dates. Stations posted 'NO GAS' signs when empty. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: Americans queued an hour for gasoline in 1973 and 1974, and many blamed the Arab oil embargo. Milton Friedman's followers pointed instead to a policy Nixon had first set in 1971. It made it illegal for the price at the pump to climb as supply fell, so stations ran dry. What was the policy?
answer: Federal price ceilings on gasoline
choices: Federal price ceilings on gasoline
The 55-mph national speed limit
Federal excise taxes on gasoline
The Alaska Pipeline delay
context: Nixon-era gasoline price ceilings were already in force before the embargo. The ceiling prevented the pump price from rising to clear the market; the resulting shortage was rationed by queuing. Without the ceiling, prices would have risen sharply and lines would not have formed. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: Arab oil producers cut off sales in October 1973 to nations that had helped Israel in the Yom Kippur War. America, Britain and France soon had mile-long lines at their gas stations. Two European countries had no lines at all: their pumps stayed full, though their prices ran far higher. Which pair was it?
answer: West Germany and Switzerland
choices: West Germany and Switzerland
France and Italy
Norway and Denmark
Britain and Ireland
context: West Germany and Switzerland had no price controls and no lines during the 1973-74 shock. Prices rose sharply, demand adjusted, supply cleared. The US had controls and lines. Source: energyhistory.yale.edu.

question: Frederic Bastiat taught that every policy has two sides: the Seen, its obvious effects, and the Unseen, the hidden costs everyone forgets. Murray Rothbard's 1974 essay 'The Energy Fiasco' turned that frame on America's gasoline lines of 1973, when federal price controls held pump prices low. What did Rothbard call the Seen and the Unseen of those controls?
answer: Seen: the low pump price. Unseen: hours in line and fuel never brought in
choices: Seen: the low pump price. Unseen: hours in line and fuel never brought in
Seen: OPEC's greed. Unseen: the oil imports America kept buying
Seen: rising gas taxes. Unseen: the road repairs they never paid for
Seen: drivers' thrift. Unseen: refiners making more fuel than anyone bought
context: Rothbard's Bastiatian argument: the low pump price is what people saw; what was hidden was the time-cost paid in the line, the private importers unwilling to bring in gasoline at a loss, and the deliveries that did not happen. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in 1945 that a market runs on knowledge spread across millions of ordinary people. Shoppers choosing tomatoes at a grocery store make thousands of small decisions: what price is fair, what tastes good, what they can afford. Together those choices tell farmers what to plant. Suppose an office in the capital tried to replace them all with one central plan. What would most likely go wrong first?
answer: The office would guess wrong about what people actually want, leading to shortages and waste
choices: The office would guess wrong about what people actually want, leading to shortages and waste
Shoppers would prefer being told what to buy
Farmers would grow exactly the right amount because their instructions would be clearer
Grocery stores would run more smoothly with simpler prices
context: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay The Use of Knowledge in Society argued that the knowledge an economy runs on, of particular circumstances of time and place, is scattered among millions of people and is never given to any single mind. Prices gather it: shoppers' choices tell the grocer, and the grocer's orders tell the farmer. An office that replaced those choices with a plan would lack that knowledge and guess wrong, leaving shortages in one place and waste in another. Milton and Rose Friedman later made the 1973-74 gas lines a showcase of price-control shortages in Free to Choose (1980). Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society.

question: Frederic Bastiat taught that every policy has an obvious effect and a hidden one. In the 1970s Murray Rothbard and other Austrian economists turned that idea on price ceilings. A cap, they argued, does not remove the cost of a scarce good; it only turns one kind of cost into another that most shoppers never notice. What conversion did they name?
answer: Money-costs converted into time-costs paid in line
choices: Money-costs converted into time-costs paid in line
Money-costs converted into transportation-costs
Money-costs converted into gasoline-quality-costs
Money-costs converted into environmental-costs
context: The ceiling converts what would have been a money-cost (buyer pays higher price, seller collects it) into a time-cost (buyer pays hours in line, no seller collects). The cost is not eliminated -- and no producer receives the payment. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: Richard Nixon set a legal ceiling on the price of American oil in 1971, and Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter after him kept the caps in place. Long gas lines formed across the country in 1973 and again in 1979. Then, days after taking office in January 1981, Ronald Reagan signed an executive order that scrapped the oil price caps entirely. What happened at the pumps after that?
answer: The lines never came back, as producers could sell at real market prices
choices: The lines never came back, as producers could sell at real market prices
Lines returned because rules do not change real behavior
Lines grew much worse because prices spiked forever
Lines returned until the government built more oil wells
context: Reagan's Executive Order 12287 of January 28, 1981 ended the remaining federal price and allocation controls on domestic crude oil and refined products. The gas lines of 1973-74 and 1979 never returned, and oil prices, which peaked about then, fell through the first half of the 1980s. Source: https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/codification/executive-order/12287.html.

question: The Iranian Revolution overthrew the Shah in 1979 and cut off Iran's oil exports, sending world oil prices spiking for the second time in a decade. Gasoline lines came back to America, and California's lines were the worst: drivers there waited hours at the pump. Federal price caps were still in force, along with federal rules for sharing gasoline out among the states. Why was California hit so hard?
answer: Its federal allotment was based on its smaller past use
choices: Its federal allotment was based on its smaller past use
Its refineries were destroyed by an earthquake
Its truck-driver strike blocked deliveries
Its harbor unions refused to unload tankers
context: In spring 1979 federal price controls on crude oil and gasoline were still in force, and the Department of Energy allotted gasoline by a formula tied to how much each buyer had used in an earlier base period (1972 until March 1979, then 1978). President Carter said on May 16, 1979 that the formula had not been able to reflect California's rapid growth, so the state's allotment fell short and its lines were among the worst in the country. The natural experiment confirmed the price-ceiling-produces-lines mechanism a second time. Source: https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/gasoline-shortages-california-statement-the-president-0.

question: Drivers across America queued for gasoline in 1973 and 1974, and California's lines came back in 1979. Both times a price ceiling, a legal maximum no seller could charge above, held the pump price low. Murray Rothbard saw more in the two episodes than the bare word 'shortage.' What lesson did he draw?
answer: The shortage under a ceiling is a shortage in space AND in time
choices: The shortage under a ceiling is a shortage in space AND in time
The shortage under a ceiling is offset by tariff reductions
The shortage under a ceiling improves consumer welfare
The shortage under a ceiling requires more central planning
context: The reasoning move: the shortage manifests both as empty pumps (space) and as hours of queueing (time). Removing the ceiling ends both instantly. Source: mises.org/library/energy-fiasco.

question: Anna wants planners to run the city's traffic; Ben doubts they could ever know enough. Thomas Sowell called the rival pictures behind quarrels like theirs visions. Why that word?
answer: They come before any argument
choices: They come before any argument
They are dreams of utopia
They are forecasts of the future
They come from studying data
context: In A Conflict of Visions (1987) Thomas Sowell used the word vision for a sense of how the world works that comes before any theory is built. The constrained and unconstrained visions, he argued, decide which policies feel obviously right to each side and which feel naive, before a single fact is weighed. Ben's doubt about planners is the constrained vision speaking. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Conflict_of_Visions.

question: Thomas Sowell mapped two rival pictures of human nature in his 1987 book A Conflict of Visions. One holds that new and better institutions can remake people; the other holds that they cannot. What one-word label did he give each picture?
answer: Constrained and unconstrained
choices: Constrained and unconstrained
Left and right
Progressive and conservative
Statist and libertarian
context: Sowell uses 'constrained' as the primary label (with 'tragic' as a synonym from within the tradition) and 'unconstrained' as the paired label (with 'utopian' as a critical synonym). He explicitly rejects a 'realistic vs idealistic' framing. Source: Sowell, Conflict of Visions (1987).

question: Adam Smith and Edmund Burke wrote from one picture of what people are like, Thomas Sowell argued, and Friedrich Hayek and the American Federalists shared it. In that picture, what anyone knows is spread across millions of heads, and good rules are built up over long trial and error. What view of human beings lies under it?
answer: A view that human nature has real limits we must work around
choices: A view that human nature has real limits we must work around
A view that people can be reshaped into anything by a smart plan
A view that self-interest can be trained out of people
A view that a small group of experts can plan a whole country
context: The constrained vision runs through Smith, Burke, the American Federalists, and Hayek. Politics in this vision is about designing rules to channel imperfect people -- not about identifying who has the right vision and empowering them. Source: Sowell (1987), Chapter 2.

question: Thomas Sowell grew his 1987 book on rival visions of human nature into a trilogy over the next twelve years. The second volume, in 1995, set the hopeful vision, that people can be remade by better institutions, against the social policy of modern America, and traced what follows when self-congratulation becomes the basis of policy. What is that volume called?
answer: The Vision of the Anointed
choices: The Vision of the Anointed
The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Discrimination and Disparities
Intellectuals and Society
context: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic 1995) analyzed the unconstrained vision in operation across US social policy. It is the second book in the trilogy. Source: basicbooks.com (Sowell 1995).

question: Thomas Sowell ended his trilogy on rival visions of human nature in 1999. Its last volume followed the hope that people can be remade by better institutions all the way to its utopian end, and diagnosed the results. What did he title that final book?
answer: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
choices: The Quest for Cosmic Justice
Applied Economics
Migrations and Cultures
Ethnic America
context: The Quest for Cosmic Justice (Free Press, 1999) analyzed the unconstrained vision's aspirations to remake outcomes to match a picture of ultimate fairness. It is the closing book in the trilogy. Source: simonandschuster.com (Sowell 1999).

question: Thomas Sowell laid out both visions of human nature at their strongest in his 1987 book and followed each through named thinkers, from Adam Smith to William Godwin. Then, on purpose, he held back from one last step. Which step did he refuse to take?
answer: Declare either vision correct
choices: Declare either vision correct
Describe the visions in detail
Trace the visions through named thinkers
Apply the visions to specific policy debates
context: Sowell's methodological restraint: the book maps the disagreement without declaring which vision is right. Kids learn to RECOGNIZE which vision is speaking, not which is right. The bank replicates that restraint. Source: Sowell (1987), Introduction.

question: Thomas Sowell took up a puzzle in 1987: an economist and an activist who know the same facts still talk past each other on the same policy. In A Conflict of Visions he traced the gap to something deeper than facts. What did he say lay beneath it?
answer: Each side operates from a different picture of what humans essentially are
choices: Each side operates from a different picture of what humans essentially are
One side has poor mathematical training
One side ignores empirical data on principle
One side is paid by wealthy donors and the other is not
context: The unconstrained-vision speaker sees trade-off talk as failure of will; the constrained-vision speaker sees solution talk as naive utopianism. Both are reasoning inside internally-coherent frameworks -- the gap is the pre-analytical vision, not the argument at the surface. Source: Sowell (1987), Chapters 4-6.

question: Adam Back proposed in 1997 that every email carry a small puzzle costing the sender's computer about half a second of work, a scheme he called Hashcash. Twenty emails a day would cost a person ten seconds. What would happen to a spammer sending a million?
answer: He gives up -- a million puzzles would take days
choices: He gives up -- a million puzzles would take days
Nothing changes -- spammers have faster computers
Nothing -- he sends the puzzles along unsolved
Users suffer -- they can no longer send email
context: Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997. At half a second a message, a person's twenty emails a day cost ten seconds, but a million messages would cost a spammer's computer some 500,000 seconds, nearly six days of work, while the receiving computer checks each stamp in an instant and throws out any message without one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor sketched an early version in 1993 of the lopsided puzzle Adam Back built Hashcash around in 1997: slow for a sender's computer to solve, but checked by the receiver in a blink. Bitcoin later used the same idea to secure its blockchain. What is a puzzle of that kind called?
answer: proof-of-work
choices: proof-of-work
proof-of-stake
proof-of-authority
zero-knowledge proof
context: 'Proof-of-work' is the general name for a lopsided puzzle that costs far more to solve than to check. Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor proposed the idea against junk mail in a paper presented in 1992 and published in 1993; the name itself was coined by Markus Jakobsson and Ari Juels in 1999. Proof-of-stake, proof-of-authority and zero-knowledge proofs are separate cryptographic ideas. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Proof_of_work.

question: One giant email service put Hashcash-style postmarks to work against spam in the mid-2000s. They never spread everywhere, since all the world's email software would have had to change at the same time. Which service tried them?
answer: Microsoft's mail servers
choices: Microsoft's mail servers
Google Gmail
Apple iCloud Mail
AOL Mail
context: Microsoft integrated Hashcash-style postmark stamps into its Exchange/Hotmail anti-spam stack (Penny Black project, 2003 onward). Google, Apple, and AOL relied on other filtering (Bayesian, reputation, DKIM) rather than PoW stamps. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash.

question: Two cypherpunks, programmers in a scattered online circle who hoped for digital money without banks, took Adam Back's Hashcash and built money designs on it, one in 1998 and one in 2004. Both men would later play a part in Bitcoin's story. Which two were they?
answer: Wei Dai (b-money) and Hal Finney (RPOW)
choices: Wei Dai (b-money) and Hal Finney (RPOW)
David Chaum (DigiCash) and Nick Szabo (bit gold)
Phil Zimmermann (PGP) and Eric Hughes (remailers)
Tim May (crypto anarchy) and John Gilmore (toad.com)
context: Wei Dai's b-money (Nov 1998) and Hal Finney's Reusable Proof-of-Work (RPOW, 2004) both cited Hashcash. DigiCash used blind signatures, not PoW; PGP is encryption; Tim May and John Gilmore ran the cypherpunk community infrastructure. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt; https://nakamotoinstitute.org/rpow/.

question: Adam Back helped found a company, Blockstream, in 2014, and it became one of the teams contributing to Bitcoin Core. Yet Bitcoin itself has no chief executive and no owner, and its code is open to the public. What does that open code mean in practice?
answer: Anyone can improve the network, and competing teams keep each other honest
choices: Anyone can improve the network, and competing teams keep each other honest
Only one official company is allowed to change the code each year
A Bitcoin foundation must approve every new feature before release
Governments choose which teams may work on the software
context: Adam Back co-founded Blockstream in 2014 and later became its chief executive; the company's developers contribute to Bitcoin Core, and it runs the Liquid sidechain. Bitcoin Core's code is open source: anyone may read it, propose a change or run it, and no company, foundation or government owns the network or approves its releases. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Back.

question: Adam Back's spam stamp picked up a new task in 2008, when Satoshi Nakamoto made it the engine of Bitcoin's mining. In email the stamp had only made each message cost a little computer work; in Bitcoin it took on a further role. What new job did it take on there?
answer: settling network-wide agreement on the ordering of transactions
choices: settling network-wide agreement on the ordering of transactions
encrypting the contents of individual messages
authenticating the identity of the sender
compressing block-chain data for storage
context: In Hashcash, PoW just imposes a per-message cost. In Bitcoin, PoW plus the longest-chain rule is the consensus mechanism -- how thousands of nodes agree on the ordering of transactions without a central coordinator. Encryption, sender-authentication, and compression are separate technologies. Source: Nakamoto (2008) sec 4; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto built Bitcoin's mining on Adam Back's old spam stamp, so a Bitcoin miner mints every new coin with puzzle work. Bitcoin writers say Hashcash gave software a trait no earlier digital thing had. Which trait?
answer: digital scarcity: something expensive to produce and cheap to check
choices: digital scarcity: something expensive to produce and cheap to check
digital anonymity: transactions without identifying information
digital consensus: agreement among many nodes without a leader
digital irreversibility: a payment that cannot be reversed
context: Hashcash's specific contribution was making costly digital tokens verifiable at zero cost -- the first working demonstration of digital scarcity. Anonymity (blind signatures), consensus (Nakamoto's longest chain), and irreversibility (block confirmations) came from different later designs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashcash; Szabo's later 'shelling out' essay.

question: Congress set up the Transportation Security Administration in November 2001, after the September 11 attacks, to search bags at every American airport. What had become of the agency two decades later?
answer: Bigger -- new government agencies almost never shrink
choices: Bigger -- new government agencies almost never shrink
Smaller -- the crisis is over
Gone -- the law only lasted five years
The same size it was on day one
context: The TSA was created by Public Law 107-71, signed November 19, 2001. Founding staff about 30,000; by 2023 approximately 60,000 employees with an annual budget near $10B. Source: dhs.gov (TSA history).

question: Undercover testers for the Department of Homeland Security set out in 2015 to sneak fake guns and bombs past American airport checkpoints. When the results leaked, the number stunned Congress. What share of the fakes did the screeners reportedly miss?
answer: About 95 percent
choices: About 95 percent
About 5 percent
About 30 percent
About 50 percent
context: The 2015 DHS OIG covert red-team test found TSA screeners missed approximately 95% of test contraband. A 2017 follow-up found little improvement. Results are sensitive to test conditions but were widely reported. Source: oig.dhs.gov (2015 covert testing summary).

question: Ronald Reagan campaigned to abolish the Department of Education, and failed. Meanwhile what American public schools spent on each pupil, after inflation, more than doubled from 1970 to 2010. What do the nation's long-term reading and math tests for 17-year-olds show between the early 1970s and 2012?
answer: Scores stay roughly flat, even though spending has gone way up
choices: Scores stay roughly flat, even though spending has gone way up
Scores rise in perfect step with the extra spending
Scores double, matching the rise in per-student funding
Scores fall by about half within the first ten years
context: Average long-term-trend NAEP reading and math scores for 17-year-olds did not change significantly between the early 1970s and 2012, the last year those tests were given, despite decades of increased education spending. Source: https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/ltt_2012/.

question: Jimmy Carter created the Department of Education in October 1979. Set its officials beside the airport screeners and the tax collectors of the Internal Revenue Service, and one pattern runs through all three over the decades. What is it?
answer: Staff and budget grow, but results do not clearly improve
choices: Staff and budget grow, but results do not clearly improve
Staff and budget grow, and results rise with every dollar
Staff and budget shrink once the founding crisis fades
Staff stays level while budgets go to buildings and machines
context: The recurring pattern across all three: growing staff, growing budget, and difficulty demonstrating proportional improvement on the metric the agency was created to move. Niskanen's model predicts exactly this. Source: Niskanen (1971); GAO agency performance reports.

question: Suppose a government office is paid each year by how many people it employs, not by anything it finishes. James Buchanan and other public-choice economists spent careers tracing incentives like that one. Over a decade, how does an office like this tend to change?
answer: It hires more people and finds new tasks so its budget keeps growing
choices: It hires more people and finds new tasks so its budget keeps growing
It shrinks its own staff to save taxpayer money
It closes down once its original job is finished
Its workers refuse promotions to keep the office small
context: James Q. Wilson, Bureaucracy: What Government Agencies Do and Why They Do It (Basic Books, 1989). Wilson analyzed observable, measurable outputs versus procedural rule-following as key determinants of agency behavior. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Q._Wilson.

question: William Niskanen left citizens a test to run whenever a government agency asks for more money, and he predicted that agencies would fight any kind of measurement that made the test possible. What does his test ask the agency to show?
answer: Show that the last ten percent of prior budget produced roughly ten percent of the output
choices: Show that the last ten percent of prior budget produced roughly ten percent of the output
Show that its whole budget, taken together, bought more than a dollar of results per dollar
Show that its budget has grown no faster than the national economy as a whole
Show that most citizens surveyed approve of the job the agency is doing
context: The marginal-cost / marginal-product test: if the last dollar of prior spending bought well under a dollar of output, adding more is even less likely to be worthwhile. A bureau prefers to defend its total budget against its total output, which can look good even when the last dollars bought little. Niskanen predicts agencies systematically resist any measurement scheme that would allow the marginal comparison. Source: Niskanen (1971), Chapter 5.

question: Donald Trump won the 2024 election and chose Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy to lead a hunt for bureaus that had swollen without doing more real work, the very pattern William Niskanen had warned of in 1971. What was the effort called?
answer: The Department of Government Efficiency
choices: The Department of Government Efficiency
The Federal Streamlining Office
The Bureau of Bureaucratic Review
The Council on Public Administration Reform
context: Donald Trump announced the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) on November 12, 2024, with Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy to lead a hunt for waste in federal agencies. Ramaswamy left on January 20, 2025, the day the effort was formally set up, and Musk left at the end of May 2025. The initials echoed a famous internet meme. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Department_of_Government_Efficiency.

question: An insurance company has sold home-loan insurance to hundreds of banks. If a single bank has a poor year and a few loans sour, the insurer pays it and carries on. Then home loans start going bad everywhere at once. What danger does the insurer now face?
answer: The company runs out of money -- it sold more coverage than it could ever pay
choices: The company runs out of money -- it sold more coverage than it could ever pay
The banks cancel their policies -- they demand every premium back at once
The company loses its customers -- no bank buys new coverage in a slump
The company is fined -- it insured loans it had never checked
context: American International Group, founded 1919, was one of the largest insurance companies in the world. Its Financial Products unit had written CDS coverage on hundreds of billions in mortgage-backed securities held by every major bank. Source: Grokipedia 'American International Group' (2026-09-05).

question: Timothy Geithner, then running the New York Fed, drew up the rescue of the insurance giant American International Group in September 2008. The first loan came the day after Lehman Brothers collapsed, and the Fed took nearly 80 percent of the company in exchange. How big was that first loan?
answer: About 85 billion dollars
choices: About 85 billion dollars
About 8 billion dollars
About 300 billion dollars
About 15 billion dollars
context: The initial September 16 2008 commitment was $85 billion, later expanded to a total of $182 billion -- the largest single bailout in US history. Source: Grokipedia 'AIG bailout' (2026-09-05).

question: The Fed and the Treasury kept adding to their rescue of the insurer American International Group after its first emergency loan in September 2008. Month after month the commitment climbed, until no single American firm had ever been rescued on that scale. How high did it peak?
answer: About 182 billion dollars
choices: About 182 billion dollars
About 85 billion dollars
About 500 billion dollars
About 45 billion dollars
context: The $182 billion peak commitment, from the Fed and the Treasury together, is the largest single-firm government rescue in US financial history. Sources: Grokipedia 'AIG bailout' (2026-09-05); Wikipedia 'American International Group' ($182.3 billion in combined assistance).

question: American International Group (AIG) had written credit default swaps, insurance contracts on mortgage bonds, for nearly every big bank. The government rescued the insurer in September 2008, saying the rescue would protect ordinary families' insurance. Whose rescue was it really?
answer: The banks that had bought AIG's swaps
choices: The banks that had bought AIG's swaps
The families holding AIG's insurance policies
AIG's own stockholders and top executives
AIG's foreign subsidiaries in Asia
context: AIG immediately used the loaned money to pay CDS collateral at 100 cents on the dollar to its counterparties. Every major dealer that had bought protection was made whole through the insurance conduit. Source: SIGTARP Report, October 2009.

question: American International Group (AIG) owed its Wall Street trading partners billions when the government rescued it in September 2008, on swap contracts that had insured their riskiest mortgage bets and on loans of securities. Federal officials saw that those debts were paid in full. Which bank collected the biggest sum in all?
answer: Goldman Sachs
choices: Goldman Sachs
Citigroup
JPMorgan Chase
Wells Fargo
context: By AIG's own disclosure of March 2009, Goldman Sachs received about $12.9 billion through AIG, the largest sum, counting swap collateral, payments for the bonds the swaps insured and securities-lending repayments. Societe Generale received about $11.9 billion and Deutsche Bank about $11.8 billion; on the swaps alone Societe Generale took the most, about $11 billion to Goldman's $8.1 billion. Source: AIG release of March 15, 2009, reported by ThinkAdvisor and Calculated Risk; SIGTARP audit, November 2009.

question: Congress gave the 2008 bailout money its own watchdog, an inspector general whose job was to track where it went. The watchdog's chief issued reports between 2009 and 2011 on the insurer American International Group, tracing where its rescue money actually ended up, and later told the story in a book, Bailout. Who was he?
answer: Neil Barofsky at SIGTARP
choices: Neil Barofsky at SIGTARP
Elizabeth Warren at the COP
Sheila Bair at the FDIC
Mark Calabria at the FHFA
context: Barofsky, the Special Inspector General for TARP, published a series of reports 2009-2011 documenting exactly how AIG's rescue moved money to Goldman, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch, and others. His book Bailout (2012) tells the story. Source: SIGTARP Reports 2009-2011.

question: American International Group sold credit default swaps, promises to pay out if mortgage bonds went bad, on the strength of a top-grade triple-A rating, and it set aside no cash against them; no regulator demanded any. It lost the triple-A in 2005, and in September 2008 the rating agencies cut it again. Under its own contracts, what suddenly happened?
answer: The company owed billions in collateral overnight and could not pay
choices: The company owed billions in collateral overnight and could not pay
The banks could tear up the swaps and claim back their fees
Regulators froze its swap business until it raised fresh capital
The swaps lapsed, leaving the banks with no protection at all
context: AIG's counterparties had accepted its promise to pay without collateral, trusting the AAA rating. Standard & Poor's cut AIG from AAA in March 2005; when the agencies downgraded it again on September 15, 2008, collateral demands surged past what the firm could raise. Sources: Grokipedia 'AIG Financial Products' (2026-09-05); S&P testimony to the House Financial Services Committee (2009).

question: Every big firm on Wall Street watched in September 2008 as the government poured billions into the insurer American International Group rather than let it fail, in a rescue that kept its real winners out of sight. Public-choice economists warn that two lasting results follow rescues like that, and one of them is called moral hazard. What are the two?
answer: Big risk-takers expect more rescues, and public trust in the government shrinks
choices: Big risk-takers expect more rescues, and public trust in the government shrinks
Big risk-takers turn cautious, and public trust in the government grows
Small banks win customers from big ones, and bank fees fall
Regulators gain sharper tools, and later bubbles grow smaller
context: The AIG conduit worked in the moment but corroded institutional legitimacy over years. Every future risk-taker learned that political optics can be managed while counterparties get paid. Source: Barofsky, Bailout (2012).

question: An airline asks the Civil Aeronautics Board in Washington for leave to cut a fare; from 1938 to 1978 every airline had to. The Board also chose which airlines flew which routes. Who gained the most from that forty-year rule?
answer: The existing airlines -- they did not have to fear a cheaper competitor
choices: The existing airlines -- they did not have to fear a cheaper competitor
Passengers -- prices went down every year
New airline start-ups -- it was easy to open one
Foreign airlines -- they won the busiest American routes
context: The Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938 created the authority that became the Civil Aeronautics Board in 1940. The CAB issued 'certificates of public convenience and necessity' specifying exact endpoints and stops, and set fares. Sources: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: Officials of the Civil Aeronautics Board, which picked the routes and set the fares of every American airline from 1938 to 1978, warned the public against letting any airline fly anywhere at any price. Open skies, they said, would unleash one specific danger. Which danger?
answer: Ruinous competition that would bankrupt carriers and strand small towns
choices: Ruinous competition that would bankrupt carriers and strand small towns
Crowded skies that air traffic controllers could not handle safely
Foreign carriers taking over the profitable American routes
Airlines cutting maintenance to survive on cheaper tickets
context: The CAB's stated purpose was to avert 'destructive' or 'ruinous' competition, keep the established trunk carriers solvent, and sustain service to smaller communities by cross-subsidy. Because the Board treated large price differences as destabilising, airlines competed on meals, seat width and schedules rather than fares. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: An outside firm files an application with the Civil Aeronautics Board to start a scheduled American airline against the big established carriers. The Board received seventy-nine such applications between 1950 and 1974. How many did the Board approve?
answer: None of them
choices: None of them
Three of them
Eleven of them
Twenty-six of them
context: Between 1950 and 1974 the CAB received 79 applications from firms outside the domestic scheduled airline industry, and not one was granted; with minor exceptions the Board had not even set such applications for hearing since 1960. The protected 'trunk carriers' faced no new entrants for forty years. Source: Journal of Air Law and Commerce, vol. 41.

question: Pacific Southwest in California and Southwest in Texas sold tickets 30 to 60 percent cheaper than the regulated carriers in the 1960s and 1970s, and their planes flew fuller too. The Civil Aeronautics Board never stopped them. Why couldn't it touch them?
answer: Each flew only inside one state, so its business never reached the Board's authority
choices: Each flew only inside one state, so its business never reached the Board's authority
Each was owned by its own employees, an arrangement the Board's rules did not cover
Each carried mail under a contract that exempted its fares from Board review
Each used aircraft small enough to be classed as air taxis, which were exempt
context: The CAB regulated INTERSTATE air transport. PSA in California and Southwest in Texas flew only intrastate, escaping the Board entirely, and their fares ran roughly 30-60 percent below comparable regulated fares with higher load factors. The air-taxi exemption was real -- Part 298 covered aircraft under 30 seats -- but neither airline used it. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: Robert Timm, while he chaired the Civil Aeronautics Board, set a rule that airlines should earn 12 percent on their money. Senator Ted Kennedy's team later asked the Justice Department to look at him for a gift he took from the airlines he oversaw. What was the gift?
answer: A golf holiday in Bermuda
choices: A golf holiday in Bermuda
A seat on a carrier's board of directors
Lifetime first-class travel for his family
A consulting fee routed through a trade group
context: Timm, CAB chair until 1974, prioritised ensuring scheduled airlines made a 12 percent return on investment and was caught accepting a Bermuda golf vacation from those airlines; Kennedy's subcommittee referred him to the Justice Department. Kennedy's 1975 hearings, with Stephen Breyer as counsel, publicised both this and the low intrastate fares. Source: Wikipedia 'Civil Aeronautics Board'.

question: Jimmy Carter put Alfred Kahn, a Cornell professor and lifelong Democrat, in charge of the Civil Aeronautics Board in 1977. Kahn joked that he could not tell one plane from another, then added a line about planes that stuck to him for life. What did he say they were to him?
answer: All just marginal costs with wings
choices: All just marginal costs with wings
Buses that happen to leave the ground
Tubes full of people and kerosene
The most protected machines in America
context: Kahn (1917-2010), author of The Economics of Regulation (1970-71) and called the father of airline deregulation, said: 'I can't tell one plane from the other. To me, they're all just marginal costs with wings.' A marginal cost is what one more unit -- here one more passenger on a flight already leaving -- actually adds to cost, and Kahn's point was that fares should track it. Source: Wikipedia 'Alfred E. Kahn'.

question: Congress ended fare control in 1978, and a hidden transfer had nowhere left to hide. Under the Civil Aeronautics Board, travellers on busy trunk routes had paid fares above what competition would have set, and the surplus quietly kept flights going to small towns. So Congress built a replacement. What did it create?
answer: The Essential Air Service programme, funded as a line in the federal budget
choices: The Essential Air Service programme, funded as a line in the federal budget
A rule obliging every major carrier to keep flying a quota of rural routes
A landing-fee rebate that small airports could offer to attract carriers
A rural air mail contract system administered by the Postal Service
context: Congress created Essential Air Service alongside the 1978 act to keep flights going to low-density airports formerly cross-subsidised under the CAB regime. The economics lesson is Bastiat's: the cost had always been paid, but by invisible passengers on other routes; deregulation did not abolish it so much as move it into daylight where a legislature has to vote on it. Source: Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'.

question: Jimmy Carter signed the Airline Deregulation Act on October 24, 1978, after it cleared Congress by crushing margins: 82 to 4 in the Senate, 356 to 6 in the House. The lopsided votes hid a long and bitter fight, and economists still cite the losing side. Who fought hardest to keep the Civil Aeronautics Board's controls?
answer: The established trunk airlines and the Air Line Pilots Association
choices: The established trunk airlines and the Air Line Pilots Association
The consumer movement, with Ralph Nader leading the opposition
The Federal Aviation Administration and the big airport authorities
The aircraft manufacturers, Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, together
context: The fiercest resistance came from the incumbent trunk carriers and ALPA, the pilots' union -- the parties forty years of route protection had shielded -- which is Stigler's regulatory capture visible from the outside: an industry defending its regulator. ALPA lost, and low-fare, often non-union entrants eroded the wage premiums it had won. Ralph Nader in fact SUPPORTED deregulation, on the ground that CAB rules propped up monopoly. The 82-4 and 356-6 tallies are the final votes on the conference report, October 14, 1978. Sources: ALPA, 'From the Hill'; Cato, 'Alfred Kahn, 1917-2010'; Grokipedia 'Airline deregulation'; Wikipedia 'Airline Deregulation Act'.

question: Murray Rothbard was thirty-seven when he published a 361-page re-examination of the 1929-33 slump in 1963, writing as an economist of the Austrian school. Where others faulted free markets and the 1929 crash, he faulted Washington. What did he title the book?
answer: America's Great Depression
choices: America's Great Depression
The Road to Serfdom
A Monetary History of the United States
The General Theory of Employment
context: Published by D. Van Nostrand of Princeton in 1963, 361 pages. Rothbard (1926-1995) was 37 when the book appeared. It became the definitive Austrian-school treatment of the 1929-33 downturn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America%27s_Great_Depression.

question: Murray Rothbard re-examined, in 1963, the slump that closed thousands of American banks between 1929 and 1933 and threw nearly a quarter of workers out of work. He argued the free market was not to blame. Which two culprits did his account name?
answer: The Federal Reserve and President Hoover
choices: The Federal Reserve and President Hoover
Wall Street speculators and the gold standard
Consumer debt and rural bank failures
European war debts and immigration limits
context: Rothbard argued Fed credit expansion in the 1920s produced the boom that had to bust, and then Hoover's activist response after October 1929 turned what should have been a short liquidation into a decade-long depression. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: One Federal Reserve official, who worked closely with the Bank of England's Montagu Norman, drew Murray Rothbard's sharpest blame for the boom of the 1920s. He was the dominant force in the Fed in those years. Which official did Rothbard blame?
answer: Benjamin Strong, Governor of the New York Fed
choices: Benjamin Strong, Governor of the New York Fed
Marriner Eccles, Chairman of the Board of Governors
Paul Warburg, founding member of the Federal Reserve Board
Andrew Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury
context: Rothbard singled out Strong as the dominant force at the Fed during the 1920s. Strong pushed easy credit in part to help Britain sustain the pound after Britain's 1925 return to gold at the pre-war parity, working closely with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: Herbert Hoover called Henry Ford, Pierre du Pont and other great industrialists to the White House in November 1929, weeks after the stock market crashed, as unemployment began to rise. What did he press them to promise?
answer: That they would not cut wage rates
choices: That they would not cut wage rates
That they would suspend all foreign lending
That they would sell their gold holdings to the Treasury
That they would freeze retail prices for one year
context: The centerpiece conference was November 21, 1929, with figures like Henry Ford and Pierre du Pont. Rothbard argued Hoover's high-wage policy blocked the labor-market adjustment that had ended earlier American depressions in eighteen months or less. Source: mises.org/online-book/progressive-era/15-herbert-hoover-and-myth-laissez-faire.

question: Warren Harding became president in March 1921, in the middle of a savage slump that had struck the year before. Unemployment neared 12 percent, and the dollar value of everything the country produced had fallen about 17 percent. His government kept cutting until federal spending in 1922 was almost half that of 1920, and it let wages and prices fall. What happened next?
answer: The slump ends within about eighteen months of its start as prices reset
choices: The slump ends within about eighteen months of its start as prices reset
Falling prices feed a spiral that deepens the slump for years
Unemployment stays near 12 percent for the rest of the decade
Recovery waits until the cuts are reversed and spending resumes
context: The slump ran from January 1920 to about July 1921. Thomas Woods of the Mises Institute gives unemployment rising from 4 to nearly 12 percent and GNP falling 17 percent, and credits Harding with cutting the federal budget nearly in half between 1920 and 1922. Rothbard, and later Austrian writers, treated this 'forgotten depression' as the natural experiment showing that non-intervention produced a fast recovery, while Hoover's opposite response after 1929 produced the opposite result. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/forgotten-depression-1920.

question: Herbert Hoover created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in January 1932, and before the year was out it had spent about 1.5 billion dollars, a great share of it propping up failing banks and railroads. Franklin Roosevelt kept it and enlarged it. What is the main long-run danger of rescue programs like this one?
answer: Firms take bigger risks, expecting a rescue loan if they get in trouble
choices: Firms take bigger risks, expecting a rescue loan if they get in trouble
Firms grow more careful, because the loans come with strict rules
Rescued firms lose the right to borrow from private banks for good
Prices fall for years as rescued firms flood markets with goods
context: Signed January 22, 1932. The RFC spent about $1.5 billion in 1932, much of it in loans to banks and railroads. Roosevelt kept the agency and widened its powers from 1933. Sources: federalreservehistory.org/essays/reconstruction-finance-corporation; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Finance_Corporation.

question: Amity Shlaes went back over Herbert Hoover's four years in office for The Forgotten Man, published in 2007, as Murray Rothbard had before her. The schoolbook story says Hoover sat idle after the October 1929 crash until Franklin Roosevelt stepped in from 1933. What did the record show the two writers?
answer: The first president had run big spending and price-support programs
choices: The first president had run big spending and price-support programs
The first president had balanced his budgets and let prices fall
The first president had cut tariffs to restart world trade
The first president had kept federal spending flat to the end
context: Rothbard wrote that 'if we define New Deal as an antidepression program marked by extensive governmental economic planning and intervention, Herbert Clark Hoover must be considered the founder of the New Deal in America.' Amity Shlaes's 2007 book The Forgotten Man popularized this view. Source: mises.org/online-book/progressive-era/15-herbert-hoover-and-myth-laissez-faire.

question: Murray Rothbard pushed back in 1963 against the schoolbook line that the October 1929 crash caused the Great Depression. He used a move from Austrian Business Cycle Theory, his school's account of boom and bust. Which move did he press against the crash-caused-it story?
answer: The 1929 bust was the inevitable liquidation of Fed-created 1920s malinvestment, not itself the cause
choices: The 1929 bust was the inevitable liquidation of Fed-created 1920s malinvestment, not itself the cause
The crash was psychological panic that spread by newspaper coverage rather than by real economic forces
The crash was caused by insufficient consumer spending and could have been offset by fiscal stimulus
The crash reflected structural overproduction in American manufacturing outrunning global demand
context: ABCT holds that artificially cheap credit steers savings into projects that only look profitable while rates are suppressed. When rates normalize, those projects reveal themselves as malinvestment. On this reading the 1929 crash was the correction, not the disease. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, in their Monetary History of 1963, blamed the Federal Reserve for shrinking the supply of money by about a third after the crash. Murray Rothbard's book of the same year faulted the Fed for a different failure, spread over the whole decade before the crash. Which failure?
answer: Expanding credit through the 1920s to help Britain stay on gold, planting malinvestment
choices: Expanding credit through the 1920s to help Britain stay on gold, planting malinvestment
Holding credit too tight through the 1920s, so farm debts and bank failures piled up
Failing to enforce the Federal Reserve Act's real-bills rule on its member banks
Raising rates sharply each time stocks climbed, so the decade's recoveries stalled
context: Rothbard's account is a CAUSE-of-the-boom story; Friedman-Schwartz's is a CAUSE-of-the-post-crash-contraction story. Both blame the Fed but for opposite mechanisms. Rothbard traced the cheap-credit push to Benjamin Strong's cooperation with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman after Britain returned to gold in 1925 at the pre-war parity. Source: mises.org/library/book/americas-great-depression.

question: Andrew Jackson, a frontier general turned president in 1828, threw much of his two terms into a fight to kill the Second Bank of the United States. Its owners were wealthy Easterners and foreign investors. What danger did Jackson see in that?
answer: A small group having control over the whole country's money
choices: A small group having control over the whole country's money
The bank charging too little interest on loans
Foreign countries printing US dollars
The bank giving too many loans to poor farmers
context: Jackson won the 1828 election on a populist platform. His fight against the Bank became the defining political conflict of his two terms. Source: Grokipedia 'Andrew Jackson' (2026-09-05).

question: Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to renew the Second Bank of the United States on July 10, 1832. His veto message attacked the privilege the Bank held. What did the message say a privilege like the Bank's did?
answer: Made the rich richer and the potent more powerful
choices: Made the rich richer and the potent more powerful
Weakened the states relative to the federal center
Undermined the moral virtue of American farmers
Encouraged wasteful government spending in Washington
context: Jackson's July 10 1832 veto message named the Bank as a threat to democratic equality: 'The rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes... make the rich richer and the potent more powerful.' Source: Grokipedia 'Bank War' (2026-09-05).

question: Nicholas Biddle, president of the Second Bank of the United States, hit back with the one weapon in his hands when Andrew Jackson began moving federal deposits away from the Bank in 1833. He hoped to hurt the economy badly enough that voters would blame Jackson and push Congress to recharter the Bank, and his own letters record the plan. What did Biddle do?
answer: He contracted credit sharply to induce a recession
choices: He contracted credit sharply to induce a recession
He raised interest rates on federal loans
He refused to redeem Treasury deposits
He sold off British-owned shares en masse
context: Biddle's role in the 1833-34 credit contraction is documented in his own letters. He hoped economic pain would generate political pressure to recharter. Jackson responded by withdrawing federal deposits from the Bank and placing them in state-chartered institutions. Source: Grokipedia 'Nicholas Biddle (banker)' (2026-09-05).

question: Freshly re-elected, Andrew Jackson began moving the government's money out of the Second Bank of the United States in 1833 and parked it in a few state banks that were friendly to him. His enemies gave those banks a mocking animal nickname. What did they call them?
answer: Pet banks
choices: Pet banks
Wildcat banks
Serpent banks
Squire banks
context: The state-chartered banks Jackson favored with federal deposits were called 'pet banks' because his critics saw them as political allies rewarded for loyalty. Source: Grokipedia 'Pet banks' (2026-09-05).

question: A delegation of directors from the Second Bank of the United States came to plead with Andrew Jackson in 1834, the story goes, hoping to save the Bank's charter. Jackson is said to have answered with a furious insult that is still quoted, though historians dispute its exact source. What is he said to have called them?
answer: A den of vipers and thieves he meant to rout out
choices: A den of vipers and thieves he meant to rout out
A cabal of foreign agents he meant to expose
A pack of moneychangers he meant to drive out
A gang of swindlers he meant to see in prison
context: Tradition gives the line as 'You are a den of vipers and thieves. I intend to rout you out.' It is traditionally attributed to Jackson, but modern historians dispute its exact primary source; it captures the tone of his 1832-1834 public statements about the Bank. Source: Grokipedia 'Andrew Jackson' (2026-09-05).

question: Andrew Jackson let the charter of the Second Bank of the United States run out in 1836, ending its life as a central bank. Private and state banks then carried American money alone, with no national central bank at all, and the country lived through periodic panics. How long did that stretch last?
answer: Seventy-seven years, until 1913
choices: Seventy-seven years, until 1913
About ten years, until 1846
About thirty years, until 1866
Almost a hundred and fifty years
context: The Federal Reserve Act was signed December 23 1913 -- 77 years after the Second Bank's charter expired in 1836. The 19th-century US operated under a decentralized banking system with periodic panics. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: Richard Lawrence came at Andrew Jackson at the Capitol on January 30, 1835, with two pistols. Jackson went after him with his cane before bystanders pinned the man down, and later blamed friends of the Bank for the attack. What went wrong with the two pistols?
answer: Both caps fired, but neither pistol's main charge went off
choices: Both caps fired, but neither pistol's main charge went off
Both pistols jammed before Lawrence could cock them
Both pistols burst in his hands, hurting only Lawrence
Both shots went wide after a bystander knocked his arm
context: Lawrence's percussion-cap pistols both misfired on January 30 1835, an event so improbable that it was calculated at odds of about 125,000 to 1. Jackson attacked Lawrence with his cane; bystanders subdued him. Source: Grokipedia 'Attempted assassination of Andrew Jackson' (2026-09-05).

question: Andrew Jackson killed the Second Bank of the United States by 1836, with his veto pen and by pulling out the federal deposits. The country then went generations without a national central bank before Congress created another. What does the whole Jackson-versus-Bank episode show about central banks?
answer: Whether to have one is a political choice, not a technical necessity
choices: Whether to have one is a political choice, not a technical necessity
An economy cannot run long without one, so one always returns
Without one, a country slides quickly into runaway inflation
Each one lasts only as long as its own bankers keep it sound
context: The 77-year gap between the Second Bank's expiration and the Federal Reserve Act shows the country could and did operate without a central bank. The choice to have one is political and reversible in principle. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank War' (2026-09-05).

question: Two rival companies want the only government license to import a certain good, and each pours a million dollars into lawyers and lobbyists to talk officials into granting it. In the end one company wins and the other loses. Did the country as a whole get any richer from all that spending?
answer: No -- they only fought over a government favor
choices: No -- they only fought over a government favor
Yes -- the lawyers' fees count as new income
Yes -- the winner's license paid for the spending
Partly -- only the loser's money was wasted
context: Anne Osborn Krueger's June 1974 AER paper 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' gave a permanent name to Tullock 1967's concept. Krueger later served as World Bank Chief Economist 1982-86 and IMF First Deputy Managing Director 2001-06. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Krueger.

question: Anne Krueger looked hard at India and Turkey in the early 1970s, where the right to bring in foreign goods was handed out by government license. In a short paper of 1974 she named the effort firms spent chasing those licenses, and economists still use her name for it. What is it?
answer: Rent-seeking
choices: Rent-seeking
Regulatory capture
Moral hazard
Producer surplus
context: Rent-seeking: dissipation of real resources chasing state-created privileges. The term entered every economics vocabulary through Krueger 1974, though Tullock's 1967 paper 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' described the mechanism first. Source: aeaweb.org.

question: Anne Krueger found in Turkey, in the early 1970s, that a single government import license could fetch more than the whole shipment it let in. Her 1974 paper spelled out what firms did once a paper permit was worth more than a factory's output. What did they do?
answer: Hired whole departments to lobby for licenses instead of producing goods
choices: Hired whole departments to lobby for licenses instead of producing goods
Refused to trade with license-holding rivals
Cut prices to below-market levels to avoid inspection
Diversified into shipping instead of manufacturing
context: Firms rationally spent resources chasing licenses proportional to the licenses' rent value -- staffing whole departments, cultivating officials, making side payments. Every hour spent chasing a license was an hour not spent producing. The dissipation is pure. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: Anne Krueger added a new reason to the list of why nations stay poor, a list that until then named mostly too little capital or too little education. She came to it after studying India and Turkey in the early 1970s. What did her 1974 paper add?
answer: A large fraction of measured 'economic activity' in state-led economies is unproductive rent-seeking
choices: A large fraction of measured 'economic activity' in state-led economies is unproductive rent-seeking
Falling prices for raw-material exports keep shrinking poor countries' earnings
Fast-growing populations in poor countries eat up every gain in output
Colonial-era borders split peoples apart and keep civil wars burning
context: Krueger's insight transformed development economics. In her account, part of the poverty of state-led economies comes from institutions that burn resources chasing privileges: fix the rent-creating rules, and the wasted effort turns back toward production. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: Manmohan Singh, India's finance minister, led sweeping reforms in 1991 against a system that had kept businessmen lobbying officials in New Delhi for decades, rather than serving customers. A factory had needed government permission, from independence in 1947, to expand, to make something new or to hire more workers. Which system did his reforms target?
answer: Rent-seeking around the License Raj
choices: Rent-seeking around the License Raj
Foreign-currency speculation
Rural land redistribution
Public-sector pension liabilities
context: The 1991 Singh reforms dismantled most industrial licensing, cutting the rents that had generated the massive lobbying dissipation Krueger had documented in 1974. Growth accelerated within a few years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_liberalisation_in_India.

question: Anne Krueger's paper on Indian and Turkish firms that poured their effort into chasing import licenses is cited by economists everywhere. Later another economist widened her idea to all ways of making money without making anything, from theft and lawsuits to lobbying for tariffs. Who was he?
answer: Jagdish Bhagwati
choices: Jagdish Bhagwati
Amartya Sen
Deepak Lal
Peter Bauer
context: Jagdish Bhagwati's 1982 paper in the Journal of Political Economy, 'Directly-Unproductive, Profit-Seeking (DUP) Activities', generalized Krueger's mechanism to any activity that yields income without producing goods: theft, tariff-seeking, litigation and more. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent-seeking.

question: A young Hungarian fled Communist rule in 1948, made his way to Oxford and settled at last in France. In 1985 the Oxford publisher Basil Blackwell brought out his short, startling book on politics, which asked readers to put themselves in a government's place. Who was he?
answer: Anthony de Jasay
choices: Anthony de Jasay
Peter Bauer
William Fellner
János Kornai
context: De Jasay (1925-2019) held no permanent academic post: after Oxford, where he arrived in 1955 and was a research fellow of Nuffield College until 1962, he worked as a banker in Paris until 1979, then retired to Normandy to write. Peter Bauer and William Fellner were Hungarian-born economists who made their careers in Britain and America; János Kornai, a critic of planned economies, did most of his work in Budapest. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: Anthony de Jasay, who had fled Communist Hungary in 1948, published a short, bold book on politics in 1985. A government, he argued, will keep stretching its own power, whatever its founders intended. He named the book after his one great subject, in a single stark word. What is the title?
answer: The State
choices: The State
The Market
The Constitution
The Republic
context: The book argued that a state, once granted power, would use it in ways that predictably diverged from any theory treating the state as neutral arbiter or benevolent public servant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock founded a new field of economics in the 1960s by working out how rules might hold back politicians who serve themselves. Anthony de Jasay thought they had skipped a step. What deeper question did he ask first?
answer: Why would a state, presumed to be self-interested, honor any constraint at all?
choices: Why would a state, presumed to be self-interested, honor any constraint at all?
Which voting rule would best let citizens restrain a self-serving state?
Why do voters keep re-electing politicians who break their promises?
How can judges be kept independent enough to enforce the limits?
context: The prior question dissolves much of the constitutional-design literature: constraints only bind if the constrained actor accepts them. De Jasay pushed the logic of public choice one step deeper than most public-choice scholars had. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: Anthony de Jasay attacked the social contract, the old account, told by Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and John Rawls, that citizens once consented to be ruled. He answered it with history rather than theory. What did he point out?
answer: No such consent ever happened; real states began in conquest or seizure
choices: No such consent ever happened; real states began in conquest or seizure
Each generation would have to consent anew, and none ever had
Tribes that lived without any state proved the contract unneeded
Only property owners had ever been asked, so the consent was partial
context: The hypothetical-consent framing of Hobbes, Locke, and Rawls treated the state's legitimacy as flowing from an idealized agreement. De Jasay treated the framing as a rationalization dressed up as philosophy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay.

question: Anthony de Jasay fled Hungary in 1948 and spent seven years at Oxford. His later books won admirers among economists of the free-market tradition, yet one fact about his career set him apart from nearly all of them. What was it?
answer: He never held a professorship; he earned his living as a banker in Paris
choices: He never held a professorship; he earned his living as a banker in Paris
He wrote every book in Hungarian and left the translating to others
He wrote under a pen name, and was unmasked only after his death
He served as a minister in Hungary's first free government in 1990
context: De Jasay went to Oxford in 1955 and stayed until 1962, latterly as a research fellow of Nuffield College; he was then a banker and investor in Paris until 1979, when he retired to Normandy and wrote his books outside the universities. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Anthony_de_Jasay; dejasay.org/biography.

question: Anthony Downs asked in 1957 what two parties do when they compete on a single issue. Both, he predicted, drift toward the citizen at the dead center of opinion, because whoever wins him wins the majority. What is this result called?
answer: The median-voter theorem
choices: The median-voter theorem
The lucky-loser theorem
The consensus principle
The Condorcet convergence
context: The median-voter theorem: under simple-majority voting on a single-issue spectrum, competing platforms converge to the preference of the median voter. Duncan Black had proved the mathematical version in 1948; Downs popularized and applied it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_voter_theorem.

question: A British economist proved the mathematics nine years before Anthony Downs made the idea famous in his 1957 book: two parties chasing the voter in the middle. What was that economist's last name?
answer: Black
choices: Black
Arrow
Vickrey
Robbins
context: Duncan Black's 1948 JPE paper 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making' proved the mathematical version of what became the median-voter theorem. Downs popularized it for political-competition analysis in 1957. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Black.

question: A third-party candidate on the campaign trail complains about the two big parties in US politics. Anthony Downs's model, in which both parties chase the citizen at the exact center of opinion, explains his complaint. Which pattern does it explain?
answer: The two big parties sound alike on many issues by voting day
choices: The two big parties sound alike on many issues by voting day
The two big parties pull further apart with every election
The two big parties win by firing up voters at the extremes
The two big parties take turns in power, term after term
context: The convergence prediction: both parties chase the median voter, ending up close together on many issues. This explains the 'not a dime's worth of difference' complaint often voiced by third-party advocates. Source: Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957).

question: Anthony Downs noticed that most citizens skip the homework before an election: few read the bills, study the candidates or check the budgets. He argued that this was no sign of stupidity but a sensible answer to the incentives each voter faces. What name did Downs give the idea?
answer: Rational ignorance
choices: Rational ignorance
Adaptive expectations
Bounded rationality
Anchoring bias
context: Rational ignorance: studying candidates and issues costs time; the expected influence of any one vote is essentially zero; therefore rational voters minimize the time they spend informing themselves. Most voter ignorance is rational, not stupidity. Source: Downs (1957).

question: A citizen deciding whether to study every candidate before an election faces the arithmetic Anthony Downs worked out in 1957. Among a hundred million voters, his ballot's odds of deciding the result are about those of a lottery jackpot, and the studying costs whole evenings. In Downs's model, what are the private returns to becoming an informed voter?
answer: Near zero
choices: Near zero
Very high
Highly volatile
Perfectly aligned with public returns
context: The private return to becoming informed as a voter is near zero because the probability that one vote determines the outcome is near zero. The social return may be high, but the individual voter's incentive to learn is not. Source: Downs (1957).

question: Anthony Downs, famous since his 1957 book on democracy, turned to a very concrete problem far from voting theory. He wrote about it for decades, later at the Brookings Institution in Washington. Which field did his later work most influence?
answer: Urban traffic and expressway congestion
choices: Urban traffic and expressway congestion
Central-bank monetary policy
International trade theory
Sports economics
context: Downs wrote widely on traffic and urban planning. His 'law of peak-hour expressway congestion' -- that expanding highways induces more driving until the new capacity is filled -- is standard reference in transportation economics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: A trucker heard that a hurricane had knocked out a town's power for days, leaving food to spoil in warm refrigerators. He bought 19 generators hundreds of miles away, drove them into the disaster zone and priced them at about double what he had paid. What good did his high prices do the town?
answer: They made the trip worth it -- so the town got generators at all
choices: They made the trip worth it -- so the town got generators at all
Nothing -- they only moved the town's money to him
Little -- so few could pay that most went unsold
Cheaper goods -- local shops had to cut their prices
context: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast at the end of August 2005. John Shepperson of Kentucky bought 19 generators, rented a truck, drove them to Mississippi and planned to sell them for about twice what he had paid. Without that price the long drive would not have paid, and the generators would have stayed in Kentucky. Source: Munger, 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' (Cato Unbound, 2007); https://clips.cato.org/sites/default/files/Vandoren_reason_reg.pdf.

question: John Shepperson of Kentucky loaded 19 generators onto a rented truck in 2005 and drove south to Mississippi, where Hurricane Katrina had cut power to thousands of homes. State law made it a crime to charge far more than usual for necessities. What did the police do when he arrived?
answer: They arrested him, confiscated the generators, and jailed him for four days
choices: They arrested him, confiscated the generators, and jailed him for four days
They cited him with a small fine and let him continue
They escorted him to hurricane shelters as a preferred vendor
They asked him to sell only to registered emergency workers
context: Shepperson was arrested for price gouging, held four days, and the nineteen generators remained in police custody rather than in the hands of anyone in Mississippi. John Stossel used the case on ABC's 20/20; Mark Perry has cited it repeatedly.

question: Ice runs out in a town that a hurricane has left without power, and a man drives sixteen hours through the wreckage with a truckful to sell. He asks three times the normal price, enough to pay for his gas, his hours and his risk. Police arrest him for price gouging. Which hidden cost do economists see in the arrest?
answer: Next time, fewer people bring in supplies, since the trip will not pay
choices: Next time, fewer people bring in supplies, since the trip will not pay
Next time, insurers raise their rates for every town in the storm's path
Next time, the town's own shops raise their prices to match his
Next time, the federal government pays for every truck of ice sent in
context: Michael Munger (Duke University, formerly chair of political science) wrote 'They Clapped: Can Price Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' (Cato Unbound, 2007). It is the standard reference for the Shepperson story. Source: cato-unbound.org (Munger 2007).

question: John Shepperson drove 19 generators from Kentucky to Mississippi, where Hurricane Katrina had cut power to thousands of homes, hoping to sell them at a big markup, until the state's anti-gouging law stopped him. Read the way Friedrich Hayek read markets, what had Shepperson's trip really done?
answer: He moved scarce capital from a low-value use to a high-value one, guided by price
choices: He moved scarce capital from a low-value use to a high-value one, guided by price
He took advantage of a shortage that his own high price made worse
He drained Kentucky of generators that its own buyers needed more
He charged far more than the generators were really worth to anyone
