context: The high price in Mississippi told Shepperson, hundreds of miles away in Kentucky, that generators were desperately needed there, and his 600-mile trip made sense only because that price made the effort worthwhile. In Munger's reading, anti-gouging laws cut the signal and prevent the very coordination they claim to protect. Source: Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: Michael Munger, a Duke University economist, took on the people who demand 'fair' fixed prices after a hurricane in an essay for Cato Unbound in 2007. Residents of a storm zone, he argued, are not really choosing between a fair price and an unfair one. What pair of choices did he say they face instead?
answer: Expensive supply that arrives versus cheap supply that does not exist
choices: Expensive supply that arrives versus cheap supply that does not exist
Fair supply versus unfair supply for the wealthy
State-supplied versus corporation-supplied
Rationed supply versus black-market supply
context: Munger's line reframes the ethical debate: the anti-gouging law does not create abundance; it prevents the arrival of supply. The real trade-off is between expensive arriving supply and cheap nonexistent supply. Source: Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: Walmart trucks were carrying bottled water, food and diapers into Louisiana within days of Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, often before the official trucks arrived. The Federal Emergency Management Agency was far slower. Two economists, Sobel and Leeson, later documented the gap. Why did the private chain move so much faster?
answer: Local managers had authority to act without waiting for headquarters
choices: Local managers had authority to act without waiting for headquarters
Its headquarters planned every shipment from one central office
Federal law gave its trucks first use of the damaged roads
The government had paid it in advance to stock the region
context: Sobel and Leeson documented Walmart's post-Katrina supply-chain response as delivering food, water, and supplies to affected areas faster than federal agencies. They traced the gap to knowledge and incentives: managers on the spot knew what their own towns needed and had the authority to act on it. Source: Sobel + Leeson, 'The Use of Knowledge in Natural-Disaster Relief Management,' Independent Review (2007).

question: A man with a truckload of generators checks the price in a distant storm zone and decides whether the long drive will pay. Friedrich Hayek argued that prices pass along knowledge no planner could ever collect, knowledge scattered among many people. When a rule cuts that price signal, what happens to the coordination it made possible?
answer: It disappears
choices: It disappears
It intensifies
It becomes visible for the first time
It moves onto voluntary channels
context: Hayek's 1945 point applied as policy diagnostic: prices coordinate dispersed knowledge. Sever the signal and the coordination goes with it. The seen effect (no one 'gouged') coexists with the unseen cost (thousands in the dark for weeks). Source: Hayek AER 1945; Munger, Cato Unbound (2007).

question: A sugar grower collects his government bonus, and so do a few thousand other sugar and cotton farmers; the bill is spread over every shopper in the country at a few pennies each. Why does a rule like this almost never get repealed once it passes?
answer: The few farmers fight for it; the many taxpayers barely notice
choices: The few farmers fight for it; the many taxpayers barely notice
Voters like farmers and are glad to keep paying them
Each farmer gains too little to bother defending it
Courts treat a farm payment as a right once paid
context: The modern structure of federal farm support dates from the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933, and every Farm Bill since has kept it. Mancur Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965) explains why such programs last: the few who gain a lot organize to keep them, while the millions who each lose a little never bother. Source: usda.gov farm bill history; Olson (1965).

question: A farmer learns that the government will start paying him extra money, a subsidy, for the corn he grows. How does a subsidy like this change the amount of corn that gets planted?
answer: Farmers grow more of it than the market would want on its own
choices: Farmers grow more of it than the market would want on its own
Farmers grow less of it, since the subsidy replaces their income
Farmers grow the same amount, since buyers decide what is planted
Farmers switch to other crops the government does not pay for
context: A subsidy lifts what a farmer earns on each bushel above the price buyers alone would pay, so he plants more of that crop than the market would call for. The Farm Bill is the general name for the law Congress passes every few years to renew such programs. Source: usda.gov farm bill.

question: A shopper in an American grocery drops a bag of sugar into her cart. The sugar's price carries the cost of a federal program that shelters a few thousand domestic growers with import quotas and price supports. The program is often called the purest case of Mancur Olson's logic in modern policy. Roughly what multiple of the world price does it push US sugar to?
answer: About twice
choices: About twice
About 20 percent higher
About ten times
About the same
context: US sugar prices run roughly 2x world prices as a result of tariff-rate quotas and price supports. About 4,000 US sugar producers benefit; 330 million consumers pay the higher price on anything sweetened. Source: cbo.gov sugar program analysis.

question: Mancur Olson asked in 1965 who bothers to organize when a policy hands a few people a lot and charges everyone else a little. Some 4,000 American sugar producers take in about $1 billion a year from the federal sugar program, while 330 million shoppers each pay a few dollars for it. Under his theory, which side is easier to organize?
answer: The 4,000 producers
choices: The 4,000 producers
The 330 million consumers
Both sides equally organized
Neither side ever organizes
context: Olson's mechanism: concentrated benefits attract concentrated lobbying; dispersed costs generate almost no counter-organization. The producers form associations (American Sugar Alliance, US Sugar Corporation); the 330 million consumers do not organize to save $3 each per year. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: A young man who hopes to open a barbershop finds the state's licensing rules stiff and expensive. Rules like these hurt would-be newcomers most, yet the newcomers barely push back. Under Mancur Olson's theory of collective action, why can't they organize a strong counter-push?
answer: They are not yet in the profession and cannot organize as members
choices: They are not yet in the profession and cannot organize as members
They lack the constitutional right to petition
They are barred by antitrust law from lobbying
They earn too little to fund political action
context: Would-be barbers, hair braiders, and interior designers are not yet in the profession; they have no association to fund the counter-lobby. Olson's classic mechanism: concentrated present interests always outweigh dispersed future ones. Source: Kleiner + Krueger 2013.

question: A woman who braids hair for pay learns that her state now demands a full cosmetology license: hundreds of classroom hours and hundreds of dollars in fees. Under standard occupational-licensing analysis, what usually happens to insiders' wages, and to newcomers trying to break in?
answer: Insider wages rise because competition drops; newcomers find it much harder to start
choices: Insider wages rise because competition drops; newcomers find it much harder to start
Insider wages fall because the license costs eat into their pay
Newcomers flood in because the license is a badge of quality
Nothing changes because the customers set the wages
context: Morris Kleiner's empirical work has documented the wage premium and entry-barrier effect of state licensing across dozens of occupations and states. His work with Alan Krueger is widely cited. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Kleiner.

question: A florist in Louisiana applies for the state license she needs before she may sell arrangements for pay, and about one American worker in four needs a license of some kind, from barbers to tour guides. Such rules add training hours, exam fees and long waits before a newcomer can open shop. Who tends to lobby state capitols hardest to pass and keep these laws?
answer: Existing workers in the field who want fewer competitors
choices: Existing workers in the field who want fewer competitors
Consumers hoping to pay lower prices at every shop
Newcomers trying to enter the trade for the first time
The federal government looking for extra tax revenue
context: Louisiana licenses roughly 70 occupations including tour guide, florist, and hair braider. Wyoming and other Western states license far fewer. The variation is a natural experiment for the entry-barrier hypothesis. Source: Institute for Justice Occupational Licensing report.

question: A reformer in James Buchanan's tradition, one of Mancur Olson's heirs, looks for a way to stop lobbies like sugar's from winning in ordinary politics every year. He would lift such decisions to a level that small pressure groups cannot easily capture. Which tools make up the standard package for doing that?
answer: Constitutional-level rules, judicial review, sunset clauses
choices: Constitutional-level rules, judicial review, sunset clauses
Executive orders, administrative rulings, emergency decrees
Tariff hikes, export subsidies, price supports
Referendums, initiative petitions, recall votes
context: The remedies fit Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy tradition: move the decision from ordinary politics (where the sugar lobby wins) to constitutional-level rules or automatic sunset clauses that force periodic re-litigation with the dispersed group's attention gathered. Source: Buchanan + Wagner, Democracy in Deficit.

question: Argentine lawmakers passed a nationwide rent-control law, numbered 27,551, in June 2020, during the COVID lockdowns. It rewrote the rules for every apartment lease in the country. What did the law mainly do?
answer: Set three-year minimum leases and indexed rent adjustments
choices: Set three-year minimum leases and indexed rent adjustments
Made rentals free of any regulation
Prohibited foreign ownership of Argentine property
Established a state rental agency
context: Ley 27.551 mandated three-year minimum leases and required annual rent adjustments only via a Central Bank formula tied to wages and inflation. It also imposed other tenant protections. Source: infoleg.gob.ar (Ley 27.551).

question: Real-estate brokers in Buenos Aires counted the long-term apartments posted for rent after Argentina's strict 2020 rent-control law took effect. What happened to the number of new listings within that first year?
answer: It fell by roughly 40-50 percent
choices: It fell by roughly 40-50 percent
It rose by about 30 percent
It stayed almost exactly the same
It quadrupled
context: Buenos Aires realtor associations reported new-listing supply falling by 40-50% in the first year of the law. Rents on remaining listings rose sharply -- tripling or more in nominal terms by 2023. Source: CEMA Buenos Aires studies.

question: A landlord in Buenos Aires looked at the new controlled leases after Argentina's 2020 rent-control law and pulled his apartment off the long-term market, as thousands of others did. Rather than sign while inflation ate the payments, the landlords put their units to other uses. Where did those apartments go?
answer: Airbnb, unfurnished monthly, or held empty
choices: Airbnb, unfurnished monthly, or held empty
State-owned public housing programs
Government seizures for social housing
New industrial warehousing
context: Landlords shifted to short-term (Airbnb), unfurnished-monthly, or converted units for sale. Some kept units EMPTY rather than commit to a three-year indexed contract under Argentina's political inflation risk. Source: CEMA Buenos Aires studies.

question: Javier Milei waved a chainsaw on the campaign trail in 2023 and won Argentina's presidency that November. What label does he openly and proudly use for himself?
answer: Anarcho-capitalist and Austrian-school
choices: Anarcho-capitalist and Austrian-school
Peronist national socialism
Third-way social democracy
Latin American structuralism
context: Javier Milei, an economist and self-described anarcho-capitalist, won the November 19, 2023 runoff against Peronist Sergio Massa. Rent-control repeal was a specific campaign issue. Milei has publicly identified as an anarcho-capitalist and Austrian-school economist, citing Rothbard, Mises, and Hayek as intellectual influences in campaign speeches and interviews.

question: Landlords across Buenos Aires watched the rent caps fall away on December 29, 2023, when Javier Milei's decree took effect. What happened over the next few months to rental listings in the city, and to their rents?
answer: Supply tripled and real rents on new listings fell
choices: Supply tripled and real rents on new listings fell
Supply stayed flat while rents doubled
Supply fell further and rents rose sharply
Supply doubled but rents rose faster than incomes
context: Within a few months of DNU 70/2023 taking effect, Buenos Aires new-listing supply roughly tripled and rents on new listings fell in real terms as competition returned. Source: CEMA and Zonaprop Buenos Aires listings data.

question: Javier Milei lifted Argentina's rent caps at the end of 2023, after Congress had imposed them in June 2020, so one rental market felt the caps both go on and come off. Set side by side, what plain economic lesson do the two halves teach?
answer: Make supplying rental housing less profitable, and less of it is supplied
choices: Make supplying rental housing less profitable, and less of it is supplied
Cap rents, and tenants gain while the housing supply stays the same
Lift the caps, and rents soar so high that fewer people find homes
Rental supply follows only inflation, never the rules for leases
context: The Argentine sequence -- supply falls when the ceiling comes on, supply rises when it comes off -- confirms the standard supply-response prediction with unusual clarity because the natural experiment happened both ways within four years. Source: mises.org/library/rent-control.

question: Javier Milei's decree swept away Argentina's rent caps in December 2023, more than three years after they began. Most research on rent control watches only the years the caps are on, which leaves defenders free to claim that lifting them would not undo the damage. What about Argentina's aftermath made it an unusually clean test?
answer: The ceiling was fully lifted and supply rebounded within months
choices: The ceiling was fully lifted and supply rebounded within months
The ceiling was only partially applied
Rents were also government-subsidized
The country simultaneously changed currencies
context: Most rent-control historical cases run one way (ceiling imposed, decades of decay). Argentina's clean off-switch in December 2023 lets researchers observe both directions of the mechanism. Source: CEMA studies.

question: Richard Nixon leaned hard on Arthur Burns, his chairman at the Federal Reserve, in the early 1970s to keep interest rates low. Cheap credit would make the economy feel like a boom, and Nixon had one big personal event in mind. What was it?
answer: The November 1972 re-election
choices: The November 1972 re-election
The 1970 midterm elections
The 1973 State of the Union address
The Watergate hearings of 1974
context: Nixon wanted an easy-money environment through the 1972 presidential election. The pressure is documented in the White House tapes and in Burns's own diaries published posthumously. Source: Grokipedia 'Arthur Burns' (2026-09-05).

question: Murray Rothbard and other Austrian-school writers would not put Arthur Burns's record at the Federal Reserve down to bad luck or a weak chairman. Burns had kept money cheap under pressure from Nixon, and they saw in it proof of a built-in flaw in the institution itself. What flaw did they name?
answer: Any central bank will be captured by politicians who want a quick boom, whatever the cost
choices: Any central bank will be captured by politicians who want a quick boom, whatever the cost
Any central bank acts on figures that arrive months late, so it always steers too late
Any central bank gets blamed for shocks, like oil embargoes, that it cannot control
Any central bank is too timid to act until a crisis is already underway
context: The Austrian point: Burns's tenure is the textbook case. An academically distinguished chairman with proper theoretical training nevertheless caved to a president's re-election needs, and in their reading the dollar's purchasing power paid for it over the following decade.

question: Arthur Burns gave a lecture in Belgrade in 1979, a year after leaving the Federal Reserve, titled 'The Anguish of Central Banking.' He confessed that central bankers struggle to stand firm against inflation, because one outside force keeps leaning on them to loosen money. What pressure was he describing?
answer: Elected leaders pressing for easy money to keep jobs and incomes up
choices: Elected leaders pressing for easy money to keep jobs and incomes up
Foreign central banks pressing for low rates to steady their currencies
Commercial banks pressing for low rates to fatten their lending profits
Stock traders pressing for cheap money to keep share prices climbing
context: Burns delivered 'The Anguish of Central Banking' as the Per Jacobsson Lecture in Belgrade on September 30, 1979. He said the Fed had been 'caught up in the philosophic and political currents' of the age, and that inflation was 'continually driven by political forces.' It is a striking admission from the chair whose tenure had failed the test he was now describing. Sources: mises.org/mises-daily/anguish-central-banking-2005; Grokipedia 'Arthur Burns' (2026-09-05).

question: Arthur Burns cut interest rates when the first wave of 1970s inflation died down, and expectations of rising prices came loose. Austrian analysts hold up his mistake as a warning to every central bank tempted to ease early. What sequel do they warn an early cut invites?
answer: A second, worse inflation wave that only Volcker-style hikes can break
choices: A second, worse inflation wave that only Volcker-style hikes can break
A long slump with falling prices, like Japan's in the 1990s
A run on the dollar as foreign banks rush to swap it for gold
A glut of savings that drives interest rates below zero
context: The Volcker recession followed because Burns had eased too soon and let expectations come loose. Austrian analysts draw a warning for the 2020s from it: a central bank that eases too early may need Volcker-style hikes again. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: Richard Nixon named Arthur Burns chairman of the Federal Reserve in 1970, and Burns had every credential the job could want: a celebrated Columbia professor and an expert on business cycles. Nixon pressed him for cheap money, and the Great Inflation followed. What lesson about central-bank appointments does Burns's tenure teach?
answer: Even a superbly trained chair can bow to a president and cause the inflation he foresaw
choices: Even a superbly trained chair can bow to a president and cause the inflation he foresaw
A professor lacks the banker's feel for markets that the chair's job demands
A chair chosen for his theory will cling to it after events prove it wrong
A chair needs freer discretion, since no fixed rule can foresee every shock
context: Burns had the credentials any economist would have wanted in a Fed chair. He caved anyway. The problem is not the chair's training but the institutional structure that puts a single reappointable individual under presidential pressure at four-year intervals. Source: Grokipedia 'Arthur Burns' (2026-09-05).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin in 2009 on the same kind of chip that Hal Finney, a cryptographer, and any hobbyist at home could use. Which common chip did they all mine with in 2009 and 2010?
answer: The CPU inside every ordinary laptop and desktop
choices: The CPU inside every ordinary laptop and desktop
The GPU inside a high-end gaming card
A field-programmable gate array (FPGA)
A dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)
context: Bitcoin's early democracy meant anyone with a laptop could earn coins by running the software. The rewards were then 50 BTC per block, mostly won by a handful of hobbyists including Satoshi Nakamoto and Hal Finney. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: Bitcoin miners stumbled on a trick in 2010. The rendering chip inside a video-game card could crunch the network's hashing puzzle roughly 50 to 100 times faster than the normal computer chip they had been using. Gamers set their machines mining day and night. Which kind of chip took over mining?
answer: The GPU (graphics processing unit)
choices: The GPU (graphics processing unit)
The FPGA (field-programmable gate array)
The SSD (solid-state drive controller)
The TPU (tensor processing unit)
context: GPUs from AMD and NVIDIA, designed for parallel pixel-shading math, turned out to be accidentally excellent at repetitive hashing. Gamers' hardware became the world's best money-mint for a year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: A Bitcoin miner unplugged his old rig and switched on a chip built for narrower work, as miners did at every step from 2009 to 2013. Each generation drove the older one out of the race. Why did each new step win?
answer: Each step used less power per calculation, so old rigs lost money
choices: Each step used less power per calculation, so old rigs lost money
Each step was cheaper to buy at an ordinary computer shop
Each step earned bigger block rewards from the network
Each step needed less internet bandwidth to stay connected
context: An FPGA can be reprogrammed after manufacture to perform a specific circuit. FPGA mining lasted only about a year (roughly 2012) before purpose-built ASICs arrived. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: Butterfly Labs and Avalon shipped a new kind of Bitcoin mining chip in early 2013: application-specific integrated circuits, able to compute the network's hashing puzzle and nothing else. A laptop's general-purpose processor can run the same puzzle. Set against that processor, what is the trade-off of the single-purpose chip?
answer: The single-purpose chip is far faster and cheaper per calculation, but useless for anything else
choices: The single-purpose chip is far faster and cheaper per calculation, but useless for anything else
The single-purpose chip is slower but handles many kinds of jobs
The general-purpose chip is always faster at any specialized task
The two chips perform the same because the math is identical
context: The first Bitcoin ASICs shipped from Butterfly Labs and Avalon in early 2013. Because an ASIC's silicon is committed to one algorithm at fabrication, it cannot be repurposed if the algorithm is abandoned. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Application-specific_integrated_circuit.

question: A hobbyist mining Bitcoin on his home computer found by 2015 that he could no longer keep up. Mining farms in China, many of them in Sichuan and Inner Mongolia, had filled whole warehouses with application-specific integrated circuits: silicon designed to do only Bitcoin's hashing math. What made home mining stop paying?
answer: Purpose-built mining chips are thousands of times faster than home computers
choices: Purpose-built mining chips are thousands of times faster than home computers
The network capped how many coins one home computer could earn
Home electricity prices doubled in most countries by 2015
Mining pools began refusing to pay out to small home miners
context: MicroBT (Whatsminer) and Canaan (AvalonMiner) are Bitmain's principal competitors, both also Chinese. Butterfly Labs was an early US ASIC shop notorious for shipping delays and later shut down. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitmain.

question: A mining company sinks millions into chips that can compute Bitcoin's puzzle and nothing else: they cannot run a video game, browse the web or edit a photo. Critics call such narrow hardware centralization; Bitcoin's defenders answer that it makes the network more secure. What is the defenders' reasoning?
answer: Miners have no way to abandon Bitcoin and reuse their expensive hardware
choices: Miners have no way to abandon Bitcoin and reuse their expensive hardware
Hackers cannot copy or steal chips built for a single task
Governments cannot ban hardware that only does arithmetic
Narrow chips spread mining evenly among many small miners
context: This is a commitment property. Every ASIC owner is economically committed to Bitcoin's survival: if the network died, the hardware is scrap. Critics call this centralization; defenders call it aligned incentives. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Application-specific_integrated_circuit.

question: Miners in China packed up millions of machines after Beijing banned Bitcoin mining outright in June 2021. Over half of all the computing power securing Bitcoin had been running inside China, and the move took months. Which set of places took in many of the migrating machines?
answer: Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland and Paraguay
choices: Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland and Paraguay
France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom
Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore
Australia, New Zealand, Chile and Peru
context: Each destination offered cheap and often stranded electricity: Texas wind and gas, Kazakhstan coal, Iceland geothermal, Paraguay hydro. Total hash power reached new all-time highs within nine months of the China exit. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: John Maynard Keynes blamed the swings of boom and bust in 1936 on shifting moods, the slide from hope into fear. Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek pointed somewhere else: at one policy tool being misused. Which tool did the Austrians blame?
answer: Artificially low interest rates set by a central bank
choices: Artificially low interest rates set by a central bank
The gold standard and its fixed exchange rates
Free international trade in manufactured goods
The private ownership of the means of production
context: Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT) says the boom-bust cycle is a MONETARY phenomenon: when a central bank pushes rates below the rate that would balance real saving against real investment, entrepreneurs start projects that the actual supply of savings cannot support. The bust is the market discovering the truth. Keynes's animal-spirits account made the swing psychological; Austrians made it institutional and monetary. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: Ludwig von Mises refused a senior job at Austria's great Kreditanstalt bank in 1929, and told his fiancée why: a great crash was on its way. The bank collapsed in May 1931, setting off a banking crisis across Europe. Which of his own theories lay behind the forecast?
answer: Austrian business cycle theory
choices: Austrian business cycle theory
Rational expectations
Efficient markets
The Keynesian multiplier
context: Kreditanstalt, Austria's largest bank, collapsed in May 1931, and its failure rippled through central European banking and deepened the Great Depression across the continent. Mises's warning rested on his business cycle theory: years of cheap credit had paid for a boom that real savings could not support, so a bust had to follow. The story of the refused post comes from Margit von Mises, the fiancée in question, in her memoir My Years with Ludwig von Mises (1976). Source: mises.org/online-book/skyscraper-curse-and-how-austrian-economists-predicted-every-major-economic-crisis-last-century/chapter-13-who-predicted-great-depression.

question: A developer takes a loan at just 1 percent and starts a fifteen-year housing project, and builders in other long-term industries follow. Two years later rates rise to 4 percent. Many of the projects no longer make sense, and some are abandoned mid-build. What do Austrian economists call projects like these?
answer: Malinvestment
choices: Malinvestment
Overproduction
Excess capacity
Speculation
context: MALINVESTMENT is the core ABCT concept -- resources committed to structures of production that cannot in fact be sustained. Not 'bad investment' in the ordinary sense but investment that would have been correct if the rate signal had been true; the misallocation is traceable to the rate distortion, not to entrepreneurial stupidity.

question: Alan Greenspan drove the Federal Reserve's key rate down from 6.5 percent late in 2000 to 1 percent by mid-2003, then kept it there for a year. Austrian analysts at the time named one market, especially sensitive to long-term interest rates, as the main sink for projects that cheap money would set going. Which market did they name?
answer: Housing and residential real estate
choices: Housing and residential real estate
US Treasury bonds
Grocery-store retail
Municipal utilities
context: Housing depends on long-duration mortgage financing, so it is the most rate-sensitive major asset class in the American economy -- exactly the market that stretched furthest when rates were held at 1%. Peter Schiff and other Austrian-influenced analysts made the housing-crash call publicly and repeatedly in 2005-2007; the crash arrived in 2007-2008. Treasuries respond to rate cuts in price but do not overbuild; groceries and utilities are short-horizon and rate-insensitive. Source: cato.org/publications/commentary/how-greenspan-bernanke-fed-created-bubbles.

question: A lending boom ends, and a town is left with empty office towers that buyers will not touch at boom-era prices. The government now steps in and buys the towers at those boom prices. What do Austrian-school economists say happens to the correction?
answer: The correction drags on, because bad projects are kept alive instead of cleared
choices: The correction drags on, because bad projects are kept alive instead of cleared
The correction ends quickly and demand fully returns
Deflation is prevented and prices stay stable
The length of the correction is unchanged
context: The Austrian argument is that a bust is DIAGNOSTIC as well as painful: the projects that fail are the ones that never should have been started, and liquidating them frees capital and labour for uses that DO reflect real time preferences. Keynesian stimulus -- keeping demand up for the malinvested projects -- protects them from liquidation and stretches the correction. Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) presses this reading of the 1930s: Hoover's and Roosevelt's interventions prolonged the depression they were supposed to cure. Source: mises.org/online-book/skyscraper-curse-and-how-austrian-economists-predicted-every-major-economic-crisis-last-century/chapter-24-what-wrong-abct.

question: Knut Wicksell, a Swedish economist, asked where borrowing costs would settle if no central bank touched interest rates. His answer: at the level where the total people choose to save equals the total businesses want to borrow for factories, farms and new equipment. That level is the yardstick behind Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek's account of boom and bust. What is that reference rate called?
answer: The natural rate of interest
choices: The natural rate of interest
The federal funds rate
The prime rate
The risk-free rate
context: Mises and Hayek inherit the 'natural rate' concept from the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell (Interest and Prices, 1898): it is the interest rate at which voluntary saving and voluntary investment would balance in the absence of monetary distortion. When the central-bank rate is BELOW the natural rate, credit expands beyond real saving and malinvestment follows. The federal funds rate is the Fed's actual operating target, the prime rate is a commercial-bank benchmark, and the risk-free rate is the yield on the safest government debt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: John Maynard Keynes put a new driver of the boom-bust cycle into his 1936 book, The General Theory: not money but a force in the mind. Keynes described spontaneous urges to invest that swing between confidence and panic, and gave them a memorable two-word name. What was it?
answer: Animal spirits
choices: Animal spirits
Bounded rationality
Rational expectations
Adaptive expectations
context: Keynes: 'Most, probably, of our decisions to do something positive... can only be taken as a result of animal spirits -- of a spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction.' The clash is direct: Austrians say the cycle is a MONETARY event with a specific institutional cause and a specific remedy (stop suppressing the rate); Keynes says it is a PSYCHOLOGICAL event with no simple institutional cause and a specific remedy (stabilise demand). Bounded rationality is Herbert Simon 1955; rational and adaptive expectations are 1960s-70s macro developments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_spirits_(Keynes).

question: Thomas Sowell, a former Marxist trained at the University of Chicago, wrote a book in 2000 for adults with jobs who had never taken a class in the subject. Five editions later it runs to roughly 800 pages. What is it called?
answer: Basic Economics
choices: Basic Economics
Free to Choose
Economics in One Lesson
The Wealth of Nations
context: Basic Economics grew across five editions from about 500 pages in 2000 to over 700 by 2015. Each new edition added case studies rather than abstract theory. Free to Choose was Milton and Rose Friedman's 1980 book; Economics in One Lesson was Henry Hazlitt's 1946 one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: A reader opening the fifth edition of Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics finds roughly 800 pages built from real cases rather than abstract theory. One deliberate choice sets the book apart from nearly every other economics textbook. What is it?
answer: No graphs, no equations, no algebra anywhere in the book
choices: No graphs, no equations, no algebra anywhere in the book
A short biography of a famous economist opens every chapter
Every case is drawn from a single country's history
Each chapter ends with graded homework problems and answers
context: Sowell's earlier 1971 textbook 'Economics: Analysis and Issues' had used the traditional graph-and-equation format. Basic Economics was his conscious departure from that model, aimed at a working adult reader without prior training. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Thomas Sowell filled Basic Economics with real cases: Ghana's rice farms, American rent control, apartheid's labor rules, post-Soviet Europe. Rather than march through theories one at a time, Sowell grouped his chapters another way. How did the book group them?
answer: By institution, such as prices, production, and work and pay
choices: By institution, such as prices, production, and work and pay
By region of the world, from Africa and Asia to the Americas
By era, from the ancient world to the post-Soviet economies
By difficulty, from the simplest ideas to the hardest ones
context: Each chapter examines the institution through case studies, then returns repeatedly to the same handful of questions: What are the trade-offs? At what cost? Compared to what? What are the incentives? Who bears the unseen costs? Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Lionel Robbins, a British economist, wrote in 1932 that economics is the study of how people use scarce means that could serve many different ends. Thomas Sowell built Basic Economics on that definition. Time, money and effort are always limited, but human wants are not. What kind of decision does that force on every person, every day?
answer: A tradeoff -- picking one use means giving up others
choices: A tradeoff -- picking one use means giving up others
A calculation with a single correct answer
A random guess with no real consequences
A vote where the majority always gets more
context: Robbins's 1932 'An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science' put the scarcity-with-alternative-uses definition into the modern discipline's vocabulary. Sowell adopts and popularizes it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lionel_Robbins.

question: Britain's Corn Laws taxed wheat brought in from abroad. The landlords who owned the wheat fields loved the tax, since it kept their grain dear. But bread is made from wheat, and nearly everyone ate it every day. Who was hurt most by the tax?
answer: Poor families -- the tax makes bread more expensive every day
choices: Poor families -- the tax makes bread more expensive every day
Farm laborers -- the tax cuts the wages paid in the fields
City bakers -- the tax caps the price they can charge for bread
Wool merchants -- the tax is charged on every fleece they sell
context: The grain tax fell hardest on poor families, who paid extra for every loaf while the landlords pocketed the higher price. The families who rallied to the Anti-Corn Law League, founded in Manchester by Richard Cobden and John Bright, wanted the tariffs gone because they made bread more expensive than it needed to be. The League was the classic 19th-century mass free-trade movement, and Bastiat traveled to its Manchester headquarters in 1845 specifically to study its methods. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Anti-Corn_Law_League; grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Two Lancashire cotton men led a campaign in the 1840s to repeal Britain's Corn Laws, the tariffs that kept bread dear. They founded the Anti-Corn Law League, toured the country making speeches, and won free trade in grain in 1846. Who were the pair?
answer: Richard Cobden and John Bright
choices: Richard Cobden and John Bright
William Gladstone and Benjamin Disraeli
Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington
Lord Palmerston and Lord John Russell
context: Cobden (1804-1865) and Bright (1811-1889) led the League from Manchester through seven years of relentless public campaigning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Anti-Corn_Law_League.

question: Frederic Bastiat traveled to England in 1845 to study the Anti-Corn Law League, the British mass movement against the tariffs that made bread dear for ordinary families. Back home he wrote a book introducing the League's campaign to French readers, and the publisher Guillaumin brought it out in Paris that same year. What is the book's short title?
answer: Cobden et la Ligue
choices: Cobden et la Ligue
Sophismes economiques
Harmonies economiques
La Loi
context: Cobden et la Ligue, ou l'agitation anglaise pour la liberte des echanges (Guillaumin, 1845) translated the League's speeches and pamphlets for French audiences. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Frédéric Bastiat founded a free-trade association in Bordeaux in 1846 and edited its weekly paper, Le Libre-Échange. French tariffs of the day kept cheaper foreign goods out to shield makers at home. What did the association say such a tariff really does?
answer: It helps a few producers and raises prices for everyone else
choices: It helps a few producers and raises prices for everyone else
It makes foreign makers pay, since they must cut their prices
It saves home jobs at no cost, as the money stays at home
It raises revenue that lets the state cut other taxes
context: The French Free Trade Association (Association pour la liberte des echanges) was founded in Bordeaux in February 1846 and expanded to Paris later that year. Le Libre-Echange (from November 1846) was its weekly paper, edited by Bastiat during his most productive years. Across the Channel, Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws on June 25, 1846 was the classic case of a free-trade movement winning against a landed political interest. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat; grokipedia.com/page/Repeal_of_the_Corn_Laws.

question: Richard Cobden, a cotton merchant, and John Bright, a fiery orator, led a band of free traders from an English factory city. Their campaign forced Parliament to repeal Britain's Corn Laws in 1846. History named the group after its industrial home. What is its two-word name?
answer: The Manchester School
choices: The Manchester School
The Birmingham School
The Liverpool School
The Leeds School
context: The Manchester School was the British counterpart to Bastiat's French free-trade tradition and gave English a shorthand for classical-liberal political economy. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Manchester_School.

question: A decree issued in Paris on April 27, 1848 freed every enslaved person on Martinique, Guadeloupe and Réunion and in French Guiana. Its author, a junior minister for the colonies, had fought slavery for twenty years. Who drafted it?
answer: Victor Schoelcher
choices: Victor Schoelcher
Alexis de Tocqueville
Victor Hugo
Frédéric Bastiat
context: Victor Schoelcher (1804-1893), under-secretary of state for the Navy and Colonies in the Provisional Government, drafted the decree of April 27, 1848, which covered Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana and Réunion. It was France's second and final colonial abolition, after Napoleon had restored slavery in 1802. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Victor_Schœlcher.

question: A woman freed on Martinique in 1848 could now pick her own job, quit it and keep her wages. Compared with forced labor, what does free labor tend to become over time?
answer: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
choices: More productive -- people work harder when they choose the work and keep the pay
Exactly the same -- pay and freedom do not affect effort
Less productive -- nobody works without being forced
Less steady -- free workers keep quitting for better pay
context: Victor Schoelcher (1804-1893) drafted and championed the April 27, 1848 decree. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Victor_Schoelcher.

question: A new French ruler sent soldiers across the Atlantic in 1802 to force slavery back onto Saint-Domingue and France's other Caribbean colonies. He wanted their sugar profits restored, and he was undoing an abolition the Revolution had decreed in 1794. Who was he?
answer: Napoleon Bonaparte
choices: Napoleon Bonaparte
King Louis XVI
Robespierre
King Louis Philippe
context: Napoleon's 1802 reversal restored slavery in French colonies until Schoelcher's 1848 decree ended it definitively. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Abolition_of_slavery_in_France.

question: Frédéric Bastiat, the economist of the broken-window tale and the free-trade pamphlets, ran for France's new National Assembly in 1848, soon after a revolution toppled King Louis Philippe. He won. Which French department elected him?
answer: Landes
choices: Landes
Paris
Bouches-du-Rhone
Nord
context: Bastiat represented Landes, his native southwestern department, in the Constituent Assembly from May 1848. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Frédéric Bastiat turned his usual method on slavery: compare what people see with what they miss. Slavery's defenders held up the cotton crop and the fortunes it made. Bastiat pressed on what they failed to see. Which argument did he make?
answer: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
choices: The slave has no incentive to be productive and the master's character is corrupted
The abolitionist movement had no chance of political success
The Caribbean colonies were unprofitable regardless of the labor system
The moral case for slavery outweighed the economic case against it
context: Bastiat argued that the slave region SEES the free labor and its products but does not see the incentive-destroyed population, the strangled free-labor market, and the corrupted master class. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: British lawmakers who abolished slavery across most of the empire in 1833 had to get the law past a powerful plantation lobby. They wrote it in a way that has stirred debate ever since, and France followed a version of the same model in 1848. What choice did the British act make?
answer: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
choices: Compensating the former slave owners rather than the freed slaves
Compensating the freed slaves directly for years of unpaid labor
Confiscating the plantations and redistributing them to the freed slaves
Requiring the freed slaves to purchase their freedom over 20 years
context: The 1833 British Act paid GBP 20 million in compensation to former slave owners; freed slaves received an 'apprenticeship' period rather than direct compensation. This became the framework for later 19th-century abolitions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833.

question: Voters elected Frédéric Bastiat to France's new National Assembly in 1848, after his years of attacking slavery in print. The Provisional Government issued the decree abolishing colonial slavery after his election but before the new Assembly had ever met. Which description of his voting record on slavery is accurate?
answer: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
choices: He did not vote on the initial decree; he supported the abolition publicly and voted for its implementation
He voted against the abolition decree because he opposed the Provisional Government
He drafted the abolition decree in his role as under-secretary of the Navy
He was absent from the Assembly for the entire 1848-1850 session
context: Sequencing: Bastiat elected April 23, decree April 27, Assembly opens May 4. He supported the abolition, had a decades-long antislavery record in print, and voted for the implementation and compensation measures the Assembly took up. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Ludwig von Mises, teaching in Geneva after leaving Austria in 1934, wrote a German treatise that came out in 1940. Henry Hazlitt pressed him to translate it into English; Mises rewrote it for American readers instead, and it became Human Action. What was the 1940 German book called?
answer: Nationaloekonomie
choices: Nationaloekonomie
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Kritik des Interventionismus
Grundprobleme der Nationaloekonomie
context: Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens was published in Geneva in 1940. When Henry Hazlitt urged an English translation, Mises insisted on rewriting for the American audience -- the result was Human Action (1949). The other three titles are real earlier Mises books but not the direct precursor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Action.

question: Joseph Schumpeter, an Austrian-born economist at Harvard, dismissed Frédéric Bastiat in one short line in History of Economic Analysis, a book that came out in 1954, after his death. Bastiat's admirers say that line kept university economists from reading him for decades. Which line did Schumpeter write?
answer: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
choices: I do not hold that Bastiat was a bad theorist. I hold that he was no theorist.
Bastiat's errors are so many that only his wit has kept him in print.
Bastiat is an amateur whom only the French still mistake for a master.
Bastiat understood free trade and nothing else in economics at all.
context: Schumpeter's dismissal in History of Economic Analysis (published posthumously in 1954) is often blamed for academic economists' long neglect of Bastiat. Rothbard's later Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995) answered it, treating Bastiat as a genuine French classical-liberal theorist. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: Murray Rothbard, who carried Ludwig von Mises's school into the next generation, answered Joseph Schumpeter's put-down of Frédéric Bastiat in his last great work. Its two volumes treat Bastiat as a real theorist rather than a mere pamphleteer. Edward Elgar published it in 1995, the same year Rothbard died. What is its title?
answer: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
choices: An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
The Panic of 1819
context: Rothbard's two-volume An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought was published posthumously by Edward Elgar in 1995 (Rothbard died in January 1995). The book devotes serious attention to Bastiat and the wider French classical-liberal tradition -- a rebuke of Schumpeter's 1954 dismissal. The three other choices are all real earlier Rothbard books. Source: https://mises.org/library/book/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought.

question: Frédéric Bastiat wrote his essays in plain French; a century later Ludwig von Mises rebuilt the argument as a full system in his treatise of 1949, and in 1962 Murray Rothbard made it more formal still in Man, Economy, and State. Each teaches the same reasoning move, more carefully than the last. Which move is that shared backbone?
answer: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
choices: That because human action is purposive, economic reasoning must trace the seen and unseen consequences of every choice
That empirical macro-econometrics is the only rigorous form of economic knowledge
That all economic laws must be established through controlled laboratory experiments
That government spending stimulates growth by expanding aggregate demand
context: Mises's praxeology -- reasoning from the axiom that human action is purposive -- is the formal core of Human Action, and it inherits Bastiat's plain-language habit of tracing consequences past the seen effect to the unseen. Rothbard rebuilds the same method in Man, Economy, and State (1962). The reader can accept or reject Austrian conclusions; the reasoning MOVE is the seen/unseen chain of consequences. Source: https://mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bastiats-legacy-economics.

question: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a printer from Besançon, put a question on the cover of a small book in 1840: what is property? He answered it in three words, and the line has been quoted ever since. What was his answer?
answer: That property is theft
choices: That property is theft
That property is sacred
That property is order
That property is labour
context: Proudhon's answer, 'La propriété, c'est le vol' (property is theft), comes from his 1840 book Qu'est-ce que la propriété? (What Is Property?). He meant the phrase strictly of ABSENTEE property that draws rent or interest without labour, not of a workman's tools -- a distinction later socialists frequently blurred. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Pierre-Joseph Proudhon'.

question: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon opened a lending house in Paris in late January 1849 to lend to workers at zero interest, using notes its members could trade for one another's goods. Thousands joined but put in only some 18,000 francs, and within months a court sent its founder to prison. What was the house called?
answer: The Bank of the People
choices: The Bank of the People
The Society of the Rights of Man
The National Workshops
The Society of the Seasons
context: Proudhon's Banque du peuple was the concrete institutional test of his mutualist idea that competing lenders could organise credit gratuit -- interest-free lending -- outside the state and outside profit. Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux (National Workshops) were a different 1848 scheme; the Society of the Rights of Man and the Society of the Seasons were older republican secret societies. Source: recma.org 'Proudhon et la Banque du Peuple'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon traded long public letters through the winter of 1849 to 1850 over whether it was fair to charge interest on a loan. Almost every letter ran in Proudhon's own Paris daily, which he kept editing from a cell in Sainte-Pélagie prison. What was the paper called?
answer: La Voix du Peuple
choices: La Voix du Peuple
Le National
La Presse
Le Constitutionnel
context: La Voix du Peuple ran from October 1849 into the summer of 1850 as Proudhon's third and last major daily; he continued editing it from Sainte-Pelagie prison. Publishing the exchange in his OWN paper meant Bastiat argued in front of Proudhon's readership. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat argued against interest-free lending in front of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's readers, and he did not claim that lenders deserve a prize for lending. On his account, interest on a loan of 1,000 francs for a year is the price of exactly what?
answer: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
choices: The lender's foregone use of the money for that year
The paperwork and risk of writing the loan
The borrower's expected profit from the loan
The scarcity of gold coin in the economy
context: A century before the Austrian school named it 'time preference', Bastiat had the argument's core: a lender is a person who does without his capital for a period; the interest compensates him for that period of doing without, not for any labour of lending. Paperwork, risk, and borrower profit are separate items. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Frédéric Bastiat pressed Pierre-Joseph Proudhon on a result Proudhon refused to face. Suppose the law forced the interest on loans down to zero, Bastiat said: borrowers would not get cheap loans at all. What would happen instead?
answer: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
choices: Savings would stop flowing into loans, and there would be nothing left to borrow
Only the wealthy would still be able to borrow, at higher secret rates
The state would have to nationalise every bank at once
Prices of all consumer goods would fall by about the old interest rate
context: The disappearance-of-lenders argument runs: at zero interest, savers cease to LEND -- they hold cash or hoard specie instead -- so the volume of loanable funds collapses toward nothing. This is the same reasoning modern economists use against binding usury caps. Source: praxeology.net Letter 2b.

question: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon insisted, in his exchange with Frédéric Bastiat, that ending interest on loans would need no force from the state at all. Let one arrangement take hold, he claimed, and the interest rate would fall all the way to zero by itself. Which mechanism did Proudhon propose?
answer: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
choices: Free competition among mutually organised lenders
A single state monopoly bank issuing paper money
Public shaming of anyone charging any interest at all
A universal tax on capital equal to the interest rate
context: Proudhon insisted his scheme was not coercive: multiply the number of mutual banks, let them compete for borrowers, and the rate would fall organically to zero. Bastiat rejoined that competition could push the rate down only to the value of time-preference itself, and no further. Source: praxeology.net Letter 13.

question: Guillaumin, a Paris publisher, brought out Frédéric Bastiat's letters with Proudhon as one volume in 1850. For its title Bastiat borrowed, with irony, Proudhon's own slogan for lending without interest: one French noun and its qualifier. What was the title?
answer: Gratuite du credit
choices: Gratuite du credit
Interet et principal
Contradictions economiques
Solutions du probleme social
context: Gratuite du credit -- literally 'Free Credit' or 'The Gratuity of Credit' -- was Proudhon's own slogan for the interest-free-lending idea, and Bastiat used it as the book's ironic title. Proudhon in turn published a rival edition of the same letters under his own preferred title Interet et Principal. Source: worldcat.org record 4078594.

question: Frédéric Bastiat printed his debate with Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in Paris as fourteen letters, and that is the count most people cite. Proudhon brought out a rival edition of the same exchange. How did its count differ?
answer: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
choices: Thirteen letters -- Proudhon dropped Bastiat's closing letter
Twelve letters -- Proudhon dropped both the opening piece and Bastiat's last
Fifteen letters -- Proudhon added a summary letter of his own
Ten letters -- Proudhon printed only his own contributions
context: The opening letter of the exchange was by C.F. Cheve, a Proudhon disciple; then twelve letters ran between Bastiat and Proudhon in strict alternation. Bastiat added a closing fourteenth letter (Letter 14) which Proudhon refused to answer, and Proudhon's Interet et Principal simply omitted it. Source: praxeology.net 'The Bastiat-Proudhon Debate on Interest'.

question: An Austrian economist began publishing Kapital und Kapitalzins, Capital and Interest, in parts from 1884, and counted Frédéric Bastiat among the forerunners of its theory. The work gave Bastiat's answer to Proudhon on interest its full formal statement. Who wrote it?
answer: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
context: Bohm-Bawerk's Kapital und Kapitalzins appeared in three parts between 1884 and 1889, with a second edition into the 1890s. He credited Bastiat as one of the nineteenth-century predecessors of the theory. Menger founded the Austrian school (1871) but did not write on interest at that length; Wieser worked on opportunity cost; Mises came a generation later. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Eugen Bohm von Bawerk'.

question: A Viennese exile teaching in the United States brought the Austrian argument about interest back to English readers in 1949, at the core of a thousand-page treatise. The book treats time preference as part of every choice between now and later, not a quirk of capitalism. Which book was it?
answer: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
choices: Human Action, by Ludwig von Mises
The Road to Serfdom, by Friedrich Hayek
Man, Economy and State, by Murray Rothbard
The Theory of Money and Credit, by Ludwig von Mises
context: Human Action (Yale University Press, 1949) is Mises's systematic English treatise; its chapters on interest treat originary time-preference as an inescapable category of acting man. The Road to Serfdom (1944) was Hayek's political tract; Rothbard's Man, Economy and State came later (1962); Mises's Theorie des Geldes was much earlier (1912). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Ludwig von Mises'.

question: The banks that lend a Wall Street investment firm enormous sums every night, just to keep it running the next day, take fright one Monday and stop lending. What is likely to happen to the firm by Friday?
answer: It collapses -- it cannot last days without the borrowed money
choices: It collapses -- it cannot last days without the borrowed money
It carries on -- its own cash can cover months of business
It carries on -- the law obliges the Fed to lend it the money
It shrinks -- but keeps running on its daily profits
context: Bear Stearns, founded in 1923, was heavily exposed to subprime mortgages and mortgage-backed securities. Its two internal hedge funds collapsed in July-August 2007, previewing the firm's own collapse eight months later. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: US officials spent one weekend in March 2008 rushing to find a buyer for the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns before Monday's trading began. JPMorgan Chase agreed to buy it, with the Federal Reserve's help. Why did officials hurry to arrange the sale?
answer: To keep the collapse from scaring every other bank
choices: To keep the collapse from scaring every other bank
To make sure the shareholders lost nothing
To let the government run the bank itself
To punish its leaders before markets opened
context: JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, was the buyer, and the Fed's help made the sale possible on a compressed timeline. Officials feared that a Bear failure on Monday, with its web of lenders and trading partners, would spread panic to every bank that dealt with it. Bear's shareholders were nearly wiped out. Source: Grokipedia 'JPMorgan Chase acquisition of Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: Jamie Dimon agreed over one weekend in March 2008 to have JPMorgan Chase buy the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns, whose shares had sold for $172 fourteen months before. His first offer per share was famously low; a week later, after shareholders threatened to sue, JPMorgan raised it. What was the first price?
answer: Two dollars
choices: Two dollars
Ten dollars
Fifty cents
Twenty dollars
context: The initial Sunday-night announcement was $2 per share. Bear shareholders threatened lawsuits over the price; JPMorgan raised it to $10 the following week. The stock had traded at $172 fourteen months earlier -- a 99% loss for shareholders in a single weekend. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: Bankers at JPMorgan Chase agreed in March 2008 to buy the collapsing investment bank Bear Stearns, but only after some $30 billion in Bear's worst mortgage securities had been moved into a new company called Maiden Lane. JPMorgan took only the healthier parts. Who ended up owning those bad securities?
answer: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
choices: The Federal Reserve, and through it US taxpayers
The failing bank's original shareholders
The buyer paid full price for them
Foreign central banks
context: Maiden Lane LLC, named after the New York Fed's address, held $30 billion of Bear's worst mortgage-backed securities. The Fed took the assets off JPMorgan's books via a non-recourse loan. Source: Grokipedia 'Maiden Lane Transactions' (2026-09-05).

question: Bear Stearns's shareholders and executives lost heavily when the Federal Reserve helped JPMorgan Chase buy the bank in March 2008. One group was paid in full. Which group did the rescue protect at 100 cents on the dollar?
answer: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
choices: Creditors and counterparties whose panic had caused the run
Junior employees at the collapsing firm
Retail brokerage clients
Municipal pension funds holding the stock
context: The Bear precedent: shareholders got wiped out but creditors and counterparties were paid in full. This was designed to prevent a broader panic but also trained the market to expect similar rescues in future crises. Source: Grokipedia 'Bear Stearns' (2026-09-05).

question: Traders across Wall Street had watched the Federal Reserve broker the Bear Stearns rescue in March 2008. By September, Lehman Brothers was failing the same way, its overnight lenders refusing to renew. What did the firms still lending to Lehman and trading with it expect the Fed to do?
answer: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
choices: Broker a similar rescue so Lehman's creditors would also be paid in full
Let Lehman fail immediately to punish executive risk-taking
Nationalize Lehman directly under a special Treasury charter
Merge Lehman with Bank of America without Fed involvement
context: Markets had priced in the Bear precedent. When Lehman was allowed to fail on September 15 2008, the counterparty network priced in exactly the outcome the Bear rescue had trained them not to expect. The moral-hazard trap sprung the other way. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: One economist on the political left and one on the right warned in the spring of 2008, as the Federal Reserve helped JPMorgan Chase buy Bear Stearns, that the rescue would encourage even bigger risks at the next bank. Few listened to either at the time. Which two made the argument?
answer: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
choices: Nouriel Roubini on the left; Peter Schiff on the right
Paul Krugman on the left; Larry Kudlow on the right
Alan Blinder on the left; Milton Friedman on the right
Joseph Stiglitz on the left; John Taylor on the right
context: Roubini (NYU) and Schiff (Euro Pacific Capital) both publicly warned in spring 2008 that the Bear rescue was setting up worse crises. Both were widely dismissed at the time and vindicated within six months. Source: Grokipedia 'Nouriel Roubini' (2026-09-05).

question: Bankers saw the Federal Reserve save Bear Stearns in March 2008 and let Lehman Brothers fail that September, and Lehman's fall was violent. Austrian-school critics draw one lesson from the pair of decisions. What lesson?
answer: Each rescue resets what markets expect, so pulling an expected rescue can set off the panic it meant to prevent
choices: Each rescue resets what markets expect, so pulling an expected rescue can set off the panic it meant to prevent
Each rescue should go to the biggest banks first, since size alone is what spreads a panic
Each rescue breeds moral hazard only when the bank being saved is foreign rather than American
Each rescue works only if a buyer is strong enough to absorb all of the failing bank's losses
context: The Bear rescue trained markets to expect the Lehman rescue; the September 15 Lehman failure violated that trained expectation. The Fed's discretionary rescue policy is not neutral -- each intervention writes the script for the next crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Jimmy Cayne, chairman of the investment bank Bear Stearns, was reportedly away at a bridge tournament in July 2007 while two hedge funds inside his firm collapsed. Less than a year later Bear itself failed. What lesson do critics draw from stories like this about the leaders of giant firms?
answer: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
choices: Top leaders can lose touch with what is really happening inside their own firm
A firm's fate is set by the markets, not by what its leaders do
Losses in a firm's hedge funds rarely threaten the firm itself
Leaders who delegate freely keep their firms safer, not riskier
context: Jimmy Cayne, then Bear's chairman, was playing at a bridge tournament while the July 2007 collapse of Bear's internal hedge funds unfolded. The anecdote became emblematic of Wall Street executive detachment during the run-up to the crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'James Cayne' (2026-09-05).

question: Benjamin Strong pioneered a tool at the new Federal Reserve Bank of New York that is still central today: the Fed buys government bonds from private banks, pumping in new reserves and pulling interest rates down, and sells them to do the reverse. What is the tool called?
answer: Open market operations
choices: Open market operations
Reserve requirements
The discount window
Margin requirements
context: Open market operations became the Fed's most important standing tool. Strong built the New York Fed's Open Market Committee into the operational center of American monetary policy. Source: Grokipedia 'Open market operation' (2026-09-05).

question: Across the Atlantic, Benjamin Strong of the New York Fed found his closest friend in finance. That friend ran the Bank of England from 1920 all the way to 1944, and together the two men steered world money policy through the 1920s. Who was he?
answer: Montagu Norman
choices: Montagu Norman
John Maynard Keynes
Winston Churchill
Hjalmar Schacht
context: Montagu Norman led the Bank of England for 24 years -- one of the longest tenures at any major central bank. His friendship with Strong shaped 1920s international monetary coordination. Source: Grokipedia 'Montagu Norman' (2026-09-05).

question: Three foreign central bankers met Benjamin Strong in secret at a Long Island estate in July 1927. Days later the Fed lowered the rate it charges banks that borrow from it, from 4 to 3.5 percent. The cut was meant to help Europe stay on gold. Which three central bankers came?
answer: Montagu Norman of Britain, Charles Rist of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
choices: Montagu Norman of Britain, Charles Rist of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany
John Maynard Keynes of Britain, Raymond Poincaré of France, and Hans Luther of Germany
Winston Churchill of Britain, Aristide Briand of France, and Gustav Stresemann of Germany
Reginald McKenna of Britain, Joseph Caillaux of France, and Rudolf Hilferding of Germany
context: The July 1927 Long Island meeting brought Benjamin Strong together with Montagu Norman of the Bank of England, Hjalmar Schacht of Germany's Reichsbank and Charles Rist, deputy governor of the Bank of France, sent by its governor, Émile Moreau. It produced the rate cut that Austrian economists later blamed for the final phase of the 1920s boom. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Wall Street was roaring in July 1927 when Benjamin Strong pushed the Fed's discount rate down from 4 to 3.5 percent, days after his secret Long Island meeting with three European central bankers. In private he reportedly described the cut with a drinker's metaphor, an image of what cheap money would do to the boom. Which phrase did he use?
answer: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
choices: A little coup de whiskey to the stock market
A friendly nudge to the bond market
A helping shot for the London Fund
A quiet toast to European stability
context: The 'coup de whiskey' phrase is attributed to Strong via Adolph Miller's later Senate testimony. It captured the sense in which the rate cut was calculated to lift asset markets rather than to serve any narrow domestic policy purpose. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: A factory owner is deciding whether to build a new plant just after the Fed has pushed its rate down. In the Austrian account, a rate held below where savers and borrowers would settle on their own sends him a false message. What does the low rate wrongly tell him?
answer: That people want to save more, so long-term projects look profitable
choices: That people want to save more, so long-term projects look profitable
That the economy is already at full production capacity
That the government wants prices to fall next year
That businesses should invest less than they normally would
context: Rothbard's 1963 book America's Great Depression built the Austrian case that the 1927 Strong-Norman coordination directly seeded the 1929 crash. Rothbard identified Strong as the pivotal Fed figure of the whole 1920s. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Cheap money poured into New York after Benjamin Strong pushed American interest rates down in 1927, partly so that Europe's central banks could hold their currencies to gold. What do critics of the 1927 easing say those low rates did?
answer: They fueled a stock-market bubble that later burst
choices: They fueled a stock-market bubble that later burst
They pulled gold out of London and toward New York
They cooled Wall Street by sending money abroad
They helped Europe and left America's economy untouched
context: Adolph Miller, a Fed Board member 1914-1936, was the dissenter on the 1927 rate cut and later Senate witness against Strong's legacy. His testimony is the traceable source of the 'coup de whiskey' quote. Source: Grokipedia 'Adolph Miller' (2026-09-05).

question: Winston Churchill put Britain back on gold in 1925 at a rate that overvalued the pound, and gold threatened to flow out of London toward New York. Benjamin Strong held American interest rates low to keep the gold in London, and cut them further in 1927. What does the episode show about central banks working together across borders?
answer: Easing to defend another country's currency can inflate asset prices at home
choices: Easing to defend another country's currency can inflate asset prices at home
Easing to defend another country's currency leaves the easing country untouched
Central banks working together can keep any fixed exchange rate safe for good
Cooperation across borders works only when every central bank eases at once
context: Strong cut US rates in 1927 to help Britain defend the pound. The unintended domestic consequence was a US stock-market bubble that broke in 1929. International cooperation solved one problem by creating another. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: A young couple goes hunting for a brand-new apartment in a city that froze every rent at a low level a few years ago, for five years, no matter what heating and repairs cost. What has likely happened to the number of new apartments being built?
answer: It drops -- builders will not build for a rent they cannot raise
choices: It drops -- builders will not build for a rent they cannot raise
It rises -- builders hurry to finish before the freeze ends
Nothing changes -- builders follow demand, not rent rules
It rises -- cheap rents draw more renters and more building
context: Mietendeckel means 'rent lid' in German. The rule applied only inside Berlin, so neighboring Brandenburg municipalities kept market pricing -- creating a natural experiment economists rarely have. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Economists in Munich and Berlin seized on Berlin's 2020 rent freeze, the Mietendeckel, as a rare experiment: two sets of apartments in the same country and the same months, one under the lid and one not. What feature of the law made that comparison possible?
answer: It stopped at Berlin's city line, so the towns beyond kept market rents
choices: It stopped at Berlin's city line, so the towns beyond kept market rents
It began on different dates in different districts of the city
It covered only flats owned by large landlord companies
It applied only to flats let to tenants with low incomes
context: Economists at the ifo Institute in Munich and the DIW in Berlin used the border discontinuity to compare rental-market outcomes in Berlin against adjoining non-Berlin municipalities. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Economists at the ifo Institute and the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) counted the flats offered for rent in Berlin in the months after its 2020 rent freeze. They also checked the market in Potsdam and the other towns just past the city line, where the freeze did not reach. What did they find?
answer: Listings inside the city fell sharply, while rents just outside climbed
choices: Listings inside the city fell sharply, while rents just outside climbed
Listings rose inside the city, while flats just outside stood empty
Rents fell on both sides, as the lid's low prices spread outward
Listings and rents barely moved on either side of the line
context: Landlords held units off the market, listed them as furnished shares (exempt from the freeze), or sold them. An ifo study of 2022 found Berlin's supply of rental listings shrank by up to 60 percent, and a DIW paper found rents climbing fast in the uncapped towns next door, Potsdam among them. Sources: ifo Institute study, April 2022 (reported by fundresearch.de); DIW Discussion Paper 1999 (Hahn, Kholodilin, Waltl and Fongoni).

question: A nurse arrives in a big city for a new hospital job a year after it froze the rents on every apartment already leased. She finds almost nothing listed, and the few flats on offer cost far more than before the freeze. Why have rents jumped on the leftover listings?
answer: The freeze shrank the pool of listings, so movers now compete for the few left
choices: The freeze shrank the pool of listings, so movers now compete for the few left
Building costs soared, and landlords passed them on to every tenant
The central bank raised rates, so mortgages and rents climbed together
The city taxed landlords to pay for the freeze, and they passed it on
context: Applied Bastiat: seen benefit (protected sitting tenants) was real; unseen cost fell on the mover who now faced a smaller and more competitive market for the units that remained available. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: Judges in Karlsruhe, on Germany's Federal Constitutional Court, struck down Berlin's rent freeze on April 15, 2021. They never weighed whether the price cap was good or bad economics. On what legal ground did they strike the law down?
answer: Only the national government could regulate rents, not the state of Berlin
choices: Only the national government could regulate rents, not the state of Berlin
The freeze took landlords' property without the payment the Basic Law requires
The freeze treated tenants in old and new buildings unequally
The freeze broke European Union rules on the free movement of capital
context: The Court did not rule on the economic merits of the freeze; it ruled that the wrong level of government had enacted it. Retroactive rent had to be paid back by Berlin tenants who had been paying the frozen rate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Berlin_rent_cap.

question: A trader on the Pacific island of Yap accepted a giant stone disc as payment. Cowrie shells did the same work in West Africa, gold in Rome, silver bars in China and wampum belts in North America. Each of them had one trait in common that let it hold its value. What was it?
answer: It was difficult to produce more of
choices: It was difficult to produce more of
It was universally beautiful to look at
It was easy to divide into small units
It was heavy enough to be hard to steal
context: Difficulty of production is the property that made gold, silver, and every other commodity money resist debasement. Easy-to-produce goods flooded markets and lost value; scarce goods held it. Source: Menger, Principles of Economics, 1871.

question: Carl Menger set out to explain why one good, and not another, wins out as money. Beauty, size and toughness, he answered, matter less than one feature: whatever the widest circle of traders will take most easily slowly becomes the money everyone uses. What one word names that feature?
answer: Marketability
choices: Marketability
Divisibility
Portability
Durability
context: Menger's Principles (1871) grounds money in MARKETABILITY -- the depth of the network of would-be trading partners. High marketability historically correlated with difficulty of production. Source: mises.org/library/principles-economics.

question: A miner in Nevada pours fresh gold into the world's stock of gold ever mined and still kept in vaults and jewelry, as mines in South Africa and Australia do each year. Austrian economists call that stock's slow growth the true strength of gold as money. By about what percentage does the stock grow each year?
answer: About 1 to 2 percent
choices: About 1 to 2 percent
About 5 to 6 percent
About 10 to 12 percent
Effectively zero, at the geological limit
context: New annual mining runs about 1-2% of above-ground stock. This is why gold's 'issuance rate' has been the historical benchmark for a hard money against which every fiat currency was measured. Source: World Gold Council annual supply data.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto wrote a hard limit on how many coins can ever exist into Bitcoin's code when he launched it in 2009. Gold's stock keeps creeping upward year by year, and no metal or paper money had ever had a fixed upper bound written into it. What short phrase names Bitcoin's property?
answer: Absolute scarcity
choices: Absolute scarcity
Relative scarcity
Digital fungibility
Cryptographic uniqueness
