context: Gold is relatively scarce (~1-2% annual growth); Bitcoin is absolutely scarce (fixed upper bound). No prior commodity money has been absolutely scarce; even the tightest fiat central bank grows supply several percent yearly. Source: saifedean.com (Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard, 2018).

question: Saifedean Ammous made popular a yardstick for money: divide all the supply that already exists by the fresh supply added each year. For gold the figure is about 60, and a higher figure means a money that is harder to inflate. What is the ratio called?
answer: Stock-to-flow
choices: Stock-to-flow
Price-to-earnings
Debt-to-equity
Money velocity
context: Ammous's argument: gold's stock-to-flow is about 60, meaning some sixty years of mining at the present pace would match the gold already above ground. Bitcoin's ratio jumps at every halving and climbs toward infinity as new issuance approaches zero around 2140. Source: saifedean.com/thebitcoinstandard.

question: Germans watched the Weimar mark lose its value in 1923, as Romans had watched Diocletian's denarius and savers since 1971 have watched paper money. Austrian-school writers make a narrower case for Bitcoin than world conquest: all three lost value the same way, they argue, and Bitcoin's fixed cap shuts that way off. Which mechanism does the cap block?
answer: Debasement by the issuing authority
choices: Debasement by the issuing authority
Counterfeiting by private forgers
Loss of physical stock to warfare
Substitution by more convenient rival currencies
context: Roman denarius under Diocletian, medieval coin-clipping, Weimar mark 1923, every post-1971 fiat currency: the issuing authority has always been the debasement channel. Bitcoin's protocol removes that channel by making supply not-decidable by any actor. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: A Bitcoin defender in the Austrian school, asked where his case for hard money begins, points to a single book that came out in Vienna in 1871. Every Austrian book on money since has built on it. Which book is it?
answer: Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
choices: Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
Ludwig von Mises's Theory of Money and Credit
Friedrich Hayek's Denationalisation of Money
Murray Rothbard's What Has Government Done to Our Money
context: Menger's Principles of Economics (Vienna, 1871) is the founding Austrian text on money's market emergence via marketability; every later Austrian monetary book (Mises 1912, Hayek 1976, Rothbard 1963) builds on it. Source: mises.org/library/principles-economics.

question: A Bitcoin wallet guards a secret number far too long to memorize or copy by hand without mistakes. So nearly every wallet turns it into a friendlier backup: a short list of everyday words to write down and lock away. What is that backup called?
answer: a seed phrase
choices: a seed phrase
a private key
a public key
a wallet address
context: Bitcoin wallets turn the underlying secret into a mnemonic seed phrase, usually 12 or 24 English words, from which every key in the wallet can be rebuilt (the BIP-39 standard). The private key is the secret number itself; the public key is derived from it, and a wallet address is a short code made from the public key for receiving coins. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: A Ledger owner writes her backup words on paper, and a Trezor owner does the same with his. Every word on both sheets comes from one fixed list of common English words, which countless phone wallets use too. How many words are on that list?
answer: 2,048 words
choices: 2,048 words
500 words
10,000 words
12 words
context: The BIP-39 wordlist is exactly 2,048 English words (11 bits per word). 12 is the number of words in a short seed phrase, not the wordlist size. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/english.txt.

question: Suppose you cross a border with no phone, no wallet and not a scrap of paper, only your seed phrase in your memory. Gold would set off the scanner, a bank account could be locked from far away, and a case of cash would draw the sniffing dogs. What can customs officers find?
answer: nothing — no search reveals the memorized words in your head
choices: nothing — no search reveals the memorized words in your head
border scanners can read memorized information
customs freezes coins tied to any traveler crossing a border
the network refuses to sign anything from the new country
context: A memorized seed phrase leaves no physical trace; the coins remain moveable from any internet-connected machine that can reconstruct the wallet. Contrast: gold triggers metal detectors, cash triggers currency-dog searches, bank balances can be frozen from any jurisdiction. The novel property is that ownership can be reduced entirely to a memorized sequence of words in a human mind; every prior monetary asset had a physical or ledger footprint outside the owner.

question: Police search a Bitcoin owner's house and carry off the sheet of paper his seed phrase is written on. Had the phrase lived only in his memory, American defense lawyers argue, the state could not force him to say it aloud. They cite the amendment to the US Constitution that protects anyone from being made to testify against himself. Which amendment is it?
answer: the Fifth Amendment
choices: the Fifth Amendment
the First Amendment
the Fourth Amendment
the Second Amendment
context: The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination has been invoked in US courts to argue that compelling password disclosure is compelled testimony. First Amendment covers speech; Fourth covers search and seizure; Second covers arms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution.

question: A suspect refuses to give police the password to his laptop, saying no one can force him to testify against himself. American courts have split over refusals like his. Some judges will not compel the password. Others order it, reasoning that a password reveals nothing new once the state already knows the files exist, where they sit and that they are real. What is that rule called?
answer: the foregone-conclusion doctrine
choices: the foregone-conclusion doctrine
the Miranda rule
the exclusionary rule
the plain-view doctrine
context: Some US courts have used the 'foregone-conclusion' doctrine to compel password disclosure when the state can show the material's existence, location and authenticity are already established. Miranda concerns warnings; the exclusionary rule bars illegally seized evidence; plain-view relates to warrantless observation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foregone_conclusion.

question: A Bitcoin owner learns one morning that the company behind his hardware wallet is closing for good: no more updates, no more support. His backup is a seed phrase built to Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39, published free for any maker to use without asking permission, and makers from Ledger to Trezor to countless phone apps have adopted it. What can he do?
answer: Restore the phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard
choices: Restore the phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard
Nothing -- the coins are lost once the vendor turns off its servers
Wait for the largest surviving vendor to migrate the coins automatically
Convert the phrase into a new secret format before any other wallet reads it
context: BIP-39 phrases are portable across compliant wallets -- the whole design intent. No vendor server is involved in signing; migrations and format conversions are not needed. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: A slick website promises 1 percent a day on any crypto deposited with it. At that pace $100 would top $3,700 within a year. A Treasury bond issued by the United States, among the safest loans there are, pays about 4 percent a year. What is such a promise almost always a sign of?
answer: A scam -- no real business can pay that much
choices: A scam -- no real business can pay that much
A breakthrough -- new tech beats bank rates
A gamble -- risky, but honest about its odds
A promotion -- a bonus rate for new customers
context: A promise of 1 percent a day compounds $100 into about $3,700 in a year, while a United States Treasury bond pays about 4 percent a year. No real business earns that much, so such a promise almost always means a scam. BitConnect, launched in 2016, made just this kind of promise, claiming its returns came from a secret trading bot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BitConnect.

question: An Italian immigrant in Boston promised investors huge profits in 1920 from trading international postal coupons, with no real business behind the pitch. He paid a bonus to whoever recruited fresh depositors, and the whole operation collapsed within a year. What is a fraud of that shape called?
answer: a Ponzi scheme
choices: a Ponzi scheme
a hedge fund
a mutual fund
a public offering
context: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors from new investors' contributions and typically recruits through a pyramid of downstream depositors. Named for Charles Ponzi (1920). Hedge funds, mutual funds, and public offerings are legitimate structures. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponzi_scheme.

question: Satish Kumbhani launched BitConnect in 2016 on the claim that a hidden trading bot, which no outsider could examine, earned its returns. In January 2018 regulators in Texas and North Carolina told it to take no more deposits, and its coin crashed from roughly $400 to nearly zero in a few days. How much did depositors lose in all?
answer: about $2.4 billion
choices: about $2.4 billion
about $50 million
about $30 billion
about $200 million
context: Estimated depositor losses were about $2.4 billion. BitConnect founder Satish Kumbhani was indicted by the US Department of Justice in 2022 and remains a fugitive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BitConnect.

question: Ruja Ignatova sold OneCoin around the globe as Bitcoin's successor, staging glitzy promotions for it, before she vanished in 2017 with billions of investors' dollars gone. What makes a scheme like hers a Ponzi rather than a real investment?
answer: Old investors were paid with new investors' money, not real earnings
choices: Old investors were paid with new investors' money, not real earnings
The scheme mined real Bitcoin with special hardware
The scheme was audited by real accountants
Every investor got paid back at the end
context: Ruja Ignatova launched OneCoin around 2014 and styled herself the Cryptoqueen. Like Charles Ponzi's scheme of 1920, OneCoin paid its early investors with money from later ones rather than from real earnings, so it needed an ever-growing stream of new recruits. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin.

question: Investigators finally took OneCoin apart after Ruja Ignatova, a Bulgarian-born businesswoman with a German doctorate in law, had sold it worldwide as the next Bitcoin and packed London's Wembley Arena for its promotions. They found one piece missing that every real cryptocurrency needs. What did OneCoin lack?
answer: any working blockchain behind the coins it said it issued
choices: any working blockchain behind the coins it said it issued
any independent trading pair on any external exchange venue
any legally registered corporate address or filing history
any bug-bounty program or third-party security review
context: OneCoin had no blockchain; the 'ledger' was entries in an internal SQL database that Ignatova and her staff controlled. That means the entire operation was them typing numbers by hand. It had registered companies, celebrity appearances, and its own internal exchange rate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin; BBC 'The Missing Cryptoqueen' podcast.

question: Prosecutors in Germany, Britain and the United States pieced together how much money investors had poured into OneCoin, the coin Ruja Ignatova sold as the next Bitcoin. Their estimate dwarfed what BitConnect's depositors had lost. What range do they give for OneCoin?
answer: roughly 4 to 15 billion US dollars
choices: roughly 4 to 15 billion US dollars
roughly 40 to 60 billion US dollars
roughly 100 to 200 million US dollars
roughly 500 million to 1 billion US dollars
context: OneCoin fundraising estimates range from $4B to $15B depending on the accounting; even the low end is larger than BitConnect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneCoin; US DOJ indictments.

question: Ruja Ignatova boarded a Ryanair flight out of Sofia, Bulgaria, on October 25, 2017, as investigators from America and Germany closed in on her OneCoin scam. She has not been seen in public since. Which country did that last flight land in?
answer: Greece (Athens)
choices: Greece (Athens)
Germany (Frankfurt)
the United Arab Emirates (Dubai)
the United States (New York)
context: The last confirmed public sighting was her Sofia-to-Athens Ryanair flight on October 25, 2017; she vanished from Athens. Investigative reporters have pursued leads through several countries since. Source: BBC 'The Missing Cryptoqueen' podcast (2019).

question: Ruja Ignatova, the self-styled Cryptoqueen behind OneCoin, had been missing since a flight out of Sofia in 2017, with investigators in several countries still on her trail. On June 30, 2022, American authorities gave her a new status in the hunt. What did she receive that day?
answer: placement on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
choices: placement on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
a US federal indictment sealed under national-security law
an Interpol Blue Notice
designation as a specially designated national by the US Treasury
context: The FBI added Ruja Ignatova to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on June 30, 2022. Federal indictments against her had already been unsealed. Source: https://www.fbi.gov/wanted/topten/ruja-ignatova.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos, who wrote Mastering Bitcoin, the standard technical book on the protocol, objects whenever reporters lump every coin together under the single word crypto. He and other longtime Bitcoin teachers say the word blurs a real distinction. Which point do they insist reporters recognize?
answer: That Bitcoin, a 2009 protocol with a fixed supply, is a different thing from most 'crypto'
choices: That Bitcoin, a 2009 protocol with a fixed supply, is a different thing from most 'crypto'
That all cryptocurrency including Bitcoin should be regulated identically by financial authorities
That any project using a blockchain is legitimate regardless of its economics
That the SEC alone should decide which cryptocurrencies are legitimate
context: The Bitcoin-vs-crypto distinction (Antonopoulos, Ammous, Song) treats Bitcoin as a specific rule-bound engineering artifact; most 'crypto' projects have an issuer who can change the rules, which is what BitConnect and OneCoin exploited. Regulatory framings and blockchain-as-legitimizer are precisely the moves the distinction refuses. Source: Antonopoulos, Mastering Bitcoin (2017 ed.).

question: A Boston promoter promised huge returns from international postal coupons in 1920, and his scheme collapsed within a year. Austrian-minded writers set BitConnect and OneCoin, both sold as cryptocurrencies, beside his fraud. Which historical claim about the pattern do they press?
answer: That the pattern of promising fixed high returns with a vague mechanism and paying them from new deposits is older than the technology it dresses in
choices: That the pattern of promising fixed high returns with a vague mechanism and paying them from new deposits is older than the technology it dresses in
That fraud of this specific shape was invented by the cryptocurrency industry and had no prior counterpart in twentieth-century finance
That government regulation of financial products reliably prevents Ponzi schemes if the enforcement budget is high enough
That Ponzi schemes structurally require a specific new financial technology to attract depositors and cannot succeed with older tools
context: The Austrian pattern-recognition argument treats BitConnect and OneCoin as a 1920 Ponzi rewrapped in 2016 clothing -- the technology is decoration; the structure is ancient. Government regulation did not prevent either; the technology did not create the Ponzi form (Ponzi himself had none). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponzi_scheme.

question: A devout Baptist in a Southern town campaigns to keep the Sunday liquor ban, sure that drinking on the Sabbath is wrong. A moonshiner backs the ban too, because closed liquor stores send Sunday drinkers his way. What kind of coalition is this?
answer: An alliance of two groups wanting the same rule for opposite reasons
choices: An alliance of two groups wanting the same rule for opposite reasons
A vote trade, where each side backs the other's pet rule in return
A compromise, where each side gives up part of what it wanted
A front, where one side pays the other to pretend to believe
context: Bruce Yandle spent 1982-84 as Executive Director of the FTC. His 1983 essay in Regulation magazine, then published by the American Enterprise Institute, coined the 'Bootleggers and Baptists' framing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Yandle; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_(magazine).

question: Bruce Yandle, a Clemson economist running the Federal Trade Commission's staff in the early 1980s, saw the same odd partnership behind rule after rule. In a 1983 essay he gave that partnership a short name. What did he call it?
answer: Bootleggers and Baptists
choices: Bootleggers and Baptists
The Iron Triangle
Concentrated benefits and dispersed costs
Regulatory capture
context: The 1983 essay is titled 'Bootleggers and Baptists -- The Education of a Regulatory Economist'. Southern Baptists supported Sunday liquor bans on moral grounds; bootleggers supported them because Sunday legal sales would compete with their illegal operations. The pairing has become one of the most-cited concepts in modern political economy.

question: A Southern bootlegger sells his liquor on a Sunday with no legal store open to compete, and he helps pay for the fight to keep the Sunday-closing law. The Baptists, in Bruce Yandle's telling, bring something else, which lets lawmakers defend the rule without blushing. What do the Baptists give the rule?
answer: Moral cover
choices: Moral cover
Legal defense
Election financing
Media coverage
context: The Baptists' visible moral rhetoric provided political legitimacy; the bootleggers' quiet profit interest supplied resources. Together the coalition was more effective than either could be alone. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983).

question: A hearing opens at city hall on new limits for Uber and Lyft: where their drivers may pick up riders, and what they may charge. Bruce Yandle's pattern predicts two unlikely allies at the microphone backing the limits, one with money at stake and one with a moral cause to plead. Which pair usually shows up?
answer: Taxi-medallion holders (economic) and pedestrian-safety advocates (moral cover)
choices: Taxi-medallion holders (economic) and pedestrian-safety advocates (moral cover)
Uber shareholders (economic) and consumer-rights groups (moral cover)
Ride-share drivers (economic) and disability advocates (moral cover)
Hotel operators (economic) and neighborhood groups (moral cover)
context: Taxi-medallion holders benefit economically from restrictions that raise the cost of ride-share entry. Pedestrian-safety and passenger-protection advocates provide moral cover. Yandle's pattern applied to a modern case. Source: mercatus.org ride-share studies.

question: Environmentalists rally behind a new green rule, sincere in wanting to protect the planet. Bruce Yandle's lens looks for a quieter partner cheering the rule on: a business that gains because the rule weighs more heavily on its rivals than on itself. Which kind of business often plays that bootlegger's part?
answer: Domestic producers seeking barriers against foreign competitors
choices: Domestic producers seeking barriers against foreign competitors
Foreign producers seeking easier access to the home market
Importers seeking lower prices on goods brought from abroad
Banks seeking new lending to firms forced to retool
context: Environmental rules that raise costs on all producers can disadvantage foreign competitors more than domestic ones (particularly under carbon-adjustment or content-labeling schemes). Domestic producers become the bootleggers behind the environmental moral coalition. Source: cato.org environmental economics.

question: One group fought for the 18th Amendment, which banned alcohol across America from 1919 to 1933; another grew rich from the ban while it lasted. Economists read that ban as the biggest case of Bruce Yandle's pattern. Which two groups were they?
answer: Moralists and organized-crime beneficiaries
choices: Moralists and organized-crime beneficiaries
Farmers and factory owners
Suffragists and railroad barons
Immigrants and native-born citizens
context: Prohibition united moralists (temperance movements, WCTU, Anti-Saloon League) with organized-crime beneficiaries who would run the resulting black market. The 18th Amendment (1919) and the Volstead Act became the American case study. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States.

question: Bruce Yandle made his insight into a way of reading the news. In a working coalition of moralists and profit-seekers, he said, each side plays its own part in public, and it takes a regulatory economist years to learn to see past the moral speeches to the bootlegger behind them. What part does the moral side play?
answer: The visible lobbying while the profit coalition supplies the resources
choices: The visible lobbying while the profit coalition supplies the resources
The private financing while the profit coalition takes the public credit
The economic analysis while the profit coalition provides the theory
The election donations while the profit coalition writes the laws
context: Yandle wrote that regulatory economists spend years learning to look past the moral rhetoric to identify the bootlegger. The moral side gets the microphone; the profit side gets the check. Recognition-not-verdict: the kid learns to spot the pattern. Source: cato.org (Yandle 1983, 2014).

question: A Baptist preaches in defense of the South's Sunday-closing law, while a bootlegger quietly loves it, since it shuts his legal rivals for the day. Their reasons are opposite, yet for Bruce Yandle's pattern one thing must match. What must the two share?
answer: Identical policy positions on the rule's specific design
choices: Identical policy positions on the rule's specific design
Identical philosophies of government
Shared electoral organization
Common demographic background
context: Yandle's insight: the moral coalition provides political cover; the commercial coalition provides funding and lobbying muscle. Both need identical detail-level policy to succeed. Source: Yandle, Regulation (1983).

question: General Motors and Ford publicly backed California's goal that every new car sold in the state from 2035 run without tailpipe emissions, standing beside the environmental groups that cheered it. Why would two of America's biggest established carmakers welcome so strict a rule?
answer: They can afford the switch, but smaller rivals cannot
choices: They can afford the switch, but smaller rivals cannot
They had already sold more electric cars than any rival
The state paid them a bonus for every gas car they dropped
Their buyers had already stopped wanting gas-powered cars
context: Large incumbent automakers such as GM and Ford publicly backed the goal when California's air board approved the Advanced Clean Cars II rule in August 2022. Their compliance capital is a moat: smaller automakers and independent parts suppliers who cannot afford the transition are the unrepresented losers. In June 2025 President Trump signed resolutions of Congress revoking the federal waiver that let California enforce the rule, and California sued. Source: reuters.com (2022 CARB rulemaking coverage); https://www.dwt.com/blogs/energy--environmental-law-blog/2025/06/california-epa-clean-air-emission-waivers-lawsuit.

question: The justices of the US Supreme Court ruled in June 2018, in South Dakota v. Wayfair, that states may require online sellers based in other states to collect their sales tax. Tax collectors in the states and champions of a level playing field made the moral case, and a small online seller must now handle more than forty-five different state tax systems. Which businesses quietly welcomed the ruling?
answer: Large brick-and-mortar retailers and Amazon
choices: Large brick-and-mortar retailers and Amazon
Online marketplaces such as eBay and Etsy
Overnight shippers such as UPS and FedEx
Card networks such as Visa and Mastercard
context: Wayfair was a classic Bootleggers-and-Baptists case: state revenue officials and 'level-playing-field' advocates (Baptists) with big-box retailers and Amazon (Bootleggers, since both already had physical nexus and were already collecting). Small e-commerce sellers now face 45+ state sales-tax regimes. Source: supremecourt.gov (Wayfair 585 US ___).

question: A licensed cannabis shop in California paid heavy taxes in 2023 and filled out piles of paperwork, while unlicensed dealers nearby paid no tax at all. California had legalized marijuana, following Colorado and Washington, the first to do so in 2012, but boxed the legal trade in with scarce licenses. What share of the cannabis sold in California that year still came from the illegal market?
answer: About two-thirds
choices: About two-thirds
About one-tenth
About one-third
Essentially none
context: California's licensed cannabis market has been repeatedly estimated to supply only about one-third of total consumption, with the illegal market preserving roughly two-thirds -- a structural gift to Bootleggers-and-Baptists coalitions of anti-drug advocates and licensed incumbents. Source: California DCC market reports; New Frontier Data.

question: Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson and Lorillard signed the Master Settlement Agreement in 1998 with forty-six state attorneys general. It looked like a punishment for the tobacco industry. Yet the per-pack payments it required made it ruinously expensive for any new cigarette maker to break in. Which two groups found themselves allies, for opposite reasons?
answer: Public-health advocates and the four largest tobacco companies
choices: Public-health advocates and the four largest tobacco companies
Tobacco farmers and cigarette retailers
State attorneys general and independent smoke shops
Advertising firms and pharmaceutical companies
context: The MSA locked in the Big Four tobacco companies' market share by imposing per-cigarette payments that made new entry prohibitively expensive. Public-health advocates got funding; Big Four got a moat. Source: naag.org (MSA 1998); Viscusi, Smoke-Filled Rooms (Chicago 2002).

question: Bruce Yandle wanted analysts to learn one habit. When moral reformers line up behind a new rule, do not settle for the moral story told up front, even though the moralists often mean every word. Look one layer down. What should the analyst look for there?
answer: A concentrated commercial beneficiary hiding behind the moral advocate
choices: A concentrated commercial beneficiary hiding behind the moral advocate
A single ideological cause explaining the whole coalition
A single geographic region driving the outcome
A hidden foreign influence campaign
context: The Yandle move: when moral rhetoric and commercial interest happen to align on identical policy detail, look for the commercial beneficiary. This is a diagnostic tool, not a policy verdict on the substantive goal. The moral coalition may be sincere; the commercial coalition may be following naked incentive.

question: Delegates of forty-four Allied nations gathered at a grand mountain resort hotel for three weeks of July 1944, with World War II almost won. Their job was to design the money system the world would run on after the war. In which hotel did they meet?
answer: the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
choices: the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
the Greenbrier in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia
the Homestead in Hot Springs, Virginia
the Balsams in Dixville Notch, New Hampshire
context: The July 1-22, 1944 Bretton Woods Conference was held at the Mount Washington Hotel in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. The Greenbrier, the Homestead and the Balsams were grand mountain resorts of the same era; the Homestead hosted the 1943 Allied food conference, not the money one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_Conference.

question: Harry Dexter White drafted the plan that won at Bretton Woods in 1944: every Allied currency pegged to the dollar, and the dollar fixed by law to gold. Any foreign central bank could hand its dollars to the American Treasury and take gold at that fixed price. What was the price per ounce?
answer: $35 per ounce of gold
choices: $35 per ounce of gold
$20 per ounce of gold
$100 per ounce of gold
$400 per ounce of gold
context: The Bretton Woods peg was $35 per ounce of gold. The classical US gold-standard price before Roosevelt's 1934 devaluation was ~$20.67; $100 and $400 are later 1970s prices after the peg broke. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: John Maynard Keynes led Britain's team and Harry Dexter White the Americans' when delegates of forty-four Allied nations met at Bretton Woods in July 1944. They pegged currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold, and they founded two new bodies to run the system, both of which survive today. Which pair did they found?
answer: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank
choices: the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank
the United Nations and the World Trade Organization
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the European Central Bank
the Bank for International Settlements and the League of Nations
context: Bretton Woods created the IMF (for exchange-rate stability) and the World Bank (formally IBRD, for postwar reconstruction). The UN and WTO were established elsewhere; NATO and the ECB came much later; BIS predates Bretton Woods (1930) and the League of Nations was already dissolving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_Conference.

question: Keynes came to Bretton Woods in 1944 with a rival to the American plan. He wanted a reserve currency that no single nation owned, issued by a body he called the International Clearing Union to settle the trade accounts between countries. What did he name the new currency?
answer: the Bancor
choices: the Bancor
the Euro
the Special Drawing Right
the ECU
context: John Maynard Keynes proposed the Bancor at Bretton Woods; the US design (Harry Dexter White's dollar anchor) was adopted instead. The Euro (1999) and ECU (1979) came from European monetary integration; SDRs (1969) were the IMF's much later reserve asset. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bancor.

question: The delegates who left Bretton Woods in July 1944 had tied every Allied currency to the dollar at a fixed rate, and the dollar itself to gold, on Harry Dexter White's design. What was the arrangement meant to do?
answer: To keep exchange rates steady and stop countries from printing money without limit
choices: To keep exchange rates steady and stop countries from printing money without limit
To let each country's currency float freely against every other
To create a single world currency to replace all national money
To make the dollar the only money allowed in world trade
context: Harry Dexter White's plan pegged each Allied currency to the dollar at a fixed rate and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce. Fixed rates were meant to give postwar trade steady prices, and the gold link was meant to stop governments from printing money without limit: a country that inflated would see its currency strain against its peg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: Code-breakers in the Second World War cracked a trove of Soviet cables, and the National Security Agency began releasing their files in 1995. The files identified Harry Dexter White, who had drafted the American plan at Bretton Woods, as a Soviet source; the cables called him Jurist and Richard. What was the code-breaking project called?
answer: the Venona project
choices: the Venona project
the Manhattan Project
Operation Paperclip
the Bletchley Park archive
context: Venona (public releases 1995-96) provided the strongest forensic evidence that White was a Soviet source (codenames 'Jurist' and 'Richard'). The Manhattan Project built the atomic bomb; Paperclip recruited German scientists; Bletchley Park broke Enigma. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venona_project.

question: Whittaker Chambers, a former Soviet courier, named Harry Dexter White before a congressional committee in 1948, and decoded wartime Soviet cables later marked White as a Soviet source. White had drafted the American plan that won at Bretton Woods. What risk in designing the world's money does his story expose?
answer: A few insiders with hidden agendas can steer rules that bind everyone else
choices: A few insiders with hidden agendas can steer rules that bind everyone else
Fixed exchange rates can hide a currency's weakness until it breaks
A single reserve currency hands its issuer a privilege over all others
Rules drafted in wartime may not suit the needs of peacetime trade
context: Whittaker Chambers named Harry Dexter White before the House Un-American Activities Committee on August 3, 1948. White denied the charge before the committee on August 13 and died of a heart attack three days later. The Venona decrypts released from 1995 identified him as a Soviet source under the code names Jurist and Richard. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Harry_Dexter_White.

question: Murray Rothbard and Saifedean Ammous looked back at the gold peg Richard Nixon abandoned in August 1971. The world's hunger for dollars, they said, had kept America running a deficit, paid for in dollars it issued itself. What did they argue the peg's design meant from the start?
answer: That any peg that required the peg-setter to run payments deficits in its own currency was arithmetically doomed the moment those deficits exceeded gold reserves
choices: That any peg that required the peg-setter to run payments deficits in its own currency was arithmetically doomed the moment those deficits exceeded gold reserves
That the peg would have held indefinitely if postwar political leaders had shown more discipline about deficit spending and had chosen to defend the peg with fiscal restraint
That the peg was purely a matter of international communication and could have been sustained by careful rhetoric and coordinated central-bank statements to hold public confidence
That the peg was an accidental byproduct of postwar chaos rather than a deliberately designed monetary system and had no coherent architecture to defend once challenged
context: The Austrian argument (Rothbard, Ammous): the Bretton Woods gold-exchange standard collapsed by arithmetic. Once the dollars the United States owed abroad outran its gold, the peg could not survive any test, whatever leaders said or did. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States; Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: A British shopkeeper before 1914 handed a banknote across his bank's counter and walked out with gold coins, a swap any ordinary person could make. Under Bretton Woods, from 1944 to 1971, no private citizen had that right; the swap was open to foreign central banks alone, which could trade their dollars for gold. Strictly speaking, what kind of standard was Bretton Woods?
answer: a gold-exchange standard rather than a classical gold standard
choices: a gold-exchange standard rather than a classical gold standard
a bimetallic standard rather than a silver standard
a floating peg rather than a fixed peg
a currency board rather than a central bank
context: Bretton Woods was a gold-EXCHANGE standard: only foreign central banks could redeem dollars for gold, not ordinary citizens. A classical gold standard makes gold coins the actual circulating money. The other pairs address different distinctions. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_exchange_standard.

question: India, Brazil, China and Russia began meeting as a formal club in 2009, and South Africa joined them in 2010. Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs had given the first four a catchy label back in 2001. What short name does the group go by?
answer: BRICS
choices: BRICS
G7
OPEC
APEC
context: The original 2009 BRIC grouping became BRICS in 2010 when South Africa joined. It is a coordination forum, not a treaty organization. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS' (2026-09-05).

question: At Goldman Sachs in 2001, Jim O'Neill bet that four big emerging economies, China, India, Brazil and Russia, would grow fast for the next twenty years. What did the four share that made him pick them?
answer: Huge populations and lots of room to catch up to richer countries
choices: Huge populations and lots of room to catch up to richer countries
Vast oil and gas reserves that would pay for their growth
Democratic governments with strong courts and a free press
Close trade ties through a shared customs union
context: Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill coined the term BRIC in a 2001 paper titled 'Building Better Global Economic BRICs.' The label described projected economic weight; the actual political group formed later. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS' (2026-09-05).

question: Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates joined the bloc of rising economies on January 1, 2024, and its members now speak openly of settling trade without dollars. Why do they want payment channels of their own?
answer: They fear the US could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them
choices: They fear the US could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them
Their central banks are barred by law from holding foreign money
Their exporters are now paid in gold, so they no longer need dollars
Their own currencies already pay higher interest than the dollar
context: The January 1 2024 expansion added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the UAE. The expanded group is often called BRICS+ and represents roughly 45% of global population and 35% of world GDP. Source: Grokipedia 'BRICS+' (2026-09-05).

question: Russian troops invaded Ukraine in the last days of February 2022. The United States, Britain, Japan and the European Union answered by freezing the reserves Russia's central bank kept in Western banks, money built up over years of oil and gas sales. Reserve holders beyond the West took note. About how much was frozen?
answer: About 300 billion dollars
choices: About 300 billion dollars
About 30 billion dollars
About 3 trillion dollars
About 3 billion dollars
context: The February 2022 freeze of roughly $300 billion in Russian central-bank reserves was the largest such action in modern history. Non-Western reserve holders read the precedent and accelerated their interest in alternative payment rails. Source: Grokipedia 'Sanctions during the Russo-Ukrainian War' (2026-09-05).

question: Russia and China moved fast from 2022 on to shift their trade with each other out of dollars and into rubles and yuan, and Indian buyers began settling Russian oil purchases in rupees and Emirati dirhams. By Chinese customs figures, what share of Russian-Chinese trade now settles in rubles and yuan?
answer: Over 90 percent
choices: Over 90 percent
About 20 percent
About 50 percent
Under 5 percent
context: Chinese customs data show over 90% of Russia-China trade now settles in ruble-yuan, up from a small fraction pre-2022. India began paying for Russian oil in rupees and UAE dirhams. Saudi Arabia signaled acceptance of yuan for some Chinese oil purchases at the 2023 Beijing summit. Source: Grokipedia 'De-dollarisation' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises described how a government's debts can end in ruin. One that can no longer raise enough in taxes to carry what it owes turns to inflation, he argued, until the public decides the inflation will never stop, rushes to swap its money for real goods, and the currency breaks. What did Mises call that final stage?
answer: The crack-up boom
choices: The crack-up boom
The liquidity trap
The Great Moderation
The deflationary spiral
context: Mises described the crack-up boom in Human Action (1949): once people expect prices to keep rising without end, they rush to swap their money for real goods at any price, and the currency breaks down. By the Congressional Budget Office's count, US federal debt held by the public was about 100 percent of GDP in 2025, up from about 79 percent in 2019; high debt and the freezing of Russia's reserves both push central banks to diversify. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949); Congressional Budget Office, The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2025 to 2055 (https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61187).

question: A central banker outside the West, uneasy after the United States froze Russia's dollar reserves in 2022 and watching American federal debt mount, signed off on a purchase of a reserve asset that sits outside any government's control. Central banks' buying in 2022 was the heaviest in fifty-five years and stayed high through 2024. What did the central banks buy?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Bitcoin
Chinese sovereign debt
Swiss francs
context: World Gold Council data show central-bank gold purchases hit a 55-year high in 2022 at roughly 1,082 tonnes. The 2023 and 2024 totals remained above 1,000 tonnes each year -- historically extraordinary. Source: World Gold Council, Central Bank Gold Statistics.

question: Saifedean Ammous, Lyn Alden and Luke Gromen, analysts in the Austrian camp, read two trends side by side: central banks moving part of their reserves out of dollars, and an American federal debt past 34 trillion dollars. What do they conclude is happening?
answer: A slow shift toward neutral assets is starting, but the dollar isn't immediately replaced
choices: A slow shift toward neutral assets is starting, but the dollar isn't immediately replaced
The dollar will collapse within two years and be replaced by the Chinese yuan
A shared new currency will launch worldwide within twelve months
Gold will be dropped by every central bank as too old-fashioned
context: The Austrian read (Luke Gromen, Lyn Alden, Ammous): near-term dollar hegemony intact; long-term directional shift is real. Weaponized reserves plus rising sovereign debt drive rational holders toward assets no state can freeze. Source: Lyn Alden, Broken Money (2023).

question: A merchant settled a far-off sale in British pounds, as traders before him had done in Dutch guilders, Spanish dollars and Venetian ducats; each of those currencies in turn lost its place. Historians of these currencies note that rivals had usually lurked for decades first. What do they say finally tipped the balance?
answer: The issuing country's own choices to overspend or freeze others' savings
choices: The issuing country's own choices to overspend or freeze others' savings
Being outcompeted by a bigger rival economy
Losing a major war to a smaller country
Being displaced by a new currency pegged to gold
context: The BRICS+ story is not really about the yuan or rupee. It is about the choices the US made -- freezing reserves, running large deficits -- that made non-Western holders want alternatives. The reserve-currency issuer is the primary driver of its own displacement. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Paul Krugman wrote, just three days after the attacks of September 11, that the country would suddenly need fresh office space. Readers of Frédéric Bastiat, Don Boudreaux among them, answered that rebuilding what was destroyed adds no growth. Why not, by Bastiat's reasoning?
answer: The money for rebuilding was going to be spent on other things people wanted
choices: The money for rebuilding was going to be spent on other things people wanted
Builders were already fully booked, so no extra building could happen
Insurers paid for it, and their losses abroad cancelled the gains
New towers cost more to build than the old ones had been worth
context: Krugman, then a new Times columnist and later the 2008 Nobel laureate in economics, wrote in the column: 'Now, all of a sudden, we need some new office buildings.' Boudreaux, a former president of the Foundation for Economic Education, co-founded Cafe Hayek with Russ Roberts in 2004 and writes the recurring 'Quotation of the Day' invoking Bastiat.

question: Frédéric Bastiat told in 1850 of a shopkeeper's boy who broke a window. The glazier pocketed six francs for the new pane, and the neighbors called it good for trade. But the shopkeeper had meant to spend those coins on shoes or a book. What did Bastiat call that lost second purchase?
answer: That which is not seen
choices: That which is not seen
The dead-weight loss
The unpaid labour
The hidden surplus
context: The essay is titled Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas -- 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen'. Bastiat's move is that the six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or a book is the UNSEEN loss the broken window caused. Source: oll.libertyfund.org, Bastiat, 'That Which is Seen'.

question: Russell Roberts, who hosts the economics podcast EconTalk, put Bastiat's way of seeing into fiction. His novel of 2008 set an earthquake loose on Palo Alto, where sky-high prices sent bottled water and generators to the people who needed them most. What is the novel called?
answer: The Price of Everything
choices: The Price of Everything
The Choice
The Invisible Heart
How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life
context: The Price of Everything (Princeton University Press, 2008) uses a post-earthquake supermarket to show how sharply rising prices coordinate the movement of bottled water and generators to where they are most needed -- Bastiat's method dramatised. The Choice (first published 1994) and The Invisible Heart (2001) are Roberts's other novels; How Adam Smith Can Change Your Life is his 2014 non-fiction. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Russ Roberts'.

question: Robert Higgs, an economic historian, took a fresh look in the 1990s at the claim that the Depression was cured by the Second World War. Factories had poured out tanks, ships and planes, and the war's output figures soared. So he looked past the output figures to daily life at home. What did he find?
answer: Everyday goods for families barely improved on Depression levels during the war
choices: Everyday goods for families barely improved on Depression levels during the war
Families bought more than ever before, as war wages flowed home
Rationing ended early in the war, and shops soon filled with goods
War wages rose so fast that families stopped saving altogether
context: Higgs's point is that GDP counts what is SPENT, including tanks and shells; what an ordinary American could actually buy at home -- meat, sugar, tires, gasoline, new cars -- was under strict rationing, and real private per-capita consumption sat near 1938-39 levels until demobilisation. The other three claims are false. Source: eh.net review, 'Depression, War, and Cold War' (Higgs).

question: The neighbors in Frédéric Bastiat's broken-window story of 1850 consoled the shopkeeper: at least the glazier would be paid. Bastiat ended the story with a four-word answer in French, aimed at every claim that wrecking things is good for trade. What were the four words?
answer: 'Destruction n'est pas profit'
choices: 'Destruction n'est pas profit'
'Ruine n'est pas richesse'
'Briser n'est pas gagner'
'Dépense n'est pas richesse'
context: The full French sentence reads: 'Casser, briser, dissiper, ce n'est pas encourager le travail national', ou plus brièvement: 'destruction n'est pas profit.' Those four words are the essay's own closing formula; the other phrases are made-up lines in Bastiat's style. Source: Bastiat, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (1850), iedm.org edition.

question: A hiring manager offers more pay to the applicant with a college diploma. Bryan Caplan argues that most of the extra pay has little to do with what the graduate learned in class: the diploma shows the manager that its holder can see hard, dull work through. What do economists call this idea?
answer: Signaling
choices: Signaling
Human capital
Credential inflation
Moral hazard
context: Michael Spence modeled job-market signaling in 1973: a credential pays because it tells employers something about its holder, not because of what it taught. Bryan Caplan, an economist at George Mason University, argues in The Case Against Education (2018) that most of college's payoff works this way. Human capital theory, the usual rival account, says the extra pay rewards skills learned. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalling_(economics).

question: A student weighs four years of classes against the diploma at the end. Bryan Caplan argues that a diploma pays off mostly by proving to employers that its holder is bright and patient, not by teaching job skills. If so, what will students pay dearly to get?
answer: The degree, even if the classes taught nothing useful
choices: The degree, even if the classes taught nothing useful
The hardest courses, which teach the most skills
The cheapest school, since diplomas all look alike
The internships, which employers check most
context: Bryan Caplan, The Case Against Education: Why the Education System Is a Waste of Time and Money (Princeton UP, 2018). Source: press.princeton.edu (Caplan 2018).

question: Two classmates take almost the same courses, but one quits a single class short of graduating. Over his working life he earns much less than the one who got the diploma, so the paper itself seems worth a small fortune. Bryan Caplan points to this jump in the data. What do economists call the earnings jump at graduation?
answer: The sheepskin effect
choices: The sheepskin effect
The credential trap
The Peter principle
The reservation-wage gap
context: The sheepskin effect: substantially higher earnings for degree-holders than for those with the same coursework but no completed credential. It is a classic empirical marker consistent with signaling. Source: Jaeger + Page, Review of Economics and Statistics (1996).

question: Bryan Caplan offered an estimate in his 2018 book The Case Against Education: about 80 percent of the extra pay college graduates earn comes from the message the diploma sends employers rather than from anything learned. It is a claim heterodox even among economists friendly to him. What is his main policy recommendation?
answer: Cut education subsidies
choices: Cut education subsidies
Free college for all
More STEM funding
Extend the school year
context: Caplan's book-length estimate is that ~80% of the college wage premium is signaling. It is heterodox even among economists sympathetic to public choice; treat as Caplan's specific claim, not a settled number. Source: Caplan (2018), Chapter 6.

question: A voter who believes trade destroys jobs casts his ballot and pays nothing for the mistake, though a shopper who buys something foolish pays at the checkout. Bryan Caplan coined a two-word term for why voters keep such systematically wrong views, a term distinct from an older idea of Anthony Downs's. What did Caplan call it?
answer: Rational irrationality
choices: Rational irrationality
Structural bias
Systemic error
Cognitive drift
context: Caplan's 'rational irrationality' extends Downs 1957. Downs said voters rationally do not INFORM themselves; Caplan adds that voters rationally do not THINK CLEARLY, because clear thinking on politics is personally costly and privately worthless. Source: Caplan (2007), Chapter 4.

question: Bryan Caplan drew on studies of twins and adopted children for a book of 2011. Parents shape how their grown children turn out far less than most of them assume, he argued, so child-rearing can be more relaxed than they fear. What did he title the book?
answer: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids
choices: Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids
The Nurture Assumption
Nurture Shock
The Parent Trap
context: Bryan Caplan, Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids (Basic Books, 2011). Draws on twin-adoption studies and Judith Rich Harris's Nurture Assumption (Free Press 1998). Source: basicbooks.com (Caplan 2011).

question: A farmer in a poor country brings in his harvest, about $500 worth of crops for a year's work using an ox and hand tools. Moved to a rich country of tractors, paved roads and reliable power, the same man doing similar work could earn around $40,000. What does the gap show, in Bryan Caplan's case for freer immigration?
answer: That where people work, not just effort, sets what they can produce
choices: That where people work, not just effort, sets what they can produce
That workers everywhere produce roughly the same value
That richer countries owe poorer ones direct payments
That trade always hurts the poorer country
context: Bryan Caplan + Zach Weinersmith, Open Borders: The Science and Ethics of Immigration (First Second, 2019). Standard economic-gains-from-trade case for free migration, presented in graphic-novel format as a popularization experiment. Source: firstsecondbooks.com (Caplan 2019).

question: A family moves to San Francisco for a tech job and goes house-hunting in a city that smothers new building in permits, zoning rules and neighborhood vetoes. Thousands of newcomers arrive the same way every year. Bryan Caplan's 2024 book Build, Baby, Build asks what basic supply-and-demand reasoning predicts. What happens to home prices?
answer: They go way up, because supply cannot keep up with demand
choices: They go way up, because supply cannot keep up with demand
They fall, because building slows down
They stay flat, because people leave the city
They swing wildly with no clear pattern
context: Bryan Caplan + Ady Branzei, Build Baby Build: The Science and Ethics of Housing Regulation (Cato Institute, 2024). Argues for sweeping housing-supply reform on affordability, mobility, and welfare grounds. Source: cato.org (Caplan + Branzei 2024).

question: Zach Weinersmith drew Bryan Caplan's 2019 case for open borders as a nonfiction graphic novel, and Ady Branzei drew his 2024 housing book the same way. Few tenured professors do anything of the kind. What problem does the comic form solve that scholarly prose cannot?
answer: Reaching general readers who do not read academic prose
choices: Reaching general readers who do not read academic prose
Presenting the data more precisely than tables can
Making the argument harder for critics to quote out of context
Letting the author skip the notes a scholarly book needs
context: Popularization is the specific problem. Caplan's graphic-novel books on open borders and housing deregulation are aimed at readers who would never open a Princeton UP monograph, extending public-choice arguments to a wider audience. Source: Caplan blog Bet On It; interviews 2019-24.

question: Suppose Bryan Caplan is right that a degree mostly shows employers its holder is bright and diligent, rather than building useful skills. Taxpayers fund college through grants, low-cost loans and state-run universities. What follows for that money?
answer: Subsidies pump up signals without producing corresponding productive skills
choices: Subsidies pump up signals without producing corresponding productive skills
Subsidies create additional productive skills proportional to enrollment
Subsidies always reduce total educational credentials issued
Subsidies convert signals to human capital by definition
context: Caplan's payoff: if degrees mostly SIGNAL that a student is smart, conscientious, and conformist, then subsidizing more degrees inflates the signal without increasing the underlying trait. The wage premium erodes as more people hold the same signal. Source: Caplan (2018), Chapter 12.

question: A shopper fooled about a product hands over his own money for it, while a voter fooled about trade casts one ballot among tens of millions. Bryan Caplan argued that the voter can afford his comforting error. Why can the voter afford it?
answer: The private cost of one wrong belief is essentially zero
choices: The private cost of one wrong belief is essentially zero
Other voters' errors cancel his out, so the result stays sound
Elected leaders ignore what voters believe once they take office
Courts strike down the bad laws that such beliefs produce
context: The private cost of holding an economically wrong belief is essentially zero because the belief influences one vote out of tens of millions. Consumers with wrong beliefs about products suffer directly; voters do not. Caplan argues that this is why democracies choose bad policies, and he rejects the hope that voters' random errors cancel out, because their errors lean the same way. Source: Caplan, The Myth of the Rational Voter (2007).

question: Anthony Downs had said in 1957 that voters skip the homework because a single vote seldom counts. Bryan Caplan pushed further in 2007: voters are not merely uninformed, he argued, but wrong in systematic ways. His book's subtitle was 'Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies.' What is its main title?
answer: The Myth of the Rational Voter
choices: The Myth of the Rational Voter
The Case Against Democracy
The Voter's Fallacy
Rational Ignorance
context: The Myth of the Rational Voter: Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies (Princeton UP, 2007). Caplan's argument: voters are not just uninformed but systematically wrong on economic questions in identifiable ways. Source: press.princeton.edu.

question: Bryan Caplan set ordinary Americans' answers about the economy beside those of economists with doctorates. He found four slants that voters shared and economists of every party lacked. Which pair are two of the four?
answer: Anti-market and anti-foreign biases
choices: Anti-market and anti-foreign biases
Anti-tax and anti-bank biases
Anti-Congress and anti-Fed biases
Anti-education and anti-labor biases
context: The four biases: (1) anti-market, (2) anti-foreign, (3) make-work, (4) pessimistic. Anti-market: voters underestimate market benefits. Anti-foreign: voters underestimate trade gains. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: Voters in a town watched a new machine take over a pointless job and saw only a loss, though the worker was freed for better use. Bryan Caplan saw voters prizing jobs for their own sake, the more work the better, rather than for what the work produces. What did he name this bias?
answer: Make-work bias
choices: Make-work bias
Job-security bias
Employment worship
Career preservation
context: Make-work bias: voters treat job counts as ends in themselves rather than as means to produce goods. It underlies opposition to labor-saving technology, automation, and free trade. Source: Caplan (2007).

question: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok run the blog Marginal Revolution from the university where Bryan Caplan and Peter Boettke also teach. The university grew into the chief home of James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's public choice school, and it runs the Mercatus Center. Which university is it?
answer: George Mason University
choices: George Mason University
Harvard University
Yale University
Stanford University
context: The GMU-Buchanan-Tullock tradition includes Peter Boettke (Austrian-tradition), Alex Tabarrok (co-founder of Marginal Revolution), and Tyler Cowen (also Marginal Revolution, GMU chair). All are Caplan's colleagues. Source: gmu.edu economics department.

question: The Swedish academy chose the words of its citation carefully when it gave James Buchanan the 1986 economics Nobel, the first for the public-choice school. The citation named the idea beneath his work, not the school. What did it honor him for?
answer: The contractual and constitutional bases of political decision-making
choices: The contractual and constitutional bases of political decision-making
The empirical study of federal tax and spending policy
The mathematical theory of general market equilibrium
The saving and technology behind economic growth
context: The 1986 Nobel citation, October 16, 1986: 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The committee generalized rather than saying 'public choice.'

question: James Buchanan stood up in Stockholm on December 8, 1986, aged sixty-seven, to give his Nobel lecture. A fight over one tax rate, he argued, skips an earlier question: which rules govern the fight. He put that idea into the lecture's title. What was it?
answer: The Constitution of Economic Policy
choices: The Constitution of Economic Policy
The Calculus of Consent
Public Finance in Democratic Process
Cost and Choice
context: 'The Constitution of Economic Policy' (December 8, 1986, Stockholm) argued that economic policy should be evaluated by the rules governing choices, not just by outcomes of individual choices. Published in AER March 1987. Source: nobelprize.org (Buchanan lecture 1986).

question: Paul Samuelson reportedly grumbled, when James Buchanan's Nobel was announced, that it was really a prize for political science. Many economists disliked public choice's picture of politicians, regulators and bureaucrats as people chasing reelection, budgets and influence like everyone else. Why did that picture bother them so much?
answer: It removes the assumption that officials always act for the public good
choices: It removes the assumption that officials always act for the public good
It ignores how markets actually set prices
It only applies to small local governments, not national ones
It refuses to use any mathematics
context: Samuelson reportedly complained the prize was for political science -- which, if true, was exactly the point Buchanan had been making since 1962: the artificial disciplinary wall between economic analysis of markets and of politics was itself the mistake. Source: widely reported anecdote.

question: A senator weighs a bill to build a costly bridge in his home state, paid for out of federal taxes, though engineers rank it far down the nation's list of needs. Public-choice economists, Mancur Olson and James Buchanan among them, expect him to vote yes. Why would he?
answer: The benefits are focused on a few, while the costs are spread thin over many
choices: The benefits are focused on a few, while the costs are spread thin over many
He expects the bridge to pay back more than it costs the nation
Voters everywhere always want more spending, so he obeys them
The senator does not understand the true cost of the bill
context: This is Mancur Olson's logic of concentrated benefits and dispersed costs: the few local firms that gain from the bridge notice, organize and reward the senator, while taxpayers who each lose a few dollars barely notice. Home-state projects of this kind are called pork-barrel spending. Source: Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: Ronald Coase noticed that neighbors quarreling over smoke could settle the matter themselves if bargaining were free, and won the economics Nobel in 1991, after James Buchanan in 1986. Douglass North followed in 1993, and another laureate joined their line in 2009. They studied constitutions, property rights, courts and the rules villagers set for a common fishery, each resting on an idea Buchanan had pressed decades before. What was the idea?
answer: Taking institutions seriously as objects of economic analysis
choices: Taking institutions seriously as objects of economic analysis
Formalizing rational-expectations models mathematically
Building general-equilibrium computer simulations
Applying game theory to industrial organization
context: Buchanan's Virginia-school move: the rules of the game are as much a subject for economic analysis as the play within the rules. Coase's transaction costs, North's institutions, and Ostrom's commons all extend that analytical stance. Source: nobelprize.org economics laureates.

question: Two children grab for the same ball at recess, as they do every day, until one of them proposes a standing rule to settle whose turn it is each day. James Buchanan made that kind of choice, the choice of the rulebook itself, the subject of a whole field. What did he call it?
answer: Constitutional political economy
choices: Constitutional political economy
Positive political science
Behavioral macroeconomics
Institutional public finance
context: Constitutional political economy: the right level for political-economic analysis is not the individual policy choice but the rules that govern how such choices are made. Buchanan pioneered the term. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_economics.

question: James Buchanan argued that a fight over a tax rate of 20 percent or 25 turns every new law into a fresh brawl, drawing lobbyists and favor-seekers each time. He wanted the debate raised a level, above any single policy. Where did he want it moved?
answer: The rules governing how policy is made
choices: The rules governing how policy is made
The individual voter's preferences
The Fed's monetary policy
The federal budget process
context: Buchanan's move: analyzing whether a constitutional rule should require a supermajority to raise taxes relocates the debate to a level where interest-group pressure operates differently. Rules bind both majority and minority in ways particular policy debates cannot. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: James Buchanan wrote a book with Geoffrey Brennan, an Australian philosopher and economist, in 1985, a year ahead of his own Nobel. It became the standard case that firm rules, not the goodwill of officials, must bind government. What is the book called?
answer: The Reason of Rules
choices: The Reason of Rules
The Calculus of Consent
The Limits of Liberty
Cost and Choice
context: The Reason of Rules: Constitutional Political Economy (Cambridge University Press, 1985) is the standard modern statement. Brennan (Australian philosopher-economist) was Buchanan's most important later co-author. Source: cambridge.org (Brennan + Buchanan 1985).

question: Geoffrey Brennan and James Buchanan asked people to pick a country's political rulebook without knowing whether luck would leave them rich or poor, powerful or ordinary. They gave that thought experiment a name. What did they call it?
answer: The veil of uncertainty
choices: The veil of uncertainty
The Rawlsian curtain
The choice horizon
The Hobbesian mist
context: The 'veil of uncertainty' is Buchanan and Brennan's device (adapted from Rawls's veil of ignorance): constitutional rules agreed to when the choosers do not know their future position bind both majority and minority. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: James Buchanan and Richard Wagner argued in 1977 that an unwritten rule had held American politicians in check for well over a century. John Maynard Keynes's teaching, they said, licensed deliberate spending beyond tax revenue, the rule dissolved, and the gap ratcheted upward ever after. Which older rule did they say had been lost?
answer: The old constitutional norm of balanced budgets
choices: The old constitutional norm of balanced budgets
The gold-standard convertibility rule
The Fed's independence from Treasury
The Senate's supermajority rule for tax hikes
context: Democracy in Deficit: The Political Legacy of Lord Keynes (Academic Press, 1977) argued that the old constitutional norm of balanced budgets had disciplined politicians for a century. Once Keynes's General Theory legitimized deliberate deficit spending, the norm dissolved and deficits ratcheted upward. Buchanan's move: individual deficits are not the problem; the erosion of the RULE that had disciplined all politicians is.

question: Geoffrey Brennan and James Buchanan held up the posted speed limit as a model in their book of 1985: a clear rule everyone follows, in place of officials who weigh each case on its own. Why is the fixed rule better, in their view?
answer: Fixed rules limit favoritism and let people plan ahead
choices: Fixed rules limit favoritism and let people plan ahead
Fixed rules give the best result in every single case
Fixed rules cost less to enforce than hiring skilled officials
Fixed rules remove any need for courts to settle disputes
context: In The Reason of Rules (1985), Geoffrey Brennan and James Buchanan argue that a known, fixed rule leaves officials little room to favor friends and lets citizens plan, since they know in advance how it will apply; wide discretion invites the abuse of power. Brennan, a philosopher-economist at the Australian National University, also wrote The Power to Tax (1980) with Buchanan. Source: Brennan + Buchanan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: A gym class agrees on how kickball will be scored before anyone picks teams. After the teams are chosen, each side can see which rules help it. Thinkers in James Buchanan's tradition judge every rule from that earlier moment, before anyone knows his team. What does that do to the argument?
answer: It moves the debate from picking winners to picking fair rules
choices: It moves the debate from picking winners to picking fair rules
It reduces every choice to a single number
It applies only to changes in a country's constitution
It makes every policy choice look equal
context: The constitutional-political-economy move: from OUTCOMES (is this policy good?) to CONSTRAINTS (would we have consented to the rules that produced it, behind the veil of uncertainty?). This is the mature analytical stance Buchanan is remembered for. Source: Buchanan + Brennan, The Reason of Rules (1985).

question: A fisherman on a lake can grab a few fish by hand this morning, or spend the day tying a net, go home empty-handed, then haul in far more each day for weeks. What did the Austrian school call that second, longer path?
answer: Roundabout production
choices: Roundabout production
Marginal utility
Spontaneous order
Comparative advantage
context: Boehm-Bawerk's word for longer, more indirect production processes -- using tools to make tools to make consumer goods -- was 'roundabout production' (German Produktionsumweg). The extra day spent on the net produces far more fish over the following weeks; the extra season spent making a plough produces far more grain the next season. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Bohm-Bawerk's Roundaboutness' (https://www.fff.org/explore-freedom/article/bohm-bawerks-roundaboutness-why-the-longest-path-to-wealth-is-usually-the-shortest/).

question: An Austrian economist took up an old puzzle in Vienna in the 1880s: what makes anyone pay interest in the first place? His first volume came out in 1884; the second appeared in 1889 and offered what came to be called the time-preference account of interest. Who was he?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Carl Menger
Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises
context: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk published 'Kapital und Kapitalzins' in three volumes: Volume 1 in 1884, Volume 2 in 1889, Volume 3 posthumously in 1921. Menger was his teacher; Wieser his brother-in-law; Mises his student a generation later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Capital and Interest' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest).

question: Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk pointed to a farmer who builds his plow before he sows a single field, and to a carmaker who sets up an assembly line before one car rolls out. He saw a plain fact behind interest in scenes like these. What feature of making things did he mean?
answer: That production takes time
choices: That production takes time
That production yields joint products
That production faces diminishing returns
That production requires cooperation
context: The insight the whole Positive Theory rests on: production is a process across TIME, not an instant. Because the saver must release resources today for output that will only exist next month or next year, and because people prefer present to future goods, someone must be paid a premium to bridge the wait. Interest is the market price of that time gap. Source: Econlib, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html).

question: Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk rested his theory of interest on three grounds. People expect to be better off later, so a future good is worth less to them now, and they undervalue their future wants. His third ground, the most disputed, would hold even if the first two collapsed: interest would still stay above zero. What does that third ground appeal to?
answer: The technical superiority of longer production processes
choices: The technical superiority of longer production processes
The moral virtue of self-denial by the saver
The bargaining power of capitalists over workers
The state's legal enforcement of debt contracts
context: Ground three -- the technical superiority of longer, more roundabout production methods -- is Boehm-Bawerk's most disputed claim. It says that even without shortsightedness or expected prosperity, more roundabout methods yield more output per unit input, so waiting is intrinsically worth something. The American economist Frank Fetter later argued ground two (time preference) does all the real work and ground three is redundant; John Bates Clark defended a rival pure-productivity account. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: Karl Marx called interest theft from the workers. A modern socialist agrees: a saver who lends $100 for a year and gets $105 back did no work, as the cash just sat there. How did Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk answer?
answer: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
choices: The saver supplies waiting -- releasing present resources so future output can exist -- and interest is the market price for that waiting
The saver takes on the risk that the borrower will default, and interest is the premium compensating that risk
The saver exercises entrepreneurial judgment about which projects deserve capital, and interest is the reward for that judgment
The saver enjoys legal protection under contract law, and interest is the state-enforced return on lawful lending
context: The clean Boehm-Bawerkian move: production takes time; someone must release today's resources for tomorrow's output; that release is what the saver contributes; the interest payment is the market price of that contribution. It is not stolen from the worker; it is compensation for the postponement of consumption. Risk, entrepreneurship, and legal enforcement are separate real phenomena but they answer different questions.

question: Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, building on Böhm-Bawerk, held that an interest rate is no ordinary price. Austrians in their line object whenever a central bank forces rates down to zero. Which price does such a policy distort?
answer: The price of time itself -- how much people value goods now versus later
choices: The price of time itself -- how much people value goods now versus later
The value of the dollar against foreign money
The wages paid to workers who make exports
The price tag on things people buy on credit
context: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory, developed by Mises and Hayek on the Boehm-Bawerkian foundation, treats the interest rate as the price of time -- the price coordinating how much of today's resources get released for tomorrow's output through more roundabout production. Forcing that price down artificially misleads entrepreneurs into starting more roundabout projects than real savings can complete; when the bust arrives the malinvested projects have to be liquidated. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Eugen Von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/social-sciences-and-law/economics-biographies/eugen-von-bohm-bawerk).

question: At Wabash College in Indiana in 1956, Milton Friedman gave a series of talks, and his wife Rose helped him recast them in plain English for a book of 1962. Buyers took home more than half a million copies over the years. What was the book called?
answer: Capitalism and Freedom
choices: Capitalism and Freedom
Free to Choose
A Monetary History of the United States
A Theory of the Consumption Function
context: Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (University of Chicago Press, 1962). Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo25839091.html.

question: Milton Friedman set out a one-way link in 1962 between two freedoms: the freedom to trade and produce, and the freedom to vote and speak. One, he argued, is the ground the other stands on. Which link did he argue for?
answer: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
choices: Economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom
Political freedom always suffices for economic freedom
Economic freedom is irrelevant to political freedom
Political freedom is a sufficient condition for economic freedom
context: Friedman's move: once government controls the means of employment, the media, and the currency, dissent cannot be sustained -- the dissenter cannot eat. Economic freedom is necessary though not sufficient for political freedom. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 1.

question: A reader opening Milton Friedman's slim new book in 1962 found it packed with reforms that sounded strange at the time, each one argued from the same case for economic freedom. Which reform was never in the book?
answer: Universal single-payer health insurance
choices: Universal single-payer health insurance
School vouchers for parents
The negative income tax
An all-volunteer military
context: Capitalism and Freedom (1962) proposed school vouchers, a negative income tax in place of the tangle of welfare programs, an all-volunteer army, floating exchange rates and an end to licensing rules that kept newcomers out of trades. Universal single-payer health insurance, the Canadian model, was never among its proposals. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962).

question: A shopper walks the aisles of a supermarket with her family's weekly budget, picking freely among thousands of items. In Free to Choose, Milton and Rose Friedman set beside her a committee of nutrition experts choosing everyone's groceries, with the same budgets at the same store. What would most likely happen?
answer: Many would get food they did not want, while unwanted goods piled up
choices: Many would get food they did not want, while unwanted goods piled up
Families would eat better, since experts know nutrition best
Costs would fall, since one committee could buy in bulk
Little would change, since experts would copy shoppers' choices
context: Milton and Rose Friedman's point in Free to Choose (1980): a shopper knows what her own family wants, and her choices tell the store and its suppliers what to stock. A committee spending the same budget would have to guess, so families would get food they did not want while unwanted goods sat on the shelves. Source: Friedman and Friedman, Free to Choose (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1980).
