question: Milton and Rose Friedman took their case to public television in 1980 with a ten-part series filmed in Hong Kong, Chicago, Washington and other cities. A companion book carried the same title, Free to Choose. How did the book fare with American readers that year?
answer: It reached number one on the New York Times list
choices: It reached number one on the New York Times list
It sold well only as a college textbook
It sold poorly until the 1990 series revived it
It was handed out only to public-TV donors
context: Free to Choose spent weeks at number one on the New York Times best-seller list in 1980. Some accounts call it the year's best-selling nonfiction book, though other year-end lists rank Douglas Casey's Crisis Investing first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_to_Choose_(book).

question: Milton Friedman recalled in his memoirs that Free to Choose, translated into more than a dozen languages, was smuggled into one bloc of countries in illegal underground translations. A reformer there later counted the book among the sources of his country's reforms. Which region was that bloc?
answer: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
choices: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
Central African republics
Southeast Asian dictatorships
Latin American military regimes
context: Free to Choose was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in samizdat translations. Vaclav Klaus later credited the book as an intellectual source of Czechoslovakia's post-1989 economic reforms. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Robert Solo edited a volume in 1955 that carried an essay by Milton Friedman, who later folded the essay's proposal into his book of 1962. What was the essay called?
answer: The Role of Government in Education
choices: The Role of Government in Education
The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
A Monetary and Fiscal Framework
The Methodology of Positive Economics
context: Milton Friedman, 'The Role of Government in Education' (in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest, Rutgers UP 1955). The voucher proposal was collected into Capitalism and Freedom (1962). Source: JSTOR (Solo 1955 collection).

question: Richard Nixon in August 1971 shut the gold window, and the Bretton Woods order of fixed rates collapsed. Milton Friedman had pressed since 1953 for the change that came next. What regime had the world's leading currencies moved to by 1973?
answer: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
choices: Floating exchange rates for major currencies
A permanent gold-based monetary system
A single global fixed-rate regime
Complete abolition of national currencies
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 closing of the gold window ended dollar-gold convertibility; the international regime shifted to floating major-currency exchange rates by 1973. Friedman had argued the case since 1953. Source: Friedman, 'The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates' (1953, in Essays in Positive Economics).

question: Milton Friedman offered a list of reforms in a slim book of 1962, and many readers found them odd. Historians looking back decades later noticed something striking about that list. What did they notice?
answer: Many of its eccentric-seeming ideas later became mainstream policy
choices: Many of its eccentric-seeming ideas later became mainstream policy
Most of its proposals were tried and then quickly repealed
Its proposals caught on abroad but never in America
Nearly all its proposals were already law when it appeared
context: The all-volunteer military (1973), floating exchange rates (1971-73), and state-level voucher programs (1990s-2020s) all trace to Capitalism and Freedom proposals that were dismissed as eccentric at the time. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Carl Menger brought out his book Principles of Economics in 1871, while on the staff of the prime minister's press office, and two years later it earned him a university chair. His students carried his ideas into the next century. What did the circle around him come to be called?
answer: The Austrian School
choices: The Austrian School
The Chicago School
The Keynesian School
The Marxist School
context: Carl Menger (1840-1921), the founder of the Austrian School, published 'Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre' (Principles of Economics) in 1871 while still working in the prime minister's press office; the book won him a Vienna chair in 1873. Wieser and Boehm-Bawerk were his students; Mises a generation later still. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger: The Founding of the Austrian School' (https://mises.org/articles-interest/carl-menger-founding-austrian-school).

question: Carl Menger's two brightest followers had been friends since school, and one married the other's sister. Between them they carried his school through its next stage, writing on capital, on tracing value back to the things that make a good, and on taking apart Marx's labor theory of value. Who were the two?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
Israel Kirzner and Murray Rothbard
Joseph Schumpeter and Otto Bauer
context: Menger's two most important early followers were Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk (capital theory, the refutation of Marx) and Friedrich von Wieser (imputation, opportunity cost). They met as schoolboys in Vienna, and Boehm-Bawerk later married Wieser's sister Paula. Mises and Hayek belong to later generations, Kirzner and Rothbard later still; Schumpeter and Otto Bauer were Boehm-Bawerk's own students. Source: https://mises.org/library/eugen-bohm-von-bawerk-economist-minister-aristocrat.

question: Carl Menger, who came to economics by way of law rather than mathematics, took his doctorate in 1867 in a city whose medieval royal castle stands on a hill above the Vistula river. The university that granted it is the oldest in its country. Which university was it?
answer: Jagiellonian University in Krakow
choices: Jagiellonian University in Krakow
Charles University in Prague
Humboldt University in Berlin
University of Vienna
context: Menger took his doctorate in jurisprudence at Jagiellonian University in Krakow in 1867, then joined the Austrian civil service. Charles University in Prague was where he studied earlier; Humboldt in Berlin was the leading German university of the era but not his; Vienna was where he later held his chair. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Two friends wait in line at a food truck. One orders a taco and the other orders nothing, though the taco would cost each of them the same and hold the same fillings. Carl Menger built a whole theory of prices on what a moment like this shows. What idea does the scene demonstrate?
answer: Value depends on the person, not the object
choices: Value depends on the person, not the object
Value is fixed by the cost of making the item
Value is set by the price the seller posts
Value is decided by what most people want
context: Carl Menger's Principles of Economics (1871) argued that value is subjective: a good is worth what it is to the person judging it, given his wants and how much of it he already has. The same taco, at the same price and with the same fillings, is worth a great deal to the friend who loves tacos and nothing to the one who does not. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: The heirs of Carl Menger sold his vast private library abroad after he died in Vienna in 1921. His books, journals and pamphlets, one of the biggest economics collections anywhere in Europe, survive together under the name of the Menger Library. Which university keeps them?
answer: Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo
choices: Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo
Harvard University in Cambridge
Cambridge University in England
Chicago University in Illinois
context: Menger's private economics library, one of the largest in Europe, was sold by his heirs to Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo after his 1921 death; the collection is still catalogued there as the 'Menger Library.' Harvard, Cambridge (England), and the University of Chicago all built major economics libraries in the same era but not from Menger's holdings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carl Menger' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger).

question: Jimmy Carter's 1980 tax on oil profits was sold as a way to take back unearned gains American producers made when one event of 1979 cut the world's oil supply almost overnight. Which event?
answer: The revolution in Iran
choices: The revolution in Iran
The Arab oil embargo
The Suez Canal closure
The Venezuelan oil strike
context: The 1979 revolution overthrew the Shah and disrupted Iranian oil exports; world crude went from about $15/barrel in 1978 to over $35 by 1981. The Carter administration argued domestic producers should not keep the price increase as pure profit. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1979_oil_crisis.

question: Jimmy Carter's backers promised in 1980 that his new tax on oil profits would skim off an undeserved bonanza and change nobody's behavior. Ten years later the Congressional Research Service, which does nonpartisan research for Congress, reported what the tax had done to American oil production. What did it find?
answer: Domestic output fell about 3 to 6 percent, and imports rose
choices: Domestic output fell about 3 to 6 percent, and imports rose
Domestic output rose about 3 to 6 percent, and imports fell
Domestic output held steady, and so did imports
Domestic output fell by half, and imports doubled
context: The tax raised the effective cost of producing each additional barrel of US oil, so marginal wells were not drilled, and the country produced less of its own oil. The 3 to 6 percent figure is the 1990 Congressional Research Service estimate; a later CRS study, in 2006, gave a wider range. Source: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/RL33305.html.

question: A Texas senator rises on the Senate floor in 1985 to complain that Carter's tax on oil profits has cost his state's oil patch thousands of jobs. An economist answers with one reasoning move about what the tax does to every extra barrel a producer might pump. Which move is he pressing?
answer: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue; the undrilled barrels are the unseen cost
choices: The tax acts as a price ceiling on producer revenue; the undrilled barrels are the unseen cost
The tax is a Keynesian aggregate-demand stimulus that raises drilling investment
The tax is a Coasean bargaining solution that internalizes drilling externalities
The tax is a Pigovian correction that equates marginal social benefit and marginal social cost
context: A tax on the return to production at the margin reduces production at the margin. Applied Bastiat: the seen is oil-company profit recovery for the public; the unseen is domestic supply that never enters the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Crude_Oil_Windfall_Profit_Tax_Act_of_1980.

question: Britain's chancellor imposed an Energy Profits Levy on North Sea oil firms in 2022. The same kind of tax had been proposed for drugmakers in 2020 and, after the crisis of 2008, for American banks. Each time, one question in Frederic Bastiat's tradition came back with it. Which question was it?
answer: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
choices: What will the taxed producers do less of, and who bears that cost invisibly?
What is the highest tax rate the affected industry can bear before bankruptcy?
How does the tax score under the Congressional Budget Office static model?
How much revenue will the tax collect in its first fiscal year?
context: The Bastiat pattern: measure the seen benefit against the unseen response. Any tax on the reward for producing during a shortage removes some of the incentive to produce during the crisis when society most needs it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Windfall_tax.

question: Barack Obama signed the Car Allowance Rebate System into law in June 2009. A buyer who handed over a running older car got $3,500 to $4,500 toward a more fuel-efficient new one, but first the trade-in had to be wrecked so it could never be resold. How were the engines destroyed?
answer: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
choices: Pouring sodium silicate into the oil to seize the engine, then crushing the car
Draining the fuel tank and towing the car to a landfill for compaction
Removing and melting the catalytic converter, then junking the shell
Shipping the vehicle intact to a licensed scrapyard for parts recovery
context: The mandate that engines be seized with sodium silicate (liquid glass) was written to keep the trade-ins from being resold as running cars; some 690,000 running vehicles were destroyed this way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Allowance_Rebate_System.

question: A dealer scrapped a running trade-in in the summer of 2009, one of some 690,000 wrecked under Cash for Clunkers, a federal program meant to sell new cars and lift the economy. Frederic Bastiat had warned in 1850 against exactly this mistake, in a parable about destruction mistaken for wealth. Which of his arguments does the program match?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The negative railway
The candlemakers' petition
The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: Bastiat's broken-window: destruction of a usable good is not creation. Cash for Clunkers spent $3B destroying about 690,000 usable cars to make the subsidized new-car sale look like fresh economic activity. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: A dealer crushed one more running trade-in in the summer of 2009, among some 690,000 cars, most of them low-priced, destroyed under Cash for Clunkers. Austrian economists predicted what would follow. What happened in the year after?
answer: Used-car prices rose about 10%
choices: Used-car prices rose about 10%
New-car prices fell about 10%
Fuel prices rose about 10%
Auto-insurance premiums fell about 10%
context: Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index for 2009-10 showed a roughly 10% jump in used-car prices, pricing out the very households the auto-stimulus was said to help. Source: manheim.com/used-vehicle-value-index (2010 press releases).

question: Ted Gayer and Emily Parker, economists at the Brookings Institution, published a study of Cash for Clunkers in 2013. Most of the new cars sold under it, they found, would have been bought within six to nine months anyway, and it left no lasting gain in jobs. What did they call the effect on sales?
answer: Pulled-forward sales
choices: Pulled-forward sales
Aggregate multiplier
Rationing tax
Deadweight loss
context: Gayer & Parker (Brookings, October 2013) estimated the program pulled forward about 380,000 vehicles, generated no long-run net jobs, and produced CO2 savings at $91-$301 per ton -- well above the EPA's own social cost of carbon. Source: brookings.edu/articles/cash-for-clunkers-an-evaluation-of-the-car-allowance-rebate-system.

question: A buyer drove a new car home under Cash for Clunkers in 2009, the benefit anyone could see. Austrian and Chicago-school critics, following Frederic Bastiat's seen and unseen, kept pointing at a group the program hurt directly but out of sight. Which group?
answer: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
choices: Poor households who buy in the used-car market that the destruction thinned out
Auto-parts manufacturers whose supply contracts came under EPA review
Insurance companies whose collision policies subsidized the rebate
Foreign auto brands excluded from the eligibility criteria
context: Destroying 690,000 vehicles in the $1,500-$4,500 range is destroying exactly the price band low-income buyers actually shop; used-car prices rose accordingly. This is Bastiat's UNSEEN victim: the low-income family that no longer finds a cheap running car. Source: cato.org/commentary/cash-clunkers-textbook-example.

question: Frederic Bastiat argued that every government spending program carries one visible benefit and many hidden costs. Cash for Clunkers spent about $3 billion in roughly two months of 2009. Beyond the 690,000 wrecked cars, Austrian economists point to a much larger loss that appears in no count. What is it?
answer: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
choices: The alternative goods and jobs the same $3B could have supported if left with taxpayers or lenders
The additional carbon emissions from the mandated new-car manufacturing
The regulatory-compliance staff the auto dealers had to hire to process claims
The tax revenue foregone on the salvage value of the destroyed trade-ins
context: Every $3B of federal spending had to come from a taxpayer or a lender; that money's alternative use is the Bastiat UNSEEN. The seen is the DOT sales figure; the unseen is the private consumption and investment that never happened. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/cash-clunkers-and-broken-window.

question: A young organizer, a Kansas oil industrialist and a fiery Austrian economist started a libertarian think tank together in San Francisco in 1977. The organizer became its first president, the industrialist was its biggest early funder, and the economist led its thinking. Who were the three?
answer: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
choices: Ed Crane, Charles Koch, and Murray Rothbard
William Buckley, Milton Friedman, and Barry Goldwater
James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Douglass North
Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, and Wilhelm Ropke
context: Crane served as founding president, Koch was the principal early funder, and Rothbard was the intellectual leader. The institute relocated to Washington DC in 1981. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: Two English writers filled the London papers between 1720 and 1723 with political essays signed 'Cato,' after the Roman senator Cato the Younger, who defied Julius Caesar. Their letters railed against corruption, stood up for liberty and were reprinted throughout the colonies in America, where they helped inspire the revolutionary generation. Who were the two writers?
answer: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon
choices: John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon
Alexander Hamilton and James Madison
John Locke and John Stuart Mill
Edmund Burke and Adam Smith
context: 'Cato's Letters' were published in London and reprinted heavily in the American colonies, where they influenced the founders. Hamilton and Madison wrote The Federalist Papers as Publius, a different pen-name project. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato%27s_Letters.

question: The Cato Institute's co-founders pushed out their intellectual leader in 1981, after a bitter fight over strategy and staff. A year later he set up a rival institute with Lew Rockwell, one whose Austrian line ran more radical than Cato's policy work in Washington. Who was he, and what did he found?
answer: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: Murray Rothbard, who founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute
James Buchanan, who founded the Center for Study of Public Choice
Milton Friedman, who founded the Free To Choose Network
Friedrich Hayek, who founded the Mont Pelerin Society
context: The Mises Institute (Auburn, Alabama, 1982) took a more radical Austrian direction than Cato, which pursued a Washington-focused policy engagement. The split defined two wings of the modern American libertarian movement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: William Niskanen, the Cato Institute's long-serving chairman, argued in a 1971 book that the people who run government offices work to swell their budgets and staffs, since a larger office brings more pay, more prestige and more sway to those at the top. What follows from his argument?
answer: Agencies will keep growing whether or not their problem gets solved
choices: Agencies will keep growing whether or not their problem gets solved
Agencies will shrink once the problem they fight is solved
Agencies will cut costs to win praise for their thrift
Agencies will hold budgets flat to avoid oversight
context: Niskanen was best known for his 1971 book 'Bureaucracy and Representative Government,' a foundational public-choice analysis of bureaucratic behavior. His long chairmanship shaped Cato's public-choice orientation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: The Cato Institute ended a legal fight of 2012 that had threatened its independence for several anxious months and made national news, and the banker John Allison took over as its president. What was that fight?
answer: Charles and David Koch sued over control of its board; the case was settled
choices: Charles and David Koch sued over control of its board; the case was settled
The US Department of Justice charged Cato with tax fraud; the case was dismissed
The Ludwig von Mises Institute sued Cato for trademark infringement over the name 'Cato'
Congress subpoenaed Cato's donor list under the Foreign Agents Registration Act
context: The dispute concerned Cato's board structure. Under the settlement, Ed Crane was succeeded as president by former BB&T CEO John Allison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education in New York in 1946 to teach the general public, and Friedrich Hayek began the Mont Pelerin Society a year later as a private network of scholars meeting at Swiss resorts. What set the Cato Institute, founded in 1977, apart from both?
answer: Day-to-day influence on policy and bills in Washington
choices: Day-to-day influence on policy and bills in Washington
Granting master's and doctoral degrees in economics
Running its own candidates for Congress and president
Seeding free-market think tanks in other countries
context: The Foundation for Economic Education (Leonard Read, 1946) focused on general educational outreach; the Mont Pelerin Society (Hayek, 1947) organized scholarly networks. Cato uniquely aimed at the real-time DC policy process. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cato_Institute.

question: Romanians rose up in the streets against Nicolae Ceausescu in December 1989, after years of empty shops under his rule. He had held power since 1965, and his government fell in about a week. What kind of government were the Romanians throwing off?
answer: A communist dictatorship
choices: A communist dictatorship
A constitutional monarchy
A parliamentary democracy
A free-market republic
context: Nicolae Ceausescu ruled Socialist Romania from 1965 as party general secretary. His wife Elena served as effective co-ruler. Both were tried and shot on December 25, 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Ceausescu.

question: Nicolae Ceausescu raised a gigantic palace in Bucharest in the 1980s with 700 architects and 20,000 workers. Much of the old city, churches among it, was flattened to make room, and only one office building anywhere has more floor space. What is it called today?
answer: The Palace of the Parliament
choices: The Palace of the Parliament
The Casa Batlló
The People's Ministry
The Ceausescu Museum
context: Built as Casa Poporului (House of the People), 365,000 square meters, using 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. It now houses Romania's Parliament. It remains one of the heaviest and most expensive buildings ever constructed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_the_Parliament.

question: Foreign reporters walked into Romania's state institutions in 1990, after Ceausescu's fall, and put what they found on Western television. His ban on abortion and contraception had run for over twenty years and brought far more babies into the world than the state could care for. What did the reporters find?
answer: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
choices: About 100,000 children in appalling state orphanages
A mass wave of infant mortality on farms
Widespread hunger among rural schoolchildren
A polio outbreak in three major cities
context: By 1989 roughly 100,000 children were in Romanian state institutions. Western television footage after 1990 showed severe neglect and drove international adoption reform for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_orphans.

question: Nicolae Ceausescu sent bulldozers into thousands of Romania's farming villages in the 1980s under a program called systematization. Their families were moved by force from the old houses into rows of identical concrete blocks beside state factories. Why is a top-down plan like this typical of central planning?
answer: A few planners decide how everyone lives, overriding what people want
choices: A few planners decide how everyone lives, overriding what people want
The state owns the land, so moving families costs it nothing
Concrete blocks are cheaper to heat than scattered farmhouses
Factories need workers close by, and only a plan can place them
context: Ceausescu's systematization (sistematizare) set out to remake Romania's villages and towns by plan, razing old houses and moving families into apartment blocks near state industry. Planners in Bucharest chose where and how families would live, and what the families themselves wanted counted for nothing: central planning in miniature. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematization_(Romania).

question: Townspeople in Timisoara turned out on December 16, 1989, to stop a pastor, Laszlo Tokes, from being evicted, and troops fired on them. Within a week the uprising had reached Bucharest, and the regime soon fell. What does that cascade show about a dictator's grip?
answer: Obedience can vanish fast once people see others dare to defy
choices: Obedience can vanish fast once people see others dare to defy
A regime that fires on crowds always ends the protest
Uprisings spread only where foreign radio can be heard
Unrest in one city stays local unless leaders plan it
context: Timisoara protests defending Laszlo Tokes on December 16, 1989 spread across the city and were met with lethal force. Within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: A crowd ordered out to hear Nicolae Ceausescu gathered below the Central Committee building's balcony in Bucharest on December 21, 1989, and his speech went out live to every home in the country. Halfway through, the crowd did something it had never once done in his twenty-four years in power. What did it do?
answer: Booed him live on state television
choices: Booed him live on state television
Threw stones at the balcony
Chanted Ceausescu's name louder
Sang the national anthem
context: The recording of Ceausescu's stunned face as the crowd's boos rose is preserved. Within four days he had fled by helicopter, been captured, tried, and shot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution.

question: Nicolae Ceausescu set out to clear every last dollar Romania owed abroad, and through the 1980s he sent its grain, meat and fuel overseas to earn hard currency. Winter after winter, families waited in cold apartments for whatever the state allowed them. What everyday hardship did the debt drive force on them?
answer: Electricity blackouts and food rationing
choices: Electricity blackouts and food rationing
Universal barter for basic goods
State confiscation of home appliances
Mandatory sale of family land
context: Ceausescu personally decided to pay off Romania's foreign debt at all cost. The 1980s saw scheduled blackouts, chronic queues for meat, sugar, and cooking oil, and gasoline severely rationed while agricultural goods were exported for hard currency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania.

question: Doctors at an American hospital ask a state board for permission to add a new wing, as the law in many states requires before any hospital grows. Backers of these laws give one main reason for keeping them. What do they say the laws guard against?
answer: Duplicative healthcare investment
choices: Duplicative healthcare investment
Insurance fraud
Prescription drug abuse
Foreign medical school competition
context: Advocates argue CON prevents duplicative capacity and concentrates patients at higher-volume facilities. The empirical record does not bear out the cost-reduction claim. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Certificate_of_need.

question: A company files plans to build a new hospital in one of some thirty-five American states, and first it must prove at a formal state hearing that the area needs more beds. When the hearing opens, one group almost always shows up in numbers to insist the area has all the beds it needs. Who shows up?
answer: The hospitals already in the area
choices: The hospitals already in the area
Patients hoping for lower prices
Local home-nursing agencies
State insurance regulators
context: The incumbent-veto mechanism: existing hospitals routinely file objections to competitor CON applications, delaying approvals by years or defeating them entirely. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: Matthew Mitchell, an economist at the Mercatus Center, compared states that make hospitals win a board's permission to build with states that have no such rule. The rules' backers had promised lower costs. What did he find in the states that keep them?
answer: Fewer hospitals open, fewer scanners get bought, prices go up
choices: Fewer hospitals open, fewer scanners get bought, prices go up
More hospitals open and prices fall as new ones compete
Hospital count stays the same but wait times drop sharply
Rural areas gain more clinics because the board favors them
context: CON states show fewer hospitals per capita, fewer MRI machines per capita, and higher per-service prices -- the opposite of the stated 'lower costs from consolidation' rationale. Source: mercatus.org/research/policy-briefs/certificate-need-laws.

question: The Institute for Justice sued Kentucky in 2019 for two Nepali immigrants who had been barred from opening a home-health agency, arguing that the state's rule denies people their Fourteenth Amendment right to earn a living. Under the rule, a newcomer must first prove to a state board that the area needs another home-health office. What does such a rule mostly end up doing?
answer: It protects the businesses already in the market from new competition
choices: It protects the businesses already in the market from new competition
It lowers prices for patients by adding more providers
It guarantees each new company a share of the market
It stops fraud by making applicants pay a filing fee
context: Dipendra Tiwari and Kishor Sapkota wanted to open a home-health agency for Nepali-speaking clients and were turned down under Kentucky's certificate-of-need rule in 2019. The Institute for Justice sued for them, the Kentucky Hospital Association joined the state in defending the law, and a federal appeals court upheld it in 2022. Source: https://ij.org/press-release/appeals-court-rules-against-nepali-immigrants-seeking-to-open-home-health-care-agency/.

question: The families of Xiaogang, a poor village in China's Anhui province, decided one night in December 1978 to split the commune's land among themselves. Each would farm its own plot, deliver the state's grain quota and keep any extra. What happened to how much food they grew?
answer: It soared past the commune's best
choices: It soared past the commune's best
It fell; plots were too small
It held steady without tractors
It rose a bit, then sank back
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang, Fengyang County, Anhui, signed the secret pact in December 1978. In the first year the village's grain output rose about six times over, too much for local officials to hide, and neighboring villages copied the idea. The contract is kept today at the National Museum in Beijing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: Farmers in a neighboring village copied Xiaogang's secret pact, and the idea spread county by county until, by 1983, the arrangement was legal across China. Each household owed the state a fixed amount of grain but could keep or sell any extra harvest. What was the arrangement called?
answer: The Household Responsibility System
choices: The Household Responsibility System
The Free Farming Program
The Village Enterprise Reform
The New Rural Charter
context: Jiating lianchan chengbao zeren zhi (Household Responsibility System) was legalized nationwide by 1983. It restored the family plot and let households keep above-quota production. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household-responsibility_system.

question: Each signer of Xiaogang's secret pact of December 1978 promised to raise the others' children should he be jailed or executed, for private farming was still forbidden. Years on the commune had left the village's families in one steady condition. What was it?
answer: Chronic hunger despite constant work
choices: Chronic hunger despite constant work
Chronic surplus with no market
Chronic under-employment on rich land
Chronic conscription for army service
context: Xiaogang villagers had been sending members to beg for food in other counties for decades under the commune system. The famine memory of 1959-61 was still living. The life-and-death contract was a rational response to a chronic shortage economy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: Justin Yifu Lin, an economist, later picked apart the rise of about a third in China's grain output over the six years after the family-plot reform. He traced roughly half of the gain to one main cause. What was it?
answer: Farmers worked harder because the extra grain was theirs
choices: Farmers worked harder because the extra grain was theirs
The government sent new tractors and fertilizer to every village
Weather across China was unusually good for six straight years
The state simply raised the quota each year
context: Justin Yifu Lin's paper 'Rural Reforms and Agricultural Growth in China' (American Economic Review, 1992) traced close to half of the farm-output growth after the reform to the household system's incentives, rather than to fertilizer, weather or better seed. Lin later served as the World Bank's chief economist from 2008 to 2012. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Yifu_Lin.

question: China's own Communist Party admitted that its farm communes had failed. Austrian economists call the episode a natural experiment that bore out an argument from 1920: that planners without real prices and property cannot weigh one cost against another. Whose argument was it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
choices: Ludwig von Mises on economic calculation
John Maynard Keynes on effective demand
Karl Marx on primitive accumulation
Alfred Marshall on partial equilibrium
context: Mises's 1920 argument that socialist commonwealths cannot calculate rationally without market prices was empirically confirmed at the largest possible scale by the Chinese state's own reforms. Same land, same farmers, radically more output when prices returned. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: Eighteen Xiaogang farmers pressed red thumbprints onto their secret contract under a kerosene lamp in December 1978, knowing the pact could cost them their lives. China now counts the crumbling paper among the treasures of its modern history. Where is it on display?
answer: The National Museum in Beijing
choices: The National Museum in Beijing
The village schoolhouse in Xiaogang
The Ministry of Agriculture in Beijing
The Shanghai Museum
context: The original contract, marked with the farmers' red thumbprints, is displayed at the National Museum in Beijing. It marks the practical starting point of China's Reform and Opening.

question: A farmer in Xiaogang worked the same field with the same seed after the village's secret pact, yet far more grain came up; the only thing that changed was who kept the surplus. Austrian economists boil the story down to two words. What are the two words?
answer: Incentives matter
choices: Incentives matter
Scale matters
Prices coordinate
Trade enriches
context: 'Incentives matter' is the compressed lesson of the Chinese agricultural reform, taught in every introductory economics course. It captures the incentive-recognition side of the calculation debate. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Ronald Coase, still an undergraduate, crossed to America on a travel scholarship in 1931 to tour its great integrated companies and see why they did so much of their own work. In Detroit he called on the giant of the day. Which company?
answer: Ford
choices: Ford
General Electric
American Tobacco
US Steel
context: Coase's Cassel Scholarship US visit included Ford in Detroit, US Steel, and other integrated firms. Watching those hierarchies is what led him to ask why the firm existed rather than the market coordinating everything through prices. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: Ronald Coase put a puzzle to his profession in 1937. If market prices guide people so well, why does a carmaker keep salaried workers on its books instead of hiring someone new for every bolt tightened or letter typed? Coase said companies exist for one reason. Which?
answer: Because using the market for every tiny task has its own hidden costs
choices: Because using the market for every tiny task has its own hidden costs
Because governments make it illegal to hire freelancers
Because workers refuse to be paid by the task
Because companies get big tax breaks that freelancers don't get
context: Coase's key move: using markets is costly (finding partners, negotiating, monitoring, enforcing). When those costs exceed the costs of managing inside a firm, hierarchies replace market transactions. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: A growing company decides, job by job, whether to do its own cleaning, accounting and deliveries or buy them from outside firms. On Ronald Coase's account in his 1937 paper, where does the company stop growing?
answer: The point where doing one more job inside costs the same as buying it
choices: The point where doing one more job inside costs the same as buying it
The point where its profit on each worker is at its highest
The point where it has bought out all of its own suppliers
The point where it controls most of the market it sells in
context: Coase's boundary condition: the firm grows until the marginal in-house transaction cost equals the marginal market transaction cost. Cheaper in-house transactions are absorbed; cheaper market transactions are outsourced. Source: Coase, Economica (1937), section III.

question: Ronald Coase's 1937 paper explained where a firm's boundary falls, the line between what it makes for itself and what it buys. Since then shipping and the internet have cut the cost of finding, hiring and checking on outside suppliers. What broader shift in how companies make things has followed?
answer: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
choices: A move from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains
A move from outsourced supply chains toward vertical integration
A move from stock ownership toward partnership structures
A move from public listing toward private ownership
context: Apple once made much of its own hardware; today it designs its chips in California and has contract factories in Asia, such as Foxconn's, build them. When dealing with outside firms grows cheaper, Coase's logic says firms buy more and make less themselves. Source: Baldwin and Clark, Design Rules (MIT 2000).

question: A carmaker is about to buy a load of steel. Ronald Coase's 1937 framework, which changed how economists study any industry, has an analyst ask one comparative question about any such deal. What is the question?
answer: Why is this deal done inside a firm rather than across a market?
choices: Why is this deal done inside a firm rather than across a market?
Is the steel's price above what it cost to make?
Does one seller hold enough of the market to set the price?
Would a tax on the deal correct its harm to others?
context: Coase's move: for every transaction, ask why it is organized the way it is. The answer is always the relative transaction cost of the two arrangements. Source: Coase, Economica (1937).

question: Arnold Plant taught a young Ronald Coase to be wary of the central-planning schemes fashionable among British intellectuals in the 1930s, and Coase gave his teachers the credit. Coase took his commerce degree in 1932 at the school where Plant taught. Which school?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Cambridge
The University of Chicago
Harvard University
context: Coase took his BCom at the London School of Economics (1932). His US Cassel Scholarship trip in 1931-32 provided the empirical observations behind Nature of the Firm. Source: Coase, Nobel biographical essay (1991).

question: A steel mill on the edge of town blows black smoke over the houses next door. The families start coughing, but the mill's owner does not pay a cent of their doctors' bills. What do economists call a cost that falls on others instead of on whoever causes it?
answer: An externality
choices: An externality
A subsidy
A windfall
A dividend
context: Arthur Pigou (1877-1959) had argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) that pollution should be corrected by government tax. Coase said the Pigouvian analysis was incomplete because it treated the causation as one-directional. Source: Pigou (1920); Coase (1960).

question: Arthur Pigou called in 1920 for a tax to correct the harm a factory's smoke does its neighbors. Ronald Coase answered in 1960 that the harm cuts both ways. What did he mean?
answer: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
choices: A no-pollution rule also harms the factory by preventing production
The neighbor is legally required to endure the pollution
The neighbor loses standing to sue in federal court
The factory automatically owes triple damages
context: Coase's move: the economic question is not who is at fault. It is which use of the resource creates more value. Both parties have legitimate uses; a rule imposes costs on whichever party is prevented from its use. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960).

question: A rancher's cattle keep straying into a neighboring farmer's crops, in Ronald Coase's most famous example. If the two of them can bargain cheaply, the rancher may pay for a fence, or the farmer may pay the rancher to pen his cattle in. Either way, one outcome always shows up. Which one?
answer: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
choices: The resource ends up with its highest-value user
The side the law protects always gets its way
The two split the land and the cost evenly
The crops are always protected from the herd
context: The initial rights determine WHO PAYS in the bargain; they do not determine the final resource allocation if transaction costs are low enough for the parties to negotiate. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (1960), section IV.

question: Two neighbors quarrel over a harm one does the other, and striking a bargain costs them little, so they reach the same efficient result whichever one the law sides with. George Stigler named the result in his 1966 textbook. What did he call it?
answer: The Coase theorem
choices: The Coase theorem
The tragedy of the commons
The invisible hand
The prisoner's dilemma
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase Theorem' in his 1966 textbook Theory of Price. Coase himself argued the textbook version was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: Ronald Coase complained that readers misread his 1960 paper as saying the state should never step in when a factory causes harm. In a book of 1988 he set out his real view for cases where hundreds of neighbors are harmed and striking a bargain is expensive. What was it?
answer: Government may step in, but its own costs of acting count too
choices: Government may step in, but its own costs of acting count too
A tax on the polluter is always the best fix
Nothing can be done; the neighbors must live with it
Only judges, never lawmakers, may step in
context: Coase's actual argument in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: when private bargaining is too costly, government intervention may be superior -- provided the analysis honestly counts the transaction costs of government administration too. Source: Coase, The Firm, the Market, and the Law (Chicago 1988).

question: Ronald Coase's 1960 paper changed how economists handle harms like factory smoke and overfished seas. Two kinds of systems later built on its ideas took hold in America, Europe, Iceland and New Zealand, one for smoke from power plants and one for fishing grounds at sea. What were they?
answer: Tradeable pollution permits and transferable fishing quotas
choices: Tradeable pollution permits and transferable fishing quotas
Pollution taxes and fees for fishing licenses
Fixed emission limits and closed fishing seasons
Clean-energy subsidies and state fish hatcheries
context: The 1990 US SO2 cap-and-trade Acid Rain Program, EU ETS (2005), and Iceland + New Zealand fisheries individual transferable quotas all trace their intellectual pedigree to Coase 1960. Source: Ellerman + Joskow, Markets for Clean Air (Cambridge 2000).

question: Ronald Coase set out his two great ideas in short papers of 1937 and 1960 that together fill only about sixty pages: the first on why firms exist, the second on smoke, noise and quarrels between neighbors. The Swedish academy awarded him the 1991 Nobel for that work. What did the academy say the papers had discovered and clarified?
answer: The significance of transaction costs and property rights
choices: The significance of transaction costs and property rights
The mathematical foundations of general equilibrium
The theory of comparative advantage in international trade
The empirical measurement of national income
context: The 1991 Nobel citation named Coase 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Both 1937 and 1960 papers are the pillars. Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: Textbooks soon boiled Ronald Coase's 1960 paper down to a tidy rule about neighbors who strike bargains over a harm. Coase called that textbook version a misreading of his work. In his own writing, what did the paper really show?
answer: Real bargaining is costly, so who holds the rights at the start matters
choices: Real bargaining is costly, so who holds the rights at the start matters
Bargaining is cheap, so who holds the rights at the start never matters
Harm runs one way, so the one who causes it must always pay
The state must never step in when neighbors quarrel
context: Coase in his 1988 book The Firm, the Market, and the Law: the zero-transaction-cost world of the textbook Coase Theorem does not exist. In the real world, transaction costs are high, so initial rights and institutional design matter enormously. Source: Coase (1988).

question: Two American families go shoe shopping, one earning $30,000 a year and the other $200,000. The cheap canvas sneakers the first family buys carry a tariff of 15 to 20 percent; the leather dress shoes the second buys carry 5 to 8 percent. Measured against income, which group pays more of this tax?
answer: Low-income households
choices: Low-income households
High-income households
Both income groups equally
Only foreign-based importers
context: Because low-income households spend a larger share of income on the tariffed low-end goods, they bear a disproportionately higher effective burden. Source: usitc.gov/tariff_affairs/tariff_databases.

question: Edward Gresser, a trade researcher at the Progressive Policy Institute, laid out in a 2002 paper who really pays America's tariff bill. He set the tariff bill of the poorest fifth of households against their income, and did the same for the richest fifth. How many times heavier was the poorest fifth's burden?
answer: 3 to 4 times
choices: 3 to 4 times
1.1 to 1.2 times
10 to 15 times
About 30 times
context: Bottom-quintile households pay roughly 3-4x the top-quintile burden as a share of income; the schedule targets specifically the goods the poor buy most. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: Thomas Sowell took on, in his book Basic Economics, the claim that tariffs on imported goods protect American workers. He found a hidden twist in that claim which the tariff's backers do not admit. What did he say?
answer: The workers the tariff claims to protect are the ones it taxes hardest
choices: The workers the tariff claims to protect are the ones it taxes hardest
The foreign makers the tariff shuts out are the ones who pay it
The rich buyers of imports are the ones who pay most of the tariff
The workers the tariff protects gain more in wages than they pay
context: Sowell's Basic Economics distills the incidence result: protectionism sold as pro-worker functions economically as a regressive consumption tax hitting working-class families most. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_Economics.

question: Anna bakes faster than Ben and paints signs faster too, yet she leaves the sign-painting to him while she bakes, and the two trade. An idea David Ricardo published in 1817 explains why both of them come out ahead, even though one is better at everything. What is the idea called?
answer: Comparative advantage
choices: Comparative advantage
Absolute advantage
Diminishing returns
Economies of scale
context: David Ricardo's Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) set out comparative advantage: each side gains by doing what costs it least to give up, even when the other side is better at everything. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comparative_advantage.

question: A shopper at the register pays a higher price for an imported shirt because of a tariff on it. Which kind of tax does a tariff most closely resemble?
answer: A consumption tax
choices: A consumption tax
A payroll tax
A corporate income tax
A capital gains tax
context: A tariff raises the domestic price of the imported good and is paid, in economic incidence, by the domestic consumer -- like a targeted sales tax. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tariff.

question: A shopper in an American shoe store pays a far higher tariff on cheap sneakers than on fine leather shoes, and cheap clothes carry far higher rates than fancy ones too. Congress built that pattern into the tariff schedule one bill at a time over many decades. Which mechanism best explains how the schedule came to look this way?
answer: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
choices: The domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection
The World Trade Organization mandates the pattern
Congress taxed cheap goods more because they sell in bulk
Foreign governments retaliated against US textile exports
context: The schedule is not accidental. Producers of low-end goods (footwear, apparel) had the strongest incentive to lobby for protection and the tariff schedule reflects their trade-lobby lawyers' work. Source: progressivepolicy.org/toughest-on-the-poor.

question: A law-abiding adult in one of more than two dozen states slips a hidden pistol into his pocket, and the law asks for no permit, fee or class. Supporters say the rule restores the original meaning of the Second Amendment. What do they call it?
answer: Constitutional carry
choices: Constitutional carry
Castle doctrine
Stand your ground
Red-flag law
context: Constitutional carry, also called permitless carry, lets an adult who may lawfully own a handgun carry it concealed without any permit; more than two dozen states allowed it by 2024. The other extreme was 'may-issue' permitting at officials' discretion, largely struck down by the Bruen decision. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_carry.

question: A burglar sizing up a street knows that some of its homes may hold an armed owner, so he thinks twice before breaking in. On a street where he knows no home is armed, he has far less to fear. What idea from economics does his choice show?
answer: Incentives change behavior
choices: Incentives change behavior
Sunk costs should be ignored
Scarcity raises prices
Trade makes both sides richer
context: The burglar weighs what he stands to gain against the risk he runs, and the chance of meeting an armed owner raises that risk. John Lott's More Guns, Less Crime (Chicago, 1998; 3rd ed. 2010) is the most-cited, and most disputed, empirical study of concealed-carry laws. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: John Lott, author of More Guns, Less Crime, argues that cutting the fees and paperwork for a concealed-carry permit changes who applies. In his telling, one group signs up in far greater numbers once permits get cheaper. Which group?
answer: Poorer residents of high-crime neighborhoods
choices: Poorer residents of high-crime neighborhoods
Retired military officers and veterans
Suburban homeowners with families
College-educated city professionals
context: Lott and his Crime Prevention Research Center argue that high permit fees fall hardest on the poor, and that cheaper permits bring many more applicants from poorer, heavily minority neighborhoods, where residents cannot count on a fast police response. Other researchers dispute much of his work. Source: https://m.washingtontimes.com/news/2023/nov/30/more-people-carrying-concealed-weapons-even-as-per/.

question: A rifle and pistol association in New York State challenged the state's may-issue law, which let officials refuse a carry permit unless the applicant proved some special need. The Supreme Court struck the law down on June 23, 2022, and gun-rights supporters count the case among their landmark wins. What is its short name?
answer: Bruen
choices: Bruen
Heller
McDonald
Rahimi
context: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen (2022), majority opinion by Justice Clarence Thomas, invalidated may-issue regimes requiring 'proper cause'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: Justice Clarence Thomas wrote the Supreme Court's opinion in June 2022 striking down New York's rule that carry-permit applicants show a special need. New York, New Jersey and California had kept carry permits rare, and they did not give up. Which set of tools did they turn to instead?
answer: Higher fees, long training rules and lists of banned places
choices: Higher fees, long training rules and lists of banned places
A lottery handing out a fixed number of permits
A rule that permits be good only inside the home
A minimum age of thirty for every applicant
context: Restrictive states shifted from discretionary denial to cost-based and geography-based restriction after Bruen. The Bastiat move: the SEEN policy changed; the UNSEEN restriction on the low-income permit-seeker did not. Source: grokipedia.com/page/New_York_State_Rifle_%26_Pistol_Association,_Inc._v._Bruen.

question: Frederic Bastiat taught economists to hunt for the person a rule harms but nobody ever counts. Turned on a state's gun-permit fees, training hours and paperwork, his method brings to light a person who appears in no government statistic on gun policy. Who is it?
answer: The victim who could not afford a permit and faced her attacker unarmed
choices: The victim who could not afford a permit and faced her attacker unarmed
The gun dealer who lost a sale when the buyer gave up
The licensing office that lost fee revenue to the rules
The taxpayer who paid for the permit office's extra staff
context: The seen: revenue-generating fees and training requirements. The unseen: the woman being stalked who could not afford the $400+20-hours barrier and could not lawfully carry for self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/More_Guns,_Less_Crime.

question: Two criminologists published a national household survey in 1995 estimating that Americans draw guns to defend themselves about 2.2 million times a year, many more times than guns are used in crimes. Groups favoring gun control still contest the number. Which pair wrote it?
answer: Gary Kleck and Marc Gertz
choices: Gary Kleck and Marc Gertz
John Lott and David Mustard
Franklin Zimring and Gordon Hawkins
David Hemenway and Deborah Azrael
context: Kleck and Gertz's estimate of ~2.2 million annual defensive gun uses in the US is contested but remains a widely-cited figure in the empirical literature on self-defense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Defensive_gun_use.

question: Regulators in Washington rescued one of America's largest banks in May 1984, after big depositors had begun pulling billions out of it. The bank had loaded up on oil-and-gas loans in Oklahoma and Texas, a large share bought from Penn Square Bank, which had already failed. Which bank was it?
answer: Continental Illinois
choices: Continental Illinois
First Chicago
Manufacturers Hanover
Chase Manhattan
context: Continental Illinois had about $40 billion in assets at the time of its 1984 crisis -- roughly $120 billion in 2026 dollars. It had bought energy loans from the failed Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma in 1982. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental Illinois' (2026-09-05).

question: Todd Conover, the Comptroller of the Currency, went before a House banking committee in September 1984 to explain the rescue of Continental Illinois. He told lawmakers that one group of large American banks would not be allowed to go under. Which group did he name?
answer: The 11 largest US banks
choices: The 11 largest US banks
The 3 largest money-center banks
The 25 largest banks by branch count
The 5 largest investment banks
context: Comptroller of the Currency C. Todd Conover testified in September 1984 that regulators would not let any of the eleven largest banks fail. At the same hearing Congressman Stewart McKinney popularized a phrase for the policy: too big to fail. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_big_to_fail.

question: Congressman Stewart McKinney heard Todd Conover tell a House banking hearing in September 1984 that the government would never let the very largest banks go under. Months before, regulators had made good every account at Continental Illinois, even balances beyond the $100,000 insurance limit. McKinney gave the policy a name that stuck. What was it?
answer: Too big to fail
choices: Too big to fail
Systemic risk exception
Lender of last resort
Money-center backstop
context: Congressman Stewart McKinney popularized the phrase, which had turned up now and then in the press before, at the September 1984 House hearing on the Continental Illinois rescue, and it became shorthand for the moral-hazard structure of modern banking regulation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_big_to_fail.

question: Regulators saved Continental Illinois in May 1984, and Austrian and public-choice critics say the rescue taught America's biggest banks a lesson that changed how they lent for decades afterward. Once the precedent was set, big banks expected a certain kind of federal protection whenever they got into trouble. What did they learn?
answer: Regulators would shield uninsured depositors and creditors, so big risks were safer
choices: Regulators would shield uninsured depositors and creditors, so big risks were safer
Regulators would rescue any bank, large or small, that ran into trouble
Regulators would repay only insured deposits, up to the legal limit
Regulators would prop up the share prices of troubled big banks
context: This is the moral-hazard structure of every subsequent bailout episode -- LTCM 1998, Bear Stearns 2008, TARP 2008, SVB 2023. All extended the Continental Illinois precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Moral hazard' (2026-09-05).

question: A saver deposits her pay at a bank, trusting a federal promise dating from 1933, made in the wake of the Depression's bank runs: if the bank fails, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation will repay her. Austrian and free-market economists warn that the promise breeds what they call moral hazard. Why would deposit insurance push a bank toward bigger risks?
answer: The bank keeps profits from big bets, but taxpayers cover the loss if it fails
choices: The bank keeps profits from big bets, but taxpayers cover the loss if it fails
Insurance fees eat its profits, so it must chase higher returns
Depositors punish risky banks by moving their money quickly
Insured savers demand higher interest, so it must lend riskily
context: Deposit insurance takes away a depositor's reason to watch her bank, since her money is safe whatever the bank does. Its owners keep the gains when risky loans pay off, while the insurance fund, and behind it the taxpayer, carries the loss when they go bad; critics call that moral hazard. After the 1984 rescue the FDIC itself took majority ownership of Continental Illinois, which Bank of America absorbed in 1994. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard.

question: Big depositors at Continental Illinois, then the nation's seventh-largest bank, got every dollar back in 1984, even the wealthy ones the law was never meant to cover. The rescue was billed back then as a one-off. Which reasoning move does the story teach?
answer: An exception granted once hardens into a precedent that shapes later risk-taking
choices: An exception granted once hardens into a precedent that shapes later risk-taking
A one-off rescue ends once the crisis passes and leaves no mark
A rescue teaches only the bank that was saved, not its rivals
An exception can be withdrawn later at no political cost
context: The 1984 above-cap protection was framed as an exception. Every subsequent major rescue extended the pattern until 'too big to fail' was a well-understood implicit guarantee. The 2023 SVB extension of full protection was the direct heir of the 1984 precedent. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: A depositor weighs a giant bank against a small one, knowing after the Continental Illinois rescue that only the giant would be saved in a crisis. Austrian economists press one step further than other critics of the rescue. Which reasoning move do they press?
answer: A guarantee for only the biggest banks is a subsidy that drives concentration
choices: A guarantee for only the biggest banks is a subsidy that drives concentration
A guarantee for only the biggest banks protects small savers most of all
A guarantee for only the biggest banks gets dropped once they grow safe
A guarantee for only the biggest banks costs nothing unless a crisis strikes
context: The Austrian point: too-big-to-fail is not just moral hazard for the biggest banks; it is an active subsidy over their smaller competitors. Depositors rationally prefer the guaranteed bank. Consolidation is the mechanical result. Source: Selgin, Bagehot's Legacy (Cato commentary, 2013-2020).

question: Milton Friedman argued that a company is a creature of the law, not a person, so no company can really pay a tax. When the government taxes a company, every dollar is taken from real people. Which three groups of people?
answer: Its workers, customers or owners
choices: Its workers, customers or owners
Voters, judges or civil servants
Its auditors, lawyers or tax collectors
Rival firms, critics or neighbors
context: Friedman's line summarizes the incidence point: a corporation is a legal fiction and every dollar of tax comes from a real human's pocket -- a consumer, a worker, or a shareholder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose.

question: A senator promises voters that the corporate income tax makes big companies pay their fair share. An economist in Frederic Bastiat's tradition asks who ends up poorer. The law names the company as payer, but much of the cost quietly lands on one group as smaller earnings. Which group takes the largest hit?
answer: Workers via lower wages
choices: Workers via lower wages
Retirees via smaller Social Security checks
Foreign investors via US border tariffs
Landlords via higher property tax
context: Empirical research (Suarez Serrato and Zidar, AER 2016; CBO 2012 distributional update) shows a large share of the corporate income tax is ultimately borne by workers through lower wages. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: Lawmakers in one country raise the tax on corporate profits, and, as often happens, the wages of its workers fall the most. The reason lies in a difference between the two things every business needs to produce, money and workers, and in how each responds when a tax bites. Which difference is at work?
answer: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
choices: Capital is more mobile internationally than labor
Labor is more mobile internationally than capital
Capital and labor are equally mobile
Neither capital nor labor moves across borders
context: Mobile capital's after-tax return is set by world markets; when the US taxes capital, mobile capital exits or requires a compensating gross return, and the burden shifts to less-mobile labor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: Two economists set out to learn whether workers, landowners or shareholders carry the cost when American states raise or cut their corporate taxes, using numbers from local labor markets in every state. Their 2016 paper in the American Economic Review became the standard modern study. Who were they?
answer: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
choices: Juan Carlos Suarez Serrato and Owen Zidar
Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
David Card and Alan Krueger
Anthony Atkinson and Thomas Piketty
context: Suarez Serrato and Zidar, 'Who Benefits from State Corporate Tax Cuts? A Local Labor Markets Approach with Heterogeneous Firms' (AER, 2016), is the workhorse modern study of state corporate-tax incidence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: A candidate tells a rally that a higher corporate tax will make rich shareholders pay. Part of the burden does land on the company's owners, but its owners are not just the wealthy: one huge group of them holds enormous amounts of American stock and rarely comes up in such speeches. Which group?
answer: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' savings
choices: Pension funds holding teachers' and firefighters' savings
Credit unions holding members' savings deposits
Labor unions holding their members' strike funds
City governments holding their road-repair budgets
context: The shareholder class is not only 'the rich' -- large pools of public-employee and private-sector pension fund savings hold corporate equity, so the incidence that falls on capital hits ordinary retirement accounts too. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Corporate_tax_in_the_United_States.

question: One small Central American country handed every adult citizen $30 in bitcoin through its new Chivo wallet on September 7, 2021, the day it became the first nation to give Bitcoin legal-tender status alongside the dollar. Its young president had unveiled the plan in Miami that June. Which country, under which president?
answer: El Salvador, under Nayib Bukele
choices: El Salvador, under Nayib Bukele
Argentina, under Alberto Fernandez
Panama, under Laurentino Cortizo
Honduras, under Xiomara Castro
context: Bukele announced the plan at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference in Miami. Same-day September 7 the government launched the Chivo Wallet and issued each adult citizen a $30 Bitcoin allocation. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: Javier Milei praised Bitcoin after taking office in Argentina in December 2023 and let Argentines write contracts in it, but he did not make it legal tender. One small Central American country had already done that in 2021. What did that status mean for the shops of that country?
answer: They had to accept it by law in payment
choices: They had to accept it by law in payment
They had to show every price in it
They had to turn it into dollars each day
They could take it only from foreign visitors
context: Legal tender is money the law says must be accepted in payment. El Salvador's Bitcoin Law of 2021 required every business to accept bitcoin when a buyer offered it. An amendment passed on January 29, 2025, to meet the terms of a loan from the International Monetary Fund, made acceptance voluntary. Source: https://www.theblock.co/post/337885/el-salvador-passes-bill-to-revise-bitcoin-adoption-strategy-per-imf-deal-reuters.

question: Javier Milei waved a real chainsaw over his head at an Argentine campaign rally in 2023 while the crowd cheered. Argentines elected the libertarian economist president, and he was sworn in on December 10, 2023. The chainsaw stood for something he had promised to do to the government. What was it?
answer: Slashing the government's spending and cutting whole agencies
choices: Slashing the government's spending and cutting whole agencies
Cutting down forests to sell the timber
Breaking apart a big state-owned oil company
Ending trade with neighboring countries
context: Milei was sworn in on December 10, 2023. He had long praised Bitcoin as a way of returning money to the private sector, and his deregulation decree of December 2023 allowed contracts written in it; as of 2025 he had not made it legal tender. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Javier_Milei.

question: Bhutan, a Buddhist kingdom of about 700,000 people between India and China, chose a quieter path than Argentina's from about 2019, while other countries argued over whether to embrace Bitcoin. Rivers tumbling down the Himalayas power the kingdom's dams. What has Bhutan been doing since?
answer: Mined Bitcoin with its hydropower and built a large state reserve
choices: Mined Bitcoin with its hydropower and built a large state reserve
Banned Bitcoin entirely and criminalized possession
Made Bitcoin its sole legal tender, replacing the ngultrum
Issued a state-backed stablecoin as an alternative to Bitcoin
context: 2024 disclosures revealed Bhutan holds an estimated 13,000+ BTC. The mining is run through Druk Holding & Investments, the country's sovereign wealth fund. The scale, on a population of 700,000, is proportionally very large. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Bhutan.

question: The International Monetary Fund pressed the first nation to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender to undo its 2021 law, warning of risks to financial stability. To Bitcoin's backers, the real worry lay deeper, in something about Bitcoin that the managers of government money cannot copy. Which feature?
answer: No central bank controls its supply, so policy cannot inflate it
choices: No central bank controls its supply, so policy cannot inflate it
Its price is pegged to gold, so it cannot fall
Its payments are hidden from every tax office
Its supply grows with the economy, keeping prices steady
context: The International Monetary Fund pressed El Salvador to reverse its Bitcoin law from 2021 on, citing risks to financial stability, consumer protection and public finances. Bitcoin's supporters answered that the deeper difference is supply: new bitcoin is issued on a fixed schedule toward a cap of 21 million coins, and no central bank can change it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: A high-school student asks which national Bitcoin experiment was the right one: the Central African Republic's short-lived legal tender, Argentina under Javier Milei, or Bhutan's quiet path. A Hayekian economist refuses to name a single winner. Which reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Different tradeoffs suit different countries' circumstances
choices: Different tradeoffs suit different countries' circumstances
Only central-bank digital money can be legitimate
Any state embrace of Bitcoin succeeds whatever the context
Only the largest economies can adopt a new money
context: The CAR reversal warns that infrastructure prerequisites matter as much as legal declarations. Milei's legal-friendliness lets adoption grow organically. Bhutan converts stranded hydro energy into a portable savings asset. Different national situations, different fits. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: A hurricane leaves Florida's stores nearly out of bottled water, and the last bottles sell for $10 instead of $2. Buyers call it gouging, but Thomas Sowell and other economists say the high price is doing useful work for the whole state. What work?
answer: It signals sellers to rush more water in
choices: It signals sellers to rush more water in
It lets stores recoup their storm losses
It raises sales tax for the cleanup
It warns buyers the water may be bad
context: Prices signal both scarcity (to buyers, to conserve) and profit opportunity (to sellers, to bring more supply). Ceilings that suppress the signal degrade both responses. This is the operating mechanism behind every emergency-supply anti-gouging analysis. Source: mercatus.org, mises.org.

question: John Shepperson of Kentucky saw Hurricane Katrina leave Mississippi without power in 2005, hired a truck and drove it about 600 miles south, planning to sell its load at roughly twice what he had paid. What had he loaded into the truck?
answer: 19 generators
choices: 19 generators
500 gallons of gasoline
100 chainsaws
50 portable radios
context: Shepperson bought 19 generators in Kentucky and drove them about 600 miles to Mississippi after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, planning to sell them at about twice what he had paid. Police arrested him under the state's anti-gouging law and impounded the generators. Source: John Stossel and Gena Binkley, 'A Jail for Heroes', New York Sun (2006); https://www.nysun.com/article/opinion-jail-for-heroes.

question: Michael Munger of Duke University boiled his long argument about emergency prices down to one short slogan. In his telling, the high price is what pulls trucks of supplies through the night from far away. What is his slogan?
answer: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
choices: Price gouging is the solution, not the problem
The market always clears eventually
Consumers pay whatever the seller demands
Regulation is the answer to shortages
context: Munger's framing: the high price is the market's shout to producers and importers 'HERE, RUSH SUPPLY HERE'; the anti-gouging law silences the shout and prolongs the shortage. Source: EconTalk, Munger episodes on gouging.

question: Thomas Sowell, author of the widely read Basic Economics, wrote against the laws, kept on the books in most American states, that punish sellers for charging high prices in a disaster. He named one reasoning error that lies under every such law. What is it?
answer: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
choices: They mistake a price signal for a moral offense
They ignore consumer welfare entirely
They assume unlimited government resources
They confuse macroeconomic and microeconomic scales
context: Sowell's move: the high price is information about scarcity, not evidence of bad character. The law that criminalizes the messenger destroys the message the market was trying to send. Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Bitcoin's creator, who wrote under the name Satoshi Nakamoto, mined the earliest coins after putting out the white paper in 2008, then disappeared without ever showing a face. Many people have claimed the name since. Experts put one simple test to every such claimant. What is it?
answer: Move some of Satoshi's original bitcoins as a signature
choices: Move some of Satoshi's original bitcoins as a signature
Show a passport issued in the name Satoshi Nakamoto
Move some bitcoins from any address he happens to control
Show early drafts of the white paper on his own computer
context: Coins mined in Bitcoin's first days sit at addresses everyone links to Satoshi, so only the holder of those keys could move them; signing a fresh message with one of those keys proves the same thing in seconds. Moving coins from some other address proves nothing about Satoshi, and passports and old drafts can be forged. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: A handful of reporters sat through private sessions in London in May 2016 as Craig Wright walked them through what seemed a cryptographic proof that he was Satoshi Nakamoto. Within hours Dan Kaminsky, a security researcher, and others had exposed it as a recycled old signature of Satoshi's, not a fresh one. Why could Wright's trick not hold up?
answer: Bitcoin proofs can be checked openly by anyone with a computer
choices: Bitcoin proofs can be checked openly by anyone with a computer
The reporters recorded him confessing later
Satoshi came online personally to deny the claim
A government agency ran a background check on him
context: Dan Kaminsky (1979-2021), a well-known security researcher, publicly explained within hours that Wright's 'proof' was a copy-pasted old Satoshi signature rather than a fresh one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Craig Wright doubled down after his London demonstration was exposed in 2016. He joined in launching a new coin that broke away from Bitcoin Cash in November 2018. Which coin did he help launch?
answer: Bitcoin Satoshi's Vision (BSV)
choices: Bitcoin Satoshi's Vision (BSV)
Bitcoin Gold (BTG)
Bitcoin Diamond (BCD)
Bitcoin Private (BTCP)
context: BSV split from Bitcoin Cash in November 2018 and made 'Satoshi's Vision' part of its name -- an identity claim embedded in the ticker. Bitcoin Gold (2017), Bitcoin Diamond (2017) and Bitcoin Private (2018) were other offshoots, with no tie to Wright. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_SV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bitcoin_forks.

question: Bitcoin programmers and companies took Craig Wright to London's High Court after he had threatened and sued programmers for calling him a fraud. In March 2024 the judge ruled on his claim to be Satoshi Nakamoto. Which case gave the ruling?
answer: COPA v Wright
choices: COPA v Wright
Kleiman v Wright
Wright v Bitcoin Core
Wright v Twitter
context: The Crypto Open Patent Alliance (COPA) brought the London High Court action; Mr Justice Mellor issued the March 14, 2024 ruling. Kleiman v Wright was the earlier Florida case (2018-21) over disputed early Bitcoin holdings; the other cases are hypothetical or minor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright#COPA_v._Wright.

question: Mr Justice James Mellor heard Craig Wright's claim to be Satoshi Nakamoto in London's High Court and ruled against him in March 2024. His language about the documents and messages Wright had brought as proof was unusually blunt. What did the judge find?
answer: The man had forged and backdated them
choices: The man had forged and backdated them
The man had forgotten crucial details under stress
The proof was scattered but real
The man had refused to answer any questions about them
context: Mr Justice Mellor found that Wright had forged and backdated his documents; many showed forensic evidence of manipulated fonts and metadata inconsistent with claimed dates. Wright testified extensively; the ruling was not about incomplete or forgotten details but affirmative fabrication. Source: COPA v Wright, oral ruling 14 March 2024, written judgment 20 May 2024.
