question: Jack Dorsey's company Square founded an alliance of crypto firms in 2020, and in 2021 the alliance took Craig Wright to court. Wright had been threatening and suing programmers who branded him a fraud. What problem did pooling their money against him solve?
answer: A cost too big for one small developer, but cheap when split across many
choices: A cost too big for one small developer, but cheap when split across many
A shortage of programmers willing to work on Bitcoin
A need to find the real Satoshi so a court could name him
Programmers' fear that speaking out would cost them their jobs
context: The Crypto Open Patent Alliance (COPA) was formed by Square in September 2020 to pool crypto patents and keep the technology open; in April 2021 it asked the UK High Court to declare that Wright did not own the copyright in the Bitcoin white paper. Square was renamed Block in 2021. Sources: https://open-crypto.com/about; decrypt.co (April 2021).

question: Craig Wright, the Australian computer scientist who had spent years claiming to be Satoshi Nakamoto, kept repeating the claim even after a London judge ruled in March 2024 that he was not. What did the court do to him next?
answer: He was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
choices: He was held in contempt of court and referred for possible criminal prosecution
He was ordered to hand the court the keys to Satoshi's early coins
He was barred from setting foot in Britain for ten years
He was sent to prison at once for six months
context: In July 2024 Mr Justice Mellor referred the papers to the Crown Prosecution Service to consider prosecuting Wright for perjury and forgery; in December 2024 the court found him in contempt for breaching its order against repeating the claim, and gave him a suspended prison sentence. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Steven_Wright.

question: Craig Wright pointed to old writings, public speeches and court papers to back his claim to be Satoshi Nakamoto, yet he never offered the one thing that counts as proof in Bitcoin's world. Bitcoin teachers draw a single lesson from the affair. What reasoning move do they make?
answer: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only identity claim that counts in Bitcoin
choices: That cryptographic proof of key control is the only identity claim that counts in Bitcoin
That the courts alone should adjudicate who Satoshi is
That academic credentials and public speaking are the correct grounds for accepting an identity claim
That anonymous founders should be legally required to reveal themselves
context: The Bitcoin argument (Antonopoulos, Song, Kaminsky) is that in a system built on private-key signatures, the only relevant proof of any 'is-Satoshi' claim is a fresh signature -- courts and credentials cannot substitute for the primitive the system is built on. Legal-adjudication, credentialing, and forced-doxxing responses are precisely what the argument rejects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright.

question: Fidel Castro lost Cuba's lifeline in December 1991, when the Soviet Union dissolved and its billions of dollars a year in support stopped almost overnight. Food, fuel and power ran short from 1990 to 1994, and hunger reached every province. What did his government call those years?
answer: The Special Period in Time of Peace
choices: The Special Period in Time of Peace
The Great Leap Forward
The Cultural Revolution
The New Economic Policy
context: In Spanish, 'Periodo Especial en Tiempo de Paz.' The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and its subsidy to Cuba (fuel at below-world-market prices, guaranteed sugar purchases at above-world prices) ended essentially overnight. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: A Cuban family sat down to a thin supper in 1993. Daily calories per person on the island had dropped to about 1,900, from some 3,100 in 1989, once the Soviet aid that kept Cuba afloat had stopped. Medical journals later reported how much weight the average adult lost. What range did they give?
answer: Between 5 and 25 pounds
choices: Between 5 and 25 pounds
Between 1 and 3 pounds
Between 50 and 100 pounds
Essentially no change
context: Per-capita daily caloric intake fell from roughly 3,100 kcal in 1989 to roughly 1,900 kcal in 1993. The Special Period is one of the few modern rich-data natural experiments in what a fully price-controlled economy does when hit by a supply shock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: A Havana family opened its ration book in the hungry years after Soviet aid stopped and found the meat all but gone. Across the city one group of animals nearly vanished as well, and hungry neighbors caught and ate some of them. Which animals nearly disappeared from Havana?
answer: Urban cats and dogs
choices: Urban cats and dogs
Domesticated cattle
Chickens on state farms
Racing pigeons
context: Some pets were eaten; many others starved or were abandoned. Zoo animals faced similar pressure. The pet-population collapse became one of the visible human-scale markers of how deep the caloric shock had gone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: Fidel Castro let the market into Cuba's hungry economy in two ways after Soviet aid stopped, and slowly the economy began to mend. Which two openings did he allow?
answer: City vegetable plots and self-employment, plus legal US dollars
choices: City vegetable plots and self-employment, plus legal US dollars
Full price freedom and selling off all state factories
Leaving the socialist bloc and joining the North American free trade zone
Returning all farms and buildings to the families that owned them before 1959
context: The recovery lever was NOT more planning; it was permitting Cubans to grow and sell food and hold dollars. Where the market was let in, calories followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: A high-school student asks an economist in Ludwig von Mises's tradition why Cuba's hunger of the early 1990s makes a useful test of central planning. When the Soviet Union came apart in December 1991, its subsidy of billions a year vanished almost overnight, and calories per person crashed from about 3,100 to about 1,900. The economist points to one feature that makes the case a rare natural experiment. Which feature?
answer: Only the Soviet subsidy changed; the planning, embargo and weather stayed put
choices: Only the Soviet subsidy changed; the planning, embargo and weather stayed put
Cuba ran a planned and a free economy side by side
Cuba's planners kept a record of every ration handed out
Cuba dropped central planning in that same year
context: The US embargo had been in place since 1962; weather was normal; the planning apparatus was retained. The subsidy loss isolates central planning's ability (or inability) to adapt to a supply shock. This is Mises's 1920 calculation-debate prediction played out in body-weight units. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cuba%E2%80%93Soviet_Union_relations.

question: Fidel Castro, ruler of Cuba since 1959, gave a series of speeches in 1993 that finally admitted the hunger on the island. Two years earlier the Soviet Union had dissolved, ending the sugar-for-oil subsidy that propped up his planned economy, and the average Cuban had lost about a third of a normal day's calories. What did Castro blame for the shortage?
answer: The US trade embargo
choices: The US trade embargo
Cuba's own central planners
Local corruption and mismanagement
Climate change and poor rainfall
context: The embargo had been in place since 1962, while the collapse was timed to the loss of the Soviet subsidy in 1991. Critics call Castro's move blaming a constant for a sudden change. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Special_Period.

question: David Chaum, a cryptographer, worked out a trick in 1982 that let a bank stamp a digital coin without seeing it. Spent later at a shop, the coin could not be traced to whoever had withdrawn it. What was he protecting for the customer?
answer: The buyer's privacy
choices: The buyer's privacy
The bank's profit
The shop's records
The buyer's credit rating
context: David Chaum invented blind signatures in 1982: a bank could sign a digital coin without seeing it, so when the coin was later spent, nobody could link it to the person who had withdrawn it. The aim was privacy, the digital version of cash in a pocket. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Chaum.

question: David Chaum founded DigiCash in Amsterdam in 1989, sure that banks and shops would rush to offer his private digital cash. Instead the banks moved slowly, few shops joined and buyers stayed away. Why were most people so slow to switch?
answer: Cash and cards already worked well enough
choices: Cash and cards already worked well enough
Banks charged too much to issue the coins
Hackers had cracked its code early on
Most laws forbade digital money
context: DigiCash was founded in Amsterdam in 1989. Banks were slow to sign on, few merchants accepted its coins, and most customers saw no reason to switch from paper money and credit cards; the company filed for bankruptcy in 1998. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: A customer withdrew a DigiCash coin from a bank in the 1990s and later spent it at a shop. The bank could check that the coin was real and unspent, yet it never learned who had received it. David Chaum had invented the math trick that made this possible. What is it called?
answer: blind signatures
choices: blind signatures
ring signatures
Schnorr signatures
elliptic-curve signatures
context: Blind signatures (Chaum 1982) let a signer authenticate a message whose contents are hidden from them. Ring signatures (Rivest, Shamir, Tauman 2001) provide sender-anonymity from a group; Schnorr signatures are a different signing scheme; elliptic-curve is a mathematical family used by many signature schemes including Bitcoin's. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_signature.

question: Giants of the software business came knocking at David Chaum's DigiCash in the mid-1990s. Microsoft reportedly put a nine-figure sum on the table while it hurried to ship Windows 95, wanting his anonymous electronic cash built into the new system. Why did the big software firms want it so badly?
answer: Private payments would let users buy online with no bank in the middle
choices: Private payments would let users buy online with no bank in the middle
Governments were starting to require payment systems in software
Its code would guard their programs against viruses
Banks had promised them a fee for every account opened
context: Bill Gates and Microsoft reportedly offered David Chaum a nine-figure sum, widely cited as either $100 million or $180 million, to build DigiCash into Windows 95. Chaum turned it down. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: Besides Microsoft, two more American giants made offers for David Chaum's DigiCash technology in the mid-1990s, and he turned both of them down. One made the browser that then ruled the young web; the other ran a huge credit-card network. Which pair was it?
answer: Netscape and Visa
choices: Netscape and Visa
Netscape and MasterCard
AOL and American Express
Yahoo and Diners Club
context: Besides Microsoft, Netscape, the dominant early web-browser company, and Visa made offers that Chaum declined. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto put out the Bitcoin paper in 2008, ten years after David Chaum's DigiCash went bankrupt and every coin it had issued died with it. Its math had held up. Wei Dai, Nick Szabo and Satoshi himself all drew one lesson from the collapse, and Bitcoin was built without the piece that had sunk DigiCash. What was the lesson?
answer: Even brilliant cryptography fails as money if it still needs a central issuer
choices: Even brilliant cryptography fails as money if it still needs a central issuer
Cryptography can never make sound money, whatever the design around it
Digital cash can succeed only with explicit government backing
Money must be physical, since users will not trust intangible balances
context: The DigiCash lesson (Dai, Szabo, Nakamoto) was that removing the trusted issuer was the central task, because whoever ran issuance was a single point of failure; without a partner bank there were no coins at all. Bitcoin keeps signatures and units of value but has no trusted issuer: new coins come from proof-of-work and a distributed network checks every transaction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: An economist argued in a book of 1973 that private firms and voluntary groups could take over police, courts, roads and money. His father was the Nobel laureate Milton Friedman, and he taught economics and law at Santa Clara University. What was the book called?
answer: The Machinery of Freedom
choices: The Machinery of Freedom
For a New Liberty
Anarchy, State, and Utopia
The Road to Serfdom
context: David Friedman, born in 1945, the son of Milton and Rose Director Friedman, took a doctorate in theoretical physics before turning to economics and law. His 1973 book, The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism, argued that competing businesses and voluntary groups could supply everything from policing and courts to roads and money. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: Milton Friedman argued for a small state that kept to defense, the courts and a handful of other jobs. His son David, born in 1945, became an economist too and took a different view of the state itself. What is the difference between the two Friedmans?
answer: David is an anarcho-capitalist; Milton was a classical liberal
choices: David is an anarcho-capitalist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a democratic socialist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a monarchist; Milton was a classical liberal
David is a technocratic centrist; Milton was a classical liberal
context: Milton Friedman defended a minimal state (national defense, courts, some social insurance). David Friedman argues no state is necessary at all, with all such functions in principle providable by competing private firms. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: David Friedman set out in a book of 1973 to show how a society could run with no state at all. Its chapters take up competing private courts, rival police agencies, money printed by private firms and roads paid for by the drivers who use them. What was his core move?
answer: Describe how specific mechanisms would work and let the reader judge
choices: Describe how specific mechanisms would work and let the reader judge
Argue from natural rights that the state is inherently illegitimate
Prove mathematically that no state can ever be efficient
Chronicle past societies that lived without any state
context: Friedman insists on institutional specifics rather than doctrinal claims. Chapters like 'How Would Private Law Enforcement Really Work?' walk through the contract-and-arbitration architecture with realistic edge cases. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: Murray Rothbard built his case on natural rights: every person owns himself, so any tax the state collects is theft. David Friedman reached the same goal, anarcho-capitalism, a free market with no government at all, but he set the rights argument aside. On what ground did Friedman build his case instead?
answer: Consequences: a stateless society would serve most people better
choices: Consequences: a stateless society would serve most people better
Consent: no one ever agreed to be ruled by a state
History: every state slides in the end into tyranny
Virtue: free people grow more moral without rulers
context: Rothbard defended the same conclusion from natural rights (the state as an inherent violator of self-ownership). Friedman's consequentialist framing lets the reader compare outcomes without accepting the underlying rights premise. The distinction matters inside libertarian debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: David Friedman teamed up with two other scholars in 2019 to survey real societies that resolved quarrels without any central state: Somali xeer, Icelandic saga law, Jewish rabbinical courts, Amish community rules, Roma kris and more. What was the book called, and who were his co-authors?
answer: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
choices: 'Legal Systems Very Different from Ours,' with Peter Leeson and David Skarbek
'Free to Choose,' with Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
'The Constitution of Liberty,' with Friedrich Hayek
'The Sovereign Individual,' with James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg
context: Peter Leeson is a George Mason University economist; David Skarbek is a Brown University political scientist. The book presents these historical cases as natural experiments in the decentralized private legal architecture 'The Machinery of Freedom' described in theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/David_D._Friedman.

question: Patri Friedman, grandson of Milton and Rose Friedman, started a group in 2008 that hopes to found new communities beyond the reach of any government's rules, with early money from Peter Thiel. His father David had argued for a society with no state at all. What was Patri's project?
answer: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
choices: Patri Friedman founded the Seasteading Institute
Patri Friedman founded the Institute for Justice
Patri Friedman founded the Cato Institute
Patri Friedman founded the American Enterprise Institute
context: The Seasteading Institute proposes floating city-states on the high seas as a physical experiment in the polycentric governance David Friedman describes in theory. The Institute was funded early by Peter Thiel. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Patri_Friedman.

question: David Friedman brought out a third edition of his 1973 book in 2014, and he changed how it reached readers in a way neither earlier edition, of 1973 or 1989, had done. The choice fit the book's own theme of removing gatekeepers. What was the change?
answer: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
choices: It was released as an open-source text, freely available online
It was translated into every major world language simultaneously
It was published exclusively as an audio book
It was released only through university-press subscriptions
context: Consistent with the book's political stance, Friedman made the third edition freely downloadable. Any curious reader with internet access can read the complete text at no cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Machinery_of_Freedom.

question: A Labor Department official sat down with a city's pay survey to set the prevailing wage for a federal building job under the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931. As in most cities, the survey landed on one wage as its answer. Which wage?
answer: The union scale
choices: The union scale
The state minimum wage
The federal minimum wage
The Bureau of Labor Statistics median
context: The DOL wage-survey process defaults to the union scale in most metropolitan areas, making Davis-Bacon a de-facto union-wage protection on federally-funded projects. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: A school district builds a new school with federal money under the Davis-Bacon Act, while a private builder across town puts up a similar one at market wages. Economists at the Beacon Hill Institute measured in 2008 the extra cost the act adds to federal building. What premium did they find?
answer: About 10 percent
choices: About 10 percent
About 1 percent
About 50 percent
No premium at all
context: The Beacon Hill Institute's 2008 study found that the act's wage rules raised costs on covered federal projects by about 9.9 percent, some $8.6 billion a year; other estimates run higher or lower. Source: https://beaconhill.org/BHIStudies/PrevWage08/PRPrevailingWage0802.htm.

question: Several backers of the Davis-Bacon Act said openly on the House floor in 1931 whom they wanted kept off federal building sites. They meant lower-paid newcomers moving north in the Great Depression to compete for federal construction jobs. Which group did the bill's backers name?
answer: Southern Black workers
choices: Southern Black workers
European immigrant workers
West Coast Chinese workers
Mexican migrant workers
context: The 1931 debate shows sponsors explicit that the point was to keep Southern Black workers, who had been migrating north to compete for federal-project work at lower wages, off federal jobsites. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Davis%E2%80%93Bacon_Act_of_1931.

question: Congressman Miles Allgood of Alabama rose on the House floor in 1931 to back the Davis-Bacon Act. He told of a contractor from his home state who had landed a federal building contract in New York, and his words later became infamous in histories of the law. What did Allgood say the contractor had brought north with him?
answer: Cheap colored labor, in competition with white labor
choices: Cheap colored labor, in competition with white labor
Steel girders shipped in from Germany
Machines that put carpenters out of work
Union crews hired away from Chicago
context: The 1931 House-floor remarks of Congressman Miles Allgood of Alabama are in the Congressional Record. The racial-exclusion motive was overt, and critics argue the Act keeps its exclusionary effect even though the language was dropped. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_C._Allgood.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught his readers to hunt for the hidden second side of every law, what is seen and what is not seen. Read that way, the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, which lifts wages on federal building sites, has a side everyone sees and a side few notice. Which two-sided pattern is it?
answer: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
choices: Concentrated benefit to unions, dispersed cost to taxpayers
Concentrated benefit to taxpayers, dispersed cost to unions
Uniform benefit and uniform cost across the population
Concentrated benefit to foreign contractors, dispersed cost to domestic firms
context: Mancur Olson's Logic of Collective Action (1965) explains the pattern: organized construction unions capture the concentrated benefit while every federal-project taxpayer bears a small share of the dispersed cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Logic_of_Collective_Action.

question: A French official counting his country's dollar reserves in the mid-1960s began to doubt America's promise to swap them for gold at $35 an ounce. Washington was printing dollars to pay for two vast projects at the same time, and every new dollar made the peg harder to defend. Which two projects drained the dollar?
answer: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
choices: the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs
the Korean War and the Marshall Plan
the Cold War missile buildup and the Interstate Highway System
the Iraq War and the Bush tax cuts
context: The 1960s fiscal pressures came from Vietnam War spending and Johnson's Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty). Korea/Marshall Plan (1950s), missile buildup/highways (1950s), and Iraq/Bush tax cuts (2000s) are the wrong eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: The president of France walked into a Paris press conference in February 1965 and called the dollar's tie to gold, at $35 an ounce, a huge and unfair advantage for America. France, he announced, would turn in its dollars for gold bars and ship them home. Which French leader was he?
answer: Charles de Gaulle
choices: Charles de Gaulle
Georges Pompidou
Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
François Mitterrand
context: Charles de Gaulle, French President 1959-69, made the February 1965 press conference challenging the dollar peg. Pompidou succeeded him; Giscard was his finance minister at the time; Mitterrand came to the presidency in 1981. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle.

question: Reporters gathered at a Paris press conference in February 1965 to hear Charles de Gaulle attack the dollar. The phrase people quote for America's advantage, the exorbitant privilege, gets credited to him, but his finance minister coined it, a rising young politician who would himself take the French presidency in 1974. Who was that minister?
answer: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
choices: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
Georges Pompidou
Jacques Chirac
François Mitterrand
context: Giscard d'Estaing coined 'exorbitant privilege' as de Gaulle's finance minister and later served as president from 1974 to 1981; the phrase is often credited to de Gaulle himself. Pompidou, Chirac and Mitterrand were other presidents of France. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: A European central banker added another batch of American dollars to his reserves in the 1960s, as central banks the world over did. France's finance minister had a stinging name for the edge this gave the United States: the exorbitant privilege. What could America do that no other country could?
answer: the US could pay for imports with new dollars others had to hold
choices: the US could pay for imports with new dollars others had to hold
the US could raise tariffs without any trade-treaty review
the US could veto UN Security Council decisions
the US could station troops abroad without permission
context: The asymmetry: the US paid for imports in dollars that were the world's reserve currency, so foreign banks accumulated dollar reserves -- effectively lending the US real goods in exchange for paper claims. Tariffs, Security Council vetoes, and troop stationing are separate political privileges. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exorbitant_privilege.

question: Charles de Gaulle tested America's word in 1965 by cashing in French dollars for gold at the US Treasury, so that America had to pay out real bullion to hold its peg. Larger conversions came later, and other central banks quietly followed. Roughly how much did France convert that first year?
answer: about $150 million
choices: about $150 million
about $2 billion
about $10 million
about $50 billion
context: France converted about $150 million of dollar reserves to gold in 1965. Larger conversions followed over the next several years; other central banks followed France's lead more quietly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: Charles de Gaulle demanded in the mid-1960s that France's dollars be turned into gold bars and shipped home across the Atlantic. The bars did not go straight to Paris: first they sat in a vault cut eighty feet into the rock beneath lower Manhattan. Which vault was it?
answer: the New York Fed's gold vault
choices: the New York Fed's gold vault
the Stock Exchange's basement vault
the Chase Manhattan Bank's vault
the old Sub-Treasury at Federal Hall
context: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's vault at 33 Liberty Street, cut into Manhattan bedrock about eighty feet below the street, holds gold for foreign central banks. Source: https://www.newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/goldvault.html.

question: Private bidders pushed the price of gold past $35 an ounce as the 1950s drew to a close, threatening the dollar's peg. In 1961 eight Western central banks agreed to sell gold from a shared stockpile every time private buying pushed the price up, pinning it back down. What was the arrangement called?
answer: the London Gold Pool
choices: the London Gold Pool
the Basel Gold Consortium
the Zurich Gold Compact
the Frankfurt Gold Alliance
context: The London Gold Pool (1961-68) joined eight central banks: those of the United States, Britain, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Gold_Pool.

question: Frédéric Bastiat's doctors sent him south in 1850, hoping warmer air would ease his tuberculosis. He went first to Pisa, then on to the city Pope Pius IX ruled as capital of the Papal States, and he died there on Christmas Eve. Which city was it?
answer: Rome
choices: Rome
Florence
Naples
Milan
context: Bastiat left Pisa for Rome in the autumn of 1850, hoping the warmer air would ease his failing throat and lungs. He died there on 24 December 1850 and is buried in the French national church of San Luigi dei Francesi.

question: Prosper Paillottet brought out a fuller edition of his friend Frédéric Bastiat's last book in 1851, piecing the rest together from the papers Bastiat left. Bastiat had been correcting its proofs in his sickroom until he died, and he had meant it as his answer to the socialists. What was the book?
answer: Economic Harmonies
choices: Economic Harmonies
Economic Sophisms
The Law
Cobden and the League
context: Harmonies economiques, Bastiat's one attempt at a positive systematic theory and the work he expected to be remembered for, was being corrected from the sickroom right up to his death; only about half was in print when he died. Prosper Paillottet, his friend and chosen editor, prepared the expanded 1851 edition from his manuscripts.

question: Frédéric Bastiat asked in his last big book what happens when many strangers buy and sell freely, with no person or committee in charge of the whole. He had watched shopkeepers, farmers and craftsmen trade in ordinary French markets. What did he say emerges from all that trading?
answer: A working order that meets needs with no planner in charge
choices: A working order that meets needs with no planner in charge
A guaranteed equal outcome for every worker
A slide into disorder that only a state can stop
A slow drift into monopoly by the richest sellers
context: In Economic Harmonies (1850; expanded edition 1851), Bastiat argued that when people trade freely, their interests fit together into a working order that no one designs or directs. Prosper Paillottet, his friend and chosen editor, prepared the expanded edition from his manuscripts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: A visitor near Piazza Navona finds the plaque that marks Frédéric Bastiat's grave, in the church where he was buried after his death on Christmas Eve 1850. The same church holds three Caravaggio paintings of Saint Matthew's life. What is the church called?
answer: San Luigi dei Francesi
choices: San Luigi dei Francesi
Santa Maria del Popolo
Sant'Andrea della Valle
Santa Maria Sopra Minerva
context: San Luigi dei Francesi (Saint Louis of the French) is the French national church in Rome. A memorial plaque marks Bastiat's tomb inside. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: A visitor strolls into the church where Frédéric Bastiat lies buried and stands before three paintings by Caravaggio, painted around 1600. Nobody charges him a cent to look, yet at auction the paintings would sell for hundreds of millions of dollars. What does the scene show about market value?
answer: Value comes from what buyers would pay, not from being for sale
choices: Value comes from what buyers would pay, not from being for sale
Value comes from the cost of the paint and the canvas
Value comes from the hours of work the painter put in
Value vanishes when anyone can see a work for free
context: Caravaggio's Contarelli Chapel cycle (The Calling, The Inspiration, and The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew), 1599-1600, in San Luigi dei Francesi, are among the most-visited paintings in Rome. Source: grokipedia.com/page/San_Luigi_dei_Francesi.

question: Deirdre McCloskey wrote three books to explain one great turn in history. For ages almost every family lived poor and hungry much of the time; then, from about 1800, incomes in northwestern Europe and later America climbed year after year. What does she call that leap?
answer: The Great Enrichment
choices: The Great Enrichment
The Great Depression
The Great Migration
The Great Awakening
context: Deirdre McCloskey (born September 11, 1942) is a Chicago-trained economic historian who taught at the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois at Chicago. Her Bourgeois Trilogy pressed the culture-of-innovation thesis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: A reader picking up Bourgeois Dignity, the middle book of Deirdre McCloskey's trilogy, in 2010 found her argument summed up in a subtitle. What is the subtitle?
answer: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
choices: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World
Institutions and the Wealth of Nations
The Cultural Origins of Capitalism
How the West Grew Rich
context: Bourgeois Dignity: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World (Chicago 2010). The provocation is that the standard economic inputs (capital, geography, institutions) do not account for the timing and place of the Great Enrichment. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo8474162.html.

question: Deirdre McCloskey closed her trilogy in 2016 with Bourgeois Equality and put her whole thesis on its cover, in the subtitle. Her story turns on what drove the West's great leap in wealth. What does the subtitle say?
answer: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
choices: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World
The Rise of the Middle Class in Northwestern Europe
Merchants, Inventors, and the Industrial Revolution
Culture and Commerce Since 1600
context: Bourgeois Equality: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World (Chicago 2016). The subtitle is McCloskey's thesis in one sentence -- IDEAS about the merchant and inventor, not stocks of capital or formal rules, produced the modern world. Source: press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/B/bo22269023.html.

question: Deirdre McCloskey pointed to a shift in Holland and England between about 1600 and 1800, which she calls the missing ingredient in the usual story of growth. Two kinds of people whom nobles and churchmen had long looked down on began to earn moral respect. Which two?
answer: The merchant and the inventor
choices: The merchant and the inventor
The soldier and the magistrate
The scholar and the theologian
The landholder and the aristocrat
context: McCloskey argues that before roughly 1600, aristocratic and clerical cultures held merchants and inventors in contempt. After the shift, businesspeople acquired dignity, and millions of ordinary people started trying to invent things. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (2010), introduction.

question: A gentleman of 1700 sneered at the shopkeeper who sold him his gloves; a century later ordinary opinion had come round to admiring men in trade. Deirdre McCloskey calls that shift the unseen ingredient that made capital, institutions and geography pay off. What one word does she use for it?
answer: Dignity -- treating regular business people with real respect
choices: Dignity -- treating regular business people with real respect
Property -- stronger legal ownership of land and tools
Machinery -- new steam and factory technology
Empire -- wealth pulled in from colonies
context: Bourgeois Dignity (2010) argues that once innovation and trade were DIGNIFIED in ordinary talk, ordinary people started innovating in earnest. In McCloskey's Bastiat-style reading the SEEN inputs are capital, institutions and geography; the UNSEEN one that made them productive is the cultural legitimation of the merchant and inventor.

question: A student hears Deirdre McCloskey's culture story of how the West grew rich and worries that it throws out secure property rights, enforceable contracts and honest courts. Which statement best fits her stance on institutions?
answer: Respect for innovators complements institutions; it does not replace them
choices: Respect for innovators complements institutions; it does not replace them
Institutions are a purely illusory factor with no growth effect
Institutions matter only in societies that never industrialized
Institutional analysis should be abandoned in favor of pure rhetoric studies
context: McCloskey argues that the new respect for merchants and inventors worked alongside secure property, enforceable contracts and honest courts: she adds a missing ingredient to the list of causes and removes none of the others. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Equality (Chicago 2016), preface.

question: Deirdre McCloskey jolted her own profession in 1985 with a short book about how economists really persuade one another in their journals: not with mathematics alone, but with vivid metaphors, little stories and appeals to famous names. What did she call the book?
answer: The Rhetoric of Economics
choices: The Rhetoric of Economics
The Language of Growth
The Persuasion of Markets
Style in the Dismal Science
context: The Rhetoric of Economics (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985) opened the field of rhetorical study of economic writing and argued that economists persuade each other by narrative and metaphor as much as by proofs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deirdre_McCloskey.

question: To sharpen her puzzle, Deirdre McCloskey sets two societies side by side with much the same people, land, tools and trade, and opposite fortunes. Her trilogy asks why wealth exploded in one part of the world and not another, and the difference, she argues, lay in the culture around the merchant. Which pair does she use?
answer: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
choices: Ming-dynasty China's stagnation versus Britain's Industrial Revolution
Roman North Africa's decline versus medieval Italy's revival
Iberian empires' silver imports versus Dutch banking innovation
Ottoman guild economies versus Persian bazaars
context: McCloskey argues that Ming China had comparable capital, technology, and formal institutions to early-modern Britain -- but the culture around the merchant differed. Same inputs, different cultural legitimation, opposite outcomes. Source: McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: A European farmhand took home his day's wage in the 1700s, some three dollars in today's money, much as his great-grandfather had. Deirdre McCloskey set that beside the two centuries since. By roughly what factor has real income per person grown in the countries that industrialized first?
answer: About 30-fold (3,000 percent)
choices: About 30-fold (3,000 percent)
About 3-fold (300 percent)
About 100-fold (10,000 percent)
About 3-fold, only in the richest cities
context: The 3,000-percent figure (roughly 30x) is the standard estimate from Angus Maddison and OECD historical statistics for real per-capita income growth in Western countries since 1800. McCloskey uses it as the puzzle to explain. Source: Maddison Project Database (2020 update); McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity (Chicago 2010).

question: Joseph Stalin gave a Moscow speech on December 27, 1929, that set Soviet farm policy for years. He targeted the kulaks, peasants a little better off than their neighbors, and used a chilling phrase for what the state would do to them. What was the phrase?
answer: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
choices: Liquidation of the kulaks as a class
Correction of the peasant question
Reorganization of rural labor
Cleansing of the villages
context: The phrase 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class' (likvidatsiya kulachestva kak klassa) was delivered at the December 27, 1929 conference and formalized in a Politburo decree of January 30, 1930. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: The Politburo, the Communist Party's ruling council, turned Stalin's speech into policy on January 30, 1930. Its decree sorted the kulak families of the Soviet countryside into three categories, each with a different fate. What were the three fates?
answer: Executed, deported, or resettled locally
choices: Executed, deported, or resettled locally
Taxed, fined, or warned
Retrained, retained, or reassigned
Relocated, redistributed, or repatriated
context: The Politburo's January 30, 1930 decree sorted kulak families: category one shot, category two deported to the far north / Siberia / Kazakhstan, category three resettled locally on marginal land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dekulakization.

question: Soldiers and police crammed a whole Soviet village into cattle cars in 1931 and sent it to a labor settlement far to the east. Between 1930 and 1932 the campaign against the kulaks deported people this way to Siberia, the Kazakh steppe and the far north. Roughly how many were deported?
answer: About 2 million
choices: About 2 million
About 20,000
About 200,000
About 20 million
context: About 30,000 alleged kulaks were shot; about 2 million were deported to the far north, Siberia, and Kazakhstan; another 4-5 million were dispossessed of property and reassigned. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (Oxford UP, 2007).

question: Lynne Viola rebuilt Stalin's deportation system from newly opened Soviet police archives for her book The Unknown Gulag. She concluded the campaign against the kulaks was meant to drive farmers from the land so the state could take over every farm and run it. What did the deportations achieve?
answer: It stripped villages of the farmers best able to resist collectivization
choices: It stripped villages of the farmers best able to resist collectivization
It gave the land of the rich to the poorest peasants
It raised grain output by putting experts in charge
It filled the Red Army's quotas for new recruits
context: The most competent farmers were destroyed because they were the most competent, so the villages that remained had lost their most capable people before collectivization and before the 1932-33 famine. Lynne Viola's The Unknown Gulag (Oxford, 2007) uses newly opened OGPU archives to reconstruct the settlement system for deported peasants.

question: A deported kulak family stepped off a train at a special settlement in the Urals in the winter of 1931-32, when death rates there were catastrophic. One Soviet agency ran the deportations and built such settlements in the far north, Siberia and the Urals. Which agency was it?
answer: The OGPU (later the NKVD)
choices: The OGPU (later the NKVD)
The Red Army Corps of Engineers
The Ministry of Agriculture
The Comintern Executive
context: The OGPU (unified state political directorate, renamed NKVD in 1934) built 'special settlements' in Siberia and the Urals to hold deported kulak families. Winter 1931-32 death rates in these settlements ran to hundreds of thousands. Source: Lynne Viola, The Unknown Gulag (2007).

question: A party activist in a Soviet village pointed in 1930 at a peasant who had refused to join the collective farm and branded him a class enemy in disguise, fit for deportation to Siberia. Activists stretched the label this way across the countryside until any resister could be caught by it. What did they call the move?
answer: Unmasking someone as a kulak
choices: Unmasking someone as a kulak
Registering someone as a class enemy
Naming someone as a saboteur
Marking someone for rectification
context: 'Unmasking' (razoblachenie) redefined kulak-status as anyone who resisted collectivization. The label became a catch-all administrative tool for eliminating opposition. Source: Fitzpatrick, Stalin's Peasants (1994).

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to set every policy's visible effects beside its hidden ones. Turned on Stalin's campaign against the kulaks, his test finds the seen in what party newspapers printed: rich peasants' property seized in the name of social justice. What was the unseen cost the villages paid in the years that followed?
answer: The loss of farming skill, and the famine that followed
choices: The loss of farming skill, and the famine that followed
A flood of cheap grain that ruined the poorer farmers
A shortage of workers for Moscow's new factories
The loss of the rent the kulaks had paid the state
context: The Bastiat move: the SEEN was 'redistributing kulak property'; the UNSEEN was the collapse of village agricultural knowledge (which farmer knew which fields, which seed variety, which threshing techniques) and the famine that used the resulting vulnerability. Source: mises.org/library/theft-of-a-nation-holodomor.

question: Friedrich Hayek published a short pamphlet in London in 1976 urging governments to give up their monopoly on money. His publisher was a small think tank that Antony Fisher, a chicken farmer, had founded on Hayek's own advice. Which think tank put it out?
answer: The Institute of Economic Affairs
choices: The Institute of Economic Affairs
The Cato Institute
The Adam Smith Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: The IEA, founded 1955, is Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank; Hayek personally counselled Antony Fisher to start it after Fisher read The Road to Serfdom. The Cato Institute (1977) and Adam Smith Institute (1977) did not yet exist. The Mont Pelerin Society is a scholarly society, not a publisher. Source: iea.org.uk/publications/research/denationalisation-of-money.

question: Friedrich Hayek watched inflation rip through the Western world in the 1970s. Two years after sharing the 1974 Nobel Prize, he wrote a short pamphlet tracing the whole problem to one source: governments held a monopoly on printing money. He made a single bold proposal for what they should do about it. What was it?
answer: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
choices: Give up their monopoly on issuing money and let private issuers compete
Return to a fixed exchange rate anchored on a single ounce of gold
Adopt a common global reserve currency issued by the International Monetary Fund
Delegate all monetary policy to an independent panel of academic economists
context: Hayek (1899-1992) had shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics two years earlier, in 1974, with Gunnar Myrdal. The 1976 pamphlet was the most radical monetary proposal of his career. He argued that money is no different from any other good: competition between private issuers, checked by consumer choice, would supply it better than a state monopoly. The idea is called currency competition. The proposal was radical enough that even some fellow Austrian economists, Murray Rothbard among them, rejected it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek went back through the record of every currency a government had ever issued as its own monopoly money. That record, he argued in his 1976 pamphlet against the state's monopoly on money, showed one clear pattern. What was it?
answer: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
choices: Every such currency has been debased or destroyed over long enough time
Every such currency has appreciated against gold across the twentieth century
Every such currency has stabilized once its central bank became independent
Every such currency has held value so long as its government retained a fiscal surplus
context: Hayek's examples ran from the Roman denarius under Diocletian to the Weimar mark of 1923 to modern post-war fiat currencies. His conclusion was that debasement is not a scandal but the predictable equilibrium of a monopoly issuer facing short-run political incentives. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Friedrich Hayek wanted governments to give up their monopoly on money and let private issuers compete side by side. Readers asked the obvious question: if anyone can print money, how would competing currencies stay honest? Hayek pointed to one discipline. Which force did he say would keep the issuers honest?
answer: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
choices: Consumers refusing to hold or accept currencies whose value was falling
Government auditors inspecting each issuer's reserve ratios annually
International treaty obligations enforced through the World Bank
A gold-parity peg required by domestic constitutional law
context: Hayek's mechanism was identical to the market discipline any producer faces. Issuers whose currency lost purchasing power would see it refused in commerce, lose deposits, and fail; issuers who kept it stable would win business. No government auditor, treaty, or peg was needed. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/hayeks-plan-private-money.

question: An economist of the Austrian school argued that governments should not be the only ones allowed to print money: private banks and companies could each issue their own currencies, and people could choose freely among them. What did he predict that competition would do?
answer: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
choices: Only currencies that held their value would survive, and inflation would fall
One firm would win the market and then print more than any government
Rival currencies would multiply until no shop could price anything
Issuers would race to print more, and inflation would climb everywhere
context: In the second edition Hayek added the speculation that a free monetary market would not sustain an unmanageable number of currencies but would converge on a limited number of stable standards. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Murray Rothbard, a fellow Austrian economist, agreed with Friedrich Hayek that the government should not run the money supply. But when Hayek argued in 1976 that private banks should be free to issue their own paper currencies and compete for users, Rothbard drew a line. He wanted one more rule for any honest free-market money. What did he require?
answer: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
choices: That the currency be backed by a commodity such as gold
That the currency circulate only within a single sovereign jurisdiction
That the currency be issued exclusively by chartered depository institutions
That each issuer hold government bonds as reserves for its notes
context: Rothbard remained a strict commodity-money advocate: free banking, yes, but the notes had to be redeemable claims on a real commodity such as gold. On this account Hayek's proposal for competing PAPER currencies with no commodity backing was more radical than Rothbard would go. Source: cameronharwick.com/writing/hayek-vs-rothbard-on-money.

question: A high-school student raises her hand in class: 'The US government prints all the dollars right now, so why should we let different companies compete to supply money?' An economist in Hayek's tradition answers, 'For the same reason we let many bakeries compete to sell bread, and many companies compete to sell phones.' What reason is he giving?
answer: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
choices: Competition gives customers choice and pushes suppliers to serve them better
Bakeries and phone makers are private, so money should be too
Rival suppliers drive prices down, so loans would get cheaper
The law treats bread, phones and money as the same kind of goods
context: The Austrian methodological move: reject the special-pleading claim that money is uniquely unsuited to markets. Hayek argued the same competitive discipline that improves other goods would improve currency; the burden falls on defenders of the state monopoly to say why money is the exception. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Denationalisation_of_Money.

question: Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by an anonymous programmer known as Satoshi Nakamoto, was built to run without any government or bank. Its champions, Saifedean Ammous among them, call Friedrich Hayek's 1976 pamphlet Denationalisation of Money the project's grandfather: competing currencies keeping each other honest. But Bitcoin uses one engineering trick no one could have used in 1976. Which trick?
answer: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
choices: A cryptographically fixed supply schedule that no issuer can debase
A supply set by computer to grow with the size of the economy
Digital coins backed one for one by gold held in a secure vault
A central computer that records every coin's owner by name
context: Hayek imagined competing private BANKS disciplined by consumer refusal to hold debased notes; Bitcoin, launched thirty-three years later by Satoshi Nakamoto, hard-codes the discipline into the protocol itself with a 21-million-coin cap and a halving schedule no operator can override. Ammous's 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard makes the intellectual-descent argument explicit; the European Central Bank has publicly noted the same theoretical lineage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saifedean_Ammous.

question: The Communist Party's Third Plenum set Deng Xiaoping's market turn in motion in December 1978, two years after Mao Zedong died. Market prices came back to farming first, then to industry. What is the program usually called?
answer: Reform and Opening
choices: Reform and Opening
The Great Leap
The Hundred Flowers
The Cultural Revolution
context: Gaige kaifang -- Reform and Opening -- was launched at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee, December 18-22, 1978, under Deng Xiaoping. It ended pure central planning first in agriculture, then in industry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform.

question: Eighteen households in Xiaogang, a poor village in Anhui province, secretly carved up their commune's fields into family plots late in 1978. They knew they risked arrest or worse, and they promised to bring up each other's children if any parent was taken away. Why did they take the risk?
answer: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew itself
choices: So each family would be rewarded for the food it grew itself
So each family could leave the commune and move to the city
So they could sell the land and split the money among themselves
So the families could hide their grain from the state's collectors
context: Eighteen households in Xiaogang village, Fengyang County, Anhui signed a secret agreement late in 1978 (on November 24, by some accounts) to divide land plots, pledging to raise each other's children if any were arrested. They also pledged to deliver the state's quota first. Local officials tolerated the pact after harvest yields rose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiaogang,_Anhui.

question: Deng Xiaoping let China's farmers keep and sell any grain above their state quota at market prices, starting in 1978. The land was essentially the same as before, and so were the people working it. Roughly what happened to China's total grain output between 1978 and 1984?
answer: It rose about 34 percent
choices: It rose about 34 percent
It fell by about half
It stayed roughly flat
It quadrupled
context: Chinese grain output rose about 34% from 1978 to 1984 on essentially the same land and labor -- once farmers again had market price signals to guide planting and keep the surplus. The famine of 1959-61, which killed some 36 million people by the journalist Yang Jisheng's count, was still a living memory. Source: World Bank data; Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (2008).

question: A foreign company built a factory in Shenzhen in the early 1980s, inside one of four walled-off coastal enclaves where the market, not the state, set prices. Deng Xiaoping's China had opened the four in 1980; the others were Xiamen, Shantou and Zhuhai. Shenzhen, a fishing town of about 30,000, has since grown past 17 million people. What were the four called?
answer: Special Economic Zones
choices: Special Economic Zones
Free Trade Territories
Foreign Investment Bureaus
Coastal Enterprise Parks
context: The first four SEZs were Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, and Xiamen (1980); Hainan Island became a fifth SEZ in 1988. Shenzhen grew from a fishing village of 30,000 to a metropolis of over 17 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_economic_zones_of_China.

question: A Chinese steel mill of the 1980s handed over its planned quota at the old set price, then sold whatever it made beyond that at market prices. Deng Xiaoping ran his reforms as this kind of hybrid rather than scrapping the plan overnight, so market signals could reach production. What is the scheme called?
answer: Dual-track pricing
choices: Dual-track pricing
Ratchet planning
Convertible planning
Ratcheted quotas
context: Dual-track pricing (shuang gui zhi) let firms sell state quotas at planned prices and any additional output at market prices. This let market signals reach production margins without a shock discontinuation of the plan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual-track_pricing.

question: Deng Xiaoping answered the old guard of the Communist Party, who accused him of betraying Mao, with an old folk saying about a cat, one he had used in a speech of 1962. What was the heart of his saying?
answer: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
choices: It does not matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice
The best cat sleeps by day and hunts by night
One cat is not enough for a granary of rats
Feed the cat with rice and it will forget the mice
context: Deng's cat saying, from a 1962 speech and revived in the reform era, meant that results should outweigh ideological purity. His 1962 wording, from a Sichuan proverb he credited to General Liu Bocheng, set a yellow cat beside the black one; the white cat came into the popular version later. It became the shorthand slogan of Reform and Opening. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_theory_(Deng_Xiaoping).

question: Deng Xiaoping refused the kind of grand blueprint that had given China the Great Leap Forward, which had killed tens of millions. He tried each policy in one place first, watched whether it worked, and moved on only once it had. What saying, which his colleague Chen Yun had applied to economic policy as early as 1950, came to stand for that method?
answer: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
choices: Crossing the river by feeling the stones
Climbing a mountain step by step
Planting a forest one seed at a time
Building a wall from small bricks
context: 'Mo zhe shi tou guo he' -- crossing the river by feeling the stones -- began as a folk idiom; Chen Yun used it of economic policy at a State Council meeting in April 1950, but it has always been associated with Deng. It became a rule for the whole reform: experiment locally, adopt what works, avoid theoretical grand plans. Xiaogang, then Anhui, then nationally. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_river_by_touching_the_stones.

question: Deng Xiaoping began his reforms in 1978, and the World Bank later counted how many Chinese rose out of extreme poverty between 1981 and 2015. Readers in the line of Mises and Hayek call those reforms the biggest test the argument over socialist calculation has ever had. What is the World Bank's figure?
answer: About 800 million
choices: About 800 million
About 80 million
About 400 million
About 250 million
context: World Bank data show roughly 800 million Chinese moved above the extreme-poverty line between 1981 and 2015 as market pricing extended sector by sector. This is the largest sustained poverty reduction ever measured. Source: worldbank.org China country data.

question: Deng Xiaoping's reforms brought market prices to some parts of China's economy and left others in the planners' grip. Economists who compared the sectors through the 1980s and 1990s found a clear pattern in which grew fastest and which slowest. Which parts grew slowest?
answer: The state-owned banks and factories the planners still ran
choices: The state-owned banks and factories the planners still ran
The rural family farms working their own plots again
The coastal export factories inside the special zones
The township and village workshops in the countryside
context: Chinese state-owned banks and SOEs continued to underperform the private and township-enterprise sectors through the 1990s and 2000s. The Austrian reading of Chinese growth attributes it to the market-priced sectors, not to state industrial policy. Source: mises.org/library/china-and-austrian-school.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto built Bitcoin, launched in 2009, to add a fresh block of transactions about every ten minutes. Some blocks arrive in a minute and others take thirty, and miners join and leave all the time, yet the long-run average holds near ten. What keeps it there?
answer: The difficulty adjustment
choices: The difficulty adjustment
The halving schedule
The proof-of-stake vote
The Federal Reserve's discount rate
context: Every node in the Bitcoin network computes the difficulty target identically from the timestamps of recent blocks. It is Bitcoin's homeostatic clock. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: A Bitcoin node reaches a scheduled checkpoint and measures how long the last batch of blocks actually took, using the blocks' own timestamps. Then it turns the mining puzzle harder or easier, so blocks keep coming about every ten minutes however many miners join or leave. The check comes after a fixed number of blocks. How many?
answer: 2,016 blocks
choices: 2,016 blocks
1,000 blocks
10,080 blocks
210,000 blocks
context: 2,016 blocks equals two weeks at exactly ten minutes per block. If blocks came faster than expected, difficulty rises; slower, it falls. The 210,000-block figure is the halving interval (roughly four years), a separate protocol constant.

question: New miners switch on their machines, and a batch of Bitcoin blocks arrives faster than the ten-minute pace calls for. At the next scheduled retarget every node in the network applies the same rule and responds the same way. What does the network do?
answer: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
choices: Increases difficulty so miners must find hashes with more leading zeros
Rewards existing miners with a one-time bonus in newly minted coin
Reduces the block-reward payout for the next 2,016 blocks
Shuts out the newest miners until the next retarget
context: The target hash gets a smaller numerical value, making valid hashes rarer. Miners then take longer per block on average, restoring the ten-minute cadence. If blocks had been slow, the adjustment goes the other way. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin.

question: Beijing outlawed Bitcoin mining across China in May and June 2021, and about half of all the computing power securing the network went dark within weeks. Bitcoin's rules call for a fresh block about every ten minutes, but blocks began arriving well behind that pace. What did Bitcoin do next?
answer: At the July 3, 2021 retarget, difficulty fell about 28 percent, its biggest drop ever
choices: At the July 3, 2021 retarget, difficulty fell about 28 percent, its biggest drop ever
The remaining miners voted to switch the algorithm to proof-of-stake
The Bitcoin Core developers issued an emergency patch changing the block interval
Coinbase paused all Bitcoin trading until the network recovered
context: Every node computed the adjustment independently and identically. Blocks returned to a ten-minute cadence immediately after the retarget. Chinese miners then physically relocated to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_China.

question: A high-school student asks how Bitcoin kept its ten-minute pace in July 2021, when half the world's miners had just been forced offline, and the blocks soon came back on time. A Hayekian economist points to one property of the network. Which property?
answer: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
choices: The homeostatic self-correction of a rule-based network that requires no human decision-maker
The discretionary override of a benevolent central authority
The one-off emergency bailout mechanism triggered by a supervisory committee
The centrally-planned reallocation of hashing capacity by a global regulator
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument is exactly this: no central agency could set the correct difficulty target in real time across a global mining industry it did not know intimately. A rule-based system aggregates the dispersed information automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: Displaced miners shipped their machines out of China after the mining ban of mid-2021, to Kazakhstan, Texas and elsewhere, and plugged them back in on new ground. By March 2022, about nine months after the ban, what had the network's total mining power done?
answer: Recovered to a new all-time high
choices: Recovered to a new all-time high
Remained roughly half of pre-ban levels
Fallen further as miners quit permanently
Migrated entirely to a single US state
context: Displaced Chinese miners physically shipped their hardware to Texas, Kazakhstan, Iceland, and Paraguay. The rule-based difficulty adjustment absorbed a 50-percent supply shock in weeks and then handled the recovery just as automatically. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_mining.

question: Roman shoppers headed to market in 301 AD under Diocletian's new edict, which set top prices on bread, wine, olive oil, boots and a thousand more goods. His mint had been cheapening the silver coin for decades. Within weeks the same thing happened in market after market. What did the shoppers find?
answer: Empty shelves and shortages
choices: Empty shelves and shortages
Cheaper goods for everyone
Prices rising openly anyway
Nothing changed at all
context: Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) is the best-documented price control of the ancient world; fragments of it survive on stone across the eastern empire. Sellers withdrew goods rather than sell at a loss: they hoarded, sold only to family, or carried goods to black markets in other cities.

question: Diocletian issued a price edict across the Roman Empire in 301 AD that capped the price of over a thousand goods and wages: bread, olive oil, wagon wheels and haircuts among them. What penalty did it set for selling above the ceiling?
answer: Death
choices: Death
Exile
Slavery
A fine of ten denarii
context: The edict's own text prescribed death for sellers exceeding the fixed prices. Enforcement was uneven but the threat was real; the historian Lactantius records that 'much blood was shed for the sake of small and cheap things'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: Murray Rothbard and Thomas Sowell both hold up Diocletian's price edict of 301 as the classic case of a mistake rulers keep making. For decades Rome had paid its soldiers by mixing cheap metal into the silver denarius, and prices kept climbing. Whom did the edict's own preamble blame for the rising prices?
answer: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
choices: The merchants for their 'unbridled fury' and 'greed'
The Sassanid Persians for currency counterfeiting
The African provinces for hoarding grain
The Christian communities for boycotting Roman markets
context: The edict's preamble cursed the sellers for their 'unbridled fury' and greed rather than admit that the emperor's own mint had cheapened the coin. Rothbard and Sowell treat it as the archetype: currency debasement raises prices; the state blames sellers; a ceiling is imposed; goods disappear; the ceiling is eventually withdrawn.

question: Lactantius, a Christian writer who had lived through Diocletian's persecution, described the grim results of the emperor's price edict of 301 in his book On the Deaths of the Persecutors. Diocletian himself stepped down in 305 and is the only Roman emperor who gave up the throne of his own will. Roughly how long after the edict was issued did the government quietly let it lapse?
answer: About a decade
choices: About a decade
About a century
About a year
About a millennium
context: The edict was allowed to fall into disuse within roughly a decade. Diocletian himself abdicated in 305 AD -- the only Roman emperor to voluntarily step down. Source: Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum c. 315 AD.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to look for two things behind every law: what is seen, the obvious surface result, and what is not seen, the result hiding behind it. Turned on Diocletian's price edict of 301, which capped the prices of more than a thousand goods, the seen is the low legal price carved into the stone tablet in the market square. What is the unseen part?
answer: The seller who hoards rather than sell at a loss, and the hungry buyer
choices: The seller who hoards rather than sell at a loss, and the hungry buyer
The soldiers whose pay now buys more bread
The merchants who grow rich selling at the legal price
The farmers who plant more wheat to meet demand
context: Bastiat's method applied 15 centuries earlier: the visible ceiling gives the illusion of low prices; the invisible cost is the goods that disappear because their sale at the ceiling would be at a loss. Source: bastiat.org.

question: An archaeologist fits together fragments of the stone tablets that carried Diocletian's price edict of 301, pieces scattered across the eastern Mediterranean. From such fragments scholars have pieced back hundreds of the edict's price entries. Where is the most complete surviving copy?
answer: Aphrodisias in Turkey
choices: Aphrodisias in Turkey
Delphi in Greece
Palmyra in Syria
Ravenna in Italy
context: Aphrodisias, in southwestern Turkey, has the fullest surviving copy of the edict inscribed on stone. Archaeologists reconstructed hundreds of specific price lines from the fragments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisias.

question: Elizabeth Warren, a Harvard professor at the time, championed a brand-new federal agency written into the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010. Its job was to police the loans families depend on most: home mortgages, credit cards and payday loans. What kind of agency was it?
answer: A consumer financial protection agency
choices: A consumer financial protection agency
A bank-charter licensing agency
A housing-finance regulator
A public-company accounting overseer
context: The CFPB was the signature institutional creation of Dodd-Frank, championed by then-Harvard-professor Elizabeth Warren. It absorbed consumer-protection authority previously spread across the Fed, OCC, FDIC and other agencies. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Consumer_Financial_Protection_Bureau.

question: Paul Volcker, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve, helped design a new banking rule after the crisis of 2008, and Congress wrote it into the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 under his name. What principle stood behind the Volcker Rule?
answer: Banks with government-insured deposits should not gamble with those deposits
choices: Banks with government-insured deposits should not gamble with those deposits
Banks should hire more government inspectors
Banks should pay their executives less
Banks should offer higher interest rates on savings accounts
context: Named for Paul Volcker (Fed chairman 1979-87), who argued that banks with federal deposit insurance should not be running hedge-fund-style trading books. The rule took years to finalize and became a byword for the compliance-cost burden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Volcker_Rule.

question: A small-town banker watched Congress pass the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, when America had about seven thousand commercial banks. In the years that followed, most of the vanished banks were bought up by bigger competitors, not shut down. How many commercial banks were left by 2023?
answer: About 4,700 -- down by roughly a third
choices: About 4,700 -- down by roughly a third
About 6,200 -- barely changed
About 3,000 -- down by more than half
About 5,900 -- down by only a small amount
context: A decline of roughly one third in thirteen years. Consolidation into regional and money-center banks accelerated after 2010; most community banks were acquired rather than closed. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: A banker filed papers for a brand-new local bank before the Dodd-Frank Act passed in 2010; regulators were then approving about 130 such start-ups a year. They had also begun taking longer to vet new banks in 2009. In the six years after the law, how many new banks won charters each year?
answer: Fewer than six per year
choices: Fewer than six per year
About thirty per year
About eighty per year
About a hundred per year
context: The 2022 Congressional Research Service report (R47014) documents the collapse. In 2009 regulators had also raised the de novo review period from three years to seven years and stiffened capital requirements for new-bank applicants. Source: congress.gov/crs-product/R47014.

question: Suppose Congress orders every bank to take on five more lawyers. JPMorgan spreads their pay over sixty million customers; a hometown bank serving a few hundred families pays the same salaries. Which bank feels the rule more?
answer: The small bank
choices: The small bank
The giant bank
Both feel it equally
Neither bank much
context: Charles Calomiris of Columbia Business School and Stephen Haber made this the standard critique in Fragile by Design (Princeton 2014). Compliance-officer and legal staffing is largely a fixed cost per institution, so it consumes a much larger share of a small bank's revenue. A law signed May 24, 2018 by President Trump, sponsored by Senator Mike Crapo, was a bipartisan concession that fixed compliance costs on small banks had shrunk community banking without protecting the system from another 2008.

question: A crowd at the American Enterprise Institute heard Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve, worry on December 5, 1996, that stock prices had climbed too high. He summed up the investors' mood in a two-word phrase famous ever since. What was the phrase?
answer: Irrational exuberance
choices: Irrational exuberance
Speculative excess
Bubble psychology
Investor overconfidence
context: Greenspan's December 5 1996 speech to the American Enterprise Institute used 'irrational exuberance' to describe asset markets. The warning was widely quoted; the policy response was minimal. Source: Grokipedia 'Irrational exuberance' (2026-09-05).

question: A trader who bought into the Nasdaq, the index of technology shares, at its peak in March 2000 watched it slide until October 2002, as dot-com firm after dot-com firm went under. How much of its value had the index lost from top to bottom?
answer: About three-quarters of its value
choices: About three-quarters of its value
About one-third of its value
About one-tenth of its value
About half of its value
context: The NASDAQ fell from 5,048 to 1,114 -- a 78% decline over 31 months. Trillions of dollars of paper wealth vanished and hundreds of dot-com companies failed. Source: Grokipedia 'Dot-com bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued that when a central bank pushes interest rates below what a real market would set, it lures people into borrowing they cannot sustain, and the boom must end in a bust. Their followers read America's run from 2001 to 2008 as one chain, and they add that no central bank escapes the cycle without letting the bad investments be liquidated. Which chain do they trace?
answer: The 2001-03 rate cuts, made to cure one crash, inflated the bubble behind 2008
choices: The 2001-03 rate cuts, made to cure one crash, inflated the bubble behind 2008
The 2001-03 rate cuts had no relationship to the housing bubble that followed
The 2001-03 rate cuts prevented all subsequent financial crises
The 2001-03 rate cuts caused a sustained fall in commodity prices
context: The Austrian reading: each bubble is caused by the monetary response to the previous one. The 1990s cheap money produced the dot-com bubble; the 2001-03 cheap money produced the housing bubble. The boom-bust cycle is not an outside shock to a stable economy but generated by discretionary monetary policy, and trying to prevent each bust by easing produces a larger next one.

question: Christopher Foote, Kristopher Gerardi and Paul Willen, economists at the Federal Reserve Banks of Boston and Atlanta, combed through the subprime mortgage records after the housing crash of 2007 and 2008. In 2012 they asked why so many people had made choices that went so badly. What did they find the boom had fed on most?
answer: A shared belief that house prices would keep rising
choices: A shared belief that house prices would keep rising
Lenders deceiving borrowers who misread their loans
Complex new mortgage products nobody could price
Foreign savings flooding into American bonds
context: Foote, Gerardi and Willen, 'Why Did So Many People Make So Many Ex Post Bad Decisions? The Causes of the Foreclosure Crisis' (2012), argued that borrowers and investors acted reasonably given overly optimistic beliefs about house prices, and rejected the popular story that industry insiders had deceived uninformed borrowers. Source: https://ideas.repec.org/p/fip/fedbpp/12-2.html.

question: Alan Greenspan warned in a speech of December 5, 1996, that investors might be bidding stocks beyond what company earnings could justify, and over the next year the Fed raised its rate only once, by a quarter point. The boom ran on, and in March 2000 the market crashed. What lesson does the episode teach about central bankers?
answer: A chair who warns of a bubble but barely acts has in effect endorsed it
choices: A chair who warns of a bubble but barely acts has in effect endorsed it
A chair's warning alone is enough to deflate a bubble safely
Central banks have no tools to move prices in a bubble
Words from a chair work better than any change in rates
context: Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' warning became famous because the Fed did so little to follow through: one quarter-point rise in March 1997, then cuts in the autumn of 1998. Austrian critics say markets read that as a green light. Source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket_archive.htm.

question: East German planners ran short of sheet steel for the little Trabant built at Zwickau, so the car got a Duroplast body, a hard plastic stiffened with waste cotton: cheap, light and rustproof. What does that improvised body show?
answer: No small group can plan every material a country needs
choices: No small group can plan every material a country needs
Planners can replace anything that runs short
Plastic had proved stronger than steel
East Germany led the world in plastics
context: Duroplast was phenol resin from the East German dye industry reinforced with recycled cotton waste: cheap, light, rustproof and made from materials the country could get without hard currency. Austrian economists read the improvisation as the limit of planning: no small group can arrange every material a whole country needs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to look past the seen, the obvious surface fact, and hunt for the unseen behind it. East Germany set the price of its little Trabant so low that, on paper, any worker could afford one. If that cheap sticker was the seen price, what was the unseen one?
answer: A wait of a decade or more, and used cars dearer than new
choices: A wait of a decade or more, and used cars dearer than new
The hard currency spent importing its parts
The environmental cost of two-cycle engines
The cost of yearly repairs at state garages
context: The visible low price hid an invisible time-cost: the waiting list often ran to a decade or more (up to thirteen years by one count), and families sometimes signed up when a baby was born. A secondhand Trabant sold for more than twice the price of a new one, because a buyer could have it today. The waiting list was the real price. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.
