question: An East German family drove home a new Trabant in the 1980s, a smoky two-stroke car built around essentially the 1957 engine. Its engineers had drawn up newer models more than once, and the state rejected every one. In the Austrian reading, why could the state get away with that?
answer: No rival maker could enter and win its buyers away
choices: No rival maker could enter and win its buyers away
Buyers loved the old design and wanted no change
Western patents blocked any newer engine design
Soviet rules barred East Germany from new models
context: Zwickau's engineers built prototypes of more modern successors, but the East German government rejected each one, citing shortages. With no rival maker allowed into the market, buyers had nowhere else to go, so nothing forced a change. Trabants ran on essentially the same two-stroke engine until a Volkswagen engine arrived in 1990, a year before production ended in April 1991. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: Thousands of little Trabants puttered across into West Berlin once East German guards stood back on November 9, 1989. Within months East Germans could buy whatever car they could afford. What happened to the Trabant?
answer: Buyers switched to used Western cars and sales collapsed
choices: Buyers switched to used Western cars and sales collapsed
Its waiting list grew longer than ever
West Germans bought it up as a cheap second car
Its price doubled as demand spread west
context: Once the border opened, Volkswagens and other Western cars, many of them secondhand, poured into the East, and there was no place left for the Trabant. Sales collapsed, and the last model, the Trabant 1.1 with a Volkswagen engine, was dropped in April 1991. Photographs of Trabants at the checkpoints became one of the symbols of East Germany's collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabant.

question: Workers at Zwickau built Trabants for more than thirty years around essentially the same two-stroke engine the car had started out with in 1957. Austrian economists read three of their reasoning moves into that frozen design, one of them Bastiat's seen and unseen in the cheap sticker price. Which other two does it show?
answer: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
choices: The knowledge problem plus the incentive-to-improve problem
The Cantillon effect plus the Fisher effect
The Kondratiev cycle plus the Kuznets curve
The Phillips curve plus Okun's law
context: The knowledge problem: planners cannot know when a design needs updating. The incentive problem: with no competition, no one has a reason to bear the cost of a redesign. Together they froze the design for more than thirty years. Source: mises.org/library/east-germany.

question: An Austrian economist of thirty-nine brought out an essay in German in 1920. In English it is called Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth, and it started a debate that ran for decades. Who wrote it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Mises (born 1881) was 39 in 1920, working as chief economist for the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Hayek was still a 21-year-old student who would later attend Mises's private seminar. Boehm-Bawerk had died in 1914. Schumpeter was a contemporary Austrian but held Keynesian-adjacent views on money. Source: Wikipedia, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises asked in 1920 not whether socialism, with the state owning every factory, farm and mine, was cruel or kind, but whether such a system could function at all. He pressed the point again in a 1922 book whose one-word title named the system itself. What did he argue?
answer: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
choices: That rational economic calculation under socialism is impossible
That socialist regimes will always turn to political violence
That socialism destroys the incentive to work hard
That planners will inevitably use their power to enrich themselves
context: Mises deliberately set aside every other objection, laziness and corruption included, to isolate a technical one: without market prices for capital goods, a planner has no way to compare the cost of alternatives. It is not that planning is unwise; it is that no rational plan can be drawn up at all. In 1922 he expanded the argument into Die Gemeinwirtschaft, translated in 1936 simply as Socialism.

question: A Soviet planner in 1925 is deciding whether to lay a new railway line in rolled steel or in aluminum. Both are available, both would work, and each pulls labor and raw material from other uses. By Ludwig von Mises's argument of 1920, the planner cannot choose between them rationally. What exactly is missing?
answer: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
choices: Exchange-generated prices for the capital goods involved
A larger central-planning bureau with more statisticians
Better labor-hour accounting for each metal
A more accurate five-year forecast of demand
context: Prices arise only when privately-owned goods change hands. Abolish private ownership of the means of production, and iron ore and aluminum ore are no longer exchanged -- they are merely moved from one state enterprise to another. Without money prices, there is nothing to compare. More statisticians, better labor-hour books, and better forecasts all presuppose a common unit of value the planner does not have. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: Friedrich Engels promised that socialist bookkeeping would be simple: society could just add up the hours of work that went into a steam engine or a bushel of wheat. Ludwig von Mises quoted the passage in 1920 and rejected it. What reasoning move did he press against Engels?
answer: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
choices: That labor hours cannot capture how scarce the different material inputs are
That workers will always misreport how many hours they worked
That machines age at different rates, so hours-per-output changes
That some labor is skilled and some unskilled
context: Two goods can each embody ten hours of labor, yet the first may swallow scarce iron ore while the second uses abundant clay -- the labor count is identical, the real cost is not. Only exchange-set prices reflect scarcity across all inputs at once. The skilled/unskilled point was actually granted by Marx himself and does not touch the calculation problem. Source: mises.org/online-book/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth/3.

question: Friedrich Hayek recast Ludwig von Mises's argument in 1945, in a paper for the American Economic Review. Prices, he wrote, boil the private knowledge of millions down into signals no planner could ever collect. What did he title the paper?
answer: The Use of Knowledge in Society
choices: The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretence of Knowledge
Economics and Knowledge
The Meaning of Competition
context: Published September 1945 in the American Economic Review, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' is now the most-cited paper in the whole Austrian tradition. 'Economics and Knowledge' was Hayek's 1937 warm-up; 'The Meaning of Competition' was his 1946 follow-up; 'The Pretence of Knowledge' was his 1974 Nobel lecture. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: Robert Heilbroner wrote on the failure of the planned economies in a 1990 article for The New Yorker. Soviet planners had fixed some 22 million prices at their peak, yet shops stood empty of staples while depots overflowed with things no one would buy. What did Heilbroner and other Western economists conclude?
answer: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
choices: That Mises's 1920 calculation argument had been vindicated
That Keynesian demand management would have saved the East
That the Soviet failure was due chiefly to a shortage of computers
That the fault lay only with Stalin's personal cruelty, not with planning
context: Heilbroner wrote in 1990: 'Mises was right.' The other three explanations were all offered during the Cold War and all set aside once the archives opened: computing power was irrelevant if the prices being computed did not track real scarcity; the same shortages appeared in every planned economy, not just Stalin's. Source: econlib.org/the-collapse-of-the-soviet-union-and-the-continued-relevance-of-ludwig-von-mises; fee.org/articles/the-soviets-tried-to-run-an-economy-without-market-prices.

question: Karl Marx would soon argue that workers and factory owners must fight as class enemies until one side wins. Frédéric Bastiat, studying the same free markets in the 1840s, reached the opposite verdict. What was Bastiat's idea about how people's interests fit together?
answer: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
choices: Interests in a free society are naturally harmonious rather than antagonistic
Interests in any society always trend toward violent revolution
Interests are always aligned only under state central planning
Interests are unknowable and unpredictable in every case
context: Bastiat argued that when exchange is voluntary, one party's gain does not require another's loss, so class interests are not fundamentally opposed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Frédéric Bastiat told of two diamonds, equally useful, in a famous passage of Economic Harmonies: one found by chance in a mountain stream, the other dug from a mine after years of hard labor. Buyers want both alike. What did Bastiat say the two share equally?
answer: Value
choices: Value
Weight
Origin
Reservation price
context: The diamond example: value depends on the service rendered to the user, not on labor spent producing the good. This move anticipated Menger's 1871 subjective-value revolution. Source: bastiat.org/en/harmonies.html.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in 1945 that prices let millions of strangers across the world coordinate their work, with no central planner giving orders. Bastiat's diamonds had pointed the same way nearly a century before. Why, on Hayek's account, does that coordination work?
answer: Each price carries news no single planner could know
choices: Each price carries news no single planner could know
Each price is fixed by experts who study the market
Each price simply adds up the labor put into a good
Each price follows orders from a central bank
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' made the same point about price signals aggregating dispersed information -- ninety-five years after Bastiat. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Prosper Paillottet gathered his late friend Frédéric Bastiat's drafts and fragments into an expanded edition of Economic Harmonies in 1851. Tuberculosis had killed Bastiat in Rome on Christmas Eve 1850, while he was still revising the book he had begun in Paris in the late 1840s. How many chapters had Bastiat finished?
answer: Ten
choices: Ten
Two
Twenty
Fifty
context: Bastiat completed ten chapters and drafted portions of ten more; Prosper Paillottet edited the drafts into an expanded 1851 second edition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: Fire takes a farmer's barn, and the man next door says that at least the carpenters will have work. A follower of Frédéric Bastiat grants that they will be paid, then points to the new plow the farmer's savings were meant for, which will now never be bought or built. What did Bastiat call this habit of mind?
answer: The seen and the unseen
choices: The seen and the unseen
The invisible hand
Comparative advantage
Marginal utility
context: Bastiat's name for the habit comes from his 1850 essay Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen, whose own example is a broken shop window. In the barn story the carpenters' pay is seen and the plow that is never bought is not. The invisible hand is Adam Smith's image, comparative advantage is David Ricardo's, and marginal utility belongs to the economists of the 1870s.

question: Frédéric Bastiat published the first series of his short satires in Paris in 1845 and the second in January 1848: thirty-nine essays, each setting up a protectionist or socialist argument from the French Chamber in its best form, then knocking it down. What is the collection's short title?
answer: Economic Sophisms
choices: Economic Sophisms
Economic Harmonies
The Law
Cobden and the League
context: Sophismes economiques (Guillaumin, 1845 and 1848) is Bastiat's satirical corpus, comprising 39 short essays across two series. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: A carpenter writes to France's minister of commerce in a satire by Frédéric Bastiat, asking for a little protection of his own: a decree banning one tool from the shaping of beams, so that work now done in an hour would take three. Which tool does he want banned?
answer: The sharp hatchet
choices: The sharp hatchet
The steam-powered saw
The foreign-made adze
The carpenter's plane
context: Bastiat's 'The Two Hatchets' (Second Series, 1848) is the petition of Jacques Bonhomme, carpenter, to the protectionist minister Cunin-Gridaine: let no beams be used but those shaped by dull hatchets, so that a hundred blows become three hundred. It is a reductio of make-work arguments. Source: econlib.org, Economic Sophisms, Second Series, ch. 3.

question: Frédéric Bastiat put one essay at the head of his first series of satires in 1845. In it he argued that a policy which makes goods dearer has the whole goal of producing backward. What is the essay's title?
answer: Abundance and Scarcity
choices: Abundance and Scarcity
Cause and Effect
Effort and Result
Obstacle and Cause
context: 'Abundance and Scarcity' is the opening essay of the First Series (1845); it clarifies the direction of economic reasoning. Source: bastiat.org/en/es1.html.

question: Frédéric Bastiat turned his short satires of the 1840s on two favorite policies of his day, one beloved of the French left and the other of the right, and used the same method on both. Which pair did the satires attack most often?
answer: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
choices: Make-work schemes and tariffs for domestic producers
Central banking and gold-standard restoration
Personal income tax and corporate income tax
Antitrust regulation and price controls
context: Bastiat's seen/unseen method is applied to left-flavored make-work schemes and right-flavored protective tariffs alike; that even-handedness makes the collection a METHOD text. Source: bastiat.org/en/economic_sophisms.html.

question: A shoemaker cheers when his country shuts out cheap foreign shoes. A tailor across the street, who used to sell the jackets that paid for those imports, loses sales. Which kind of cost does Bastiat teach readers to look for?
answer: The hidden cost paid by many, spread thin enough to overlook
choices: The hidden cost paid by many, spread thin enough to overlook
The cost of the higher wages the shoemakers will now demand
The cost the state pays to police the closed border
The cost to shoemakers of new machines to meet demand
context: Stirling's 1873 English edition, retitled Economic Sophisms, was the standard English text until the FEE editions of the mid-20th century and the Liberty Fund Collected Works of the 2010s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_Sophisms.

question: Nayib Bukele, El Salvador's young president, pushed a law through in 2021 that made Bitcoin legal money in his country, beside the currency it already used. What sets Bitcoin apart from the paper bills in a Salvadoran shopper's pocket?
answer: No government or bank issues it
choices: No government or bank issues it
The US Federal Reserve issues it
It is backed by El Salvador's gold
Its value is fixed to the US dollar
context: The Bitcoin Law passed the Salvadoran Legislative Assembly on June 9 2021 and took effect September 7 2021, making Bitcoin legal tender alongside the US dollar, which had been El Salvador's official currency since 2001. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador.

question: A Salvadoran family spent its last colones in 2001, when El Salvador gave up its own money and took a foreign currency as its official one. Twenty years later Nayib Bukele added Bitcoin beside it. Which currency had El Salvador taken up?
answer: The US dollar
choices: The US dollar
The euro
The Mexican peso
The Central American peso
context: El Salvador dollarized in 2001, abandoning its colon; the dollar remained the official currency after the 2021 Bitcoin adoption -- Bitcoin was added ALONGSIDE the dollar, not as a replacement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_El_Salvador.

question: A Salvadoran working in the United States wired part of his pay home to his family, as Salvadorans abroad did with billions of dollars every year. El Salvador's Bitcoin law of September 2021 was meant to help workers like him. What did the government hope it would do for them?
answer: Let them send money home faster and more cheaply
choices: Let them send money home faster and more cheaply
Let them earn interest on savings sent home
Let them pay their US taxes in bitcoin instead
Let them buy land at home without a bank loan
context: Nayib Bukele, elected 2019, announced the Bitcoin plan at the Bitcoin 2021 conference in Miami in June 2021 and pushed the Bitcoin Law through the assembly within days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nayib_Bukele.

question: A corner-shop owner in El Salvador took a tiny payment on his phone through a free national wallet the government launched in 2021. It ran on the Lightning Network, a faster layer of payments built on top of Bitcoin, so small sums cost little to send. What was the wallet called?
answer: Chivo
choices: Chivo
Colibri
Cabal
Cortez
context: Chivo (Salvadoran slang for 'cool') was distributed to every adult who signed up, with a $30 Bitcoin signing bonus. It had significant early bugs but did drive initial mass adoption. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivo_(wallet).

question: A Salvadoran farmer downloaded the new national Bitcoin wallet in September 2021 and found a sign-up gift of free bitcoin waiting for him. Millions downloaded the app in the first weeks, even though it was badly buggy at first. How big was the gift?
answer: $30 in Bitcoin
choices: $30 in Bitcoin
$300 in Bitcoin
$3 in Bitcoin
$100 in Bitcoin
context: The $30 signing bonus (paid at Bitcoin's market rate at the moment of registration) was intended to hard-launch wallet adoption; it drove millions of downloads in the first weeks. Source: reuters.com (September 2021 rollout coverage).

question: Officials of the International Monetary Fund, the global lender based in Washington, urged El Salvador to abandon the Bitcoin law it had passed in 2021. Nayib Bukele refused and kept going. What lay at the root of the Fund's objection?
answer: That its price swings too wildly to be safe as money
choices: That its price swings too wildly to be safe as money
That its transfers are too slow for daily use
That it cannot be broken into small units
That its software could be switched off by its makers
context: The Fund's staff tied the problem to price: given Bitcoin's high volatility, they wrote in November 2021, making it legal tender carried large risks to consumer protection, financial integrity and financial stability. In January 2022 the Fund's board urged El Salvador to strip Bitcoin of its legal-tender status. El Salvador refused. Source: imf.org (Article IV consultation with El Salvador, January 2022).

question: Nayib Bukele announced in November 2022 that El Salvador would buy bitcoin for its national reserves on a fixed schedule, whatever the price, rather than guess the best moment to buy. He meant to build up the country's holdings steadily. What was the pace?
answer: One Bitcoin per day
choices: One Bitcoin per day
Ten Bitcoin per week
One Bitcoin per hour
One Bitcoin per week
context: Bukele announced in November 2022 that El Salvador would buy one BTC per day into national reserves; treasury holdings grew accordingly over 2022-2024. Source: bloomberg.com (El Salvador BTC treasury coverage, 2022-24).

question: Nayib Bukele planned to mine Bitcoin at El Salvador's Tecapa volcano, and in November 2021 he unveiled plans for a Bitcoin City by the Conchagua volcano, to be funded by Bitcoin bonds. Where was the power for the mining computers to come from?
answer: Steam from the volcano's heat driving generators
choices: Steam from the volcano's heat driving generators
Solar panels across the volcano's sunny slopes
Wind turbines along the crater's rim
Dams on the rivers that run off the volcano
context: Bukele's plan was geothermal: steam from the volcanoes' heat drives generators, and their electricity runs the mining computers, starting at the Tecapa volcano. Bitcoin City, near the Conchagua volcano in La Union, was announced in November 2021, to be powered the same way and funded by Bitcoin-denominated bonds; building has been slow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_City.

question: A professor from Indiana University went out to lobster harbors and the high pastures of the Swiss Alps to check a gloomy textbook story about shared land against the real world. That fieldwork won her the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics, the first ever given to a woman. Who was she?
answer: Elinor Ostrom
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Anna Schwartz
Joan Robinson
Deirdre McCloskey
context: Elinor Ostrom (1933-2012) won the 2009 economics Nobel with Oliver Williamson 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.' She was the first woman to win in the field. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom.

question: Elinor Ostrom published a book in 1990 full of real cases from around the world: villages sharing pastures, fisheries and irrigation water among their own people. What is the book's main title?
answer: Governing the Commons
choices: Governing the Commons
Understanding Institutional Diversity
Rules, Games, and Common-Pool Resources
Bloomington and the Public Choice
context: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (Cambridge University Press, 1990). Its case studies became the empirical spine of her Nobel citation. Source: cambridge.org/core/books/governing-the-commons.

question: A herder turns one more cow out onto a pasture open to everyone: the whole gain from that cow is his, while the cost of the extra grazing is shared by all. Garrett Hardin, a biologist, set out this picture in the journal Science in 1968. What did he say becomes of the pasture?
answer: The shared resource gets overused and eventually ruined
choices: The shared resource gets overused and eventually ruined
The herders agree on limits, and the pasture recovers
The richest herder buys out the rest and fences it in
The grass regrows each spring, so no lasting harm is done
context: Garrett Hardin's 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (Science, December 13, 1968) became the standard citation for the pessimistic view. Ostrom argued that Hardin's tragedy was conditional, not inevitable. Source: science.org (Hardin, Science 1968).

question: A Törbel herder drove his cows up to the village's summer pasture in the Swiss Alps, under rules his neighbors had kept for over five centuries. Nobody owned the slopes outright; the herders had written the rules themselves, down to the number of cows each household could send up. Elinor Ostrom studied the village's pastures. What lesson did she draw?
answer: A community can share a resource well if it makes and enforces its own rules
choices: A community can share a resource well if it makes and enforces its own rules
Only private ownership can protect land from overuse
Only government control can protect land from overuse
Shared land always ends up destroyed within a generation
context: Swiss alpine grazing commons (Toerbel and other villages in Valais) have been governed by user-written rules since at least 1483, when Torbel's villagers formally set up an association to regulate their alp; a rule of 1517 let no one send more cows up than he could feed through the winter. Ostrom found such commons held together by local rules and social pressure the users themselves invent and enforce, with fines, gossip and lost privileges; her case studies documented a third path beside state ownership and privatization: user groups governing the resource themselves, given the right institutional design.

question: An outsider dropped his lobster traps in water a harbor gang had claimed on a rocky stretch of the American coast, and before long his buoy lines were cut. Each gang carved up the water among its own boats, with no state fisheries police in charge, and Elinor Ostrom held the fishery up as a commons its users governed themselves. Which state's coast was it?
answer: Maine
choices: Maine
Massachusetts
Oregon
Alaska
context: The Maine lobster fishery's informal harbor gangs enforce territorial boundaries with cut buoy lines and social pressure. The anthropologist James Acheson described them in The Lobster Gangs of Maine (1988), and Ostrom drew on his work. Source: Acheson, The Lobster Gangs of Maine (University Press of New England, 1988).

question: Elinor and Vincent Ostrom founded a research institute at Indiana University in Bloomington in 1973, where Elinor taught for decades. It trained scholar after scholar, and its way of working came to be called the Bloomington School. What did they name it?
answer: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
choices: The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis
The Center for the Study of Public Choice
The Bureau of Applied Political Economy
The Institute for Constitutional Governance
context: The Ostroms founded the Workshop at IU Bloomington in 1973. Its research program became known as the 'Bloomington School' of institutional analysis. Source: ostromworkshop.indiana.edu.

question: Garrett Hardin issued his famous warning about shared pastures in 1968, and Elinor Ostrom, for all her cases of commons kept healthy for centuries, refused to say she had proved him wrong. His tragedy was real, she argued. How did she describe the link between his prediction and her fieldwork?
answer: Hardin's tragedy is a conditional outcome, not an inevitable one
choices: Hardin's tragedy is a conditional outcome, not an inevitable one
Hardin's tragedy applies only to fisheries
Hardin's paper contained a mathematical error
Hardin's tragedy holds only where users lack literacy
context: Ostrom argued Hardin identified a real failure mode that occurs when users cannot communicate, monitor, or enforce rules. Her cases showed that when those conditions are present, tragedy is avoided. She did not deny his mechanism; she conditioned it. Source: Ostrom, 'A General Framework for Analyzing Sustainability of Social-Ecological Systems' (Science, 2009).

question: The emperor Julian rode into Antioch in the summer of 362 to ready his war on Persia and found bread short and costly. Eager to win the poor's favor, he decreed a low fixed price for all the grain sold in the city. What happened to the grain supply?
answer: Merchants and farmers held their grain back
choices: Merchants and farmers held their grain back
Merchants rushed in more grain to meet demand
Grain sold steadily at the new price all winter
Rival cities sent grain to win the emperor's favor
context: Antioch's merchants and the farmers around it held their grain back rather than sell at a loss. Julian blamed their greed, but the cap itself caused the shortage: hauling grain to Antioch now cost more than the law let sellers charge. The imperial grain he shipped in was quickly bought up, and over the following months merchants stopped sending grain to the city at all.

question: Antioch's citizens had jeered at the emperor Julian's philosopher's beard, and early in 363 he answered them with Misopogon, the 'Beard-Hater,' a pamphlet blaming the empty grain shops on the sellers' greed; he never lifted his cap on grain. Opponents of price caps give his mistake a name. What is it?
answer: Blame the messenger for the message
choices: Blame the messenger for the message
Rescind the policy at the first sign of failure
Introduce competing state agencies
Return to gold-backed money
context: Julian saw the empty shelves and blamed the sellers' character rather than his own ceiling. Critics of price controls call the move blaming the messenger: an empty shelf is news that the legal price is too low, and the seller who carries the news is the one punished.

question: Diocletian fixed maximum prices across the Roman Empire in 301, and the emperor Julian capped the price of grain in Antioch in 362. Austrian economists pair the two rulers because, they argue, one pattern keeps returning, from Richard Nixon's price controls of 1971 to Venezuela's after 2013. What is the pattern?
answer: Ruler sets a low price; goods vanish; ruler blames the seller
choices: Ruler sets a low price; goods vanish; ruler blames the seller
Ruler sets a low price; supply rises; consumers benefit
Ruler sets a high price; demand falls; producers benefit
Ruler sets a high price; foreign supply floods in
context: The three steps of cap, disappearance and blame show up with Diocletian in 301, Julian in 362, Nixon's controls of 1971 and Venezuela after 2013. The reasoning error is not modern.

question: An Albanian farmer still steers his plow around a little concrete dome. Enver Hoxha, sure that foreign armies might invade any day, had pillboxes like it poured across his country from the late 1960s. Roughly how many, among 2.8 million people?
answer: About 173,000
choices: About 173,000
About 5,000
About 30,000
About 900,000
context: The usual count is about 173,000 bunkers, roughly one for every sixteen Albanians, built between the late 1960s and the 1980s for an invasion that never came; many still stand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Albanian_bunkers.

question: Enver Hoxha suspected everyone, the rulers who shared his creed included, and he broke with three powerful patrons in turn, every split leaving his country lonelier, until it was the most isolated in Europe. Which sequence of breaks did he lead?
answer: With Yugoslavia in 1948, with the USSR in 1961, and with China in 1978
choices: With Yugoslavia in 1948, with the USSR in 1961, and with China in 1978
With China in 1949, with Cuba in 1965, and with Yugoslavia in 1978
With North Korea in 1953, with the USSR in 1963, and with Romania in 1980
With Poland in 1956, with East Germany in 1968, and with Bulgaria in 1975
context: Hoxha sided with Stalin against Tito in 1948, with Mao against Khrushchev in 1961, and with orthodoxy against Deng's Reform and Opening in 1978. Each rupture left him more isolated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enver_Hoxha.

question: A priest in Albania watched his church become a warehouse in 1967, when Enver Hoxha closed every mosque, church and monastery in the land, jailed the clergy and outlawed prayer even at home. With that decree Albania claimed a first in world history. What was it?
answer: The first officially atheist state
choices: The first officially atheist state
The first state with no state church
The first officially secular state in Europe
The first state to ban religion from schools
context: Hoxha declared Albania the world's first atheist state in 1967. Secular states such as France and the United States, which keep church and government apart, are far older, but none had declared itself officially atheist. Source: grokipedia.com/page/People%27s_Socialist_Republic_of_Albania.

question: A man in Enver Hoxha's Albania told a joke about the dictator at dinner, and a neighbor paid by the secret police, the Sigurimi, reported him; a joke like that could cost years in prison. The Sigurimi held a file on nearly every family. What is the purpose of watching on that scale?
answer: To make people afraid to speak, so no group can organize
choices: To make people afraid to speak, so no group can organize
To catch ordinary thieves and smugglers faster
To plan how much food each town would need
To find skilled workers for the five-year plans
context: Sigurimi (short for Drejtoria e Sigurimit te Shtetit, 'Directorate of State Security') is the Albanian analogue of Romania's Securitate, East Germany's Stasi, and Czechoslovakia's StB. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sigurimi.

question: A scholar worked through the files of the secret police and the prison camps of Hoxha's Albania after the regime fell in the early 1990s, and found an honest death count hard to reach. Why is the count so hard, even with the papers in hand?
answer: Regimes hide deaths, mislabel prisoners and burn files
choices: Regimes hide deaths, mislabel prisoners and burn files
Too few scholars can read the Albanian files
The camps wrote their records in secret code
Most of the files rotted in damp storerooms
context: Even with the archives open, the count is hard: regimes like Hoxha's hid deaths, recorded prisoners under false labels and burned files before they lost power. Scholars still count thousands executed for political crimes and tens of thousands sent to labor camps; the toll is small beside the Soviet Union's or China's but large for so small a country.

question: Ramiz Alia, Enver Hoxha's successor, chose in December 1990 not to fire on the students marching in Albania's streets, and three months later Albanians cast ballots in their first election with more than one party. Once the frontier opened, they could see what it had hidden. What had the sealed border mostly hidden from them?
answer: How far behind their planned economy had fallen
choices: How far behind their planned economy had fallen
How much better central planning worked than markets
That their neighbors were secretly starving too
That the rulers had been giving away too much foreign aid
context: Alia had been Hoxha's designated heir and party first secretary from 1985. His decision not to shoot the December 1990 student demonstrators ended the regime. The March 1991 elections were the first multi-party vote in Albanian communist history. Source: grokipedia.com/page/History_of_Albania.

question: A student of Frédéric Bastiat stands beside one of Enver Hoxha's concrete bunkers on an Albanian beach, built for an invasion that never came, and asks what is not there beside it. Which reasoning move names what the bunker cost?
answer: Opportunity cost: the houses and schools never built
choices: Opportunity cost: the houses and schools never built
The Laffer curve: high taxes reduced total revenue
The Coase theorem: property rights would have solved the externality
The Phillips curve: unemployment traded off against inflation
context: By the end of the regime Albania had the lowest per-capita income in Europe and the most decayed infrastructure -- and 173,000 bunkers for an invasion that never came. The reasoning move is Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen applied to state investment. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Albanian_bunkers.

question: Timothy May, Eric Hughes and John Gilmore began meeting near San Francisco in the early 1990s to ask who would guard ordinary people's privacy in a wired world. Their answer left out every phone company and every state. What tool did they trust instead?
answer: Encryption that only the receiver can undo
choices: Encryption that only the receiver can undo
Firewalls guarding every home computer
Long passwords changed every week
Meeting only in person, never online
context: Strong encryption scrambles a message so that only the holder of the right key can read it: privacy rests on mathematics, not on any company's or state's promise. Eric Hughes wrote A Cypherpunk's Manifesto on March 9, 1993; Timothy May wrote the earlier Crypto Anarchist Manifesto of 1988. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Eric Hughes sent A Cypherpunk's Manifesto out to his fellow cypherpunks by email on March 9, 1993. Its most quoted line defines privacy in a single sentence. What does that line say privacy is?
answer: The power to reveal oneself selectively to the world
choices: The power to reveal oneself selectively to the world
The right to be left alone in all of one's life
A human right that every free nation recognizes
Freedom from being watched without one's consent
context: Hughes wrote: 'Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.' He defined privacy as choice, not concealment. The right to be let alone is Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis's phrase of 1890. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Eric Hughes's manifesto of March 1993 aimed three words at one kind of privacy campaigner: the man who lectured and published but never released a program that ran. The cypherpunks took the words as their motto. What were they?
answer: 'Cypherpunks write code.'
choices: 'Cypherpunks write code.'
'Code is law.'
'Don't be evil.'
'Trust no one.'
context: 'Cypherpunks write code' is the manifesto's working motto: privacy would exist only if someone actually built and shipped the software. 'Code is law' is Lawrence Lessig's line of 1999, 'Don't be evil' was an early Google motto, and 'Trust no one' was a tagline of The X-Files. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Eric Hughes warned readers of his manifesto not to mix up privacy with a word that sounds close to it. A private matter, he wrote, is one a person would rather the whole world not learn; the other kind is one he wants nobody at all to learn. Which word did he set against privacy?
answer: secrecy
choices: secrecy
anonymity
encryption
freedom of speech
context: Hughes: 'Privacy is not secrecy. A private matter is something one doesn't want the whole world to know, but a secret matter is something one doesn't want anybody to know.' Anonymity, encryption, and free speech are related tools or rights but not what Hughes contrasted here. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Hughes's friends took his manifesto at its word: privacy would exist only if they built the tools themselves, and in the early 1990s they set to work. They wrote encryption programs and designed digital cash for a world of networked computers. Which freedom were they chiefly after?
answer: Sending messages and payments with no one watching
choices: Sending messages and payments with no one watching
Copying software without paying its makers
Getting cheap internet access in every home
Trading stocks with no broker in the middle
context: The cypherpunks' aim, in money as in speech, was to send messages and payments that no one could watch: encryption programs for the first, digital-cash designs for the second. John Gilmore, Sun Microsystems's fifth employee and a co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, hosted the group's mailing list at toad.com. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Hal Finney and his friend Eric Hughes helped build a tool for the cypherpunks in the early 1990s. Each of these servers accepted an email, stripped off the sender's address and forwarded it through a string of other computers, so no one watching could follow it back to the person who wrote it. What were the servers called?
answer: anonymous remailers
choices: anonymous remailers
public-key encryption libraries
mailing-list servers
packet sniffers
context: Hughes and Finney's remailers took in an email, stripped off the sender's address and passed it along a chain of other machines, so an eavesdropper could not trace it back. Encryption libraries such as PGP were written by others (Phil Zimmermann); an ordinary mailing-list server forwards mail but keeps the sender's name; a packet sniffer is a tool for watching traffic, not hiding it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Eric Hughes refused, in his manifesto of 1993, to wait for privacy as a gift. He named the large, faceless bodies that would never hand it over out of kindness, since they were the very ones that wanted to watch and follow ordinary people. Which bodies did he rule out?
answer: governments and corporations
choices: governments and corporations
the mathematics community
the free-software community
internet service providers
context: Hughes explicitly wrote that we cannot expect governments, corporations, or other large faceless organizations to grant us privacy out of their beneficence; we must build it ourselves. Mathematicians, free-software developers, and ISPs were tools or allies, not the actor being ruled out. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto sent out the plan for Bitcoin late in 2008, fifteen years after Eric Hughes's manifesto told cypherpunks to build privacy with their own hands instead of waiting for anyone to grant it. Satoshi carried that playbook through to its end. Which sequence did he follow?
answer: publish a paper, ship working code, deploy a live network, then step aside
choices: publish a paper, ship working code, deploy a live network, then step aside
petition governments to legalize the technology first
sell the technology to a large corporation for integration
form a nonprofit foundation to lobby for adoption
context: Satoshi followed the Hughes pattern precisely: October 2008 paper, January 2009 running network, April 2011 disappearance. Petitioning, corporate sale, and nonprofit lobbying are precisely the paths Hughes ruled out as sources of everyday privacy. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html; Nakamoto white paper 2008.

question: A historian of the cypherpunks, looking back at Eric Hughes's manifesto of 1993, argued that it should be read as a working plan rather than a hope. At its heart sits a three-word motto for coders. Which reasoning move does the historian make about that motto?
answer: That 'cypherpunks write code' is a rule about proof: aspiration without a shipping working tool is not itself a privacy technology at all
choices: That 'cypherpunks write code' is a rule about proof: aspiration without a shipping working tool is not itself a privacy technology at all
That academic publication of privacy research alone is sufficient to protect ordinary users without any actual software being written or deployed
That waiting for privacy-protective legislation to pass is the correct path for cryptographers, and shipping software prematurely is counterproductive
That privacy tools must be sold in a competitive marketplace to be legitimate, and free-of-charge distribution undermines the professionalism of the field
context: The Hughes argument treats shipping software as the only proof that a privacy technology actually exists in the world for ordinary users. Academic publication, legislative advocacy, and commercial sale can all coexist with zero privacy actually reaching users. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: A big American company holds its shareholder meeting, and roughly a quarter of the votes come from just three investment firms. They run the index funds that hold the retirement savings of millions of ordinary people, and the press has nicknamed them the Big Three. Which three are they?
answer: BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street
choices: BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street
Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Morgan Stanley
Fidelity, Schwab, and Wells Fargo
Berkshire Hathaway, Citadel, and Millennium
context: As of the mid-2020s, BlackRock (~$10T+ AUM), Vanguard (~$8T+), and State Street (~$4T+) collectively manage more than $22 trillion and hold roughly 20-25% of the average S&P 500 company's shares. Source: Bebchuk + Hirst, 'The Specter of the Giant Three' (Boston University Law Review, 2019).

question: Larry Fink, head of the giant investment firm BlackRock, pressed companies in his yearly letters to chase climate and other social goals, graded under the label environmental, social and governance (ESG). What happens to a firm's aims once its largest shareholders grade it on a score like that?
answer: Managers chase the score, not just a good, cheap product
choices: Managers chase the score, not just a good, cheap product
Nothing changes, since only profits matter to managers
Only small firms respond, since big ones can ignore it
Scores fade, since customers never look at them
context: ESG labels spread fast through investing from about 2015 to 2022, and how to count 'ESG assets' is disputed. The point is about incentives: once the biggest owners grade a company on a new score, its managers start working to the score, not only to the old job of making a useful product cheaply. Source: Grokipedia 'Environmental, social, and corporate governance.'

question: Lucian Bebchuk and Scott Hirst, two legal scholars, measured the voting power of the three index-fund giants in 2019 for the Boston University Law Review. They titled the paper with a nod to the famous first line of Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto. What did they call it?
answer: The Specter of the Giant Three
choices: The Specter of the Giant Three
The Rise of the Index Titans
The Silent Concentration
The Age of the Asset Manager
context: Bebchuk + Hirst, 'The Specter of the Giant Three' (Boston University Law Review, 2019). The paper documented that Big Three ownership of the S&P 500 had roughly quadrupled since 1998 and would continue growing under passive-fund trends. Source: bu.edu/bulawreview (Bebchuk-Hirst 2019).

question: Managers at a listed firm open the yearly letter from Larry Fink, BlackRock's chief executive, pressing them on climate and other social causes. His company's funds hold pieces of almost every firm on the stock market. Why does his letter weigh so much more than an ordinary shareholder's?
answer: BlackRock can vote against managers who ignore it
choices: BlackRock can vote against managers who ignore it
BlackRock can fine firms that ignore its advice
BlackRock writes the stock exchange's listing rules
BlackRock decides which firms banks may lend to
context: BlackRock's funds own a slice of nearly every listed company, so it can vote against a company's managers at the annual meeting when they shrug off the letter. Larry Fink co-founded BlackRock in 1988 and has long been its chief executive; his yearly letters to chief executives are among the most-read documents in finance. Source: blackrock.com (Fink annual letters archive).

question: Jimmy Patronis, Florida's chief financial officer, pulled two billion dollars of state money out of the giant asset manager BlackRock in December 2022 over the way it voted on environmental, social and governance (ESG) causes. Florida, he said, had never signed up to pay for BlackRock's social engineering. What was he objecting to?
answer: The asset manager was using other people's money to push a political agenda
choices: The asset manager was using other people's money to push a political agenda
The asset manager had lost money on its investments
The asset manager refused to invest in the state's biggest employer
The asset manager charged higher fees than its rivals
context: Florida's chief financial officer, Jimmy Patronis, announced the move on December 1, 2022: the state treasury would freeze about $1.43 billion of long-term securities BlackRock managed and take away about $600 million of short-term investments. In August 2022 Governor Ron DeSantis and the other trustees of the state's pension board had told its fund managers to weigh financial returns only, not ESG goals. BlackRock said it was surprised by the decision, given the strong returns it had earned for Florida. Source: Bloomberg (December 1, 2022).

question: A fund manager votes a block of savers' shares at a company's annual meeting for a cause that many of those savers oppose, while his firm goes on charging them fees. What problem does that show?
answer: The manager may serve his own goals, not the savers'
choices: The manager may serve his own goals, not the savers'
The fees are too low to pay for careful voting
The company's managers face too many owners
The vote breaks the stock exchange's rules
context: The worry is about agents: a manager who votes savers' shares for causes many of them oppose, while still charging them fees, may be serving his own goals rather than theirs. BlackRock began a 'Voting Choice' program in 2022 that lets some clients choose their own voting policies. Source: blackrock.com/corporate/about-us/investment-stewardship/voting-choice.

question: George Stigler described in 1971 how an agency meant to police an industry can end up working for it, and he named the pattern regulatory capture. A few employees at the three biggest index-fund firms cast the votes on shares belonging to tens of millions of savers, none of whom were consulted on any given ballot. Public-choice economists see Stigler's shape in the arrangement. What lesson do they draw from the case?
answer: Capture can run through private gatekeepers, not only regulators
choices: Capture can run through private gatekeepers, not only regulators
Capture can only occur in government agencies
Capture requires formal legislative delegation
Capture is prevented by any private-sector alternative
context: Stigler's 1971 regulatory-capture framework identified the pattern. Bebchuk-Hirst extends the recognition to private financial infrastructure that operates on behalf of dispersed principals. Same alignment problem, different institutional venue. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Bebchuk + Hirst (2019).

question: Thomas Sowell proposed one test for anyone acting on other people's behalf. The Big Three asset managers cast the shareholder votes of tens of millions of retirement savers who were never asked what they wanted. What question would an analyst following Sowell put to that arrangement?
answer: Whether the intermediaries' incentives align with the principals' interests
choices: Whether the intermediaries' incentives align with the principals' interests
Whether the intermediaries beat the market for their clients
Whether the intermediaries publish annual sustainability reports
Whether the intermediaries obey every rule the regulators set
context: The test asks whether an agent's incentives match what the people he acts for actually want; where they do not, expect the agent to follow his own preferences at their expense. It applies whether the agent is a regulator, a legislator or a fund manager.

question: An Austrian finance minister walked out of the emperor's cabinet in 1904 rather than approve spending the budget could not bear. He returned to teaching in Vienna, and his university seminar trained the next generation of the Austrian school. Who was he?
answer: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Eugen von Philippovich
Emil Sax
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) served three separate stints as Austrian Finance Minister (briefly in 1895, again in 1897, and 1900-1904), resigned in 1904 rather than approve further deficits, and returned to Vienna where his 1905-06 seminar became the training ground for the next generation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk, three times Austria's finance minister, believed a state should spend no more than it takes in. In 1904 one branch of the imperial government demanded more money than the budget could carry, and he resigned rather than approve the deficit. Whose spending was he refusing?
answer: The army's
choices: The army's
The imperial court's
The pension office's
The state railway's
context: Boehm-Bawerk resigned as Austrian Finance Minister in 1904 when the army's demand for increased military expenditure threatened to unbalance the budget beyond what he thought fiscally sustainable. The imperial court, pensions, and state railway were all separate calls on the budget of the era; but the specific breaking point in 1904 was army spending. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Marx argued that the labor poured into a good is the sole source of its value. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk answered him in 1896 with a book-length essay, arguing that the theory falls apart once a reader follows Marx's own Capital through to its third volume. What is the essay called in English?
answer: Karl Marx and the Close of His System
choices: Karl Marx and the Close of His System
The Positive Theory of Capital
Principles of Economics
The Theory of Money and Credit
context: Boehm-Bawerk's 1896 essay 'Zum Abschluss des Marxschen Systems' -- translated as 'Karl Marx and the Close of His System' -- showed that Capital Volume 3, edited by Engels in 1894, contradicted the labor theory of value defended in Volume 1, opening a gap Marxists have argued about ever since. The Positive Theory of Capital (1889) was Boehm-Bawerk's own Volume 2 on capital; Principles of Economics (1871) was Menger's; The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was Mises's early book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: Two young Austrians who would become household names in twentieth-century economics sat in Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk's seminar at the University of Vienna in 1905 and 1906, after he had quit the finance ministry and gone back to teaching. Who were they?
answer: Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter
choices: Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter
Friedrich Hayek and Lionel Robbins
Israel Kirzner and Murray Rothbard
Milton Friedman and George Stigler
context: The 1905-06 Boehm-Bawerk seminar took a leading target of Austrian criticism as its topic and drew Ludwig von Mises and Joseph Schumpeter from the Austrian side alongside two future Marxist statesmen. Hayek, Kirzner, and Rothbard came in later generations; the Chicago-school figures Friedman and Stigler were a different tradition. Source: Mises Institute, 'Uncovered Audio of Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk from 1905' (https://mises.org/power-market/uncovered-audio-eugen-von-bohm-bawerk-1905).

question: A future foreign minister of Austria and a future finance minister of Weimar Germany sat as students in Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk's Vienna seminar of 1905 and 1906. Week after week the two young Austro-Marxists defended Karl Marx against the professor's critique. Who were they?
answer: Otto Bauer and Rudolf Hilferding
choices: Otto Bauer and Rudolf Hilferding
Karl Kautsky and Eduard Bernstein
Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht
Antonio Gramsci and Georg Lukacs
context: Austro-Marxists Otto Bauer (1881-1938, later Foreign Minister of Austria 1918-19) and Rudolf Hilferding (1877-1941, later Reich Finance Minister of Weimar Germany 1923 and 1928-29) both attended Boehm-Bawerk's 1905-06 seminar as young students defending the Marxian position. Kautsky, Bernstein, Luxemburg, Liebknecht, Gramsci and Lukacs were separately famous Marxist theorists of the era who did not attend the seminar. Source: Wikipedia, 'Otto Bauer' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Bauer).

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk walked out of the emperor's cabinet in 1904 rather than approve a deficit, and he died ten years later, on 27 August 1914. Historians mark the date because another event had started just a month earlier, one that would sweep his budget discipline away. What had begun?
answer: The First World War had broken out
choices: The First World War had broken out
The Austrian schilling had been introduced
The Habsburg monarchy had abdicated
The Federal Reserve had opened its doors
context: The First World War began on 28 July 1914 when Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; Boehm-Bawerk died a month later on 27 August 1914, as war finance began to sweep away the fiscal discipline he had defended in cabinet. The Austrian schilling was introduced in 1924; the Habsburg monarchy abdicated in November 1918; the US Federal Reserve opened in November 1914. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_B%C3%B6hm_von_Bawerk).

question: A merchant in Sichuan, in western China, paid with a printed paper note in the 1000s, sparing himself the heavy iron coins he had hauled along the trade roads. Around 1023 the government took over issuing such notes. Which dynasty ruled China then?
answer: the Song dynasty
choices: the Song dynasty
the Han dynasty
the Tang dynasty
the Ming dynasty
context: The Song dynasty took over jiaozi paper-money issuance around 1023 AD in Sichuan. The Han (206 BC-220 AD), Tang (618-907), and Ming (1368-1644) belong to other centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: A Scottish banker who ran France's new bank for the child-king Louis XV flooded the country with paper money from 1716 to 1720 to inflate the Mississippi Company. When the bubble burst, his notes became almost worthless. What was his paper currency called?
answer: The Banque Royale livre
choices: The Banque Royale livre
The French assignat
The mandat territorial
The billet de monnaie
context: John Law's Banque Generale, renamed the Banque Royale in 1718, issued livre notes that lost almost all their value when the Mississippi bubble burst in 1720. The assignat and the mandat territorial were the French Revolution's paper money of the 1790s, and billets de monnaie were Louis XIV's war paper of the 1700s. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Law_(economist).

question: A baker in a small central-European country charged more for a loaf at supper than at breakfast in July 1946, soon after the Second World War ended. Prices there doubled roughly every fifteen hours, the worst runaway rise ever measured, while the government printed ever-bigger banknotes. Which country's money set that record?
answer: Hungary (the pengő)
choices: Hungary (the pengő)
Germany (the papermark)
Zimbabwe (the Zimbabwean dollar)
Venezuela (the bolívar)
context: The Hungarian pengő (1946) holds the world record for hyperinflation speed. The German papermark (1923), Zimbabwean dollar (2008), and Venezuelan bolívar (2016-) also hyperinflated but at slower peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Hungary.

question: A defender of paper money holds up the British pound, called 1,300 years old by its admirers, as proof that a fiat currency can endure. An Austrian economist answers him. What does the Austrian say about the modern paper pound?
answer: it has lost about 99.5% of its purchasing power since 1750, and its physical composition has repeatedly changed
choices: it has lost about 99.5% of its purchasing power since 1750, and its physical composition has repeatedly changed
the pound has held its value steadily against gold since the early 1900s and remains a reference standard for stability
the modern pound has never been formally debased or inflated by the Bank of England in its 300-year history of issuing paper
the British pound was formally re-linked to gold in the 2000s and now sits under a working gold-exchange standard again
context: The counter: the modern paper pound has lost about 99.5% of purchasing power since 1750; its coin composition changed from silver to nickel; the medieval silver penny and today's paper pound are different monetary regimes with a shared name. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Murray Rothbard, like Ludwig von Mises before him, argued that money resting on nothing but a government's decree fails again and again, and not by accident. Joseph Salerno and Saifedean Ammous took up the case after them. What do they say drives the failure?
answer: politicians promise citizens more than tax revenue supports, monetary authorities close the gap by printing, printing debases the currency, savers absorb the loss, and the cycle accumulates until confidence breaks
choices: politicians promise citizens more than tax revenue supports, monetary authorities close the gap by printing, printing debases the currency, savers absorb the loss, and the cycle accumulates until confidence breaks
a shortage of gold and silver forces rulers in every age to print paper simply to keep trade moving, so the debasement follows from scarce metal rather than from any choice by the people in power
central bankers in every generation are personally corrupt and enrich themselves through undisclosed transactions before the currency they oversee inevitably loses its value against real goods
ordinary citizens demand ever-higher wages that force the money supply to grow to accommodate them, and the resulting debasement is a downstream effect of labor rather than monetary decisions
context: The Austrian claim is that fiat failure is structural, not personal: politicians overspend, the central bank prints, savers pay through debasement, and the pattern builds. Scarce metal, corrupt individuals and wage demands are rival explanations the argument rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021); Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?.

question: Saifedean Ammous, writing after Mises and Rothbard, argued that fiat currencies have ended in debasement or collapse again and again throughout history. From that record he drew a lesson about how money should be reformed. Which reasoning move did the argument press?
answer: That sound money is an engineering problem to be solved with fixed rules, not a political problem to be solved with better leaders
choices: That sound money is an engineering problem to be solved with fixed rules, not a political problem to be solved with better leaders
That sound money requires only better central-bank governance and improved appointment processes for the officials who run the system
That sound money is fundamentally a matter of tax policy alone, so fiscal reform inside each government can restore monetary discipline
That sound money will emerge automatically over time without any deliberate change in monetary institutions or protocols by anyone
context: The 5,000-year pattern-argument culminates in Satoshi's 2008 Bitcoin white paper: solve the political-money problem with cryptography and consensus rather than with trust in better leaders. Better central-bank governance, tax policy alone, and passive emergence are precisely what the argument denies is sufficient. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018); The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Franklin Roosevelt signed an executive order in 1934, in the depths of the Great Depression, setting up a federal lender in Washington. Its loans, backed by taxpayers, helped buyers abroad pay for goods made in America. Which agency did the order create?
answer: The Export-Import Bank of the United States
choices: The Export-Import Bank of the United States
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Reconstruction Finance Corporation
The Overseas Private Investment Corporation
context: Ex-Im's stated mission is to level the playing field for US exporters competing against foreign firms whose governments provide similar export credits. FDIC, RFC, and OPIC were other 1930s-1970s federal financial vehicles for different purposes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: Analysts at one think tank went through the Export-Import Bank's lending from 2007 to 2013. The federal agency helps foreign buyers purchase American-made goods, and they found that about 40 percent of its support had backed the sales of just one American firm, a textbook case of corporate welfare. Which company was it?
answer: Boeing
choices: Boeing
Walmart
General Electric
Apple
context: Boeing's foreign airline customers used Ex-Im-guaranteed financing to buy commercial aircraft. Critics call Ex-Im the 'Boeing Bank' because of this concentration. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: The Club for Growth, FreedomWorks and the Heritage Foundation took on the Export-Import Bank's big corporate defenders in Congress in June 2015 and won a rare fight. The federal agency lends taxpayer-backed credit to foreign buyers of American goods. What happened to the bank as a result?
answer: Congress declined to renew the bank's charter and it lapsed for about five months
choices: Congress declined to renew the bank's charter and it lapsed for about five months
Congress capped the bank's lending at a tenth of its former level
Congress barred the bank from backing more than a set share of any firm's sales
Congress voted to sell the bank's loan book to private lenders
context: The lapse was a rare successful mobilization of dispersed opposition against a concentrated-benefit program. Ex-Im's authority to finance new deals was suspended from June 30 to December 2015. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: Lawmakers renewed the Export-Import Bank's charter in December 2015 in a way that made it costly for any member to vote against the bank: they attached the renewal to a bill few members of Congress dared oppose. What was that bill?
answer: A big highway bill with road money for every district
choices: A big highway bill with road money for every district
A defense bill with pay raises for the troops
A disaster-relief bill for victims of that year's storms
A farm bill renewing crop insurance for every state
context: The bill was the FAST Act, Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act, signed on December 4, 2015. The bundling shows the logrolling move public-choice economists describe: pair a concentrated-benefit program with widely popular legislation so that opposing it becomes politically costly. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: The Export-Import Bank's biggest corporate allies warned Congress in 2015 that sales of American goods abroad would collapse without its loans behind them. From July to December that year the bank could not sign a single new deal. What did the bank's critics find happened to American export volume in those months?
answer: No measurable fall from the lapse; Boeing turned to commercial loans
choices: No measurable fall from the lapse; Boeing turned to commercial loans
A sharp fall, as buyers switched to European and Asian suppliers
A fall of about a tenth, nearly all of it in jet sales
A rise, as buyers rushed to sign before new rules arrived
context: The bank's critics concluded that the case for its necessity was weaker than its defenders had claimed: commercial bank financing cost slightly more than Ex-Im guarantees, but not enough to stop export deals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Export%E2%80%93Import_Bank_of_the_United_States.

question: Frances Kelsey, a reviewer at the Food and Drug Administration, refused to approve a sleeping pill called thalidomide for sale in America. A European firm had sold it to expectant mothers for morning sickness, and it left thousands of European babies with deformed arms and legs. What lesson did American lawmakers take from the disaster?
answer: Test new medicines carefully before sale
choices: Test new medicines carefully before sale
Let doctors, not the FDA, judge new drugs
Ban all medicines made by foreign firms
Make drug firms pay for every injury
context: Kelsey received the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service from John F. Kennedy on August 7, 1962, only the second woman to be given it; Kennedy said her judgment 'has prevented a major tragedy of birth deformities in the United States.' Samples distributed to American physicians were still linked to 17 birth defects. Sources: JFK Library; Wikipedia 'Frances Oldham Kelsey'; NLM.

question: John F. Kennedy honored Frances Kelsey in August 1962 for keeping thalidomide off American shelves, and within the year Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendment. Until then a drugmaker had needed to show only that a new medicine was safe. What extra proof did the new law demand?
answer: Proof that it actually worked
choices: Proof that it actually worked
Proof that it cost less than older treatments
Proof that it had been tested abroad first
Proof that the maker could supply the country
context: The 1962 amendments introduced a proof-of-efficacy requirement for the first time in American law: safety was no longer enough, and a manufacturer now had to satisfy the FDA that a drug worked before selling it. The amendments also set rules for advertising and labelling. Source: Wikipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment'.

question: Sam Peltzman of the University of Chicago counted, in a study of 1973, the brand-new medicines reaching American patients each year, before and after the 1962 drug amendments. About forty a year had been arriving before the law, and his model said about forty-one a year would have kept coming if the old rules had stayed in force. What did the yearly count fall to instead?
answer: About 16
choices: About 16
About 25
About 33
About 38
context: Peltzman found pre-1962 introductions averaging about 40 new chemical entities a year against about 16 afterwards, with his model predicting 41 absent the amendments -- roughly a 60 percent reduction in the flow of new medicines. Source: Peltzman (1973), JPE 81(5), summarised at fdareview.org.

question: Sam Peltzman weighed the 1962 drug amendments in 1973: the gain from keeping worthless medicines off the shelves on one side, the harm from good ones delayed or never launched on the other. He stated the net result in a form any shopper would recognize. What did he say the amendments came to?
answer: A 5 to 10 percent tax on every prescription sold
choices: A 5 to 10 percent tax on every prescription sold
A delay of one year in every patient's access to new medicine
A transfer of about a billion dollars a year to the largest makers
A doubling of the price of the average brand-name medicine
context: Peltzman concluded the efficacy amendment imposed a net consumer cost comparable to a 5-10 percent excise tax on all prescriptions sold, and judged that 'the penalties imposed by the marketplace on sellers of ineffective drugs prior to 1962 seem to have been enough of a deterrent to have left little room for improvement.' Source: Peltzman (1973), p.1086; fdareview.org.

question: Alexander Schmidt, commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration in the 1970s, pointed out that no committee of Congress had ever looked into a drug his agency failed to approve, while hearings over drugs it did approve were too many to count. What incentive does that one-sided pressure give the agency?
answer: To be over-cautious and delay approving new medicines
choices: To be over-cautious and delay approving new medicines
To approve every medicine as fast as possible
To ignore all political pressure equally
To hold public hearings before every decision
context: Schmidt, FDA Commissioner 1973-76: 'In all our FDA history, we are unable to find a single instance where a congressional committee investigated the failure of FDA to approve a new drug. But the times when hearings have been held to criticize our approval of a new drug have been so frequent that we have not been able to count them.' The asymmetry is the point: one kind of mistake summons a hearing, the other summons nothing. Source: quoted in Hoover Institution, 'The FDA at 100'.

question: Alex Tabarrok of George Mason University sorts a drug regulator's mistakes into two kinds. Approving a drug that harms people brings a name, a face and a hearing; blocking a drug that would have kept patients alive means they die of their disease, and their deaths pass as ordinary ones. Tabarrok has a phrase for where those uncounted dead lie. What is it?
answer: The invisible graveyard
choices: The invisible graveyard
The regulatory ratchet
The precautionary principle
The safety premium
context: Tabarrok's phrase: when a regulator fails to approve a good drug, people die, but they lie in an 'invisible graveyard', because their deaths look like ordinary deaths from the disease and nobody records them as an outcome of the decision. A ratchet is Robert Higgs's image for government power that grows in each crisis and never shrinks back; the precautionary principle is a real doctrine of erring toward caution. Sources: marginalrevolution.com, 'The Invisible Graveyard is Invisible No More' (2021); Wikipedia 'Alex Tabarrok'.

question: A senator proposes stretching the Food and Drug Administration's review of new medicines so that not one unsafe pill ever gets onto a pharmacy shelf. Sam Peltzman and Alex Tabarrok would not call safety a poor aim, but they put one question to the plan. Which question?
answer: What happens to the patients still waiting in the queue, and who is counting them?
choices: What happens to the patients still waiting in the queue, and who is counting them?
Which companies helped write the review standards now in force?
How much will the extra months of review cost the taxpayer each year?
Why do European regulators reach different conclusions from the same trials?
context: This is Bastiat's method at the level of institutional design. The seen: a harmful medicine kept off the shelf, with a headline attached. The unseen: people dying of a disease whose treatment is still in the queue. Peltzman measured the second in 1973; Tabarrok named it. Regulatory capture, budget cost and comparisons with Europe are real lines of criticism, but none of them is the seen-versus-unseen move.

question: Franklin Roosevelt signed the Agricultural Adjustment Act in May 1933, in the worst stretch of the Depression, to push collapsed farm prices back up. Farmers were paid to let fields lie empty, plow under cotton already growing and slaughter animals. Why would growing less food on purpose push prices up?
answer: Buyers bid more for each pound of a smaller supply
choices: Buyers bid more for each pound of a smaller supply
Farmers must charge more to cover idle land
Smaller harvests cost more to ship to market
Idle farm workers demand higher wages
context: The Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) of May 12, 1933 paid farmers to plow up crops already planted, kill livestock, and leave acreage idle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Adjustment_Act.

question: Henry Wallace, Roosevelt's agriculture secretary, went on national radio to defend paying farmers to kill some six million pigs in the fall of 1933, many of them piglets, while city families struggled to afford a meal. What does the slaughter show about wrecking valuable goods to raise their price?
answer: It hurts hungry families most, since they need the goods most
choices: It hurts hungry families most, since they need the goods most
It helps the poor, since farmers then hire more hands
It costs no one, since the goods were surplus anyway
It hurts farmers most, since they lose their animals
context: Roughly 6 million pigs were slaughtered under the AAA hog program in fall 1933. Millions of pounds of pork were rendered into fertilizer or dumped rather than shipped to the tens of millions of unemployed Americans in breadlines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Adjustment_Act.

question: Frederic Bastiat told his readers to judge every policy by its hidden effect as well as its obvious one. When the United States government paid farmers in 1933 to kill about six million pigs to raise pork prices, the seen was the better price the surviving hogs fetched, a lift to some farmers' cash flow. What was the unseen?
answer: Pork turned into fertilizer while children went hungry
choices: Pork turned into fertilizer while children went hungry
The federal tax revenue lost on the destroyed animals
Pork shipped abroad at a loss to clear the glut
Feed corn left to rot in the farmers' bins
context: Bastiat's method: the visible benefit was to farm cash flow; the hidden destruction was food that never reached the millions of hungry Americans in the same cities. Source: bastiat.org.

question: The justices of the Supreme Court struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 in January 1936. They found that the tax on food processors which paid the farmers to grow less went beyond Congress's power to tax. What was the case called?
answer: United States v. Butler
choices: United States v. Butler
Wickard v. Filburn
Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States
West Coast Hotel v. Parrish
context: US v. Butler (297 US 1, January 6, 1936) struck down the AAA's processing tax as beyond Congress's taxing power. Congress passed a modified version in 1938 that survived and still forms the skeleton of US farm-subsidy programs today. Source: supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/297/1.

question: Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian, two economists from the University of California, Los Angeles, went back over the figures for Roosevelt's New Deal, above all the factory codes of the National Industrial Recovery Act. They argued the measures kept the Depression going for years longer. Why, on their account?
answer: They held wages and prices above what markets would set
choices: They held wages and prices above what markets would set
They left investors afraid for the safety of their property
They shrank the money supply by draining the banks
They paid so many people to stay idle that few sought work
context: Cole and Ohanian's 'New Deal Policies and the Persistence of the Great Depression' (Journal of Political Economy, 2004) argued that the National Industrial Recovery Act let industries collude so long as they paid high wages, which kept wages and prices well above market levels and choked off recovery; they put these cartel policies behind much of the slump after 1933. Source: minneapolisfed.org (Working Paper 597).

question: William Graham Sumner, who taught sociology at Yale, wrote in the 1880s about the person politics leaves out. When the state takes from one citizen to help another, everyone talks about the citizen helped and the politician who arranged it, while the one who paid and got nothing back drops from view. What did Sumner call him?
answer: The forgotten man
choices: The forgotten man
The silent partner
The hidden victor
The unseen hand
context: Amity Shlaes's The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression (HarperCollins, 2007) reintroduced the Rothbard-Friedman critique of the New Deal to a general audience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Forgotten_Man_(Shlaes_book).

question: Lawmakers rewrote the farm law in 1938 after the Supreme Court struck down the first version, and the farm bill Congress renews about every five years still rests on that 1938 law. Franklin Roosevelt had signed the original in 1933 as a stopgap for an emergency. Milton Friedman had a famous line about the pattern. What does the farm bill's story teach?
answer: Temporary programs turn permanent once a group depends on the checks
choices: Temporary programs turn permanent once a group depends on the checks
Farm prices stay stable only with permanent federal support
Laws written in a hurry need decades of fixing
The Supreme Court cannot stop Congress from spending
context: The farm bill is the omnibus farm law Congress renews about every five years; the 2018 bill, the Agriculture Improvement Act, was extended more than once after it ran out in 2023. Its programs descend directly from the 1938 act. Friedman's line: nothing is so permanent as a temporary government program. Source: usda.gov farm bill.
