question: Franklin Roosevelt ordered Americans in April 1933 to hand in their gold coins, bars and certificates in exchange for paper dollars, and keeping a large stash of gold became a crime. Why would a government want every citizen's gold in its own vaults?
answer: So it could print paper money with no gold limit
choices: So it could print paper money with no gold limit
So it could pay foreign lenders in gold
So banks would have gold to lend to farmers
So it could sell the gold abroad at a profit
context: Executive Order 6102 required Americans to turn in gold at the official rate of $20.67 per troy ounce. It was signed under authority of the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 (a wartime law) as amended by the March 9 1933 Emergency Banking Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: Franklin Roosevelt presented his gold order of April 5, 1933, Executive Order 6102, as a way to stop 'hoarding' in the Depression. It spared small holdings, a hundred dollars' worth of coins or less, and rare coins kept by collectors. Whoever held on to a large hoard faced a stiff punishment. What was it?
answer: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
choices: A fine of up to $10,000 and up to 10 years in prison
A fine of up to $500 and six months in jail
A fine of up to $1,000 and a year in jail
A fine of twice the gold's value but no jail
context: $10,000 in 1933 dollars is roughly $240,000 in 2026 dollars. Citizens could keep small amounts (up to $100 face value in coins) and coins of recognized numismatic value. Bulk holdings were confiscated. Source: Grokipedia 'Executive Order 6102' (2026-09-05).

question: Franklin Roosevelt fixed a new official price for gold on January 31, 1934, in a proclamation under the Gold Reserve Act passed the day before. Less than a year earlier he had ordered Americans to hand in their gold at the old official price of $20.67 an ounce. What was the new price?
answer: $35.00 per troy ounce
choices: $35.00 per troy ounce
$25.00 per troy ounce
$50.00 per troy ounce
$100.00 per troy ounce
context: The January 31 1934 proclamation raised the official gold price from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce -- a 40.94% devaluation of the dollar against gold. Anyone who had turned in gold the previous year could not buy it back at the new rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: A saver who had obeyed Roosevelt's gold order in 1933 was paid $20.67 an ounce in paper dollars. Within a year the government had repriced gold far higher and cut the dollar's gold content, and a slice of that saver's wealth passed to the Treasury, with no way to buy the gold back at the old price. Roughly how big was that slice?
answer: About two-fifths of his gold's worth
choices: About two-fifths of his gold's worth
About a seventh of his gold's worth
About a twentieth of his gold's worth
About seven-tenths of his gold's worth
context: Gold went from $20.67 to $35.00 an ounce, a rise of about 69 percent. Put the other way, each dollar lost about 41 percent of its gold value (20.67 divided by 35 is about 0.59), and that slice of the gold savers' wealth went to the Treasury. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: Five of the nine Supreme Court justices ruled in 1935, in the Gold Clause Cases, that holders of bonds promising payment in gold could collect no damages, after Roosevelt had taken the metal and cut the dollar's gold value. Cancelling those promises, the Court said, was a breach of the Constitution where the government's own bonds were concerned. What did the ruling mean for savers?
answer: The government could reduce the real value of what it and others owed them
choices: The government could reduce the real value of what it and others owed them
The government now had to repay every gold contract in full
Private gold ownership was fully restored
Contracts written in dollars were no longer enforceable
context: The 1935 Gold Clause Cases (5-4) upheld the seizure and devaluation while declaring unconstitutional the government's abrogation of gold-clause obligations in its own bonds. But the Court also held that bondholders were not entitled to damages -- a limited victory that was in practice a full defeat. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold Clause Cases' (2026-09-05).

question: Congress at last lifted the ban on owning gold that Franklin Roosevelt had imposed on Americans in 1933, more than four decades after he signed it. The ban had blocked ordinary Americans from holding real gold as savings. When did the ban end, and under which president?
answer: December 31 1974, under President Gerald Ford
choices: December 31 1974, under President Gerald Ford
August 15 1971, under President Richard Nixon
January 20 1981, under President Ronald Reagan
October 3 2008, under President George W. Bush
context: Congress repealed the ban on private gold ownership effective December 31 1974. Americans could once again legally own gold bullion for the first time in over 40 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold ownership laws in the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: The Treasury finished a fortress at an Army base in Kentucky in 1936 for the gold Americans had handed in after Roosevelt's order of 1933. The fortress still keeps the greater part of the nation's official gold. What is it called?
answer: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository
choices: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository
The New York Fed Vault
The Denver Assay Office
The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Vault
context: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository was completed in 1936 in Kentucky to house the seized gold. It remains one of the most secure facilities in the world and holds the majority of official US gold reserves. Source: Grokipedia 'United States Bullion Depository' (2026-09-05).

question: Frederic Bastiat taught readers to ask of every policy what is seen and what is unseen. Franklin Roosevelt's order of 1933 took Americans' gold at $20.67 an ounce, and his Gold Reserve Act of 1934 then repriced it far higher. Which pairing of seen and unseen fits the seizure and devaluation together?
answer: Seen: banks shielded from gold hoarding; unseen: savers' wealth moved to the Treasury
choices: Seen: banks shielded from gold hoarding; unseen: savers' wealth moved to the Treasury
Seen: gold holders paid a fair price; unseen: banks left with too little gold
Seen: a cheaper dollar for exporters; unseen: factory jobs lost to imports
Seen: new revenue for the Treasury; unseen: interest rates pushed sharply up
context: The stated purpose was banking stability. The invisible mechanism was a targeted wealth transfer from the group that had chosen the specifically prudent monetary asset. Bastiat's frame fits the episode exactly. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: Franklin Roosevelt made it a crime in 1933 for Americans to keep a large stash of gold, and a year later, with the metal in Treasury vaults, he valued it far higher. John Law had tried something like it in France in 1720. What lasting lesson do Austrian economists draw?
answer: A state can outlaw hard money, seize it, then devalue against it
choices: A state can outlaw hard money, seize it, then devalue against it
Gold hoarding in a slump must be stopped to save the banks
Courts will undo any seizure that breaks a written contract
Devaluing a currency hurts the state that issues it most
context: The 1933 American episode was not the first. In 1720 John Law's France forbade any private person to keep more than 500 livres in gold and silver coin. The Austrian lesson is that a determined state can make hard money a crime, collect what exists, and then devalue its paper against the metal it holds. Source: encyclopedia.com, 'Law's System'.

question: The Federal Reserve bought another batch of government bonds to hold Washington's borrowing costs down, as it did all through the Second World War, in effect printing fresh dollars for the Treasury. That money was all still circulating when the war ended in 1945 and when the price controls came off. What followed?
answer: Rising prices as too much money chased the same goods
choices: Rising prices as too much money chased the same goods
Falling prices as factories made peacetime goods
Steady prices, since the Fed soaked the money up
A rush to hoard gold coins at home
context: During the war the Fed pinned interest rates low by buying as many government bonds as it took, in effect creating dollars for the Treasury. When price controls came off in 1946, prices jumped as those dollars met a supply of goods that had not grown as fast. The Treasury-Fed Accord of March 4, 1951 later freed the Fed to set rates on its own. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: A roomful of New York investment bankers heard William McChesney Martin, chairman of the Federal Reserve, sum up his job in October 1955: the Fed has to end the drinking just as a party warms up. In his image the drink was the cheap credit and loose cash that make an economic party feel lively. What did he mean?
answer: Cut off easy money before the boom ends in a crash
choices: Cut off easy money before the boom ends in a crash
Cut off easy money to punish reckless bankers
Cut off easy money so savers earn more interest
Cut off easy money to keep wages from rising
context: Martin served as Fed chairman for nearly 19 years (April 1951 to January 1970) under presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Harry Truman picked William McChesney Martin to chair the Federal Reserve in April 1951, expecting a loyal ally. Martin had just helped negotiate the Accord of March 4, 1951, which restored the Fed's freedom to set its own interest rates, and he had argued one side at that table. Which side?
answer: The Treasury side
choices: The Treasury side
The Federal Reserve side
The Senate Banking Committee side
The Council of Economic Advisers side
context: Martin had negotiated the Accord as a Treasury official. Truman assumed a Treasury man would keep monetary policy accommodating to fiscal needs. Instead Martin became a fierce defender of Fed independence, and Truman felt betrayed. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: William McChesney Martin addressed the New York Group of the Investment Bankers Association on an October evening in 1955, reaching for an image of what the Fed does when the economy runs hot. The line he found became one of the most quoted in central banking: the Fed, he said, was like a certain figure at a party. Which figure?
answer: The chaperone who orders the punch bowl removed
choices: The chaperone who orders the punch bowl removed
The bartender who refuses to serve one more drink
The host who quietly turns down the music
The doorman who admits only sober guests
context: Martin's words in October 1955: the Federal Reserve is 'in the position of the chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up.' The image became the classic description of anti-inflationary central banking. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: William McChesney Martin stepped down as chairman of the Federal Reserve in 1970 after almost nineteen years, a longer run than anyone else has had in the job. He had taken over in 1951, the year of the Fed's accord with the Treasury. Which five presidents, in order, did he serve under?
answer: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
choices: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon
Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Ford
Roosevelt, Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson
Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, and Ford
context: Martin's tenure ran from April 1951 through January 1970. He served under five presidents across three decades -- the longest continuous Fed chairmanship in modern history. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Negotiators for the Treasury and the Federal Reserve reached an accord on March 4, 1951, ending the arrangement that had kept interest rates pinned low for Washington's borrowing. The central bank had spent the war buying government bonds to hold rates down. What lesson does the episode teach about wartime finance and a central bank's independence?
answer: War ties a central bank to the Treasury, and freedom must be won back openly
choices: War ties a central bank to the Treasury, and freedom must be won back openly
War ties a central bank to the Treasury, but peace frees it on its own
Pinning rates low is harmless once the war debt is paid off
Only a new act of Congress can free a central bank after a war
context: The 1951 Accord was a political victory hard-won by insiders who understood the inflationary consequences of continued Treasury-bond pegging. Fed independence is not a natural equilibrium; it is a political achievement that must be actively maintained. Source: Grokipedia 'Fed-Treasury Accord' (2026-09-05).

question: A central banker who raises rates to cool a boom, William McChesney Martin told bankers in 1955, is like someone taking the drink away from a party just as it gets lively. Financial writers turned the line into shorthand for tight money in a boom. What point does the image press about fighting inflation?
answer: Tightening is unpopular because it comes just as the boom feels best
choices: Tightening is unpopular because it comes just as the boom feels best
Tightening is technical, so politics plays no part in it
Tightening is popular, since the public fears rising prices
Tightening works only after a crash has already begun
context: Martin's point: anti-inflation policy is unpopular exactly when it matters most, because it arrives while everyone is enjoying the boom. The tension helps explain why Arthur Burns gave way to Nixon's pressure in 1971-72 and why later chairs have struggled with the same choice. Source: Grokipedia 'William McChesney Martin' (2026-09-05).

question: Leonard Read wrote an essay in 1958 in the voice of a yellow pencil, whose cedar, graphite, rubber and brass come from different countries. The pencil brags that no one on earth knows how to make it, and Milton Friedman retold its story on his television program Free to Choose. What does the essay teach about a market economy?
answer: Millions of people cooperate through prices without any single planner in charge
choices: Millions of people cooperate through prices without any single planner in charge
Trade between countries matters more than any factory at home
Big companies that own every step of making a product work best
Simple goods are cheap because machines now do nearly all the work
context: Leonard E. Read (1898-1983) founded the Foundation for Economic Education in March 1946 as the first American institutional home of the classical-liberal reading tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_for_Economic_Education.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in his essay of 1949, 'The Intellectuals and Socialism,' that elections matter less to where a country goes than the ideas its teachers, journalists and writers take in and hand on, since politicians follow them in the end. Leonard Read's foundation and other free-market think tanks, magazines and student reading programs try to do something no campaign can. What is it?
answer: Slowly change what people take for common sense about how the economy works
choices: Slowly change what people take for common sense about how the economy works
Win the next election by funding the candidates who agree with them
Pass laws faster by drafting bills for friendly lawmakers to file
Train economists to run government agencies after each election
context: FEE moved its offices to Atlanta, Georgia in the 21st century and continues its student-education mission from there. Source: fee.org.

question: Six Cubans crashed a stolen city bus through an embassy gate in Havana in April 1980 and asked for asylum. Fidel Castro, furious, pulled the police guard off the gate, and in two days about 10,800 people had packed the grounds asking to get out of Cuba. Which embassy was it?
answer: The Peruvian embassy
choices: The Peruvian embassy
The Spanish embassy
The Canadian embassy
The Mexican embassy
context: On April 1, 1980 six Cubans drove a bus through the Peruvian embassy gates in Havana. When Castro withdrew the Cuban security guards for 48 hours, 10,800 Cubans poured into the embassy grounds asking for asylum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: Fidel Castro told Cubans in 1980 that whoever wished to leave might sail from the harbor at Mariel. From April to October families packed into boats and crossed to Florida. What does a mass flight like that say about the system people were leaving?
answer: People were fleeing a system that had failed them
choices: People were fleeing a system that had failed them
Cuba had more people than its farms could feed
A storm season had wrecked the island's homes
The United States had paid them to come over
context: Castro announced that Cubans who wished to leave could sail from Mariel harbor. From April through October 1980 about 125,000 Cubans crossed to Florida. Castro emptied several prisons and mental hospitals into the flow to embarrass the US. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: A Cuban family crowded into a boat at the port of Mariel in 1980 and crossed to Florida, one of many that sailed between April and October after Fidel Castro told the unhappy they were free to go. His government sent convicts and mental patients along with them to embarrass the United States. About how many Cubans made the crossing?
answer: About 125,000
choices: About 125,000
About 12,500
About 1.2 million
About 15,000
context: About 125,000 Cubans left Mariel between April and October 1980. The exodus overwhelmed South Florida's absorption capacity and became a defining political event of the Carter presidency. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariel_boatlift.

question: A family on a beach near Havana lashed a raft together from inner tubes, truck tires and wooden pallets in mid-1994 and pushed off for Florida, ninety miles away across waters full of sharks. Some 35,000 of the balseros, as the rafters were called, made it across in six weeks. What does their flight say about the shortages at the depth of Cuba's post-Soviet slump?
answer: Want was so deep that people risked death at sea to leave
choices: Want was so deep that people risked death at sea to leave
Florida jobs paid well enough to lure them over
Food was plentiful, but there was little work
Most rafters meant only to fish and drifted north
context: 'Balseros' means raft-people. About 35,000 crossed to Florida in six weeks in 1994 aboard improvised rafts (balsas). The US shifted policy afterward to the 'wet foot / dry foot' rule that stood until 2017. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Cuban_rafter_crisis.

question: Armando Valladares, a young poet, refused to display a pro-Castro sign at his desk, and Fidel Castro's government jailed him in 1960. Valladares came out twenty-two years later, freed in 1982 under pressure from France, and wrote a memoir of Castro's prisons, Against All Hope. Why did the book change many minds abroad?
answer: It gave first-hand proof from a man who lived it
choices: It gave first-hand proof from a man who lived it
It was the first book on Cuba printed in English
It was based on official Cuban prison records
It was praised by Castro's own newspapers
context: Armando Valladares was arrested in 1960 and released in 1982 after French intervention. His memoir Against All Hope (1985) documented the Cuban prison system for a global readership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armando_Valladares.

question: Fidel Castro put Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, a guerrilla fighter who had never studied economics or business, in charge of Cuba's National Bank in 1959 and then of its Ministry of Industry. What tends to happen to the main crop when plantations are seized and untrained commanders run the economy?
answer: Output of the crop falls sharply
choices: Output of the crop falls sharply
Output rises as workers own the land
Output holds steady but quality drops
Output rises at first, then levels off
context: Ernesto 'Che' Guevara ran the National Bank of Cuba 1959-61 and the Ministry of Industry 1961-65. Cuban sugar output fell sharply during his industrial-diversification push. He left Cuba in 1965 and was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara.

question: Christina Romer and Jared Bernstein, two of Barack Obama's incoming economists, put out a memo in January 2009 on the $787 billion stimulus Congress was weighing. They forecast how high unemployment would climb with the stimulus in place. Below what rate did the memo say it would peak?
answer: Below 8 percent
choices: Below 8 percent
Below 6 percent
Below 10 percent
Below 12 percent
context: The Romer-Bernstein memo of January 2009 ('The Job Impact of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan') published a chart showing unemployment peaking below 8%. In fact it reached 10.0% in October 2009, with ARRA fully in effect. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Recovery_and_Reinvestment_Act.

question: Lawmakers passed the $787 billion stimulus in February 2009, after Barack Obama's economists Christina Romer and Jared Bernstein had forecast how far joblessness would climb with it in place. Joblessness climbed past the forecast anyway and stayed high for years. What lesson does the gap teach?
answer: Even experts often cannot predict a whole economy
choices: Even experts often cannot predict a whole economy
Unemployment figures are too rough to trust
Forecasts fail only when Congress delays a law
Joblessness lags, so the forecast was still right
context: Christina Romer chaired the CEA; Jared Bernstein was Vice President Biden's chief economist. Their multiplier assumption of about 1.55 (each stimulus dollar raising GDP by $1.55) drove the under-8% forecast. Source: whitehouse.archives.gov (Romer-Bernstein memo, January 9 2009).

question: Christina Romer's team assumed in 2009 that each dollar of stimulus would add about $1.55 to the economy as it moved from hand to hand. Later independent studies often found a smaller payoff than that. What does the gap say about the White House predictions?
answer: They were often too optimistic
choices: They were often too optimistic
They were far too pessimistic
They exactly matched later measurements
They were required by law to be conservative
context: The 1.55 multiplier assumption is what generated the sub-8% unemployment forecast; recalculated with standard New-Keynesian frictions and crowding-out, the same models produce multipliers in the 0.6-0.7 range. Source: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland, Journal of Economic Dynamics 2010.

question: Frederic Bastiat asked the same thing of every dollar a government spends: where did it come from? Anyone who claims that public spending grows the economy by more than it spends has to answer him honestly, and Bastiat's method allows only three answers. Which three?
answer: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
choices: Taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank
Confiscated from a corporation, appropriated from foreign trade, or drawn from reserves
Levied on tariffs, extracted from monopoly rents, or issued as certificates
Deducted from savings, garnisheed from wages, or redistributed from land
context: Bastiat's method: whatever the government spends, that dollar came from a taxpayer's foregone consumption, a lender's foregone loan to a private borrower, or a printed dollar whose Cantillon-effect winners capture it before prices adjust. The SEEN is the road crew; the UNSEEN is the private capital that dollar would have financed. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Valerie Ramey looked at the giant jumps in federal spending during the Korean War and the Second World War, then measured what an added federal dollar did in ordinary peacetime, on offices, gear and salaries. On average, how much extra economic activity did each added dollar bring in normal times?
answer: Less than one extra dollar
choices: Less than one extra dollar
About two extra dollars
About three extra dollars
About five extra dollars
context: Ramey's careful VAR estimates find defense multipliers of 0.6-1.1 depending on specification, and civilian peacetime multipliers below 1. Sub-1 means net crowding-out of private activity. Source: Journal of Economic Literature 49(3), 2011.

question: A government borrows heavily to pay for a stimulus program. Soon a furniture maker finds that loans cost him more, and he shelves the new workshop he had planned. Which hidden cost of the government's borrowing does the shelved workshop show?
answer: Crowding-out of private investment
choices: Crowding-out of private investment
The Cantillon effect of new money
Moral hazard from a public safety net
Regulatory capture of the lenders
context: A government that borrows heavily competes with businesses and families for the same pool of savings, and the private projects that lose out, like the workshop never built, are what economists call crowding-out, the modern name for Bastiat's unseen. When crowding-out is large, the stimulus multiplier falls below one. The Cantillon effect concerns who gets newly printed money first, moral hazard the extra risk a safety net invites, and regulatory capture a watchdog that comes to serve the industry it watches.

question: John Taylor and three colleagues reran Christina Romer's 2009 stimulus model in 2010, starting from its payoff of $1.55 per dollar and adding a drag real economies carry: taxes that rise later to pay the bill. What much smaller payoff did their adjusted models give?
answer: About 0.6-0.7
choices: About 0.6-0.7
About 1.3-1.4
About 2.0-2.2
About 2.8-3.0
context: Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland showed the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 assumed away the crowding-out; realistic frictions bring the multiplier below 1. Source: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 34(3), 2010.

question: A mayor stands on the courthouse steps and promises the town a handsome new bridge and many good jobs. A critic in Frederic Bastiat's line puts one question to him before the first paycheck goes out: where does the money come from? What is the honest one-line answer?
answer: Public works mean taxes on the people who would have spent that money elsewhere
choices: Public works mean taxes on the people who would have spent that money elsewhere
The bridge pays for itself because the workers spend their new wages in town
The Federal Reserve prints the money at no cost to anyone
Foreign banks lend the money and never ask to be paid back
context: Hazlitt's chapter 4 title, 'Public Works Mean Taxes,' compresses the whole Bastiat objection: the ribbon-cutting is seen; the tax that paid for it is unseen. Every 2009 ARRA critique is an application. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: Friedrich Hayek and three colleagues from the London School of Economics, Lionel Robbins and Arnold Plant among them, warned on October 19, 1932 that Keynes-style public works paid for with borrowed money would not cure the Depression. Which newspaper carried their letter?
answer: The Times of London
choices: The Times of London
The Manchester Guardian
The Daily Telegraph
The Financial Times
context: The letter to The Times of October 19, 1932, signed by Hayek, T. E. Gregory, Lionel Robbins and Arnold Plant, objected on classical and Austrian grounds to public works paid for with borrowed money. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynes-Hayek_letters.

question: The publisher Macmillan brought out Murray Rothbard's most popular book in 1973, under the subtitle The Libertarian Manifesto. It pictured private courts and roads, with neither a draft nor an income tax. What was its main title?
answer: For a New Liberty
choices: For a New Liberty
The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
Power and Market
context: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto (Macmillan, 1973) was Rothbard's popular-audience movement statement, distinct from his systematic 1982 political ethics and his 1962 economic treatise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard rested every argument of his 1973 manifesto on one rule, and he held the state to it as strictly as a street criminal, so that taxes and the draft counted as breaking it too. He called it the non-aggression principle. What does it say?
answer: No person or group may start force against another's person or property
choices: No person or group may start force against another's person or property
Every person owes society a positive duty to reduce inequality where able
Government exists by the consent of the governed and rules only within that consent
The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right action
context: Rothbard called this the non-aggression axiom. He argued that the whole libertarian program, on schools, roads, police, courts and foreign policy, follows from applying the axiom to the state as consistently as to private crime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_a_New_Liberty.

question: Even a minimal government was too much for Murray Rothbard. He wanted a society with no state at all, where people pay for every service by choice and never through taxes. What did he call his position?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism
choices: Anarcho-capitalism
Anarcho-syndicalism
Mutualism
Objectivism
context: Rothbard's name for his position joined anarchism's rejection of the state to capitalism's private property and free exchange. Anarcho-syndicalism would put workers' unions in the state's place, mutualism is the market of cooperatives and free credit that Pierre-Joseph Proudhon proposed, and Ayn Rand's Objectivism kept a limited state. Source: britannica.com/money/anarcho-capitalism.

question: A worried reader of Murray Rothbard's manifesto of 1973 asks who would keep order in a society with no state at all, and pictures plain lawlessness. Rothbard answered that it would mean law provided by other hands, and his chapter on private roads was his test case. Who, in his scheme, would provide the police, the courts, the roads and even the army?
answer: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
choices: Competing private organizations bound by property-rights contracts
Voluntary local militias governed by direct town-hall vote
A single elected but powerless minimal state of night-watchman scope
International arbitration panels enforcing global common law
context: Rothbard's central move: not the ABSENCE of law but the private-market PROVISION of it. The famous test case in the book is his chapter on private roads. Source: mises.org/library/book/for-new-liberty-libertarian-manifesto.

question: Murray Rothbard reached back to John Locke in 1982, nine years after his popular manifesto, for a longer and more philosophical book. It rests libertarianism on the old conviction that a person's body, labor and earnings are his own before any government exists. What is its title?
answer: The Ethics of Liberty
choices: The Ethics of Liberty
Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
What Has Government Done to Our Money?
context: The Ethics of Liberty was published in 1982 by Humanities Press of Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey. If For a New Liberty was the popular manifesto, The Ethics of Liberty was the systematic treatise. A later edition (1998, NYU Press) carried an introduction by Hans-Hermann Hoppe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: Robert Nozick, a Harvard philosopher, built his book of 1974, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, on an older idea he took from John Locke: that a person owns himself, his labor and what he earns before any government exists to hand out permission. What is that idea called?
answer: Natural rights
choices: Natural rights
Divine right of kings
Government-granted rights
Might makes right
context: Rothbard secularizes Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689): self-ownership, the labor theory of homesteading, and the strict limits on legitimate coercion. Rothbard drops Locke's theological grounding but keeps the natural-rights framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: Murray Rothbard turned critic in Part IV of his treatise of 1982, after building his own case for liberty on John Locke. He weighed four other champions of freedom one after another and argued that none of them defended liberty with full consistency. Which four did he examine?
answer: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
choices: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek, Isaiah Berlin, and Robert Nozick
Milton Friedman, James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and Ronald Coase
John Rawls, Ronald Dworkin, Amartya Sen, and Michael Sandel
Ayn Rand, Nathaniel Branden, Leonard Peikoff, and Tibor Machan
context: Rothbard reviews Mises's utilitarianism, Hayek's rule-of-law liberalism, Berlin's two-concepts-of-liberty essay, and Nozick's minimal-state derivation, and argues each falls short of a fully consistent libertarian position. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ethics_of_Liberty.

question: A little-known farmer from Mugron, in southwestern France, became famous almost overnight in October 1844, when a Paris journal printed his piece on English and French tariffs. The farmer, Frédéric Bastiat, had spent some twenty years reading about trade and money on the family estate. Which journal was it?
answer: Journal des Economistes
choices: Journal des Economistes
Revue des Deux Mondes
Le Constitutionnel
La Gazette de France
context: The Journal des Economistes was founded in 1841 by the Guillaumin house as the flagship of the French free-trade school. Bastiat's article 'The Influence of English and French Tariffs on the Future of the Two Peoples' appeared in the October 1844 issue. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat made a deliberate choice of style when he wrote for ordinary French readers in the 1840s. He wanted a shopkeeper or a farmer to follow every link in his reasoning. Which academic style did he refuse to use?
answer: Mathematical formalism
choices: Mathematical formalism
Historical narration
Satirical dialogue
First-person voice
context: Bastiat wanted his readers to be able to check the argument at each step without algebra. He used satirical dialogue (the Candlemakers' Petition), historical narration (the Sophisms), and first-person voice (Ce qu'on voit) freely; the one continental fashion he refused was the equation. Source: fee.org 'The Life of Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat took a seat in France's new National Assembly in 1848, after the revolution drove King Louis-Philippe from his throne. Voters returned Bastiat the next year, and he sat on its finance committee. Which group did his speeches there mostly attack, believing its schemes would ruin France?
answer: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
choices: The socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
The legitimists of Henri de Chambord and Berryer
The Bonapartists of Louis-Napoleon and Persigny
The Orleanists of Thiers and the Duke de Broglie
context: Bastiat's parliamentary speeches, published in the Assembly journals of 1848-49, mostly opposed Louis Blanc's Ateliers Nationaux and Proudhon's Bank of the People. He was not primarily engaged with the royalist, Bonapartist or Orleanist blocs. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat, gravely ill with tuberculosis, rushed two short works to his printer a few weeks apart in June and July 1850. They became the most-quoted pages he ever wrote and remain his two best-known short works. Which pair was it?
answer: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
choices: La Loi and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas
Sophismes economiques and Petition des fabricants de chandelles
Harmonies economiques and Cobden et la Ligue
Propriete et loi and Capital et rente
context: La Loi (The Law) appeared in June 1850 and Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen) in July 1850. The Sophismes had appeared as two earlier collections (1845, 1848); Harmonies was his unfinished positive treatise; Propriete et loi and Capital et rente were earlier short pieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Prosper Paillottet kept watch at Frédéric Bastiat's bedside in Rome on Christmas Eve 1850, when his friend died at forty-nine. Paillottet later reported that Bastiat, in his final hour, kept murmuring the same two French words, and his friends took them as the summary of his life's work. What were the words?
answer: 'La verite, la verite'
choices: 'La verite, la verite'
'La liberte, la liberte'
'La justice, la justice'
'La patrie, la patrie'
context: The account of the deathbed scene comes from Prosper Paillottet, one of the editors of the posthumous Oeuvres completes, who was in the room. Bastiat had built his method around the discipline of not lying about consequences; the reported dying words -- 'the truth, the truth' -- were taken by his friends as the summary of that vocation. Legend, but well-attested. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: A student opening a modern economics textbook meets two ideas credited to Frédéric Bastiat's essays of 1848 to 1850. One is the parable of the broken window, which counts what a policy destroys as well as what it creates. What is the other?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Comparative advantage
Diminishing marginal utility
The velocity of money
context: Bastiat argued that every choice must be judged against the foregone alternative -- what the broken-window essay calls 'that which is not seen' -- and modern textbooks credit him with the first clear statement of opportunity cost. Comparative advantage is Ricardo (1817); marginal utility is Menger, Jevons and Walras (1871-74); the velocity of money goes back to the classical quantity theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Frederic Bastiat'.

question: Milton Friedman answered, in the New York Times Magazine on September 13, 1970, those urging companies to take up social causes along with profit. Both sides now call his argument the Friedman Doctrine. What headline did the Times print over the essay?
answer: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
choices: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
The Modern Corporation and Private Property
The Shareholder Value Myth
Capitalism and Freedom
context: The essay ran under the heading 'A Friedman doctrine' as 'The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits' (New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970). The Modern Corporation and Private Property is Adolf Berle and Gardiner Means's book of 1932, The Shareholder Value Myth is Lynn Stout's of 2012, and Capitalism and Freedom is Friedman's own book of 1962. Source: nytimes.com/1970/09/13/archives.

question: Milton Friedman opened his argument of 1970 by asking whom a company's boss actually works for. The answer, he said, defines the boss's job: to make the business as profitable as possible for those people. Who are they?
answer: The shareholders
choices: The shareholders
The customers
The federal government
The neighborhood community
context: Friedman: the executive is an employee of the shareholders and should generally maximize corporate profits within the rules of law and ethical custom. Any expenditure of shareholder money on the executive's own social projects is other people's money on his priorities. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (September 13, 1970).

question: Milton Friedman drew his sharpest line in his essay of 1970 between two kinds of money a company boss might hand to a cause: his own salary, and the company's funds. What did Friedman say about the boss's own salary?
answer: He is free to give it to any cause he likes
choices: He is free to give it to any cause he likes
He may give it only to causes his firm supports
He must ask the shareholders before giving it
He should not give it, since profit is his duty
context: Friedman's distinction: an executive who gives his own money to a cause is spending his own money, which is his right; an executive who gives the company's funds is spending someone else's money without the owners' consent. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Milton Friedman defended honest business, not fraud, in his essay of 1970. A company's boss should chase as much profit as he can, Friedman wrote, but only while obeying his society's ground rules. Which rules did Friedman say the boss must obey?
answer: Both law and ethical custom
choices: Both law and ethical custom
The written law alone
His own conscience alone
The stock exchange's listing rules
context: Friedman's precise phrasing: the executive should run the business to make as much money as possible 'while conforming to the basic rules of the society, both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom.' He is not defending fraud or predation. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: A company's board tells its managers to serve the workers, the town, the environment and the owners all at once. Economists who build on Milton Friedman's essay of 1970 warn that a mandate like that wrecks something about holding managers to account. What problem do they name?
answer: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
choices: They answer to no one and can justify any decision
They answer to the board alone, not the owners
They spend so long consulting that nothing gets done
They must report every choice to each group they serve
context: Michael Jensen sharpened the point in 2001: a manager told to maximize several goals at once has no goal at all, so any decision can be defended by naming the group it served, and nobody can hold him to account. A single clear owner to serve is what keeps managers answerable. Source: Jensen, 'Value Maximization, Stakeholder Theory, and the Corporate Objective Function' (2001).

question: Chief executives in the Business Roundtable, a lobby of top American bosses based in Washington, put out a statement about the purpose of a corporation in August 2019, and it broke openly with Milton Friedman's rule of 1970. How many of them signed it?
choices: About 50
context: The Business Roundtable's Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation (August 19, 2019) was signed by 181 CEOs and formally endorsed stakeholder capitalism over pure shareholder primacy. It was widely read as a direct response to renewed attention to the Friedman doctrine. Source: businessroundtable.org (August 2019).

question: A chief executive gives the company's funds to a cause its owners never approved. Milton Friedman likened such a man in 1970 to a self-appointed tax collector, and his essay remains the chief answer to ESG (environmental, social and governance) investing. What did Friedman say the executive is doing?
answer: Spending someone else's money
choices: Spending someone else's money
Serving all masters at once
Building the corporate community
Protecting long-term brand value
context: Friedman wrote that in each such case 'the corporate executive would be spending someone else's money for a general social interest': the stockholders' money when returns fall, the customers' when prices rise, the employees' when wages are cut. Source: Friedman, NYT Magazine (1970).

question: Rebecca Henderson of Harvard took aim at Milton Friedman's rule of 1970 in her book Reimagining Capitalism; Michael Porter of Harvard did so with his idea of 'shared value', and Colin Mayer of Oxford with his work on what firms are for. What charge do the three professors level at Friedman's rule?
answer: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
choices: That the shareholder-only mandate misses long-term corporate value creation
That the shareholder-only mandate makes firms too timid to innovate
That the shareholder-only mandate hands control to foreign investors
That the shareholder-only mandate forces firms to raise their prices
context: The pro-stakeholder rebuttal, in various forms: attending to environmental, social, and community outcomes builds long-term corporate value that shareholder-narrow maximization misses. Friedman's response is that such considerations can be voluntarily adopted by shareholders themselves; executive imposition still lacks mandate. Source: Porter + Kramer, HBR (2011); Mayer, Prosperity (Oxford 2018); Henderson, Reimagining Capitalism (Public Affairs 2020).

question: Two economists published A Monetary History of the United States in 1963, 860 pages on a century of American money. Ben Bernanke, later Fed chairman, said its account of the Depression was the most persuasive explanation of the country's worst collapse. Who were the two?
answer: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
choices: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow
John Maynard Keynes and Roy Harrod
Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek
context: Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research through Princeton University Press. It became one of the most influential economics books of the 20th century. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: Anna Schwartz and Milton Friedman measured, in chapter seven of their history of American money, the shrinking of the money Americans held in cash and bank accounts between 1929 and 1933, while the Federal Reserve stood aside. By about what percent did it shrink?
answer: About 33 percent
choices: About 33 percent
About 10 percent
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
context: The M2 money supply contracted roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933. Friedman and Schwartz argued the Fed could have prevented this by acting as lender of last resort during bank failures. It did not. Source: Grokipedia 'A Monetary History of the United States' (2026-09-05).

question: A run on an American bank in the early 1930s wiped out its depositors' savings, for deposits went uninsured until 1933, and every failure shrank the money supply further. Some 25,000 banks were doing business when the crash of 1929 came. About how many failed between 1930 and 1933?
answer: About 9,000
choices: About 9,000
About 500
About 25,000
About 1,200
context: Roughly 9,000 US banks failed 1930-33 -- about a third of all banks. Each failure destroyed the deposits held there (no FDIC until 1933), further contracting the money supply. The Fed, chartered specifically to be lender of last resort, mostly stood aside. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Depression' (2026-09-05).

question: Friedman and Schwartz pointed to one death in October 1928: Benjamin Strong, who had steered the Fed for over ten years, died without warning. Without him, they argued, the regional reserve banks quarreled and went their own ways into the crash of 1929. What did the gap show?
answer: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
choices: A single institution can be shaped heavily by one person
Regional banks do best when they act on their own
Laws matter more to a central bank than its leaders
Markets, not officials, set a central bank's choices
context: Strong died in October 1928, less than a year before the crash. His absence left the Fed without a dominant voice able to force the system into aggressive lender-of-last-resort action during the 1930-33 bank failures. Source: Grokipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.' (2026-09-05).

question: Historians of the Fed trace its refusal to rescue failing banks in the early 1930s partly to a doctrine many of its officials followed. In its harsh form it told the central bank to turn away any bank it judged unsound and let it go under, as a purge. What is the doctrine called?
answer: The real-bills doctrine
choices: The real-bills doctrine
The gold-standard doctrine
The Bagehot doctrine
The monetarist doctrine
context: The real-bills doctrine's liquidationist descendant held that the Fed should not lend to banks whose portfolios contained questionable loans -- exactly the banks needing rescue in 1930-33. The doctrine ensured the Fed refused to provide the liquidity that could have stopped the cascade. Source: Grokipedia 'Real bills doctrine' (2026-09-05).

question: Milton Friedman spent six days in a South American country in March 1975, at a private foundation's invitation. He met the country's military ruler for about forty-five minutes and lectured in its capital on how to stop runaway inflation. Which country was it?
answer: Chile
choices: Chile
Argentina
Peru
Brazil
context: Friedman visited Chile March 1975 at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He met Augusto Pinochet briefly and wrote one follow-up letter with monetary and economic recommendations. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: Sergio de Castro and the other Chicago Boys, Chilean economists trained in Chicago, ran Chile's economic policy from 1975. They cut price controls and tariffs, sold state firms and opened the country to trade. What happened to its economy over the next twenty years?
answer: It grew much richer than before
choices: It grew much richer than before
It grew, then fell back where it began
It stalled as investors stayed away
It shrank as imports closed its factories
context: The Chicago Boys were about twenty-five Chilean economists trained at Chicago under an exchange with Chile's Catholic University begun in 1955; Sergio de Castro, finance minister from 1976 to 1982, was among their leaders. Under their reforms Chile grew much richer over the following two decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Boys.

question: Critics back home accused Milton Friedman of advising a dictatorship after his lectures in Santiago in March 1975 on Chile's runaway inflation. A general had ruled the country since a military coup on September 11, 1973. Who was the general?
answer: Augusto Pinochet
choices: Augusto Pinochet
Salvador Allende
Eduardo Frei
Juan Peron
context: Augusto Pinochet came to power in the September 11, 1973 military coup that overthrew the elected socialist president Salvador Allende. He ruled until 1990. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet.

question: Milton Friedman wrote in his Newsweek column in 1976 to answer critics who said his visit to Chile the year before meant he endorsed its military regime. How did he describe that regime?
answer: An authoritarian system he profoundly disagreed with
choices: An authoritarian system he profoundly disagreed with
A shining example of Latin American governance
The best hope for South American development
A necessary transitional phase toward liberty
context: In Newsweek on June 14, 1976, Friedman wrote of 'my profound disagreement with the authoritarian political system of Chile,' adding that it was no more evil for an economist to give its government technical advice than for a physician to help it end a medical plague. Source: Friedman, Newsweek (June 14, 1976).

question: Milton Friedman pointed to a double standard while protesters kept denouncing his 1975 visit to Chile. In 1980 he visited a much larger communist country, met its leaders and gave them much the same free-market advice, and almost no one objected. Which country was it?
answer: Communist China
choices: Communist China
The Soviet Union
Vietnam
Cuba
context: Friedman visited China in 1980, meeting Chinese leaders including Zhao Ziyang. He argued the selective outrage over his Chile visit reflected a political double standard, since the China visit went uncontested. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Two Lucky People (Chicago 1998).

question: The Chicago Boys, about twenty-five Chilean economists who had studied in Chicago, sold state companies, cut tariffs and tamed runaway inflation once they ran Chile's economic policy from 1975, and the elected governments after 1990 kept their framework. About 45 percent of Chileans were poor in 1987, by the government's own household survey. Where did the rate stand thirty years later?
answer: Under 10 percent
choices: Under 10 percent
About 25 percent
About 40 percent
About 60 percent
context: Chile's national household survey put poverty at about 45 percent in 1987 and, by a newer and stricter measure, at 8.6 percent in 2017. Source: CEDLAS working paper 19; Chile's Ministry of Social Development, survey results for 2017.

question: General Pinochet wrote into his own 1980 constitution a single vote, yes or no, on whether he would stay on for another term. Millions of Chileans went to the polls to answer it on October 5, 1988. What was the outcome?
answer: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
choices: Pinochet lost and the country returned to democracy
Pinochet won and remained in power for another decade
The plebiscite was cancelled by the military
Pinochet abdicated before the vote was counted
context: The October 5, 1988 plebiscite voted Pinochet out. Free elections in December 1989 chose Patricio Aylwin as president; the transition to democracy in 1990 was peaceful. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Chilean_national_plebiscite.

question: Chileans went to free elections after seventeen years of military rule and chose Patricio Aylwin, the first of a run of center-left leaders. Christian Democrats led the early governments and Socialist-led coalitions the later ones. The Chicago Boys had remade the economy on free-market lines under the dictatorship. What did the elected governments do with those reforms?
answer: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
choices: They kept the framework substantially in place for the next 30 years
They reversed nearly every reform within the first two years
They nationalized every privatized industry immediately
They abolished the central bank
context: Successor democratic governments substantially kept the market framework across three decades of center-left and center-right rule, and Chile stood among the richest South American economies per person through the 2010s. Source: worldbank.org (Chile long-run macro data).

question: Demonstrators followed Milton Friedman to Stockholm in 1976 and, at the very ceremony where he was honored, denounced the six days he had spent in Chile the year before. He gave his lecture anyway. Which award had he come to receive?
answer: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
The Nobel Peace Prize
The Nobel Prize in Literature
The Franklin Institute Bower Award
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economic Sciences 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' Protests at the Stockholm ceremony centered on the Chile visit. Source: nobelprize.org (Friedman 1976).

question: A. W. Phillips charted British figures in 1958: pay rose fastest in years when few were out of work. Governments in the 1960s read the chart as an offer. What did they think it offered?
answer: Fewer jobless for more inflation
choices: Fewer jobless for more inflation
Higher pay with steady prices
Fewer jobless at no cost
Growth from lower taxes
context: Phillips's curve, drawn from British wage and unemployment figures, was read in the 1960s as a menu: a little more inflation could buy a little less unemployment. Milton Friedman's address of December 1967, published in 1968 as The Role of Monetary Policy, argued that the trade-off works only briefly. Source: jstor.org (Friedman AER 1968).

question: Edmund Phelps of Columbia and Milton Friedman, working separately in 1967, reached the same conclusion. In the long run, they argued, real things set the jobless rate, not money: how fast people find new jobs, how well skills fit employers' needs, how flexible wages are, laws like the minimum wage. What did Friedman call that level?
answer: The natural rate of unemployment
choices: The natural rate of unemployment
The equilibrium wage floor
The frictional threshold
The full-employment ceiling
context: Friedman's natural-rate hypothesis: there is a rate of unemployment determined by real, non-monetary factors. Monetary policy cannot push unemployment permanently below it; it can only produce temporary reductions at the cost of accelerating inflation. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: A. W. Phillips, a New Zealand-born economist, found in British figures in 1958 that pay climbed fastest in years when few people were out of work, and governments treated his curve like a menu. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps later added a piece he had left out. What was it?
answer: Inflation expectations
choices: Inflation expectations
Federal deficit levels
International trade balances
Corporate tax rates
context: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve: workers demand nominal wages that account for expected inflation. Once expectations adjust, the trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman (1968); Phelps (1967).

question: Milton Friedman argued that extra money buys extra jobs only while rising prices take workers and shopkeepers by surprise. Sooner or later they catch on, and start asking for wages and setting prices that allow for the price rises ahead. What happens to unemployment once they do, by his account?
answer: It rises back to its natural level, only now with high inflation on top
choices: It rises back to its natural level, only now with high inflation on top
It stays permanently low forever
It falls all the way to zero
It becomes disconnected from prices entirely
context: Friedman argued that once workers expected 4% inflation, they would demand 4% higher nominal wages, and unemployment would return to the natural rate -- with 4% inflation now baked in. The trade-off vanishes in the long run. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: A Federal Reserve chairman decides to hold unemployment below its natural floor for good, printing money year after year to keep jobs plentiful. By the natural-rate theory of Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps, such a central bank faces a harsh logic. What does the theory predict must happen?
answer: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
choices: Doing so requires ever-accelerating inflation until the currency breaks
Doing so requires only a one-time inflation shock
Doing so is impossible without changing the natural rate itself
Doing so imposes no long-run inflation cost at all
context: The accelerationist implication: if the Fed keeps trying to push unemployment below natural, it must keep raising expected inflation to keep workers surprised. 4% then 8% then 16% -- eventually the monetary system breaks down. Source: Friedman, AER (1968).

question: New Zealand's central bankers began a practice in 1990 that most developed countries' central banks soon took up, one still shaped by Milton Friedman's 1967 address. Rather than chase lower unemployment, the banks promised in public to hold one number steady. Which practice is it?
answer: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
choices: Inflation targeting anchored to stable expectations
Fixed exchange rates against gold
Direct government spending controls
Complete abandonment of any monetary rule
context: Modern inflation targeting (New Zealand 1990, then dozens of countries) rests on the Friedman-Phelps insight: keep inflation expectations stable and the economy tends toward the natural rate. Wandering targets undermine expectations and produce accelerationist dynamics. Source: rbnz.govt.nz (New Zealand inflation-targeting history).

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in a 1945 essay that no committee of planners, however brilliant, can gather the countless small local facts a modern economy runs on: who wants what, what is scarce, what things cost. What is that limit now called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The counting problem
The paperwork problem
The velocity problem
context: Hayek's 1945 essay, The Use of Knowledge in Society, argued that the facts an economy runs on are scattered in millions of heads and that market prices, not any central committee, carry them to where they are needed. The limit he described is now called the knowledge problem. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Lionel Robbins invited Friedrich Hayek to London in 1931 to give four lectures, later published as Prices and Production. In them Hayek claimed that booms built on cheap credit from central banks must end in painful busts. What kind of theory was he setting out?
answer: A theory of the business cycle
choices: A theory of the business cycle
A theory of international trade
A theory of consumer choice
A theory of economic growth
context: Prices and Production (1931) set out the Austrian theory of the business cycle: credit made cheap by a central bank lures firms into long projects that real savings cannot support, and the boom ends in a bust. The lectures won Hayek a chair at the London School of Economics. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A von Hayek (1899-1992) at LSE'.

question: German bombs were falling on London while Friedrich Hayek wrote a book that sold widely in Britain and America after it came out in 1944. A government planning a whole economy from the top, it warned, drifts step by step toward ruling more of people's lives, however kind its aims. What is the book called?
answer: The Road to Serfdom
choices: The Road to Serfdom
Human Action
Man, Economy, and State
The General Theory
context: Published 1944, the book was a wartime bestseller in Britain and the United States. Human Action (1949) was Mises's magnum opus; Man, Economy, and State (1962) was Rothbard's; The General Theory (1936) was Keynes's. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Robert Hutchins, chancellor of the University of Chicago, found Friedrich Hayek a professorship in 1950 after the university's economics department refused to hire him. The William Volker Fund paid for the post, outside the economics department. Which part of the university was it in?
answer: The Committee on Social Thought
choices: The Committee on Social Thought
The Cowles Commission
The Chicago Law School
The Booth School of Business
context: The William Volker Fund financed Hayek's chair on the Committee on Social Thought, outside the economics department. The Cowles Commission was the university's mathematical-economics research group, and the Law School and the business school (then the Graduate School of Business, now Booth) were separate schools. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Hayek.

question: Friedrich Hayek called about forty classical-liberal scholars, Ludwig von Mises, Milton Friedman and Karl Popper among them, to a mountain resort over Lake Geneva in April 1947. Central planning was fashionable everywhere, and they hoped to save the free-market tradition. What did they found there?
answer: The Mont Pelerin Society
choices: The Mont Pelerin Society
The Fabian Society
The Cato Institute
The Institute of Economic Affairs
context: The founding meeting was April 1-10, 1947, at Mont Pelerin above Lake Geneva. The Fabian Society was the older British socialist group Hayek argued against; Cato (1977) and the IEA (1955) came later, both influenced by Mont Pelerin alumni. Source: Mont Pelerin Society, Friedrich Hayek page.

question: Friedrich Hayek published his last book in 1988, at eighty-nine. Morals, the family, property and markets, he argued, grew over countless generations into a living order no group of planners could redesign without breaking it. Trying to rebuild society by pure reason was, he said, one particular mistake. What did he name it?
answer: The fatal conceit — believing reason can build from nothing what history took ages to grow
choices: The fatal conceit — believing reason can build from nothing what history took ages to grow
The knowledge problem — planners lack the local details that prices reveal
The utopian mirage — the idea that a perfect society is within easy reach
The rationalist error — the belief that anything old must be worth keeping
context: The Fatal Conceit (1988), edited by W. W. Bartley III, was Hayek's last book. The knowledge problem names what planners cannot gather; the fatal conceit is the pride that thinks reason can rebuild society from a blank page anyway. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A farmer sows wheat on his field, and the barley that ground might have grown is what the wheat really costs him. Friedrich von Wieser called that cost Alternativkosten. What is that in English?
answer: Opportunity cost
choices: Opportunity cost
Sunk cost
Fixed cost
Marginal cost
context: Wieser's Alternativkosten translates as OPPORTUNITY COST -- the value of the next-best alternative use foregone. Sunk cost is spent-and-unrecoverable; marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; fixed cost does not vary with output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Friedrich Wieser came home to Vienna in 1903 to take over Carl Menger's chair, after nearly twenty years of teaching elsewhere in the Habsburg empire. He had spent them at a German-language university in a city where most people spoke another language. Which city?
answer: Prague
choices: Prague
Berlin
Heidelberg
Budapest
context: Wieser held the chair at the German-language Charles University in Prague from 1884 until his 1903 move to Vienna. Prague was then the second university city of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: A traveller lost in the desert would give a fortune for his first canteen of water and next to nothing for his tenth, because each one helps less than the one before. Friedrich Wieser coined a German word in 1884 for the usefulness of that last unit: Grenznutzen. What is its English form?
answer: marginal utility
choices: marginal utility
consumer surplus
producer surplus
elasticity of demand
context: Grenznutzen is marginal utility: the value of the last unit consumed, and the reason a thirsty man in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and almost nothing for the tenth. Consumer surplus, producer surplus and elasticity of demand are other terms of price theory, all made famous by Alfred Marshall. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Workers at a steel mill turned iron ore and coal into train wheels. The classical economists found a wheel's value by adding up the labor and fuel spent making it, but Friedrich von Wieser stood that on its head with his theory of imputation. Where did he say a wheel's value begins?
answer: With the customer's use for the final product
choices: With the customer's use for the final product
With the hours of labor put into each part
With the amount of coal burned to smelt the iron
With the age of the machinery used
context: Wieser's theory of imputation (Zurechnung) works from the top down: a good's value comes from what the customer will use the finished product for, and that value is then credited back to the inputs, the steel, the ore and the labor. The classical labor theory ran the other way, adding up the work and fuel spent. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Emperor Karl I raised Friedrich Wieser to the nobility in 1917, turning plain Friedrich Wieser into Friedrich von Wieser, a baron. The same year the emperor seated him in the upper house of the imperial parliament. What was that house called?
answer: the House of Lords
choices: the House of Lords
the Imperial Council
the Diet of Bohemia
the Reichsrat lower chamber
context: Wieser was elevated to hereditary nobility (Freiherr, Baron) in 1917 and appointed to the Austrian House of Lords (Herrenhaus) the same year, alongside his Ministry of Commerce cabinet role -- an unusually rapid political promotion for an academic. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Fritz Machlup, teaching at Princeton in 1962, published the first attempt to count a slice of the American economy nobody had measured: its schools, research labs, publishers and media. What was the book called?
answer: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
choices: The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States
The Coming of Post-Industrial Society
The Age of Discontinuity
The Affluent Society
context: The 1962 Princeton book defined and measured what Machlup called the knowledge industry: schools, research and development, media, communication and information services. The Coming of Post-Industrial Society is Daniel Bell's book of 1973, The Age of Discontinuity is Peter Drucker's of 1969, and The Affluent Society is John Kenneth Galbraith's of 1958. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: Fritz Machlup reckoned that the schools, labs, publishers and media he counted came to about 29 percent of everything America produced in 1958. His figure launched a whole field of study, years before its name became a business-magazine cliché. What is that part of the economy now called?
answer: The knowledge economy
choices: The knowledge economy
The attention economy
The gig economy
The information age
context: Machlup spoke of a knowledge industry; his 29 percent estimate for 1958 launched the study of what is now called the knowledge economy. The gig economy and the attention economy are later names for other things. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Production_and_Distribution_of_Knowledge_in_the_United_States.

question: Fritz Machlup's fellow economists elected him to the summit of their profession in 1966, a rare height for a man trained in Vienna's Austrian school. Which post did they give him?
answer: President of the American Economic Association
choices: President of the American Economic Association
Chair of the Federal Reserve
Director of the National Bureau of Economic Research
Chief Economist of the World Bank
context: Machlup's 1966 AEA presidency was a rare case of a Mises-trained Austrian reaching the summit of the American mainstream without abandoning his tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/American_Economic_Association.

question: Fritz Machlup began, late in life, to grow his 1962 study into a huge work of several volumes. Princeton University Press brought out its volumes between 1980 and 1984. What is the set called?
answer: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
choices: Knowledge: Its Creation, Distribution, and Economic Significance
Knowledge and Decisions
The Constitution of Liberty
A Monetary History of the United States
context: Machlup planned ten volumes, but only three reached print, the third in 1984, after his death in 1983; the series was never finished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup.

question: A husband and wife send dollars overseas to Japan and Colombia. Austrian economists, reading the trade figures past the headlines, say the two have lost nothing. What do the husband and wife get for those dollars?
answer: Goods they freely chose to buy
choices: Goods they freely chose to buy
A debt the country must later repay
Fewer jobs for workers at home
A weaker dollar for everyone else
context: Buying an import is a trade, not a loss: the family hands over dollars and gets a car or coffee it valued more than the money. Austrian economists read a trade figure the same way, as a record of voluntary exchanges, and the dollars that go abroad come back as purchases of American goods or investments in American assets.

question: A Vienna economist supervised Fritz Machlup's doctorate, finished in 1923, and Machlup was among the youngest regulars of that man's private seminar. The supervisor had shown in 1920 why socialist planners, without real market prices, cannot work out what anything costs. Who was he?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk
Friedrich von Wieser
context: Machlup took his Vienna doctorate in 1923 under Mises and became one of the youngest members of the Mises Privatseminar. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fritz_Machlup.

question: A customer of Sam Bankman-Fried's crypto exchange tried to pull his money out in November 2022 and found withdrawals frozen. The exchange, the world's second-largest and based in the Bahamas, filed for bankruptcy days later. What was it called?
answer: FTX
choices: FTX
Binance
Coinbase
Kraken
context: FTX, founded 2019 by Sam Bankman-Fried, filed for Chapter 11 on November 11 2022 after a run triggered by a CoinDesk leak about its sister trading firm Alameda Research. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried's customers lost billions in November 2022 when his crypto exchange collapsed after secretly spending their deposits on a sister firm's bets. Bitcoin's own network kept adding blocks the whole time. What did the collapse show about where the failure lay?
answer: In one dishonest company, not in Bitcoin
choices: In one dishonest company, not in Bitcoin
In Bitcoin's code, which let coins vanish
In the Bahamas' weak banking laws alone
In crypto as a whole, which cannot work
context: FTX had secretly spent its customers' deposits to cover its sister firm's losses, so when customers ran for the exits the money was gone. Through it all the Bitcoin network kept adding blocks as usual: the failure was the company's, not Bitcoin's. Sam Bankman-Fried was arrested in the Bahamas on December 12, 2022. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: Tom Brady and Shaquille O'Neal appeared in TV ads for Sam Bankman-Fried's crypto exchange, which also paid about $135 million to put its name on the Miami Heat's arena. Months later, in November 2022, the exchange collapsed. Why do risky firms buy stadium names and celebrity ads?
answer: It buys the look of trust before anyone asks hard questions
choices: It buys the look of trust before anyone asks hard questions
Sports leagues require it of every sponsor
It proves to regulators that the firm holds reserves
Celebrities vouch for the firm's audited books
context: FTX bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's arena in a 2021 19-year, $135M deal. The naming reverted after the bankruptcy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaseya_Center.

question: Readers of the crypto news site CoinDesk saw a leaked balance sheet on November 2, 2022: Alameda Research, the trading firm tied to Sam Bankman-Fried's exchange, held as its biggest asset a token that the exchange had invented itself and could create more of at will. Why was leaning on that token unsafe?
answer: Its value hung on the exchange surviving, so it backed nothing
choices: Its value hung on the exchange surviving, so it backed nothing
Its price was set by regulators, not by the market
It was too new to have any market price yet
Its trades were too slow to settle in a crisis
context: FTT was FTX's own exchange token. Alameda's balance sheet holding its sister exchange's own token as its largest asset was the market signal that led competitor Binance to announce it would sell its FTT holdings -- and that triggered the run. Source: coindesk.com (November 2 2022 report).

question: Changpeng Zhao, who ran Binance, the largest crypto exchange, announced on November 6, 2022, that Binance would sell every FTT token it held. FTT (the FTX Token) was a token FTX (short for Futures Exchange) had invented itself, and FTX's sister firm leaned on it. What happened at FTX within hours?
answer: Customers rushed to pull their money out in a run
choices: Customers rushed to pull their money out in a run
Buyers rushed in to scoop up the cheap token
The token's price jumped as traders bought in
Customers moved more money into FTX for safety
context: Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao's November 6 2022 announcement that Binance would sell its FTT holdings after the CoinDesk leak triggered mass customer withdrawals from FTX; the run began within hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX.

question: The owner of a crypto exchange promises his customers in writing that their deposits sit safe in separate accounts and can be withdrawn at any time. Behind the scenes he moves customer money out of those accounts to cover what his private investment firm has lost on bad bets. When customers try to withdraw, the vault is empty. What is this called in finance and law?
answer: Commingling customer funds with the firm's own trading
choices: Commingling customer funds with the firm's own trading
A legal short-term loan customers agreed to
Standard fractional-reserve banking
An audited overnight sweep account
context: The commingling-and-use of customer funds was the criminal act; it is the same failure mode as Mt Gox (2014) and MF Global (2011). Every exchange collapse of this shape has taught the same lesson: not your keys, not your coins. Source: cnbc.com (FTX bankruptcy filings coverage).

question: Judge Lewis Kaplan sentenced Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of a collapsed crypto exchange, in a Manhattan courtroom on March 28, 2024. A jury had found him guilty in November 2023 on all seven counts against him. What sentence did Kaplan hand down?
answer: Twenty-five years in federal prison
choices: Twenty-five years in federal prison
Life in federal prison
Ten years in federal prison
Five years in federal prison and a fine
context: Kaplan's 25-year sentence covered wire fraud, securities fraud, and money-laundering conspiracy. FTX creditors were later paid back close to dollar-value on their claims by the bankruptcy estate, but of course missed the Bitcoin appreciation over the recovery years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Sam_Bankman-Fried.

question: Sam Bankman-Fried told reporters and donors that his ethics came from one movement. Its followers try to do the most good they can with their money and their work, often by getting rich and then giving to whatever cause saves the most lives per dollar. What is the movement called?
answer: Effective altruism
choices: Effective altruism
Rational optimism
Stoicism
Utilitarian pragmatism
context: Bankman-Fried had been publicly linked with effective altruism since his Jane Street days; his stated plan was to earn as much as possible and give it away. He then took billions from his own customers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism.

question: Suppose Congress sets up a safety agency to watch the country's carmakers. Over the years it hires their former lobbyists and writes rules that suit the three biggest firms, burying smaller rivals in paperwork. What is it called when a watchdog ends up serving the industry it was meant to police?
answer: Regulatory capture
choices: Regulatory capture
Consumer surplus
Market discipline
Free enterprise
context: Stigler argued in 1971 that regulation is, as a rule, acquired by the industry and run mainly for its benefit; a watchdog that ends up serving the firms it watches is the pattern called regulatory capture. Stigler won the 1982 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on industrial structure and regulation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stigler.

question: George Stigler published 'The Theory of Economic Regulation' in a journal paid for by AT&T's research arm, in the spring of 1971. Which journal was it?
