question: Joseph Schumpeter told a stormier story about entrepreneurs than Israel Kirzner did: inventors of new technology charge in and sweep away established firms and whole industries. Schumpeter gave that stormy process a famous two-word name. What did he call it?
answer: Creative destruction
choices: Creative destruction
Perfect competition
Rent-seeking
Moral hazard
context: Schumpeter cast the entrepreneur as a disruptive innovator in The Theory of Economic Development (1911) and made the phrase creative destruction famous in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942). Kirzner's 1973 book is the deliberate Austrian counter-account. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: Israel Kirzner parted from Joseph Schumpeter over where chances for profit come from. Schumpeter said entrepreneurs invent brand-new opportunities out of thin air. In Kirzner's view, what does each of those entrepreneurs really do?
answer: Discovers opportunities that were already there
choices: Discovers opportunities that were already there
Bears the risks that others will not take on
Organizes land, labor and capital to produce
Saves for years to build up the capital he needs
context: Kirzner's language of DISCOVERY versus Schumpeter's CREATION is the standard shorthand for the two accounts in the entrepreneurship literature. Source: mises.org, 'Schumpeter vs. Kirzner on Entrepreneurs'.

question: Israel Kirzner, in his mid-seventies, received a prize in Stockholm in 2006. Many Austrians thought he deserved a Nobel Prize, which never came. Which honor did he receive?
answer: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
choices: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research
The Schumpeter Prize of the Schumpeter Society
The Templeton Prize for progress in religion
The John Bates Clark Medal in economics
context: The Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research, presented in Stockholm, went to Kirzner in 2006; it is often called the top honor in the study of entrepreneurs. Source: Wikipedia, Israel Kirzner.

question: Israel Kirzner wrote his doctoral thesis at New York University on how economists across the centuries had drawn the edges of their own subject, and in 1960 the thesis became his first book. What title did he give it?
answer: The Economic Point of View
choices: The Economic Point of View
The Theory of Money and Credit
The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science
The Constitution of Liberty
context: The Economic Point of View (1960) was Kirzner's revised dissertation, a history of how economists have defined their own field. The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was Mises's; The Ultimate Foundation of Economic Science (1962) was Mises's late methodological book; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was Hayek's. Source: EconJournalWatch author page, Israel M. Kirzner.

question: A trader finds oranges selling for one dollar in one town and three in the next, and carts some across. Israel Kirzner argued that profit like his carries information. What does the trader's profit signal to everyone else?
answer: That resources were being wasted in the low-value place
choices: That resources were being wasted in the low-value place
That he has cheated the town where he bought cheap
That oranges cost more to grow in the dearer town
That prices between towns can never be equal in a free market
context: In Kirzner's account a price gap is a sign that goods are not where people value them most. The trader's profit rewards him for noticing it and tells others the gap is there, and each crate he moves shifts oranges toward the town that values them more, narrowing the gap. Source: Kirzner, Competition and Entrepreneurship (1973).

question: Frank Knight, a Chicago economist, split the unknown in two in a book of 1921. A tossed coin lands heads half the time, so its odds can be measured; whether war breaks out somewhere next year has no honest odds at all. What did Knight call that second kind?
answer: Uncertainty
choices: Uncertainty
Risk
Interest
Depreciation
context: Buchanan later insisted that six weeks in Frank Knight's price-theory course flipped his intellectual orientation. He took his 1948 Chicago PhD under Knight's supervision. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: Warren Nutter and James Buchanan set up a research center at the University of Virginia in 1957. They named it for a champion of small farmers and of government kept small. What did they call it?
answer: The Thomas Jefferson Center
choices: The Thomas Jefferson Center
The Mercatus Center
The Center for Study of Public Choice
The Cato Institute
context: Buchanan and Nutter founded the Thomas Jefferson Center at UVa in 1957. It was Buchanan's first institutional home before Tullock arrived and the two founded the Public Choice Society together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson_Center_for_Political_Economy.

question: Gordon Tullock and James Buchanan refused to treat people in government as saints. Their school spent years studying how citizens vote, how lobbies push and how agencies spend, and the studies kept turning up one finding about officials and lawmakers. What was it?
answer: They respond to incentives, just like people in business do
choices: They respond to incentives, just like people in business do
They mostly act on party ideology, not self-interest
They know too little to manage what they control
They mostly follow the experts on their staffs
context: Public choice is politics without romance. Buchanan's contribution: strip the assumption that politicians act from pure public spirit; treat them as ordinary humans responding to ordinary incentives. The Center moved to George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, in 1983.

question: Luigi Einaudi, a former president of Italy, was among the public-finance scholars James Buchanan met on a Fulbright year in 1955-56. They wanted limits on spending set in a country's constitution, above everyday politics. Why not simply trust politicians to hold the line?
answer: Politicians face short-term pressure to spend and print money
choices: Politicians face short-term pressure to spend and print money
Elected leaders lack the expertise to draw up a budget
Courts move too slowly to stop a bad spending bill
Parliaments change too often for any plan to last
context: Buchanan spent 1955-56 in Italy on a Fulbright, working with Luigi Einaudi (former President of Italy 1948-55) and the Italian public-finance tradition. He credited that year with shaping his constitutional-fiscal focus. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: John Price Buchanan, a Populist farmer-politician, won election on a Farmers' Alliance platform, and the family's tales of his campaigns later fed his grandson James's early interest in public life. What office did the grandfather hold from 1891 to 1893?
answer: Governor of Tennessee
choices: Governor of Tennessee
US Senator from Tennessee
Chief Justice of the Tennessee Supreme Court
Mayor of Nashville
context: John Price Buchanan served as Governor of Tennessee from 1891 to 1893, elected on a Farmers' Alliance platform. James Buchanan often noted the family political inheritance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_P._Buchanan.

question: Back from the war, in which he had served on a Navy staff in Honolulu, James Buchanan arrived at the University of Chicago as a student in 1945. Years later he described the young man he had been as a 'libertarian socialist,' until six weeks in one price-theory course made him a market-order man. What had he really been, politically, when he arrived?
answer: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
choices: He was a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to redistribution
He was a Northern union organizer drawn to the Socialist Party
He was a Midwestern farm-state Republican wary of the New Deal
He was a New York progressive loyal to Roosevelt's brain trust
context: Buchanan was the son of Tennessee farming Democrats and sympathized with New Deal redistribution when he arrived at Chicago; he had no early conservatism. The 'libertarian socialist' label was his own description of that starting point. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (1992).

question: Jeff Booth, a Canadian who had built and sold companies for thirty years, published a book about money and technology in January 2020. Bitcoin's defenders soon embraced it. What is its title?
answer: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
choices: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future
The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Sovereign Individual: Mastering the Transition to the Information Age
The Ascent of Money: A Financial History of the World
context: Written by Jeff Booth, formerly the founder of BuildDirect, an online building-materials company. He had spent 30 years building and selling companies before turning to monetary writing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth argued in his 2020 book that central banks and politicians treat one feature of the modern economy as a threat, when it is really a gift that would let ordinary families grow richer every year without a raise. Which trait of technology does Booth call the misunderstood gift?
answer: Technology keeps making things cheaper, from computer chips to solar power
choices: Technology keeps making things cheaper, from computer chips to solar power
Technology keeps replacing jobs, so workers must keep retraining
Technology keeps pulling work into cities, where wages run higher
Technology keeps shortening the working week for everyone
context: Moore's Law captures the classical case: Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling every year, and in 1975 revised the pace to about every two years. Solar photovoltaics, LEDs, memory, and storage follow parallel curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Moore%27s_law.

question: A saver finds that her pay has crept up only slightly since 2010, while share prices have more than tripled. Jeff Booth blames central banks, which create new money to keep prices from falling. Read in Frédéric Bastiat's way, the seen fact is steady prices in the shops, which look like proof that the Fed did its job. What is the unseen?
answer: The price drops technology owed her were soaked up by rising asset prices
choices: The price drops technology owed her were soaked up by rising asset prices
Cheap imports, not the central bank, were what held shop prices steady
Shares rose only because companies earned far more each year
Her savings earned enough interest to more than close the gap
context: The seen: relatively stable consumer prices, a 'successful' Fed inflation target. The unseen: the prices should have fallen substantially given the underlying productivity gains. The gap accrues to asset holders. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth, the Canadian tech entrepreneur, argues that technology should let a working family's savings buy more every year, but central banks print new money to prop prices up, so the gain never reaches the family. Booth says one form of money escapes that trap. Which money does he pick?
answer: Bitcoin, whose supply is capped at 21 million coins
choices: Bitcoin, whose supply is capped at 21 million coins
Gold, whose supply grows only as fast as miners dig
A digital dollar issued by the central bank under a fixed rule
A basket of world currencies run by the International Monetary Fund
context: Booth's argument connects Bitcoin to technology-optimism in a way that reaches audiences who resist harder Austrian or goldbug framings. The point is monetary design, not price prediction. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Jeff Booth shares the stage, in the Bitcoin argument about money, with two other leading voices: a software boss who put his listed company's cash reserves into Bitcoin, and the author of The Bitcoin Standard. Who are the other two?
answer: Michael Saylor and Saifedean Ammous
choices: Michael Saylor and Saifedean Ammous
Vitalik Buterin and Sam Bankman-Fried
Peter Thiel and Elon Musk
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger
context: Saylor (MicroStrategy chairman, corporate-treasury Bitcoin advocate) and Ammous ('The Bitcoin Standard') provide the corporate and Austrian frames; Booth provides the technology-optimist frame. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jeff_Booth.

question: Bankers and a senator spent about nine days in secret on Jekyll Island, off the Georgia coast, in November 1910, drafting a plan for a new American central bank. Only one body could make such a plan law. Which body had to pass it?
answer: Congress
choices: Congress
The Treasury
The courts
The states
context: The plan went to Congress as the Aldrich Plan and stalled; Congress then passed a modified version as the Federal Reserve Act, which President Woodrow Wilson signed on December 23, 1913. Nelson Aldrich, the senator who led the party, chaired the National Monetary Commission. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: Frank Vanderlip rode the private railroad car to Jekyll Island in November 1910 as president of a huge New York bank, the one tied to the Rockefeller fortune. Which bank did he lead?
answer: National City Bank of New York
choices: National City Bank of New York
Chase National Bank
First National Bank of New York
Bankers Trust
context: Frank Vanderlip led National City Bank of New York -- the Rockefeller bank, later Citibank and eventually Citigroup. His part in the Jekyll Island trip was kept quiet for years; he told his side in a 1935 magazine article. Source: Grokipedia 'Frank Vanderlip' (2026-09-05).

question: Henry Davison rode with the party to Jekyll Island in November 1910. His companions included Senator Nelson Aldrich of Rhode Island, Kuhn Loeb's Paul Warburg, Frank Vanderlip and the Treasury's Piatt Andrew. What post did Davison hold on Wall Street?
answer: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
choices: Senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company
President of Chase National Bank
Chairman of Kuhn Loeb and Company
President of First National Bank of New York
context: Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company, there for the House of Morgan. Source: Grokipedia 'Henry Pomeroy Davison' (2026-09-05).

question: Paul Warburg, Frank Vanderlip and the other bankers at Jekyll Island in November 1910 drew up, in private, the plan that would pass in modified form as the Federal Reserve Act. Why do public-choice economists think it matters that those bankers wrote it?
answer: The regulated helped write the rules that would govern them
choices: The regulated helped write the rules that would govern them
No small group could know enough to design a money system
Rules drafted in secret can never be legally binding
Bankers lacked the training to design a central bank
context: Public-choice economists, following George Stigler's theory of regulatory capture, expect the industry a regulator oversees to shape its rules. At Jekyll Island the bankers who would live under the new system drafted it themselves, with Senator Aldrich and A. Piatt Andrew, an Assistant Treasury Secretary, beside them. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/jekyll-island-conference.

question: Frank Vanderlip, president of a great New York bank and one of the Jekyll Island party, told his own side of the story in print in 1935, and he described his conduct on the trip in blunt terms. Which phrase did he use?
answer: Furtive, as any conspirator
choices: Furtive, as any conspirator
Formal, as a governmental commission
Cheerful, as a social gathering
Studious, as an academic seminar
context: Vanderlip wrote in the Saturday Evening Post of February 9, 1935: 'I was as secretive -- indeed as furtive -- as any conspirator', and he called the trip the actual conception of what became the Federal Reserve System. Source: saturdayeveningpost.com (From Farm Boy to Financier).

question: Song officials took over Sichuan's private paper receipts in 1023 and began issuing the notes themselves, the first paper money any government ever put out. What were the notes called?
answer: jiaozi
choices: jiaozi
chao
yuan
cash
context: Jiaozi was the Song dynasty government paper (from ~1023 AD). Chao was the later Mongol Yuan dynasty paper; yuan is the modern name for the Chinese currency unit; 'cash' is the English name for old Chinese round coins with a square hole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: Song China's rulers, the first anywhere to issue government paper money, ordered yet another batch of notes printed, far beyond what their reserves could back. What pressure drove them to print so much?
answer: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
choices: military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols
the construction of the Great Wall extensions
irrigation projects in the Yangtze delta
famine relief after the Yellow River floods
context: Military spending against the Jin (the northern rival) and later the Mongols drove the over-issue of the Song's later paper notes, the huizi, which came after the jiaozi; by the 1230s the notes in circulation had multiplied many times over and lost much of their value. Great Wall extension (a Ming project), Yangtze irrigation and flood relief were not the driver. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huizi_(currency); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiaozi_(currency).

question: Kublai Khan, the Mongol emperor who ruled China from Beijing in the late 1200s, printed a paper money called chao and made every merchant and peasant take it by law. When a ruler can print at will and force people to take it, what tends to happen to his money?
answer: The ruler prints more to pay his bills and each note buys less than before
choices: The ruler prints more to pay his bills and each note buys less than before
The ruler stops printing and the money holds its value for centuries
Merchants refuse the notes, and trade moves back to silver at once
Prices fall as the new notes draw more goods into the markets
context: Kublai Khan (reigned 1260-94) issued the chao from the first year of his reign; his second issue of 1260 was tied to silver, but later Yuan issues lost their backing and suffered devaluation and, at the end, hyperinflation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_(currency).

question: Marco Polo, the Venetian merchant who spent the 1270s and 1280s in Kublai Khan's service, described the Khan's paper money, the chao, and how the Khan kept the notes moving through the markets. What punishment did Polo report for anyone who refused them?
answer: death for refusing to accept the notes
choices: death for refusing to accept the notes
banishment for two years
a fine of one hundred silver taels
public flogging
context: Marco Polo reported that refusing the chao was punishable by death under Kublai. Banishment, fines, and flogging were common Mongol punishments for other offenses but Polo specifies death for chao refusal. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels of Marco Polo (c. 1298), Book II ch 24.

question: Marco Polo gave a whole chapter of the book he wrote in 1298, his Travels, to Kublai Khan's paper money. He said the notes were cut from the inner bark of one kind of tree and sealed in vermilion ink with the emperor's stamp. Which tree?
answer: the mulberry tree
choices: the mulberry tree
the English oak
the white willow
the silver birch
context: Polo described the chao as being made from mulberry bark. Oak, willow, and birch bark have been used for other papers in other places but Polo specifies mulberry for the chao. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: Marco Polo came from a Europe where money always meant gold and silver coin, and in Kublai Khan's China he watched the emperor issue paper notes. In his Travels, Polo described the Khan's paper money with a striking comparison. Which comparison did he use?
answer: a kind of alchemy that turned bark into wealth
choices: a kind of alchemy that turned bark into wealth
a form of taxation the citizens paid willingly
a religious offering the citizens made to the Khan
a military tribute the conquered peoples paid
context: Polo compared the chao system to alchemy: bark being transmuted into wealth by the Khan's stamp. He did not frame it as tax, offering, or tribute in the passage. Source: Marco Polo, The Travels (Book II ch 24).

question: Kublai Khan forced his paper money, the chao, on China from Beijing, and Marco Polo marveled at it in his Travels. Kublai himself died in 1294; the Yuan dynasty he founded lasted until 1368. What happened to the chao in the decades after his death?
answer: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
choices: successor emperors printed at will to fund crises, and by the 1350s the chao was worthless
the chao was formally backed by silver and stabilized for another two centuries
the Ming dynasty adopted it as its own currency in 1368
the notes were called in and swapped for copper coins at full value
context: After Kublai, later Yuan emperors printed chao at will; by the 1350s it was worthless and the Yuan dynasty was collapsing. The Ming (founded 1368) inherited the ruin, not the currency; silver backing did not stabilize it, and no one redeemed the notes at full value. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty.

question: Song officials in the 1000s and Kublai Khan in the 1200s issued two of the earliest paper moneys any state ever put out, and both ended nearly worthless. Modern Austrian economists draw one pointed conclusion from that record. Which reasoning move do they make?
answer: That the earliest government paper currencies in world history all collapsed, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
choices: That the earliest government paper currencies in world history all collapsed, suggesting the failure pattern is structural rather than a modern accident
That Chinese culture was uniquely unsuited to paper money, so the Song and Yuan collapses tell us nothing about later fiat currencies elsewhere in the world
That the paper-money failure in both dynasties was caused primarily by insufficient literacy among the population handling the notes rather than by over-issuance
That the Song and Yuan governments simply lacked modern accounting tools, so a modern central bank with proper spreadsheets would not repeat the same mistake
context: The Austrian move: paper money is nearly a thousand years old, and the first states to try it, the Song, then the Jin and the Mongol Yuan, all watched it lose nearly all its value; the failure pattern is structural, not modern-specific. Cultural, literacy, and accounting explanations are the alternative arguments the Austrian analysis specifically rejects. Sources: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021); Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money?; Wikipedia 'Chao (currency)'.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught his readers in the 1840s to look for both the seen and the unseen consequences of every policy. A Bastiat-style retelling of Kublai Khan's paper money applies that lens to what Marco Polo witnessed at the Khan's court. Which claim does it make about the mechanism?
answer: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
choices: That the SEEN was the Khan turning bark into wealth, and the UNSEEN was the future price collapse absorbing the wealth of every current chao holder within a generation
That Marco Polo simply misunderstood Chinese economics and misreported what Kublai's paper system actually did in daily commerce inside the Mongol empire
That paper money worked reliably in Kublai's China as long as the Khan personally guaranteed it, and no monetary lesson generalizes to any later fiat system elsewhere
That the chao would have lasted indefinitely if the Mongol empire had lasted longer, and the collapse says nothing about paper money's structural incentive to over-issue
context: The Bastiat move: SEEN (the wealth Kublai's paper appeared to create); UNSEEN (the future currency collapse quietly transferring that wealth away from every holder). Personal guarantee, imperial duration, and mistaken observer are the standard alternative theories the argument rejects. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: John Law talked the French regent into letting him found the Banque Generale in Paris in 1716, a bank that issued paper notes. Two years later the king's government took it over, gave it a new name, the Banque Royale, and let it issue notes with no real limit. What happened next to Law's paper money?
answer: It crashed, and people lost their savings in a giant bubble
choices: It crashed, and people lost their savings in a giant bubble
It held its value, since the crown backed every note
It was swapped for silver coin at full value
It kept circulating for decades at a small discount
context: Law founded the Banque Generale in 1716. In 1718 the crown nationalized it and renamed it the Banque Royale, guaranteeing its notes as legal tender. Banque de France (a different institution) was founded by Napoleon in 1800. Source: Grokipedia 'Banque Royale' (2026-09-05).

question: Small investors in Paris piled into John Law's Mississippi Company in 1719, and many of them grew rich on paper as its shares soared. The French language coined a brand-new word for these newly rich shareholders. Which word came out of the mania?
answer: Millionaire
choices: Millionaire
Bourgeois
Rentier
Speculateur
context: The word 'millionaire' first appears in French in about 1719 to describe the newly rich shareholders in Law's Mississippi Company. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Oxford English Dictionary etymology entry.

question: Investors in Paris paid about 500 livres for a share of John Law's Mississippi Company in mid-1719, a company that held the right to develop France's Louisiana territory. By early 1720 the shares had climbed to a peak that made the scheme famous across Europe. Roughly what peak price did they reach?
answer: About 10,000 livres per share
choices: About 10,000 livres per share
About 1,000 livres per share
About 100,000 livres per share
About 3,000 livres per share
context: Mississippi Company shares climbed roughly twenty-fold from about 500 livres in mid-1719 to around 10,000 livres by early 1720 -- one of the sharpest speculative rises in monetary history. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: John Law had promised France's regent that paper money would cure the debts left by Louis XIV's wars. Between 1716 and 1720 he bound his state-backed Banque Royale to his Mississippi Company, which held a monopoly on French trade with Louisiana. How did his scheme tie the bank and the company together?
answer: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
choices: The bank printed notes that were used to buy shares, whose rising price fed demand for more notes, which the bank printed
The bank taxed foreign trade and used the revenue to buy shares back from the public at a fixed price
The company shipped Louisiana silver to France, and the bank issued notes backed 100 percent by that silver
The bank borrowed from Dutch and English merchants and lent the proceeds to the company at low interest
context: The circular mechanism was the core of Law's scheme: paper money financed share purchases, rising share prices created demand for more paper, and the bank obliged. This is the shape every asset-inflation bubble since has followed. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997).

question: Big shareholders in John Law's Mississippi Company began cashing out in February 1720, demanding hard metal for their paper notes. Law, by then controller-general of French finances, reached for one legal weapon to keep his paper system alive. What did he try to do to gold?
answer: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
choices: He banned private ownership of gold coin and bullion
He fixed the price of gold at half its market rate
He required all gold to be deposited with the Mississippi Company
He nationalized every French goldsmith's shop
context: Law's February 1720 edict forbade private holdings of gold and silver bullion above small amounts, hoping to force the public back into paper. It failed within weeks. Source: Murphy, John Law (1997); Grokipedia 'Mississippi Bubble' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises later explained a pattern of boom and bust, and the Austrian economists who follow him call John Law's Mississippi scheme of 1719 and 1720 its earliest modern case. Paris filled with new fortunes on paper, and then it all went bust in 1720. Which Austrian reading fits Law's scheme most exactly?
answer: Easy credit floods one favored venture, then collapses when holders demand real money
choices: Easy credit floods one favored venture, then collapses when holders demand real money
Government spending lifts total demand and drives growth that lasts for good
A fixed supply of money brings falling prices and long-lasting unemployment
Free banking floods the country with an excess of small paper notes
context: The Austrian business-cycle pattern: newly created money distorts capital toward a favored project (Louisiana), the boom looks like prosperity, and when holders of the new money try to convert it back to real goods or hard money, the whole edifice collapses. Ludwig von Mises named the mechanism in 1912. Source: Mises, Theory of Money and Credit (1912).

question: One economist at Pace University took a side in 1990 in an old Austrian argument over Ludwig von Mises's 1920 essay on whether socialism can calculate. He defended a strict reading of Mises over the milder one drawn from Friedrich Hayek. Who is he?
answer: Joseph Salerno
choices: Joseph Salerno
Peter Boettke
Israel Kirzner
Don Lavoie
context: Joseph T. Salerno (born 1950) is professor emeritus at Pace University's Lubin School of Business and academic vice president of the Ludwig von Mises Institute. Source: mises.org/profile/joseph-t-salerno.

question: Joseph Salerno has long edited a journal of scholarship that the Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama, has published since 1998 as the flagship outlet for research in the school's Rothbardian wing. Its plain title names its school. What is the journal called?
answer: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
choices: Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics
Review of Austrian Economics
Journal of Political Economy
American Economic Review
context: Salerno has long edited the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics, which the Mises Institute launched in 1998 in place of the Review of Austrian Economics; the Review moved to George Mason University and is a separate journal. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mises_Institute; mises.org/profile/joseph-t-salerno.

question: Ludwig von Mises pointed out in 1920 that where the state owns every factory, tool and field, nobody can bid for any of them, and goods nobody can bid for never get real market prices. What problem does that leave a central planner trying to run the whole economy?
answer: The planner has no way to know which uses of resources are worth it
choices: The planner has no way to know which uses of resources are worth it
The planner cannot stop managers shirking without profits
The planner will be captured by the managers he oversees
The planner must print money to cover factory losses
context: Salerno's strict-Misesian reading: without real market prices for producer goods, no cost comparison is possible; the calculation problem is a monetary problem, not primarily a knowledge problem. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Socialist_calculation_debate.

question: Joseph Salerno published his key statement on Mises's 1920 calculation essay in the Review of Austrian Economics in 1990, arguing for a strict reading of the master, and many Austrians around the Mises Institute came round to his view. What was the article's short title?
answer: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
choices: Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist
The Use of Knowledge in Society
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
The Meaning of Market Process
context: 'Ludwig von Mises as Social Rationalist' (Review of Austrian Economics, 1990) is the paper in which Salerno set out his strict reading of Mises's argument, a reading many Austrians in the Mises Institute tradition came to share. Source: mises.org/library/ludwig-von-mises-social-rationalist.

question: Joseph Salerno turned Ludwig von Mises's theory of money on the gold standard and on the Federal Reserve in essays written over twenty-five years, and the Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama, collected them in 2010. What is the book's title?
answer: Money: Sound and Unsound
choices: Money: Sound and Unsound
The Theory of Money and Credit
Human Action
America's Great Depression
context: Money: Sound and Unsound (Mises Institute, 2010) collects 26 of Salerno's essays, among them four on the gold standard and several attacking Alan Greenspan's Fed, with a new introduction tying them to the recent crisis. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/what-we-need-know-about-money.

question: Joseph Salerno wrote a new introduction in 2009 for the Mises Institute's scholar's edition of the great treatise Murray Rothbard had left. That edition, first out in 2004, put two books first published apart back under one cover. Which work was it?
answer: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
choices: Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
context: The Mises Institute's Scholar's Edition of 2004 reunited Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State (1962) with Power and Market (1970), the material cut before first publication; its second edition of 2009 carries a new introduction by Salerno. Sources: store.mises.org (Scholar's Edition, 2009); mises.org/free-market/treatise-his-own.

question: Ludwig von Mises published an essay in 1920 in a German journal of social science, the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, and it opened decades of argument over whether a planned economy can work. What is the essay called in English?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Pretense of Knowledge
The Nature and Significance of Economic Science
context: 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' (1920) is Mises's founding contribution; the entire subsequent Austrian tradition, including the intra-tradition dispute Salerno intervened in, argues about how to read it. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: Milton Friedman, who won the Nobel Prize in 1976, warned again and again of one great mistake people make in judging laws meant to help the poor or protect renters. Which rule did he urge instead?
answer: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
choices: Judge policies by their results, not their intentions
Judge policies by their fairness, not their cost
Judge policies by experts' forecasts, not by polls
Judge policies by their aims, not their side effects
context: 'One of the great mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results' -- Milton Friedman, in his 1975 interview with Richard Heffner on The Open Mind, a line he repeated often. Source: pbs.org (Free to Choose archive).

question: Milton Friedman took aim at the old American welfare system that ran from the 1960s through the 1990s. Its rules, he argued, quietly damaged family structure among the poor. What flaw did he find built into them?
answer: A marriage penalty in how household income was counted
choices: A marriage penalty in how household income was counted
A rule ending aid once a child turned twelve years old
A rule paying more to families who moved to big cities
A rule barring grandparents from raising children on aid
context: The pre-reform welfare system counted household income for eligibility, so a two-parent household could lose more in benefits by marrying than the added income was worth. Friedman pressed the point in Free to Choose. Source: Friedman + Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), Chapter 4.

question: Thomas Sowell, Milton Friedman's student at Chicago, added two questions of his own to his teacher's rule for weighing a policy, and together they make a three-part test. Which sentence states it?
answer: What does it intend, what does it actually do, and at what cost compared to what alternative
choices: What does it intend, what does it actually do, and at what cost compared to what alternative
Which party sponsors it, which lobbyists back it, and which president signed it
Is it legal, is it popular with voters, and can it pass both houses of Congress
How much does it cost, how much revenue does it raise, and what do budget forecasters say
context: The Friedman-Sowell three-part diagnostic: (a) intended outcome; (b) actual result; (c) cost, compared to the honest alternative. Skipping any of the three is standard practice in unserious policy debate. Source: Sowell + Friedman across their popular books.

question: A depositor walked into an American bank in the years before 1933 and traded his paper dollars for a set weight of gold. Under that gold standard, which held nearly everywhere before 1914, a government could print no more paper than its gold would cover. What did the rule stand guard against?
answer: Endless money printing
choices: Endless money printing
Bank runs and panics
Falling farm prices
Cheap foreign imports
context: In 1933 Franklin Roosevelt's government ended Americans' right to trade paper dollars for gold, and in 1971 Richard Nixon closed the dollar's last link to gold, which foreign governments had still been able to claim. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard.

question: Donald Trump picked the economist Judy Shelton in 2020 for a seat on the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors. She was known for an idea about money that almost no Fed nominee in decades had held. What had she long argued for?
answer: Tying the dollar's value to gold
choices: Tying the dollar's value to gold
Letting private banks issue their own money
Sending every citizen new money each month
Replacing cash with Fed digital money
context: Shelton has long argued for a gold-linked dollar and a stable international monetary system, and she has favored a zero inflation target over the Fed's 2 percent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Shelton.

question: A senator on the Banking Committee questions a president's nominee for the Federal Reserve's Board, which runs America's central bank. Like many economists, he wants the Fed's governors kept somewhat free of the White House once they take their seats. What reason do such economists give?
answer: So money decisions are not bent to help one politician win the next election
choices: So money decisions are not bent to help one politician win the next election
So the Treasury can always borrow at whatever interest rate it picks
So the private member banks can choose the Fed's governors themselves
So the Fed can buy up government debt whenever Congress overspends
context: The 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord ended the Fed's wartime duty to hold down the Treasury's borrowing costs. Defenders of independence argue that a central bank answering to the White House would be pressed to print money before elections. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_Accord.

question: Judy Shelton blamed the shaky, drifting exchange rates that followed the collapse of Bretton Woods for much economic harm in Money Meltdown, her book of 1994, and she argued for sound money in their place. In her argument, what does 'sound money' mean?
answer: Money that keeps its value because it cannot be printed at will
choices: Money that keeps its value because it cannot be printed at will
Money a central bank keeps stable by steering interest rates
Money backed by the full faith and credit of the government
Money whose value floats freely against every other currency
context: Money Meltdown: Restoring Order to the Global Currency System (Free Press, 1994) criticized the floating exchange rates of the post-Bretton Woods era and called for a stable, rule-bound international money. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Judy_Shelton; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Shelton.

question: Senators were still weighing Judy Shelton's nomination when the Federal Reserve promised, as the first COVID lockdowns began in the spring of 2020, to buy government bonds in any amount, flooding the economy with new dollars. Austrian critics called the policy a hidden tax on ordinary Americans. Why did they call it a tax?
answer: The new money makes existing dollars worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power
choices: The new money makes existing dollars worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power
The government adds a special new line to every income tax return
Banks are forced to charge higher fees on every checking account
The government takes a share of every bank deposit each year
context: The Fed's pledge of March 23, 2020, to buy Treasury and mortgage bonds 'in the amounts needed' came while her nomination was still pending. Whether one more vote on the Board would have changed policy is unknowable. Source: Federal Reserve press release, March 23, 2020.

question: Judy Shelton had once called America's central bank 'almost a rogue agency', and in writings and interviews before her nomination to its Board she openly doubted one long-standing arrangement there. Democrats and some Republicans took alarm in 2020. Which arrangement had she questioned?
answer: Federal Reserve independence from the executive branch
choices: Federal Reserve independence from the executive branch
The rotation of regional Fed presidents on the FOMC
The publication of FOMC minutes with a lag
The chair's twice-yearly testimony before Congress
context: In a 2019 interview Shelton said she saw no reference to independence in the law that governs the Fed. Democrats framed her doubts as a threat to the Fed's political neutrality; Republicans on the fence were also uneasy about her gold-standard views. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Shelton.

question: Susan Collins and Mitt Romney sided with every Democrat in November 2020 to deny Judy Shelton a vote on her nomination to the Federal Reserve's Board, though the Senate Banking Committee had approved her. Analysts in the Austrian tradition drew a public-choice lesson from her defeat. What lesson?
answer: An institution's own veterans tend to block a nominee who would rein it in
choices: An institution's own veterans tend to block a nominee who would rein it in
Senators trade votes on nominees to pass their own pet bills
Voters ignore Fed nominations because each one's stake is tiny
Lawmakers back nominees who will steer federal money home
context: The letter signed by dozens of former Fed economists and Reserve Bank presidents is the mechanism these analysts point to: an institution defends itself against reform-minded appointees by mobilizing its retired officials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Shelton.

question: Tim May, Eric Hughes and the other coders of the 1990s cypherpunk mailing list set out to write software that no government, however powerful, could shut off. What must be true of a tool for it to stay beyond every government's reach?
answer: No single person or place controls it
choices: No single person or place controls it
It has a very strong password
It runs only on its makers' own computers
It is kept secret from every government
context: Julian Assange joined the cypherpunk mailing list around late 1995 and wrote to it regularly until 2002, years before he founded WikiLeaks in 2006. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: A girl locks her diary with a code so strong that no computer on Earth could ever crack it. Then a bully corners her and threatens to hurt her until she opens it herself. Bitcoin holders face the same danger when an attacker can reach the person who knows the private key. What does the story show about even a perfect code?
answer: A code can still be broken by force applied to the person who knows it
choices: A code can still be broken by force applied to the person who knows it
A code is only ever as strong as the computer that runs it
A code must be changed every few months or it will wear thin
A code stays safe as long as nobody ever writes it down
context: Cryptographers call this rubber-hose cryptanalysis: the attack goes around the mathematics to the person who holds the key. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber-hose_cryptanalysis.

question: Julian Assange co-wrote a disk-encryption program in 1997 and named it Rubberhose, after cryptographers' grim slang for beating a password out of a captive. He built it for human-rights workers who might be captured and tortured. Its key idea let a captive give up one password and still keep other data hidden. What was the idea?
answer: Several hidden volumes on one disk, so no one can prove that more exist
choices: Several hidden volumes on one disk, so no one can prove that more exist
Automatic deletion of all data after a wrong password attempt
A one-time pad shared physically with a trusted friend
A password split into pieces held by several trusted friends
context: An attacker cannot tell how many volumes exist, only how many the captive has chosen to reveal; cryptographers call this plausibly deniable encryption. Assange wrote Rubberhose with Suelette Dreyfus and Ralf Weinmann as a tool for human-rights workers protecting sensitive data in the field. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubberhose_(file_system).

question: Julian Assange helped write a disk-encryption program called Rubberhose in 1997, for human-rights activists who might one day face an interrogator. The program faded, but its trick of hidden volumes a captive could deny having reappeared in two encryption programs that many people adopted. Which two?
answer: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013)
choices: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013)
PGP (1991) and GnuPG (1999)
Kerberos (1988) and SSL (1995)
Signal (2014) and Wire (2014)
context: TrueCrypt, first released in 2004, could hide a second encrypted volume inside its first, opened by a different password; VeraCrypt, begun in 2013, carried TrueCrypt's code on after TrueCrypt was abandoned in 2014. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TrueCrypt; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VeraCrypt.

question: Julian Assange founded WikiLeaks in 2006, a website that published leaked government documents from around the world. Governments tried to knock the site offline, yet it kept reappearing. The site rested on one design drawn from the cypherpunk mailing list's ideas about networks that are hard to censor. What was that design?
answer: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
choices: Documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many jurisdictions
Every document was split into pieces held by different volunteers
Only paying subscribers could read the documents, behind encryption
The servers ran from a ship anchored in international waters
context: A direct scale-up of 1990s cypherpunk censorship-resistance principles. No single government could shut all the mirrors down without cross-border legal cooperation that was often unavailable. Source: grokipedia.com/page/WikiLeaks.

question: Julian Assange walked into a small embassy in London in 2012 and asked for political asylum, after WikiLeaks had put out secret American war logs and diplomatic cables. He stayed within its walls for seven years, until, in 2019, the country behind it withdrew his asylum and British officers arrested him inside. Which country's embassy sheltered him?
answer: The Ecuadorian embassy
choices: The Ecuadorian embassy
The Russian embassy
The Cuban embassy
The Swedish embassy
context: Ecuador granted him asylum in 2012; the asylum was revoked in April 2019 and British police arrested him inside the embassy the same day. He was then held in Belmarsh prison until his 2024 plea deal and release. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Julian_Assange.

question: A student asks a cryptographer how the cypherpunks of the 1990s, coders like Tim May and Eric Hughes who fought government control of encryption, led on to WikiLeaks and, after that, to Bitcoin. The cryptographer names one idea that runs through all three. Which idea does he name?
answer: Censorship resistance: what many independent copies hold, no one can seize
choices: Censorship resistance: what many independent copies hold, no one can seize
Peer review: experts check every claim before it is published
Open source: anyone may read, copy and change the code
Digital cash: payments that leave no trail back to the payer
context: The thread runs from the mailing list's tools that no government could switch off, to WikiLeaks's mirrored documents, to Bitcoin's ledger copied on thousands of independent computers: what many copies preserve, no single power can seize. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cypherpunk.

question: Julian Simon backed his claim with the prices of raw materials such as copper, tin, wheat and iron, tracked as the world's population multiplied over two centuries. Which way have their inflation-adjusted prices moved over the long run?
answer: They have fallen
choices: They have fallen
They have risen
They have remained essentially flat
They have oscillated randomly
context: Simon documented that the inflation-adjusted prices of copper, tin, wheat and iron had fallen over the long run even as the world's population multiplied. If resources were growing scarcer, prices would rise; they did not. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Paul Ehrlich, a biologist, warned in his 1968 bestseller The Population Bomb that overpopulation would starve hundreds of millions of people to death in the 1970s. The famines never came; harvests grew bigger and the world's population went on rising. What does the story teach about big, scary forecasts?
answer: Confident doomsday predictions often turn out to be very wrong
choices: Confident doomsday predictions often turn out to be very wrong
Scientists' forecasts are more reliable than economists' forecasts
Harvests grow only when governments plan what farmers sow
A larger population always brings famine sooner or later
context: Paul Ehrlich, The Population Bomb (Ballantine, 1968), predicted global famines in the 1970s. The predicted famines did not occur; food supply per capita rose. Simon spent much of his career debating Ehrlich. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Population_Bomb.

question: Julian Simon dared the doomsayers to a public bet in 1980: name whatever raw materials they liked and a settlement date at least a year off, and he would bet their real prices would fall. Paul Ehrlich accepted, with John Harte and John Holdren. Which five metals did they pick?
answer: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
choices: Chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten
Gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and rhodium
Iron, aluminum, lead, zinc, and magnesium
Cobalt, manganese, molybdenum, titanium, and vanadium
context: Ehrlich, Harte, and Holdren chose chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten for a 10-year wager ending September 1990, totaling $1,000 ($200 per metal). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Matt Ridley and other optimists carried forward the case Julian Simon had made against Paul Ehrlich, whose 1968 book The Population Bomb warned that population growth would use up the Earth's resources and bring mass famine. Which idea never belonged to Simon's counter-argument?
answer: That governments should impose one-child policies
choices: That governments should impose one-child policies
That people are producers as well as consumers
That human ingenuity finds substitutes as scarcity rises
That real prices are the honest measure of scarcity
context: Simon's argument is anti-Malthusian, not pro-population-control. He argued people are producers of ideas as well as consumers, that ingenuity finds substitutes, and that real prices are the honest scarcity measure. One-child policies belong to the opposing Ehrlich tradition. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Julian Simon published The Ultimate Resource in 1981, a book that answered the doomsayers of the 1970s. The true limit on human progress, he argued, was not oil, copper or grain. What did he say the ultimate resource is?
answer: Human ingenuity and problem-solving
choices: Human ingenuity and problem-solving
Government stockpiles of raw materials
International trade agreements
Nationwide recycling programs
context: John Holdren served as Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and science advisor to President Obama from 2009 to 2017. He had signed onto the losing Ehrlich side of the 1980 Simon wager. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holdren.

question: Matt Ridley, a British science writer, carried Julian Simon's outlook forward in his 2010 book The Rational Optimist. Human progress, Ridley argued, does not come from clever planners running the economy from above. Where did he say most new ideas come from?
answer: Ideas meeting and combining, like people, through free exchange
choices: Ideas meeting and combining, like people, through free exchange
A few great inventors whose lone breakthroughs change everything
Big universities that train scientists in pure research
Military rivalry that drives nations to out-invent each other
context: Matt Ridley, The Rational Optimist (Harper 2010) and How Innovation Works (Harper 2020), popularizes the Simon case for continued improvement in human welfare through ingenuity. Hans Rosling's Factfulness (2018) also fits the tradition. Source: mattridley.co.uk.

question: Julian Simon staked his case against Paul Ehrlich in 1980 on five metals and ten years of population growth, a wager many call the closest thing there is to a real-world test of the fear that people were running out of resources. What point about measuring scarcity did Simon draw from the bet?
answer: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
choices: Falling real prices are the honest empirical marker of decreasing scarcity
Shrinking known reserves are the honest empirical marker of rising scarcity
Faster population growth is the honest empirical marker of rising scarcity
Expert demand forecasts are the honest empirical marker of future scarcity
context: Simon's move: real prices, not headlines, are the honest measure of scarcity, and a falling real price means a thing is growing less scarce. Ehrlich and his allies answer that one decade of prices cannot settle the long-run question. Source: Simon, The Ultimate Resource 2 (1996).

question: Paul Ehrlich has maintained since the bet closed that the decade of his wager with Julian Simon, September 1980 to September 1990, was unusual, and that his larger warnings remain sound. Ehrlich and his two partners had bet that the metals they picked would grow dearer as the world ran short; Simon bet they would grow cheaper. What does the wager's own record show?
answer: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
choices: All five metals fell in real price; Ehrlich lost every commodity
The metals rose in real price; Simon lost every commodity
The outcome was too close to call between the two
Four metals fell and one rose; Simon won on balance
context: The record on the wager itself: all five metals fell in inflation-adjusted price between September 1980 and September 1990, and in October 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a check for $576.07. Ehrlich's broader argument is a separate question from that outcome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon%E2%80%93Ehrlich_wager.

question: Karl Marx argued in Das Kapital that no family should own a mill or a field as its private property. Who did he say should own the factories and farms instead?
answer: The government, for the workers
choices: The government, for the workers
The churches, for the poor
The guilds, for their craftsmen
The crown, for the nation
context: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto (1848) called for all the instruments of production to be centralized in the hands of the state; Das Kapital supplied the economic theory behind that aim. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto.

question: Karl Marx brought out the opening volume of Das Kapital in Hamburg in 1867 with one sharp rule for prices. When two goods are exchanged, he said, the ratio of their prices reflects how much of one thing each contains. What thing?
answer: labor-hours
choices: labor-hours
raw materials
capital equipment
land area used
context: This is the LABOR THEORY OF VALUE: a coat that took twice as many socially necessary labor-hours to make as a pair of shoes should exchange for two pairs of shoes. Marx inherited the theory from Ricardo and made it the foundation of Volume 1. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Kapital.

question: Careful readers spotted a gap in Karl Marx's first volume of 1867, and he promised to close it in a later one. Real prices did not follow his rule: a factory full of machines sold its goods for more than the rule predicted, a workshop full of hands for less. What was the puzzle called?
answer: the transformation problem
choices: the transformation problem
the calculation problem
the socialization problem
the accumulation problem
context: The transformation problem: turning Volume 1's labor values into Volume 3's prices of production. Mises's later calculation problem is a different critique: under socialism there are no market prices for capital goods at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_problem.

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk set the opening volume of Das Kapital beside the one Friedrich Engels released in 1894. His 1896 charge did not rest on any test against real prices; it needed no data at all. What flaw did he charge Marx's system with?
answer: internal contradiction
choices: internal contradiction
empirical falsification
mathematical over-simplification
definitional circularity
context: Boehm-Bawerk's charge was NOT that Marx failed a data test; it was that Marx's own two volumes CONTRADICT each other. Volume 3 quietly drops what Volume 1 confidently asserted -- and no data are needed to see the internal inconsistency. This is why his essay is called the CLASSICAL critique of Kapital: the flaw is logical, not empirical. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk read the volume of Das Kapital that Engels released in 1894 and argued in 1896 that Marx had quietly dropped his own labor theory of value there. In its place, he said, Marx had slipped in an older theory of price linked to Adam Smith. What is that older theory called?
answer: A cost-of-production theory of price
choices: A cost-of-production theory of price
A supply-and-demand theory of price
A subjective marginal utility theory of price
A quantity theory of money
context: Boehm-Bawerk showed that Marx's Volume 3 prices are effectively determined by the sum of costs (wages plus capital-input costs plus average profit) -- the classical COST-OF-PRODUCTION theory of price associated with Adam Smith. That is not a transformation of the labor theory; it is a quiet substitution for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx_and_the_Close_of_His_System.

question: A young Vienna mathematician, son of the Austrian school's founder, described a strange solid in 1926. He bored a square tunnel through the middle of each face of a cube, then did the same to every smaller cube left, forever. What is the shape called?
answer: The Menger sponge
choices: The Menger sponge
The Cantor set
The Sierpinski triangle
The Mandelbrot set
context: Karl Menger the younger described the sponge in 1926. It is a 3-dimensional analogue of the 1D Cantor set. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: Karl Menger the younger took his doctorate in Vienna in 1924 under the mathematician Hans Hahn. His field asks how many numbers are needed to pin down each point in a space. What is that field called?
answer: Dimension theory
choices: Dimension theory
Number theory
Group theory
Probability theory
context: Menger's 1924 doctorate under Hans Hahn produced original work on the topological definition of what it means for a space to be n-dimensional. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: A cube bored through with square tunnels at every scale, forever, ends up with endless surface but almost no volume. Mathematicians give such a shape a fractional dimension. About what is this one's dimension?
context: The Menger sponge's Hausdorff dimension is log(20)/log(3), approximately 2.727 -- a solid cube that is dimensionally between a 2D surface and a full 3D volume. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Menger_sponge.

question: Karl Menger the younger wrote late in life about the two worlds he had lived in: the logical positivists whose meetings he sat in on, and the mathematicians, Kurt Gödel among them, who argued at his own gathering. The book came out in 1994, after his death. What is it called?
answer: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle
choices: Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle
The Open Society and Its Enemies
Logical Syntax of Language
Wittgenstein's Vienna
context: Menger's memoir, Reminiscences of the Vienna Circle and the Mathematical Colloquium (Kluwer, 1994), is one of the best insider accounts of Vienna's twin scientific-philosophical circles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Menger.

question: Molotov and Ribbentrop, the foreign ministers of Stalin and Hitler, signed a pact in Moscow late in August 1939, and its public text pledged peace between their two countries. What did its secret protocol do?
answer: Divided Poland and the Baltics between the two
choices: Divided Poland and the Baltics between the two
Pledged a joint war against Britain and France
Promised to leave Poland's borders untouched
Set up a joint navy to patrol the Baltic Sea
context: The public treaty promised non-aggression; a secret protocol, whose existence Moscow denied until 1989, split Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Romania's Bessarabia into German and Soviet spheres. Germany invaded Poland on September 1 and the Soviet Union on September 17. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: Hitler sent his armies over Poland's western border on September 1, 1939, starting the war in Europe. Sixteen days later, on September 17, a second great power invaded Poland from the east. Which power came from the east?
answer: The Soviet Union
choices: The Soviet Union
Fascist Italy
Imperial Japan
Francoist Spain
context: The USSR annexed eastern Poland immediately, and in June 1940 annexed the three Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), all consistent with the pact's secret territorial protocol. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: Stalin's secret policemen arrested thousands of Polish officers, policemen, priests, teachers and lawyers, and in the spring of 1940 their squads shot them in the Katyn Forest and at other sites. The victims were picked by design. Why would a regime like Stalin's, bent on ruling a conquered people, go after the educated first?
answer: Educated people can organize resistance to the new rulers
choices: Educated people can organize resistance to the new rulers
Educated people owned the land the state meant to seize
Educated prisoners could fetch a ransom from the West
Educated people were the likeliest to flee abroad
context: Katyn was one of three main execution sites; the other two were the NKVD facilities at Kalinin and Kharkiv. The category of victim was deliberately chosen to decapitate Polish national leadership. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: Squads of Stalin's secret police led captured Polish army officers, priests, professors and policemen into the Katyn Forest in April and May of 1940 and shot them over pits. More were shot in Kalinin's and Kharkiv's prisons, and the bodies went into mass graves. About how many people did they kill?
answer: About 22,000
choices: About 22,000
About 500
About 200,000
About 1.5 million
context: The victims were specifically the categories most likely to lead a Polish national resistance or postwar state. The class-decapitation intent is what NKVD execution lists document. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: Soviet officials blamed Nazi Germany for the Katyn massacre of 1940 once German soldiers came upon the graves in 1943, and they held to that story for almost fifty years. On April 13, 1990, the Soviet government at last admitted that its own police had done the killing. Which Soviet leader was in power that day?
answer: Mikhail Gorbachev
choices: Mikhail Gorbachev
Leonid Brezhnev
Yuri Andropov
Nikita Khrushchev
context: Gorbachev's glasnost policy made possible the archival admission that Stalin's Politburo, not Nazi Germany, had ordered the Katyn executions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: Boris Yeltsin, Russia's president, gave Poland's leaders the secret Politburo papers on the Katyn massacre on October 14, 1992, once the Soviet state had ceased to exist. One paper among them was dated March 5, 1940. What did that paper carry?
answer: Stalin's own signature on the execution order
choices: Stalin's own signature on the execution order
Molotov's diplomatic notes on the Ribbentrop pact
Ribbentrop's telegrams to Berlin
Beria's private diary from 1940
context: The Politburo order of March 5, 1940 was signed by Stalin personally. Its transfer to Poland closed a fifty-year denial. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_massacre.

question: Andrzej Wajda, a Polish director, released a film in 2007 named just Katyn, seen through the eyes of Polish families looking for their lost men after Stalin's secret police shot thousands of Polish officers and professionals in 1940. What personal history gave Wajda a direct claim to the story?
answer: Wajda's own father, an officer, had been killed at Kharkiv
choices: Wajda's own father, an officer, had been killed at Kharkiv
Wajda had served in the NKVD before defecting to Poland
Wajda had personally filmed the German 1943 exhumations
Wajda had led the March 1990 protests demanding acknowledgment
context: Wajda was one of Poland's most decorated filmmakers (director of 'Man of Iron' and 'Man of Marble'). The 2007 'Katyn' won multiple international awards. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Katyn_(film).

question: Vyacheslav Molotov signed a pact with Joachim von Ribbentrop, Hitler's foreign minister, in Moscow in August 1939. Moscow went on to annex Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in June 1940, and Stalin's police carried out the Katyn massacre, all before Hitler attacked Stalin in June 1941. What hard fact do these events establish about the Soviet state in the twenty-two months between?
answer: The Soviet Union was a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany from August 1939 to June 1941
choices: The Soviet Union was a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany from August 1939 to June 1941
The Soviet Union stayed neutral, acting only to defend its own borders
The Soviet Union was allied with the United Kingdom throughout 1939-41
The Soviet Union was itself at war with Germany from 1939 onward
context: The pact and its secret territorial protocol, the September 1939 Soviet invasion of Poland, the June 1940 annexation of the Baltics, and the 1940 Katyn massacre are one continuous historical arc. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact.

question: Susette Kelo, a nurse, refused in 2000 to sell her little pink house by the shore in New London, Connecticut, which the city wanted for a private development beside Pfizer's new research center. The city moved to take it anyway, under a power the Fifth Amendment allows for public use with just compensation. What is that power called?
answer: Eminent domain
choices: Eminent domain
Sovereign immunity
Regulatory taking
Manifest necessity
context: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause authorizes eminent domain -- government seizure of private property for public use, with just compensation. Historically 'public use' meant roads, schools, or military bases. Source: constitution.congress.gov (Fifth Amendment).

question: New London's lawyers told the Supreme Court in 2005 that a developer's new office park beside a Pfizer plant counted as 'public use' under the Constitution, reason enough to take Susette Kelo's little pink house. The Court sided with the city. Why do critics say the ruling stretches the meaning of public use too far?
answer: The property is going to another private owner, not to a park or a road
choices: The property is going to another private owner, not to a park or a road
The owners were offered less than their homes were worth
The development would raise taxes on the neighbors who stayed
The project would serve tourists rather than the city's residents
context: Justice John Paul Stevens wrote for the majority in Kelo v. City of New London, 545 US 469 (2005), joined by Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Source: supremecourt.gov (Kelo 545 US 469).

question: Five justices of the Supreme Court let New London take Susette Kelo's home for a private developer in 2005. One of the four dissenters wrote the case's most quoted warning: under the ruling, the state could now replace any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton, or any home with a shopping mall. Which justice wrote it?
answer: Sandra Day O'Connor
choices: Sandra Day O'Connor
Antonin Scalia
Clarence Thomas
William Rehnquist
context: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor's principal dissent was joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas. The Motel-6-to-Ritz-Carlton passage became the most-quoted line of the case. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), dissent.

question: New London's planners built their redevelopment of Susette Kelo's street around Pfizer's big new research center beside it, which was supposed to revive the city. After the Supreme Court's 2005 ruling, Kelo lost her pink house. What happened to the Pfizer center that was the whole point of the plan?
answer: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
choices: Pfizer closed the facility within about five years
Pfizer doubled the campus size
Pfizer moved its global headquarters there
Pfizer turned it into its main vaccine factory
context: Pfizer closed the New London research facility in 2009-10. The cleared land where Kelo's house and her neighbors' homes had stood then remained vacant for more than a decade. Source: nytimes.com and courant.com (Pfizer New London closure coverage).

question: Susette Kelo's lawyers lost her case in the Supreme Court in 2005, when five justices let New London take her home for a private developer, and the anger that followed cut across party lines. State legislatures passed statutes or amendments to their constitutions that curbed takings for private projects. Within a decade of the ruling, roughly how many states did so?
answer: About 45
choices: About 45
About 15
About 5
About 30
context: Roughly 45 states enacted post-Kelo constitutional amendments or statutes restricting economic-development takings, largely driven by campaigns from the Institute for Justice, Kelo's counsel. Source: ij.org (post-Kelo state legislation tracker).

question: Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick founded a public-interest law firm in 1991, and its lawyers later carried Susette Kelo's fight for her pink house in New London all the way to the Supreme Court in 2005. It has since become one of the nation's leading firms suing on behalf of property owners. What is it called?
answer: The Institute for Justice
choices: The Institute for Justice
The Pacific Legal Foundation
The Federalist Society
The Cato Institute
context: The Institute for Justice, founded in 1991, represented Susette Kelo and has litigated dozens of eminent-domain cases since. Source: ij.org.

question: Susette Kelo, a nurse, lost her little pink house in 2005 when New London handed the land to a private developer to build offices beside Pfizer's new research center. Public-choice economists find a familiar story in the case. It explains, they say, why takings from one private owner for another keep happening, though critics call them a stretch of the Constitution. Which story do the economists tell?
answer: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
choices: A politically connected developer captures takings power over dispersed homeowners
A benevolent city planner balances competing public interests
A federal environmental review paralyzes local government
A random judicial error assigns rights inefficiently
context: The public-choice reading combines Tullock 1967 rent-seeking (real resources burned on the political process) with Olson 1965 concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost (one organized developer versus many un-organized neighbors). Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: Defenders of the Supreme Court's 2005 Kelo ruling pointed to the public purpose New London had named in its redevelopment plan, the plan that gave Susette Kelo's land to a private developer to build offices beside Pfizer's new plant. What was that stated purpose?
answer: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
choices: Increased jobs and expanded tax base for the city
Federal defense readiness in New England
Access to a natural harbor for shipping
Preservation of a historic Colonial neighborhood
context: The New London plan's stated purpose was economic development -- jobs and tax base -- which the Kelo majority accepted as satisfying 'public use' under the Fifth Amendment. The public-choice reading focuses on WHO actually benefited concentrated-ly, and how organized they were. Source: Kelo, 545 US 469 (2005), majority opinion.

question: An analyst trained in public choice is handed a case like Kelo's, in which a Connecticut city forced a nurse to give up her little pink house so that a private developer could build offices. The city gave a public reason for the taking. Behind any such stated reason, what should the analyst look for?
answer: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
choices: Who is the concentrated beneficiary and who bears the concentrated cost
Whether the stated public purpose is sincere or only a pretext
Whether the city's total benefits outweigh its total costs
Whether the owners were paid a fair market price for the land
context: The stated public purpose is often sincere but incomplete. The public-choice reading identifies the concentrated beneficiary (developer) and concentrated cost-bearers (individual homeowners) whose organizational asymmetry drives the outcome. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965); Kelo (2005) as case study.

question: Susette Kelo lost her pink house in the Supreme Court in 2005, but the homeowners on her side won in another arena, as state lawmakers moved to curb such takings. In public-choice terms that is unusual: a small group usually beats a scattered crowd, and the homeowners were the scattered crowd. What do public-choice analysts credit for the reversal?
answer: The Institute for Justice's years of lawsuits and advocacy organized them
choices: The Institute for Justice's years of lawsuits and advocacy organized them
Developers lost interest once Pfizer closed its New London center
A new federal law forced every state to rewrite its takings rules
Cities themselves lobbied to give up the power to take homes
context: The Institute for Justice ran years of litigation, model bills and publicity that helped turn scattered public anger into new limits on takings in roughly 45 states. Mancur Olson argued that a scattered group wins only when something organizes it; here a public-interest law firm did. Source: ij.org.

question: Kenneth Arrow published his famous proof in 1951 in a slim book that grew out of his doctoral thesis at Columbia University. Its title set the group beside the single person, the two halves of the question he studied. What is the book called?
answer: Social Choice and Individual Values
choices: Social Choice and Individual Values
General Equilibrium and Welfare
The Theory of Voting Systems
Preferences and Aggregation
context: Social Choice and Individual Values (Wiley, 1951; second edition 1963). The book launched the modern field of social-choice theory. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (2012 reprint of the second edition).

question: A group of friends ranks pepperoni, cheese and mushrooms for a pizza, and the votes go round in a circle: each topping beats one rival and loses to the other, and no clear winner emerges. Kenneth Arrow's mathematics speaks to cases like theirs. What does it show about a flawless way of counting votes, fair to every group?
answer: No such perfect voting rule exists
choices: No such perfect voting rule exists
One exists only when there are exactly three voters
Ranked-choice voting solves every possible case
It works only if every voter is completely honest
context: Arrow's impossibility theorem: once a group faces three or more alternatives, no method of ranking them can meet all of his fairness conditions at once. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Kenneth Arrow found that a group choosing between just two options can use plain majority rule and keep every one of his fairness rules. The paradox he proved waits for groups facing more options than that. How many options must voters face before it can appear?
answer: Three
choices: Three
Two
Five
Seven
context: With only two alternatives, majority rule satisfies every Arrow condition. The impossibility appears once voters face three or more alternatives; the classic Condorcet paradox is a case of three voters and three options. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951).

question: Kenneth Arrow shook democratic theory with his proof of 1951. If two ways of counting can crown two different winners from one identical pile of ballots, the counting rule has a hand in who wins, and a phrase heard on every election night, used to justify the winner, names nothing that was ever there to be found. Which phrase does Arrow's mathematics dissolve?
answer: The will of the people
choices: The will of the people
The consent of the governed
The public interest
The rule of law
context: If different voting methods produce different winners from the same voter preferences, there is no method-independent 'will of the people' waiting to be discovered. The winner is jointly produced by voters AND the aggregation rule. Source: Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (1951/1963); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (Freeman 1982).

question: James Buchanan, a public-choice economist, drew his own lesson from Kenneth Arrow's theorem of 1951 on voting, the result that helped win Arrow the 1972 Nobel Prize. In Buchanan's reading, what follows from Arrow's theorem?
answer: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
choices: Constitutional rules that set the aggregation method matter enormously
The particular slate of candidates matters more than the rules
Party discipline can substitute for any voting-method choice
Judicial review can always correct impossibility results
