context: James Buchanan built on this insight: rules that determine HOW votes are aggregated do not merely process a preexisting will; they partly DEFINE what the aggregate looks like. Constitutional political economy takes the rules-choice question with new seriousness. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962); Riker, Liberalism Against Populism (1982).

question: Steve Jobs brought Apple's iPhone to market in June 2007, when BlackBerry, Nokia and Motorola led the phone market and all three kept their old designs. In Israel Kirzner's terms, what opportunity had Jobs noticed?
answer: A touchscreen, music player and phone could be one product
choices: A touchscreen, music player and phone could be one product
Phones would sell best with bigger physical keyboards
Cheap phones for poorer countries were the real market
Music players would soon replace phones altogether
context: Jobs unveiled the iPhone in January 2007 and it went on sale that June. Touchscreens (LG Prada 2006), music players (Apple's iPod since 2001) and phones (Nokia, BlackBerry, Motorola) all existed; the Kirznerian alertness was seeing they could be combined. BlackBerry's Jim Balsillie publicly brushed off the iPhone in 2007. Source: Isaacson, Steve Jobs (Simon & Schuster 2011).

question: Elon Musk set up SpaceX in 2002 to go after a chance that the big rocket makers had walked past for forty years. What was it?
answer: Rockets that land and fly again
choices: Rockets that land and fly again
Rockets built more cheaply overseas
Rockets launched from ships at sea
Rockets powered by nuclear engines
context: The launch industry had assumed rockets were disposable for decades. Musk's insight was that per-launch cost drops dramatically if the first stage lands and is reused. Falcon 9's first successful landing was December 21, 2015. Source: spacex.com (Falcon 9 mission archive).

question: Jeff Bezos started Amazon out of a garage outside Seattle in July 1994, selling just one kind of product at first rather than everything. His choice is a test case for Israel Kirzner's theory of the entrepreneur. What made that category the perfect launch point for an internet store?
answer: Books are identical copies that ship well, from a vast catalog
choices: Books are identical copies that ship well, from a vast catalog
Books have the highest per-unit profit margins in retail
Publishers gave web stores deeper discounts than shops
Books are exempt from state sales tax on federal statute
context: Bezos's Kirznerian alertness: books were the perfect starting product for internet-scale retail. No physical bookstore could stock the long-tail catalog. Chain bookstores had the same information but did not move decisively online. Source: Stone, The Everything Store (Little Brown 2013).

question: A student of Israel Kirzner's theory sizes up Jeff Bezos at Amazon, Elon Musk at SpaceX and Steve Jobs with the iPhone. The theory boils down to a single question for each of them. What question does it put to a founder?
answer: What did the founder see that rivals with the same tools missed
choices: What did the founder see that rivals with the same tools missed
How much money did the founder raise before launch
Which rivals did the founder buy out or drive off
How many patents did the founder hold on the technology
context: Kirznerian analysis: technology and capital are usually accessible to many; alertness is not. The reason a new firm succeeds where competitors failed is usually a specific perception of an integration or application others considered impossible. Source: Kirzner (1973), Chapter 2.

question: Israel Kirzner offered a third picture of the entrepreneur beside Frank Knight's bearer of true uncertainty and Joseph Schumpeter's inventor of new combinations that destroy old industries. Real founders such as Elon Musk and Steve Jobs mix all three. What is gained by pulling the three theories apart when studying one founder?
answer: It shows which theory fits which particular move
choices: It shows which theory fits which particular move
It shows which single theory fits the founder best
It shows how much of the success was simple luck
It shows which founder took the biggest risk
context: The point is not that a founder is 'a Kirznerian' or 'a Schumpeterian' in every action. The point is that different moves within a founder's career fit different theories: Bezos's book-choice was Kirznerian alertness; Musk's Mars ambition is Schumpeterian innovation; both took Knightian risks. Source: Kirzner (1973); Schumpeter (1911); Knight (1921).

question: Friedrich Hayek tells of tin growing scarce, whether a mine floods or someone finds a fresh use for it. Its price rises, and factories in a dozen trades cut back on tin, though not one of them learns the reason. What does Hayek say no central planning board could manage here?
answer: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
choices: Gathering into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin
Proving in advance that the scarcity was real and not a speculator's rumour
Keeping its own officials honest once tin was valuable enough to bribe over
Matching the speed with which foreign factories would switch to substitutes
context: Hayek's point is not that planners are stupid but that the knowledge is not theirs to have: it exists only as millions of particular circumstances of time and place. The price is not a summary of that knowledge -- it is the only form in which it can travel. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hayek' and 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society,' American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: An interviewer asked Thomas Sowell in 2018, as he neared eighty-eight, which of his own books he liked best. He passed over his big economics books and named a shorter one from 1987. Which book did he name?
answer: A Conflict of Visions
choices: A Conflict of Visions
The Vision of the Anointed
Intellectuals and Society
Basic Economics
context: Sowell to Reason, November 26 2018: Knowledge and Decisions 'certainly was at the time, and it's certainly among the books that I'm proudest of now,' but his 'own personal favorite is Conflict of Visions, which is perhaps a third of the size and more readable.' Source: Reason, 'Thomas Sowell Returns' (https://reason.com/2018/11/26/thomas-sowell-returns/).

question: Friedrich Hayek, eighty-two and seven years past his 1974 Nobel Prize, took up Thomas Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions in the pages of Reason magazine in December 1981. Sowell had built the whole book on an essay Hayek wrote in 1945 about how prices carry what no central office could gather. What did Hayek do there?
answer: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
choices: Reviewed it under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'
Objected in a letter to the editor that his 1945 essay had been flattened into slogans
Listed it among ten books he wished that he had written himself before the war
Warned readers that Sowell had confused his 1945 essay with Mises's 1920 one
context: Hayek's review ran in Reason, December 1981, under exactly that title. He wrote that Sowell had expanded admirably on his original concepts and made them clear to lay readers, with examples of economic activity drawn from the real world. Sources: Reason, December 1981 (https://reason.com/1981/12/01/the-best-book-on-general-econo/); Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Tom McCall, Oregon's governor, faced filling-station queues hours long in the autumn of 1973, while federal ceilings held the pump price of gasoline down. He had no power to move the price, so he changed the rule about who could fill up, and other states soon copied it. What was Oregon's rule?
answer: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
choices: Odd-numbered licence plates could buy on odd days, even-numbered plates on even days
Every registered household received a coupon book good for a fixed number of gallons
The first two hours of every morning were reserved for commercial and farm vehicles
Each station auctioned off its remaining supply to the highest bidders at opening time
context: Oregon adopted odd-even rationing in the autumn of 1973, Governor Tom McCall urging stations to sell by the last digit of the plate. It is the clean illustration of Sowell's point: stop the price from rationing scarce gasoline and something else must ration it -- a queue, a coupon, a calendar. Source: Grokipedia, 'Odd-even rationing' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Odd-even_rationing) and '1970s energy crisis'.

question: Thomas Sowell won the Law and Economics Center's prize in 1980 for Knowledge and Decisions, and the citation called the book a landmark. It did not praise the book in general terms; it named one thing the book had helped its readers understand. What did it name?
answer: The differences between the market process and the process of government
choices: The differences between the market process and the process of government
The reasons wage and price controls had failed in every decade since 1940
The drift of American courts away from the intentions of the Constitution's framers
The gap between what academic economists publish and what voters actually believe
context: The Law and Economics Center called Knowledge and Decisions a landmark work, chosen 'because of its cogent contribution to our understanding of the differences between the market process and the process of government.' Sources: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions); ContemporaryThinkers.org, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A driver in 1973 waited for hours in a gasoline line that news reports blamed on the oil simply running out. The Arab embargo was a genuine shock, but national stocks were in fact adequate, and Washington had put a legal ceiling on the price of American oil and gasoline. On Thomas Sowell's account, what did that ceiling do?
answer: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
choices: Silenced the one message that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder
Moved the shortage from the pump back to the refinery, where it could be managed out of public sight
Raised the cost of hoarding so sharply that drivers ran their tanks down to fumes before refilling
Concentrated the loss on the oil companies while spreading the gain thinly across every single driver
context: The 1973 Arab embargo was a real supply shock -- crude went from about $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Sowell's argument is not that the controls caused the shortage but that they made it far worse: with the price frozen, refiners had little reason to produce more, drivers little reason to buy less, and hoarding paid. Source: Grokipedia, '1970s energy crisis' (https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s_energy_crisis) and 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Thomas Sowell set markets, legislatures and courts side by side in Knowledge and Decisions, his book of 1980, and through it ran one worry about modern societies: a gap he saw widening. Which gap did he mean?
answer: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
choices: Between the people who know the particulars firsthand and the people who hold the authority to decide
Between what a government promises at election time and what it can actually afford to pay for later
Between the wealth held by a country's oldest households and the wealth held by its youngest ones
Between the speed at which a society's technology changes and the speed at which its laws get rewritten
context: Sowell's framing worry is a widening gap between firsthand knowledge and decision-making authority: the further a decision travels from the person who knows the particulars, the more it must run on somebody's general theory instead. Source: Hoover Institution book page (https://www.hoover.org/research/knowledge-and-decisions).

question: A student summed up Knowledge and Decisions as 'markets good, government bad.' Thomas Sowell had built the book differently: he took markets with their prices and profits, elected legislatures with their votes and lobbying, and courts with their rules of evidence, and ran every one of them through the same single test. What is that test?
answer: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
choices: Which facts the process can actually pick up, and which ones it is simply blind to
Whether the people who designed the process meant well by those it would govern
How thinly the process spreads its costs and how narrowly it piles up its benefits
Which rival process would otherwise do the same job, and how badly it would do it
context: This is why the book is not a market-versus-state pamphlet: Sowell asks the identical question of every institution, markets included, and the answers come out different by institution rather than by team. Sowell's own 'compared to what?', Mancur Olson's dispersed costs and concentrated benefits, and Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions' are real analytic moves too, but none of them is the book's single test. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'; Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: Thomas Sowell argued that a racial preference in admissions can seat a student among classmates who came in far better prepared, and so hurt the very students it was meant to help. His complaint, he made clear, was not about the student's ability. What did he say the admissions office never actually checks?
answer: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
choices: How this particular student would fare against this particular programme's pace
Whether this particular student's own high school was underfunded next to its neighbours
Whether the programme's faculty would end up marking this student harder than the others
How many students from the same background that programme had already admitted before
context: Sowell calls this mismatch. It grew out of what he saw teaching at Cornell in the late 1960s, where students admitted under preferences were disproportionately on academic probation -- not, he argued, because they could not do college work, but because the fit was wrong. He made the case at book length in Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study (Yale University Press, 2004). The argument is a claim about what admissions data can and cannot tell an admissions office, not a claim about who deserves a place. Sources: H-Net Reviews, DasGupta on Sowell, 'Affirmative Action Around the World'; Claremont Review of Books, Sowell, 'The Perversity of Diversity'.

question: Thomas Sowell, known for his writing on economics and race, turned in the 1990s to a subject far from either: bright children who begin to speak much later than most, children often mislabeled as autistic or slow. Something in his own home drew him to it. What was it?
answer: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
choices: Sowell's own son John was one of these children
Sowell's own younger brother had been misdiagnosed as deaf
Sowell had witnessed a neighbor's child undergo similar mislabeling
Sowell had been asked to consult by a Stanford developmental clinic
context: When John was young, doctors and specialists variously diagnosed him as autistic, mentally retarded, or hearing-impaired -- all of which turned out to be wrong. John talked late and grew into a highly intelligent adult with a technical career. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell.

question: Thomas Sowell named a pattern he found in bright late-talking children after a famous physicist whose family said he spoke no full sentences until he was about three. What did Sowell call it?
answer: The Einstein Syndrome
choices: The Einstein Syndrome
The Turing Pattern
The Newton Cluster
The Feynman Presentation
context: Albert Einstein was reported to have been a late talker (his family said he did not speak in sentences until about age 3). The 2001 book carried the name in its title: 'The Einstein Syndrome: Bright Children Who Talk Late.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Thomas Sowell argued, in two books on late-talking children, that the professionals who assess such children were not impartial judges: pediatricians, speech therapists and the special-education offices of schools. Their work, he said, ran on one particular incentive. What incentive did he point to?
answer: To sort children into named conditions, each with its own funding
choices: To sort children into named conditions, each with its own funding
To avoid lawsuits by never naming any condition at all
To pass each child on to the cheapest specialist
To keep waiting lists short by sending children home
context: Sowell's argument is a Hayekian knowledge-problem move applied to a medical-institutional case. No single specialist could see the pattern because it crossed specialties, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded diagnosis-and-treatment over watchful waiting. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Thomas Sowell, writing two books on late-talking children, carried one reasoning move he had long used on markets into pediatric medicine, a subject far from his usual economics. Which move carried over?
answer: Hayek's knowledge problem: no single specialist sees the whole pattern
choices: Hayek's knowledge problem: no single specialist sees the whole pattern
Comparative advantage: each specialist sticks to what he does best
Revealed preference: parents' choices show what they truly value
Collective action: small groups organize while large ones cannot
context: The same Hayekian analytical style Sowell applies to economic-policy questions carries over to a medical-institutional question. The books are often the first Sowell book recommended to non-economists because they show his method on a subject no one has a political axe about. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Einstein_Syndrome.

question: Friedrich Hayek, in his seventies and long famous for The Road to Serfdom, began a work on the order a free society truly has, and on why clever lawmakers so often get it wrong. It filled three volumes, from 1973 to 1979. What is it called?
answer: Law, Legislation and Liberty
choices: Law, Legislation and Liberty
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Individualism and Economic Order
context: Law, Legislation and Liberty, Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1973 / 1976 / 1979. The Constitution of Liberty (1960) is a distinct earlier single-volume work; The Road to Serfdom (1944) is the wartime polemic; Individualism and Economic Order (1948) collected essays. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: A gardener sets each flower in its bed by hand, while in a forest each tree finds its own place. Friedrich Hayek set the two side by side to explain how societies come by their order, and he gave the forest's kind its own name. What kind of order did he say the forest has?
answer: A grown order that no one designed on purpose
choices: A grown order that no one designed on purpose
A hierarchical order commanded from the top
A random order with no pattern at all
A legal order backed by government force
context: Kosmos (grown) versus taxis (made) is Hayek's central pair -- a forest is a kosmos, a garden is a taxis. Hierarchical command is a species of taxis; randomness is Hayek's opposite of both; legal codification is legislative taxis. Source: Knowledge Problem blog, 'Hayek on Order: Cosmos and Taxis'.

question: Friedrich Hayek pointed to human language, the prices of a market and the common law, systems that come from countless people's own choices and local customs, though no one plans them. He gave such systems a two-word name, crediting the scientist Michael Polanyi, who had used it back in 1951. What is the phrase?
answer: Spontaneous order
choices: Spontaneous order
Central planning
Constructivist rationalism
Positive liberty
context: Hayek's canonical Kosmos examples of spontaneous order: language, the common law, market prices, and cultural norms. Central planning is the opposite; constructivist rationalism is the intellectual error Hayek attacks; positive liberty is Isaiah Berlin's concept, not Hayek's. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: A judge settles one real dispute, and the next judge who meets a case like it follows the ruling; over centuries the rules pile up that way. Elsewhere learned men draft a full code, and courts follow its text to the letter. Friedrich Hayek admired the first kind of law for the same reasons he admired markets. Which tradition of law is famous for it?
answer: English common law
choices: English common law
Continental civil-code law
Roman imperial edicts
Islamic sharia jurisprudence
context: Common law grows precedent by precedent through judicial decision, without any single legislator; continental codes (Napoleonic Code 1804 and its successors) are deliberate taxis; Roman edicts and sharia have their own histories but are not Hayek's paradigm of a Kosmos-legal-order. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Rules and Order.

question: Friedrich Hayek went after a phrase in the second volume of his trilogy of the 1970s, a phrase people often apply to the results of a market: who ends up rich and who poor, who earns high wages and who low. He called it a category mistake, since those results are no one's deliberate act. Which phrase did he target?
answer: Social justice
choices: Social justice
Economic freedom
Political liberty
Public reason
context: Hayek's argument: justice is a property of intentional individual conduct; the distribution that emerges from millions of separate voluntary acts is un-designed, so calling it 'just' or 'unjust' misapplies the concept. Economic freedom, political liberty, and public reason are terms Hayek uses positively or neutrally. Source: Libertarianism.org, review of Volume 2.

question: Adam Ferguson, a Scottish philosopher, wrote a line in 1767 on where things such as language, money and law come from, and Friedrich Hayek quoted it often. What does the line teach about how such systems come about?
answer: They grow from many small choices, with no one planning the whole
choices: They grow from many small choices, with no one planning the whole
A wise ruler must sit down and design them from the top
They need central experts to keep them working properly
Only a written national constitution can ever create them
context: The phrase comes from Part III of Ferguson's 1767 Essay on the History of Civil Society: nations 'stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design.' Source: Online Library of Liberty, Adam Ferguson quote page.

question: Friedrich Hayek feared, by the late 1970s, that democracies run by plain majorities were drifting away from stable general laws toward daily political deal-making. In the third volume of his trilogy, published in 1979 and the most political of the three, he proposed a constitutional change to slow the drift. What did he propose?
answer: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
choices: A two-chamber legislature separating rule-making from ordinary government business
A single-chamber assembly directly elected by universal proportional franchise
The abolition of parliament in favor of binding national referenda on major questions
The devolution of central authority to autonomous chartered city-states of Swiss size
context: Hayek's design: a rule-making chamber elected on a long, lifetime-scale franchise to insulate it from short-term political pressures, and a separate government-making chamber on ordinary franchises -- an explicit bicameral proposal to protect the rule of law from majoritarian drift. Source: University of Chicago Law Review, review of Volume 3.

question: A clever committee sits down to redesign human language, as though it were an engine to be taken apart and put back together. Friedrich Hayek saw the same mistake in schemes to remake the common law and market prices, and he gave it a name. What did he call it?
answer: Constructivist rationalism — the belief that reason can build a society from scratch
choices: Constructivist rationalism — the belief that reason can build a society from scratch
Methodological individualism — explaining groups by starting from persons
Analytical positivism — the view that only measurable claims count
Evolutionary skepticism — the doubt that old customs still fit new problems
context: Constructivist (or naive) rationalism is Hayek's label for the mistake of thinking that reason can design social institutions from scratch, as against evolutionary rationalism which recognizes tested-through-time rules. Methodological individualism is a separate Austrian commitment; analytic positivism belongs to the Vienna Circle Hayek argued against. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: A Harvard philosopher made one phrase the central topic of political philosophy with a huge book in 1971. Five years later Friedrich Hayek published the second volume of his trilogy, partly to answer that book. Which 1971 book was it?
answer: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
choices: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls
Anarchy, State, and Utopia by Robert Nozick
The Open Society and Its Enemies by Karl Popper
The Concept of Law by H. L. A. Hart
context: Rawls's A Theory of Justice (Harvard, 1971) put social justice at the center of Anglophone political philosophy; Hayek's 1976 argument is the counter-tradition's reply. Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) was itself a reply to Rawls; Popper (1945) and Hart (1961) are earlier works Hayek shared intellectual ground with. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: An experienced doctor glances at a patient and knows at once that it is appendicitis, yet she cannot spell out on paper all that told her. A carpenter knows how to steady a warped board but cannot put every finger position into words. Michael Polanyi named this kind of skill, genuine and handed on by practice, and Friedrich Hayek took it as further evidence that no one place can hold all an economy knows. What did Polanyi call it?
answer: Tacit knowledge
choices: Tacit knowledge
Practical wisdom
Analytic proof
Formal theory
context: Michael Polanyi (1891-1976), in Personal Knowledge (1958) and The Tacit Dimension (1966), argued that 'we can know more than we can tell', a claim Hayek treated as support for his own case that dispersed knowledge cannot be gathered by a central planner. Source: Wikipedia, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: Dick Fuld ran out of buyers for Lehman Brothers, a Wall Street bank 158 years old, and in September it filed for the biggest bankruptcy the country had seen. Credit markets around the world froze as big banks' hidden, risky bets on home mortgages came to light. What did the collapse help set off?
answer: The 2008 financial crisis
choices: The 2008 financial crisis
The Great Depression
The 1970s oil crisis
The dot-com bubble
context: Lehman Brothers filed at 1:45 AM on September 15 2008 with $639 billion in assets, primarily mortgage-backed securities and commercial real estate. The S&P 500 fell 4.7% that day. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Dick Fuld, Lehman Brothers' chief executive, hunted all summer in 2008 for someone to buy his failing firm. One suitor paused its talks on September 9, and another broke off on the final weekend to buy a rival firm instead, leaving Lehman to file for bankruptcy on September 15. Which pair walked away?
answer: Korea Development Bank and Bank of America
choices: Korea Development Bank and Bank of America
Wells Fargo and Deutsche Bank
HSBC and Citigroup
UBS and Goldman Sachs
context: Lehman's shares fell 45 percent on September 9 after reports that the state-run Korea Development Bank had put its talks on hold. Bank of America bought Merrill Lynch on the final weekend instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers.

question: The Treasury Secretary and the president of the New York Federal Reserve called the heads of Wall Street's biggest banks to the New York Fed one weekend in September 2008, trying to line up private buyers for the failing Lehman Brothers. They failed. Who were the two officials?
answer: Hank Paulson and Tim Geithner
choices: Hank Paulson and Tim Geithner
Robert Rubin and Alan Greenspan
Larry Summers and Janet Yellen
Jack Lew and Jerome Powell
context: Paulson (former Goldman Sachs CEO, now Treasury Secretary) and Bernanke (Fed chair) worked with New York Fed president Tim Geithner over that weekend. The private-rescue attempt failed when the strongest candidate buyer walked away. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Bankers at Barclays, a British bank, moved to buy the failing Lehman Brothers in September 2008, hours before the end. They could close in time only if someone backed Lehman's trading obligations until Barclays shareholders voted, and the Treasury Secretary would not commit public money to that backing. What did Barclays most likely do next?
answer: Walked away, since it would now bear all the risk alone
choices: Walked away, since it would now bear all the risk alone
Bought Lehman anyway, betting the Fed would cover losses later
Cut its offer to a dollar a share to cover the extra risk
Signed at once and left its shareholders to vote later
context: Barclays was the last serious buyer standing. British regulators refused to bless the deal without a US backstop, and Paulson would not provide one. Barclays walked away on Sunday, September 14. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Managers of the Reserve Primary Fund, a fund where savers parked spare cash, said on the day after Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008 that its shares were now worth less than a dollar; it held more than $700 million in short-term loans to Lehman. Savers had trusted such funds to be as safe as cash. What did nervous savers do next?
answer: They rushed to pull their money out of other money-market funds
choices: They rushed to pull their money out of other money-market funds
They shrugged it off, since each share had lost only a few cents
They held on, trusting the Treasury to make the fund whole
They bought the fund's cheap shares, betting they would recover
context: The Reserve Primary Fund held over $700 million in Lehman commercial paper. It broke the buck on September 16 2008, triggering a broad run on money-market funds and forcing the Treasury to guarantee the whole sector. Source: Grokipedia 'Reserve Primary Fund' (2026-09-05).

question: Ben Bernanke, the Fed's chairman, and the Treasury Secretary each wrote a memoir after the crisis defending their choice not to rescue Lehman Brothers in September 2008. Each claimed his hands were tied: one legal rule, they argued, kept the Fed from lending to Lehman that weekend. What did they say the constraint was?
answer: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
choices: The Fed lacked legal authority to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral
The Fed was prohibited by the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act
The Fed needed prior congressional approval for the specific loan
The Fed's charter forbade any loan to an investment bank
context: Paulson and Bernanke both maintained that Lehman lacked the good collateral required under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act. Whether this claim was accurate has been sharply disputed by later historians. Source: Grokipedia 'Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers' (2026-09-05).

question: Two developers published a white paper in January 2016 setting out how Bitcoin users could pay each other quickly and cheaply without writing every payment onto the main chain. The network they described went live in March 2018. Who were the two authors?
answer: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja
choices: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja
Vitalik Buterin and Gavin Wood
Nick Szabo and Wei Dai
Adam Back and Hal Finney
context: The paper proposed payment channels secured by Bitcoin smart contracts. The mainnet went live in March 2018 with implementations from Lightning Labs (LND), Blockstream (c-lightning), and ACINQ (Eclair). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Two friends expect to trade often over Bitcoin's fast second layer. Their first step is to lock some bitcoin into a joint account on the main chain; from then on they can send payments back and forth off the chain, and when they stop, only the closing balance goes onto the main chain. What is that first step called?
answer: Opening a payment channel
choices: Opening a payment channel
Making an atomic swap
Running a full node
Mining a fresh block
context: The funding transaction commits Bitcoin to a two-party multisignature address. Off-chain updates rebalance the split without touching the chain. When the channel closes, only the final balance is settled on-chain. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Alice and Bob have a channel between them on Bitcoin's fast second layer, and so do Bob and Carol. Alice has none with Carol, yet she can still pay Carol by sending the money through Bob. What does Bob get for passing the payment along?
answer: A small routing fee, paid by the sender
choices: A small routing fee, paid by the sender
A share of the next block reward
A subsidy from the Lightning Labs company
An interest charge on Carol's balance
context: Routing fees are voluntary market prices set by each node. The network structure depends on nodes with well-funded channels making themselves available for routing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Engineers built a second layer on top of Bitcoin's main chain for small, quick payments, since the chain, with a block about every ten minutes, is too slow and dear for a two-dollar coffee. What is that layer called?
answer: The Lightning Network
choices: The Lightning Network
The Merkle Tree
The Mempool
The Proof-of-Stake Ledger
context: Mallers appeared alongside President Nayib Bukele at the June 2021 Bitcoin conference where the legal-tender law was announced. Strike allowed US-El Salvador remittances via Lightning at negligible cost. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Mallers.

question: A high-school student buys a two-dollar coffee in San Salvador with a Bitcoin app on her phone, and the payment settles in under a second for a fraction of a cent. An economist in Hayek's tradition finds a quiet feat in that purchase. Which problem does he say Bitcoin's fast layer has solved?
answer: Keeping settlement auditable while competing nodes price tiny payments
choices: Keeping settlement auditable while competing nodes price tiny payments
Letting one central body set a fair fee for every small payment
Fixing bitcoin's dollar price so a coffee always costs the same
Writing every small payment onto the main chain within a second
context: Lightning fees are set by node operators competing for routing volume, not by any central body. Bitcoin's settlement layer stays fully auditable. The design is analogous to how the internet has TCP/IP at the base and higher-level protocols on top. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Lightning_Network.

question: Myron Scholes and Robert Merton shared the 1997 economics Nobel for showing how to price options, and their hedge fund, Long-Term Capital Management, traded by models of the same high-powered mathematics. A year later the fund collapsed. What lesson did that teach the world?
answer: Complex math models don't guarantee safety in markets
choices: Complex math models don't guarantee safety in markets
Options can't be priced with math
Big funds ride out panics best
Bond price gaps always close in time
context: LTCM's founder team included Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who had won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on options pricing (the Black-Scholes model). Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: Long-Term Capital Management held about $125 billion of bets on only $4.7 billion in capital, so it owed some twenty-seven dollars for each dollar it owned. What does borrowing like that do to a fund's gains and losses?
answer: It magnifies both
choices: It magnifies both
It shrinks both
It shrinks losses only
It locks in gains
context: LTCM held roughly $125 billion in positions against only $4.7 billion in capital, a ratio of about 27 to 1. Using borrowed money to multiply a bet this way is called leverage: it multiplied the fund's gains in its good years and its losses in 1998, when the loans still had to be repaid. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: Traders at a big fund bet that two nearly identical bonds would drift back to the same price. Then a large country stopped paying its debts, panic sent investors running for the safest assets, and the two prices moved far apart instead. What happened to the fund?
answer: It nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to prevent wider damage
choices: It nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to prevent wider damage
It lost a little but recovered within weeks on its own
It was shut by regulators and its partners were jailed
It sold its bets at once and returned the cash to investors
context: The Russian government defaulted on August 17, 1998, devaluing the ruble and defaulting on domestic debt. The flight to safety that followed made LTCM's leveraged spread bets go against the fund across every desk. Source: Grokipedia '1998 Russian financial crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: Wall Street's bank chiefs gathered in one room at the New York Federal Reserve's call, and on September 23, 1998, fourteen of their banks agreed to pool their own money, not a cent from taxpayers, to take over the failing hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management and wind down its trades bit by bit. How big was the rescue?
answer: About $3.6 billion
choices: About $3.6 billion
About $700 million
About $30 billion
About $250 million
context: The $3.6 billion September 23 1998 rescue was entirely privately funded. Each of the 14 banks contributed and took a stake in the fund's positions, unwinding them slowly over months. No federal money was used, but the Fed's coordination power was central. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: The president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York summoned Wall Street's chiefs to a conference room in September 1998, as the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management collapsed after Russia's default, and pressed them to organize a private rescue. His deputy, Peter Fisher, ran the details. Who was that president?
answer: William McDonough
choices: William McDonough
Timothy Geithner
William Dudley
E. Gerald Corrigan
context: William McDonough led the New York Fed 1993-2003. Peter Fisher ran the actual operation of coordinating the private banks. The rescue was a formative moment in Fed practice of coordinating rescues without directly using federal funds. Source: Grokipedia 'William McDonough' (2026-09-05).

question: Federal Reserve officials in New York stepped in when the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management collapsed in September 1998, though it had no depositors, no branches and no small savers to protect, nothing the Fed is supposed to backstop. They gave one specific reason for stepping in. What was it?
answer: The banks that traded with it could be dragged down in a fire sale
choices: The banks that traded with it could be dragged down in a fire sale
Its partners had broken federal law and had to be stopped
Its trades had pushed interest rates above the Fed's target
Its Russian bonds had to be kept out of hostile hands
context: The 1998 justification: LTCM's counterparties (the 14 banks that would organize the rescue) were also its potential victims. A disorderly unwind of $125 billion in leveraged positions could damage them enough to trigger a broader crisis. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: Warren Buffett, with the insurer American International Group and Goldman Sachs beside him, offered $250 million in September 1998 to take over the collapsing hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, an offer that would have left its partners with nothing. The talks broke down, and a rescue by other banks came instead. Free-market critics wish Buffett's offer had gone through. Why do they prefer private buyouts over rescues the government organizes?
answer: They do not teach big firms that the government will save them
choices: They do not teach big firms that the government will save them
They settle a failure faster than a meeting of rival banks
They keep the deal secret from markets until it is done
They make sure investors get back every dollar they put in
context: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, together with AIG and Goldman Sachs, offered $250 million for LTCM's positions in early September 1998. The offer would have wiped out the LTCM partners entirely. Negotiations broke down; the Fed rescue came days later. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: Traders at Long-Term Capital Management placed their bets in 1998 with models promising that a market move as large as the one that August should strike only once in many hundreds of years. It came anyway, and the fund nearly collapsed. What did the math miss?
answer: Rare events are not as rare as models built on calm years suggest
choices: Rare events are not as rare as models built on calm years suggest
The fund's computers were too slow to trade in a panic
The firm's traders ignored the models when it mattered
Russia's bonds carried no risk because Russia was so big
context: LTCM's risk models, fitted to years of calm markets, treated a move as large as August 1998's as a once-in-centuries event. Real markets produce such big moves far more often than those models allow, a pattern known as fat tails. Scholes and Merton had won the Nobel less than a year before. Source: Grokipedia 'Long-Term Capital Management' (2026-09-05).

question: A critic of bailouts lists the rescues in order: a big bank first, then an investment fund in 1998, later a giant insurer and a money-market fund. Each one is billed as a one-time exception. What pattern does his list show in who ends up protected from failure?
answer: The circle of firms treated as too big to fail quietly grows over time
choices: The circle of firms treated as too big to fail quietly grows over time
Each rescue was a true one-off with its own special cause
The government can protect big firms while still keeping others cautious
Rescues shift over time from big firms toward small ones
context: The LTCM pattern extended through AIG (2008), the Reserve Primary Fund (2008), and eventually to any entity whose failure would cascade into the banking system. The Continental Illinois principle grew steadily across categories over four decades. Source: Grokipedia 'Too big to fail' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig Lachmann, a student of Hayek's who spent over twenty years teaching in Johannesburg, published a short, influential book in 1956 about lathes, trucks and factory buildings and the ways such tools fit together. What did he title it?
answer: Capital and Its Structure
choices: Capital and Its Structure
The Theory of Money and Credit
Human Action
Prices and Production
context: Capital and Its Structure (Bell, London, 1956) argued that a lathe is not a truck is not a factory building, and that aggregating them into a single 'K' hides the actual complementarities the cycle disrupts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Ludwig Lachmann objected in 1956 to the way mainstream textbooks treated a lathe, a delivery truck and a factory building, arguing that their habit wiped out exactly the fit among different tools that a boom and bust throws into disorder. Which idea was he attacking?
answer: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
choices: That capital can be aggregated into a single number K
That capital is always privately owned
That capital depreciates at a constant rate
That capital is measured in labor-hours
context: The heterogeneous-capital claim: because specific goods have specific complementarities, adding them into aggregate K erases the very structure that matters to production and to booms and busts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: Frank Knight drew a line in 1921 between risk that can be measured and real uncertainty, and Ludwig Lachmann took it up against the rational-expectations school of the 1970s, which pictured business owners working out tomorrow by the laws of probability. Which view did Lachmann defend?
answer: The future is truly unknowable, so entrepreneurs reasonably expect different things
choices: The future is truly unknowable, so entrepreneurs reasonably expect different things
The future is unknowable, so entrepreneurs all copy the market leader
The future follows long cycles that careful study can predict
The future is irrelevant because entrepreneurs only respond to present prices
context: Lachmann invoked Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between measurable risk and genuine uncertainty; there is no such thing as 'the' rational expectation of a market participant. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_Lachmann.

question: George Shackle and Ludwig Lachmann argued that the economic future is not risky the way a dice roll is. Dice have known odds; tomorrow will bring inventions, firms and decisions no one has made yet, and nobody can put fair odds on what does not exist. If they are right, what follows for ten-year economic forecasts?
answer: They are basically guesses, not to be trusted like weather reports
choices: They are basically guesses, not to be trusted like weather reports
They grow more accurate the further ahead they look
They are reliable once enough past data is fed in
They work as long as forecasters agree with each other
context: 'From Mises to Shackle: An Essay on Austrian Economics and the Kaleidic Society' (JEL, 1976) argued the tradition should follow Shackle's radical-uncertainty picture rather than any equilibration story. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: Ludwig Lachmann pushed the Austrian school to its most radical position in an essay of 1976, From Mises to Shackle. Markets, he wrote, never come to rest; plans and expectations change without end and the whole pattern keeps reshuffling. Borrowing a word from George Shackle, he gave that restless view a two-word name. What was it?
answer: The kaleidic society
choices: The kaleidic society
The knowledge economy
The spontaneous order
The equilibrium constellation
context: 'Kaleidic' -- from kaleidoscope -- captures Lachmann's picture of markets in constant pattern-shifting flux, as opposed to any tendency toward stable equilibrium. Source: jstor.org/stable/2722553.

question: A planner in a communist ministry sets prices by decree, with no free market to tell him anything. Ludwig von Mises taught that every free price tells two things at the same time: what buyers want and what the goods cost to produce. What goes wrong for that planner?
answer: He can't tell what is scarce or what people need
choices: He can't tell what is scarce or what people need
Shoppers refuse to pay legal prices
Prices rise each month whatever he does
Workers quit once wages are equal
context: Mises held that a free price carries two messages at once: how much buyers want a thing and what it costs to make. A price set by decree carries neither, so the planner cannot tell what is scarce or what people need. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises drew on two thinkers above all as he studied in Vienna, where he took his doctorate in 1906: the founder of the Austrian school of economics and the school's leading thinker on capital. Which pair was it?
answer: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
choices: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
Alfred Marshall and Arthur Pigou
Leon Walras and Vilfredo Pareto
context: Menger (1840-1921) had founded the school with his 1871 Principles of Economics; Boehm-Bawerk (1851-1914) developed the theory of capital and interest and demolished the Marxian labor theory of value. Marx and Engels were Vienna's ideological opponents, not teachers; the other two pairs were English and Franco-Italian schools respectively. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises never drew a professor's salary in Vienna, where his university lecturing was unpaid. From around 1909, for a quarter of a century, another Vienna institution paid him to draft its briefs on money, tariffs and labor law. Which institution paid his salary?
answer: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce
choices: The Austrian Chamber of Commerce
The Austro-Hungarian National Bank
The Vienna Stock Exchange
The Austrian Ministry of Finance
context: The Kammer fuer Handel, Gewerbe und Industrie (Chamber of Commerce, Trade and Industry) paid Mises to draft economic policy briefs on tariffs, labor law, and monetary reform. He held his unpaid University of Vienna Privatdozent title from 1913 to 1938 in parallel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises published a paper in 1920 attacking the whole idea of full socialism, on economic rather than moral grounds. Under full socialism the state owns every factory, farm and tool, so none of them ever changes hands in a market and none has a genuine price tag. Why, in his argument, are the planners then stuck when they decide what to produce and how?
answer: Without real prices, they cannot tell which uses create the most value
choices: Without real prices, they cannot tell which uses create the most value
Workers grow lazy once everyone is paid the same wage
Inflation makes any long-term plan impossible to keep
Central bankers can never agree on the rate of interest
context: Mises's 1920 essay, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth, argued that when the state owns all the means of production they are never bought or sold, so they carry no market prices, and planners have no way to compare one use of resources with another. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Ludwig von Mises founded a research body in Vienna in 1927 and made a young Friedrich Hayek its first director; the Rockefeller Foundation later helped pay for its work. What was it called?
answer: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
choices: The Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research
The Vienna School of Political Economy
The Austro-Hungarian Monetary Union
The Kreditanstalt Research Bureau
context: The Oesterreichisches Institut fuer Konjunkturforschung was directed by Mises's young protege Friedrich Hayek from its founding; Hayek's monthly reports on the American boom made his name in Britain and led to Lionel Robbins's 1931 invitation to the LSE. The other three are inventions or unrelated institutions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Lew Rockwell, an American organizer, founded a research institute in Ludwig von Mises's name in October 1982. Mises's widow Margit backed him, as did Murray Rothbard, Henry Hazlitt and Ron Paul. Which Alabama town has been the institute's home ever since?
answer: Auburn
choices: Auburn
Tuscaloosa
Birmingham
Montgomery
context: Llewellyn H. Rockwell Jr. founded the Mises Institute in October 1982 and placed it in Auburn, home of Auburn University, whose economics department at the time had several Austrian-friendly faculty. Tuscaloosa is Alabama's other main university town; Birmingham is the largest city; Montgomery is the state capital. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/story-mises-institute.

question: Ludwig von Mises would not settle for the title of economist. Economics, he held, was just one branch of a wider deductive science of purposeful human action, and he preferred to describe himself by that science's Greek-derived name. Which self-description did he prefer?
answer: praxeologist
choices: praxeologist
monetarist
microeconomist
econometrician
context: Praxeology (from Greek praxis, action) was Mises's own coinage for the general science of purposive action; economics is the best-developed branch of it. Monetarism was Milton Friedman's Chicago-school program; microeconomist and econometrician are 20th-century academic labels Mises specifically resisted. Source: mises.org/mises-daily/human-action-purposeful-action.

question: Murray Rothbard, then thirty-six and living in New York, set out to retell Ludwig von Mises's whole system for an American audience, and in 1962 he published a treatise in two volumes, close to a thousand pages long. It ran from human choice and prices through capital and money to booms and busts. What is the treatise called?
answer: Man, Economy, and State
choices: Man, Economy, and State
America's Great Depression
For a New Liberty
The Ethics of Liberty
context: Published in 1962 by D. Van Nostrand of Princeton, New Jersey, in two volumes running 987 pages. America's Great Depression (1963), For a New Liberty (1973) and The Ethics of Liberty (1982) are later Rothbard books. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man,_Economy,_and_State.

question: Murray Rothbard took a job from the William Volker Fund late in 1949: turn a dense Austrian classic of that year into a textbook students could manage. The job swelled into a treatise of his own. Whose book was he first asked to simplify?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action
choices: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action
Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom
Carl Menger's Principles of Economics
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest
context: The William Volker Fund's president, Herbert Cornuelle, gave Rothbard the assignment in the fall of 1949. Under his hand the textbook grew into a full original treatise. Source: mises.org/library/treatise-his-own.

question: Murray Rothbard wrote for a Kansas City donor group, the William Volker Fund, at a time when big commercial publishers turned down free-market manuscripts and most colleges leaned toward central planning and Keynes. The fund paid to print such books anyway. Why does a story like this matter for the world of ideas?
answer: It lets unpopular ideas find an audience without needing official approval
choices: It lets unpopular ideas find an audience without needing official approval
It proves good ideas always win out without anyone's help
It shows that only state-funded research can stay independent
It shows bestseller lists are the best judge of an idea's worth
context: The Kansas City-based Volker Fund, run by Harold Luhnow after 1947, was a major financier of American classical-liberal scholarship in the postwar decades, when the biggest foundations funded mostly mainstream research. Source: Gary North, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State: A Memoir', Mises Institute.

question: Murray Rothbard followed his teacher Ludwig von Mises when he wrote the opening chapter of his 1962 treatise, and he built every later chapter on it. Rothbard, like Mises, called the method praxeology. What starting move does that opening chapter make?
answer: It takes the axiom that humans act and deduces economic law from it
choices: It takes the axiom that humans act and deduces economic law from it
It gathers price records and finds patterns in them by statistics
It builds a model of one typical shopper who maximizes his pleasure
It starts from the rule that a nation's total spending sets its output
context: This is the Misesian method Rothbard calls praxeology: the science of human action, built by deduction rather than by statistics, by models of maximizing shoppers, or by Keynesian totals. Source: FEE, 'Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State at 50'.

question: Murray Rothbard's sponsors at the William Volker Fund read his huge manuscript, some 1,900 typed pages by his own count, before it went to press in 1962. On their reviewer's advice they set one big condition for backing it. What did they demand?
answer: That its final part, on government intervention, be cut as too political
choices: That its final part, on government intervention, be cut as too political
That the entire manuscript be rewritten in the third person to sound less polemical
That the footnotes citing Ludwig von Mises be removed to avoid appearing derivative
That the two-volume format be compressed into a single introductory paperback
context: Frank Meyer, the fund's reviewer, judged Part III (chapters 12 to 19) fundamentally political; it was replaced by a short summary chapter, and the cut material became Power and Market in 1970. The restored Scholar's Edition of 2004 runs to about 1,500 pages. Source: mises.org/library/treatise-his-own.

question: Murray Rothbard saw a new book of his come out in 1970 from F. A. Harper's Institute for Humane Studies, eight years after his big treatise, built from chapters cut from the treatise before it went to press. What was the 1970 book called?
answer: Power and Market
choices: Power and Market
America's Great Depression
The Ethics of Liberty
For a New Liberty
context: America's Great Depression (1963), For a New Liberty (1973) and The Ethics of Liberty (1982) are other Rothbard books; Power and Market is the one that printed the chapters cut from Man, Economy, and State. Source: Mises Institute library, Power and Market.

question: Murray Rothbard divided all the ways the state uses force in an economy into three kinds in his book of 1970, sorting each act by who is forced and what he is made to do or forbidden to do. Which three kinds did he name?
answer: Autistic, binary, and triangular intervention
choices: Autistic, binary, and triangular intervention
Fiscal, monetary, and regulatory intervention
Progressive, proportional, and regressive intervention
Executive, legislative, and judicial intervention
context: The scheme is original to Rothbard and is the analytic backbone of Power and Market. The three-name scheme lets him treat drug bans, taxes, and rent control as three structurally different coercions rather than one blurry 'government activity'. Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: Two adults strike a deal freely, and a third party, the government, steps in to set its terms for them. Murray Rothbard gave that shape of state force a place of its own in his book of 1970. Which real-world policy is a textbook example of it?
answer: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
choices: A rent-control law capping what a landlord may charge a tenant
A federal income tax withheld from a worker's paycheck
A statute making private possession of a drug a crime
A conscription order drafting a citizen into the army
context: Triangular intervention: state + two private parties whose exchange is dictated (rent controls, minimum wages, tariffs, licensing). Income tax and conscription are BINARY interventions (state extracts from the individual directly). A private-drug ban is AUTISTIC intervention (state forbids a solitary act, no exchange). Source: Mises Wiki, 'Intervention'.

question: Milton Friedman brought out Capitalism and Freedom in 1962, the year of Murray Rothbard's treatise, from the rival Chicago tradition. Suppose you lived where officials assign every job, every flat and every loaf of bread. What core claim did Friedman draw from a picture like that?
answer: A people cannot be politically free while the state controls the whole economy
choices: A people cannot be politically free while the state controls the whole economy
Political freedom and economic freedom are unrelated in practice
Political freedom must be won first, and economic freedom follows
Voting is enough to protect freedom no matter who runs the economy
context: Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago, 1962) and Man, Economy, and State (D. Van Nostrand, 1962) reach overlapping political conclusions from opposite methods: Chicago's empirical economics and Austrian praxeology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism_and_Freedom.

question: A young economist raised on a farm in North Dakota published a short book about groups with Harvard University Press in 1965, and it reshaped what economists and political scientists believed about them. His name was Mancur Olson. What did he title the book?
answer: The Logic of Collective Action
choices: The Logic of Collective Action
The Rise and Decline of Nations
Power and Prosperity
The Theory of Groups
context: The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of Groups (Harvard University Press, 1965). Source: hup.harvard.edu (Logic of Collective Action).

question: Lawmakers take up a subsidy bill: if it is defeated, ten million taxpayers each save $10, and if it passes, a hundred or so people on the inside each gain a million dollars. Mancur Olson worked through cases like this one. Which side, by his reasoning, will organize a serious lobbying campaign?
answer: The hundred insiders
choices: The hundred insiders
The ten million taxpayers
Both sides organize equally
A neutral consumer coalition organizes both
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern. Each farmer has $1M at stake; each taxpayer has $10. The math of individual incentives, not moral character, produces the asymmetric lobbying. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965).

question: A middle-school class of twenty takes on a big group project, and every student will get the same grade no matter how much he does. Some coast, counting on the rest to get it done. Economists have a name for that temptation, which turns up in taxes, unions and climate treaties too. What is it called?
answer: Free-riding
choices: Free-riding
Regulatory capture
Adverse selection
The prisoner's dilemma
context: Free-riding is central to Olson's account: in large groups no individual has enough at stake to bear the cost of organizing, so each rationally hopes others will do it. The result is under-organization. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 1.

question: Mancur Olson pointed in his 1965 book to one mechanism that lets some large groups organize after all, though readers often misread him as saying they never can. What did he call the mechanism?
answer: Selective incentives
choices: Selective incentives
Coercive taxation
Charismatic leadership
Federal grants
context: Selective incentives are private benefits available only to members: union-negotiated contracts, professional certifications, discount insurance for AARP members. They give individuals a private reason to join what would otherwise be an under-organized group. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), Chapter 6.

question: A couple signs up for one huge American group, mostly for its cheap insurance, hotel deals, travel discounts and low-priced prescription drugs. Tens of millions of members have joined for the same perks, and scholars applying Mancur Olson's idea hold the group up as a classic case of members drawn in by private benefits rather than shared political passion. Which group is it?
answer: AARP
choices: AARP
The Elks
The Grange
The Lions
context: AARP offers its members insurance and travel discounts as selective incentives, private benefits that sustain what would otherwise be an under-organized group of older Americans. Olson's own 1965 example was the Farm Bureau, which drew farmers with cheap auto insurance into a lobby for farm subsidies. Source: econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/Olson.html.

question: Mancur Olson took up a hard question in a book of 1982: why do some countries grow rich over generations while others slide into stagnation? It came between his famous first book of 1965 and his last, published after his death. What is the title of that middle book?
answer: The Rise and Decline of Nations
choices: The Rise and Decline of Nations
Power and Prosperity
The Political Economy of Growth
Sclerosis and Stagnation
context: The Rise and Decline of Nations: Economic Growth, Stagflation, and Social Rigidities (Yale University Press, 1982). It applied the Logic to macro-history. Source: yalebooks.yale.edu (Rise and Decline).

question: Mancur Olson worked through the arithmetic of policies that give a large gain to a few people and a small loss to each of millions, even where the total cost exceeds the total benefit. What did he say becomes of such policies?
answer: They survive
choices: They survive
They accelerate
They collapse
They backfire
context: The beneficiaries organize to defend the policy; the victims never organize to oppose it. Farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, occupational licensing, and thousands of similar policies survive for decades despite failing cost-benefit tests. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: Mancur Olson's students finished his last book after he died in 1998, and it came out in 2000. It set bandits who rove and plunder against bandits who settle down and tax, to explain why some countries grow rich while others stay poor. What was the book called?
answer: Power and Prosperity
choices: Power and Prosperity
The Wealth and Poverty of Nations
Institutions and Growth
Coalitions and Collapse
context: Power and Prosperity: Outgrowing Communist and Capitalist Dictatorships (Basic Books, 2000) was completed by Olson's students after his 1998 death. It introduced his 'stationary bandit' / 'roving bandit' framework. Source: basicbooks.com (Power and Prosperity).

question: Mancur Olson knocked down, in his 1965 book, an assumption that most political scientists of his day took for granted about workers, consumers and taxpayers. Which assumption did his book undo?
answer: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
choices: Large groups with shared interests will readily organize to advance them
Small groups always fail against large coalitions
Politicians act from pure public spirit rather than self-interest
Voting systems always produce coherent group preferences
context: Pre-Olson pluralist theory (David Truman, Arthur Bentley) assumed shared interests produce organization. Olson showed the opposite: shared interest is not enough; a large group needs selective incentives, small numbers or compulsion. Source: Olson, Logic of Collective Action (1965), preface.

question: Investors were fleeing in panic as COVID-19 spread into the United States when, on Tuesday, March 3, 2020, the Federal Reserve made an emergency rate cut between its scheduled meetings. No surprise cut had come since the financial crisis of October 2008. By how much did the Fed cut its rate that day?
answer: 50 basis points
choices: 50 basis points
25 basis points
100 basis points
75 basis points
context: The March 3 2020 emergency cut moved the target range from 1.50-1.75% to 1.00-1.25%. It was the first out-of-meeting emergency cut in 12 years. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: Traders on Wall Street heard a Sunday announcement on March 15, 2020: twelve days after its first emergency cut, the Federal Reserve was cutting its rate again, by a full percentage point. The new rate stayed there for two years. What was the new range?
answer: Zero to 0.25 percent
choices: Zero to 0.25 percent
0.75 to 1 percent
0.25 to 0.5 percent
Negative 0.25 percent
context: The Sunday March 15 2020 emergency action cut an additional 100 basis points to a range of 0.00-0.25%. It also announced $700 billion in initial asset purchases. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell, the Fed's chair, told markets on March 23, 2020, that the central bank would buy government debt and mortgage-backed bonds in any amount it took, with no ceiling. Critics called it money printing and repeated an old warning. What long-term effect did they warn of?
answer: Prices in the economy rise as more dollars chase the same goods
choices: Prices in the economy rise as more dollars chase the same goods
Banks sit on the new money, so prices fall for years
The dollar grows too strong for American exporters
Wages race ahead of prices and workers grow richer
context: The March 23 2020 announcement removed any dollar cap on Treasury and mortgage-backed-security purchases. It also launched unprecedented new lending facilities. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: Peter Schiff, an Austrian critic, called it a dangerous step when the Federal Reserve began in 2020 to create money to buy the bonds of single companies like Apple, Ford and AT&T, something it had never done before. Why did he and other Austrian critics say so?
answer: The central bank was now picking which companies to prop up
choices: The central bank was now picking which companies to prop up
Buying company bonds would push interest rates up
The companies would owe the Fed their future profits
The Fed was buying only from foreign bondholders
context: The Primary and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facilities let the Fed buy corporate bonds directly for the first time; before, it had bought only Treasuries and agency debt. On April 9, 2020 it also opened a Municipal Liquidity Facility for state and city bonds, so the central bank itself was choosing which borrowers got credit, a job traditionally left to legislatures. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve response to the COVID-19 pandemic' (2026-09-05).

question: A Wall Street bond trader watched the Federal Reserve stretch its buying in April 2020 to company bonds that Moody's and S&P had rated investment grade before the pandemic and had just cut to junk. Traders already had a nickname for bonds like these. What was it?
answer: Fallen angels
choices: Fallen angels
Zombie bonds
Toxic tranches
Widow-makers
context: The April 9 2020 expansion covered 'fallen angels' -- formerly investment-grade debt now trading as high yield. The Fed had crossed the line from Treasury-and-agency-only purchases into direct corporate credit allocation, including junk. Source: Grokipedia 'Fallen angel (finance)' (2026-09-05).

question: Critics of the Federal Reserve watched it begin buying Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities in huge amounts when the pandemic hit in March 2020. Its balance sheet, near $4.2 trillion before COVID, more than doubled by the peak in spring 2022, the largest growth the Fed had ever seen. Roughly how big was it at that peak?
answer: About $8.9 trillion
choices: About $8.9 trillion
About $5.5 trillion
About $12 trillion
About $6 trillion
context: The Fed's assets peaked at roughly $8.9 trillion in April 2022 -- larger in dollar terms than QE1 plus QE2 plus QE3 plus Operation Twist combined. It was the largest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-22).

question: Congress wrote a clause into the Federal Reserve Act in 1932 that lets the Fed lend to nearly any borrower, not just banks, in what the statute calls 'unusual and exigent circumstances.' Every one of the Fed's emergency programs of March 2020 rested on it. Which section of the act is it?
answer: Section 13(3)
choices: Section 13(3)
Section 10(b)
Section 24A
Section 15
context: Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, dating to 1932, allows the Fed to lend to non-bank borrowers in emergencies. Its 2020 use was the broadest invocation in the section's history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Act' (2026-09-05).

question: A Mises Institute economist sets the Federal Reserve's programs of March 2020 beside its rescues of 2008 to 2014 and finds them far larger. He draws a lasting lesson about what an emergency leaves behind. What is his point?
answer: Emergency programs set a new baseline that the next crisis starts from
choices: Emergency programs set a new baseline that the next crisis starts from
Emergency programs are always fully unwound within two years
Emergency programs affect only asset prices, not consumer prices
Emergency programs are politically neutral and leave incomes alone
context: The Fed's 2020 balance sheet ($8.9T at its 2022 peak) became the new reference point; on this reading, any future crisis response starts from at least that level. The Cantillon-effect gains to the first receivers of new money (asset holders, primary dealers, government contractors) were correspondingly larger. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Two economists at George Mason University in Virginia started a blog together in 2003 and have posted on it daily ever since, for more than twenty years. Few economics blogs online have run as long. Who started marginalrevolution.com?
answer: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
choices: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
Russ Roberts and Michael Munger
Bryan Caplan and Robin Hanson
Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner
context: Cowen (born 1962) and Tabarrok (born 1966) both teach economics at GMU, where they succeeded the Buchanan-Tullock generation as the public face of the George Mason public-choice and Austrian-adjacent tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Marginal_Revolution_(blog).

question: A George Mason economist looked back, in The Great Stagnation of 2011, at the airplane, the car, electricity and indoor plumbing, all arriving before the 1970s, and argued that inventions on that scale have been far rarer since. What did he say the shortage of big new inventions has caused?
answer: A slowdown in productivity growth
choices: A slowdown in productivity growth
A trade deficit
A currency devaluation
A liquidity trap
context: Cowen followed 'The Great Stagnation' (2011) with 'Average Is Over' (2013, on labor-market polarization from technology), 'The Complacent Class' (2017), and 'Big Business' (2019, a partial defense of large corporations). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: An economist at George Mason University, one of the two who had blogged daily since 2003, launched an interview podcast in 2015. Each episode gives about an hour to a single guest, and the guests have run from chefs and chess players to novelists, historians and fellow economists. What is the show called?
answer: Conversations with Tyler
choices: Conversations with Tyler
EconTalk
Freakonomics Radio
Odd Lots
context: EconTalk is Russ Roberts's older podcast (started 2006); Freakonomics Radio is Stephen Dubner's; Odd Lots is Bloomberg's Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway. Conversations with Tyler is Cowen's own long-form interview series. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock brought their center for public choice to George Mason University in 1983 and built the school's academic structure there. A generation later two economists there, the pair behind the Marginal Revolution blog, added something of their own. What did the pair add to the Mason tradition?
answer: They carried its reasoning online and into popular debate
choices: They carried its reasoning online and into popular debate
They swapped public choice for Keynesian economics
They took over editing the profession's leading journal
They moved the public-choice center to Washington
context: Where Buchanan and Tullock built the academic apparatus, Cowen and Tabarrok made the reasoning-move tradition accessible to a general reader without a degree -- through Marginal Revolution (daily blog since 2003), MRU (free courses since 2012), Cowen's podcast (since 2015), and their principles textbook. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tyler_Cowen.

question: Milton Friedman argued in his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom that a state license to practice medicine shields doctors from competition as well as protecting patients. In each American state, who decides who gets that license?
answer: The state medical board
choices: The state medical board
The US Department of Health
The American Medical Association
The Federal Trade Commission
context: State medical boards, staffed largely by licensed physicians, control entry to the profession within each state. Friedman argued that boards run by the profession use entry rules to hold down competition, a pattern George Stigler later built into his theory of regulatory capture. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (Chicago 1962), Chapter 9.

question: Abraham Flexner, in a 1910 study for the Carnegie Foundation, urged the states to shut the small medical schools that failed the strict new standards and to model medical training on Johns Hopkins. School after school shut while America's population kept growing. What did that do to the price of seeing a doctor?
answer: It pushed prices higher because fewer new doctors entered the field
choices: It pushed prices higher because fewer new doctors entered the field
It pushed prices lower as doctors grew better trained
It left prices flat as surviving schools grew
It pushed prices lower by driving out quacks
context: The Flexner Report (Abraham Flexner for the Carnegie Foundation, 1910) recommended consolidating US medical education on the Johns Hopkins model. The number of US medical schools fell from 160 in 1904 to 85 by 1920 and 66 by 1935. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexner_Report.

question: A hair braider in one American state applied for a government license before she could charge her neighbors for braiding their hair. Morris Kleiner, a labor economist, has spent years measuring what rules like that do to pay. What do his studies find about the pay of workers who already hold a license?
answer: Wages rise, because new competitors are kept out
choices: Wages rise, because new competitors are kept out
Wages drop, because rules push customers away
Wages stay the same, since customers do not notice
Wages rise only for the newest license holders
context: Morris Kleiner, in Licensing Occupations: Ensuring Quality or Restricting Competition? (Upjohn Institute, 2006), estimates that licensed workers earn about 15 percent more on average, with little measurable gain in quality. With Alan Krueger he found in 2013 that the share of American workers needing a license had risen from about one in twenty in the 1950s to more than one in four by 2008. Source: Kleiner and Krueger, Journal of Labor Economics (2013).

question: A nurse practitioner, a nurse with advanced clinical training, opened her own primary-care clinic with no doctor supervising her, in one of about half the states that allowed it by 2024. Researchers compared those states with the ones where only a physician could run such a clinic. What did they keep finding?
answer: Lower primary-care prices and no measurable change in quality
choices: Lower primary-care prices and no measurable change in quality
Sharply worse patient outcomes and higher malpractice rates
Sharply higher primary-care prices and lower quality
Identical prices and quality but shorter waits
context: Multiple studies, including RAND Corporation work and AANP meta-analyses, find lower primary-care prices with no measurable quality difference. State medical societies routinely oppose scope expansion; state nursing associations support it. Source: rand.org (NP scope-of-practice studies).
