question: A patient choosing a doctor deserved, in Milton Friedman's view, to know who was well trained, yet Friedman did not want the state deciding who may practice at all. He set out his alternative in Capitalism and Freedom in 1962. What did he propose in place of licensing?
answer: Certification rather than licensing
choices: Certification rather than licensing
Free-for-all with no state role at all
Federal licensing replacing state licensing
Direct government provision of the service
context: Friedman's certification / licensing distinction: the state may certify credentials, but should not forbid uncertified practitioners from offering services to informed adults who accept the trade-off. Quality signaling without monopoly. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962), Chapter 9.

question: The people who write a profession's entry rules in one state are nearly all members of that profession: dentists judging dentists, lawyers judging lawyers. Public-choice economists have a default rule for a body like this. What should a reader suspect first about the rules it writes?
answer: That its entry limits protect members' incomes more than safety
choices: That its entry limits protect members' incomes more than safety
That its rules will be the strictest and safest that can be had
That the state legislature will watch its every decision closely
That patients can see exactly how every one of its rules is made
context: The Stigler-Olson combined move: incumbents are the concentrated beneficiary organized to write the entry rules; patients are the dispersed party unable to organize. The default should be suspicion; specific safety justifications must be shown, not assumed. Source: Friedman (1962); Stigler (1971); Kleiner (2006).

question: Ludwig von Mises laid one rule about method at the foundation of his great treatise of 1949, and Murray Rothbard opened his own treatise of 1962 the same way. Where did that rule say the study of economics has to begin?
answer: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
choices: With the choices of individual people acting on purpose
With the total amount of money in the country
With the government's official five-year plan
With the average behavior of a whole social class
context: Human Action (Yale, 1949) makes methodological individualism the foundation of praxeology in chapter 1 section 2, 'The Fundamental Task of Praxeology'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: A news report says a country has decided something, and an Austrian-school economist stops at once to ask who, exactly, did the deciding. Which founding rule of his school makes him ask?
answer: Methodological individualism
choices: Methodological individualism
Methodological holism
Structural functionalism
Popperian falsificationism
context: Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies (Routledge, 1945) uses the same phrase and endorses the same doctrine from outside the Austrian tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies.

question: A Marxist writer declares: the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat. A follower of Ludwig von Mises takes the sentence and rewrites it, so that the choices and incentives hiding behind its class words come out where a reader can see them. What move does the follower make?
answer: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
choices: Replace class terms with specific persons acting in specific transactions
Replace class terms with abstract aggregate demand curves
Replace class terms with statistical correlations across populations
Replace class terms with equilibrium price vectors
context: The analytical payoff of methodological individualism: 'the government intervened' hides everything; 'this senator, facing this lobby, cast this vote for this reason' opens up the incentive picture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Methodological_individualism.

question: Friedrich Hayek, following the Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson, stressed one point about the Austrian rule that every social outcome traces back to what persons did. Some critics read the rule as a claim that someone consciously planned every language, market and custom. What did Hayek say the rule leaves room for?
answer: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
choices: Outcomes can be the result of human action but not of any human design
Outcomes are always the intended plan of a central authority
Outcomes can be reduced to statistical population means
Outcomes emerge from unconscious biological instincts
context: The doctrine coexists with spontaneous order: a market price is not chosen by anyone yet emerges from individuals choosing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: Company treasurers watched the Federal Reserve create new dollars at a record pace in 2020, and Michael Saylor, fearing for his software company's cash reserves, began moving them into Bitcoin. What makes Bitcoin different that he counted on to protect those savings?
answer: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
choices: Bitcoin has a fixed supply and can't be printed
Bitcoin pays interest every month
Bitcoin is backed by the US government
Bitcoin is guaranteed by the Federal Reserve
context: MicroStrategy, headquartered in Tysons Corner Virginia and founded in 1989, was the first US public company to make Bitcoin a corporate-treasury reserve asset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MicroStrategy.

question: The dollar was a losing bet, Michael Saylor said in August 2020, as his software company, MicroStrategy, began holding Bitcoin in its place. He laid the blame on one pandemic-era policy of the Federal Reserve. Which Fed policy did Saylor blame?
answer: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
choices: Trillion-dollar balance-sheet expansion
Setting the federal-funds rate at 5 percent
Selling off Treasury holdings under quantitative tightening
Raising bank reserve requirements sharply
context: The Fed's balance sheet grew by trillions in 2020-21 as it bought Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities to backstop pandemic markets. Saylor argued this made cash a certain loser and Bitcoin the hedge. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2020-21).

question: Michael Saylor's software company, MicroStrategy of Tysons Corner, Virginia, made news on August 11, 2020: it had swapped cash from its reserves for Bitcoin, a first for any big public company. The money was cash already on its books, not borrowed. Roughly how much did that first purchase cost?
answer: $250 million
choices: $250 million
$25 million
$2.5 billion
$50 million
context: MicroStrategy's August 11 2020 announcement: $250M converted from cash into Bitcoin. Subsequent purchases over 2020-2025 pushed total holdings well above 200,000 BTC. Source: microstrategy.com (August 11 2020 press release).

question: Michael Saylor kept buying Bitcoin through the crypto slump of 2022, though his company's coins had sunk billions below what it paid for them. He raised the money for new purchases by selling the same kind of corporate debt again and again. Which kind of debt did MicroStrategy use?
answer: Convertible bonds
choices: Convertible bonds
Preferred stock
Bank revolvers
Municipal bonds
context: MicroStrategy issued multiple tranches of convertible senior notes 2020-2024 and used the proceeds to buy Bitcoin, effectively increasing its Bitcoin-per-share leverage. The stock ticker MSTR became a leveraged Bitcoin proxy. Source: microstrategy.com (investor filings 2020-2024).

question: Michael Saylor's MicroStrategy built its whole identity around Bitcoin: it put on a logo in Bitcoin orange in February 2025, and that August it took the legal name Strategy. What does Saylor tell shareholders the company holds its Bitcoin as?
answer: A long-term store of value
choices: A long-term store of value
A short-term trading position
A payment currency for customers
A hedge to sell once inflation cools
context: The rebrand was announced February 5 2025 and the legal name change to Strategy Inc took effect August 11 2025; the MSTR ticker was retained. Source: cnbc.com/2025/02/05/bitcoin-treasury-pioneer-microstrategy-rebrands-with-a-new-name-strategy.html.

question: Michael Saylor turns a habit of corporate finance upside down. A company that sits on cash under a central bank that keeps printing, he argues, is quietly losing its shareholders' money, so guarding them against dollar debasement is no optional extra for management. What does he say it is instead?
answer: A requirement of fiduciary duty
choices: A requirement of fiduciary duty
A public-relations decision
A regulatory-compliance obligation
A shareholder-vote matter
context: Saylor's move: if directors have a fiduciary duty to preserve shareholder value, and cash certainly loses purchasing power at a debasing central bank, then holding a scarce non-state asset is the fiduciary-consistent trade. It shifts the corporate-finance default. Source: saylor.org (public speeches 2020-2024).

question: A company disclosed in a regulatory filing early in 2021 that it had put about $1.5 billion into Bitcoin, following the path Michael Saylor's MicroStrategy had opened, and the price jumped. Within a year and a half it had sold off about three-quarters of the stash. Which company was it?
answer: Tesla
choices: Tesla
Block (formerly Square)
Marathon Digital
Coinbase
context: Tesla disclosed the $1.5 billion purchase in its 10-K filing of February 8, 2021, sold about a tenth of the coins in the first quarter of 2021, and by the end of June 2022 had converted about 75 percent of its Bitcoin purchases into dollars. Block (formerly Square) and Marathon kept theirs. Source: theblock.co (Tesla sold $936 million in bitcoin in the second quarter, July 2022).

question: Rose Friedman, a trained economist herself, and her husband Milton carried one claim about spending to readers and television viewers in 1980: no one watches someone else's money as closely as his own. Whose spending did they set out to rein in?
answer: Government officials spending taxpayers' money
choices: Government officials spending taxpayers' money
Banks lending out their depositors' money
Charities spending their donors' money
Insurers investing their customers' premiums
context: Free to Choose (1980) sorted spending into four kinds and held that spending other people's money on other people, as government does with taxes, is the least careful of all. Rose Director Friedman was a Chicago-trained economist in her own right. Source: Grokipedia, 'Free to Choose' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose).

question: Milton Friedman had left the University of Chicago for Stanford's Hoover Institution by 1980, when he and his wife Rose took their case for free markets to public television in ten parts, alongside a best-selling book of the same title. What was the title?
answer: Free to Choose
choices: Free to Choose
Capitalism and Freedom
The Road to Serfdom
A Monetary History
context: Free to Choose (1980) was a book and a PBS series, with Rose Friedman as associate producer. Capitalism and Freedom (1962) is Milton's earlier book, The Road to Serfdom (1944) is Hayek's, and A Monetary History (1963) is the Friedman-Schwartz volume. Source: Grokipedia, 'Free to Choose' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Free_to_Choose).

question: General William Westmoreland, Army chief of staff, told a commission on ending the draft that he did not want to lead an army of mercenaries. Richard Nixon had set it up under Thomas Gates in 1969. Milton Friedman, a member, answered with one question. What did Friedman ask?
answer: Whether he would rather command an army of slaves
choices: Whether he would rather command an army of slaves
What he would pay to keep the men he commanded
What price his own patriotism carried
Who was paying for the army he commanded
context: Friedman's words were 'General, would you rather command an army of slaves?' Westmoreland objected that he did not like hearing patriotic volunteers called slaves; Friedman answered that he did not like hearing them called mercenaries -- 'If they are mercenaries, then I, sir, am a mercenary professor, and you, sir, are a mercenary general.' The commission's February 21 1970 report unanimously recommended ending conscription. Sources: Friedman and Friedman, Two Lucky People; Duke HOPE working paper, 'Slaves or Mercenaries'; Cato Institute centennial appreciation.

question: Anna Jacobson Schwartz, Milton Friedman's full co-author, tracked America's money with him from 1867 to 1960 in their book A Monetary History, published in 1963. The book's hardest-won lesson came out of the 1930s. What did it tell central bankers?
answer: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
choices: Do not let the money supply collapse during a banking panic
Print unlimited money whenever growth slows down
Fix the exchange rate to gold once every ten years
Ignore money entirely and focus only on interest rates
context: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 (Princeton, 1963) is by Milton Friedman AND Anna Jacobson Schwartz. She was a full co-author, not an assistant, spent seven decades at the NBER, and lived until 2012. Source: Grokipedia, 'Anna Schwartz' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Anna_Schwartz).

question: The Swedish academy named three of Milton Friedman's achievements when it gave him the economics Nobel in 1976. Which three did it name?
answer: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
choices: Consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilization policy
Price theory, the economics of the family, and the measurement of national income accounts
Monetary history, the theory of public choice, and the analysis of regulatory institutions
Consumption analysis, international trade theory, and the design of central-bank independence
context: The full citation: 'for his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy.' The three strands map onto A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957), A Monetary History (1963), and the natural-rate argument. Sources: NobelPrize.org, Economic Sciences 1976 press release; NBER.

question: Congress mails every household a one-time rebate cheque of $600 to lift spending, and a supporter predicts most of it will be spent within the quarter. An economist who follows Milton Friedman's 1957 account of consumption, which challenged the Keynesian rule of thumb that families spend a set share of every dollar they receive, expects far less. What reasoning does he press?
answer: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
choices: The cheque changes this year's cash, not the long-run income a household budgets against
The cheque lands after the downturn has already turned, so the spending arrives unwanted
The cheque is funded by borrowing that households expect to repay in later taxes anyway
The cheque means far more to a poor household than a rich one, so the average misleads
context: This is the permanent income hypothesis doing policy work. Friedman's charge against Keynes was precise: Keynes had related consumption to measured income without separating transitory income from permanent income. The argument says the rebate will move spending less than its sponsors expect, not that the sponsors are acting in bad faith. Other real arguments about rebates, each pressed by real economists, include the lag problem, Ricardian equivalence and distributional averaging.

question: Ludwig von Mises and Milton Friedman agreed that central banks had made the century's worst slumps deeper, but neither trusted the other's method. Mises built on principles of human action and held that no statistic could overturn them. What did Friedman insist an economic claim must do instead?
answer: Stand or fall on measured data series that another researcher could check
choices: Stand or fall on measured data series that another researcher could check
Rest on a written constitution that binds the central bank before any downturn actually begins
Begin from what a policymaker intends, since intentions determine which levers ever get pulled
Be reducible to a single equation, since anything not written as one cannot be argued about clearly
context: This is why Friedman must not be filed as an Austrian. He was a Chicago-school monetarist and a methodological empiricist: A Monetary History is a hundred years of data, not a chain of deductions. Austrians answer that human action is not laboratory chemistry and that the data themselves only mean anything inside a theory -- a live argument, not a settled one. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Monetarism' and 'Chicago school of economics'.

question: A senator proposes raising the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour to help low-wage workers. Critics in the line of Frédéric Bastiat and Milton Friedman look past the workers who get the raise for the worker nobody sees. Whose job does the new $15 floor price out?
answer: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
choices: A 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8 per hour
A senior union electrician earning $42 per hour under a long-standing collective bargain
A civil-service accountant on a fixed grade paying $58,000 per year
A hospital physician with a fellowship contract paying $190 per hour
context: Friedman's Bastiat-style worked example: at $15/hr floor, no employer can legally pay $15 for $8 of work; the 16-year-old's job does not exist, it does not appear as a fired employee, and so it is UNSEEN. Source: fee.org/articles/milton-friedman-on-the-minimum-wage.

question: Milton Friedman put it in one blunt line on television and again, with his wife Rose, in their 1980 best seller Free to Choose: what a minimum wage law, rightly described, orders employers to do. Which line did he use?
answer: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
choices: A law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills
A law saying employers must pay their workers fair market value
A law saying government fixes the price of labor for all industries
A law saying workers cannot bargain individually for wages
context: Friedman said it in a television interview, and Free to Choose (1980) says the law requires employers to discriminate against persons with low skills. His 1966 Newsweek column had already argued that the floor shuts the least skilled, black teenagers above all, out of work. Source: cafehayek.com/2013/11/quotation-of-the-day-800.html.

question: McDonald's, Panera and Wendy's spread one new piece of self-service gear through their restaurants in 2017 and 2018, the years Seattle's $15 minimum wage reached full force for big employers. The gear draws no wage. Which piece of gear was it?
answer: Self-order kiosks
choices: Self-order kiosks
Robotic burger flippers
Automated deep fryers
Motion-sensor drink dispensers
context: McDonald's, Panera, and Wendy's led a mass kiosk rollout after Seattle's $15 floor took full effect; touch-screens do not need a wage, and became worth buying only once labor was made expensive by law. Source: seattletimes.com (2017-18 rollout coverage).

question: David Card and Alan Krueger phoned managers and counted staff on both sides of a state line for a famous paper of 1994. One state had lifted its minimum wage shortly before; the other had not. Jobs, they reported, had barely fallen in the short run on the side that raised it. Which two states did the paper make famous?
answer: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
choices: New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food
California vs Arizona agriculture
New York vs Connecticut retail
Texas vs Oklahoma construction
context: Card & Krueger 1994 became the standard mainstream citation for 'minimum wage does not cost jobs', and empirical work of this kind won Card a share of the 2021 Nobel Memorial Prize. Source: American Economic Review 84(4), 1994.

question: David Neumark and William Wascher took aim at the method behind David Card and Alan Krueger's famous study: a manager's word over the phone, they said, was a poor way to count jobs. They argued it at length in their 2008 book, Minimum Wages. Which kind of data did Neumark and Wascher push for?
answer: Payroll records from the restaurants themselves
choices: Payroll records from the restaurants themselves
Consumer-survey purchasing questionnaires
Store-window help-wanted sign counts
Chamber of Commerce membership rolls
context: Neumark & Wascher's response (2000 AER; Minimum Wages, MIT Press 2008) showed the Card-Krueger effect flips sign in long-run panels and in administrative payroll data rather than short phone surveys. Source: MIT Press catalog.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued that no distant planner can gather the knowledge scattered across a whole country, and the minimum wage's critics turn his argument on the wage floor. One floor, set far away, covers every worker in every town. What does the owner of the shop know that the lawmakers do not?
answer: What each worker is worth in that job and town
choices: What each worker is worth in that job and town
How many workers the whole country employs
What the average wage is across every industry
Where the central bank will set interest rates
context: Hayek's 1945 knowledge-in-society argument applied to labor: the employer's local knowledge of a worker's productivity in a specific job is not available to a legislator setting a single national floor. This is the Hayekian bite of the minimum-wage debate. Source: fee.org/articles/hayek-and-the-minimum-wage.

question: Walter Williams set two eras side by side in his 2011 book Race and Economics: the 1950s, when the federal wage floor was low once prices are counted, and the decades after the floor was raised again and again from the 1970s. What did he find had happened to teenage unemployment?
answer: It rose from about 10 percent to between 15 and 20, higher still for black teens
choices: It rose from about 10 percent to between 15 and 20, higher still for black teens
It held near 10 percent in both eras, for black and white teens alike
It fell from about 20 percent to 10, as higher pay drew teens into work
It rose from about 10 percent to 12, with no gap between black and white
context: Williams's account: US teenage unemployment averaged around 10 percent in the 1950s, when the real federal minimum was low, and 15 to 20 percent after the repeated increases from the 1970s on, with far higher rates among black teenagers. Sources: Walter E. Williams, Race and Economics (Hoover Institution Press, 2011); bls.gov historical labor-force data.

question: Slush, a Czech programmer, opened a service in November 2010 that let small Bitcoin miners combine their machines' power and split every prize they won. Which older arrangement works the same way?
answer: A lottery syndicate splitting its winnings
choices: A lottery syndicate splitting its winnings
A cartel fixing one price for its members
A bank lending out its savers' deposits
A union bargaining for all its workers
context: The service was first called Slush Pool and runs today as Braiins Pool. Like a syndicate's members, each miner gives up his slim chance of a whole prize alone for a steady share of the group's wins. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Braiins_Pool.

question: A miner in a Bitcoin pool hands in result after result: partial hashes, near-misses that would have taken a block had the network set an easier target. Each one proves he did real work, and the pool splits every reward by how many he turned in. What is one of those entries called?
answer: A share
choices: A share
A halving
A block reward
A dividend
context: A share is a hash that would have been a valid block at a much lower difficulty than the actual network target. It proves the miner did real work. Payout schemes like PPS, PPLNS, and FPPS all key off share counts. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: A Bitcoin miner running just a machine or two switches them on to race for the next block, which turns up only once every ten minutes or so across the whole network, with a prize of about 3.125 coins. Many miners like him join a big pool instead of racing alone. Why does a small miner join?
answer: Alone he may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
choices: Alone he may go months or years without ever winning a block reward
A pool's blocks carry a larger prize than any solo miner's
The pool's operator pays the electricity bill for his machines
Pooled machines solve each puzzle with far less work
context: With one block found about every ten minutes across the network, a miner holding a sliver of the total hash power can wait months or years between wins; a pool smooths that into small regular payouts, minus a fee. Foundry USA, Antpool, F2Pool and ViaBTC are among today's largest pools, and their shares rotate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: The operators of GHash.io, one of Bitcoin's big pools, watched it pass half of all the hashing power on the network for a short time in the summer of 2014. A pool that big could in theory rewrite recent blocks and spend coins twice over, yet neither a court nor a regulator stepped in. What happened next?
answer: Miners pulled their machines out, and its operators urged users to leave
choices: Miners pulled their machines out, and its operators urged users to leave
Bitcoin's developers rewrote the code to cap any one pool's share
The Bitcoin Foundation expelled GHash.io from the network
Rival pools bought GHash.io out and broke up its machines
context: The incident demonstrated that a mining pool's power depends on user trust. Pool operators knew that keeping >51 percent would undermine the network their own hardware depended on, so they chose to shrink. Source: grokipedia.com/page/51%25_attack.

question: A high-school student worries that the GHash.io scare of 2014 shows Bitcoin is fragile, now that a handful of big pools direct the bulk of the world's mining. An economist trained in public choice answers that the episode itself shows why the danger has limits. What is his reasoning move?
answer: An attack would ruin the value of the operators' own machines and fees
choices: An attack would ruin the value of the operators' own machines and fees
Regulators in each pool's home country would shut any pool past half
The next halving would cut the reward and starve an oversized pool
Rival pools would join forces and outvote any attacker's blocks
context: This is incentive recognition -- the kind of analysis Buchanan and Tullock applied to political actors. Pool operators are not benevolent; they are self-interested actors whose interests align with network security. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mining_pool.

question: Lew Rockwell, an ex-congressional aide, set up an institute beside Auburn University in Alabama in 1982. It bore the name of Ludwig von Mises, a lifelong enemy of central planning, and grew into a leading American center of one school of economics. Which school?
answer: The Austrian school
choices: The Austrian school
The Keynesian school
The Marxist school
The Monetarist school
context: The Ludwig von Mises Institute was founded in Auburn, Alabama in 1982 and is located adjacent to the Auburn University campus. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: Ron Paul, a Texas congressman, ran for president three times, and his attack on the Federal Reserve came down to three words: End the Fed. In his view the Fed's power to create dollars from nothing does one harm. What was his main complaint?
answer: Printing money makes the dollar lose value over time
choices: Printing money makes the dollar lose value over time
The Fed keeps interest rates too high for borrowers
The Fed lends too little to struggling small banks
The Fed lets the dollar's value rise too quickly
context: Ron Paul, then a Republican congressman from Texas, was an early supporter of the Mises Institute and one of its distinguished counselors; its founder, Lew Rockwell, had been his chief of staff. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mises_Institute.

question: Lew Rockwell opened his small institute in Auburn in 1982 under a famous economist's name. The right to use that name came from one person, who gave the founding her blessing and served on its board until she died in 1993. Who was she?
answer: Margit von Mises
choices: Margit von Mises
Bettina Bien Greaves
Sylvia Nasar
Hazel Kyrk
context: Margit von Mises, Ludwig's widow, gave her personal blessing to the founding and remained on the board until her death in 1993. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: A college student travels to Auburn, Alabama, one summer for Mises University, an intensive week of lectures run by the Mises Institute, and students from many countries do the same. She could have stayed home and taken a summer course. Why does she make the trip?
answer: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
choices: Most universities teach little or none of the Austrian tradition
Its week of lectures counts as credit at most US colleges
It trains students for careers at the Federal Reserve
It is the only place Austrian books can still be found
context: Mises University is the Institute's annual weeklong summer program for undergraduates, taught by senior Austrian-school faculty. Source: mises.org/mises-university.

question: Murray Rothbard, Ludwig von Mises's leading American student, founded a hard-money branch of Mises's school, and after Rothbard's death in 1995 its home was the Mises Institute in Auburn. Which money reform is that branch best known for?
answer: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
choices: 100 percent reserve banking and abolition of the Fed
A Milton Friedman k-percent money-supply rule
Explicit nominal-GDP targeting
A permanent zero-interest-rate policy
context: The Rothbardian branch is monetarily hard-line: 100% reserves and immediate abolition of the Federal Reserve. The Hayekian branch at George Mason has a different institutional emphasis. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mises_Institute.

question: Jörg Guido Hülsmann, an economist, wrote the standard modern life of Ludwig von Mises, the twentieth century's great enemy of central planning, and the Mises Institute published it in 2007. Its subtitle gives Mises a heroic title. What is the subtitle?
answer: The Last Knight of Liberalism
choices: The Last Knight of Liberalism
The Prophet of Vienna
The Austrian Socrates
The Chancellor's Economist
context: Mises: The Last Knight of Liberalism (2007), by the economist Jörg Guido Hülsmann, is the standard scholarly biography of Ludwig von Mises. Source: mises.org/library/mises-last-knight-liberalism.

question: A student opens mises.org on a laptop and finds the school's great names there, Menger, Böhm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek and Rothbard alike, all free to read. Why does a free library like that spread a school further than any advertising could?
answer: Students anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
choices: Students anywhere can read the original arguments and decide for themselves
Readers trust a free book more than one they had to pay for
Free books rank higher in search results than paid ones
Giving books away brings in more donations than sales would
context: Mises.org hosts freely readable editions of Menger, Bohm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Rothbard, and modern Austrian scholars. Source: mises.org.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued that a market economy run with price caps, subsidies and targeted taxes cannot stand still: each fix breeds a problem that calls for another fix. He gathered those essays into a German book in 1929. What is its German title?
answer: Kritik des Interventionismus
choices: Kritik des Interventionismus
Die Gemeinwirtschaft
Nationaloekonomie
Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel
context: Full title: Kritik des Interventionismus: Untersuchungen zur Wirtschaftspolitik und Wirtschaftsideologie der Gegenwart. Hans F. Sennholz translated the essays into English as A Critique of Interventionism, first published in 1977 by Arlington House. Source: Mises Institute, 'A Critique of Interventionism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises spoke at the University Club in New York in April 1950, ten years after he had fled Europe, and gave a short version of his long case against the mixed economy. He packed his warning into the talk's title. What was the speech called?
answer: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
choices: Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism
Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth
Bureaucracy and the Free Market
The Anti-Capitalistic Mentality
context: The Commercial and Financial Chronicle first printed the address on May 4, 1950, and the Libertarian Press collected it in Planning for Freedom in 1952. It remains one of the most quoted short statements of his case against the interventionist ratchet. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Officials cap the price of one basic food so the poor can buy it. Farmers make less on it and raise less, the shelves go bare, and the officials cap the price of what goes into it, then of what goes into that. Which food does Ludwig von Mises's example of 1950 start with?
answer: Milk
choices: Milk
Bread
Coal
Rental housing
context: Mises walked from a milk-price ceiling to caps on what goes into milk, then on what goes into those, until the government was fixing, step by step, the prices of all consumers' goods and of all factors of production. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: A New York audience heard Ludwig von Mises argue in April 1950 that a mixed economy offers no real middle ground. Production, he said, answers either to the prices consumers pay or to the state's decrees. What three-word rule did he pack that either-or into?
answer: Control is indivisible
choices: Control is indivisible
Prices reveal knowledge
Property implies liberty
Money is neutral
context: Mises's argument: either consumers direct production through the prices they are willing to pay, or the state does through decree. Any attempt to split the difference leaves neither mechanism doing its job; the resulting malfunction forces an escalation to full state direction. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises closed his talk at New York's University Club in 1950 with his most famous line. The mixed economy of price controls, subsidies and quotas, he said, is no lasting system at all, only a way of reaching one destination. Where did he say it leads, and how?
answer: Socialism, by installments
choices: Socialism, by installments
Poverty, in a single generation
Central banking, over a business cycle
Fascism, within a decade
context: Full sentence: 'The middle-of-the-road policy is not an economic system that can last. It is a method for the realization of socialism by installments.' The metaphor is deliberate: no single intervention looks like socialism, but the running total does. Source: FEE, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Ludwig von Mises insisted in 1950 that his pattern was history, not just theory, and he pointed to one European country. It went to war in 1914 with price ceilings on just a few consumer goods, and before the war was over its whole economy had been bent to making munitions. Which case did Mises cite?
answer: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
choices: Germany's progression to the 1917 Hindenburg Plan
Britain's slide under the 1914 Defence of the Realm Act
France's move to the 1916 Loucheur decrees
Austria-Hungary's Kriegswirtschaft of 1915
context: The Hindenburg Programme of 1916-17, driven by General Erich Ludendorff, subordinated the whole German economy to munitions production. Mises's point was that Germany did not vote for the Hindenburg Plan in 1914; each intervening step looked reasonable given the last one, and the accumulated total was total control. Source: Mises Institute, 'Middle-of-the-Road Policy Leads to Socialism'.

question: Robert Higgs traced the growth of the American federal government in his 1987 book Crisis and Leviathan. The government swelled in wars, depressions and panics, he found, and shrank back only partway once the crisis passed. What did Higgs name that one-way pattern after?
answer: Ratchet
choices: Ratchet
Cascade
Spiral
Escalator
context: Higgs's Crisis and Leviathan: Critical Episodes in the Growth of American Government (Oxford, 1987) surveys the First World War, the Great Depression, the Second World War and the Cold War, showing that after each emergency the government shrank back only partway, so each crisis left it larger than before. Source: Wikipedia, 'Crisis and Leviathan'.

question: A wheat farmer planted more once the New Deal's price supports guaranteed him a floor price, and growers like him raised more grain than buyers wanted at that price. Surpluses piled up. What was Washington's next fix for the surplus?
answer: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
choices: Paying farmers to leave land idle under set-aside and payment-in-kind programs
Nationalizing the grain elevators to store the surplus at cost
Declaring a temporary tariff to force domestic bakeries to buy the surplus
Rationing consumer purchases to draw down accumulated stocks
context: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 first paid farmers to plow crops under; postwar set-aside acreage programs and the 1983 Payment-in-Kind program paid producers in surplus grain not to grow more of it. Ninety years later the policy is still running -- exactly the ratchet Mises described in 1929: the intervention that fixed the last intervention's malfunction generates the next malfunction to fix. Source: Mises Institute, 'Farm Bill Folly'.

question: Ludwig von Mises read protective tariffs, farm supports and rent control as half-measures bound to slip back toward markets or on toward full state control, never as resting points. He had one short phrase for a lasting resting point of that kind, and he used it only to deny that one could exist. Which phrase?
answer: A third system
choices: A third system
A guided economy
Managed capitalism
The mixed economy
context: Mises used 'a third system' precisely because he thought it did not exist as a stable system. Either consumer sovereignty through prices rules production or the state does; the intermediate cases he documented -- rent-controlled housing, price-supported farming, tariff-protected industry, rate-suppressed banking -- were the disequilibria that generated the ratchet toward the second pole. Source: Mises Institute, 'Why Intervention Persists'.

question: Friedrich Hayek went to work under Ludwig von Mises in 1921 at a Vienna government office. He came to see every market price as a signal summing up what countless people know and want. What did he say no central planner could ever do?
answer: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
choices: Gather all the knowledge that prices already carry
Set prices low enough for every family to afford
Pay workers as much as private firms would pay
Raise enough in taxes to pay for all his plans
context: Hayek (1899-1992) was hired at the Vienna claims-settlement office on a letter of introduction from his professor, Friedrich von Wieser, and won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974. Source: mises.org/online-book/last-knight-liberalism/hayek-and-bureau-claims-settlements.

question: Murray Rothbard sat down in Ludwig von Mises's New York University seminar in 1949 and later put a simple point about incentives. What did he say happens to what people produce as a government's taxes and rules pile up?
answer: People produce less because their reward for effort shrinks
choices: People produce less because their reward for effort shrinks
People produce more to catch up on taxes
Output holds steady, since people still need the same things
Output rises, since rules push firms to work more carefully
context: Rothbard (1926-1995) attended the NYU Mises seminar from 1949 and stayed for two decades, becoming the seminar's most important American product. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Israel Kirzner put one human activity at the very center of the Austrian school in a book of 1973, calling it the real wellspring of profit and of economic progress. He had studied under Ludwig von Mises at New York University in the 1950s. Which activity did he put at the center?
answer: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
choices: Entrepreneurship as alertness to opportunity
Consumption as revealed preference
Saving as time preference
Central planning as knowledge aggregation
context: Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973) put alertness to unnoticed opportunities in disequilibrium at the center of Austrian microeconomics. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: Henry Hazlitt, a journalist, squeezed economics into one rule in a short book of 1946, written in the spirit of Bastiat, and it sold strongly for decades. What is the one lesson of Economics in One Lesson?
answer: Look at all the effects on all the people, not just the visible ones now
choices: Look at all the effects on all the people, not just the visible ones now
Judge a policy by the good intentions of the people behind it
Count only the jobs created, since jobs are what matter most
Let prices alone decide, and never let the government act at all
context: Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (Harper, 1946) grew out of Bastiat's essay on what is seen and what is not seen, as Hazlitt acknowledged, and it has stayed in print ever since. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Hazlitt.

question: George Reisman, a graduate of Mises's New York seminar, published Capitalism in 1996, a book of more than a thousand pages. In it he set out to weld Mises's economics to the philosophy of one famous novelist into a single vast system. Whose philosophy was it?
answer: Ayn Rand's
choices: Ayn Rand's
Leo Tolstoy's
Albert Camus's
Jean-Paul Sartre's
context: George Reisman (born 1937) came through Mises's New York seminar and wrote Capitalism: A Treatise on Economics (Jameson Books, 1996), an attempt to join Austrian economics to Ayn Rand's Objectivism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/George_Reisman.

question: Ludwig von Mises took a professorship in Geneva in 1934, and there, as in Vienna before and New York after, he warned against governments free to print new money at will. What did he say such printing does?
answer: Prices go up and people's savings lose value
choices: Prices go up and people's savings lose value
Everyone grows richer as more money circulates
Prices fall as shops compete for the new cash
Factories run out of workers to hire
context: Mises accepted a professorship at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva, Switzerland in 1934. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Gestapo agents searched Ludwig von Mises's empty Vienna flat after Nazi Germany swallowed Austria in 1938, and they hauled his private papers away to Berlin. Soviet troops seized the papers when the war ended and shipped them on, to sit hidden in an archive for some fifty years. Where did the papers end up?
answer: Moscow
choices: Moscow
Prague
Warsaw
Leningrad
context: The papers sat in a secret Moscow archive for about fifty years. In October 1996 the economist Richard Ebeling, then teaching at Hillsdale College, reached them and brought back photocopies of almost the whole collection, some ten thousand pages by his own count, for Hillsdale. Source: fee.org (Ebeling, 'Mission to Moscow: The Mystery of the Lost Papers of Ludwig von Mises').

question: Ludwig von Mises found safety in America in 1940, but not a job: no major American university offered him a paid post, and he had to start over in New York with almost nothing. Why, in most accounts, did the leading economics departments keep him at arm's length?
answer: His views clashed with the Keynesian consensus of the day
choices: His views clashed with the Keynesian consensus of the day
He would lecture only in German, never in English
He refused any post outside New York City
He asked for a salary above any American professor's
context: Mises held an unpaid visiting professorship at NYU from 1945 until 1969 and ran his seminar there; private backers, the businessman Lawrence Fertig among them, paid his salary. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Margit fled Geneva with her husband, the economist Mises, in the summer of 1940, while German armies poured into France: they rode a bus through a continent at war to Portugal and took ship at Lisbon for New York. In 1976, three years after his death, she told the story in a memoir that is still the chief eyewitness account of their escape. What is it called?
answer: My Years With Ludwig von Mises
choices: My Years With Ludwig von Mises
The Vienna I Loved
A Life With an Economist
Escape from Europe
context: Margit von Mises's 1976 memoir My Years With Ludwig von Mises is the primary source for the escape and the early American years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Margit_von_Mises.

question: Stephanie Kelton of Stony Brook University carried Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) to a wide public in 2020 with her best seller The Deficit Myth. Her critics answered that the theory plays down one danger. What do they say it misses?
answer: Printing extra money causes inflation, which hurts savers and the poor
choices: Printing extra money causes inflation, which hurts savers and the poor
Printing extra money makes exports too cheap for foreign buyers
Printing extra money forces banks to raise interest rates too much
Printing extra money pushes the dollar's value up abroad
context: Kelton's The Deficit Myth: Modern Monetary Theory and the Birth of the People's Economy (PublicAffairs, 2020) reached the New York Times bestseller list. Its argument was that the traditional view of federal deficits as a constraint is a myth. Source: Grokipedia 'The Deficit Myth' (2026-09-05).

question: Warren Mosler and Stephanie Kelton made the case for Modern Monetary Theory (MMT): a government issuing its own currency, they argued, is limited neither by its tax revenue nor by the size of its debt. Only two things, in MMT's own account, hold such a government back. Which two?
answer: Inflation and real resources
choices: Inflation and real resources
Foreign lender willingness and gold reserves
Bond markets and credit ratings
Interest rates and unemployment
context: MMT says deficit financing is fine as long as excess capacity exists; taxes are for controlling inflation and redistributing resources, not for 'paying for' spending. The framing sounds new but is a modern repackaging of an old inflationist position. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020).

question: Larry Summers, a former Treasury secretary and a Democrat, went after Modern Monetary Theory in 2019 by likening it to an old target. George H. W. Bush had thrown an insult at Ronald Reagan's tax cuts in the 1980 campaign. Which insult did Summers call back?
answer: Voodoo economics
choices: Voodoo economics
Trickle-down economics
Zombie economics
Snake-oil economics
context: Summers's Washington Post op-ed of March 4, 2019, 'The left's embrace of modern monetary theory is a recipe for disaster', set MMT beside the supply-side economics George H. W. Bush had mocked as voodoo economics in 1980, and headlines reported it as Summers calling MMT voodoo economics. Summers was a Democratic economist speaking against a left-favored school. Sources: hks.harvard.edu (op-ed listing); bloomberg.com (Tom Orlik, March 11, 2019).

question: Robert Murphy, an Austrian-school economist, took aim at one claim of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT): that new money is safe while a country has unused capacity, with idle workers, empty factories and machines standing still. What objection did he and other Austrians press?
answer: No idle pool exists economy-wide, so new money bids prices up
choices: No idle pool exists economy-wide, so new money bids prices up
Idle capacity exists, but new money reaches it only after long lags
Unused capacity is too small to matter, so new money mostly gets saved
New money flows abroad first, so it lifts import prices, not output
context: The Austrian point (Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff): an economy-wide pool of unused capacity is a Keynesian fiction. Resources are always in some use, so monetary expansion bids competing uses higher, and prices adjust to absorb the excess. Source: Murphy, Contra Krugman (podcast archive 2019-2021).

question: Joe Biden put his name to the American Rescue Plan in March 2021: $1.9 trillion of new spending, funded by borrowing and by newly created money. Larry Summers, a former Treasury secretary, predicted a hard push on prices. What happened over the next two years?
answer: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
choices: The worst US price inflation in about forty years
The worst US price inflation since the Civil War
A rise that never passed 4 percent a year
A rise smaller than the one of the late 1980s
context: The American Rescue Plan Act, signed March 11 2021 at $1.9 trillion, was an MMT-adjacent bet that fiscal stimulus of that size would not overheat prices. Summers had warned publicly against it in February 2021. Source: Grokipedia 'American Rescue Plan Act of 2021' (2026-09-05).

question: A camp of economists nicknamed Team Transitory offered its own explanation as US prices climbed through 2021 and 2022, and many advocates of Modern Monetary Theory took the same line. What did the camp blame for the climb?
answer: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
choices: Supply-chain problems caused it, not the new money
Store owners across the country got greedy at the same moment
Foreign oil producers alone drove up every price
Consumers suddenly switched from spending to saving
context: MMT proponents echoed the Fed's 'transitory' framing, blaming supply chains. But the core MMT claim -- that political will, not math, was the constraint -- was falsified by exactly the mechanism its critics had predicted: prices adjusted to absorb the excess demand. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: Critics of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) looked back on the price surge of 2021 and 2022, which followed the theory's rise in the late 2010s, and drew a broad lesson about how schools of economics rise and fall. What lesson did they draw?
answer: Schools fall fastest when a live test in the real economy goes against them
choices: Schools fall fastest when a live test in the real economy goes against them
Schools fall fastest when a rival wins the argument in the journals
Schools fall fastest when a new generation of professors replaces the old
Schools fall fastest when they lose the backing of a major party
context: In the critics' telling, a year of inflation above 7 percent did what a decade of Austrian critique could not: it settled the empirical question and drained the political oxygen from the movement. Source: Grokipedia 'Modern Monetary Theory' (2026-09-05).

question: Warren Mosler, who traded bonds before he ran a hedge fund, argued in a pamphlet of the 1990s, Soft Currency Economics, that a government which prints its own currency can never run out of it. Mainstream economists accepted the narrow claim but threw out the sweeping version. Why did they throw it out?
answer: Each new bill buys less, so inflation is the real limit
choices: Each new bill buys less, so inflation is the real limit
Each new bill needs gold behind it, so gold is the real limit
Each new bill must be taxed back, so taxes are the real limit
Each new bill cheapens exports, so trade is the real limit
context: Warren Mosler's Soft Currency Economics, from the 1990s, is the founding text. The term 'MMT' itself was popularized by the Australian economist Bill Mitchell at the University of Newcastle. Source: Grokipedia 'Warren Mosler' (2026-09-05).

question: Mt Gox's customers learned in February 2014 that about 850,000 of the bitcoins they had left in its accounts were gone. The Tokyo exchange had carried the bulk of the world's Bitcoin trading. What blunt lesson did Bitcoiners draw from the loss?
answer: Coins left with someone else are only as safe as that someone
choices: Coins left with someone else are only as safe as that someone
Bitcoin's own code was broken and had to be rewritten
Exchanges must hold a government license to keep coins
Big exchanges are safest, since their size proves honesty
context: Mt Gox at its 2013 peak handled roughly 70-80 percent of global Bitcoin trading volume. The bankruptcy set the world's expectations of what could go wrong with a centralized custodian. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: A Frenchman living in Japan bought Mt Gox in 2011 from the American who had started it. The Frenchman was still running the exchange in February 2014, when about 850,000 customer bitcoins, then worth some half a billion dollars, vanished from its books. Who was he?
answer: Mark Karpeles
choices: Mark Karpeles
Craig Wright
Charlie Shrem
Ross Ulbricht
context: Karpeles had bought Mt Gox from Jed McCaleb in 2011. He was later convicted in Japan in 2019 of falsifying data (padding balance records) but acquitted of the theft charges; he received a suspended sentence. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mark_Karpel%C3%A8s.

question: Mt Gox's customers had lost about 850,000 bitcoins when the Tokyo exchange collapsed in February 2014, and a hunt for them began at once. Weeks later its staff reported finding some 200,000 of the coins. Where had those coins been sitting?
answer: In an old offline wallet nobody had checked
choices: In an old offline wallet nobody had checked
In a hacker's account that police had seized
In Mark Karpeles's own private trading account
In a rival exchange that had borrowed them
context: Mt Gox reported in a court disclosure of March 20, 2014 that it had found about 200,000 bitcoins in an old digital wallet. The trustee held the recovered coins through a decade of legal proceedings, and repayments began in July 2024. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: Jed McCaleb, an American programmer, registered Mt Gox in 2007 as a site for trading Magic: The Gathering cards, turned it over to Bitcoin trading in 2010, and sold it a year later. He kept building. Which two projects did he co-found afterward?
answer: Ripple in 2012 and Stellar in 2014
choices: Ripple in 2012 and Stellar in 2014
Ethereum in 2015 and Cardano in 2017
Binance in 2017 and FTX in 2019
Coinbase in 2012 and Kraken in 2013
context: McCaleb had sold Mt Gox by 2011. Ripple and Stellar run on ledgers kept by networks of validators that vote, not on proof-of-work mining. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jed_McCaleb.

question: The trustee named by a Tokyo court began repaying Mt Gox's creditors from the salvaged coins in 2024, a decade after the exchange collapsed. One fact eased the years of waiting for the customers who had lost their bitcoin. What was it?
answer: The recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
choices: The recovered coins were worth many times their 2014 dollar value
The Japanese government covered every creditor's loss in yen
An insurer paid each creditor the full value of his lost coins
Mark Karpeles repaid the losses from his own fortune
context: Creditors could take repayment in bitcoin, and most did, so the coins they received were worth far more than the 2014 dollar value of their losses. The custody lesson held, but so did Bitcoin's long climb. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mt._Gox.

question: Murray Rothbard walked into an economics seminar as a young man and never left its leader's school. Like his teacher he fought for a smaller state, free markets and sound money, and he became the school's most radical voice. Which school was it?
answer: The Austrian school
choices: The Austrian school
The Marxist school
The Keynesian school
The behavioral school
context: Rothbard enrolled at Columbia at sixteen in 1942 and took his doctorate there in 1956; Mises's New York seminar made him an Austrian for life. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: David Rothbard, a Jewish chemist, left Poland and made his home in an American city, where his son Murray arrived in March 1926. In which city, and which part of it, was Murray born?
answer: New York City, in the Bronx
choices: New York City, in the Bronx
Chicago, in Hyde Park
Vienna, in Leopoldstadt
Boston, in Back Bay
context: Rothbard was born in the Bronx on March 2, 1926; his father David was a chemist who had emigrated from Poland, and the family were Jewish immigrants. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard finished his doctoral thesis at Columbia University in 1956, on money and banking in the young American republic. The Panic of 1837
The Long Depression of 1873
The Panic of 1907
context: Rothbard argued the Panic of 1819 followed the credit expansion of the Second Bank of the United States, a foreshadowing of his later Austrian account of 1929. His dissertation, The Panic of 1819: Reactions and Policies, came out as a book from Columbia University Press in 1962. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard became a regular at a weekly economics seminar while he was still a graduate student, and the William Volker Fund was quietly paying its leader's salary. Which seminar did Rothbard attend?
answer: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
choices: Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at NYU
Milton Friedman's Chicago money workshop
Kenneth Arrow's Stanford theory workshop
John Kenneth Galbraith's Harvard institutional seminar
context: Mises ran the seminar at NYU until 1969, his salary paid by private backers, the William Volker Fund among them. Rothbard became his most influential American follower. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Murray Rothbard called taxation theft, and to the economics profession he was far too radical. Despite his Columbia doctorate, no leading economics faculty would hire him for twenty years. Where did he teach from 1966 to 1986?
answer: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute, an engineering school in New York
choices: Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute, an engineering school in New York
Grove City College, a small Christian college in Pennsylvania
Auburn University, a large state university in Alabama
George Mason University, a state university in Virginia
context: Rothbard taught part-time at Brooklyn Poly from 1966 to 1986, an engineering-school post, while he wrote For a New Liberty (1973) and the four volumes of Conceived in Liberty. Grove City housed Hans Sennholz; George Mason built its Austrian program later; Auburn is where the Mises Institute would later be based, but Rothbard never taught for Auburn University itself. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard took up a named professorship of economics in 1986, after a career the economics profession had kept at arm's length, and kept it until his death from a heart attack in January 1995. Which chair, at which university, did he take?
answer: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
choices: S.J. Hall Distinguished Professor of Economics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas
Ludwig von Mises Chair in Economics at Grove City College
F.A. Hayek Chair in Political Economy at George Mason University
Adam Smith Chair in Free Enterprise at Auburn University
context: UNLV hired Rothbard in 1986 into the S.J. Hall chair, and he taught there until his death from a heart attack in January 1995. Source: Wikipedia, Murray Rothbard.

question: Murray Rothbard traced the American colonies from their earliest settlers to the war with Britain in four volumes that came out between 1975 and 1979, his biggest work of history. A fifth, put together from his notes, followed in 2019. What is the work called?
answer: Conceived in Liberty
choices: Conceived in Liberty
The Discovery of Freedom
The American Testament
Empire of Liberty
context: Conceived in Liberty is Rothbard's four-volume libertarian retelling of American colonial history and the Revolution; a fifth volume was assembled posthumously from his notes in 2019. The Discovery of Freedom (1943) is Rose Wilder Lane. The American Testament and Empire of Liberty are titles of unrelated later works. Source: Mises Institute, 'Toward a Science of Liberty' (Salerno).

question: Ludwig von Mises published the largest book of his career so far in 1940, as Hitler's armies swept into France. He wrote it in German while teaching at a graduate institute in a neutral country. Where did it first come out, and from which publisher?
answer: Geneva, published by Editions Union
choices: Geneva, published by Editions Union
London, published by George Allen & Unwin
New York, published by Yale University Press
Vienna, published by Julius Springer
context: Mises had been at the Geneva Graduate Institute since 1934, having left Vienna. The book, in German, was 'Nationaloekonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens' ('Economics: A Theory of Action and Enterprise'). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nationalokonomie.

question: Ludwig von Mises printed a thick German treatise, Nationalökonomie, in 1940, with Europe at war. His books had been blacklisted in Nazi Germany since 1933. What became of the book?
answer: Almost no one read it, with its German-speaking market closed or small
choices: Almost no one read it, with its German-speaking market closed or small
It sold widely in Switzerland and was smuggled into Germany
It was translated into English and French within two years
It became the standard economics text in Swiss universities
context: Mises's works had been blacklisted in Nazi Germany since 1933, Europe was at war, and neutral Switzerland was too small a market for a thick German treatise, so the book found almost no readers. Source: mises.org (Nationalökonomie: Theorie des Handelns und Wirtschaftens).

question: Ludwig von Mises crossed to America in the summer of 1940, carrying the German treatise he had just published, and spent years rewriting and enlarging it in English. When did the new version appear, and under what title?
answer: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
choices: 1949; 'Human Action: A Treatise on Economics'
1945; 'The Theory of Money and Credit'
1944; 'Bureaucracy'
1957; 'Theory and History'
context: Yale University Press published Human Action in 1949. The English version was longer, more polished, and updated for the postwar American context (Keynesianism, the Cold War, the New Deal experience). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: Ludwig von Mises wrote a thick German treatise in neutral Geneva in 1940 and then, after his escape to America, brought the book out again in English through Yale University Press. A reader sets the two side by side. How are the two books related?
answer: Same ground, but the English book is longer, more polished and answers postwar debates
choices: Same ground, but the English book is longer, more polished and answers postwar debates
A word-for-word translation of the German chapters, with nothing added
The English book rejects the German one's arguments and argues the opposite
The English book is a short abridgment that cuts over half the German original
context: Nationaloekonomie is the tighter German-language original; Human Action is the mature English restatement. Scholars now read both to trace how Mises's arguments evolved between Geneva 1940 and New York 1949. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Action.

question: A freshman signed on with a college team under a century-old rule of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA): he could accept a scholarship, a room, his meals and a little stipend, but not a wage for playing. What did the NCAA call the rule?
answer: Amateurism
choices: Amateurism
Professionalism
Free agency
Salary cap
context: The National Collegiate Athletic Association, founded 1906, governed approximately 500,000 US college athletes across ~1,100 member institutions. Its amateurism rules held from founding through 2021. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association.

question: The colleges of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) all agreed through its rulebook that none of them would pay a player, though any single school might have won the top recruits with a paycheck. Economists have a blunt name for an agreement like that. What is it?
answer: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
choices: Price-fixing among employers who should be competing
Fair-share bargaining between rival workplaces
A friendly market-sharing custom
A legal minimum-wage floor
context: Roughly 1,100 nominally competing 'employers' (universities) collectively agreed to fix the price of athlete labor at zero above standardized in-kind compensation. In any other industry this would be a per-se Sherman Section 1 violation. Source: Zimbalist, Unpaid Professionals (Princeton 1999).

question: Ed O'Bannon, who had starred in basketball for the University of California, Los Angeles, sat in a friend's living room and saw his own face and jersey number in a college basketball video game. Millions of copies had sold, and he had never seen a penny of it. He sued. What did his case rest on?
answer: People own their name and likeness, so a seller of them owes payment
choices: People own their name and likeness, so a seller of them owes payment
A college owns a player's likeness only while he is enrolled
Game makers must ask the NCAA before showing any real team
A player's likeness belongs to whoever films his games
context: O'Bannon v. NCAA (Ninth Circuit, August 8, 2015, upholding partial 2014 district-court ruling by Judge Claudia Wilken). Wilken held NCAA amateurism rules violated Sherman Section 1 as an unreasonable restraint of trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%27Bannon_v._NCAA.

question: A college basketball player signed his first paid deal for his name, image and likeness (NIL) on July 1, 2021, the day athletes became free to make such deals. Within three years NIL deals topped a billion dollars a year. How has the change tended to affect how long top players stay in college?
answer: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
choices: Some stay longer because they can earn real money without turning pro
Most leave sooner, using their NIL fame to go pro early
Nothing has changed, since NIL money is too small to matter
Most must leave, since NIL deals end college eligibility
context: NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) compensation became legal for college athletes on July 1, 2021. Within three years the NIL market was estimated at over $1 billion annually flowing to athletes from endorsement deals. Source: ncaa.org (NIL policy history).

question: The regents of the University of Oklahoma took the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) to the Supreme Court, and in 1984 the Court let each college sell the right to broadcast its own football games. Until then the NCAA had picked which games were televised and how many. What happened after the ruling?
answer: Many more games aired, and television money soared
choices: Many more games aired, and television money soared
Almost no games aired, because schools could not organize alone
The same number aired at the same prices — nothing changed
Fans lost interest and stopped watching college football
context: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, 468 US 85 (1984), held that NCAA control over member schools' television contracts violated Sherman Section 1. It was an earlier stage of the same antitrust unwinding. Source: supremecourt.gov (468 US 85).

question: An economist in the public-choice tradition looks back on the no-pay rule of the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which kept the pay of even a star player at nothing for about a century. He draws a lesson for any industry that keeps a key input priced well under its market value, whether by law or by custom. What does he expect of the rule keeping that price low?
answer: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
choices: The legal or cultural rule holding the low price in place will eventually break
The rule will hold for good, since the buyers who gain from it organize
The buyers will raise the price by choice once shortages bite
The government will step in and set a fair price by statute
context: The amateurism-as-noble-tradition framing was a cultural prop for the price-fixing structure. Once courts began applying standard antitrust analysis, the prop eroded and the cartel collapsed within about a decade. Source: Zimbalist (1999); Alston (2021); House settlement (2025).

question: Assar Lindbeck, who stood on Sweden's democratic left, wrote in 1971 that one housing policy seemed the most efficient way known to destroy a city, except for bombing it. Which policy did he mean?
answer: Rent control
choices: Rent control
Public-housing high-rises
Zoning height limits
Property taxes
context: Assar Lindbeck, The Political Economy of the New Left (1971): 'In many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city—except for bombing.' Lindbeck was a Social Democrat until he left the party in 1982 and later chaired the committee for the economics Nobel, so his line is cited across the political spectrum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assar_Lindbeck.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to weigh every policy by what is seen and what is not. Turned on New York's rent control, his test finds the seen on a lucky tenant's lease: the low rent printed there. What does it find in the unseen?
answer: Apartments never built, repairs put off, units kept off the market
choices: Apartments never built, repairs put off, units kept off the market
New towers rising as builders compete for rent-capped tenants
Lower rents spreading to the uncontrolled apartments nearby
Bigger landlord profits from tenants who never move out
context: Bastiat's method: the visible benefit was to the specific rent-regulated tenant; the hidden cost was future tenants who could not find apartments, current tenants of deteriorating buildings, and landlords who warehoused units. Source: bastiat.org, mercatus.org.

question: Block after block of the South Bronx went up in flames in the 1970s, and critics blamed New York's rent laws for the fires. What connection did they draw?
answer: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
choices: The incentive to burn a rent-controlled building for the insurance
The lack of fire-code enforcement in regulated buildings
The crowding of extra boarders into cheap regulated flats
The greater density of gas heaters in old apartments
context: In the critics' account, a controlled building that could not cover its mortgage and upkeep became a liability, and an insurance payout on a total loss could be worth more than the building itself. They point to the South Bronx arson wave of the 1970s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx.

question: New York tightened its rent rules again in 2019 with the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act: smaller rent increases, more apartments kept under regulation, evictions harder to win. Two years on, the law's critics said they could measure its effects. What were they?
answer: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
choices: More warehoused units and less new rental construction
Rising landlord investment in maintenance
Faster tenant turnover across boroughs
Reduced construction permit backlogs
context: Critics of the 2019 law, the landlords' Rent Stabilization Association among them, reported regulated units held off the market ('warehoused') rather than renovated for capped rents, and a drop in new rental construction. Source: Rent Stabilization Association analyses 2020-22.

question: A New York landlord collects a capped rent that sits below what his building costs to keep up. Critics of rent control have told the same incentive story about landlords like him for generations, from New York to San Francisco. What does the story say?
answer: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
choices: Landlords with rent below cost have no reason to maintain, expand, or add supply
Landlords with rent below cost invest more heavily in improvements
Landlords with rent below cost lower quality but expand supply
Landlords with rent below cost mostly exit but new entrants rush in
context: The core incentive story: if rent is below what maintenance and construction cost require, the rational landlord defers maintenance, warehouses units, converts to condos, or exits. Future tenants pay the invisible cost. Source: Friedman-Stigler, Roofs or Ceilings? (1946).

question: Nick Szabo coined a term in the mid-1990s for a deal written in computer code that enforces itself: a tenant pays and the digital lock clicks open, misses a payment and it shuts, and no lawyer or judge is needed. What did he call such a deal?
answer: A smart contract
choices: A smart contract
A legal loan
A digital receipt
A payment plan
context: Nick Szabo coined the term smart contract in essays of the mid-1990s. Vitalik Buterin later built Ethereum (2015) around smart contracts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: Nick Szabo sketched bit gold in 1998, a digital money a decade ahead of Bitcoin. Dollars and yen multiply at a central bank's say-so, but one trait of bit gold mattered to him more than any other. Which trait was it?
answer: Its supply grows only as fast as fixed puzzle difficulty allows
choices: Its supply grows only as fast as fixed puzzle difficulty allows
Its payments settle instantly, with no waiting at any point
Its transfers can be recalled within a set window if mistaken
Its tokens can be printed as notes to hold in the hand
context: Szabo argues bit gold's supply is governed by puzzle difficulty, not by any issuer's discretion; fiat has always been discretionary. Instant settlement, reversibility, and physical notes are properties the essay does not claim as the differentiator. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto, whoever he was, put a mechanism into his Bitcoin white paper of 2008 that bit gold, Nick Szabo's design of 1998, had lacked, and Bitcoin ran where bit gold was never even built. Which mechanism did Satoshi add?
answer: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
choices: the longest-chain rule combined with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker for competing histories
the blind-signature bank issuance model that Chaum's DigiCash had introduced in 1989
the reusable-proof-of-work token exchange model that Hal Finney had built in 2004
the ring-signature transaction hider that later cryptocurrencies would adopt for privacy
context: Satoshi's longest-chain rule with proof-of-work as the tiebreaker specifically resolves the consensus problem bit gold left open. Blind signatures (Chaum) required a bank; RPOW (Finney) required a central server; ring signatures came later and hide senders, not resolve ordering. Source: Nakamoto 2008 sec 4.

question: A reporter puts the question to Nick Szabo once more: did he create Bitcoin under a pen name? Journalists and researchers point to Szabo's early bit gold design, the way he writes and his lifelong work on digital money. What has Szabo said in public when asked?
answer: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
choices: he has consistently denied being Satoshi Nakamoto
he has quietly confirmed the identification in later interviews
he has told journalists he cannot remember
he has been legally prohibited from discussing it
context: Szabo has denied the Satoshi identification publicly on multiple occasions. There has been no confirmation, memory-loss claim, or legal gag reported. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Szabo.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto ended his 2008 white paper with a short list of the earlier work it drew on, Adam Back's Hashcash and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping among them. One cypherpunk design of 1998, widely counted as Bitcoin's nearest forerunner, is nowhere in it. Which design is missing?
answer: Nick Szabo's bit gold
choices: Nick Szabo's bit gold
Wei Dai's b-money
Adam Back's Hashcash
Haber and Stornetta's timestamping
context: Satoshi's white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money (Ref 1), Adam Back's Hashcash (Ref 6), and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping papers, but does not cite bit gold directly, even though the design similarity is widely acknowledged. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Homeowners in a small California town packed with jobs turn out to vote down one more plan for new houses and apartments, while people keep moving to the area for work. What is probably happening to the price of the houses already standing?
answer: It keeps climbing, as more buyers chase the same houses
choices: It keeps climbing, as more buyers chase the same houses
It holds steady, since blocking projects leaves supply unchanged
It falls, since less building means less activity in town
It rises only if the town raises its property taxes
context: Palo Alto's median home price approached $3M in 2024 (Zillow/CoreLogic). By one local count about nine-tenths of the land it zones for housing is single-family only. Sources: paloaltoonline.com; zillow.com; paloaltoforward.nationbuilder.com/fact_check.

question: A builder who wants to put up an apartment block in Palo Alto, beside Stanford University, finds almost all of the city's residential land set aside for single-family houses. What name do housing economists give rules like these?
answer: Exclusionary zoning
choices: Exclusionary zoning
Inclusionary zoning
Mixed-use zoning
Transit-oriented zoning
context: By one local count about nine-tenths of the land Palo Alto zones for housing is single-family only, so a multi-family project needs special approvals and long hearings each time. Sources: Palo Alto Comprehensive Plan via paloaltoforward.nationbuilder.com/fact_check.

question: Edward Glaeser of Harvard and Joseph Gyourko of Wharton measured what tight building rules cost in places from San Francisco to Manhattan, where the price of a home runs far above what it would cost to build, often by six figures. They gave the gap the rules create a name. What did they call it?
answer: The zoning tax
choices: The zoning tax
The rent premium
The permitting spread
The metro markup
context: Glaeser + Gyourko, 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' (NBER Working Paper 8835, 2002) and follow-up work estimate the zoning tax at 30-60% in Bay Area cities. The wedge is a pure transfer from would-be residents to existing homeowners. Source: nber.org (Glaeser-Gyourko 2002).

question: A Palo Alto homeowner watches his house climb in value again, because the zoning lets nothing new go up next door. By Mancur Olson's account of how interest groups organize, his gain is big, visible and concentrated, and the cost is thinly spread among people nobody sees. Who are those hidden losers?
