answer: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
choices: What reason is there to believe the actual politicians and bureaucrats will do better?
What percentage of GDP will the new agency consume?
Which political party currently controls the executive branch?
How much did the market failure cost in dollar terms?
context: The public-choice discipline: never compare a REAL failure to an IDEALIZED alternative. Given the actual incentive structure facing the people who would design and administer the fix, is there reason to expect improvement? Often the answer is no. Source: Buchanan, 'Politics Without Romance' (1979).

question: A convoy of armed galleons gathered at Havana, its holds packed with the king's silver in bars and in coins, and set out across the Atlantic for Seville with English raiders on its trail. Such convoys sailed twice a year. What do historians call them?
answer: The Spanish treasure fleets
choices: The Spanish treasure fleets
The Portuguese caravels
The Hansa cogs
The English East Indiamen
context: The Flota de Indias sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana and then across the Atlantic, carrying the world's largest sustained cross-oceanic flow of precious metal. Source: Grokipedia 'Spanish treasure fleet' (2026-09-05).

question: Spain's king took in silver bars at Seville by the shipload, and by modern estimates prices across Europe rose roughly five or six times over between 1500 and 1650, keeping pace with the American silver. What lesson about money does this teach?
answer: When the supply of money grows much faster than goods, prices rise
choices: When the supply of money grows much faster than goods, prices rise
When a country gains more silver, its people grow richer in goods
When money is made of real silver, its value cannot fall
When merchants grow greedy, prices climb across a whole continent
context: Modern estimates put the general European price level in 1650 at roughly six times its 1500 level, with the acceleration tracking the arrival of American silver. Source: Grokipedia 'Price revolution' (2026-09-05).

question: The king of Spain saw his treasury go bankrupt yet again around 1600, while Spanish workshops closed, though no country in Europe held more silver and gold. What puzzle do economists still study in that record?
answer: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
choices: The country with the most silver was becoming poorer, not richer
The country with the most silver could not defend its ships
The country with the most silver refused to trade with its colonies
The country with the most silver banned interest on loans
context: The bullion inflow raised prices in Spain faster than in its trading partners, so Spanish goods became uncompetitive. Real wealth flowed abroad while nominal money piled up. Source: Grokipedia 'Economic history of Spain' (2026-09-05).

question: Martín de Azpilcueta wrote about silver and prices in 1556, one of a circle of priests and law scholars who studied money, prices and interest two centuries ahead of Adam Smith. Most of them taught at one ancient university, and historians name the circle after it. What do historians call the group?
answer: The School of Salamanca
choices: The School of Salamanca
The Physiocrats
The Vienna Circle
The Mercantilists
context: The School of Salamanca (Azpilcueta, Luis de Molina, Domingo de Soto, Francisco de Vitoria) is now recognized by Austrian economists such as Rothbard and Huerta de Soto as a genuine predecessor to modern economics. Source: Grokipedia 'School of Salamanca' (2026-09-05).

question: Irving Fisher put an old rule into an equation in 1911: the more money there is, the less each coin buys, so prices rise as money grows and fall as it shrinks. Martín de Azpilcueta had stated it in 1556. Modern economists lean on it when they warn that a central bank printing money for government deficits only pushes prices up. What is the rule called today?
answer: The quantity theory of money
choices: The quantity theory of money
The efficient-markets hypothesis
The Phillips curve
The Ricardian equivalence
context: The quantity theory (money supply times velocity equals prices times output) was formalized by Irving Fisher in 1911, but its European roots go back to Azpilcueta and the Salamanca scholastics in the 1550s. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantity theory of money' (2026-09-05).

question: A priest at Spain's oldest university watched the price of bread in his town climb year after year in the late 1500s, as the American mines shipped tons of silver to Spain. The prices of cloth and land there kept rising too, yet Spaniards seemed no richer in food, clothing or houses. Which belief does the puzzle warn a modern reader against?
answer: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
choices: That creating more money makes a nation richer in real terms
That international trade always benefits the exporting country
That taxation is always preferable to borrowing
That war spending stimulates long-run growth
context: The Salamanca-to-Austrian line: nominal money and real wealth are different things. Printing more units of currency raises prices, redistributes purchasing power to the first receivers, and leaves the underlying productive capacity unchanged. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective (1995).

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught economists to look past what an event shows to what it hides, to the seen and the unseen. Turned on Spain's paradox around 1600, his method splits the story in two. Which pairing captures his contrast for that case?
answer: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savings debased
choices: Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish industry hollowed out and savings debased
Seen: galleons of silver arriving; Unseen: Spanish farms quietly growing more grain
Seen: Spanish prices climbing; Unseen: Spanish wages climbing even faster
Seen: royal bankruptcies; Unseen: new wealth piling up in Spanish homes
context: Bastiat's 'seen and unseen' fits the Spanish silver flood: what looked like national wealth (bullion arriving) hid the decline of domestic industry and the quiet loss of value in every Spaniard's savings, while wages lagged behind the rising prices. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850); Grokipedia 'Price revolution'.

question: A shop owner ordered closed in the 2020 lockdowns took a Paycheck Protection Program loan, forgiven if she kept her workers on the payroll. It felt like a gift, but governments sell no products and earn nothing of their own. Where did the money come from?
answer: From taxes and borrowing that future citizens will pay back
choices: From taxes and borrowing that future citizens will pay back
From fees banks paid to take part in the program
From money left over in past years' federal budgets
From a one-time tax on big corporations' profits
context: PPP was administered by the Small Business Administration through private banks. Loans were forgiven if the borrower spent them mostly on payroll within a set window. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paycheck_Protection_Program.

question: David Autor of MIT and his colleagues went through payroll records to measure what the Paycheck Protection Program achieved. The program had handed out forgivable loans to businesses that promised to keep workers on the payroll. Roughly what did taxpayers pay for each year of each job it preserved?
answer: About $170,000 to $257,000 per job
choices: About $170,000 to $257,000 per job
About $5,000 to $8,000 per job
About $20,000 to $30,000 per job
About $2 million to $3 million per job
context: Autor and nine co-authors, 'The $800 Billion Paycheck Protection Program: Where Did the Money Go and Why Did It Go There?', NBER Working Paper 29669 (2022), later in the Journal of Economic Perspectives. The figure came out far higher than the yearly pay of the workers whose jobs were kept. Source: nber.org/papers/w29669.

question: Economists led by MIT's David Autor traced where the Paycheck Protection Program's money ended up, the forgivable loans paid to businesses that kept workers on the payroll. What share did they report went to workers whose jobs the program had actually saved?
answer: Between a quarter and a third
choices: Between a quarter and a third
Between a half and two-thirds
Between two-thirds and three-quarters
Between nine-tenths and all of it
context: The rest went to business owners, shareholders, creditors and suppliers of the firms that took the loans, most of which would not have laid workers off anyway. Autor and co-authors, NBER Working Paper 29669 (2022), later in the Journal of Economic Perspectives. Source: nber.org/papers/w29669.

question: A country store applied for a Paycheck Protection Program loan in April 2020 and came away empty-handed in the first round, while a big bank's well-connected clients were paid within days. Many minority-owned firms missed out too. Which idea does the rollout illustrate?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem of who truly needed relief
choices: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem of who truly needed relief
Milton Friedman's monetary theory that inflation is a purely monetary phenomenon
John Kenneth Galbraith's conventional-wisdom theory of institutional inertia
John Maynard Keynes's animal-spirits theory of investment
context: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' argued that the specific knowledge of who needs help, at what price, and in what shape is dispersed across millions of local actors and irreducible to any central authority. PPP defaulted to whoever had a bank relationship because the agency had no other way to allocate the money at speed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: A congressman defends the Paycheck Protection Program by pointing to the millions of business owners handed forgivable loans. A critic in Frédéric Bastiat's tradition agrees those visible winners were real, then points to a hidden cost. Which hidden cost does the critic press?
answer: Debt run up paying firms whose workers would have kept their jobs anyway
choices: Debt run up paying firms whose workers would have kept their jobs anyway
Tax revenue lost when small businesses closed during the lockdowns
Stock that spoiled on shelves while the shops stood closed
Workers who stayed home because benefits paid more than their jobs
context: Applied Bastiat: the preserved payroll is seen; the unseen is the taxpayer debt that paid firms whose workers would have stayed on anyway. Autor and co-authors found that only 23 to 34 percent of PPP dollars reached workers who would otherwise have lost their jobs. Source: nber.org/papers/w29669.

question: Alfred Espinas, a French sociologist, coined a word in 1890 that Ludwig von Mises took up in the 1940s as the name for his science of human choice, the starting point of all economic reasoning in his view. What was the word?
answer: Praxeology
choices: Praxeology
Behaviorism
Utilitarianism
Positivism
context: Praxeology (praxis + -logia) was coined in its modern sense by the French sociologist Alfred Espinas in an 1890 essay in the Revue Philosophique. Mises adopted it in the 1940s for the science that starts from human action as its single axiom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: A baker takes a shopper's dollar and hands over a warm loaf. Both leave pleased, and neither is forced to trade. Carl Menger and the Austrians after him have taught with scenes like this since the 1870s. What does this one show about the trade?
answer: Each values what he gets more than what he gives up
choices: Each values what he gets more than what he gives up
The loaf and the dollar are of exactly equal value
The shopper pays what the loaf cost the baker to make
One of them gains exactly as much as the other loses
context: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics was published by Yale University Press in September 1949. It rebuilt Mises's German-language Nationaloekonomie (1940) for an American audience and defined praxeology as the general theory of action, with economics as its most developed branch. Source: Grokipedia, 'Human Action'.

question: Ludwig von Mises built the whole of economics on one undeniable fact about people. Even a man who tries to deny it, Mises said, proves it in the trying. What is that fact?
answer: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
choices: Human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to attain preferred ends
Every good has a market price equal to its cost of production
The general price level moves in proportion to the money supply
Individuals choose the option that maximizes measurable utility
context: This is the action axiom. Mises treated it as apodictic: the very effort to argue against it is a means-and-ends act, so the axiom cannot be coherently rejected. From it he deduced the whole cascade of Austrian economics. Source: Grokipedia, 'action axiom'.

question: Milton Friedman published an essay in 1953 on how economists should judge a theory: by how well it predicts, not by whether its assumptions look realistic. The essay shaped the whole Chicago school. What was it called?
answer: The Methodology of Positive Economics
choices: The Methodology of Positive Economics
A Monetary History of the United States
Capitalism and Freedom
Free to Choose
context: Friedman's 1953 essay is often called the most influential piece of methodological writing in twentieth-century economics. It set out the positivist alternative to praxeology: economics as an empirical predictive science whose theorems stand or fall by out-of-sample data, not deduction. Source: Western Sydney University, 'Friedman 1953: The Methodology of Positive Economics'.

question: A critic says that no one can test the Austrian school's claims the way physicists test theirs. Ludwig von Mises has a stock reply, which he gave in Human Action and repeated in Theory and History. Which comparison does Mises press?
answer: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- no cause can be varied with all else held fixed
choices: Human action is not laboratory chemistry -- no cause can be varied with all else held fixed
Economics is not astronomy -- there are no cycles regular enough to fit an equation
Human action is not biology -- there are no species-level laws below the individual
Economics is not engineering -- there is no fixed material to be shaped
context: The point is not that historical evidence is worthless but that no economic episode is ever a controlled experiment: every other variable moves at the same time as the one under study. Mises concluded that economic laws have to be established by deduction from the action axiom, with history supplying cases the laws help interpret. Source: Wikipedia, 'Praxeology'.

question: Logic alone cannot explain history, Ludwig von Mises conceded. To explain one particular episode, he said, a historian needs a second kind of understanding as well, and he gave it a name of its own, thymology. What is that second kind mostly about?
answer: Reading the motives and choices of real people in their own time
choices: Reading the motives and choices of real people in their own time
Measuring how prices and output moved in the record
Finding laws of history that hold true in every age
Testing theories by how well they predict the data
context: Thymology (from Greek 'thymos', the seat of feeling) is for Mises a historical branch of the sciences of human action. Praxeology says what it means to act; thymology asks why this actor, in these circumstances, chose those ends and reached for those means. Source: Wikipedia, 'Thymology'.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe wrote a book in 1988 defending the method of Ludwig von Mises and Murray Rothbard, and one claim in particular about how the Austrian school's main laws are known to be true. What was the claim?
answer: They are true by logic, once it is granted that people act on purpose
choices: They are true by logic, once it is granted that people act on purpose
They hold only after data have tested their predictions
They are rough rules of thumb drawn from past history
They are true only within one nation's culture and era
context: Hoppe's lectures at the Mises University argued that the action axiom is a synthetic a priori proposition in Kant's sense -- informative about the world but true by the structure of thought, not by empirical test. The book has been the standard defense of praxeological method for a generation of Austrian graduate students. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: The followers of Ludwig von Mises watched the Soviet system collapse as the 1980s closed. Mises had reasoned in 1920, from logic alone, that an economy run by planners, with no market prices, would have no way to calculate. How did his followers describe the collapse?
answer: As real-world confirmation of a point already proven back in 1920
choices: As real-world confirmation of a point already proven back in 1920
As the very first honest test its argument had ever received
As a total surprise its theory could not explain
As proof that the 1920 argument had been wrong all along
context: The distinction is methodological, not rhetorical. If the calculation problem is a deduced law of action under conditions of no market prices, then the USSR could no more disprove it than a falling apple could disprove gravity; the Soviet experience showed the law working, it did not test whether the law is true. Source: Mises Institute, 'Economic Science and the Austrian Method'.

question: A king orders that no loaf of bread in his realm may cost more than one gold coin. His bakers protest that flour, yeast and firewood cost them two gold coins for every loaf they bake. What happens on the town's bread shelves in the weeks that follow?
answer: Bread will soon vanish from the bakers' shelves
choices: Bread will soon vanish from the bakers' shelves
Bread will stay plentiful at the lower price
Flour will soon get cheaper to match the law
Bakers will bake extra loaves for the crowds of buyers
context: Emperor Diocletian's Edictum de Pretiis Rerum Venalium (Edict on Maximum Prices) covered over 1,200 goods and services and hundreds of occupations, with death for overcharging. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices.

question: Richard Nixon told a national television audience in August 1971 that he was freezing nearly every wage and price in the country for 90 days, a rare control in peacetime. What usually happens when a government forces prices below the level a free market would set?
answer: Shortages, because sellers won't sell as much at the fixed low price
choices: Shortages, because sellers won't sell as much at the fixed low price
Sudden gluts, because buyers refuse the fixed low price
Lower costs, as suppliers cut their own prices to match
Steady supply, as sellers accept a thinner profit
context: Nixon's August 15, 1971 broadcast (which also closed the gold window) imposed a 90-day freeze, followed by looser Phases of control that ran until April 1974. As the controls were loosened in 1973 and then lapsed, inflation surged into double digits in 1974. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: Diocletian capped prices across the Roman Empire in 301, and rulers have tried the same thing ever since, from Richard Nixon's freeze of 1971 to Berlin's rent lid of 2020. When the law pins a price below the level where supply and demand would meet, which outcomes show up?
answer: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
choices: Queuing, black markets, and reduced supply
Higher taxes, lower wages, and unemployment
Currency devaluation, inflation, and default
Trade barriers, tariffs, and retaliation
context: When the state sets a price below what buyers would pay, demand exceeds supply. The gap is filled by non-price rationing (queues), by illegal secondary markets, or by suppliers exiting entirely (landlords convert to condos, sellers hoard, farmers plant less). Source: Sowell, Basic Economics.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that a state owning every factory and field leaves its planners with no prices to show them whether steel should go into tractors or into bridges. Rent control abolishes nothing: apartments still change hands, but a legal ceiling caps the rent. On Mises's logic, how are the two cases connected?
answer: A ceiling below market breaks the local signal, as full planning breaks it economy-wide
choices: A ceiling below market breaks the local signal, as full planning breaks it economy-wide
A ceiling leaves the signal whole, since apartments still trade at some price
Only abolishing every market breaks the signal; one cap leaves it untouched
A ceiling hands planners the very knowledge that market prices hide
context: Mises's 1920 argument applied at smaller scale: whether by abolishing exchange or by capping the price, if the market-clearing signal is suppressed the allocation goes wrong. Same mechanism, different scale. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: A student opening one popular economics book meets Diocletian's price edict of 301, Richard Nixon's wage-and-price freeze of 1971 and rent-controlled cities, each told to make the same point about prices held below their market level. Which book is it?
answer: Basic Economics by Thomas Sowell
choices: Basic Economics by Thomas Sowell
Freakonomics by Steven Levitt
The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith
The Undercover Economist by Tim Harford
context: Sowell's Basic Economics (first edition 2000; multiple later editions) is the standard introductory exposition that runs the price-control-produces-shortage argument across centuries of cases. Source: tsowell.com.

question: Four young men hired freezer trucks after Hurricane Fran blacked out Raleigh, North Carolina, in September 1996. They filled them with ice from a town with power and sold the bags for many times the pre-storm price. Police arrested them and took the truck. What did the customers waiting in line do?
answer: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
choices: Clapped and cheered as the sellers were cuffed
Blocked the police cars until the ice was freed
Emptied the truck while the officers wrote tickets
Chipped in for the sellers' bail
context: Michael Munger, who teaches political science and economics at Duke University, wrote the night up for the Library of Economics and Liberty on January 8, 2007 under the title 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' His line: 'They clapped. I can't for the life of me understand why the people would clap.' The four men had rented two freezer trucks, paid $1.70 a bag for 500 bags per truck, and chain-sawed fallen logs off the road to get in. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: A Florida hardware store owner marks up his generators one calm week, and the state's price-gouging law lets it pass. That law is not always on. Once it switches on, a price breaks it by running far above the seller's own average over the previous 30 days. What switches it on?
answer: The governor declaring a state of emergency
choices: The governor declaring a state of emergency
A hurricane making landfall inside the state
A county sheriff reporting a supply shortage
The attorney general opening an investigation
context: Florida Statute 501.160 forbids an 'unconscionable' price during a declared state of emergency, defining it as a 'gross disparity' with the average price charged in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately before the declaration. Penalties run to $1,000 per violation and up to $25,000 for violations inside a single 24-hour period. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.myfloridalegal.com/price-gouging-hotline/price-gouging-statute.

question: Friedrich Hayek asked the readers of his 1945 essay on knowledge to suppose that tin has suddenly grown scarce. Tens of thousands of people who use it must now make do with less, and Hayek's whole argument turns on what they have to be told first. What did he say they need to know?
answer: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
choices: Nothing beyond the new price they now face
Which mine closed or which war caused it
How long the shortage is expected to last
Which uses of tin the state ranks highest
context: Hayek's marvel was that 'without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' He added that it does not matter which cause made tin scarcer, and called the price system 'a system of telecommunications' whose users watch a few pointers as an engineer watches dials. Sources: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html ; https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/hayek-the-use-of-knowledge-in-society-1945.

question: Michael Munger wrote up the Raleigh ice arrests after Hurricane Fran in a 2007 essay, under a two-word title with a question beneath it. That question carries the argument of the whole essay. What did the subtitle ask?
answer: Can price-gouging laws prohibit scarcity?
choices: Can price-gouging laws prohibit scarcity?
Can a state legislate a fair price?
Does the law owe disaster victims a queue?
Should a state ration what a storm spared?
context: 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?', Library of Economics and Liberty, January 8, 2007. Munger's answer is no: a statute can forbid a price, but the ice, generators and chain saws are no less scarce for the ban. As he put it, 'all a state accomplishes by passing an anti-gouging law is to ensure that there is no ice.' Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: A state attorney general announces that any merchant who sells a generator above its pre-storm price after the hurricane will be prosecuted. The stated aim is to keep generators in reach of families who just lost everything, and the first cases are still weeks away. A critic working in Bastiat's tradition does not dispute the aim. Which cost does the critic say the announcement has already imposed?
answer: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
choices: Every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays there
The state's own emergency stockpile is drawn down faster than planned
Retailers raise prices on unrelated goods to make up the lost margin
Insurance premiums across the state rise for the following season
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' asks, after any law, what does not happen because of it. The prosecuted merchant is seen; the trucker who never loads, never drives and never arrives is not. John Shepperson's nineteen generators reached Mississippi and ended up in an impound lot; the ones that stayed in Georgia never made the news at all. Sources: Bastiat, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas (1850) (https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss.html); https://www.econlib.org/library/Columns/y2007/Mungergouging.html.

question: A critic in Friedrich Hayek's tradition looks hard at the yardstick in Florida's price-gouging law. After a storm, a price breaks that law when it runs far above the seller's own average price for the 30 days before the law switched on. What does the law quietly assume about prices?
answer: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
choices: That the pre-storm price is still the correct price after the storm
That merchants can compute their own thirty-day averages precisely
That every merchant in the state buys from the same wholesale supplier
That governors declare emergencies at the same point in every storm
context: The benchmark in Florida Statute 501.160 is the average price in the usual course of business during the 30 days immediately preceding the emergency declaration. On Hayek's account a price is a piece of information about present conditions, so freezing the benchmark at the pre-storm figure instructs the market to behave as though the storm carried no information at all. Sources: https://m.flsenate.gov/statutes/501.160 ; https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html.

question: Michael Munger once boiled his whole case against anti-gouging laws down to a single sentence, on Russ Roberts's EconTalk podcast. The sentence was about what a state has to permit if it wants a well-supplied city after a hurricane. How did Munger put it?
answer: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
choices: The only way to guarantee low prices is to allow sellers to charge high prices
The only way to protect the poor is to ration essentials by household size
The only way to stop hoarding is to cap what any single buyer may carry away
The only way to speed relief is to suspend the state's transport licensing rules
context: Munger's point is that the high price is the thing that pulls supply toward the disaster: it tells a trucker eight hundred miles away that this city is where his load is worth most, it moves the scarce stock toward the buyers who need it most, and it makes the people already holding ice or fuel stretch it. A cap removes all three at once, and the shortage the cap was meant to soften simply lasts longer. Source: https://www.econtalk.org/munger-on-price-gouging/.

question: A great copper mine floods one winter and shuts down, and copper's price shoots up. Factory owners who use the metal see the higher price and start hunting for other metals, or for ways to use less. What is the price doing for them?
answer: Carrying the news that copper has grown scarce
choices: Carrying the news that copper has grown scarce
Recording what copper costs to dig and refine
Showing that sellers have agreed to charge more
Measuring how much new money has come into the economy
context: Hayek made the point most famously in his 1945 essay The Use of Knowledge in Society, with tin as his example: a higher price tells every user to economize, though none of them needs to know why the metal grew scarce. The price carries the news in a single number. Source: Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945).

question: Cheap credit's real damage, Friedrich Hayek told his London audience in 1931, is not that prices simply rise across the board. The damage, he argued, lies in the shape of an economy's capital, which gets bent out of balance. What did he say happens to the pattern of production?
answer: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
choices: Long, roundabout capital projects are started that the underlying pool of savings cannot finish
Consumer-goods factories are shuttered as households divert spending toward government bonds
Money velocity collapses and idle cash balances swell across every stage of production
Nominal wages become sticky downward and unemployment jumps immediately in every sector
context: Artificially low interest rates falsify the natural rate of interest -- the rate at which voluntary saving would match investment demand. Firms respond as if saving were plentiful and start long-horizon capital projects that must later be abandoned. Rival accounts put the trouble in hoarded cash or in wages that will not fall, not in the shape of capital. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: Friedrich Hayek set out to show his 1931 audience production as a chain of stages: raw iron and lumber first, then factory work, then finishing, and last the goods on a shop shelf. He drew the whole chain as one simple figure, which Austrians still name after him. What shape did he draw?
answer: A triangle
choices: A triangle
A staircase
Rings, like a tree's
A rising wave
context: The Hayekian triangle: one side runs through the stages of production over time, the other measures the output of consumer goods at the end. Cheap credit, in Hayek's account, stretches the triangle into a longer, capital-heavy shape that real savings cannot sustain. Source: Mises Wiki, 'Hayekian triangle'.

question: Lionel Robbins brought Friedrich Hayek to the London School of Economics in February 1931 to lecture on booms and busts. Hayek told the story of a boom fed by artificially cheap credit and of the crash that ends it. Where in that story does the real disease lie?
answer: The boom was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
choices: The boom was the disease and the bust is the painful correction
The bust was the disease and the boom had been a healthy real expansion
Both boom and bust are neutral psychological fluctuations around a stable trend
The whole cycle is a statistical artefact with no underlying economic cause
context: This is Hayek's core diagnostic move against Keynes: the mistakes were made during the artificial boom (wrong capital projects, wrong worker locations); the bust is the market discovering the errors and reallocating resources. Stimulus that prolongs the boom prolongs the disease. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations'.

question: Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek described a central bank pushing interest rates far beneath their natural rate, fooling firms into long projects that look profitable only while credit stays cheap. Money races into factories, real estate and mines. How did they predict such a boom must end?
answer: A bust in which many of those projects fail once the cheap credit stops
choices: A bust in which many of those projects fail once the cheap credit stops
A slump in which nervous savers hoard cash and spending dries up
A gentle slowdown as firms finish their projects and growth levels off
A crash that comes only when a shock from abroad, like a war, strikes
context: In the Austrian account the bust is built into the boom: the projects were begun on credit that the public's real savings could not back, so when the cheap credit ends, many of them cannot be finished. Mises set out the credit-expansion theory in his 1912 book on money and credit; Hayek's 1931 lectures carried it to London. Source: Mises Institute, Prices and Production and Other Works.

question: Friedrich Hayek tore into a British economist's 1930 book on money with a harsh two-part review, published in the journal Economica in 1931 and 1932, and the author hit back at Hayek's own Prices and Production. Whose book had Hayek reviewed?
answer: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money
Irving Fisher's The Purchasing Power of Money
Arthur Pigou's The Economics of Welfare
Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics
context: Hayek's two-part critique of Keynes's Treatise on Money (1930) appeared in Economica in August 1931 and February 1932. Keynes's reply attacked Prices and Production rather than defending his Treatise, and in 1932 he abandoned the debate to write what became the 1936 General Theory. Fisher, Pigou, and Marshall are all real monetary or welfare theorists of the previous generation. Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: John Maynard Keynes withdrew from his quarrel with Friedrich Hayek in 1932 and spent the next four years rebuilding his ideas, and the result reached print in 1936. What was the book?
answer: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
The Economic Consequences of the Peace
A Tract on Monetary Reform
How to Pay for the War
context: The General Theory (1936) replaced the Treatise as Keynes's monetary statement and became the founding text of Keynesian macroeconomics. Keynes's earlier and later books include The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919), A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923) and How to Pay for the War (1940). Source: Mises Institute, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J.M. Keynes'.

question: One raw material suddenly runs short somewhere in the world. Within days all its users are saving it, though nobody has ordered them to and only a handful know why. Friedrich Hayek built his 1945 essay's central story on such a scene. Which raw material did he use?
answer: Tin
choices: Tin
Wheat
Coal
Copper
context: Hayek's tin story: whether tin grows scarce because a new use appears or because a source of supply is cut off makes no difference to its users. They need only the higher price to start using less, and few of them need know the cause. Source: econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in 1945 that the facts an economy runs on sit with ordinary people at work: a mechanic and his own lathe, a shopkeeper and her regular buyers, a captain and his port. No report to headquarters could carry such knowledge in time. What phrase did Hayek use for such a person?
answer: The man on the spot
choices: The man on the spot
The invisible hand of trade
The captain of industry
The knower behind the market
context: Hayek's argument: it is the man on the spot who has the knowledge of time and place that matters; even a perfectly benevolent central board cannot substitute for him, because his knowledge is precisely the sort that cannot be written up in a report and mailed to headquarters in time. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek wrote his 1945 essay as a reply to an economist who had argued in 1936 and 1937 that the planners on a central board could 'play at markets': set prices, raise them where queues formed and cut them where goods sat unsold. Whose work was Hayek answering?
answer: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
choices: Oskar Lange, On the Economic Theory of Socialism
Abba Lerner, The Economics of Control
Maurice Dobb, Political Economy and Capitalism
Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition
context: Lange's Part I appeared in RES in October 1936, Part II in February 1937. He famously opened with an ironic tribute to Ludwig von Mises as 'the great advocatus diaboli' of socialism. Hayek's 1945 answer was that Lange had missed the point: the market's prices aggregate knowledge that was never centrally gathered, so no board can duplicate them by trial-and-error alone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar R. Lange'.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that socialism, with no market prices for its factories, its land or its machines, is left without a way to do one thing. Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem sits on the far side of the same coin. What did Mises say socialism cannot do without those prices?
answer: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
choices: Compare the costs of alternative production plans
Reward its most productive workers fairly
Enforce contracts among cooperating enterprises
Distribute consumer goods on a per capita basis
context: Mises's 1920 essay Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen argued that without private ownership of the means of production there is no exchange of them, so no prices, so no way to compare the cost of one plan with another. Hayek added that even trial-and-error prices would still lack the dispersed knowledge real prices gather. Source: Mises Institute, 'The End of Socialism and the Calculation Debate Revisited'.

question: Friedrich Hayek took the 1974 Nobel Prize for economics, and the announcement surprised people, though not because of him. Socialists and libertarians alike were startled, and the reason lay with the man who shared the prize. What was odd about Hayek's co-winner?
answer: The co-winner held nearly opposite views on central planning
choices: The co-winner held nearly opposite views on central planning
The co-winner was Hayek's own former student at the LSE
The co-winner had once served as a Soviet economic adviser
The co-winner was a physicist rather than an economist
context: The joint citation honoured 'pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations' and 'penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena'. Myrdal was a leading Swedish social-democratic thinker. Source: NobelPrize.org, 'The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1974'.

question: A driver in 1979 sat in a gas line that stretched around the block, allowed to fill up only on odd days because his license plate ended in an odd digit. In Friedrich Hayek's terms, what had gone wrong at the pump?
answer: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
choices: The federal ceiling on retail gasoline prices had broken the signal that would have called forth more supply
The OPEC cartel had unilaterally halted all crude oil exports to the American market
The Federal Reserve had refused to expand the money supply enough to accommodate demand
The Environmental Protection Agency had banned all leaded gasoline sales without notice
context: The Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act of 1973 kept domestic oil prices under federal ceilings through the rest of the 1970s; in 1979 several states rationed gasoline by odd and even license plates. President Reagan ended the remaining controls in January 1981 (Executive Order 12287). Sources: Institute for Energy Research, 'Price Controls and the 1970s Oil Crisis'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_oil_crisis.

question: Thomas Sowell built Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay out in 1980 into a book-length theory reaching across markets, the law, science and everyday life. Hayek called it the best book on economics he had read in many a year. What is Sowell's book called?
answer: Knowledge and Decisions
choices: Knowledge and Decisions
Basic Economics
Wealth, Poverty and Politics
A Conflict of Visions
context: Its central theme, dispersed knowledge, comes from Hayek's 1945 essay. Hayek reviewed the book for Reason in December 1981 under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'. Source: reason.com/1981/12/01/the-best-book-on-general-econo/.

question: A committee of officials meets in Washington, as it does eight times a year, and sets a price that no market of buyers and sellers ever settles. Austrian economists call it an enormous, largely hidden price control, one that breaks the very signal Friedrich Hayek said prices must carry. Which price is it?
answer: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
choices: The interest rate, set below the market-clearing rate by the central bank
The retail price of gasoline, capped by the Department of Energy
The wage of federal contractors, floored by the Davis-Bacon Act
The exchange rate of the dollar, pegged by the Treasury
context: The Austrian argument, from Mises through Hayek to Rothbard: the interest rate is a price like any other -- the price of present goods in terms of future goods -- and when a central bank pushes it below the rate that would clear the loanable-funds market, it breaks the signal that would tell entrepreneurs whether long-lived projects can be sustained. This is the mechanism behind Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

question: Friedrich Hayek collected his most important essays in a single book in 1948 at the University of Chicago Press, with his 1945 essay at its center. Beside it he set Economics and Knowledge, which began life as a talk before the London Economic Club in 1936. What did he call the collection?
answer: Individualism and Economic Order
choices: Individualism and Economic Order
The Counter-Revolution of Science
Studies in Philosophy, Politics and Economics
The Constitution of Liberty
context: The 1948 volume was Hayek's own bid to fix the shape of the argument for postwar economists: 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) framed the problem, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) delivered it in a form any working economist could read in a lunch break, and the surrounding essays applied it to markets and planning. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Hayek: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)'.

question: Two kids swap lunches at recess. One brings an apple that cost a quarter; the other brings a sandwich that cost four dollars, sixteen times as much. Nobody is tricked and nobody is forced, yet both walk away smiling. How can that be?
answer: Value depends on what each person wants, not just the price tag
choices: Value depends on what each person wants, not just the price tag
The sandwich child is giving away value out of kindness
The apple and the sandwich are really worth the same amount
The sandwich had gone stale, so it was worth far less by noon
context: Menger (1840-1921) reported on grain and stock prices for the Lemberger Zeitung and then the Wiener Zeitung in the 1860s -- watching real traders form prices in real time is where his subjective-value instinct came from. He joined the University of Vienna law faculty in 1872 and won the economic-theory chair in 1873. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: A Vienna economist, Carl Menger, threw out an old theory of value in 1871, in a slim book called Principles of Economics. Smith, Ricardo and Marx had each held some form of it, and Menger did not patch it up; he put a theory of his own in its place. What is Menger's theory called?
answer: The subjective theory of value
choices: The subjective theory of value
The labor theory of value
The quantity theory of money
The comparative advantage argument
context: Menger's move was not to REFINE the labor theory but to REPLACE it. Adam Smith, David Ricardo, and Karl Marx all held labor-embodied theories in some form; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced them with subjective valuation. The quantity theory of money (Hume, Fisher, Friedman) explains price levels; comparative advantage (Ricardo 1817) explains trade -- neither is what Menger contributes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: Carl Menger reasoned at the margin in his Principles of Economics of 1871 but never gave the idea a single name. One of his followers supplied the German word more than a decade later: Grenznutzen, marginal utility. Who was the follower?
answer: Friedrich von Wieser
choices: Friedrich von Wieser
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Ludwig von Mises
Leon Walras
context: Wieser (1851-1926), with Boehm-Bawerk one of Menger's two most important followers, coined Grenznutzen to name a concept Menger had already set out in prose; sources date the coinage to his books of 1884 and 1889. Boehm-Bawerk developed capital and interest theory instead, and Mises belonged to the next generation. The English 'marginal utility' is a direct translation of Wieser's German. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Carl Menger wrote his Principles of Economics in 1871 holding that economics studies human choice, not numbers. Böhm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek and Rothbard all followed him in that, while Jevons and Walras went the other way. What lasting mark did that stance leave on the Austrian school?
answer: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
choices: Arguing in prose rather than in mathematical models
Building large econometric models
Founding the discipline of experimental economics
Grounding claims in national statistical surveys
context: Menger's rejection of mathematical economics was not incidental; it was a claim about the SUBJECT -- since valuation is subjective and preferences are ordinal, false precision misleads more than it clarifies. Walras and Jevons, the co-inventors of marginalism, went the other way and built the mathematical tradition. Experimental economics (Vernon Smith, Nobel 2002) came a century later; large econometric models are Cowles Commission and Klein 1940s-60s; national statistical surveys are the German Historical School Menger's 1883 Methodenstreit book attacked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: A purpose-built mining machine runs through trillions of guesses in search of one special number. Stirred together with a new Bitcoin block's data, the right number produces a fingerprint, called a hash, that begins with a long string of zeros. What is that special number called?
answer: A nonce
choices: A nonce
A hash
A seed
A salt
context: The 'nonce' (number-used-once) is what miners search for. Trillions of guesses per second per machine try different nonces until one produces a hash below the required difficulty target. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nonce.

question: A Bitcoin miner switches on his rig, and it starts guessing: billions of guesses a second, each checked and thrown away. It has no way to work the answer out, and a bigger machine simply gets more guesses. What everyday word do Bitcoin teachers use for the race?
answer: A digital lottery
choices: A digital lottery
A digital marathon
A digital auction
A digital contract
context: Every guess is a lottery ticket; more hashing power means more tickets per second; the miner with the most tickets wins most often. First to find a valid nonce broadcasts the block and other miners immediately begin building on top of it. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: America's National Security Agency designed a hash function that the US government adopted as a standard in 2001, years before Bitcoin existed. Bitcoin borrowed it whole: every miner's guess runs the block through it, and out comes a fingerprint of exactly 64 characters. Which hash function is it?
answer: SHA-256
choices: SHA-256
SHA-3
Scrypt
Ethash
context: SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) is a member of the SHA-2 family, published by NIST in 2001. Litecoin uses Scrypt; Ethereum used Ethash before the Merge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2.

question: An attacker wants to undo a Bitcoin payment he made last week. He must secretly rebuild each block from that point on and go on adding new ones until his chain overtakes the one the honest miners are building. What share of the network's mining power must he hold to be sure of winning in the end?
answer: Just over half
choices: Just over half
Just over a third
Just over a quarter
Just over a tenth
context: The classic 51% attack: an attacker with more hashing power than the rest of the network combined can, in principle, rewrite recent history. The energy is what makes such an attack expensive; that is the security. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-spending.

question: Rows of mining machines in a warehouse burn enormous amounts of electricity day and night, racing for each new Bitcoin block. Critics call it waste. Bitcoiners answer that all that spent power is no accident of the design but its purpose. What role do they say it plays?
answer: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
choices: It is the wall that protects every dollar of value on the network
It is a byproduct of the transaction-processing bandwidth
It is a subsidy that pays for the developer-team infrastructure
It is the cooling cost of the servers that broadcast transactions
context: The economic barrier to attack is what real-world energy an attacker would have to burn to redo the work faster than the honest network. Defenders call this 'the energy IS the security.' Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Leslie Lamport and two colleagues set out a famous puzzle in 1982. Several commanders surround a city and must agree by messenger on when to attack, but a messenger may lie and a commander may be a traitor. How do the loyal ones agree on a single plan? Bitcoin gave the first working answer for strangers on an open network. What is the puzzle called?
answer: The Byzantine Generals Problem
choices: The Byzantine Generals Problem
The Two Generals Problem
The Dining Philosophers Problem
The Prisoner's Dilemma
context: Byzantine Generals (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, 1982): how do untrusted, distributed parties reach agreement on a shared record without a central authority? Nakamoto Consensus is the first known solution using proof-of-work as the coordinating mechanism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_fault.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto joined two rules together when he designed Bitcoin. Every new block must cost real work to add, and when two rival chains turn up, everyone sticks with the chain that has the most work piled behind it. Computer scientists have a name for that pairing. What is it?
answer: Nakamoto Consensus
choices: Nakamoto Consensus
Byzantine Consensus
Cascade Consensus
Deterministic Consensus
context: 'Nakamoto Consensus' is the standard name in cryptography and computer-science literature for the proof-of-work + longest-chain rule Satoshi introduced with Bitcoin. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Nakamoto_consensus.

question: An Austrian-school defender of Bitcoin hears a critic call its giant mining farms an environmental waste. Plain old money eats huge amounts of energy as well, he replies, only where nobody sees it, spread across a whole industry rather than packed into one warehouse. Which hidden costs does he list?
answer: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
choices: Bank branches, armored trucks, printing, and the entire regulatory apparatus
Gold mines, smelters, and the guarded vaults that store the bullion
Coal plants, power lines, and the grid that feeds the mining farms
Stock exchanges, trading floors, and the brokers who buy and sell shares
context: The defender's move: fiat's energy cost is spread across every branch, every armored truck, every printing plant, every ATM, every regulatory apparatus. Bitcoin makes its energy cost visible and concentrated; fiat hides its energy cost. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Somewhere in the world, a miner finds the winning number for the next Bitcoin block and broadcasts it. Once the other miners accept the block, he collects a payment in two parts: coins the Bitcoin software itself creates out of nothing, and the fees of every payment packed into the block. What is the standard name for that payment?
answer: The block reward
choices: The block reward
The transaction cascade
The mining tip
The confirmation fee
context: 'Block reward' = newly-issued coins from the current issuance schedule plus fees on the transactions the miner has included in the block. Issuance falls to zero around 2140; by then miners live on fees alone. Source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Block_reward.

question: Vitalik Buterin got his wish on September 15, 2022, when Ethereum dropped Bitcoin-style mining in the Merge. Its block-makers now pledge coins of their own as collateral, and a cheat forfeits his. What is the new method called?
answer: Proof of stake
choices: Proof of stake
Proof of work
Proof of authority
Proof of burn
context: The Ethereum Foundation's post-Merge figure is a roughly 99.95% cut in network electricity use. That is the strongest engineering argument PoS supporters make for the switch. Source: ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption. Vitalik Buterin published the Ethereum white paper in late 2013 and has argued for proof-of-stake since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The Merge was the culmination of an eight-year design goal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalik_Buterin.

question: Bitcoin's defenders took aim at proof-of-stake, the method Ethereum adopted in 2022. Under it, validators add blocks by putting up coins they already own as collateral. The defenders say it brings back a feature of the old banking world that proof-of-work was built to break. Which feature do they mean?
answer: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
choices: Concentration of power in the hands of existing token holders
Requirement of a central government treasury for issuance
Dependence on trusted third-party settlement rails
Delegation of block production to a small licensed authority
context: The Bitcoin-community argument: those who start with the most tokens have the most power to add blocks, entrench their position and shape network rules, with no outside check like the electricity a proof-of-work miner must burn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake.

question: A Bitcoin miner switches on his rigs and races for the next block, burning real electricity as he goes. Bitcoiners see a weakness in an Ethereum validator, who adds blocks by signing them with coins he has put up as collateral. They call it the nothing-at-stake problem. What do they say a validator can do?
answer: Sign several competing chains at once, at no real cost
choices: Sign several competing chains at once, at no real cost
Earn block rewards without ever going online to sign
Pull out his collateral before his signatures are recorded
Vote by his trading volume instead of his staked balance
context: Under PoW a miner can only mine one chain at a time (electricity is a real resource). Under naive PoS a validator can sign every fork simultaneously; the defense requires trusted checkpoints or slashing penalties that add complexity and trust assumptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_stake#Attacks.

question: Gary Gensler argued in September 2022 that a great many proof-of-stake tokens could legally count as investment contracts, judged by a test the Supreme Court set in 1946 in the Howey case. Such a label would bring heavy US registration rules, and his remarks worried the whole crypto industry. Which agency did Gensler then chair?
answer: The Securities and Exchange Commission
choices: The Securities and Exchange Commission
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
The Federal Trade Commission
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority
context: Gensler, chair of the SEC from 2021 to January 2025, made the remarks on September 15, 2022, the day of Ethereum's Merge, calling staking rewards another sign that holders expect profits from the efforts of others. Sources: kitco.com (September 16, 2022); cointelegraph.com, 'Ether staking could trigger securities laws: Gensler'.

question: Bitcoiners stayed with proof-of-work when Ethereum dropped it in September 2022, power bill and all. Bitcoin has run on it since 2009, and Bitcoiners call the bill a feature, not a flaw. What kind of feature do they say it is?
answer: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
choices: An external, real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality
A regulatory-compliance cost that satisfies environmental disclosure rules
A liquidity provision that reduces short-run mining-fee volatility
A payment to network engineers who maintain node infrastructure
context: The Bitcoiners' defense: the electricity is what makes Bitcoin's security depend on something outside the network's own token economics, while proof-of-stake keeps its costs inside the system and rests on incentives among token holders. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_work.

question: Ethereum's validators took over from its miners in September 2022, while Bitcoin kept its miners, and two great networks were left guarded in opposite ways: one by staked coins, the other by burned electricity. Neither side's argument can settle on paper which of the two bets was right. What will decide it?
answer: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
choices: Whether either network survives multiple decades of live attacks and stress tests
Whether central banks issue their own digital currencies competing with both
Whether the SEC issues a definitive ruling on token classification
Whether major derivative exchanges list futures on both consensus mechanisms
context: A verdict on proof-of-work versus proof-of-stake security will take decades of live operation through real attacks, market crashes and regulatory pressure. Bitcoin has run on proof-of-work since January 2009; Ethereum's proof-of-stake only since September 2022.

question: Miners of two older coins kept at work after Ethereum's Merge of September 2022; both coins descend from Bitcoin's code and still run on proof-of-work. One came out in 2011 billed as silver to Bitcoin's gold; the other began in 2013 as a joke coin with a Shiba Inu mascot. Which pair are they?
answer: Litecoin and Dogecoin
choices: Litecoin and Dogecoin
Cardano and Solana
Polkadot and Avalanche
Tron and EOS
context: Litecoin (2011, Charlie Lee) and Dogecoin (2013, Billy Markus & Jackson Palmer) are Scrypt-based PoW coins descended from Bitcoin's codebase. Cardano, Solana, Polkadot, and Avalanche all use PoS variants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litecoin.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock led a band of economists in the 1960s who would not split the world in two, with self-seeking shopkeepers in the market and selfless servants in government. Officials want things just as shopkeepers do, they said: reelection, bigger budgets, better jobs. What is their school called?
answer: Public choice
choices: Public choice
Public finance
Monetary policy
Central planning
context: Tullock, a lawyer by training, was one of the founders of public choice theory alongside James Buchanan. Buchanan would later win the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics for the field's development. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Gordon Tullock, trained as a lawyer, started a journal in 1966 under a first title that was long and clumsy. A few years later it took a short two-word name that soon stood for the entire field. What was the original title?
answer: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
choices: 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making'
'Studies in Political Economy'
'Journal of Institutional Analysis'
'Constitutional Economics Review'
context: The journal renamed itself 'Public Choice' in 1968, and the new name became the label for the whole scholarly field. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: James Buchanan brought his research center to a third university in 1983, where it still thrives; it had begun at one university and moved to a second. All three campuses lie in a single American state, the one where the movement grew up. Which state is it?
answer: Virginia
choices: Virginia
Massachusetts
California
New York
context: The center was originally at the University of Virginia, moved to Virginia Tech, and then followed Buchanan to George Mason in 1983 -- an unusual case of a research center migrating with its founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Public_Choice_(journal).

question: Two economists wrote The Calculus of Consent together in 1962 and co-founded a new school in the 1960s. Their field took the top honor in economics in 1986, and only one of the two partners received it. What was the award, and who got it?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to James Buchanan
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, to Gordon Tullock
The John Bates Clark Medal, to James Buchanan
The John Bates Clark Medal, to Gordon Tullock
context: The Nobel-adjacent prize (usually just called the Nobel Prize in Economics). Buchanan's citation credited his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for economic and political decision-making. Tullock never received the prize, an omission still noted by public-choice scholars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/James_M._Buchanan.

question: The clerks at a shoe store walk out on strike one morning. The owner loses sales, but his customers just buy their shoes down the street. Now every police officer in a city walks off the job on the same day. Who does that strike hurt the most?
answer: The regular people who need protecting
choices: The regular people who need protecting
The city's elected officials
The striking officers themselves
The businesses that sell to the police
context: Franklin D. Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, President of the National Federation of Federal Employees, on August 16, 1937. Roosevelt considered a public-sector strike 'unthinkable and intolerable.' Source: presidency.ucsb.edu (Roosevelt letter to Steward, 1937).

question: Luther Steward, a federal union chief, got a letter from Franklin Roosevelt in 1937: government workers, it said, are employed by the whole people. Public-choice economists add that across from a government union sit officials spending other people's money. Who faces a private union?
answer: A profit-maximizing private employer
choices: A profit-maximizing private employer
A voluntary industry trade association
A regulated common carrier
A cooperatively-owned enterprise
context: Roosevelt's letter said that officials could not fully represent or bind the real employer, the whole people, who speak through laws passed by Congress. In the private sector, wage demands trade off against the employer's profits and the firm's survival; in the public sector the bill goes to taxpayers, the same voters the union spends dues to influence. Source: presidency.ucsb.edu (Roosevelt letter to Steward, 1937).

question: Franklin Roosevelt, a hero to the labor movement, set down his view of bargaining by government workers in 1937. By 2010 unions were more than four times as common in government jobs as in private ones. What was Roosevelt's view of collective bargaining in government service?
answer: He opposed it
choices: He opposed it
He championed it
He was neutral
He never addressed it
context: In 2010, public-sector union density was ~36% while private-sector density had fallen to ~7%. The gap reflects both public-sector expansion after Kennedy's Executive Order 10988 (1962) and long-running private-sector decline. Source: bls.gov (union-membership historical series).

question: Scott Walker, Wisconsin's new governor, pushed a law called Act 10 through the state legislature in 2011. Among other things it changed how public workers' money reached the union, and it forced every union to face a fresh vote of its members each year. What kind of change did Act 10 make?
answer: Making union dues voluntary instead of automatic
choices: Making union dues voluntary instead of automatic
Capping union dues at a fixed share of pay
Routing union dues through the state treasury
Charging non-members a fee in place of dues
context: Scott Walker's Act 10 passed in March 2011 after weeks of massive protest at the state capitol and a Democratic-senator walkout to Illinois to deny quorum. The Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the law in July 2014. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Wisconsin_Act_10.

question: Fourteen Democratic state senators fled Wisconsin for Illinois in early 2011 and hid in hotels across the state line. Scott Walker, the new governor, was pushing a bill called Act 10 that would sharply limit bargaining by most public-sector unions. What was the walkout meant to do?
answer: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
choices: To deny the Wisconsin Senate the quorum needed to pass Act 10
To lobby the federal Department of Labor for intervention
To organize with unions on the Illinois-Wisconsin border
To evade personal fines imposed by Walker
context: The Wisconsin state constitution required a quorum for fiscal legislation. Democratic senators crossed the state line to make that quorum unreachable, delaying but not ultimately preventing passage. Source: madison.com and wisconsinwatch.org (2011 protest coverage).

question: A Wisconsin teacher opened her paycheck after Act 10 took effect and found no union dues taken out; paying them had become her own choice, made each year. Within a few years the Wisconsin Education Association Council, Wisconsin's largest teachers' union, had lost most of its dues-paying members. What did the drop suggest about many of them?
answer: Many were paying only because the dues had been taken automatically
choices: Many were paying only because the dues had been taken automatically
Many had joined a rival union that charged lower dues
Many had left Wisconsin's schools for jobs in other states
Many had been barred from joining by the new law
context: WEAC lost the majority of its members after the end of automatic dues deduction and mandatory annual recertification votes. It is the clearest measured effect of Act 10 on public-sector union density. Source: journalsentinel.com (WEAC membership coverage 2013-16).

question: An Illinois child-support specialist refused to pay the 'agency fees' a public-sector union charged him as a non-member, and he took his fight to the Supreme Court. On June 27, 2018, the justices split five to four and ruled that no public employee could be made to pay such fees, reshaping public-sector labor law across the country. What is the case called?
answer: Janus v. AFSCME
choices: Janus v. AFSCME
Abood v. Detroit Board of Education
Harris v. Quinn
Knox v. SEIU
context: Janus v. AFSCME Council 31, 585 US ___ (2018), overturned the 1977 Abood decision. Mandatory agency fees to public-sector unions violate the First Amendment because all public-sector collective bargaining is inherently political. Source: supremecourt.gov (Janus 585 US).

question: A teachers' union pours millions of dollars of its members' dues into a governor's race one autumn, and its candidate wins. Two years later the same union sits down across the bargaining table from that governor to settle a new contract. In the public-choice reading, what becomes of the idea of two independent sides at the table?
answer: It breaks down, because the union is in effect bargaining with itself
choices: It breaks down, because the union is in effect bargaining with itself
It holds, because voters can still remove the governor at the polls
It holds, because state law caps what any contract can pay
It breaks down, because the governor now holds all the power
context: Private-sector union dues cannot choose the chief executive across the bargaining table. Public-sector union dues can help choose the mayor, governor or school-board members who then negotiate, so a concentrated interest helps pick its own counterparty while the taxpayers who pay are scattered and absent. Daniel DiSalvo traces the pattern in Government Against Itself (Oxford, 2015), drawing on Mancur Olson's logic of concentrated and dispersed interests. Source: DiSalvo (2015); Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965).

question: A Federal Reserve official announced something the central bank had never tried before on November 25, 2008, as banks failed. The Fed would create $500 billion of new money to buy home-loan bonds from struggling banks, and more rounds followed. What do economists now call that first program?
answer: QE1
choices: QE1
TARP
PDCF
Operation Twist
context: QE1 was launched November 25 2008 and expanded in March 2009. It ran until June 2010 at a total commitment of about $1.75 trillion. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: A banker who sold a mortgage bond to the Federal Reserve during its first round of bond buying saw no truck of cash leave any vault to pay for it; his bank's reserve account simply showed a bigger balance. Where does the money for such a purchase come from?
answer: The central bank creates it out of thin air by typing in the new amount
choices: The central bank creates it out of thin air by typing in the new amount
Taxpayers pay for it through this year's taxes
Other banks lend it to the central bank first
The Treasury prints paper cash and ships it over
context: When the Fed buys a bond from a primary dealer, it pays with newly created reserves credited to the dealer's Fed account -- reserves that did not exist before the purchase. This is monetary base expansion at its most direct. Source: federalreservehistory.org 'Quantitative Easing'.

question: An investor checking the Federal Reserve's books in September 2008, the month Lehman Brothers failed, found its balance sheet, all the assets it held, standing near $900 billion. Then came the Fed's first round of bond buying. About how large had the balance sheet grown by the time that program was over?
answer: About $2.3 trillion
choices: About $2.3 trillion
About $1.2 trillion
About $4.5 trillion
About $1 trillion
context: The Fed's balance sheet more than doubled from about $900 billion pre-crisis to about $2.3 trillion by mid-2010. This 150%+ expansion in two years was unprecedented in peacetime. Source: federalreserve.gov (H.4.1 balance-sheet releases 2010).

question: Richard Cantillon, a banker born in Ireland who worked in Paris, saw in the early 1700s that fresh money never spreads evenly like rain but comes in at certain doors, a mine, say, or a royal treasury, and those nearest spend it first. In QE1 the Federal Reserve created its new reserves through a Fed-dealer window. Which group received them first?
answer: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
choices: Banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, and asset holders
Low-income wage earners on fixed hourly rates
Retirees living on Social Security benefits
Small-business owners in agricultural sectors
context: The new money enters at the Fed-dealer transaction. Asset prices (stocks, real estate, corporate bonds) rose sharply through 2009-10 while wages stagnated -- textbook first-receiver benefit. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Paul Krugman on his blog and Ben Bernanke, writing later in his memoirs, defended QE1 against its critics. Both pointed to one effect the program had in 2008 and 2009 that, as they told it, stopped something worse from happening. What did they credit QE1 with achieving?
answer: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
choices: Preventing depression by stabilizing MBS markets and keeping mortgage rates low
Directly funding the automobile-industry rescue
Preventing the collapse of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Immediately restoring pre-crisis wage growth
context: The defense: absent QE1, mortgage markets would have seized, rates would have spiked, and housing would have crashed further. Whether this defense holds up depends on counterfactuals nobody can run. Source: Bernanke, The Courage to Act (2015).

question: Three men warned loudest, while QE1 ran, that the Federal Reserve was creating money to cover Washington's deficits and that higher prices would follow, if not at once. One made the case on television, one at an economics institute and one in his own newsletter. Which three were they?
answer: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
choices: Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy, and Jim Grant
Paul Krugman, Joseph Stiglitz, and Ben Bernanke
Larry Summers, Robert Rubin, and Timothy Geithner
Janet Yellen, Donald Kohn, and Frederic Mishkin
context: Schiff on television, Murphy at the Mises Institute, and James Grant in Grant's Interest Rate Observer all publicly warned that the delay between monetary expansion and consumer-price adjustment did not mean the mechanism was broken. The 2021-23 wave was consistent with their long-horizon call. Source: mises.org and Grant's Interest Rate Observer archive.

question: A reader tracing the Federal Reserve's bond buying finds QE1 in 2008, then QE2 and QE3, and then a still larger round after the 2020 pandemic. Before 2008 the Fed had never bought bonds on anything like that scale. What does the pattern show about central banking today?
answer: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
choices: Central-bank balance-sheet expansion is now a standing policy tool rather than an emergency-only measure
Central banks always fully unwind emergency programs within two years
Balance-sheet expansion is neutral because commercial banks control final money creation
Central-bank asset purchases affect only bond markets and never asset prices generally
context: QE1 was framed as an emergency. QE2 (2010) and QE3 (2012) followed, and the pandemic round of 2020 more than doubled the balance sheet again, to nearly $9 trillion by 2022. Emergency practice has become standing doctrine. Source: FRED, Federal Reserve total assets (WALCL).

question: Ben Bernanke led the Federal Reserve back into the bond market on November 3, 2010, with the recovery limping. The Fed would create $600 billion and buy Treasury bonds at about $75 billion each month through June 2011. What is that round of buying called?
answer: QE2
choices: QE2
Operation Twist
TARP
TALF
context: QE2 pushed the Fed's balance sheet from about $2.3 trillion to about $2.9 trillion by mid-2011. It was the second round in what would become a multi-decade balance-sheet policy tool. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: A reader opening his newspaper on November 4, 2010, found a column by Ben Bernanke, the Federal Reserve's chairman, defending to the public the bond buying the Fed had announced the day before. Which newspaper printed it?
answer: The Washington Post
choices: The Washington Post
The Wall Street Journal
The New York Times
The Financial Times
context: Bernanke's November 4 2010 op-ed in The Washington Post was titled 'What the Fed Did and Why: Supporting the Recovery and Sustaining Price Stability.' He had written for newspapers as chairman before, among them a Wall Street Journal piece of July 2009 on the Fed's exit strategy. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative easing' (2026-09-05).

question: Ben Bernanke, the Federal Reserve's chairman, took his case for the Fed's new bond buying straight to newspaper readers in November 2010, the day after the Fed announced $600 billion of purchases. Critics fastened on one market among those he named. Which market was it?
answer: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
choices: The stock market, which he said would boost consumer wealth and spending
The currency market, which he said would make American exports cheaper
The commodity market, which he said would raise farm incomes
The auto market, which he said would help Detroit
context: Bernanke wrote: 'higher stock prices will boost consumer wealth and help increase confidence, which can also spur spending.' He also pointed to lower mortgage and corporate bond rates; critics seized on the stock-market line as an open admission that the Fed meant to lift share prices. Source: Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: A shopper who read Ben Bernanke's newspaper column in November 2010 learned what the Federal Reserve's new bond buying was meant to do: lift the value of the shares families owned, so that they would spend more at stores and restaurants. Economists have a common two-word name for that idea. What is it?
answer: The wealth effect
choices: The wealth effect
The multiplier effect
The crowding-out effect
The Balassa-Samuelson effect
context: The wealth effect is the standard economic label for higher household net worth leading to higher spending. Its invocation by Bernanke made explicit what critics had said was implicit in QE all along: the Fed was targeting asset prices. Source: Grokipedia 'Wealth effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Wolfgang Schäuble, Germany's finance minister, told Der Spiegel that the Federal Reserve's new round of bond buying in 2010, $600 billion of freshly created money, was clueless. His country had lived through hyperinflation in the 1920s. What was Schäuble most likely worried about?
answer: That printing more dollars would push up prices and shake other countries' economies
choices: That printing more dollars would push up prices and shake other countries' economies
