That the US had not printed nearly enough new money
That Germany would have to print money to catch up
That the US would lower taxes at the same time
context: Schauble, then German Finance Minister under Angela Merkel, called QE2 'clueless' in a 2010 Der Spiegel interview. He argued the program would export inflation to Europe and destabilize the emerging-market dollar bloc. Source: Grokipedia 'Wolfgang Schauble' (2026-09-05).

question: Rick Perry, governor of Texas and a candidate for the Republican nomination for president, told a crowd in Iowa in August 2011 that if the Federal Reserve printed more money between then and the 2012 election, it would be 'almost treasonous.' What was he accusing the Fed of doing?
answer: Bending its money policy to help one side win an election
choices: Bending its money policy to help one side win an election
Refusing to obey any orders from Congress
Secretly buying gold from foreign countries
Raising interest rates too fast during a recession
context: Perry made the remark at an August 15, 2011 campaign event in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, two days after announcing his run for the nomination. Source: Grokipedia 'Rick Perry' (2026-09-05).

question: An investor bought into the S&P 500, which tracks America's biggest companies, in late August 2010, when Ben Bernanke first signaled the Fed's new bond buying, and held on until the program ended in June 2011. Austrian critics pointed to Richard Cantillon: fresh money rewards whoever gets it first. What did the index do over that stretch?
answer: Rose approximately 24 percent
choices: Rose approximately 24 percent
Fell approximately 5 percent
Rose approximately 5 percent
Stayed roughly flat
context: The S&P 500 gained roughly 24% from late August 2010, when Bernanke signaled the program in his Jackson Hole speech, to the program's end in June 2011. The wealth effect Bernanke had named publicly was working as promised for those who owned shares. Source: Grokipedia 'S&P 500' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian critics turned Frédéric Bastiat's test on the Federal Reserve's bond buying of 2010, in which it spent $600 billion of newly created reserves on Treasury bonds. Bastiat taught that every policy has effects that are seen and effects that are not. Which seen-and-unseen pairing best captures that program's structure?
answer: Seen: a strengthening recovery; Unseen: new reserves flowing into asset prices, not wages or investment
choices: Seen: a strengthening recovery; Unseen: new reserves flowing into asset prices, not wages or investment
Seen: a strengthening recovery; Unseen: new reserves flowing into factories and fresh hiring
Seen: rising stock prices; Unseen: wages rising even faster for workers without shares
Seen: the Fed buying bonds; Unseen: its balance sheet quietly shrinking as bonds matured
context: The visible outcome (S&P 500 +24%) was framed as recovery. The invisible mechanism -- new reserves flowing directly to first-receivers who owned equities -- was the actual causal channel. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: 'Higher stock prices will boost consumer wealth,' Ben Bernanke wrote in his newspaper column of November 4, 2010, defending the Fed's new bond buying. Critics had long thought the Fed was steering asset prices on purpose; now its chairman had said so in print. Once a central bank says in public that it wants stock prices up, what changes?
answer: It becomes an openly admitted aim of policy, no longer a hidden side effect
choices: It becomes an openly admitted aim of policy, no longer a hidden side effect
Nothing changes, since markets pay no heed to what bankers write
The bank must stop buying bonds, so as not to seem political
Stock prices fall, as investors fear a sudden reversal
context: After the 2010 op-ed, critics could point to the chairman's own words: the Fed meant to lift asset prices. Who owns stocks, and who does not, became part of the argument over every later round of bond buying. Source: Bernanke, Washington Post (November 4 2010).

question: A villager on a small Pacific island east of the Philippines walked past a stone disc taller than a man, with a hole in its middle, outside a neighbor's house. It was money. Which island is famous for this stone money?
answer: Yap
choices: Yap
Guam
Tahiti
Easter Island
context: The Yap Islands are a small group in Micronesia. Their traditional currency, the rai, is one of the most distinctive monetary systems ever recorded. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: The men of one Yap village sailed about 250 miles to another island to cut a giant stone disc, because their own island had no stone fit for it. They carved it by hand from that island's limestone and towed it home behind an outrigger canoe. Which island did they quarry?
answer: Palau
choices: Palau
Guam
Bougainville
Tahiti
context: Yap has no limestone; the rai were carved from aragonite in Palau and transported by long open-ocean canoe voyage. The difficulty of transport was itself part of what made each stone valuable. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: A family on Yap traded away a giant stone disc that weighed several tons and had stood in its village for years. Nobody moved the disc an inch, before the trade or after it. How did the stone change hands?
answer: By the village agreeing in public that it had a new owner
choices: By the village agreeing in public that it had a new owner
By carving the new owner's mark into the stone's face
By handing the buyer a shell token that stood for the stone
By breaking off a small piece and giving it to the new owner
context: The ledger was social memory: everyone in the village simply agreed, and the transfer was complete. Physical possession and ownership were decoupled. Source: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: A canoe crew was towing a huge new stone disc home to Yap across the open sea when a storm struck, and the stone tore free and sank far too deep for anyone to reach. The crew swore to its size and quality. What did the islanders decide about the lost stone?
answer: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
choices: They agreed it was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable
They declared the crew liable for the full value in fish and taro
They sent the crew back to Palau to carve a replacement
They classified it as destroyed and removed it from the record
context: The crew's testimony to the stone's exact size and quality was enough. The rai continued to circulate through community memory even though it was hundreds of feet under the Pacific. Source: William Henry Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Grokipedia 'Rai stones' (2026-09-05).

question: Milton Friedman retold the tale of Yap's sunken stone in 1991, a stone still traded from owner to owner though it lay on the bottom of the sea. Modern money, he wrote, works in much the same way. What did he say the two have in common?
answer: Almost nobody sees the actual money, but everyone agrees who owns it
choices: Almost nobody sees the actual money, but everyone agrees who owns it
Both hold value only because a ruler's law demands it
Both are worth exactly what it cost to make them
Both are prized mainly for their beauty and rarity
context: Friedman's 1991 essay 'The Island of Stone Money' was later collected in his 1992 book Money Mischief. The Yap story became one of his favorite teaching devices. Source: Grokipedia 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05).

question: Clerks handling France's request in 1932 and 1933 to turn its dollars into gold never shipped a bar across the Atlantic. They shifted the bars to drawers labeled as French in the very same vault, a case Milton Friedman later set beside Yap's stone money in his essay 'The Island of Stone Money.' Whose vault was it?
answer: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York
The Bank of England in London
The Bank for International Settlements in Basel
The Bank of France in Paris
context: When France wanted to convert dollar claims to gold, staff at the New York Fed simply moved gold bars from a drawer labeled 'US' to a drawer labeled 'France' inside the same vault. National ownership changed; the metal did not move. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: Milton Friedman, and the cypherpunks after him, drew one lesson from the stone money of Yap about what money really is. The cypherpunks were programmers of the 1990s who wanted digital cash, and they took up Friedman's story. Which claim did they all draw from Yap?
answer: Money is a shared ledger; the stone or the coin is only its container
choices: Money is a shared ledger; the stone or the coin is only its container
Money must be issued by a sovereign to hold any value
Money is worthless unless each unit is backed by gold
Money is at heart a sacred or ceremonial object
context: Once the ledger is seen as the money, the shape of the container -- stone disc, gold bar, paper note, database entry -- is a secondary engineering choice. This is the conceptual bridge from rai to Bitcoin. Source: Friedman, Money Mischief (1992).

question: A Yap islander who bought a stone simply had the whole village remember that it was now his. Bitcoin gives that same job, knowing who owns which coin, to a shared record book guarded by mathematics and copied onto thousands of computers around the world. What is that record book called?
answer: The blockchain
choices: The blockchain
The mempool
The Merkle root
The lightning network
context: Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 design replaces trusted human memory with a chain of cryptographically linked blocks that every node holds a copy of. The rai villagers' shared verbal record becomes a mathematical public record. Source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008).

question: The cypherpunks, programmers of the 1990s, took up the story of Yap's stone money after Milton Friedman. On the island, the record of who owned each stone sat in the villagers' heads; Bitcoin keeps that record with cryptography instead. Seen that way, which point does the comparison make about monetary innovation?
answer: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
choices: A purely digital ledger is a natural extension of monetary tradition, not a break from it
Only physical scarcity can back a real currency
Cryptography cannot replace the role of a sovereign
Monetary systems always fail when the physical medium is lost
context: Once money is understood as a ledger, moving from community memory to cryptographic memory is a technology upgrade, not a change in category. The Yap sunken stone is functionally the same object as an unspent Bitcoin output on the blockchain. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out: The Origins of Money (2002).

question: Nick Szabo, the cypherpunk, pointed out a feature that Yap's rai stones and Bitcoin share and ordinary money lacks. A king could strike fresh coins whenever he pleased, and a government print new notes; but every rai had to be cut by hand on an island 250 miles off and carried home by canoe, and every bitcoin must be won by burning real electricity. What feature is it?
answer: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
choices: Costly proof-of-work to create each new unit
A licensed sovereign mint to stamp each unit
A physical backing in an underlying commodity
Continuous inflation to keep supply growing
context: Nick Szabo argued that a rai's cost of production (quarry, carve, canoe across open ocean) is a physical analog of Bitcoin's proof-of-work (electricity spent on cryptographic hashing). Both systems make new supply hard, and past supply cheap to verify. Source: Nick Szabo, Shelling Out (2002).

question: Harry Markopolos started studying Bernie Madoff's results in 2000. No honest fund, he worked out, could make such steady gains month after month in rising and falling markets alike. He took his proof to the Securities and Exchange Commission. What came of it?
answer: The agency ignored him and the fraud kept going for years
choices: The agency ignored him and the fraud kept going for years
The agency closed the fund within a few months of his warning
Madoff sued him and forced him to take back his charges
Other investors pulled out and the fund collapsed early
context: Harry Markopolos was a quantitative analyst at Rampart Investment Management. He determined by May 2000 that Madoff's steady ~1% monthly returns could not be produced by any real trading strategy. Source: Markopolos, No One Would Listen (Wiley 2010).

question: Bernie Madoff confessed in December 2008 that his money-management firm had been a sham for decades. Years earlier Harry Markopolos had shown the Securities and Exchange Commission that Madoff's returns were impossibly smooth, rising almost every month with hardly a dip. What kind of scam had Madoff been running?
answer: A Ponzi scheme, paying old clients with new money
choices: A Ponzi scheme, paying old clients with new money
Insider trading on secret news tips
Fake accounting to hide company losses
Selling stocks the seller did not actually own
context: Markopolos's November 7, 2005 submission was titled 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud' and listed 29 red flags. The SEC opened but did not adequately pursue the investigation. Source: sec.gov (Markopolos submissions).

question: Free-market thinkers weighed the Madoff case after his fraud fell apart in the 2008 crash, with about $65 billion lost on paper. For years the Securities and Exchange Commission had sat on detailed warnings about him from Harry Markopolos. What blunt lesson did they draw?
answer: Government watchdogs can miss huge frauds, so investors still need to think for themselves
choices: Government watchdogs can miss huge frauds, so investors still need to think for themselves
The watchdog needs a bigger budget and staff before it can catch such frauds
Funds like Madoff's should be barred from taking ordinary people's savings
Investors should trust only funds that the watchdog has fully examined
context: The SEC Inspector General's 2009 post-mortem report found approximately six substantive complaints raising significant red flags about Madoff between 1992 and 2008. None was adequately investigated. Source: sec.gov (OIG Report No. 509, August 31, 2009).

question: The Securities and Exchange Commission's own inspector general went back over the agency's handling of Bernie Madoff after the fraud collapsed in December 2008, and set down in a long report what it had missed. Which of these failures did the report name?
answer: Young staff were handed cases too complicated for their training
choices: Young staff were handed cases too complicated for their training
Senior investigators were fired for asking too many questions
The whole enforcement office was shut down for a year
The person reporting the fraud refused to talk to investigators
context: The OIG Report 509 (August 31, 2009) documented junior staff assignments, missed basic verification steps (a single call to DTCC would have revealed Madoff was not actually trading the volumes he claimed), and misunderstanding of the alleged strategy. Source: sec.gov OIG Report 509.

question: Bernie Madoff took a senior post at a major US stock market early in the 1990s, long before his fraud came out, and it made him a respected establishment figure in finance. Which post was it?
answer: Chairman of NASDAQ
choices: Chairman of NASDAQ
President of the New York Stock Exchange
Head of the Chicago Board Options Exchange
Chief Executive of AMEX
context: Madoff served as chairman of NASDAQ in the early 1990s -- an establishment credential that made SEC skepticism of a whistleblower's complaint about him structurally harder. Stigler's capture theory predicts exactly this pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Madoff.

question: Harry Markopolos, the analyst who had studied Bernie Madoff's returns since 2000, published a book about the case in 2010. Which phrase became its title?
answer: No one would listen
choices: No one would listen
Too good to be true
The wizard of lies
Madoff with the money
context: Harry Markopolos, No One Would Listen: A True Financial Thriller (Wiley, 2010), tells the story from his side, from his May 2000 discovery through Madoff's arrest. Other books on the case carry their own titles: Erin Arvedlund's Too Good to Be True (2009), Diana Henriques's The Wizard of Lies (2011) and Jerry Oppenheimer's Madoff with the Money (2009). Source: wiley.com (Markopolos 2010).

question: An accountant inside a big company finds proof of a fraud and knows that blowing the whistle could cost him his job. Since 2010 the Securities and Exchange Commission has handed tipsters between 10 and 30 percent of whatever fines their information wins, rather than a flat reward. Why does a percentage work better?
answer: The bigger the fraud they expose, the bigger their reward, so they speak up sooner
choices: The bigger the fraud they expose, the bigger their reward, so they speak up sooner
A percentage keeps every reward small, so fewer false tips come in
A percentage is cheaper to pay out than any fixed reward would be
A percentage hides each tipster's reward from his employer
context: The SEC Office of the Whistleblower (created in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act) offers 10-30% of monetary sanctions above $1M for actionable tips leading to enforcement action. It is an institutional attempt to align incentives with fraud detection. Source: sec.gov/whistleblower.

question: A student of the Madoff case asks why a regulator would ignore detailed written warnings about a well-connected Wall Street figure, again and again. The Securities and Exchange Commission had such warnings about Bernie Madoff from Harry Markopolos for years, and the fraud ran on. Where do economists of the public-choice school, after George Stigler, first look for the cause?
answer: The staff's own career incentives, which pulled them away from tough cases
choices: The staff's own career incentives, which pulled them away from tough cases
The agency's thin budget, which left too few staff to check
The agency's weak legal powers over firms of Madoff's kind
Secret bribes paid by Madoff to the agency's top officials
context: Stigler's 1971 capture theory predicts that regulators tend to identify with, defer to, and hire from established regulated figures. The SEC's staff incentive structure did not reward embarrassing a former NASDAQ chairman. Markopolos, an outsider, was on the wrong side of that capture. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); SEC OIG Report 509 (2009). Stigler-style capture analysis: work out which specific decision-makers stand to lose or gain from an investigation. When the answer is that the decision-makers see mostly downside from investigating a well-connected figure, expect systematic under-enforcement. Source: Stigler (1971); Kwak, 'Cultural Capture and the Financial Crisis' (2013).

question: Jimmy Carter signed a law in 1978 that freed America's airlines to choose their own routes and set their own fares. Since 1938 the Civil Aeronautics Board had decided both, and few but the wealthy flew much. What happened to ticket prices for ordinary people after that?
answer: They dropped, and many more people could afford to fly
choices: They dropped, and many more people could afford to fly
They rose for most travelers within a few years
They stayed about where the board had once set them
They fell at first, then climbed back above the old fares
context: The CAB, created in 1938, controlled airline routes and fares until the Airline Deregulation Act (October 24, 1978, Carter). Real airfares fell dramatically over the next two decades. Source: brookings.edu (Kahn + Deregulation history).

question: A radio station owner hires a lobbyist in Washington to keep a rival station off the air. His license from the Federal Communications Commission gives him a slice of the airwaves no rival may legally use, and license holders like him fought for years to slow cable television too. What does this behavior show?
answer: A license granted by government can become a privilege its holders fight to keep
choices: A license granted by government can become a privilege its holders fight to keep
A broadcast market can hold only one strong station, a natural monopoly
Rival stations would crowd the airwaves until no one could be heard
Incumbents lobby mainly to shield listeners from weak, unreliable stations
context: The FCC was created by the 1934 Communications Act, replacing the earlier 1927 Federal Radio Commission. Broadcast-license politics is a classic capture case: cable TV was delayed for years by broadcaster opposition mediated through the FCC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission.

question: A shipper paid smaller freight bills after a law of 1980 ended decades of Interstate Commerce Commission control over one industry's rates and routes. The commission had been set up in 1887 to watch over the railroads, and the law came two years after Congress freed the airlines. Which industry did it free?
answer: Trucking
choices: Trucking
Passenger rail
Ocean shipping
City buses
context: The Motor Carrier Act of 1980, signed July 1, 1980, deregulated interstate trucking rates and routes, ending decades of ICC-set trucking rates. Truckload shipping costs fell substantially over the following decade. Source: brookings.edu (Motor Carrier Act history).

question: Critics looking back after the 2008 crash singled out two federal bank agencies that had failed to see the risks building in home lending. They pointed to staff who went from those agencies to the banks and back again, the revolving door. Which pair of agencies did they blame?
answer: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision
choices: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision
The National Credit Union Administration and the Farm Credit Administration
The Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission
The Small Business Administration and the Export-Import Bank of the United States
context: The OCC charters and supervises national banks; the OTS supervised savings-and-loans, among them Countrywide, IndyMac and Washington Mutual, and was folded into the OCC by the Dodd-Frank Act in 2011. Critics pointed to the flow of staff between both agencies and the banks they oversaw. Source: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report (2011).

question: George Stigler argued in 1971 that an agency Congress creates to police an industry, say banking or broadcasting, often ends up working for that industry, its rules helping the industry more than the public. Economists have looked hard at why. What is the most common reason it happens?
answer: The regulators come from and go back to the industry they oversee
choices: The regulators come from and go back to the industry they oversee
The industry pays every regulator secret bribes in cash
The agency's budget shrinks until it cannot enforce its rules
Judges overturn the agency's rules whenever the industry sues
context: Marver Bernstein, Regulating Business by Independent Commission (Princeton University Press, 1955), introduced the four-stage life cycle: gestation, youth, maturity, and old age -- with capture occurring in the maturity phase. Source: press.princeton.edu (Bernstein 1955).

question: Gabriel Kolko, a historian, argued that the big railroad companies lobbied for the Interstate Commerce Commission themselves when Congress created it in 1887. The airlines' Civil Aeronautics Board and the early Federal Communications Commission ended up serving their industries too. George Stigler judged capture by an agency's results, not its intentions. Which visible behavior is the strongest sign that an agency has been captured?
answer: The agency keeps new firms out while it guards the profits of firms already in
choices: The agency keeps new firms out while it guards the profits of firms already in
The agency's budget and staff grow larger with every passing year
The agency writes long, detailed rules that few outsiders can follow
The agency hires its experts from universities, not from the industry
context: Capture is measured by outcomes, not intent. If regulation systematically raises incumbent profits and blocks new competitors, the regulation is functioning like an industry-serving barrier, whatever its stated purpose. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kleiner, Licensing Occupations (Upjohn 2006). The common thread across the ICC, CAB, and FCC: agencies whose original public-interest justification gradually gave way to protecting incumbent firms against new entrants. Stigler's 1971 paper formalized the pattern as theory. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Kolko, Triumph of Conservatism (1963).

question: Sam Peltzman, George Stigler's student, took up the testing of Stigler's 1971 paper, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation,' and followers of the two carried it on for half a century across transport, broadcasting, banking and licensing. As the Chicago school reads it, what has the broad pattern of that research been?
answer: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
choices: Stigler's theory is largely vindicated across every major regulatory agency examined
Stigler's theory holds only for transportation regulators, not others
Stigler's theory has been refuted by studies of environmental agencies
Stigler's theory applies only in states with weak public-service ethics
context: Chicago economists read the record, from transport and broadcasting to banking and occupational licensing, as confirming the Stigler-Peltzman pattern of incumbent-serving regulation. Critics such as Daniel Carpenter and David Moss, in Preventing Regulatory Capture (Cambridge, 2014), argue that capture is real but often overdiagnosed, and that it can be prevented. Source: Peltzman, 'Toward a More General Theory of Regulation' (1976); Carpenter and Moss (2014).

question: A city councilwoman proposes freezing the rent on every apartment in town to keep housing affordable. Frédéric Bastiat taught that a policy has an effect everyone sees and one nobody sees; the seen effect here is today's tenants paying less. What is the main unseen effect on future housing?
answer: Apartment buildings a developer would have put up are never built
choices: Apartment buildings a developer would have put up are never built
Apartment buildings already standing are seized by the state
Apartment buildings fill with tenants moving in from other cities
Apartment buildings raise prices to cover a rent-control fee
context: The classic price-ceiling result: capping future rents below construction cost stops the pipeline of new buildings; the units the city never gets are the Bastiat UNSEEN. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control.

question: A would-be tenant in a rent-controlled city pays the landlord, or the tenant moving out, an under-the-table sum to land the cheap lease. Payments like his have turned up under strict rent control in New York, Paris and Stockholm alike. What is the side payment called?
answer: Key money
choices: Key money
Cover fee
Lock deposit
Occupancy premium
context: 'Key money' is the standard term for the covert side payment used to acquire a rent-controlled lease; the Fraser Institute's 1981 collection Rent Control: Myths and Realities documents the pattern across cities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_money.

question: 'The most important single central fact about a free market is that no exchange takes place unless both parties benefit,' Milton Friedman wrote. A rent cap breaks that principle. Whom does the cap help, and whom does it harm the most of all?
answer: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
choices: Helps existing tenants; harms would-be tenants who never get a lease at all
Helps all tenants equally; harms only speculators and non-resident landlords
Helps first-time buyers; harms only established homeowners
Helps landlords by stabilizing income; harms the general tax base
context: This is the classic seen/unseen split for a price ceiling: the incumbent tenant is SEEN paying less; the would-be tenant who never appears on any waiting list because the building was never built is UNSEEN. Source: Friedman & Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), price-ceilings chapter.

question: Richard Cantillon, an Irish-born banker, saw around 1730 that new money does not reach everyone at once, and those who get it first can spend it before prices rise. When a central bank creates money today, who loses out in this chain?
answer: Regular workers, who get the money last after prices have already climbed
choices: Regular workers, who get the money last after prices have already climbed
Borrowers, who must pay back their loans in dearer money
The government, whose tax money buys less as prices climb
The central bank, which must one day pay the money back
context: Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734) was an Irish-born banker who lived in Paris. His trading in the Mississippi Bubble made his fortune; his shorting of it made him a rare survivor. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05). In Cantillon's day, mines and government-favored merchants received new coins first. They could buy at old prices before prices adjusted. Late-receivers -- wage earners, savers -- paid the new higher prices with old wages. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: Murray Rothbard and Jesús Huerta de Soto revived the idea of an Irish-born banker who grew rich in Paris in the early 1700s: new money comes in at certain doors, a mine, a royal treasury, a bank, and those nearest spend it before prices adjust. What name does the pattern go by today?
answer: The Cantillon effect
choices: The Cantillon effect
The Wicksell effect
The Fisher effect
The Keynes effect
context: The Cantillon effect is the standard Austrian label for the redistribution from late-receivers to first-receivers of newly created money. Whether the money is 18th-century Peruvian silver or 21st-century Fed reserves, the mechanism is the same. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05). Richard Cantillon (c. 1680s-1734), an Irish-born banker who shorted John Law's bubble before it collapsed, wrote his Essai in the 1730s. It was published posthumously in 1755. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: A student tracing a new dollar from the Federal Reserve to her own pocket starts where the Fed makes it, when it buys Treasury bonds. Richard Cantillon asked the same question of fresh money in the 1730s; in his day it came from a mine or a printing press. Where do the Fed's brand-new reserves land first?
answer: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
choices: At the Fed-dealer interface, in the accounts of primary dealers
In household checking accounts nationwide
In Treasury tax-refund payments to individuals
In the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation reserves
context: When the Fed buys a bond it credits the primary dealer's reserve account. First-receivers are banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, asset holders. Consumer prices adjust years later when velocity recovers. Source: Grokipedia 'Primary dealer' (2026-09-05).

question: A shopper in 2023 paid more for her groceries than she had in 2020, the year the pandemic rescue began. Richard Cantillon had described around 1730 how new money moves through an economy. Which part of the pattern from 2020 to 2023 best matches his account?
answer: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
choices: The lag between money creation and consumer-price adjustment, with asset prices moving first
The lag between money creation and asset-price adjustment, with consumer prices moving first
All prices rising together, at once, as soon as the new money was created
Wages rising ahead of prices, so that workers were the first to gain
context: Cantillon explicitly described the timing: new money enters at specific points, those points enjoy the old prices, prices then adjust over months and years, late-receivers pay the higher prices with wages set at the old level. The modern QE-then-CPI sequence follows the pattern precisely. Source: Cantillon, Essai (1755).

question: Richard Cantillon described a figure in his manuscript of around 1730: someone who buys materials, tools and labor now at prices he knows, betting he can sell the finished goods later at a price nobody knows yet, and who may be ruined if prices fall first. Israel Kirzner later made this figure the heart of Austrian economics. What word did Cantillon give him?
answer: Entrepreneur
choices: Entrepreneur
Capitalist
Rentier
Financier
context: Cantillon's Essai introduced 'entrepreneur' as the systematic risk-bearer in the market. Modern Austrian economics -- especially Israel Kirzner -- treats this Cantillonian concept as central to how markets discover new information. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises, Murray Rothbard and their heirs turned Richard Cantillon's insight against modern central banks like the Federal Reserve. Cantillon had seen that new money enters at one place first, and whoever gets it first can spend it before prices rise elsewhere. Which pattern do they say his idea exposes?
answer: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
choices: Central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street
Central-bank money creation is distributionally neutral across all social groups
Central-bank money creation always causes immediate consumer-price inflation
Central-bank money creation has no effect on asset prices
context: The Cantillon-effect analysis explains why QE lifts asset prices for existing owners before consumer prices rise for everyone. It is not a bug of the modern system; it is a structural feature the Austrian tradition traces back to the 1730s. Source: Rothbard, An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (1995).

question: A Londoner reading the news in May 1734 learned that fire had gutted Richard Cantillon's house, apparently with the banker inside. Whispers began at once that someone had set the fire on purpose. Which suspicion has hung over his death from that day on?
answer: Murder by a servant he had dismissed, who set the fire to hide it
choices: Murder by a servant he had dismissed, who set the fire to hide it
A killing ordered by John Law to silence an old rival
Arson by a London mob angry at a foreign banker
A rival banker's revenge for the fortune he made in 1720
context: Cantillon's death by house fire on the night of 13-14 May 1734 remains unsolved. Suspicion fell on his dismissed cook, Joseph Denier, who was thought to have killed and robbed him and set the blaze to hide the crime, and who fled abroad and was never caught. Source: Grokipedia 'Richard Cantillon'.

question: A doctor in West Germany prescribed a sedative called thalidomide to an expectant mother in the late 1950s. Before it was pulled in 1961, over 10,000 babies were born with terrible birth defects, and Congress answered in 1962 with stricter rules for proving that new medicines work. What trade-off do stricter drug rules bring?
answer: Fewer bad drugs get through, but good drugs also arrive much slower
choices: Fewer bad drugs get through, but good drugs also arrive much slower
Safer drugs get through, and they reach patients faster too
Fewer drugs reach patients, but each one costs much less
More drugs reach patients, since doctors trust them more
context: The thalidomide birth-defect crisis (1957-62, mostly in Europe) prompted Congress to pass the Kefauver-Harris Amendments in 1962, requiring proof of efficacy for FDA approval. Source: fda.gov (Kefauver-Harris Amendments history).

question: A woman with a fatal disease asks her doctor for an experimental drug that has passed early safety trials but is still years from full approval; she has run out of approved treatments. The Right to Try Act, which became law on May 30, 2018, lets patients like her use such a drug. What is the moral argument for the law?
answer: Dying patients have little to lose and should get to decide the risk for themselves
choices: Dying patients have little to lose and should get to decide the risk for themselves
Patients who try early drugs serve science as willing volunteers
Early access lets drug makers gather data faster and more cheaply
Insurers should have to pay for any drug a dying patient chooses
context: The Right to Try Act was signed by President Trump on May 30, 2018. Alex Tabarrok of George Mason University has long argued for FDA reform; in a 2000 paper he pointed to off-label prescribing, where doctors use approved drugs for unapproved purposes, as evidence of what a lighter approval rule could deliver. Sources: fda.gov (Right to Try); Tabarrok, 'Assessing the FDA via the Anomaly of Off-Label Drug Prescribing' (Independent Review, 2000).

question: A California cancer doctor, Vinay Prasad, took aim in Malignant, his book of 2020, at the way the Food and Drug Administration clears some cancer drugs. On its fast-track programs, he argues, the agency often approves a drug on an early lab signal, like a scan where a tumor has shrunk. What is Prasad's main worry about that?
answer: That short-term test results are treated as proof the drug saves lives, when they are not
choices: That short-term test results are treated as proof the drug saves lives, when they are not
That the drugs are approved too slowly by the agency
That foreign trial results are given too little weight in reviews
That drug companies fund too little research on side effects
context: Vinay Prasad's book Malignant: How Bad Policy and Bad Evidence Harm People with Cancer (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2020) argues that accelerated FDA approval on surrogate endpoints has often failed to deliver actual survival improvements. Source: jhupbooks.press.jhu.edu (Prasad 2020).

question: A nurse rolled up her sleeve for one of the first COVID-19 vaccines in December 2020, months before the Food and Drug Administration had finished its normal full approval. The agency had used an Emergency Use Authorization. What trade-off is built into that kind of authority?
answer: Faster access in an emergency in exchange for less complete safety data at first
choices: Faster access in an emergency in exchange for less complete safety data at first
Lower cost in exchange for the maker skipping clinical trials altogether
Faster access in exchange for the maker giving up its patent rights
Wider access in exchange for taking doctors out of the decision
context: Emergency Use Authorization let the first COVID-19 vaccine reach the public from December 11, 2020, months before full approval in August 2021. Source: fda.gov (Emergency Use Authorization).

question: Robert Conquest, a British historian and poet, began counting the victims of Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union during the Cold War. Stalin's police shot or jailed millions in the 1930s, and his grain seizures starved millions in Ukraine. Which line best sums up communism's real record?
answer: It caused tens of millions of deaths across the countries that tried it
choices: It caused tens of millions of deaths across the countries that tried it
Its crimes were the work of a few bad leaders, not the system
It took a heavy toll at first but soon gave its people plenty
It caused about the same deaths as any other system
context: Conquest was born 1917 in Great Malvern, England, and died 2015 at Stanford, California. He had worked at the Foreign Office Information Research Department before turning to Sovietology in the 1950s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: Joseph Stalin set his police on his own people from 1936 to 1938, and they arrested and shot huge numbers of Soviet citizens, among them loyal party members, old revolutionaries, generals and factory managers. What does the Terror teach about a state that owns every farm and factory and answers to no voter?
answer: When one group controls everything, they can turn violence on anyone with no check
choices: When one group controls everything, they can turn violence on anyone with no check
Terror breaks out only when a state is too weak to keep order
Planning works well so long as the planners mean well
Violence comes from poverty, so a rich state is safe from it
context: Published by Macmillan of London in 1968. The book drew on defector testimony, Soviet dissident samizdat, and close reading of the Soviet published record. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Great_Terror.

question: Sheila Fitzpatrick and J. Arch Getty challenged Robert Conquest's The Great Terror of 1968, arguing that he had overcounted the dead and laid too much of the blame on Stalin himself. They pointed instead to local pressures and bureaucratic chaos. What was their rival school of Western Sovietology called?
answer: The revisionist school
choices: The revisionist school
The Frankfurt school
The Annales school
The Cambridge school
context: Getty's 1985 book 'Origins of the Great Purges' argued that lower-level party officials, not Stalin personally, drove much of the terror -- and that Conquest had over-counted. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Historiography_of_the_Great_Purge.

question: Researchers opened the files of Stalin's secret police after the Soviet Union collapsed in December 1991. For two decades critics had called Robert Conquest's 1968 count of Stalin's executions anti-Soviet propaganda and said he had wildly overcounted. What did the secret police's files turn out to show?
answer: The NKVD's own records came close to Conquest's execution estimate
choices: The NKVD's own records came close to Conquest's execution estimate
The NKVD's records showed Conquest had over-counted by roughly a factor of ten
The NKVD's records could not be located and the debate remains unresolved
The NKVD's records confirmed both sides were wrong by equal amounts
context: Conquest's 1968 appendix put legal executions in 1937 and 1938 at about 700,000; the 681,692 executions found in the Soviet archives for those two years roughly confirmed it. The archives also confirmed the personal-will attribution: Stalin's handwritten annotations appear on execution lists. Getty and other revisionists partially retracted; Conquest published a 1990 'Reassessment' folding in the new material. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Terror_(book) ; grokipedia.com/page/The_Great_Terror.

question: Robert Conquest turned from Stalin's purges to the Ukrainian countryside and published a second great book in 1986, through Oxford University Press. It told how Stalin's forced grain seizures of 1932 and 1933 starved millions of peasants. What was its title?
answer: The Harvest of Sorrow
choices: The Harvest of Sorrow
The Great Terror
Bloodlands
Red Famine
context: Robert Conquest's The Harvest of Sorrow: Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine (Oxford UP, 1986) was the first major Western scholarly synthesis. It was funded partly by the Ukrainian diaspora and treated with skepticism by academic sovietology until the archives opened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvest_of_Sorrow. 'The Harvest of Sorrow: Soviet Collectivization and the Terror-Famine' (Oxford University Press, 1986) was the Western scholarly standard on the Holodomor before Snyder's 'Bloodlands' (2010). Conquest also wrote 'Reflections on a Ravaged Century' (1999). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: George W. Bush gave Robert Conquest the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. Conquest, the historian of Stalin's purges, had worked since 1981 at a research institute in California, where younger scholars of the Soviet Union learned under his guidance. Which institution was it?
answer: The Hoover Institution at Stanford
choices: The Hoover Institution at Stanford
The Brookings Institution
The RAND Corporation
The Council on Foreign Relations
context: The Hoover Institution is a policy research center on the Stanford campus. Conquest mentored a generation of Sovietologists there through the 1980s and 1990s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Conquest.

question: Ron Paul, who had delivered babies as a Texas doctor before entering Congress, blamed the Federal Reserve for the 2008 crash and wrote a book about it for ordinary readers in September 2009. It reached number six on the New York Times bestseller list. Its title was three blunt words. What were they?
answer: End the Fed
choices: End the Fed
Stop the Printing
Return to Gold
Money and Freedom
context: End the Fed (Grand Central Publishing, September 2009) argued the Fed is unconstitutional, morally objectionable, and economically destructive. Its bestseller performance signaled Fed criticism had gone mainstream. Source: Grokipedia 'End the Fed' (2026-09-05).

question: Ron Paul rose on the House floor to attack the Federal Reserve, building his speech, as he built so many, on three economists whose names he cited constantly. One of the three was his personal friend. Which trio did he draw on?
answer: Mises, Hayek, and Rothbard
choices: Mises, Hayek, and Rothbard
Marshall, Keynes, and Samuelson
Friedman, Schwartz, and Meltzer
Marx, Sraffa, and Robinson
context: Ron Paul was a personal friend of Murray Rothbard's. He made frequent floor speeches drawing on Mises's monetary theory and Hayek's calculation argument throughout the 1980s-2000s. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: Ron Paul warned the House in 2003 that a housing bubble was building across the country and would end in a crash. He blamed one Federal Reserve chairman's policy for inflating it, and the crash came five years later. Whose policy did he blame?
answer: Alan Greenspan's low-rate policy
choices: Alan Greenspan's low-rate policy
Paul Volcker's high-rate policy
Arthur Burns's political accommodations
William McChesney Martin's punchbowl removal
context: The 2003 speech, delivered as the funds rate was moving toward the 1% floor, predicted a housing bubble and eventual crash. Ron Paul was widely dismissed at the time. Five years later he was largely vindicated. Source: Grokipedia 'Ron Paul' (2026-09-05).

question: Ron Paul's supporters waved signs with a three-word slogan at a rally for his Federal Reserve Transparency Act, which he filed in February 2009. The bill would have let the Government Accountability Office, Congress's own investigators, go through the Fed's books from top to bottom. What did the signs say?
answer: Audit the Fed
choices: Audit the Fed
End the Fed
Break the Fed
Reform the Fed
context: HR 1207, the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, was informally 'Audit the Fed.' It attracted 320 co-sponsors -- extraordinary bipartisan support -- but was gutted by Senate leadership. A limited one-time audit was included in the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Transparency Act' (2026-09-05).

question: House members lined up behind Ron Paul's 2009 bill to open the Federal Reserve's books to Congress's investigators, before Senate leaders trimmed it to a single review of the Fed's emergency lending. Out of 435 House members, about how many signed on as co-sponsors?
answer: About 320
choices: About 320
About 50
About 175
About 90
context: 320 House co-sponsors is a supermajority -- extraordinary for any bill, unprecedented for a Fed-oversight bill. Democratic Senate leadership prevented a full vote, but a limited one-time audit of Fed emergency-lending programs made it into the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal Reserve Transparency Act' (2026-09-05).

question: In his 2009 book, Ron Paul charged the Federal Reserve with three wrongs: that it violates the Constitution, that creating money out of nothing is wrong in itself, and that it harms the real economy. What argument did he make for the third charge?
answer: The Fed creates the boom-bust cycles Austrian business-cycle theory predicts
choices: The Fed creates the boom-bust cycles Austrian business-cycle theory predicts
The Fed is unable to control the money supply during recessions
The Fed cannot coordinate with foreign central banks
The Fed's dot plot is inaccurate more than half the time
context: Ron Paul's economic argument drew on Austrian business-cycle theory: artificially low interest rates lure businesses into mistakes, and the bust that follows is the correction. The book came out in September 2009, a year after the crash it blamed on the Fed. Source: Paul, End the Fed (2009).

question: Ron Paul ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008 and again in 2012. Comparing how his party treated the Federal Reserve before and after those campaigns, what shift does his career show?
answer: Fed criticism moved from the fringe into ordinary Republican primaries
choices: Fed criticism moved from the fringe into ordinary Republican primaries
His Fed views left no lasting mark on his own party
His Fed views caught on with Democrats but not Republicans
His audit bill passed in full during the Obama years
context: Before Ron Paul, calls to end or audit the Fed were rare in mainstream politics. After his three decades in the House and three presidential runs, they became a normal Republican-primary stance. His son Rand Paul, a Kentucky senator since 2011, has carried Audit the Fed bills into the Senate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Transparency_Act.

question: For his constitutional case against the Federal Reserve, Ron Paul turned to the clause that gives Congress the power 'to coin money' and 'regulate the value thereof.' The Fed, created in 1913, runs money policy on its own. What did Paul argue about that arrangement?
answer: Congress cannot hand its money power over to an independent agency
choices: Congress cannot hand its money power over to an independent agency
Only the states may issue money, so a federal bank is void
Only the Treasury may run money policy, under the President
The Fed is lawful only while each dollar stays backed by gold
context: The constitutional case: Article I Section 8 assigns to Congress the power 'to coin Money, regulate the Value thereof, and of foreign Coin.' Ron Paul argues this authority cannot be delegated wholesale to the Federal Reserve without amending the Constitution. Source: US Constitution, Article I Section 8; Paul, End the Fed (2009).

question: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that clear property rights can often settle pollution fights, such as a factory whose black smoke drifted over a farmer's field and ruined his crops. If the farmer held the legal right to clean air above his land, what could he do about the factory?
answer: Sue the factory, or charge it a fee to keep polluting
choices: Sue the factory, or charge it a fee to keep polluting
Ask the state to put a tax on the factory's smoke
Claim a share of the factory's yearly profits
Order the factory to shut down by his own authority
context: Ronald Coase (1910-2013) won the 1991 Nobel 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' Source: nobelprize.org (Coase 1991).

question: Ronald Coase, a young economist, asked in 1937 why companies exist at all. If markets match buyers and sellers so well, a business could hire someone afresh for each task as it came up. Why, in Coase's answer, does it keep workers on hand instead?
answer: Making a new deal for every task costs time, effort and money
choices: Making a new deal for every task costs time, effort and money
Workers on the payroll will work for less than outsiders
Owning more lets a firm squeeze its suppliers and rivals
Managers like to command people and build ever larger firms
context: Coase called these the costs of using the price mechanism: finding a partner, haggling, writing a contract, checking the work. Economists now call them transaction costs. A firm, in his account, grows until doing one more job in-house costs as much as buying it on the market. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: Arthur Pigou, a Cambridge economist, taught that when a factory's smoke harms a neighbor, the state should tax the harm. Most economists followed him until Ronald Coase published a very different answer in 1960, one that held whenever striking a deal between the two sides cost little. What did Coase claim?
answer: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
choices: The factory and the neighbor can bargain to an efficient outcome themselves
The state should immediately shut down the factory
The neighbor should be forced to move at government expense
The state should set a legal limit on how much smoke the factory makes
context: Coase's insight: when parties can negotiate, they will bargain to the outcome that maximizes joint value, regardless of who initially holds the legal right. The initial rights determine WHO PAYS, not the final allocation. Source: Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960).

question: Ronald Coase studied fights such as one between a farmer and a factory whose smoke drifted onto the farmer's cattle, and in 1966 George Stigler gave the result a name. In Coase's view, what matters most for how such a fight ends?
answer: That the two sides can bargain cheaply, not who is given the right first
choices: That the two sides can bargain cheaply, not who is given the right first
That the right goes to the farmer, since the harm falls on him
That the state taxes the smoke at exactly the harm it causes
That whichever side was there first keeps the right
context: George Stigler named it 'the Coase theorem' in his 1966 Theory of Price textbook. Coase himself was ambivalent about the honorific and worried the theorem was widely misinterpreted. Source: Stigler, Theory of Price (Macmillan 1966).

question: Ning Wang wrote a final book with Ronald Coase, finished when Coase was 100 and published in 2012. It traced how one huge Asian country left central planning for markets after reforms that began in 1978. Which country?
answer: China
choices: China
India
Vietnam
Chile
context: How China Became Capitalist (Palgrave Macmillan, 2012), co-authored with Ning Wang. Coase was 100 at publication and 102 at his death in 2013. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase.

question: Ronald Coase, asking in 1937 why firms exist at all if markets work so well, noticed that work is coordinated in two very different ways. Between firms, prices and market bargains coordinate strangers; inside a firm, prices fall silent. What mostly does the coordinating there instead?
answer: Command relationships between manager and employee
choices: Command relationships between manager and employee
Votes among the workers on how the work is shared
A fresh contract with each worker for every task
Customs handed down from the firm's founders
context: Inside a firm a manager instructs an employee what to do. Between firms, prices coordinate. Coase's question: why draw the line here rather than there? His answer: transaction costs. Source: Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937).

question: Ronald Coase's 1937 paper asked why firms exist; his 1960 paper asked how a farmer and a smoky factory should settle their quarrel. The questions differ, but economists who study him find one method running through both. Which method do the two papers share?
answer: Weighing real markets, firms and governments, costs and all
choices: Weighing real markets, firms and governments, costs and all
Measuring each real market against a model of perfect competition
Assuming that deals cost nothing, so markets always work perfectly
Testing each claim against long runs of national statistics
context: The Coase move: never compare a real institution to an idealized alternative. Firms, markets, private bargains, and government all have their own transaction costs. Comparative institutional analysis must count them all. Source: Coase, Essays on Economics and Economists (Chicago 1994).

question: Ross Ulbricht, a young libertarian, opened a secret online market, the Silk Road, early in 2011. It ran on the hidden Tor network, and people traded drugs and fake papers there without names or credit cards. What money did they pay with, so that payments would be hard to follow?
answer: Bitcoin
choices: Bitcoin
US dollars
Gold coins
Personal checks
context: Silk Road ran as a hidden Tor site from early 2011. Bitcoin payments carry no names, only addresses, though every one is written on a public ledger that investigators later learned to follow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: The pirate in the film The Princess Bride hands his name down from one man to the next, so the real Dread Pirate Roberts can never be caught. Ross Ulbricht took that name to run his hidden market. Why would the boss of an illegal market want a name like that?
answer: So agents could never be sure they had caught the real founder
choices: So agents could never be sure they had caught the real founder
So the police would take the whole site for a harmless joke
So buyers would trust a name they already knew from a film
So rival markets could not legally copy his market's name
context: Ulbricht used the pseudonym Dread Pirate Roberts (DPR), from The Princess Bride (1987), where the title passes between wearers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Federal agents caught Ross Ulbricht on October 1, 2013, with his laptop open and logged in to his secret market's controls, and they had staged the arrest with care. Where did they find him?
answer: The science-fiction section of a San Francisco public library
choices: The science-fiction section of a San Francisco public library
A desk in a university computer lab across the bay
The doorway of his rented room in San Francisco
The arrivals hall at San Francisco's international airport
context: Agents found Ulbricht on October 1, 2013 in the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library, logged in to the site's controls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Ross Ulbricht sat at his open laptop in a public place in San Francisco on October 1, 2013, as federal agents closed in. Had he closed the lid, the laptop's full-disk encryption would have sealed the drive for good, and with it the proof that he ran the Silk Road. What did the agents do so he could not lock it?
answer: Staged a loud quarrel nearby, then grabbed the laptop while he looked up
choices: Staged a loud quarrel nearby, then grabbed the laptop while he looked up
Waited for him to step away, then took the laptop from his table
Broke into it over the library's wireless network before moving in
Tricked him into typing his password on a fake login page
context: Two agents staged an argument nearby to distract Ulbricht, and others grabbed the open laptop, still logged in to the site's controls, before he could lock it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: New York jurors convicted Ross Ulbricht in early 2015 on seven charges tied to the Silk Road, among them drug trafficking and money laundering. In May 2015 Judge Katherine Forrest passed sentence on a first-time offender who had never personally used violence. What sentence did she give him?
answer: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
choices: two life sentences plus 40 years without possibility of parole
a 20-year sentence with possibility of parole
a 10-year sentence in a minimum-security prison
a 5-year suspended sentence with community service
context: Judge Katherine Forrest sentenced Ulbricht to two life sentences plus 40 years without parole. The prosecution cited the site's roughly $1.2 billion in sales and unproven murder-for-hire allegations; the defense argued the sentence was disproportionate for a first-time nonviolent offense. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: One person close to Ross Ulbricht saw more than a decade of campaigning pay off in January 2025, when Donald Trump pardoned him. That person had led the public fight to free him, arguing the punishment was far too harsh. Who was it?
answer: Lyn Ulbricht (his mother)
choices: Lyn Ulbricht (his mother)
Kirk Ulbricht (his father)
Joshua Dratel (his trial lawyer)
Roger Ver (an early Bitcoin backer)
context: Lyn Ulbricht ran the FreeRoss.org campaign for more than a decade; Joshua Dratel defended her son at his 2015 trial. Source: https://freeross.org/.

question: Donald Trump, on the second day of his second term, January 21, 2025, pardoned Ross Ulbricht, as he had promised the Libertarian Party's national convention in 2024. Libertarian writers looked back on the eleven-year campaign that had led to it. What lesson did they draw about how a movement should push back when its ideas run into a courtroom?
answer: That a long public campaign for one named person can win where abstract advocacy fails
choices: That a long public campaign for one named person can win where abstract advocacy fails
That changing the law first does more good than fighting for any one person
That quiet lobbying wins clemency more often than loud public pressure
That a movement should keep its causes abstract, never tied to one case
context: Libertarian writers, Lyn Ulbricht among them, credited the eleven-year FreeRoss.org campaign: pressure for one named person moved a president where abstract arguments about sentencing had not. Source: https://freeross.org/.

question: Saifedean Ammous, an economist teaching in Beirut, published a book with John Wiley and Sons in 2018 making the case that Bitcoin might be the hardest form of money ever made. It has since been translated into dozens of languages. What is its title?
answer: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
choices: The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking
The Bitcoin Way: A History of Digital Currency
The Bitcoin Manifesto: A New Financial Order
The Bitcoin Book: An Introduction for Investors
context: 'The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking' (Wiley, 2018) has been translated into dozens of languages. Source: https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Bitcoin+Standard%3A+The+Decentralized+Alternative+to+Central+Banking-p-9781119473862.

question: A Bitcoin miner sees his reward for each new block cut in half at a halving, which comes once every 210,000 blocks, while the coins already mined keep piling up. Saifedean Ammous applies the central tool of his 2018 book to that schedule: the stock-to-flow ratio, a good's existing stock divided by its new supply each year. What does he say happens to Bitcoin's ratio as the halvings go on?
answer: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
choices: it doubles every four years, heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero
it halves every four years, falling toward zero as issuance slows
it stays about the same, since stock and new supply grow together
it grows by a fixed amount each year, steadily and without steps
context: Ammous's argument: because the halving cuts new issuance in half every four years while stock keeps accumulating, Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio approximately doubles each cycle -- heading toward infinity as issuance approaches zero. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 8.

question: Saifedean Ammous leans on an old Austrian contrast between two kinds of money. Some can be turned out cheaply, by a printing press, a keyboard entry at a central bank or a mine that hits a rich new seam. Gold and Bitcoin cannot: adding to gold takes real physical work, and Bitcoin's code fixes a number nobody can raise. What do economists call money whose supply will not grow quickly?
answer: hard money
choices: hard money
fiat money
narrow money
helicopter money
context: 'Hard money' (money hard to produce more of) versus 'easy money' (money easy to produce more of) is the classical Austrian distinction Ammous inherits. Fiat money, money by government decree, is his chief example of the easy kind; narrow money and helicopter money name other things, a narrow measure of the money supply and new money handed straight to the public. Source: The Bitcoin Standard (2018) ch 1.

question: San Francisco voters passed Proposition I in 1994, bringing older buildings of two to four flats under rent control while near-identical neighbors stayed free. Three Stanford economists later treated the gap as a real-world experiment. Which trio wrote the classic study?
answer: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
choices: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian
Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, and Emmanuel Saez
Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, and John Van Reenen
Milton Friedman, George Stigler, and Rose Friedman
context: The 1994 expansion created a discontinuity that let economists compare almost-identical properties on either side of the cutoff. Diamond, McQuade, and Qian are mainstream Stanford scholars, not identified with the Austrian school. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: A tenant in a small older San Francisco building learned in 1994 that her flat now fell under rent control, after voters passed Proposition I; a tenant in a nearly identical building the measure did not reach got no such protection. Three Stanford economists followed buildings like these for two decades. What did they find about the number of rental units in the newly covered buildings?
answer: It fell by about 15 percent
choices: It fell by about 15 percent
It rose by about 15 percent
It fell by about 50 percent
It stayed about the same
context: Landlords converted units to condominiums, demolished and rebuilt as unregulated new construction, or undertook renovations that removed units from the rental market, taking every route around rent control that the law allowed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: A San Francisco landlord whose small building came under rent control in 1994 turned his flats into condominiums, and other owners tore their buildings down to rebuild or moved relatives in. Three Stanford economists later traced what such moves did across the whole city. What happened to city-wide rents?
answer: They rose by about 5 percent
choices: They rose by about 5 percent
They fell by about 5 percent
They rose by about 40 percent
They were unchanged
context: The city-wide supply reduction pushed up rents on the units that remained available to move-in tenants. The policy transferred wealth from future tenants (who face higher rents in a smaller market) to current protected tenants (who save on their own units). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: Rebecca Diamond of Stanford led a study of San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion, and afterwards she said plainly that the policy was no cure for the city's long shortage of homes. How did she sum up what it did instead?
answer: Shifted wealth from future renters to today's protected tenants
choices: Shifted wealth from future renters to today's protected tenants
Shifted wealth from landlords to the city through higher taxes
Shifted wealth from builders of new towers to small landlords
Shifted wealth from richer tenants to poorer ones in each building
context: Diamond is a mainstream researcher, not an opponent of the policy on principle; her point was that the savings of sitting tenants were paid for by future renters facing a smaller, dearer market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rebecca_Diamond.

question: A housing activist dismisses the San Francisco rent-control study as biased. An economist in Thomas Sowell's tradition answers that its finding matched a prediction two young economists, Milton Friedman and George Stigler, both future Nobel winners, had published in 1946 in a short pamphlet for the Foundation for Economic Education. What was the pamphlet called?
answer: 'Roofs or Ceilings?'
choices: 'Roofs or Ceilings?'
'Capitalism and Freedom'
'Free to Choose'
'Tyranny of the Status Quo'
context: Written by Milton Friedman and George Stigler in 1946, published by the Foundation for Economic Education. The pamphlet predicted the supply-response and quality-decay mechanisms Diamond-McQuade-Qian empirically measured 73 years later. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rent_regulation_in_San_Francisco.

question: A worker at an American energy giant lost her job and her retirement savings almost overnight when the company went bankrupt in 2001, after years of hiding huge losses with accounting tricks. After a scandal of that shape, what do lawmakers usually pass?
answer: New rules forcing companies to prove their money reports are honest
choices: New rules forcing companies to prove their money reports are honest
Bailouts that repay the workers who lost their savings
Laws breaking the biggest firms up into smaller ones
Cuts in corporate tax so honest firms can hire again
context: Named for Senator Paul Sarbanes (D-Maryland) and Representative Michael Oxley (R-Ohio), the chairs of the two committees that shaped the bill. Formally the Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: Senator Paul Sarbanes and Representative Michael Oxley sponsored a sweeping law of 2002 that answered two collapses: an energy-trading company that went under in December 2001 after hiding billions in losses, and a phone company that went bankrupt in July 2002 after inflating its profits. Which two firms were they?
answer: Enron and WorldCom
choices: Enron and WorldCom
Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns
General Electric and Tyco
Adelphia and HealthSouth
context: Enron filed December 2, 2001; WorldCom filed July 21, 2002. WorldCom's collapse revealed roughly $11 billion in improperly capitalized expenses. Both scandals shattered public trust in audited financial statements. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Enron.

question: A chief financial officer picks up his pen to sign the quarterly statement that his company's numbers are true; under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 a false signature can send him to prison. His chief executive must sign one too. What is the idea behind the rule?
answer: Making real people answer in law, so none can hide behind the firm
choices: Making real people answer in law, so none can hide behind the firm
Shifting blame for bad numbers from managers to auditors
Getting quarterly reports to investors faster than before
Making the firm, not its owners, pay any fine for fraud
context: Section 302 targeted the WorldCom shape of fraud, in which senior executives had claimed ignorance of accounting irregularities. Post-SOX, that defense is legally hollow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: An accountant at a small public company works through the checks on its books that its managers must build, test and personally vouch for under Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The work can cost even a small firm about $1-2 million a year. Why do critics say the rule weighs most on small firms?
answer: The cost barely grows with size, so it eats more of a small firm's income
choices: The cost barely grows with size, so it eats more of a small firm's income
Small firms must be audited more often than big ones under the law
Small firms must file twice as many reports as big ones each year
Big firms may deduct the cost from their taxes, but small ones may not
context: Section 404's internal-controls work is a largely fixed cost: a bill of a million or two barely dents a company earning billions but can swamp one earning fifty million, which shields the giants from newcomers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sarbanes%E2%80%93Oxley_Act.

question: A retail investor in 2015 hopes to buy shares in a promising young tech firm before it grows into the next Apple, and finds it has stayed private. A critic in Bastiat's tradition grants Sarbanes-Oxley its seen benefit, fewer accounting frauds, and names an unseen cost that falls on savers like her. What is it?
answer: Retail investors miss the early growth, now open only to wealthy private backers
choices: Retail investors miss the early growth, now open only to wealthy private backers
Retail investors pay higher commissions on the shares still listed
Retail investors pay more tax on gains from the stocks they hold
Retail investors get less reliable reports from the firms still listed
context: A firm that stays private into a multi-billion valuation delivers its early gains to venture funds and wealthy accredited investors; ordinary buyers get the shares only after most of the growth. How much of the shrinking of the listed market Sarbanes-Oxley caused, and how much came from mergers and cheap private money, is still argued.

question: A writer using a pen name sent a brief note to a small cryptography mailing list on Halloween night 2008, as the world's banks reeled. It linked to a nine-page paper on a new kind of money that could run with no bank in the middle. What pen name signed the note?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto
Nick Szabo
Adam Back
Hal Finney
context: The October 31 2008 post from 'Satoshi Nakamoto' to the metzdowd.com cryptography list -- run by Perry Metzger -- announced the Bitcoin white paper and linked to bitcoin.org. Source: metzdowd.com archives (October 31 2008).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto sent a short message on Halloween night 2008 to a small cryptography mailing list, pointing readers to a nine-page paper on a new kind of digital money that needed no bank or government to run it. That paper launched Bitcoin. What is its famous title?
answer: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
choices: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
A New Digital Money for the Twenty-First Century
Foundations of Distributed Cryptographic Currency
On the Cryptographic Foundations of Trustless Value
context: Nine pages, twelve sections. The paper contained no mathematics more advanced than probability theory -- deliberately readable by any competent programmer, not just cryptographers. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto took on in 2008 a puzzle that had beaten every earlier design for internet money without a trusted firm keeping the books. A digital coin is just a file, and a file can be copied; with nobody tracking who owns what, the same coin could be paid out again and again. What is the puzzle called?
answer: The double-spending problem
choices: The double-spending problem
The dining philosophers problem
The halting problem
The traveling salesman problem
context: Double-spending: how can anyone stop the same digital coin being spent twice, without a central authority checking every transaction? Every earlier digital-cash design had needed a trusted issuer (Chaum's DigiCash, e-gold and others). Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto first showed his design in late 2008 not to a newspaper but to a small mailing list that the cryptographer Perry Metzger ran. Its members, students of cryptography, had spent the 1990s arguing over how to build digital cash without a bank. Why show it to that group first?
answer: They were the people most likely to spot flaws and try running the code
choices: They were the people most likely to spot flaws and try running the code
They were the people most likely to invest money in the new coin
They were the people most likely to keep the design a secret
They were the people best placed to win approval from regulators
context: Perry Metzger ran the metzdowd.com cryptography list, a well-known venue for reviewing cryptographic proposals throughout the 1990s and 2000s. The Bitcoin white paper appeared as a normal posting on that list. Source: metzdowd.com archives.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto mined almost alone in 2009, in the network's first months, when blocks were easy to win. Researchers have since estimated what sits in his addresses. About how many bitcoins?
answer: About one million
choices: About one million
About ten thousand
About ten million
About one hundred
context: Chain analysis of the earliest-mined addresses (the 'Patoshi pattern' studied by Sergio Demian Lerner) places Satoshi's holdings at roughly one million BTC. Not one satoshi has moved from those addresses in more than fifteen years. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto posted his white paper in October 2008, in the middle of the global banking crisis, as a plain technical proposal about cryptography, hashing and timestamps, and nowhere did he call it political. Over the next fifteen years, as governments printed trillions of new dollars and savers watched their money lose value, its deeper meaning became clear to millions. What was that deeper meaning?
answer: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
choices: That money could exist without any central issuing authority
That programming languages could enforce contracts without courts
That cryptographic proofs could replace public identity verification
That the internet could function without private-sector service providers
context: The SEEN in 2008 was a paper about digital cash; the UNSEEN was that a working solution to double-spending meant money could exist without a bank, a central bank, or any political authority. That implication took years to become visible. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-case-bitcoin.

question: Hal Finney, one of the world's most respected cryptographers, began running Bitcoin almost as soon as its network started up in January 2009. He had built a close cousin of it himself, Reusable Proofs of Work, and he received the first transaction Satoshi Nakamoto ever sent. Why does a respected expert joining early matter so much to a new open-source project?
answer: It signals to other skilled people that the system is worth their time
choices: It signals to other skilled people that the system is worth their time
It proves the code free of bugs, since an expert has checked it
It gives the project an official seal from the cryptography world
It brings in money, since experts usually invest in what they test
context: Hal Finney's 2004 'Reusable Proofs of Work' (RPOW) built on Adam Back's hashcash, which the Bitcoin white paper cites. Finney was running Bitcoin within days of its launch in January 2009 and received the first person-to-person transaction on January 12. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Bitcoin's creator left no goodbye and no farewell when he made his final post on the BitcoinTalk forum: Satoshi Nakamoto's last public message there was a plain technical note on one small subject. Which subject was it?
answer: DDoS defenses
choices: DDoS defenses
Block-reward halving
Wallet backup procedures
Merchant integration
context: The December 12 2010 post concerned defenses against distributed denial-of-service attacks on Bitcoin nodes. Nothing in the message gave any hint that it would be Satoshi's last public communication. Source: bitcointalk.org (Satoshi's final post).

question: The developer Mike Hearn got an email from Satoshi Nakamoto in April 2011: 'I've moved on to other things.' Satoshi had left the software in Gavin Andresen's care, and the network has kept running without him ever since. Why is that a strength of Bitcoin, not a weakness?
