answer: No single person needs to be alive for the network to keep working
choices: No single person needs to be alive for the network to keep working
Gavin Andresen could now steer it with a firmer hand
Satoshi's coins would pass to the developers
A company could now take legal charge of the network
context: The April 23 2011 email to Mike Hearn read (in essence): 'I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Hearn published the exchange years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: A programmer on the other side of the world downloads Bitcoin's code, reads it line by line and sends in a suggested fix, as anyone may. A bank's code, by contrast, stays locked inside the company, where only the bank's employees may look at it. Why do Bitcoin's supporters say this openness makes their money safer?
answer: Thousands of eyes can spot problems, and no boss can secretly change the rules
choices: Thousands of eyes can spot problems, and no boss can secretly change the rules
Open code can't be copied, so no rival can launch a fake Bitcoin
Open code lets regulators approve each change before it goes live
Open code runs faster, because many hands keep trimming it down
context: Bitcoin's code is published under an open-source licence, so anyone may read it, run it, copy it or propose changes; a change reaches the network only if the people running nodes choose to install it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Core.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto mined about a million coins in Bitcoin's first months, and they still sit at known addresses that anyone can watch. If he came back and sold them all at once, what would most likely happen to Bitcoin's price?
answer: It would drop sharply as buyers worried about the sudden new supply
choices: It would drop sharply as buyers worried about the sudden new supply
It would rise sharply, as his return renewed faith in the project
It would barely move, since a million coins is a small share of all
It would rise at first, then settle back where it had been
context: Chain analysis of the 'Patoshi pattern' by Sergio Demian Lerner places Satoshi's early-mined stash at roughly one million BTC. At $50,000/BTC that is $50 billion; at higher prices, far more. Source: bitslog.com (Patoshi pattern analyses).

question: A researcher checks, one more time, the addresses holding the coins Satoshi Nakamoto mined in Bitcoin's first months, as others have watched them around the clock since he went quiet in 2011. In more than fifteen years, one fact about those early coins has become the strongest sign that Satoshi truly walked away. What is that fact?
answer: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
choices: Not one satoshi from the early-mined addresses has ever moved
The coins have been repeatedly split across many new addresses
The coins have been sold off slowly, a few at a time, for years
The coins were all moved once to new addresses, then left alone
context: If Satoshi were alive and had access to the keys, he could have sold, borrowed against them, or moved them for privacy at any time in fifteen years. Instead, the coins sit untouched -- an unusually strong empirical signal that he truly walked away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: Bitcoin's inventor mined roughly one million coins in its first year and never sold a single one, even after they were worth tens of billions of dollars. Which temptation did that restraint remove from Bitcoin for good?
answer: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
choices: The founder's temptation to enrich himself at the expense of the currency's users
The founder's temptation to give press interviews that move the currency's price
The founder's temptation to hire successors from his own family
The founder's temptation to relocate the project to a favorable tax jurisdiction
context: A central banker profits by inflating; a company founder profits by manipulating stock; Satoshi could have sold his million BTC at any time. His non-action is a KEPT PROMISE the design's story needed. Source: mises.org/library/satoshi-kept-promise.

question: A British High Court judge ruled in March 2024 that Craig Wright, an Australian computer scientist who had spent years suing critics who called him a fake, was not Satoshi Nakamoto. No one has proven who Bitcoin's creator really is. Why does Bitcoin work better while its creator stays unknown?
answer: No single person can be arrested, silenced, or pressured to change the rules
choices: No single person can be arrested, silenced, or pressured to change the rules
An unknown founder cannot sell his coins, so the supply stays capped
No one can sue the project, since it has no named owner to sue
An unknown founder keeps the code secret, so no one can attack it
context: In the Crypto Open Patent Alliance v Wright case, the UK High Court ruled in March 2024 that Craig Wright is NOT Satoshi Nakamoto; the ruling cited his falsified documents and inconsistent testimony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Wright_(computer_scientist).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto went silent in April 2011, and no message signed with his private keys has appeared since. What is the honest answer, as of 2026, to why he vanished?
answer: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
choices: Nobody knows for certain, though the coins stay untouched to this day
He confirmed his retirement in a signed 2015 essay published in Wired
He handed off his private keys to Gavin Andresen in a documented ceremony
He died of a documented illness in 2013, per public medical records
context: Illness, deliberate silence, prosecution fears, or death are all live theories; none has been confirmed. What IS documented: the coins have not moved in fifteen years, and no verified message from Satoshi has appeared since April 2011. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto.

question: Milton Friedman published an essay on government and schooling in 1955, 'The Role of Government in Education.' He allowed that government might pay for schooling, but not that it had to run the schools. What did the essay propose?
answer: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
choices: A voucher parents could redeem at any accredited school
A federally-set minimum teacher salary schedule
A single national K-12 curriculum administered by the Department of Education
Direct federal ownership of all urban public schools
context: Friedman argued government financing might be justified on externality grounds, but government production of schooling did not follow. Vouchers separated the two: public money, private (or public) provider chosen by the family. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milton_Friedman.

question: A seventeen-year-old takes the national test of reading and math that has tracked students her age for half a century. Over that half century the money spent on each public-school pupil has about tripled, even after adjusting for inflation. What has happened to the scores of seventeen-year-olds over the same span?
answer: They have remained essentially flat
choices: They have remained essentially flat
They have roughly doubled
They have collapsed by more than a third
They have grown steadily at a compounded 2 percent per year
context: The NAEP long-term-trend data show the flat scores. Friedman-influenced reformers cite this as the empirical anomaly a monopoly-provider hypothesis would predict: spending rose without competitive pressure to convert it into learning gains. Source: grokipedia.com/page/National_Assessment_of_Educational_Progress.

question: Cleveland parents could spend the city's school vouchers at religious schools, and in 2002 the Supreme Court upheld the program, five votes to four. The money reached those schools only because parents chose them, the majority held, so it did not violate the First Amendment's clause against establishing a religion. What was the case called?
answer: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris
choices: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris
Everson v. Board of Education
Engel v. Vitale
Lemon v. Kurtzman
context: The 5-4 decision upheld Cleveland's voucher program on the reasoning that the aid flowed through private parental choice, not directly to religious institutions. The ruling opened the constitutional path for voucher programs to include religious schools. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zelman_v._Simmons-Harris.

question: A school board member in a big city complains that charter schools and vouchers will drain her district of pupils. An economist answers her with a grocery store that holds on to nine customers in ten by force, not by being any good. Which reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
choices: The competitive-pressure move: monopoly providers lose the discipline to improve when customers cannot exit
The externality move: education produces spillover benefits so government should fully fund it
The public-goods move: schools are non-rival non-excludable and must be publicly produced
The redistribution move: spending must equalize per-pupil funding across districts
context: This is the core Friedman-Chubb-Moe argument. John Chubb and Terry Moe developed the empirical case in Politics, Markets, and America's Schools (Brookings 1990), arguing that governance structures immune to exit block real reform. Source: grokipedia.com/page/John_Chubb.

question: Milton and Rose Friedman set up an organization in 1996, late in Milton's life, for the cause he considered his most important, one he had first proposed in a 1955 essay. Which cause did the organization promote?
answer: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
choices: K-12 school choice through vouchers and education savings accounts
The abolition of the Federal Reserve System
Universal negative-income-tax replacement of welfare programs
Repeal of federal drug prohibition
context: Milton Friedman regarded vouchers as the single application of his method with the greatest human-welfare payoff. The Friedman Foundation for Educational Choice ran advocacy, research, and litigation support until it was renamed EdChoice in 2016. Source: grokipedia.com/page/EdChoice.

question: A volunteer switches on a Bitcoin node at home, one of thousands checking every block against the same rules. Some rule changes are gentle: his older software still accepts the new blocks, so the chain stays whole. Others split the chain in two. What is the gentle kind called?
answer: A soft fork
choices: A soft fork
A hard fork
A soft peg
A hard peg
context: Soft forks preserve one shared chain; hard forks can create two chains if any subset of nodes refuses the change. SegWit was a soft fork; Bitcoin Cash was a hard fork from Bitcoin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fork_(blockchain).

question: One faction of Bitcoiners broke away in a hard fork on August 1, 2017, after two years of quarrelling that came to be called the Block Size War. Their new coin had much larger blocks than Bitcoin's. What was it called?
answer: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
choices: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
Bitcoin Gold (BTG)
Litecoin (LTC)
Dogecoin (DOGE)
context: Bitcoin Cash launched with 8 MB blocks (vs Bitcoin's ~1 MB). Jonathan Bier's 2021 book 'The Blocksize War' is the standard chronicle of the dispute. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_Cash.

question: A Bitcoin developer publishes a new version of the software, and it changes nothing at all until enough miners and users choose to install it. If most of them refuse, the upgrade never takes effect. Why must so many of them go along before anything changes?
answer: No one runs Bitcoin, so a change sticks only if enough people accept it
choices: No one runs Bitcoin, so a change sticks only if enough people accept it
Satoshi Nakamoto's old code locks out changes that lack his approval
Bitcoin's foundation must ratify each change by a board vote first
The software refuses any upgrade that fewer than half its owners sign
context: Taproot's activation was notably drama-free after the SegWit years. Over 90 percent of mining hash power signaled support during the 'Speedy Trial' window in June-August 2021. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: A Bitcoin miner signaled his support for the Taproot upgrade in 2021, as over ninety percent of miners did before it activated that November. The upgrade added Schnorr signatures, which can merge several signers into one; they take their name from the cryptographer Claus-Peter Schnorr. What did the new signatures bring to each transaction?
answer: Smaller signatures per transaction and less information leaked about the sender
choices: Smaller signatures per transaction and less information leaked about the sender
Faster mining and higher block rewards for miners
Instant payments that no longer wait for a new block
A larger total supply of coins that can ever exist
context: Named for Claus-Peter Schnorr, a German cryptographer. Schnorr signatures allow multiple signers to combine their signatures into one, saving block space and improving on-chain privacy for multisig transactions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Schnorr_signature.

question: A high-school student asks a veteran Bitcoin coder why Ethereum is updated every few months while Bitcoin hardly changes. The coder points to the miners, node operators and wallet builders, thousands of them, each separate, who would all have to accept any new rule. Which reasoning move fits the coder's answer?
answer: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
choices: The knowledge-problem move: no central architect can safely rewrite a distributed system's rules
The efficient-markets move: any upgrade will be priced in instantly
The aggregate-demand move: upgrades should follow monetary stimulus
The revealed-preference move: users always choose the fastest network
context: Hayek's 1945 argument applies to protocol governance as well as to prices. Bitcoin's slow, consensus-heavy upgrade process is the practical embodiment of that principle. Ethereum's alternative approach takes on more coordination risk. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: A veteran Bitcoin developer sets two upgrades side by side: the Block Size War of 2015 to 2017, which ended with the chain split and a bitter book-length postmortem, and Taproot in 2021, a genuine change to signature math that went through almost silently. What lesson do Bitcoin developers draw from the contrast?
answer: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
choices: Decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress when the community is broadly aligned
Decentralized consensus can deliver change only through a hard fork and a split
Decentralized consensus works only when one lead developer has the final word
Decentralized consensus stalls for good once a community has split
context: The lesson is not that all disagreements can be avoided (Bitcoin Cash still exists) but that when the network is aligned, upgrades proceed smoothly without any central authority. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taproot_(Bitcoin).

question: A Bitcoin owner signs a payment with a secret number only he knows, and the network lets his coins move. Without that number nobody, however powerful, can move them; a thief who steals it can take them all. What is the number called?
answer: the private key
choices: the private key
the block hash
the mempool ID
the nonce
context: The private key is the ~256-bit secret that authorizes spending from a Bitcoin address. The block hash is the miner-computed identifier of a completed block; the mempool is the pool of unconfirmed transactions; the nonce is the number miners adjust when hashing a candidate block. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/private-key.

question: A woman buys bitcoin on a big exchange and leaves it in her account there, while the exchange keeps the secret codes that move it. One day the exchange freezes withdrawals and then collapses. What did she really own all along?
answer: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
choices: a claim on the exchange to be paid Bitcoin
the private keys to the coins
a share of the exchange company
a government-insured deposit
context: The exchange holds the private keys; the customer holds an IOU denominated in Bitcoin. If the exchange fails, freezes accounts, or is hacked, the customer becomes an unsecured creditor. Bitcoin exchange balances are not FDIC-insured and are not equity in the exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos, who wrote the textbook Mastering Bitcoin, summed up a hard lesson for a conference crowd. Bitcoin writers, setting the two great exchange collapses of 2014 and 2022 side by side, made the same point: a coin its holder cannot sign for is not really his money. Which line did Antonopoulos make famous?
answer: Not your keys, not your coins.
choices: Not your keys, not your coins.
Fix the money, fix the world.
Don't trust, verify.
Be your own bank.
context: Antonopoulos, author of Mastering Bitcoin (2014), popularized the phrase from conference stages in the 2010s. 'Fix the money, fix the world', 'Don't trust, verify' and 'Be your own bank' circulate in Bitcoin culture too, but the custody rule newcomers hear first is the one tied to him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Antonopoulos.

question: A Bitcoin owner plugs a small device into her laptop, okays a payment on its own little screen, and unplugs it again. Trezor, Ledger and Coldcard each make one, and it holds her keys on a chip that is never online. What is the device called?
answer: a hardware wallet
choices: a hardware wallet
a paper wallet
a mining rig
a full node
context: A hardware wallet stores keys on a secure chip that signs transactions offline; the private keys never leave the device. A paper wallet is a printed key backup; a mining rig computes proof-of-work; a full node validates the whole block chain but does not by itself store spending keys. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardware_wallet.

question: A Bitcoin owner's wallet device breaks, and he rebuilds every one of his keys from a list of twelve plain English words. The standard behind that backup, written in 2013, draws its words from one fixed list of 2,048. Bitcoin's developers number such standards as Bitcoin Improvement Proposals. Which one is it?
answer: BIP-39
choices: BIP-39
BIP-32
BIP-141
BIP-9
context: BIP-39 (2013, authored by Marek Palatinus, Pavol Rusnak, Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe) standardized the 12- or 24-word mnemonic backup. BIP-32 defines hierarchical deterministic wallet key trees; BIP-141 introduced Segregated Witness in 2015; BIP-9 covered soft-fork versioning bits. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: Two customers of Mt Gox took stock after the exchange collapsed in February 2014: one had lost every coin, while the other had lost nothing. Customers of Sam Bankman-Fried's exchange split the same way when it failed in 2022. Which decision separated those who lost nothing from the rest?
answer: holding the private keys themselves rather than leaving coins on the exchange
choices: holding the private keys themselves rather than leaving coins on the exchange
buying the exchange's proprietary token before the failure
using two-factor authentication on the exchange account
trusting the exchange's audited proof-of-reserves report
context: In both 2014 and 2022, customers who had withdrawn to self-custody wallets they controlled were unaffected by the bankruptcies. 2FA protects exchange login but does nothing when the exchange itself is insolvent; exchange tokens (FTT for FTX) collapsed alongside the exchange; proof-of-reserves reports were widely absent or misleading in both eras. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX.

question: A careful Bitcoin holder keeps three keys in three different places and sets up her wallet so that any two of them together can spend her coins. Losing one device, or having one stolen, can then no longer cost her the coins. What is this kind of wallet called?
answer: a multisig wallet
choices: a multisig wallet
a hot wallet
a custodial wallet
a watch-only wallet
context: A multisig (multi-signature) wallet requires m-of-n keys to authorize a transaction (commonly 2-of-3), so no single stolen or lost device is fatal. A hot wallet is any wallet on an internet-connected machine; a custodial wallet is one whose keys are held by a service; a watch-only wallet can display balances but cannot spend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multisignature.

question: A depositor at Signature Bank in New York saw Silicon Valley Bank fail on Friday, March 10, 2023, and pulled her money out over the weekend, though no one yet knew whether Signature itself was sound. Regulators shut it that Sunday. What is a chain reaction like that called?
answer: Financial contagion
choices: Financial contagion
Moral hazard
A credit crunch
Regulatory capture
context: Signature's depositors ran less for anything found at their own bank than because Silicon Valley Bank had just failed and Signature looked like it, heavy with uninsured deposits and crypto-industry customers. New York regulators closed it on Sunday, March 12. Source: Grokipedia '2023 United States banking crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: Bankers from eleven of America's largest banks, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo among them, placed deposits with the shaky First Republic on March 16, 2023, to steady it. How much did the eleven put in together?
answer: $30 billion
choices: $30 billion
$5 billion
$100 billion
$300 billion
context: JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, US Bancorp, BNY Mellon, PNC, State Street, and Truist collectively placed $30 billion of deposits at First Republic. It did not work. Source: Grokipedia 'First Republic Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A First Republic customer woke on May 1, 2023, to find that regulators had closed her bank and sold most of it to JPMorgan Chase, already the largest bank in the country. Mergers like that had cut the number of American banks from over 14,000 in 1984 to only a few thousand. When small banks keep getting swallowed, what tends to happen over time?
answer: The biggest banks get bigger and customers have fewer choices
choices: The biggest banks get bigger and customers have fewer choices
Customers gain choices, since merged banks offer more services
New small banks open as fast as old ones are swallowed
Big banks shrink again, as regulators split them up
context: JPMorgan Chase, led by Jamie Dimon, bought most of First Republic's assets on May 1 2023. It was the second-largest US bank failure in history at that moment, surpassing Silicon Valley Bank which had held the title for seven weeks. Source: Grokipedia 'First Republic Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: An analyst went through the wreckage of Silicon Valley Bank, Signature and First Republic in 2023, setting the three failed banks' balance sheets side by side, and found one root cause behind all three failures. What was that root cause?
answer: Held-to-maturity bond losses from the Fed's rate-hike cycle
choices: Held-to-maturity bond losses from the Fed's rate-hike cycle
Mortgage-servicing scandals from the 2000s revival
Cross-border money-laundering enforcement actions
State-level insurance-regulation changes
context: All three banks had bought long-duration bonds at low rates during 2020-21, classified them as HTM, and watched their economic value collapse as the Fed hiked to 5.25-5.50% in 2022-23. The rate cycle that killed inflation also killed the banks that had loaded up on cheap-rate bonds. Source: Grokipedia '2023 United States banking crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan's chief, told the world in May 2023, after his bank bought most of the failed First Republic: 'this part of the crisis is over.' Three banks had gone down one after another that spring. What does a takeover like that do to depositors at other banks?
answer: A safe giant taking over calms depositors and stops the panic spreading
choices: A safe giant taking over calms depositors and stops the panic spreading
It frightens them, since even giants are now taking on bad banks
It makes no difference, since each depositor judges only his own bank
It sends them to small banks, which now look safer than the giants
context: Dimon's public statement was framed as a declaration of stability but also a hint at the political-economy fact that consolidation had accelerated -- JPMorgan absorbed billions in troubled deposits from failing banks while becoming even more too-big-to-fail. Source: Grokipedia 'Jamie Dimon' (2026-09-05).

question: A Bitcoin economist laid the three bank failures of spring 2023 beside the Federal Reserve's own record in the years before: near-zero interest rates and heavy bond buying, then the sharp rate rises of 2022 and 2023. What did he say the sequence shows?
answer: The central bank whose easing made those bonds attractive later turned them into losses
choices: The central bank whose easing made those bonds attractive later turned them into losses
Bank failures come from fraud inside the banks, not from shifts in rate policy
Regional banks fail on their own schedule, whatever the central bank does
Deposit insurance alone stops runs, however large the losses in the books
context: Banks bought long-duration bonds at 2020-21 low rates because the Fed's QE made them attractive. The same Fed's 2022-23 tightening made those bonds catastrophic losses. The whipsaw is a structural feature of a discretionary rate cycle, not a series of independent errors. Source: Grokipedia '2023 United States banking crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: A startup founder in Santa Clara deposits her company's payroll at Silicon Valley Bank, beside a crowd of other startups from the same industry and the same region. Then the tech boom cools. Why does a bank like hers face more danger than a typical small-town bank?
answer: Its customers are too similar, so trouble hits them all at once
choices: Its customers are too similar, so trouble hits them all at once
Its customers are wealthier, so robbers target it more often
Its deposits are small, since young firms have little cash
Its customers are newer, so they trust banks less than most
context: SVB was founded 1983 to serve the Bay Area tech ecosystem. Its deposit base was overwhelmingly startup companies with venture funding parked in the bank between funding rounds. Source: Grokipedia 'Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A venture fund manager eyes safe government bonds paying almost nothing while the Federal Reserve holds interest rates near zero. What usually happens to the money flowing into risky startups at a time like that?
answer: It floods in -- investors chase any chance of higher returns
choices: It floods in -- investors chase any chance of higher returns
It dries up -- no one wants risk at low rates
Nothing changes -- rates do not affect investing
It holds back -- investors wait for rates to rise again
context: SVB's deposits roughly tripled between 2019 and 2021, hitting about $189 billion at peak. SVB invested much of this inflow in long-duration Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities at the ultra-low rates of 2020-21. Source: Grokipedia 'Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A bank treasurer buys long-term bonds while interest rates are very low. Rates then jump, and the bonds are worth much less on the open market, but under one common accounting rule the bank need not write that loss down. What danger does this create?
answer: The bank looks healthy on paper while quietly holding big real losses
choices: The bank looks healthy on paper while quietly holding big real losses
The bank must sell the bonds right away at any price
The bank's interest income collapses as the bonds stop paying
The bank's loans to customers all fall due at the same time
context: HTM accounting hides mark-to-market losses on the balance sheet. But the economic loss is real. By year-end 2022, SVB had roughly $15 billion in unrealized bond losses -- close to its entire tangible equity of $16 billion. Source: Grokipedia 'Held-to-maturity security' (2026-09-05).

question: A Silicon Valley Bank customer read a warning on Twitter in March 2023 and moved her company's money out with a few taps on her phone. Worried savers once had to queue at the teller's window, and a run could take days. What have phones and social media done to how fast a run on a bank unfolds?
answer: Runs now unfold in hours, not days, leaving regulators less time to act
choices: Runs now unfold in hours, not days, leaving regulators less time to act
Runs now take longer, since online transfers must wait to clear
Runs now end sooner, since a bank can freeze its app at once
Runs now start later, since online rumors are slow to be believed
context: Venture firms, Peter Thiel's Founders Fund among them, reportedly advised their startups to move money out, and the warnings raced through Twitter and group chats. The run moved faster than the bank's managers could react. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A family borrowed heavily from a bank to buy a house, and then house prices across America began to fall. Washington Mutual, the largest bank failure the United States has ever had, collapsed in September 2008, and banks across the country were falling with it. What main problem pushed so many of them over the edge?
answer: They had lent against home loans that borrowers could not repay
choices: They had lent against home loans that borrowers could not repay
They had lent too much to foreign governments that defaulted
They had lost their savings in a stock-market crash that year
They had been robbed by hackers who broke into their systems
context: Washington Mutual failed September 25 2008 with $307 billion in assets, the largest US bank failure in history and larger than SVB's $209B. Lehman Brothers was an investment bank, not an FDIC-insured commercial bank. Source: Grokipedia 'Washington Mutual' (2026-09-05).

question: A startup's finance chief parked millions at Silicon Valley Bank, far above the $250,000 per account that federal deposit insurance covers; about nine in ten of the bank's dollars were uninsured. When rumors spread in March 2023, customers rushed to pull their balances out. Why does a big share of uninsured deposits make a bank more likely to face a run?
answer: Uninsured depositors have a big reason to pull money out at the first sign of trouble
choices: Uninsured depositors have a big reason to pull money out at the first sign of trouble
Uninsured deposits pay no interest, so their owners leave for better rates
Uninsured deposits must be kept in cash, so the bank earns too little
Uninsured depositors are mostly foreign, and foreign money flees first
context: 93% of SVB's deposits were uninsured -- one of the highest uninsured-deposit ratios in the banking system. Startups routinely park $10-100M in a single account, far above the $250,000 cap. This concentration made the bank uniquely vulnerable to a run. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: Officials of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation made a joint announcement about Silicon Valley Bank's depositors on Sunday, March 12, 2023, two days after the bank was seized. Insurance normally covers $250,000 per account, and many of its customers had millions there. What did the officials announce?
answer: Every dollar of deposit would be paid in full, even amounts above the cap
choices: Every dollar of deposit would be paid in full, even amounts above the cap
Losses of about 15 percent on deposits above the $250,000 cap
The seizure would be postponed 30 days for further review
The matter would be sent to Congress for emergency legislation
context: The Sunday March 12 2023 joint announcement guaranteed all deposits under the FDIC's systemic-risk exception, a power Congress wrote into law in 1991. It carried protection far beyond the statutory cap without any new vote of Congress. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A depositor reading about Silicon Valley Bank after its fall learned that one senior post there had sat empty for roughly eight months in 2022. Whoever holds it has one job: to spot dangerous mismatches between short-term debts and long-term holdings. Which post was it?
answer: Chief Risk Officer
choices: Chief Risk Officer
Chief Executive Officer
Chief Compliance Officer
Chief Investment Officer
context: SVB's Chief Risk Officer departed in April 2022. The bank operated without a CRO for the eight months through late 2022 -- exactly the period when the rate-cycle bond losses were building on its balance sheet. Source: Grokipedia 'Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank' (2026-09-05).

question: A buyer on the Silk Road, the secret drug market of 2011 to 2013, paid in Bitcoin, the only money the site would take. Some Bitcoiners cheered that it worked exactly as designed, while others feared for Bitcoin's good name. Why did an illegal market pick Bitcoin over a bank transfer or a credit card?
answer: Bitcoin can be sent without a bank or government approving it
choices: Bitcoin can be sent without a bank or government approving it
Bitcoin payments cannot be seen by anyone at all
Bitcoin was the only money that worked over the Tor network
Bitcoin payments are insured if a seller fails to deliver
context: Silk Road became the first widely known use of Bitcoin outside hobbyist circles. The 2008 white paper had promised payments sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution, and the Silk Road showed that property working at scale on an anonymous network; whether the use was legitimate is a separate question. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: A Bitcoin defender writing about the Silk Road owns up to an uncomfortable fact. The money that helps people in poor countries slip past currency controls also helped criminals sell drugs on the internet. What honest point must a fair defender of Bitcoin admit here?
answer: Any tool that gives people more freedom can also be used for wrongdoing
choices: Any tool that gives people more freedom can also be used for wrongdoing
Bitcoin is used mostly by criminals, rarely by others
Bitcoin's good uses count for nothing beside crime
Bitcoin must be banned until it can refuse criminals
context: Bitcoin's defenders point to savers in countries with currency controls or collapsing money, Venezuela and Argentina among them, who use it to keep and send value; the same property that serves them served the Silk Road's sellers. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Federal agents shut down the Silk Road in October 2013 and locked up its founder, Ross Ulbricht. Within weeks copycat markets such as Silk Road 2.0 had opened and pulled in the same buyers. What does that pattern show about shutting a market by arresting the boss?
answer: As long as buyers and sellers still want to trade, a new marketplace will appear
choices: As long as buyers and sellers still want to trade, a new marketplace will appear
A market dies for good once its servers as well as its boss are seized
A market dies for good once its biggest buyers are arrested too
A market dies for good once its founder's name is made public
context: Silk Road 2.0 opened in November 2013, about five weeks after the takedown, and later markets such as AlphaBay grew larger than the original. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Silk_Road_(marketplace).

question: Donald Trump pardoned Ross Ulbricht in January 2025, ending a case that libertarians and Bitcoiners had rallied around for ten years. That year a high-school student asked a public-choice analyst what the pardon told her about markets like the Silk Road. Which reasoning move did he press?
answer: Recognizing the case's argument without collapsing it into a universal endorsement of the underlying market
choices: Recognizing the case's argument without collapsing it into a universal endorsement of the underlying market
Enforcing a strict verdict that all Tor markets are always legitimate
Enforcing a strict verdict that all Tor markets are always illegitimate
Concluding that presidential pardons always signal a change in federal drug law
context: A pardon settles one question, whether this sentence should stand, and leaves the larger argument over drug markets where it was. Ulbricht's supporters argued that a double life sentence was out of proportion for a first-time offender. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ross_Ulbricht.

question: Herbert Hoover signed a sweeping tariff in June 1930, with the Great Depression taking hold, lifting duties on imports higher than they had stood in about a hundred years. Canada, France and other American trading partners hit back with tariffs of their own. What usually happens when trading partners swap tariffs like this?
answer: Trade shrinks and both sides get poorer
choices: Trade shrinks and both sides get poorer
Trade grows because factories work harder
Trade shifts, but each side ends up about as well off
The country that struck first comes out ahead
context: Signed June 17, 1930, formally the Tariff Act of 1930. It raised US tariff rates on over 20,000 imported goods to their highest levels in about a century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: A Utah senator who chaired the Senate Finance Committee and an Oregon congressman who chaired House Ways and Means steered a tariff through Congress in 1930. It would go down as modern history's best-known trade blunder, and it carries both men's surnames. Who were they?
answer: Reed Smoot and Willis Hawley
choices: Reed Smoot and Willis Hawley
Joseph Fordney and Porter McCumber
Sereno Payne and Nelson Aldrich
Oscar Underwood and Furnifold Simmons
context: Senator Reed Smoot (R-UT) chaired the Senate Finance Committee; Representative Willis Hawley (R-OR) chaired House Ways and Means. Both later lost their seats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: An American economist put his name to a petition in May 1930 begging Herbert Hoover to veto the tariff bill, warning that it would raise prices for shoppers and invite a tariff war abroad. The New York Times printed the petition, and Hoover signed the bill anyway. About how many names were on the petition?
answer: About one thousand
choices: About one thousand
About one hundred
About ten thousand
About fifty
context: The petition published in the New York Times on May 5, 1930 carried 1,028 signatures. It warned that higher duties would raise prices for consumers and hurt exporters, and that 'a tariff war does not furnish good soil for the growth of world peace.' Hoover signed the bill anyway. Source: nytimes.com/1930/05/05/archives.

question: A congressman fought in 1930 for the businesses back home while Congress wrote the new tariff item by item, a special rate for each good from cheese to pocket watches to industrial chemicals. Every member did the same. About how many separate goods ended up with higher duties?
answer: More than twenty thousand
choices: More than twenty thousand
About two hundred
About two thousand
More than one hundred thousand
context: The Tariff Act of 1930 set specific higher duties on over 20,000 dutiable items -- the last time Congress legislated tariff rates on that many goods directly rather than delegating to the executive branch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: Canadian lawmakers struck back at the American tariff of 1930 with duties of their own, and France, Britain, Germany and country after country closed their doors as well. Between 1929 and 1934, by about how much did total world trade shrink?
answer: About two-thirds
choices: About two-thirds
About one-tenth
About one-third
About nine-tenths
context: World trade fell by roughly two-thirds between 1929 and 1934 as Canada, Britain, France, Germany, and dozens of other countries raised barriers in response to Smoot-Hawley -- the greatest peacetime contraction of international commerce ever recorded. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoot-Hawley_Tariff_Act.

question: American factory owners cheered when the 1930 tariff took effect, and foreign goods vanished from the shelves. Frédéric Bastiat had warned decades earlier that a tariff's biggest costs are the ones nobody sees at first. What were this tariff's hidden costs, the ones that surfaced months or years later?
answer: Higher prices for shoppers and lost sales for American exporters
choices: Higher prices for shoppers and lost sales for American exporters
Lower wages and fewer jobs in the factories the tariff protected
A flood of cheap foreign goods undercutting American farmers
Shortages at home as factories shipped their goods abroad
context: Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen method: the beneficiaries of a tariff are concentrated and visible (this steel plant, this sugar planter); the costs are diffuse and hidden (every consumer pays more, every exporter loses a foreign market). Source: bastiat.org/en/twisatwins.html.

question: Secretary of State Cordell Hull championed the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act, passed in 1934, which let the president lower tariffs through deals with other governments. Congress had written the 1930 tariff item by item, each member guarding the industries in his own district. Why is it usually easier for a president to lower tariffs than for Congress?
answer: A president bargains for the whole package, so no one local industry can block its line
choices: A president bargains for the whole package, so no one local industry can block its line
A president's tariff cuts need no approval and can never be undone by Congress
A president can pay off harmed industries out of customs revenue
Foreign governments will deal only with a president, never with Congress
context: The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, championed by FDR Secretary of State Cordell Hull, let the president negotiate bilateral tariff cuts without going back to Congress on every rate. It began three decades of tariff liberalization. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocal_Tariff_Act.

question: Delegates of the United States and twenty-two other countries signed, in 1947, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, aiming never to see another tariff war like that of the 1930s. In 1995 it became the World Trade Organization. Why do shared deals like this calm tariff fights between countries?
answer: Each country promises not to raise tariffs on the others, so none has reason to strike first
choices: Each country promises not to raise tariffs on the others, so none has reason to strike first
Each country hands its tariff decisions to a single world trade court
Each country pays a fine into a shared fund for every tariff it keeps
Each country agrees to buy a fixed share of its goods from the others
context: GATT, signed 1947 by 23 founding countries, ran successive tariff-cutting rounds through the postwar era. Its explicit institutional memory was that unilateral tariff hikes and retaliation had helped internationalize the 1930s depression. GATT became the WTO in 1995. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Agreement_on_Tariffs_and_Trade.

question: Ben Stein, actor and economist, summed up the story of the 1930 tariff in a famous classroom scene of Ferris Bueller's Day Off. Congress had raised import taxes on thousands of goods early in the Great Depression. What general lesson do economists draw from the episode?
answer: Raising tariffs during a downturn usually deepens the downturn instead of fixing it
choices: Raising tariffs during a downturn usually deepens the downturn instead of fixing it
Raising tariffs during a downturn speeds recovery by keeping spending at home
Raising tariffs during a downturn is safe, so long as the rates rise slowly
Raising tariffs during a downturn helps farms, though it hurts factories
context: Ben Stein's economics-teacher scene in Ferris Bueller's Day Off is probably the most-watched pop-culture reference to Smoot-Hawley, delivering an accurate one-minute summary of why economists thought the tariff worsened the Depression. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferris_Bueller%27s_Day_Off.

question: Ida May Fuller of Ludlow, Vermont, a legal secretary in her working years, received Social Security check number 1 on January 31, 1940, for $22.54. She had paid in $24.75 in all, and she lived to 100. About how much did she collect over her retirement?
answer: About $22,900
choices: About $22,900
About $2,300
About $71,000
context: Fuller collected $22,888.92 over 35 years of benefits against $24.75 paid in between 1937 and her retirement in 1939. She was born on her family's farm in Ludlow, Vermont, on September 6, 1874. The first cohort did extraordinarily well precisely because they paid in for only a few years while a very large working generation paid the taxes. Source: Social Security Administration, 'Ida May Fuller -- The first Social Security Beneficiary' (https://www.ssa.gov/history/imf.html).

question: A worker in 1950 opened his pay envelope and found Social Security tax taken out, money bound for that year's retirees, not for his own old age. Sixteen and a half workers paid in for each person collecting. Families have since had fewer babies, and people live longer. By 2024, how many workers paid in for each person receiving benefits?
answer: About 2.7
choices: About 2.7
About 5.4
About 8.1
About 1.2
context: The Social Security Administration's historical series puts the covered-worker-to-beneficiary ratio at roughly 41.9 to 1 in 1945, 16.5 to 1 in 1950, and about 2.7 to 1 today. The ratio is load-bearing because benefits are paid out of current payroll taxes rather than from each retiree's own past contributions. Sources: SSA, 'Ratio of Covered Workers to Beneficiaries' (https://www.ssa.gov/history/ratios.html); Peter G. Peterson Foundation (https://www.pgpf.org/article/the-ratio-of-workers-to-social-security-beneficiaries-is-at-a-low-and-projected-to-decline-further/).

question: Milton and Rose Friedman took aim in Free to Choose at the Social Security law's word for what workers must pay in: a 'contribution,' as if they gave it freely. Yet a worker who refuses to pay can be sent to prison. What did the Friedmans say was wrong with the word?
answer: Calling a forced tax a contribution hides what is really happening
choices: Calling a forced tax a contribution hides what is really happening
The word is too vague for any court to enforce
The word undersells how generous the benefits really are
The word was copied from a foreign law where it meant a fee
context: Free to Choose, chapter 4, 'Cradle to Grave': a company engaged in such labeling and advertising 'would doubtless be severely castigated by the Federal Trade Commission.' On the television series Friedman put it plainly: 'It has been sold as an insurance program. It's not an insurance program. It's a program which combines a bad tax, a flat tax on wages up to a maximum, with a very inequitable and uneven system of giving benefits.' Sources: Milton and Rose Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), ch. 4; Free to Choose television series, episode 4 (https://archive.org/details/freetochoose4fromcradletogravepart1).

question: Ephram Nestor sued after the government deported him in July 1956 for his old Communist Party ties and cut off his Social Security benefits. He had come from Bulgaria in 1913 and paid the tax on his wages from 1936 to 1955. The Supreme Court ruled against him in 1960. What did the Court say about money paid into Social Security?
answer: It buys no property right, and Congress may change the benefits at will
choices: It buys no property right, and Congress may change the benefits at will
It buys a contract right that only a criminal conviction can extinguish
It buys a property right, but one forfeited by leaving the country
It buys a claim on the trust fund ranking behind federal bondholders
context: Flemming v. Nestor, 363 U.S. 603 (1960). The Court treated Social Security as social insurance subject to modification by Congress, not as a system of accrued property rights, and held that terminating a deported person's benefits was not punishment and so was neither a bill of attainder nor an ex post facto law. Sources: Justia (https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/363/603/); Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemming_v._Nestor).

question: Social Security's trustees moved the date their trust fund runs dry a year closer in their 2025 report, to 2034. By law the program cannot borrow to cover a gap between what comes in from workers' paychecks and what it owes retirees. On the day the reserves run out, what does the report say happens?
answer: Incoming payroll taxes would cover about 81% of scheduled benefits
choices: Incoming payroll taxes would cover about 81% of scheduled benefits
Benefit checks would stop until Congress appropriated new money
The Treasury would make up the gap from general income-tax revenue
The retirement age would rise automatically until the books balanced
context: The 2025 OASDI Trustees Report projects the retirement fund alone depleted in 2033 with 77% of scheduled benefits payable, and the combined funds depleted in 2034 with 81% payable. Combined reserves fell $67 billion during 2024 to $2.72 trillion. SSA's June 2026 trustees release reported the combined-fund projection as consistent with the prior year. Sources: SSA press release, June 18, 2025 (https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/press/releases/2025-06-18.html); Congressional Research Service IF13045 (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13045).

question: George W. Bush opened his second term in January 2005 by making personal Social Security accounts his signature domestic proposal, with a White House campaign directed by Karl Rove and Ken Mehlman. Congress never brought a bill to a vote. Support collapsed once voters worked out what the plan would mean for them. What did they conclude it would do?
answer: Cut the guaranteed benefit for all but the lowest-income recipients
choices: Cut the guaranteed benefit for all but the lowest-income recipients
Hand the investment decisions to the Treasury rather than to the worker
Force the payroll tax up to pay for the transition years
Bar a worker's children from inheriting the balance in the account
context: The traditional benefit would have been reduced in proportion to what a worker diverted into an account, which is what turned public skepticism into opposition; the transition-cost objection (a payroll-tax rise) was also raised, but it was the guaranteed-benefit offset that sank the initiative. Sources: Brookings, 'Why the 2005 Social Security Initiative Failed' (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/why-the-2005-social-security-initiative-failed-and-what-it-means-for-the-future/); Congressional Research Service RL32879 (https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/RL32879.html).

question: A member of Congress defends the payroll tax by pointing to the check that goes out each month to 67 million Americans, many with no other retirement income. Critics in Frederic Bastiat's tradition agree on the facts. But the defense is incomplete, they say, because it counts only what the program did with the money and never what the money would have done otherwise. What comparison do the critics demand?
answer: What forty-five years of those same payroll taxes would have compounded to in the worker's own account
choices: What forty-five years of those same payroll taxes would have compounded to in the worker's own account
What the same revenue would have built had the state spent it on roads, ports and power instead
What retirees actually live on today in countries that never created a state pension at all
What the program costs to administer measured against a private insurer's overhead ratio
context: Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen' asks, after any law or expenditure, what does not happen because of it. The retiree's check is seen; the account the same 12.4% of a working life never built is not. This is a counterfactual and a contested one -- a private account carries market risk and no survivor guarantee, which is exactly why the reform argument is about the comparison rather than about a verdict. Milton Friedman pressed the same comparison in Free to Choose; Jose Pinera built a system around it in Chile in 1981; American voters rejected it in 2005. Sources: Bastiat (https://www.econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basEss.html); Friedman, Free to Choose (1980), ch. 4.

question: Barack Obama toured the California factory of Solyndra, a solar-panel maker his administration had backed in 2009 with a $535 million federal loan guarantee. Solyndra went bankrupt in 2011 and could not repay the loan. Who ends up eating that loss?
answer: Taxpayers
choices: Taxpayers
Its bankers
Its rivals
Californians
context: Based in Fremont, California. The bankruptcy laid off 1,100 workers and became the signature failure of the Obama-era green industrial-policy portfolio. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: Federal officials bet in 2009 that Solyndra, a California solar-panel maker, would beat its rivals in America and China, and they stood behind it with a $535 million loan guarantee. It went bankrupt two years later. What is the general problem with officials picking winning firms this way?
answer: Officials guessing which private companies will win rarely guess better than the market
choices: Officials guessing which private companies will win rarely guess better than the market
Officials guess as well as anyone, but bad luck can sink any single firm
Officials back too few firms, so a single failure looks worse than it is
Officials lack the money to back each firm long enough to succeed
context: Obama's May 2010 visit to the Fremont factory was a signature endorsement of the stimulus green-energy portfolio. Sixteen months later Solyndra filed for Chapter 11. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: A Solyndra worker in California coated tube-shaped solar panels with a blend of rare metals, a design unlike the flat wafers most rivals made. Between 2008 and 2011 one massive shift in the world price of a key panel material made Solyndra's tubes far too costly next to cheap Chinese flat panels. Which shift was decisive?
answer: The world price of silicon collapsed by nine-tenths
choices: The world price of silicon collapsed by nine-tenths
The world price of aluminum for frames tripled
The world price of steel for racks doubled
The world price of plastic for backing tripled
context: Silicon is the main input for flat panels. Its world price fell from about $400 a kilogram in 2008 to about $40 by 2011, and Solyndra's whole business case, which rested on dear silicon making its cylindrical design competitive, evaporated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: Private venture investors walked away from more Solyndra funding as Chinese panel factories grew, while the Department of Energy kept standing behind its $535 million guarantee. The investors had seen the danger coming. Which economist's idea does this pattern show?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: private investors' declined bets are dispersed information a central agency lacks
choices: Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: private investors' declined bets are dispersed information a central agency lacks
John Maynard Keynes's paradox of thrift: private saving reduces aggregate demand
Milton Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis about consumption smoothing
Alvin Hansen's secular-stagnation thesis about mature economies
context: Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' argued that dispersed knowledge across many private actors is irreducible to any central authority. When many private investors independently say 'no,' that revealed preference is information. A DOE loan officer facing no personal cost of being wrong lacks the same feedback discipline. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: Members of Congress opened hearings after Solyndra, a solar-panel maker backed by a half-billion-dollar federal loan guarantee, went bankrupt in 2011. Reporters zeroed in on one private backer, an Oklahoma billionaire whose investment firm had put more into Solyndra than anyone else, and who had also raised campaign cash for President Obama. Who drew the heat?
answer: George Kaiser through his Argonaut Ventures firm
choices: George Kaiser through his Argonaut Ventures firm
Warren Buffett through Berkshire Hathaway Energy
T. Boone Pickens through BP Capital
Peter Thiel through Founders Fund
context: Kaiser was a Tulsa-based billionaire and Obama campaign fundraiser. The connection did not, on the public record, direct the DOE decision, but it fueled a regulatory-capture critique of the loan-guarantee program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Solyndra.

question: A critic in Frederic Bastiat's tradition says the reporters who fixed on Solyndra alone, after its bankruptcy in 2011, missed the larger unseen cost. Solyndra's guarantee came out of a much larger federal program. What is that unseen cost?
answer: The whole $16 billion could not be used elsewhere, and other firms it backed failed too
choices: The whole $16 billion could not be used elsewhere, and other firms it backed failed too
Solyndra's collapse pushed up solar-panel prices for every buyer
None of the program's other firms ever repaid a dollar of their loans
The hearings cost more in staff time than the loan itself had
context: Bastiat's method: compare the seen benefit to the unseen alternative use of the same capital. Abound Solar (2012), A123 Systems (2012), and Fisker Automotive (2013) also went bankrupt among Section 1705 recipients. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Loan_Programs_Office.

question: A Soviet factory boss got his targets from Moscow in the 1980s, one line on a list of boots, screws, tractors and other products kept by Gosplan, the supply committee Gossnab and the ministries. About how many products did that list hold?
answer: About 200,000
choices: About 200,000
About 200
About 2 million
About 20 billion
context: By the mid-1980s Gosplan itself drew up material balances for only about 2,000 goods; adding the supply committee Gossnab and the industrial ministries brought the products tracked to around 200,000, still far short of the roughly 24 million items the Soviet economy made. Source: O. Yun, Improvement of Soviet Economic Planning (Moscow, 1988), cited by Cockshott and Cottrell.

question: A shopper who found no shoes in the Soviet stores got a pair through a favor from a friend at work. Gosplan's plans always had gaps like that, and ordinary people filled them by trading favors with friends, cousins and coworkers. What was the Russian word for that system of favors?
answer: Blat
choices: Blat
Kvass
Duma
Zek
context: Blat was the informal favor-trading system through which Soviet citizens obtained goods the state could not deliver. It permeated every level from consumer purchases to industrial inputs. Source: Alena Ledeneva, Russia's Economy of Favours (1998).

question: A Soviet tractor-plant manager found that Moscow had forgotten to ship his steel, and there was no market where he could simply buy some. So he sent agents on the road to the capital to work their contacts and pry the steel loose. What were such travelers called?
answer: Tolkachi
choices: Tolkachi
Kulaks
Nomenklatura
Stakhanovites
context: Tolkachi ('pushers') traveled to Moscow to lobby ministries for missing components, expedite deliveries, and negotiate quotas. The role was so common it had a name, and it showed how far the plan fell short of coordinating the economy's many thousands of products in real time. Source: Berliner, Factory and Manager in the USSR.

question: A famous Soviet story tells of a nail-factory manager, paid on the total weight of the nails he shipped, who turned out a handful of huge, useless nails at the end of the month to make his number. In another, a glassworks paid by area turned out panes so thin they shattered on delivery. What is the predictable result of paying for weight or count, never for quality?
answer: Lots of heavy, poorly-made products that nobody wants to use
choices: Lots of heavy, poorly-made products that nobody wants to use
Goods built to last, since every factory wants the planners' praise
Steady output of exactly the goods that shoppers want most
Too few goods of any kind, as managers simply stop trying
context: Storming (shturmovshchina) was the last-week rush to meet monthly, quarterly, or yearly plan targets. It produced low-quality output near month-end and made the phrase 'they pretend to pay us and we pretend to work' a widespread black joke. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System.

question: A socialist economist and scholar of the Soviet economy conceded in 1983 that Ludwig von Mises's calculation problem was real, and that every big planned economy has to reckon with it. He made the admission in his book The Economics of Feasible Socialism. Who was he?
answer: Alec Nove
choices: Alec Nove
Oskar Lange
Michal Kalecki
Paul Sweezy
context: Alec Nove was a British socialist economist and Soviet-studies scholar at the University of Glasgow. The Economics of Feasible Socialism (1983) is one of the most honest inside-the-tradition confrontations with Mises-Hayek. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Nove.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that without real market prices a central planner cannot know what to make, or how much, and his critics trusted that better statistics and faster computers would save the planners. The Soviet Union collapsed instead in 1991, and market prices then did what Gosplan never could. What did those prices do?
answer: Coordinate millions of goods with no committee needed
choices: Coordinate millions of goods with no committee needed
Hold every price steady from one year to the next
Match each region's output to a plan set in advance
Set each worker's wage by the hours a job takes
context: After 1991, market prices in the former Soviet lands coordinated millions of goods with no Gosplan-style committee in charge. To Mises's followers that was the vindication of his 1920 argument: the price system did what no committee could. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation.

question: A reporter writes that two groups have ended up with different outcomes and concludes that one of them must have been treated worse. Thomas Sowell took aim at that line of reasoning in Discrimination and Disparities (2018). He agreed the gaps are real. What did he say a gap shows on its own?
answer: That something differs between them, and not yet what
choices: That something differs between them, and not yet what
That the group with less has been treated worse somewhere
That the two groups began from different places
That too few years were measured for it to mean much
context: Discrimination and Disparities (Basic Books, 2018; revised and enlarged 2019) is aimed at single-factor explanation. Sowell's list of other testable causes includes age distribution, fertility rates, geography, migration history and cultural inheritance. Sources: Hachette/Basic Books title page; Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell); Independent Institute review.

question: Thomas Sowell held up one minority as his main example: shut out of occupations, hemmed in by law and set upon by mobs, it still grew richer than the majority around it. His case comes from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines. Which group was it?
answer: The overseas Chinese
choices: The overseas Chinese
The Rohingya of Myanmar
The Ainu of Japan
The Hmong of Laos
context: The overseas Chinese communities of Southeast Asia are Sowell's most-used case. He pairs them with Lebanese traders in West Africa and Indian merchant communities in East Africa. The Rohingya, the Ainu and the Hmong are minorities whose histories did not follow that pattern. Source: Grokipedia, 'Dominant minority' and 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'.

question: A Lebanese trader arrived poor and resented in West Africa, as an Indian merchant family did in East Africa, and in time both were running a large share of the trade around them. Thomas Sowell says the two cases share one cause, and it is not the countries they landed in. What is it?
answer: The trading skills and business habits they brought, which kept working in a new place
choices: The trading skills and business habits they brought, which kept working in a new place
The colonial officials who preferred outsiders to locals when handing out import licences
The port cities they settled in, which were the only places open to newcomers at the time
The small size of each community, which made trust cheap and contracts easy to enforce
context: This is what Sowell means by human capital being portable: skills, work habits, commercial networks and educational traditions travel with people and go on working in a new country. It is why he studies the same group in several countries -- the surroundings change, the pattern does not. Source: Grokipedia, 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations' and 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell finished in 1998 the last of three linked books, Race and Culture, Migrations and Cultures and Conquests and Cultures, the fruit of fifteen years' research and two journeys around the world. He gave all three one theme. What was it?
answer: That groups carry their own way of life, and their economic histories cannot be read without it
choices: That groups carry their own way of life, and their economic histories cannot be read without it
That conquest reshapes a conquered people faster than any other force in their history
That migration is the single strongest predictor of how wealthy a country will become
That national borders explain more about a group's fortunes than any inherited habit does
context: Race and Culture: A World View (1994), Migrations and Cultures: A World View (1996) and Conquests and Cultures: An International History (1998). Sowell had begun the comparative-groups argument much earlier in Ethnic America: A History (1981). Sources: FEE and Publishers Weekly reviews of Conquests and Cultures; Hoover Institution, 'Race, Culture, and Equality'.

question: Thomas Sowell argues that one English word is doing two jobs at once, and that arguments go wrong when nobody separates them. The second job is the familiar one -- treating people badly on arbitrary assumptions about their race or sex, which is what the law goes after. He labels the first job Discrimination I. What is it?
answer: Telling real differences in quality apart and choosing accordingly
choices: Telling real differences in quality apart and choosing accordingly
Preferring one's own group when the choice is close
Applying a rule strictly to some applicants and loosely to others
Judging a stranger by someone else he happens to resemble
context: Sowell's own wording for Discrimination I is 'an ability to discern differences in the qualities of people and things, and choosing accordingly' -- fact-based distinctions, ideally judging each person as an individual. Discrimination II is 'treating people negatively, based on arbitrary assumptions or aversions.' His complaint is that public argument uses one word for both. Sources: The Federalist, 'Thomas Sowell Explains The Economics Of Discrimination'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: Thomas Sowell went looking for uneven outcomes that no group cause could explain, among children with the same parents, home, schools and family income. He found them in a study of finalists for National Merit Scholarships drawn from families of exactly five children. What did the study show about the eldest child?
answer: The first-born was the finalist more often than the other four siblings combined
choices: The first-born was the finalist more often than the other four siblings combined
The first-born was the finalist about twice as often as the youngest child was
The first-born and the youngest child together supplied nine finalists in ten
The first-born was the finalist in almost exactly one family out of every five
context: Sowell's use of the figure is careful: it is not an argument about who deserves what. It is an argument that huge disparities appear between people who share every background factor a study could control for -- so equal outcomes between whole nations would be the astonishing result, not the expected one. Sources: Walter E. Williams, 'Discrimination and Disparities II' (Creators Syndicate), quoting Sowell; Hoover Institution.

question: Thomas Sowell chose Indonesia for his sharpest case. Chinese families there were a small share of the people, barred from some jobs and hit by deadly riots. What share of the country's wealth does he say they held?
answer: About eighty per cent
choices: About eighty per cent
About fifteen per cent
About thirty-five per cent
About fifty-five per cent
context: Sowell's point is not that hostility was mild -- it was severe and sometimes lethal. It is that severe hostility and economic success sat together, which is exactly what the disparity-proves-discrimination rule says should not happen. Source: Grokipedia, 'Dominant minority' and 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'.

question: An admissions committee sees that a demanding engineering program admits students unevenly across regions and treats the unevenness as the puzzle to solve. Thomas Sowell argues that getting in takes several things at once: schooling, language, family backing, mobility and money. What does he say follows?
answer: Four of the five in place is worth nothing, so even spreading would be the astonishing result
choices: Four of the five in place is worth nothing, so even spreading would be the astonishing result
The committee should weight each of the five by how much it costs a family to supply it
Any region missing a single one of the five will catch up within about a generation
The five must be ranked, because whichever comes first will determine all the others
context: This is the prerequisites argument that opens the book: where success requires multiple prerequisites all present together, it will not be evenly or randomly distributed among individuals, groups, institutions or nations. Sources: Books At A Glance summary of Discrimination and Disparities; Shenvi Apologetics review; CultureWatch.

question: A banking regulator publishes numbers showing that applicants from one neighborhood are turned down for mortgages more often than applicants from another. The regulator concludes the lenders are biased. A reader trained by Thomas Sowell does not call the numbers wrong. Which objection does that reader press first?
answer: The two sets of applicants have to be compared on what the lender actually reads before the gap means anything
choices: The two sets of applicants have to be compared on what the lender actually reads before the gap means anything
The regulator has published only one year of figures, and a single year cannot establish a lending pattern
The lenders operating in the two neighbourhoods are different firms, so their internal rules were never the same
The applicants who expected refusal may not have applied, so the pool itself was shaped before any lender saw it
context: Note the shape of the move: the reader does not announce that the lenders are innocent. Sowell's rule is that a disparity marks the beginning of an investigation, not the end of one, so the next step is to compare the two groups on the things the decision actually turned on. Sources: Independent Institute review, 'Being Careful with Numbers, Words, and Visions'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: A reviewer writes that Thomas Sowell's books amount to a claim that discrimination is a myth. Sowell has answered this charge for forty years, and his answer is not that he has been misread on the details. He says the reviewer has mistaken the kind of claim he is making. What kind is it?
answer: A claim about what evidence is needed to establish a cause, not about whether that cause exists
choices: A claim about what evidence is needed to establish a cause, not about whether that cause exists
A claim about which century the worst mistreatment happened in, not about whether it happened
A claim about the motives of researchers, not about the figures those researchers publish
A claim about which level of government should collect the data, not about what the data show
context: Sowell does not deny that discrimination has existed or that it exists. His argument is methodological: unequal treatment is one candidate cause among several, and it has to be shown with evidence about treatment rather than inferred from the size of a gap. Readers who accept the method can still disagree with him about any particular case -- which is the point of a method. Sources: Independent Institute review; Shenvi Apologetics review of Discrimination and Disparities.

question: Two economists study the same wage gap. The first compares the groups as they stand this year and reads the remaining gap as the measure of mistreatment. Thomas Sowell studies the same groups across generations and across the countries they migrated to. He is not just adding detail; the second method can find something the first cannot even look for. What is it?
answer: Whether the pattern travels with the people when they move to a country with different institutions
choices: Whether the pattern travels with the people when they move to a country with different institutions
Whether the wage figures were gathered by employers or by the government's own statisticians
Whether the gap has widened or narrowed since the last time the same survey was carried out
Whether the two groups are counted in the same industry categories by the agency doing the survey
context: This is why Sowell spent fifteen years and two circuits of the globe on the culture trilogy. If a group's professional attainment holds up in Lagos, London and Chicago alike, the explanation cannot be entirely the treatment they met in any one of those places. Austrians and Chicago economists both use this move -- hold the people constant, change the institutions, and see what survives. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Sociology of race and ethnic relations'; FEE review of Conquests and Cultures.

question: A lawmaker drafts a rule forbidding any organization to sort applicants by any characteristic that turns out uneven from group to group. An airline answers that it screens pilots on logged flight hours, and a bank that it screens borrowers on repayment records, and both come out unevenly. Thomas Sowell's distinction between two meanings of one word predicts the collision. What does he say such a rule reaches?
answer: Fact-based sorting on real qualifications, not only sorting on arbitrary aversion
choices: Fact-based sorting on real qualifications, not only sorting on arbitrary aversion
Only the largest firms, since a small firm can rarely afford to sort applicants at all
The regulators before the firms, since the sorting rules were written by agencies first
Every industry equally, since no occupation screens applicants more heavily than another
context: This is Discrimination I and Discrimination II colliding inside one word. Sowell's claim is not that the law should permit prejudice; it is that a rule written against uneven outcomes catches the airline's flight-hours check along with the prejudice, because both produce uneven outcomes. Where to draw the line afterwards is a live political argument -- Sowell's contribution is insisting that the two things be named separately before anyone argues about it. Sources: The Federalist, 'Thomas Sowell Explains The Economics Of Discrimination'; Shenvi Apologetics review.

question: Thomas Sowell answered opponents of charter schools, who pointed to the flaws of one particular charter, with the short question he had long put to anyone calling a shortage, a high price or a low wage unacceptable. Almost no one, he said, had an answer ready. What was his question?
answer: Compared to what?
choices: Compared to what?
At what cost?
And then what happens?
Who bears the risk?
context: Thomas Sowell (born 1930), the Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution since 1980, named 'Compared to what?' as the first of three questions he said would destroy most arguments on the left; the other two were 'At what cost?' and 'What hard evidence do you have?' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'; quotefancy.com/quote/920957.

question: At a town meeting a speaker says the market has failed the town's working families and the council must step in and run things better. Thomas Sowell's reply denies none of it; it shifts a burden onto the speaker. What must the speaker now produce?
answer: The name of the institution he would put in its place
choices: The name of the institution he would put in its place
The moral case for private ownership of a business
A forecast of what local wages will do next year
A count of the families now living on credit
context: The move is a demand for a NAMED alternative. Until the speaker says which real body would run things -- a city agency, a state board, a federal programme -- there is nothing to weigh the market against, and the argument is holding a real thing up against a wish. Source: Harold Demsetz, 'Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint', Journal of Law and Economics 12 (1969).

question: A governor signs a higher tax on business, and the treasury does take in more money that first year. Thomas Sowell, in Applied Economics (2003), calls that stage one and says elected officials stop thinking right there. Why do they stop?
answer: They do not think beyond the next election
choices: They do not think beyond the next election
They are never taught any economics at all
They rely on forecasts their staff invent
They believe firms cannot afford to move
context: Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One (Basic Books, 2003; 2nd ed. 2008) argues that basic economics gets misapplied because politicians think only in stage one -- the immediate result of an action -- and, in Sowell's words, 'do not think beyond the next election.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: Harold Demsetz took aim in a 1969 paper at Kenneth Arrow, who had demonstrated that a market might produce too little of some goods, new inventions among them, and had taken for granted that government would do better. Arrow never checked, Demsetz complained: he had weighed a real, flawed market against a government found only in the imagination. What did Demsetz call that habit?
answer: The nirvana approach
choices: The nirvana approach
The scientistic approach
The aggregative approach
The positivist approach
context: Demsetz wrote that 'those who adopt the nirvana viewpoint seek to discover discrepancies between the ideal and the real and if discrepancies are found, they deduce that the real is inefficient.' Later economists relabelled it the 'nirvana fallacy.' Sources: econlib.org, Biography of Harold Demsetz; Wikipedia, 'Nirvana fallacy'.
