question: Arthur Scargill led Britain's mineworkers out on strike in March 1984 to stop the closure of pits that lost money. Margaret Thatcher's government had quietly piled up coal for years beforehand, and simply waited. A year later the strike was over. What does that year teach about the strike as a weapon?
answer: It works only if the strikers can outlast the losses of going unpaid
choices: It works only if the strikers can outlast the losses of going unpaid
It works best in an industry that is losing money anyway
It works only when the government owns the industry struck
It works as long as the strikers stay peaceful throughout
context: Scargill led the NUM from 1982 and was the strike's public face; the government had spent years stockpiling coal and had prepared for the confrontation. The miners voted to go back in March 1985 without a settlement. Source: Wikipedia, 1984-1985 United Kingdom miners' strike.

question: London's stockbrokers began trading under new rules on 27 October 1986. Fixed commissions were gone, foreign firms could join the exchange, and screens were replacing the shouting floor. The press gave the day a nickname that stuck. What was it?
answer: The Big Bang
choices: The Big Bang
Black Monday
The Quiet Revolution
The Great Opening
context: Stripping old rules off a market to open it up is deregulation, and the Big Bang is credited with making the City of London one of the two global financial centres of the following generation. Black Monday is a different day, the stock-market crash of 19 October 1987. Source: Wikipedia, Big Bang (financial markets).

question: Margaret Thatcher's chancellors cut Britain's top income tax rate from 83 percent in 1979, when a high earner kept just seventeen pence of each extra pound, to 40 percent by the budget of 1988. They leaned on a case made by Arthur Laffer, an American economist. What did they say happens when the top rate falls that far?
answer: People work and invest more, so tax receipts hold up at the lower rate
choices: People work and invest more, so tax receipts hold up at the lower rate
Revenue falls at first, so public spending has to fall to match
Prices climb as people spend their tax savings all at once
Firms cut wages, since workers now keep more of each pound
context: Geoffrey Howe cut the top rate from 83 to 60 percent in his first budget of 1979, and Nigel Lawson, Chancellor from 1983 to 1989, took it to 40 percent in the 1988 Budget. Source: OMFIF, 'Nigel Lawson: influential politician and architect of Thatcherism.'

question: Antony Fisher, a former RAF fighter pilot, read a condensed version of Friedrich Hayek's wartime book in 1945 and went to ask the author how to fight back. Hayek's advice was to keep clear of elected office and fight the battle of ideas instead, and in the mid-1950s Fisher opened a London think tank for free-market ideas. What reasoning lay behind Hayek's advice?
answer: Politicians follow what voters think possible, so ideas must be won first
choices: Politicians follow what voters think possible, so ideas must be won first
A candidate's party would bury his ideas to win the next election
Laws written in haste by one man are soon undone by the next
Elected office would leave him too little time to read and write
context: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) at 2 Lord North Street pumped out short, sharp free-market monographs from 1957 onwards and became the model for over 150 similar think-tanks Fisher would help seed worldwide. Source: Economic History Society, 'Waging the War of Ideas: the Institute of Economic Affairs.'

question: A New York broker watched panic selling sweep the Stock Exchange on two days late in October 1929. Traders named both days forever after, each name pairing a color with a weekday. Which pair marked the crash?
answer: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
choices: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
Black Monday and Black Friday
Red Thursday and Red Tuesday
Black Wednesday and Red Friday
context: Black Thursday (October 24, 1929) began the panic; Black Tuesday (October 29, 1929) broke the market. Both names have been the standard shorthand ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929.

question: A newspaperman began publishing an index in 1896 that tracked a small basket of big companies, and by the 1920s every investor watched it. It hit a record in September 1929, weeks before the crash, and took decades to climb back. Which index was it?
answer: The Dow Jones Industrial Average
choices: The Dow Jones Industrial Average
The S&P 500
The NASDAQ Composite
The Russell 2000
context: The Dow peaked at 381.17 on September 3, 1929, then bottomed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932 -- an 89% peak-to-trough decline. The S&P 500 in modern form didn't exist yet, and NASDAQ was created in 1971. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: A broker of the 1920s let a customer buy shares with borrowed money: the customer put down part of the price in cash, and the broker lent him the rest. Traders called it buying on margin. At the loosest brokers of the boom, how little of the price might a customer put down?
answer: About a tenth
choices: About a tenth
About a quarter
About a third
About half
context: In the loosest margin accounts of the 1920s a customer could put down about a tenth of the price and borrow the rest, so $100 held a $1,000 position; the Federal Reserve's history of the crash calls 10 percent typical, though by 1929 many brokers had raised their margins toward 40 or 50 percent. When prices fell, brokers issued margin calls, forcing cascading liquidation. Sources: federalreservehistory.org/essays/stock-market-crash-of-1929; Rappoport and White (1994).

question: A clerk on the New York Stock Exchange watched the ticker tape fall hours behind the market on Tuesday, 29 October 1929, as sell orders piled up faster than the machines could print prices. The day's volume stood as a record for almost forty years. Roughly how many shares changed hands?
answer: About sixteen million
choices: About sixteen million
About one million
About one hundred million
About five hundred million
context: October 29, 1929 saw about 16 million shares traded on the NYSE -- a volume record that held for nearly 40 years. The Dow fell nearly 12 percent that day. Source: nyse.com historical trading records.

question: A man who bought shares at the top in September 1929 saw prices keep sliding for almost three years after the crash, as banks failed, factories shut and one American worker in four lost his job. The market's leading index hit bottom in July 1932. About what percent of its value at the 1929 peak had it lost?
answer: About 89 percent
choices: About 89 percent
About 22 percent
About 50 percent
About 33 percent
context: Peak 381.17 on September 3, 1929; trough 41.22 on July 8, 1932 -- roughly an 89% collapse. Compare: October 1987 crash ~22% in a day, 2008 GFC ~54% peak-to-trough. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices historical data.

question: Irving Fisher, a Yale economist as respected as any in America, spoke to an audience on 15 October 1929, two weeks before the crash, and gave his view of share prices. His forecast became the most quoted in economics. What did he say the market had reached?
answer: A permanently high plateau
choices: A permanently high plateau
A dangerous speculative peak
The end of its long bull run
A short-term technical top
context: Fisher's October 15, 1929 statement -- 'stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau' -- became a cautionary quote about expert overconfidence. Fisher lost most of his personal fortune in the crash. Source: New York Times, October 16, 1929.

question: A cable from Stockholm reached Friedrich Hayek in Salzburg in the autumn of 1974: he had won the economics prize. He was best known for arguing that planning fails however brilliant the planners, because no committee can collect the facts that keep an economy running. What is that idea called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The invisible hand
Supply and demand
Diminishing returns
context: The cable from Stockholm reached Hayek in Salzburg. The knowledge problem is the argument of his 1945 paper 'The Use of Knowledge in Society': the facts an economy runs on are scattered across millions of people and reach others only as prices. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1974 press release.

question: Friedrich Hayek stood at a lectern in Stockholm on 11 December 1974 and spent his prize lecture attacking his own profession. Economists, he charged, had borrowed the equations and confident forecasts of physics and claimed they could steer a national economy like a machine. What was the lecture's title?
answer: The Pretence of Knowledge
choices: The Pretence of Knowledge
The Road to Serfdom
The Use of Knowledge in Society
The Constitution of Liberty
context: The lecture is short -- about fifteen minutes -- and reads as a compressed statement of the Hayekian critique of macroeconomics. The three other choices are all real Hayek works of other decades: Road to Serfdom (1944), 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (an American Economic Review article, 1945), Constitution of Liberty (1960). Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: A physicist can predict where a falling rock will land, Friedrich Hayek reminded his Stockholm audience in 1974, because rocks follow fixed laws while people do not. Economists, he said, were claiming to forecast a whole economy the same way. What had he been calling that imitation since the 1940s?
answer: Scientism
choices: Scientism
Positivism
Empiricism
Rationalism
context: Hayek had used 'scientism' as the target of an earlier essay, 'Scientism and the Study of Society' (1942); the Nobel lecture is the mature restatement. Positivism, empiricism, and rationalism are real philosophy-of-science labels for adjacent doctrines, but none is the name Hayek gave to the imitation move. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Friedrich Hayek asked his Stockholm audience in December 1974 where the facts that decide what a whole country produces really sit. Where did he insist they sit?
answer: Dispersed across millions of individual minds
choices: Dispersed across millions of individual minds
In the hands of the central bank's research staff
Encoded in slowly-updating statistical time series
Inside the state's national-income accounts
context: This is the direct application of Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' -- the knowledge relevant to allocation is the local, tacit, contextual knowledge of individuals, communicated through prices, not through any central agency. The three other choices describe the sources macro forecasters actually reach for; Hayek's point is that these are precisely NOT where the decision-relevant knowledge lives. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Friedrich Hayek aimed his Stockholm prize lecture of 1974 at a view that had ruled economics in Britain and America since the late 1930s: that governments can smooth out recessions by pumping up overall demand through public spending and low interest rates. Which book of 1936 founded that approach?
answer: John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Alvin Hansen's Fiscal Policy and Business Cycles
Paul Samuelson's Economics
Joan Robinson's The Economics of Imperfect Competition
context: Keynes's General Theory (1936) reframed macroeconomics around aggregate demand and government fiscal management. The three other choices are all real texts of the Keynesian tradition -- Hansen (1941) popularised Keynes in America; Samuelson's textbook (1948) taught two generations; Robinson (1933) was a Cambridge Keynesian. Hayek's Nobel lecture is aimed at the whole tradition Keynes founded. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Friedrich Hayek's Stockholm audience heard him end his 1974 lecture on a warning, not a proof. Any student of society who loses sight of how little he can know, he said, ends up helping the fatal drive to rule other men, and in the end becomes the destroyer of a civilization. How did Hayek describe that civilization?
answer: That has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals
choices: That has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals
That has been designed by the great political thinkers of the age
That has been built by the guiding hand of the modern state
That has been forged in the industrial revolutions of the nineteenth century
context: The full closing sentence: 'a striving which makes him not only a tyrant over his fellows, but which may well make him the destroyer of a civilization which no brain has designed but which has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals.' This is Hayek's spontaneous-order doctrine restated as a moral warning. Source: NobelPrize.org, Hayek prize lecture.

question: Alfred Nobel left money in his will of 1895 for five prizes, and economics was not among them. Much later, in Nobel's memory, Sweden's central bank founded an economics prize, and in 1969 it went to two European economists who built mathematical tools still used to model whole economies. Who were they?
answer: Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen
choices: Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen
Paul Samuelson and Simon Kuznets
F.A. Hayek and Gunnar Myrdal
Milton Friedman and George Stigler
context: The first economics prize (1969) went jointly to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen for econometrics; the original Nobel prizes, first given in 1901, are physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The 1974 award to Hayek and Myrdal was the sixth economics prize. Source: NobelPrize.org, Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

question: Poland's communist government outlawed the Solidarity union under martial law in December 1981, and the union lived on underground for eight years. The government claimed it alone spoke for the workers and that they needed no other voice. Why does a free union frighten a communist government?
answer: It gives ordinary workers real power the government does not control
choices: It gives ordinary workers real power the government does not control
It drives up wages until the planned budget cannot pay them
It splits the workers into rival camps that fight each other
It takes over the factories and runs them for its own profit
context: Solidarnosc was founded in August 1980 at the Gdansk shipyard strikes. It was the first independent trade union in the Warsaw Pact. Banned under martial law in December 1981, it survived underground through the 1980s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union).

question: Lech Walesa, an electrician, led the shipyard workers of Gdansk out on strike in August 1980, and they built a union the ruling Communist Party did not control: Solidarity. Their demand was never mainly about wages. What did the strikers most want that the system did not allow?
answer: The freedom to bargain and choose their own leaders
choices: The freedom to bargain and choose their own leaders
The right to emigrate freely to West Germany
A seat for the union on the Party's Politburo
A share of the profit from every ship they built
context: Lech Walesa was a shipyard electrician who became Solidarity chairman, won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize, and served as President of Poland 1990-95. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lech_Wa%C5%82%C4%99sa.

question: Solidarity's candidates ran against Poland's Communist Party in June 1989 in an election only partly free: the Party kept most seats in the lower house, the Sejm, for itself, while every seat in a brand-new Senate was open. How did Solidarity do?
answer: It won 99 of 100 Senate seats and every contested Sejm seat
choices: It won 99 of 100 Senate seats and every contested Sejm seat
It won about half the Senate and a third of the contested Sejm seats
It won 35 of 100 Senate seats and a handful in the Sejm
It won no seats at all after calling a national boycott
context: The Round Table Agreement allowed contested elections for the Senate and one-third of the Sejm. Solidarity won 99/100 Senate seats and swept the contested Sejm seats. The first Solidarity-led government followed in August 1989 under Prime Minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Polish_legislative_election.

question: Winston Churchill spoke of an iron curtain across Europe, from the Baltic down to the Adriatic, and the curtain took shape in wire, concrete and watchtowers. East Germany called its stretch through Berlin an anti-fascist protection rampart. Who was the barrier really built to stop?
answer: People trying to leave the communist side for the free side
choices: People trying to leave the communist side for the free side
Western spies and saboteurs slipping into the East
Smugglers carrying Western goods into the East
Western armies massing for an invasion
context: Hungarian border guards began cutting the barrier along the Austrian border on May 2, 1989. East Germans vacationing in Hungary began crossing on foot into Austria; the Pan-European Picnic of August 19, 1989 opened the flow to a torrent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Curtain.

question: Guenter Schabowski, a spokesman for East Germany's Politburo, botched an answer at a press conference on the evening of November 9, 1989, and declared the Berlin Wall's crossings open. Nobody had warned the guards, and within hours crowds were pouring through and dancing on the Wall. What does that stampede suggest about life under the East's planned economy?
answer: Many people had wanted out for a long time and could not say so before
choices: Many people had wanted out for a long time and could not say so before
Most had come to cheer the Party's promise of new reforms
A sudden food shortage that week had driven people to flee
The crowds were mostly Party members testing the new rules
context: Schabowski, a Politburo spokesman, botched the answer at a press conference the evening of November 9, 1989. The border guards were not warned; East Berliners walked through and danced on the Wall that night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Schabowski.

question: A crowd in Prague shook its house keys late in 1989 rather than throw stones, amid weeks of marches and a general strike. No tanks rolled, nobody was shot, and Vaclav Havel, the dissident playwright, was president of Czechoslovakia before the year was out. The country named the change for its gentleness. What is it called?
answer: The Velvet Revolution
choices: The Velvet Revolution
The Rose Revolution
The Prague Uprising
The Bohemian Turn
context: The Velvet Revolution (November 17 - December 29, 1989) was led by the Civic Forum (Czech lands) and Public Against Violence (Slovakia). The playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on December 29. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_Revolution.

question: Robert Heilbroner, a democratic-socialist economist at the New School who had argued all his life for planning over markets, wrote an essay for The New Yorker in September 1990. In it he gave the old socialist calculation debate a three-word epitaph. What were the three words?
answer: Mises was right
choices: Mises was right
The plan failed
Socialism has died
Prices always win
context: Heilbroner's September 10, 1990 New Yorker essay 'After Communism' delivered the three-word verdict from a witness who had spent his life on the other side of the calculation debate. It became the epitaph of the debate. Source: The New Yorker, September 10 1990.

question: Polish voters queued on 4 June 1989 to vote in their first partly free election in decades. That same day, on the other side of the world, the Chinese army cleared the great square at the heart of its capital with tanks and gunfire, killing citizens to keep the communists in power. What was that other event of 4 June 1989?
answer: The Tiananmen Square killings
choices: The Tiananmen Square killings
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Iran-Iraq ceasefire
The Reykjavik summit
context: June 4, 1989 saw both Solidarity's Polish election sweep and the People's Liberation Army's crackdown in Beijing. The two events on the same day frame Chinese and European responses to their 1980s reform pressures. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre.

question: Mikhail Gorbachev declined to send tanks west in 1989, and by the end of 1991 the Soviet Union itself was gone, catching most Western experts flat-footed. One small school of economists had forecast the collapse decades before, arguing from 1920 on that central planning must sooner or later seize up, because planners without real prices are working blind. Which school was it?
answer: The Austrian economists
choices: The Austrian economists
The Keynesian macroeconomists
The rational-expectations theorists
The New Keynesians
context: Mises (1920, 1922), Hayek (1935, 1945), and Rothbard (1962) all argued the Soviet-style economy was calculation-impossible and therefore ultimately unsustainable. Most Western sovietology missed it. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: Alan Greenspan began raising the Federal Reserve's overnight rate on 30 June 2004, after holding it at one percent for a year following the slump of 2001. The first step was deliberately small. How big was it?
answer: 25 basis points
choices: 25 basis points
50 basis points
100 basis points
10 basis points
context: The June 30 2004 quarter-point hike moved the funds rate from 1.00% to 1.25%. It began a tightening cycle that would prove one of the most consequential -- and most predictable in its consequences -- in Fed history. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: Ben Bernanke chaired the June 2006 meeting at which the Federal Reserve made the last of seventeen rate rises in a row, each a quarter point, a run begun under Alan Greenspan in June 2004. Where did the rate stand at its peak?
answer: 5.25 percent
choices: 5.25 percent
3.5 percent
6.5 percent
2 percent
context: The last hike, June 29 2006, was Greenspan's successor Ben Bernanke's -- Bernanke had taken the chair February 1 2006. The seventeen consecutive quarter-point hikes ended at a 5.25% federal funds rate. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: A bond trader read the Federal Reserve's statement after a meeting in 2004 and found the same two words as the time before: 'measured pace.' The Fed's rate committee chose such coded, repetitive language on purpose. Why?
answer: To signal its next move without surprising markets
choices: To signal its next move without surprising markets
To hide policy from investors
To keep Congress out of the loop
To satisfy legal reporting rules
context: The phrase 'measured pace' meant '25 basis points per meeting.' It became a Wall Street cliche through 2004-06 as traders learned to expect the predictable quarter-point cadence. Source: Grokipedia 'Alan Greenspan' (2026-09-05).

question: A family signed for an adjustable-rate mortgage in 2004 on the strength of a cheap teaser rate that would last two or three years. After that the loan would reset to market rates, in a world the Federal Reserve's seventeen rate rises had remade. What happened to many such families' monthly payments?
answer: They doubled or tripled
choices: They doubled or tripled
They dropped by half
They stayed flat
They increased by about 5 percent
context: Adjustable-rate mortgages with 2-year teaser periods reset in 2006-07 to the new market rates. Many households saw payments double or triple. Subprime foreclosure notices climbed sharply in the second half of 2006. Source: Grokipedia 'Subprime mortgage crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: A saver comparing bonds in 2006 found two-year ones paying more than ten-year ones, though a ten-year loan normally pays more than a two-year one, since time carries risk. Bond desks call that flip an inverted yield curve. In American history, what has it been the most reliable warning of?
answer: A recession within the next year or two
choices: A recession within the next year or two
A stock-market boom in the next few months
A big rise in the value of the dollar
A crash in commodity prices
context: The yield-curve inversion signal comes from Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 New York Fed research paper. Every US recession since 1968 has been preceded by a sustained inversion. The 2006 signal was accurate: NBER dated the recession start December 2007. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: Two economists at the New York Fed measured in 1996 how well one bond-market shape, short-term rates rising above long-term ones, foretold what came next for the American economy. Writers on the 2008 crisis quoted their paper again and again. Who were the two?
answer: Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin
choices: Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin
Ben Bernanke and Alan Blinder
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Krugman and Maurice Obstfeld
context: Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 paper 'The Yield Curve as a Predictor of US Recessions' documented the empirical reliability of the signal across every US recession since 1968. Source: Grokipedia 'Yield curve' (2026-09-05).

question: A mortgage lender watched delinquencies on subprime loans keep rising in 2007, while short-term rates stayed above long-term ones for most of the year, an inversion that had begun in 2006. The National Bureau of Economic Research, the private body that dates American recessions, later fixed when the Great Recession began. What date did it give?
answer: December 2007
choices: December 2007
September 2008
March 2007
January 2009
context: The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee later fixed the recession start at December 2007. Bear Stearns's hedge funds had collapsed July-August 2007; Lehman failed September 15 2008. The Fed's own recession-warning tool had rung the bell for two years before the crisis fully arrived. Source: Grokipedia 'Great Recession' (2026-09-05).

question: Ben Bernanke went before Congress in 2007 as delinquencies climbed on subprime mortgages, the risky home loans made to borrowers with poor credit. Two Bear Stearns funds blew up that summer. Bernanke and other Fed officials kept using one calming word for the trouble. What did they say?
answer: The problems were contained
choices: The problems were contained
The situation was transitory
The turbulence would soon pass
The stress was normal seasonal noise
context: Bernanke and other Fed officials used 'contained' repeatedly through 2007 to describe subprime stress. The phrase would join 'transitory' in the museum of Fed forecasting errors. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: Sheila Bair, who headed the agency that insures bank deposits during the crash of 2008, wrote afterwards that it was 'the most predictable financial crisis in American history.' Which two warning signs had been in plain view for years before it struck?
answer: A rapidly rising housing bubble and a huge boom in loans to people who could not repay them
choices: A rapidly rising housing bubble and a huge boom in loans to people who could not repay them
A sudden shortage of oil combined with a war in the Middle East
A drop in immigration combined with a colder-than-normal winter
A jump in software company failures combined with a stock split
context: Bair's phrase captured what many observers had warned about in real time: the yield curve had inverted, subprime foreclosures were climbing, and Fed officials were dismissing both signals. Source: Bair, Bull by the Horns (2012).

question: A homebuyer borrowed cheaply in 2003, while Alan Greenspan held the Fed's rate at one percent and house prices climbed. Greenspan and then Ben Bernanke raised it seventeen times in a row, and by 2006 the yield curve had inverted. The Fed's leaders kept reassuring Congress through 2007. What recognition about central banks does the sequence press?
answer: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
choices: The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year
The Fed always acts immediately on yield-curve inversion signals
Yield-curve signals are unreliable in modern markets
Central banks always respond correctly to market-based recession warnings
context: The full pattern is comic if it were not so damaging: cheap money 2003-04 built the housing bubble; tight money 2004-06 popped it; the yield-curve inversion warned of recession from late 2006; Fed leadership called the stress 'contained' through 2007. The tool rang the bell; the institution ignored the bell. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: A Wall Street bank founded before the American Civil War filed in court on 15 September 2008 for protection from creditors it owed something like $613 billion, the largest bankruptcy in American history. It had loaded its books with mortgage bonds. Which firm was it?
answer: Lehman Brothers
choices: Lehman Brothers
Bear Stearns
Merrill Lynch
Goldman Sachs
context: Lehman had 25,000 employees worldwide and was the country's fourth-largest investment bank. Bear Stearns had already been swallowed by JPMorgan in a rescue that March; Merrill Lynch was sold to Bank of America on the same weekend Lehman failed; Goldman Sachs converted to a bank holding company a week later to survive. Only Lehman was allowed to fail outright. Source: Wikipedia, Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers.

question: Peter Schiff, who ran a small brokerage in Connecticut, published a book in early 2007 foretelling, in order, a crash in housing, a crisis in the banks and a falling dollar. Within about a year all three were unfolding. What was the book called?
answer: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
choices: Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
Too Big to Fail: The Inside Story of How Wall Street and Washington Fought to Save the Financial System
House of Cards: A Tale of Hubris and Wretched Excess on Wall Street
context: Crash Proof appeared in early 2007 and reads today as an eerie sequential forecast of the events of 2007-08. The three other choices are real books about the crisis written after the fact: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010), Andrew Ross Sorkin's Too Big to Fail (2009) and William Cohan's House of Cards (2009). Source: Wikipedia, Crash Proof.

question: Ben Bernanke told Congress in March 2007 that the trouble among the riskiest home loans seemed 'likely to be contained.' Eighteen months later the financial system nearly stopped. Panelists on cable news had laughed on air at Peter Schiff when he warned of a crash. What does the episode show about experts?
answer: Even experts can miss huge risks that a few outsiders see
choices: Even experts can miss huge risks that a few outsiders see

Bernanke chaired the Fed from February 2006 to January 2014 and was in the chair when he gave the March 2007 testimony. The honest conclusion is not that anyone lied: even the top experts often cannot see a crisis coming.

question: A homeowner's adjustable mortgage payment jumped in 2006, as it did for a great mass of borrowers at once. The Fed had raised its rate in seventeen quarter-point steps from June 2004 to 5.25 percent; home prices began to fall and more borrowers stopped paying. Which theory says cheap credit had made long projects look profitable until normal rates exposed them?
answer: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
choices: The Austrian Business Cycle Theory of malinvestment revealed
The Keynesian liquidity trap
Minsky's financial-instability hypothesis of endogenous fragility
Real business cycle theory of exogenous technology shocks
context: The Austrian claim: cheap credit made long-duration projects (in this case housing developments and mortgage assets) look profitable; when rates returned to something like the natural rate, the mismatch between the projects started and the saving to sustain them was revealed and collapsed. The three other choices are real rival cycle theories from Keynes (liquidity trap), Hyman Minsky (financial instability), and Kydland-Prescott (real-business-cycle) -- all applied to the same crisis by their proponents. Source: Mises Institute, 'Hayek on Industrial Fluctuations.'

question: Ron Paul of Texas warned a House committee in 2003 that two giant mortgage firms, quietly backed by Washington, were pumping up a false boom in home prices. His bill to strip their backing went nowhere, and five years later the housing market crashed. Why does a quiet government guarantee help a private company feed a boom like that?
answer: It lets the company take huge risks because taxpayers will cover the losses
choices: It lets the company take huge risks because taxpayers will cover the losses
It forces the company to hold extra capital against every loan it buys
It caps the interest the company may charge on any home loan
It ties the company's lending to the Fed's rate every quarter
context: Paul's Free Housing Market Enhancement Act would have stripped Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac of their government sponsorship; it went nowhere. Barney Frank, the ranking Democrat on the same committee, defended the two companies against warnings like Paul's. Source: RonPaulQuotes, 2003 testimony.

question: The Federal Reserve cut its key rate to the floor after the crash of 2008 and began buying government and mortgage bonds that would not mature for years, paying with freshly created reserves. Three rounds ran between 2008 and 2012, and the Fed's balance sheet grew from under $1 trillion to more than $4 trillion by 2014. What is the name for buying on that scale?
answer: Quantitative easing
choices: Quantitative easing
Open-market operations
The discount window
Reserve-requirement adjustment
context: Quantitative easing (QE) was the label the Fed adopted for buying long-dated Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities directly with newly-created reserves, once the funds rate had hit its zero lower bound. The three other choices are all real, older Fed policy tools: open-market operations (routine short-Treasury buying and selling), the discount window (direct emergency lending to banks), and reserve-requirement adjustment (changing the fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves). QE was the historically new instrument. Source: Brookings, 'The Fed's Balance Sheet.'

question: Thomas Woods, a senior fellow of the Mises Institute in Alabama, wrote the Austrian school's answer to the crash of 2008, and it came out in 2009. The book laid the blame on easy Federal Reserve money and on Washington's drive to put families into mortgages, and it made the New York Times bestseller list. What did Woods call the book?
answer: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
choices: Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed
The Big Short: Inside the Doomsday Machine
This Time is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
Stress Test: Reflections on Financial Crises
context: Thomas E. Woods Jr.'s Meltdown (February 2009) frames the crash as a straight Austrian-Business-Cycle case study -- Fed cheap credit, malinvestment in housing, inevitable liquidation, bailouts prolonging the disease. It reached number 11 on the New York Times hardcover nonfiction list. The three other choices are real books about the crisis: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010), Reinhart and Rogoff's This Time is Different (2009), and Timothy Geithner's Stress Test (2014). Source: Wikipedia, Meltdown (Woods book).

question: Jerome Powell's Federal Reserve bought debt at record speed in 2020, and M2, the count of dollars in checking and savings accounts and money funds, grew faster than in any peacetime stretch America had known. answer: About $21.7 trillion
choices: About $21.7 trillion

context: M2 rose from about $15.4T in February 2020 to a peak near $21.7T in April 2022 -- a 40%+ jump in about two years, the fastest peacetime monetary expansion in US history. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2023/may/the-rise-and-fall-of-m2).

question: A small group of American analysts warned in the spring of 2020 that the Federal Reserve's flood of new money would reach consumer prices within a year or two, and that the rise would last. Which school of economics did they draw on for that call?
answer: The Austrian school (Mises, Hayek, Rothbard)
choices: The Austrian school (Mises, Hayek, Rothbard)
The Keynesian school (Samuelson, Krugman)
The Modern Monetary Theory school (Kelton, Wray)
The New Classical school (Lucas, Sargent)
context: Schiff and other hard-money analysts used Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1931) to argue in 2020-21 that the Fed's monetary expansion would produce persistent inflation on a two-year lag. Milton Friedman's monetarist tradition, though not strictly Austrian, made a parallel prediction. Source: SchiffGold podcast archive 2020-21 (https://www.schiffgold.com/peters-podcast/peter-schiff-2021-the-year-of-inflation).

question: Milton Friedman put his rule for inflation into a single sentence in a talk he gave in India in 1963. What does his sentence say produces inflation?
answer: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output
choices: It is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output

context: From Friedman's 1963 talk 'Inflation: Causes and Consequences' delivered in India: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon in the sense that it is and can be produced only by a more rapid increase in the quantity of money than in output.' Source: Wikiquote / Hoover Institution reprints.

question: Jerome Powell's Federal Reserve raised its target 525 basis points within roughly sixteen months from March 2022, taking it from near zero to 5.25 to 5.5 percent, to bring prices back down. Which earlier chairman's campaign is the only one people alive today can compare with it?
answer: Paul Volcker's 1979-1982 campaign
choices: Paul Volcker's 1979-1982 campaign
Alan Greenspan's 1994-1995 campaign
Arthur Burns's 1972-1974 campaign
Ben Bernanke's 2015-2018 campaign
context: The FOMC raised its target 525 bp between March 2022 and July 2023, the fastest tightening cycle in four decades -- rivalled in pace only by Paul Volcker's 1979-82 campaign, which pushed rates near 20% to crush inflation. Sources: San Francisco Fed Economic Letter June 2024; Richmond Fed Economic Brief 23-26.

question: Stephanie Kelton and other modern-monetary-theory writers argued that government spending paid for with freshly created dollars is limited only by real things, workers, factories and materials, not by political will, and that the point where prices would take off was still far away. By June 2022 American prices were rising over nine percent a year, up from about one percent early in 2021. What did critics say the sequence demonstrated?
answer: The limit Kelton's school called far off had already been reached
choices: The limit Kelton's school called far off had already been reached
The rise came from snarled supply chains, so the theory stood
The theory held, but Congress had ignored its advice on taxes
Deficits matter only once foreign lenders stop buying bonds
context: Kelton's 2020 book argued the binding constraint on federal spending was not deficits but real resources and inflation; critics point to 2021-23 CPI running 1.4% -> 9.1% as real-time falsification of the practical judgment that the resource constraint was not yet close. Source: 'The Deficit Myth' (2020); Mises Institute review (https://mises.org/mises-wire/review-stephanie-keltons-deficit-myth).

question: Jerome Powell had used one calming word for rising prices over and over through 2021. He finally told senators at a hearing that the time had probably come to retire the word, and the Fed began raising rates the next March. In which month did he drop it?

question: Jesse Felder, a hedge-fund manager, argued around 2018 that a single cause was lifting houses, shares, art and collectibles all at once, unlike the dot-com craze, which had lifted a single sector. He made a phrase for it popular. What is the phrase?

question: Karl Case and Robert Shiller built the index Americans use to track house prices, and from January 2020 it climbed about 45 percent in thirty months. What was its fastest twelve-month gain in that stretch?

question: A small investor bought into the S&P 500, the index of America's five hundred largest companies, at its pandemic low on 23 March 2020. The Federal Reserve kept its rate at zero and bought bonds by the trillion, and the index peaked at the turn of 2022. About what percent had it risen?

question: A Bitcoin buyer paid about $4,000 a coin in the panic of March 2020. The Federal Reserve then created trillions of new dollars, while the supply of bitcoin is capped at twenty-one million coins. The price peaked in November 2021. About how high did it go?

question: A small trader on the Reddit board WallStreetBets bought shares in January 2021 in two struggling companies that short-sellers were betting would fall. question: A collector paid a large sum in 2021 for a picture of a cartoon ape, buying not the image itself but a record of ownership kept on a blockchain. Such non-fungible tokens crashed by more than ninety percent within two years. What did sales of them total in 2021?

question: A startup founder took his private company public in 2021 without the usual listing process, simply by merging it with a cash shell that had listed itself first. Shells like that raised well over $160 billion that year, then all but vanished by 2023. What are they called?

question: Cathie Wood bet her fund heavily on trendy technology shares and beat the market by a wide margin, a run that made her famous. From its peak in February 2021 the fund fell about 80 percent. What lesson does the fall teach about a fund packed into a few hot stocks?

question: A finance minister with an empty treasury seizes the lands of his country's largest organization and prints paper money said to be backed by those acres. What is the danger in this kind of paper money?

The livre tournois

question: A trader in revolutionary France who priced gold above paper assignats in 1793 broke a new law of the Convention. Farmers and traders had lost faith in the notes and wanted coin, and the state answered not by printing less but by raising the penalty. What was the top penalty?

question: Frederic Bastiat taught readers to set what a policy shows beside what it hides. The revolutionaries printed assignats against seized Church land through the 1790s until the notes were nearly worthless. Which pairing does Bastiat's test give for that episode?

question: A Viennese economist argued in a book on money of 1912 that anything which becomes money must first have been prized for another use, or no one could say what it was worth on its first day. Who was he?

question: Peter St Onge and Saifedean Ammous argued that Frank Shostak had read Bitcoin's history too narrowly. Shostak had said Bitcoin failed Mises's test because it had never been anything but a digital token before people traded it as money. What did the two claim instead?

question: Bitcoin's defenders answered the Austrians who said it failed Mises's rule by tracing how a hobby item came to work as money. Bitcoiners still celebrate one step on that road every May, the first known purchase anyone made with bitcoin. What did ten thousand coins buy that day?

question: Frank Shostak and Saifedean Ammous applied Mises's rule of 1912 to Bitcoin and reached opposite verdicts, and the Austrian school argued over it for years. What broader lesson does the dispute teach about how a serious school should treat a new case?

question: A banker pledges a Treasury bond with ten years to run that sells for about eighty cents on the dollar, since yields have climbed. The Federal Reserve lends against it as if it were worth a hundred. Why do critics call that a hidden bailout?

question: A loan officer at the Federal Reserve's ordinary discount window sizes up a bond that a bank wants to borrow against. The Fed takes care never to lend as much as the bond could sell for today. How does the window normally value such collateral?

question: Jim Bianco watched the Federal Reserve's balance sheet swell again in March 2023, just when the Fed was supposed to be shrinking it, as each loan from its new window for banks pushed it up. He, Peter Schiff and Lyn Alden had a nickname for the window within days. What was it?

question: A trader who read the fine print noticed the Federal Reserve reaching in March 2023 for a clause of 1932, the same one it had used in March 2020. question: A Federal Reserve lending officer accepts a bank's damaged bond in a crisis at the price it carried before the damage, and lends the bank cash against it. What is the risk when a central bank treats shaky assets as worth more than they really are?
answer: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
choices: It hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing
It pushes long-term interest rates up for every borrower
It forces healthy banks to pay for the losses of weak ones
It drains the reserves banks need to keep making loans
context: Valuing a damaged bond at its old price keeps a weak bank's books looking whole: the loss is still there, only moved out of sight, and the bank can go on operating as if it had not happened. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: Frederic Bastiat taught readers to set a policy's visible result beside its hidden one. The Federal Reserve's Bank Term Funding Program of March 2023 took banks' sunken bonds at full face value as security for year-long loans. Which reading does Bastiat's test give?
answer: Seen: the banks steadied. Unseen: a subsidy for losses the Fed's low rates had caused
choices: Seen: the banks steadied. Unseen: a subsidy for losses the Fed's low rates had caused
Seen: the banks steadied. Unseen: the extra loans those banks went on to make
Seen: the bonds sank. Unseen: a quiet gain for savers holding bank deposits
Seen: higher interest rates. Unseen: the exports a stronger dollar cost
context: The banks had bought long bonds at low rates because the Fed's earlier policy made them attractive. When the same Fed's tightening exposed those bonds to loss, the BTFP quietly reimbursed the losses. The whole cycle -- create the incentive, expose the loss, cover the loss -- was internal to Fed choices. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: A banker who had leaned on the Federal Reserve's window for underwater bonds watched it close on 11 March 2024, a year after it opened in the bank panic of March 2023. Critics feared banks would gamble bigger, counting on another rescue, and Austrians said the closing changed nothing. Why?
answer: Every bank now expects the Fed to lend against bad bonds in the next crisis too
choices: Every bank now expects the Fed to lend against bad bonds in the next crisis too
Banks had already sold their underwater bonds before it closed
The Fed kept the program running quietly under a new name
Rates fell back, so the bond losses vanished on their own
context: The BTFP ran its course but its precedent is now baked into every bank's implicit risk framework. Duration mismatch is less risky when the central bank has demonstrated willingness to cover the loss. Moral hazard accumulates one precedent at a time. Source: Grokipedia 'Bank Term Funding Program' (2026-09-05).

question: A college president learns that every student he admits next year brings a new $10,000 federal grant. He knows how much more each family can now pay, and his seats have not multiplied. Where, by William Bennett's argument, does most of that money end up?
answer: Colleges, through higher tuition
choices: Colleges, through higher tuition
Students, through lower net cost
Federal loan servicers, through fees
State governments, through matching grants
context: The Bennett Hypothesis: subsidies to a demand-side party (student) can be substantially captured by the supply-side party (college) when supply is constrained and demand is inelastic. Source: Bennett, NYT (1987).

question: A college student in the 1990s borrowed from a pool of federal student loans then worth about $100 billion in all. The pool kept growing, until the debt outweighed every credit-card balance in America combined. By the mid-2020s, about how large had it grown?
answer: About $1.7 trillion
choices: About $1.7 trillion
About $170 billion
About $17 trillion
About $170 million
context: Total federal student loan debt grew from ~$100B in the 1990s to ~$1.7T in the early-to-mid 2020s. The debt is largely the mirror image of the tuition inflation the Bennett Hypothesis predicts. Source: newyorkfed.org (Household Debt and Credit Report).

question: A family opened a public four-year college's bill in 2017. After inflation, tuition there stood about 213 percent above its level of 1987, and at private colleges about 129 percent above. One stream of federal money grew right alongside that climb. Which stream was it?
answer: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
choices: Federal student loan and Pell Grant programs
Federal defense procurement contracts
Federal highway trust fund grants
Federal agriculture price supports
context: The tuition rise tracks federal aid expansion tightly -- the 1965 Higher Education Act reauthorizations, the 1992 direct-loan program, and the 2010 elimination of private-lender intermediation each expanded federal aid. Source: nces.ed.gov (tuition historical series); collegeboard.org (Trends in Student Aid).

question: David Lucca, an economist at the New York Fed, led a team that lined up college price tags against the moments when federal student-loan limits jumped. They set each added dollar of government-backed lending beside the change in the posted price. What did they find?
answer: Each added loan dollar raised sticker tuition by about 60 cents
choices: Each added loan dollar raised sticker tuition by about 60 cents
Each added loan dollar cut sticker tuition by about 5 cents
Each added loan dollar raised sticker tuition by about $2
Each added loan dollar left sticker tuition unchanged
context: Lucca + Nadauld + Shen, New York Fed Staff Report 733 (2015, revised 2019). The 60-cent tuition pass-through is a direct market-mechanism confirmation of the Bennett Hypothesis using discontinuities in loan-limit rules. Source: newyorkfed.org (staff report 733).

question: Grey Gordon and Aaron Hedlund simulated American college pricing from 1987 to 2010 in a computer model, to test how much of the tuition rise came from Washington's growing aid. Their result leaned on the model's assumptions. How much of the rise did it lay on the aid?
answer: Essentially all of it
choices: Essentially all of it
About one-quarter
About half
None of it
context: Gordon + Hedlund's model attribution was approximately 106% of the observed rise -- essentially all of it, with a slight overshoot other model features offset. Note the model dependency in interpreting the exact number. Source: NBER Working Paper 21967 (Gordon + Hedlund 2016).

question: Ronald Reagan's Secretary of Education charged in a New York Times essay of February 1987 that colleges raised tuition to swallow every increase in federal aid: the more Washington lent, the more they charged. Economists named the claim after him. What is it called?
answer: Bennett Hypothesis
choices: Bennett Hypothesis
Baumol effect
Cantillon effect
Rent-seeking loss
context: William Bennett made the charge in a New York Times essay of February 1987, while serving as Ronald Reagan's Secretary of Education; economists have tested it under his name ever since. Source: Bennett, NYT (1987).

question: William Bennett aimed his charge of 1987 at American colleges, but the same machinery runs outside the campus too: money given to buyers in a market whose supply cannot grow to meet it. Where else does it turn up in American policy?
answer: Section 8 housing vouchers that push up rents in tight markets
choices: Section 8 housing vouchers that push up rents in tight markets
Farm price supports that pile up surplus grain in storage
Rent control that caps what landlords may charge tenants
Minimum wages that price unskilled workers out of jobs
context: Housing vouchers can raise the rents landlords charge where few new flats are being built; health-insurance subsidies and the 2008-10 homebuyer credit have been read the same way. Source: Collinson and Ganong (2018) on Section 8 vouchers.

question: A senator is about to vote for a new subsidy that helps buyers pay for something they want. Before he does, an analyst who has learned William Bennett's lesson from the college market runs one check on the sellers. What does she ask?
answer: Who has the power to raise prices against the buyers' new money
choices: Who has the power to raise prices against the buyers' new money
Whether the sellers earn higher profits than firms elsewhere
Whether the sellers are run for profit or as charities
Whether the sellers pay their own workers a living wage
context: The reasoning move: when a subsidy is proposed, ask whether the supply side is constrained and whether the specific suppliers have pricing power. If yes, expect substantial subsidy capture through prices. Source: Bennett (1987); Lucca + Nadauld + Shen (2015).

question: Richard Vedder asked in a book of 2004 why college had grown so expensive. American colleges added over 517,000 administrators and professional staff between 1987 and 2012, about 87 for every working day, and those ranks grew twice as fast as the student body. What, as economists refined William Bennett's claim, does federal aid do?
answer: It pays for offices and amenities rather than more teaching
choices: It pays for offices and amenities rather than more teaching
It lowers the price families pay for each hour of class
It moves students toward cheaper two-year colleges
It lets colleges hire more professors for each student
context: The three-part mechanism: demand-side pricing effect, administrative expansion of aid-funded revenue, and amenity-competition arms race in place of price competition. All three point in the same direction. Source: Gordon + Hedlund (2016); Vedder (2004); Delta Cost Project reports.

question: Walter Ulbricht sealed off West Berlin overnight on 12 August 1961: barbed wire first, strung in the dark, then concrete. The barrier did not follow the border between the two Germanys; it ringed West Berlin. Roughly how long was it?
answer: About 155 kilometers
choices: About 155 kilometers
About 15 kilometers
About 1,550 kilometers
About 500 kilometers
context: The Wall was roughly 155 km (96 miles) long, encircling West Berlin -- not running along the East-West German border. It included concrete, watchtowers, a 'death strip', anti-vehicle trenches, and patrol roads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: East German border guards shot twenty-year-old Chris Gueffroy as he tried to cross the Berlin Wall in February 1989; he was the last person the guards shot dead there. Machine guns stood in the Wall's watchtowers. Which way did they point?
answer: East, at East Germans
choices: East, at East Germans
West, toward free Berlin
West, at the Allied garrisons
Both directions equally
context: The Wall's fortifications faced inward: guns and mines aimed at East Germans trying to leave, not westward at any invading force. Chris Gueffroy (5 February 1989) was the last person shot dead trying to cross to West Berlin. The design fact is the argument: the state had to wall its own citizens in.

question: A young East German walked across Berlin into the western half of the city in the summer of 1961, as East Germans had done since 1949, until those leaving made up roughly a fifth of everyone in East Germany. Then the Wall went up. Roughly how many had left?
answer: About 3.5 million
choices: About 3.5 million
About 350,000
About 35 million
About 35,000
context: About 3.5 million East Germans left through Berlin between 1949 and August 1961 -- roughly a fifth of the country's population. The Wall was built to stop the flow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall.

question: A guard on the Berlin Wall opened fire on a man sprinting across the raked sand of the border strip, under orders to shoot to kill. The Berlin Wall Memorial has since documented every death it can confirm at the Wall itself in the 28 years it stood. About how many were there?
answer: About 140
choices: About 140
About 14
About 1,400
Over 14,000
context: The Berlin Wall Memorial documents about 140 confirmed deaths at the Wall itself; several hundred more died at the wider inter-German border. The first was Ida Siekmann (22 August 1961); the last to be shot dead was Chris Gueffroy (5 February 1989). Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: An East German husband filed reports on his own wife with the Stasi, the Ministry for State Security. The Stasi kept about one uniformed officer for every 180 citizens, and about two unpaid informers for every officer. What does watching on that scale say about the East German state?
answer: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
choices: It had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control
It feared Western spies far more than its own citizens
It ran its economy by tracking what each family needed
It trusted informers to report crimes the police missed
context: Ministerium fuer Staatssicherheit -- Ministry for State Security -- gave East Germany the highest surveillance-to-population ratio of any modern state. Source: bstu.de (Stasi Records Archive).

question: Ida Siekmann leapt from a fourth-floor window of her Bernauer Strasse flat nine days after East Germany strung its barbed wire through Berlin in August 1961; her house was in the East, the street below it in the West. She died of the fall. What does her death show?
answer: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
choices: People were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside
The new border was so badly marked that people strayed onto it
Guards had orders to let pass anyone who leapt from a house
Most escapes in those first days were planned by Western agents
context: Ida Siekmann (August 22, 1961) died jumping from her fourth-floor Bernauer Strasse apartment on the border. She is the first of the Berlin Wall Memorial's documented victims. Source: berliner-mauer-gedenkstaette.de.

question: A woman from East Germany read the file the Stasi had kept on her, a right a German law of December 1991 gave every former East German. The secret police left behind millions of pages on ordinary people. Why does opening such an archive matter once a police state falls?
answer: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
choices: It lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known
It lets the courts punish every informer named in the files
It proves most of the files were forged by the secret police
It lets the new state reuse the files to keep watch on people
context: The Stasi Unterlagen Gesetz (Stasi Records Act, December 1991) established the office administering the archive and gave individuals the right to read their own files. The former ministry headquarters at Normannenstrasse is now the Stasi Museum. Source: bstu.de.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that central planning has no way to price anything rationally, since without markets nothing tells a planner what people want; Friedrich Hayek pressed the case for fifty more years. In Berlin the border between the two systems stayed open for twelve years, from 1949 until 1961. In the Austrian reading, which argument did the Wall turn into masonry?
answer: Free to compare, people pick the market side, so planning must wall them in
choices: Free to compare, people pick the market side, so planning must wall them in
Open borders drain any state of its workers, whatever its economy
Planning works once the most mobile workers are kept at home
Rival powers will always lure each other's people across a border
context: The argument is exit-as-verdict: given free comparison across an open border for twelve years, the population had voted with its feet. The Wall's inward-facing design is the calculation-debate answer made physical. Source: mises.org/library/socialism-economic-and-sociological-analysis.

question: A Twitter user read a news story on a frozen bank account around 2019 and typed a three-word reply beneath it. The same reply turned up under story after story about collapsing currencies and governments printing money, half joke and half argument. What was it?
answer: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
choices: 'Bitcoin fixes this'
'To the moon'
'Diamond hands'
'When Lambo?'
context: No single person coined it; the reply spread across Bitcoin social media from about 2019, half meme and half genuine argument that most modern financial ills trace to monetary debasement. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A speaker at a Bitcoin meet-up argued that one broad label hid the only thing he valued in his coin: a supply nobody can expand. Which label did he want Bitcoin kept apart from?
answer: 'Crypto', the umbrella that takes in altcoins
choices: 'Crypto', the umbrella that takes in altcoins
'Fintech', the umbrella for payment apps
'Tech', the umbrella for internet stocks
'Digital payments', the umbrella for card apps
context: Bitcoin advocates argue Bitcoin is monetary infrastructure with a specific design; altcoins are, in their view, mostly speculative tokens or venture-capital exit vehicles. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A buyer with twenty dollars bought a sliver of one bitcoin, counted in satoshis, the tiny units named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator. Each coin divides into a fixed number of them. How many satoshis make up one bitcoin?
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC. Named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto. Naming the smallest unit for the creator is analogous to naming a small currency unit for a founder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Satoshi_(unit).

question: A young saver put the same small sum into bitcoin on payday, as on every payday before, without a glance at the price. Wall Street's name for the habit is dollar-cost averaging, and refusing to time the market counts as a virtue among Bitcoiners. What does the Bitcoin community call it?
answer: Stacking sats
choices: Stacking sats
Rebalancing the portfolio
Hedging the position
Rolling the futures
context: Formally this is dollar-cost averaging. The community identity built around stacking emphasizes the discipline of not trying to time the market. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A Bitcoin holder told a friend who would not buy any, 'Have fun staying poor,' a line the community throws at anyone who refuses to own the coin. The community means it as a forecast, not an insult. What does the line claim?
answer: Inflation eats dollar savings, so those who refuse Bitcoin grow poorer
choices: Inflation eats dollar savings, so those who refuse Bitcoin grow poorer
Bitcoin rises so fast that every holder is sure to grow rich
People who refuse Bitcoin are too foolish ever to earn much
Taxes on Bitcoin will soon fall, leaving refusers behind
context: The line is meant as a forecast about money rather than a judgment of anyone: dollar savings lose buying power to inflation, and holders expect bitcoin's fixed supply to do the opposite. It also carries the impatience of holders who have watched skeptics predict Bitcoin's death for years while the network keeps functioning. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_culture.

question: A Bitcoin fan ran a node on a computer at home, joined a city meet-up and went to a yearly conference, and no committee had planned any of it. The whole culture grew out of countless separate decisions, with nobody in charge. Whose idea describes it?
answer: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
choices: Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order
John Maynard Keynes's animal spirits
Milton Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis
Paul Samuelson's revealed preference
context: Spontaneous order is Hayek's term for shared norms and institutions -- like language, common law, and open-source software -- that arise without any central planner. Bitcoin culture emerged with no central architect. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Spontaneous_order.

question: A newcomer walked into a Bitcoin conference in Nashville, one of a circuit that runs to Prague and Riga, expecting the stock tips of an ordinary investment event. The keynote speakers on the main stage barely mentioned price forecasts or trading. What filled their talks instead?
answer: Monetary history, sound money and Austrian economics
choices: Monetary history, sound money and Austrian economics
Tax planning, estate law and how to report gains
Startup pitches from new coins seeking investors
Digital art, collectibles and the metaverse
context: The culture's emphasis on long time preference (deferring consumption today for a stronger monetary position later) and monetary-history education distinguishes the Bitcoin conference circuit from the mainstream investment-conference culture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_conference.

question: Laszlo Hanyecz, a Florida programmer, posted an offer on a web forum in May 2010: ten thousand bitcoins for anyone who would get him a meal delivered, with some left over for the next day. What did he ask for?
answer: two large pizzas
choices: two large pizzas
a hamburger and fries
a case of beer
a bucket of fried chicken
context: Hanyecz wrote 'I'll pay 10,000 bitcoins for a couple of pizzas... like maybe 2 large ones so I have some left over for the next day.' The transaction settled on May 22, 2010. Source: https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=137.0.

question: A delivery driver brought two pizzas to a Jacksonville house on 22 May 2010, and the programmer inside had paid for them with ten thousand bitcoins, worth a fraction of a cent each. Why is that dinner famous now?
answer: Those 10,000 bitcoins would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars
choices: Those 10,000 bitcoins would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars
The pizzas were the best pizzas ever made
The bitcoin transaction failed
The programmer got the pizzas for free
context: The pizzas were ordered from Papa John's through its normal website by a UK forum user with the handle 'jercos'; Papa John's had no direct involvement with the crypto side of the deal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: A Florida programmer handed over ten thousand bitcoins for two pizzas on 22 May 2010, when a single coin was worth only a small fraction of a cent. Roughly what were his coins worth in dollars that day?
answer: about $41
choices: about $41
about $8,000
about $2
context: 10,000 BTC at the prevailing rate of roughly $0.004 per BTC came to approximately $41 -- so Hanyecz paid about $20 per pizza in dollar terms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Laszlo Hanyecz traded ten thousand bitcoins for two pizzas on 22 May 2010, and Bitcoiners still count the trade a milestone. Bitcoins had already been swapped for dollars and for other tokens, but his order was the first of a special kind. Which milestone did it set?
answer: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
choices: the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin
the first Bitcoin mined by a home computer
the first Bitcoin exchange listing
the first Bitcoin transaction between two people who had never met
context: Bitcoin had been mined, sent between hobbyists, and traded for other cryptocurrencies before May 22, 2010 -- but Hanyecz's pizzas were the first documented exchange of BTC for a real physical good, marking Bitcoin's crossing from experiment to money. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: A Bitcoin holder posted a photograph of his dinner online on 22 May, as holders around the world do each year, to honor a purchase Laszlo Hanyecz made in 2010 with ten thousand coins. What do they call the day?
answer: Bitcoin Pizza Day
choices: Bitcoin Pizza Day
Genesis Day
Satoshi Day
The Halving Anniversary
context: The community holiday Bitcoin Pizza Day is celebrated every May 22. Genesis Day (January 3) marks the mining of Block 0; Satoshi has no official birthday; the halving happens roughly every four years, not annually. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: A Bitcoiner looking back from the 2020s winced at the price of Laszlo Hanyecz's dinner of 2010: two pizzas for ten thousand bitcoins, bought for him by a forum user who paid Papa John's in dollars. At the highs Bitcoin reached in the 2020s, what were those coins worth?
answer: over one billion US dollars
choices: over one billion US dollars
about one hundred million US dollars
about ten million US dollars
about one million US dollars
context: 10,000 BTC at prices above $100,000 -- reached in Bitcoin's 2024-25 cycle -- crosses the one-billion-dollar mark. At earlier peaks the figure was measured in hundreds of millions; by any 2020s-era peak the paper value ran well into the ten-figure range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day.

question: Laszlo Hanyecz told one interviewer after another that he did not regret the two pizzas he had bought for ten thousand bitcoins in 2010, through a forum user who ordered them from Papa John's for him. What was his main reason?
answer: The trade proved bitcoin could really be spent on real goods
choices: The trade proved bitcoin could really be spent on real goods
He said the coins had never really belonged to him personally
He said other developers pressured him into making the trade
He said he had spent years trying to undo the trade
context: Hanyecz has said in multiple interviews that Bitcoin needed to be spent before it could be money, and that being the first person to spend it on a physical good was worth more to him than the coins were then. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day; Cointelegraph interview archives.

question: Six European historians, led by Stephane Courtois, worked through archives thrown open by the Soviet collapse, tallying the dead of every communist regime, Lenin's Russia, Mao's China and Pol Pot's Cambodia among them. Their 900-page book came out in Paris in 1997. What is its short title?
answer: The Black Book of Communism
choices: The Black Book of Communism
The Gulag Archipelago
Bloodlands
The Rise and Fall of Communism
context: Le Livre noir du communisme was published by Editions Robert Laffont, Paris, on November 6, 1997; Harvard University Press released the English translation in 1999 as The Black Book of Communism: Crimes, Terror, Repression.

question: Stephane Courtois added up the country chapters of The Black Book of Communism in his introduction of 1997: shootings under Stalin, Mao's famine, the labor camps, the killing fields of Cambodia. What total did he reach for the dead of communist rule in the twentieth century?
answer: About 85-100 million
choices: About 85-100 million
About 8-10 million
About 25-30 million
About 200-250 million
context: The Black Book's country breakdown: China about 65 million, the USSR about 20 million, North Korea about 2 million, Cambodia about 2 million, Africa about 1.7 million, Afghanistan about 1.5 million, Vietnam about 1 million, Eastern Europe about 1 million, Latin America about 150 thousand: about 85-100 million in all, the figure rounded to 'around 100 million' in general use.

question: Nicolas Werth worked from the newly opened Soviet files to write the Soviet chapter of The Black Book of Communism, counting the camps, the shootings of the Great Purge and the Ukrainian famine of 1932-33. What total did he reach for the Soviet Union?
answer: About 20 million
choices: About 20 million
About 2 million
About 200 million
About 50,000
context: Nicolas Werth (CNRS) wrote the USSR chapter based on Soviet archival access after 1991. His later monograph Cannibal Island (2007) covered a specific 1930s Siberian deportation atrocity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Werth.

question: Mao Zedong drove China into the Great Leap Forward, whose famine ran from 1959 to 1961, and then into the Cultural Revolution. The Black Book of Communism added the dead of both to the deaths in the laogai labor camps. What total did it give for China?
answer: About 65 million
choices: About 65 million
About 6.5 million
About 650,000
About 160 million
context: The Black Book's China total of ~65M has been refined by later Chinese archival scholarship. Yang Jisheng's Tombstone (2008) estimates the Great Leap famine alone at ~36M. Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine (2010) argues for a higher famine total. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: Stephane Courtois set communism's crimes beside Nazi Germany's in his introduction to The Black Book of Communism, and asked why the public remembers the two so unequally. Compared with the communist count in his book, roughly how big were the Nazi regime's killings, the Holocaust included?
answer: About one-fourth
choices: About one-fourth
About equal
About four times as many
About ten times as many
context: Courtois put the Nazi regime's killings at about 25 million, against the book's ~85-100 million communist total, roughly a quarter, and asked why the two had such unequal public memory. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: Alvin Hansen, the Harvard economist known as the American Keynes, told the public what would happen as the war budget was cut and more than eight million soldiers came home. What did he say the economy would be doing?
answer: Slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn
choices: Slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn
Sustaining wartime full employment for at least another decade
Entering a mild recession that would end within six months
Experiencing runaway inflation as pent-up demand met limited supply
context: Hansen and other 'secular stagnation' Keynesians argued the war had 'lifted' the US out of the 1930s and removing wartime spending would collapse it back. Every major Keynesian forecast in 1945-46 predicted renewed depression. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Hansen.

question: A returning soldier looked for a civilian job in 1946, one of more than eight million home by midyear, while federal spending dropped like a stone. Famous economists were forecasting a second Great Depression. What happened to the American jobless rate in 1946 and 1947?
answer: Stayed around 4 percent
choices: Stayed around 4 percent
Rose to about 15 percent
Rose to about 25 percent as in 1933
Stayed exactly at wartime levels near 1 percent
context: Despite the Keynesian prediction of depression, unemployment averaged around 4% in 1946-47 as private demand and investment absorbed the released wartime resources within months. Source: bls.gov historical LFS series.

question: Paul Krugman suggested in a New York Times column of 14 September 2001 that the wreckage might help the economy, so much would need rebuilding. The column became the modern textbook case of the fallacy in a Frederic Bastiat parable; Henry Hazlitt had read the demobilization of 1946 as the same parable run backwards. Which parable?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The candlemakers' petition
The negative railway
The petition of the merchants of Bordeaux
context: The postwar experience was Bastiat's broken-window in reverse: the destruction (of massive government spending) did not impoverish the country because the released resources were used privately. Hazlitt makes this the anchor chapter of Economics in One Lesson. Source: mises.org/library/economics-one-lesson.

question: A Mississippi family moved back into its rebuilt house in late 2006, after Hurricane Katrina; putting the Gulf coast back together had cost on the order of a hundred billion dollars. Some had said the storm would lift the Gulf economy. Set beside life before the storm, what had the families of the Gulf ended up with?
answer: The same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries
choices: The same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries
Better houses than before, thanks to the stimulus multiplier on federal spending
The same houses they had before, plus a year of higher aggregate income
Fewer houses than before, but with matching insurance-industry compensation
context: The Bastiat UNSEEN: the resources that rebuilt destroyed homes could not build new homes elsewhere. The Gulf ended 2006 no better off in housing stock than it had been in mid-2005, minus everything the same labor and capital could have produced instead. Source: cato.org/commentary/broken-window-fallacy-still-fooling-people.

question: Henry Hazlitt pointed, in his book of 1946 for ordinary readers, to the demobilization of that year, when federal spending fell faster than in any peacetime year ever recorded and millions of soldiers came home. By about how much did federal spending fall from 1945 to 1946?
answer: By close to two-thirds
choices: By close to two-thirds
By about one quarter
By about one tenth
By slightly less than half
context: Federal outlays fell from $84B (1945) to $30B (1946), a two-thirds cut in a single year, at the same time as 8M soldiers returned to the labor force. The Austrian-Bastiat prediction (private demand absorbs the released resources) beat the Keynesian one on the largest peacetime test available. Source: whitehouse.gov OMB historical tables.

question: A sailor came home in 1946, one of millions released from the forces as some fifty-four billion dollars a year of federal spending vanished. Frederic Bastiat's reasoning and the gloomy forecasts of the day disagreed about where such men and dollars would go. What became of all those released workers and dollars?
answer: Were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition
choices: Were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition
Were absorbed by state and local government spending that replaced federal outlays
Were absorbed by an inflation surge that ate the released resources' real value
Were absorbed by involuntary unemployment for a full decade after 1946
context: The Austrian-Bastiat prediction: released resources go back into private hands and are put to their next-best use quickly. Empirically, 1946-47 US private consumption and private nonresidential investment surged as government spending fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-World_War_II_economic_expansion.

question: Frederic Bastiat answered an error in 1850 that every generation has made again since: that a world war ended the Depression, that the September 2001 attacks were a boon to business, and that a hurricane could lift the Gulf economy. Which two things does each claim treat as one?
answer: Destruction and production
