choices: Destruction and production
Saving and investment
Income and wealth
Consumption and inflation
context: Bastiat's one-line diagnosis in the broken-window chapter: 'Destruction is not profit.' Every destruction-as-stimulus claim collapses the difference between a country that built new things and a country that rebuilt destroyed things. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Frederic Bastiat told of a shopkeeper's careless son who broke the shop window. The neighbours who gathered round called it good for trade, since the pane would have to be replaced. What were they forgetting?
answer: The other thing the shopkeeper would have bought with the money
choices: The other thing the shopkeeper would have bought with the money
The glazier had other work waiting and did not need this job
The new pane would cost more than the old one had cost
The glazier would spend his fee outside the town at once
context: Bastiat's French calls the shopkeeper Jacques Bonhomme, the French everyman; English translations render him James Goodfellow. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: A careless boy smashes his father's shop window in Frederic Bastiat's parable of 1850, and the father must pay for new glass. Bastiat names the exact price, since everything in the story hangs on that sum. How many francs?
answer: Six francs
choices: Six francs
Ten francs
Twenty francs
Fifty francs
context: Bastiat specifies six francs, and the whole rest of the chapter turns on those exact six francs and where they came from. Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: The shopkeeper in Frederic Bastiat's essay of 1850 stands before the window his son has smashed while the neighbours try to cheer him up. They point to one tradesman the accident has just handed a job. Which trade do they name?
answer: The glazier
choices: The glazier
The blacksmith
The mason
The carpenter
context: The glazier's six-franc replacement job is the SEEN benefit; the bystanders' whole consoling argument is that if panes were never broken, glaziers would starve. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: Frederic Bastiat closed his broken-window chapter with a plain sum. Before the accident the shopkeeper had both his money and his pane; after it, he had a pane and no money. What did Bastiat conclude about the community as a whole?
answer: The community is exactly one window poorer
choices: The community is exactly one window poorer
The community is exactly six francs richer
The community is no better and no worse off
The community has traded consumption for investment
context: Bastiat's summary line: 'Destruction is not profit.' The community's total wealth is one pane of glass smaller than it was five minutes earlier, and that is the whole result. Source: fee.org/resources/what-is-seen-and-what-is-not-seen.

question: The shopkeeper's neighbours in Frederic Bastiat's broken-window story remind him that everybody has to earn a living, and ask what the glass trade would do if panes never broke. They open their speech with an old English proverb, now the folk name of the very error Bastiat refutes. Which proverb?
answer: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good
choices: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good
Every cloud has a silver lining
One man's loss is another man's gain
Necessity is the mother of invention
context: The bystanders' opening line: 'It is an ill wind that blows nobody good. Everybody must live, and what would become of the glaziers if panes of glass were never broken?' Source: mises.org/library/what-seen-and-what-not-seen.

question: Milton Friedman carried Bastiat's habit of looking for hidden effects to a mass audience in 1980, in a ten-part public-television series and a book written with his wife Rose, both called Free to Choose. Its episodes ran from schools and welfare to consumer safety and inflation. In whose hands, he argued, do the everyday choices of a life belong?
answer: Ordinary people's own hands, not central planners'
choices: Ordinary people's own hands, not central planners'
Trained experts' hands, since they see the whole picture
Elected officials' hands, since voters can remove them
Local councils' hands, since they know their towns best
context: Free to Choose (Harcourt, 1980) applies the Bastiat move across public education, welfare, consumer protection, and inflation; the ten-part PBS series aired the same year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_to_Choose.

question: Two Virginia economists, James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, brought out a book through the University of Michigan Press in 1962 that founded a field. It treated the state not as a referee but as people with interests of their own. What is its title?
answer: The Calculus of Consent
choices: The Calculus of Consent
The Politics of Bureaucracy
The Logic of Collective Action
The Theory of Economic Regulation
context: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy (University of Michigan Press, 1962). Both authors were then at the University of Virginia. Source: press.umich.edu (Calculus of Consent).

question: Gordon Tullock and James Buchanan threw out, in 1962, the old picture of government as a referee standing above everyone's self-interest. Whom did they treat as just as self-interested as any shopper or factory owner?
answer: Voters, politicians, and bureaucrats
choices: Voters, politicians, and bureaucrats
Only wealthy business owners
Only foreign leaders
Only judges
context: The Calculus of Consent's central methodological move: treat political actors with the same self-interest assumption economics uses for consumers and firms. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 1.

question: A voter fights over a tax or a tariff within the rules already in place, on the lower of the two floors of politics in James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's book of 1962. On the upper floor, the rules themselves are chosen. What did the two authors call that upper floor?
answer: The constitutional level
choices: The constitutional level
The judicial level
The bureaucratic level
The electoral level
context: The constitutional level is where individuals choose the rules that will bind all subsequent political choices. Buchanan's whole later career built out this idea as 'constitutional political economy.' Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: John Rawls, a philosopher, asked in 1971 which rules a man would pick for his society before learning whether he would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick. Choosing rules without knowing one's own future place is reasoning from behind what, in his phrase?
answer: A veil of ignorance
choices: A veil of ignorance
A curtain of doubt
A wall of silence
A cloud of neutrality
context: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard 1971), asked what redistributive principles rational agents would choose from behind a 'veil of ignorance.' Buchanan reached the parallel constitutional move nine years earlier from an independent starting point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Theory_of_Justice.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock asked in their book of 1962, written at the University of Virginia, what a bare majority's vote, fifty-one percent against forty-nine, really reveals about the people who cast it. What did they say drives most such outcomes?
answer: Interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance
choices: Interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance
The moral wisdom of the median voter
The efficient aggregation of correct beliefs
The natural convergence of common purposes
context: Once you model voters, politicians, and bureaucrats as self-interested individuals, majority outcomes reflect the balance of organized pressures, vote-trading across issues, and voter apathy on issues with low per-capita stakes. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 10.

question: A delegate sits down to help write a constitution, not knowing whether he will end up among the winners or the losers of the votes it will govern. By James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's reasoning, a margin of fifty-one percent is too slim to trust with a minority's rights on the gravest questions. Which kind of rule does he insist on for those?
answer: Supermajority rules
choices: Supermajority rules
Plurality rules
Runoff rules
Proportional rules
context: Buchanan + Tullock analyzed the trade-off between decision costs (higher thresholds are harder to reach) and external costs (lower thresholds impose more harm on losing minorities). Supermajority rules for consequential choices minimize expected total cost. Source: Calculus of Consent (1962), Chapter 6.

question: Gordon Tullock left the US Foreign Service in 1958 and met James Buchanan at the University of Virginia, where the two began the work that became public choice. Early money for their Virginia program came from one big American foundation, an irony given what the program later said about organized interests. Which foundation?
answer: The Ford Foundation
choices: The Ford Foundation
The Rockefeller Foundation
The Carnegie Corporation
The Mellon Foundation
context: Buchanan's autobiographical essays document early Ford Foundation support for the Virginia research program that produced the Calculus of Consent. Source: Buchanan, Better than Plowing (Chicago 1992).

question: A student hunts through James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's book of 1962 for the founding ideas of public choice. She finds most of them, but one idea first appears three years later, in a book by someone else. Which idea is missing?
answer: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern of collective action
choices: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern of collective action
The constitutional-versus-post-constitutional distinction
The veil of uncertainty behind rule choice
Vote-trading and logrolling analysis
context: The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern comes from Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (Harvard 1965) -- three years after the Calculus. The other three are all in the Calculus. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); Olson (1965).

question: James Buchanan took the 1986 Nobel for work built on one distinction from the book he wrote with Gordon Tullock in 1962. Two neighbours can fight hard about a tax rate yet agree completely on the way tax rates should be set. What lesson did Buchanan draw, in a single line?
answer: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
choices: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules
The bigger the majority, the wiser the decision
Politicians are always more knowledgeable than voters
Economic policy should never be constrained by any constitution
context: Buchanan's whole later career built out this insight. Constitutional rules that bind majorities are the deepest form of consent, because they are agreed to when the future distribution of winners and losers is still unknown. Source: Buchanan, The Reason of Rules (Cambridge 1985).

question: Isaac Newton fixed the price of gold at Britain's Mint in 1717. In 1821 the Bank of England went back to paying gold for paper pounds at his price, and the industrial world followed. What is that system called?
answer: The gold standard
choices: The gold standard
The silver standard
The bimetallic standard
The gold-exchange standard
context: The 1821 resumption of gold payments by the Bank of England is the conventional start of the classical gold standard, a system Britain led until 1914. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: A London merchant read the pound-dollar rate in his trade paper before 1914 and found the figure that had stood there decade after decade, quoted like a constant in physics. About how many dollars did one pound buy?
answer: About 4.86 dollars
choices: About 4.86 dollars
About 2.20 dollars
About 10 dollars
About 1.60 dollars
context: The pound-dollar rate stayed at 4.8665 for decades before 1914, held there by the two currencies' independent gold parities. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Otto von Bismarck set out in 1871 to move his newly unified Germany from silver to gold, and the switch needed an enormous hoard of the metal. The hoard came from a power Germany had just beaten in a short war. Which payment funded the move?
answer: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
choices: The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War
The Austrian tribute after the Austro-Prussian War
The Ottoman payment for the Berlin conference
The Danish settlement over Schleswig-Holstein
context: France paid Germany 5 billion francs in gold after its 1871 defeat, giving Chancellor Bismarck the reserves he needed to move Germany to the mark on a full gold basis. Source: Grokipedia 'Franco-Prussian War' (2026-09-05).

question: A London shopper spent a pound on bread and coal in 1914, after a century in which Britain had built its railways and factories. What word describes British prices since 1821, under gold-backed money?
answer: Stable
choices: Stable
Hyperinflationary
Deflationary by two-thirds
Volatile in a wide upward trend
context: The British price level fluctuated within a range but showed no sustained trend across the 93 years of the classical gold standard. A pound in 1914 bought roughly what a pound in 1821 bought. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: A labourer in London posted five pounds home to his family in Naples before 1914, sure that the lire they received would be worth just what he had mailed, with nothing lost to shifting rates. What made him so sure?
answer: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
choices: Both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed
The Bank of England guaranteed all foreign remittances at face value
The Italian government subsidized the Lira-Pound conversion
International trade unions negotiated the exchange rates
context: The pound was fixed to gold at one ratio, the Italian lira at another; their cross-rate followed mechanically. A worker's remittance kept its purchasing power across borders because both currencies shared a real anchor. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises argued after the Second World War that money anchored to gold had tied governments' hands, since a government that cannot print must persuade taxpayers or lenders to pay for what it wants. How did he describe the gold-based system of 1815 to 1914?
answer: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
choices: The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom
The unavoidable relic of a pre-industrial economy
A middle-class conspiracy against wage earners
A technical convenience of no political significance
context: Mises argued that gold discipline restrained state power more effectively than any written constitution. Governments unable to inflate had to persuade taxpayers or lenders to fund their projects. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: A finance minister sat down before 1914 to find the money for a larger budget, knowing that every note he issued could be redeemed in gold on demand. He could raise it only through taxes that lawmakers would pass or loans that investors would take up. What did that discipline make too costly to fund?
answer: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
choices: Fighting long industrial wars by inflation
Building public schools and hospitals
Maintaining diplomatic embassies abroad
Sponsoring scientific expeditions
context: Under gold, wars had to be paid for by taxes or borrowing. Neither scaled to modern industrial slaughter. Governments could inflate only by first suspending convertibility -- which is what all major belligerents did within days in August 1914. Source: Mises, Nation State and Economy (1919).

question: A family paid its own way from Europe to America before 1914, in an age when people and capital moved between countries on private money and most of Europe ran on gold. What do people remember as the economic mark of that era, from 1871 to 1914?
answer: Rising trade, a growing middle class, and long stretches of stable prices
choices: Rising trade, a growing middle class, and long stretches of stable prices
Constant inflation that quietly shrank most family savings
Rapid money printing used to pay for many small wars
Bank collapses in almost every country every few years
context: The Belle Epoque -- 'beautiful era' -- runs from roughly 1871 to 1914. Its economic character (free capital movement, stable prices, mass migration funded by private savings) was inseparable from the shared gold basis of world money. Source: Grokipedia 'Belle Epoque' (2026-09-05).

question: A Berliner who brought a banknote to be paid in gold on the fourth day of one month in 1914 was turned away, and the other warring powers shut their gold windows within the week. A century of gold-backed money was not defeated; it was switched off. In which month?
answer: August 1914
choices: August 1914
January 1914
November 1914
October 1918
context: Germany suspended gold payments August 4 1914; Britain effectively followed within days; France, Russia, and Austria-Hungary within the week. The century of stable prices ended not because gold discipline failed but because states wanted to fight a war that gold discipline would have made unaffordable. Source: Grokipedia 'Gold standard' (2026-09-05).

question: A Briton took a paper pound to the Bank of England before 1914 and walked out with gold, as anyone could, so no chancellor could quietly print his way to a bigger budget. Austrian economists value the old standard less for its economics than for its politics. Which effect do they stress?
answer: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
choices: It imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful
It prevented all business-cycle fluctuations
It ensured full employment across the developed world
It equalized income across social classes
context: The Austrian point: the value of gold discipline is not perfect stability -- there were still recessions and shocks -- but the constraint it placed on government power. Every 20th-century abandonment of gold was driven by governments that wanted to be freed from that constraint. Source: Mises, Human Action (1949).

question: Horst Siebert, a German economist, told a tale from British India in a book of 2001 about policies that backfire. In it, colonial officials set out to rid one great city of cobras, though no archive confirms the scheme ever ran. Which city?
answer: Delhi
choices: Delhi
Bombay
Calcutta
Madras
context: The parable is traditionally set in British colonial Delhi in the late 19th century. The historical base is disputed; Siebert used it as an illustrative parable in 2001 for the general perverse-incentive pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: A British official, as the story goes, wanted the capital rid of its venomous snakes and set up a payment to get the city's people to help. What, in the tale, did he offer?
answer: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
choices: A cash bounty for every dead cobra brought in
A tax rebate for landowners who eradicated cobras from their plots
A trained mongoose delivered to each household that requested one
A public-works job for anyone willing to clear cobra dens
context: The bounty was the seen policy: kill more cobras, get paid, cobra population should fall. Straight, intuitive, and completely wrong once the incentive was actually running. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: A man in British Delhi, in the old story, found a better way to earn the money officials paid for dead cobras than hunting the snakes. The scheme gave the cobra effect its name. What did he and his neighbours do?
answer: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
choices: Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty
Began smuggling cobras in from neighboring provinces
Began stealing cobras from public zoo enclosures
Began falsely reporting non-cobra snakes as cobras
context: Farming dead cobras in the back yard was more profitable than hunting wild ones. The bounty had created a farming operation, not a hunting one -- exactly the unseen behavioral response the policy did not price in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: Officials in British Delhi, in the tale, cancelled their payments for dead cobras once they noticed what the payments had produced. The cobras in the city's back yards were suddenly worth nothing. What did their owners do with them?
answer: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
choices: Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets
Petitioned the government for a compensation payment
Killed and buried their cobra stock privately
Sold the cobras through underground exotic-pet markets
context: Delhi's cobra population ended the program HIGHER than it started; the released breeder-stock hit the streets after the bounty ended. The parable's whole punch is this cancellation-worse-than-nothing outcome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_effect.

question: A rat-catcher in a French colonial city snipped the tail from a live rat in 1902, turned it in for the bounty, and let the animal go to breed. The scheme is better documented than the cobra tale. In which city did it happen?
answer: Hanoi
choices: Hanoi
Saigon
Phnom Penh
Vientiane
context: The French Hanoi rat-bounty (1902) is better historically documented than the Delhi cobra story. Rat-catchers began FARMING rats and turning in the tails while releasing the tail-less rats to breed more. Source: Michael Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race,' French Colonial History 4 (2003).

question: Charles Goodhart, a British economist, was watching the Bank of England try to control the money supply in 1975 when he spotted a pattern. Once officials chose one figure to be graded on, it stopped measuring what it used to, because everyone began managing the figure itself. By his rule, a measure stops telling the truth once it becomes what?
answer: A target
choices: A target
A budget item
A regulation
A subsidy
context: Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Originally a Bank of England paper on monetary aggregates, it generalized to name the whole pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law.

question: A Wells Fargo banker facing a monthly quota of new accounts in the mid-2010s, with her bonus at stake, opened accounts that customers never requested. Her colleagues opened millions more, and whole families found credit cards they had never signed up for. What lesson does the episode teach?
answer: Reward a target instead of the real goal and people will hit the target in harmful ways
choices: Reward a target instead of the real goal and people will hit the target in harmful ways
Bonuses always make workers more honest with their customers
Extra accounts do no real harm since customers rarely notice
Big banks are usually the fastest to spot their own fraud
context: Wells Fargo's 2016 cross-sell fake-accounts scandal: employees hit incentive targets by opening real accounts customers had not requested. The bounty on 'accounts opened' produced accounts, not customer value. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo_cross-selling_scandal.

question: An American teacher in the 2000s drilled her pupils on what the state test would ask, under a federal law that tied part of her school's funding to its scores. Teachers called the habit teaching to the test. What was the law's popular name?
answer: No Child Left Behind
choices: No Child Left Behind
Race to the Top
Every Student Succeeds
Elementary and Secondary Education
context: NCLB (2001), signed by George W. Bush, made federal funds contingent on test-score improvements; schools optimized on the specific tested items, sometimes at the expense of everything else. The 2015 Every Student Succeeds Act replaced it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act.

question: A hospital administrator studied the 2010 American health law that fined a hospital whenever a discharged patient came back within thirty days. Some hospitals found a way to avoid the fine that improved the measured number without necessarily helping patients. What did they do?
answer: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
choices: Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them
Refused to accept transfers from other hospitals with high readmission rates
Reduced the length of stay for all admitted patients uniformly
Charged patients directly for care that would trigger a readmission classification
context: The ACA's CMS 30-day-readmission penalties incentivized hospitals to keep returning patients in ED observation status (which is not counted as an admission), reducing the measure without necessarily improving the outcome. Standard Cobra-Effect / Goodhart pattern. Source: healthaffairs.org/do/10.1377/hpb20180216.35660.

question: Friedrich Hayek finished a book at Chicago in 1959, when most experts held that the state should run more of the economy. It defended an older tradition, in which free people choose for themselves rather than planners choosing for all. What is that tradition called?
answer: Classical liberalism
choices: Classical liberalism
Socialism
Mercantilism
Fascism
context: F. A. Hayek completed the manuscript in May 1959; University of Chicago Press published it as 'The Constitution of Liberty' in February 1960. Source: Wikipedia article on The Constitution of Liberty (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constitution_of_Liberty).

question: Friedrich Hayek began The Constitution of Liberty by pinning down a word most people use loosely: liberty. It is not wealth, he wrote, nor a political voice, nor power over one's circumstances. What is it?
answer: The absence of coercion by another person
choices: The absence of coercion by another person
The satisfaction of one's most fundamental preferences
The equal exercise of political voice in the public sphere
The material means to pursue one's chosen ends
context: Hayek: liberty is the absence of coercion by another person -- being made to serve another's will. Not power, not wealth, not political participation. Source: Cato Institute review and Online Library of Liberty essay by Ronald Hamowy (https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/hamowy-s-critique-of-hayek-s-concept-of-freedom).

question: A driver is fined for jumping a red light, under a rule fixed beforehand for everyone alike. Another man pays the same sum because an official decides on the spot that he owes it. Friedrich Hayek sets the two side by side in The Constitution of Liberty. Which contrast is he drawing?
answer: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
choices: The rule of law versus administrative discretion
Private property versus common ownership
Positive freedom versus negative freedom
Judicial review versus legislative supremacy
context: Hayek's core Part II thesis: the rule of law -- general, prospective, equal, published in advance -- is a distinct kind of political order from administrative discretion, even when the practical results coincide. Source: True North Ideas summary (https://truenorthideas.org/the-constitution-of-liberty-hayeks-lessons-for-today-and-tomorrow/).

question: Friedrich Hayek asked in the last part of The Constitution of Liberty why a free order outdoes a planned one, and his answer did not rest on people being wise. It rested on one claim about knowledge and discovery. Which claim?
answer: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
choices: That the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it
That elected representatives are systematically better informed than administrators
That most citizens correctly rank their long-term interests over short-term ones
That common law judges reason more reliably than legislators about complex trade-offs
context: Hayek's argument: freedom matters because we do not know in advance what discoveries a free society will make; only a free order can produce them, precisely because a planner would have to know them already to permit them. Source: Cato Institute Regulation review (https://www.cato.org/regulation/spring-2026/book-review-constitution-liberty).

question: Friedrich Hayek ended The Constitution of Liberty with a postscript that startled many of his readers. In it he refused a label most of them had pinned on him and claimed instead an older British name that Edmund Burke had once taken for himself. What was the postscript called?
answer: Why I Am Not a Conservative
choices: Why I Am Not a Conservative
The Errors of Progressivism
The Old Whig's Defense
Beyond Left and Right
context: The postscript is titled 'Why I Am Not a Conservative.' Hayek identifies himself as an 'Old Whig,' the term Burke had used for himself. Source: Hayek, postscript, reprinted at Cato (https://www.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/articles/hayek-why-i-am-not-conservative.pdf).

question: A reader who had taken Friedrich Hayek for a conservative reached the postscript to his book of 1960 and found him turning the label down for Edmund Burke's old name, an Old Whig. Which objection to conservatism did Hayek press?
answer: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
choices: That conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands
That conservatism has always been captured by throne-and-altar aristocracy and cannot be democratized
That conservatism confuses the value of tradition with the value of the particular customs it inherits
That conservatism is incompatible with the constitutional limits on royal power the Whigs defended
context: Hayek: conservatives want to keep things as they are; he wants to move toward greater freedom -- so conservatism cannot be a real alternative to socialism, only a brake on it. Source: Hayek, 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' (https://soonersentinel.substack.com/p/fa-hayek-why-i-am-not-a-conservative).

question: Margaret Thatcher, as one account has it, stopped a colleague urging a middle course in 1975 by pulling Friedrich Hayek's book from her bag and setting it down hard on the table: 'This is what we believe.' What core belief does the book press?
answer: Individual liberty and free markets are what makes a free society possible
choices: Individual liberty and free markets are what makes a free society possible
Expert planning of the economy keeps a free society prosperous
A strong welfare state is what keeps a free society stable
Old customs and inherited ranks are what hold a society together
context: The anecdote is told in John Ranelagh's 'Thatcher's People' (1991); the Margaret Thatcher Foundation itself calls it 'perhaps a little too perfect to be actually true,' so it should be treated as reported testimony rather than settled fact. Sources: Sotheby's essay (https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/this-is-what-we-believe-margaret-thatcher-and-f-a-hayek); Margaret Thatcher Foundation archive note.  (Legend.)

question: John Ranelagh told the story of Margaret Thatcher slamming Hayek's book on a table in his 1991 history of her circle. The Margaret Thatcher Foundation cautions in its archive that the tale may be too perfect to be true. What does that warning point to?
answer: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
choices: That vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact
That John Ranelagh's 1991 book was later fully retracted by its publisher
That Margaret Thatcher denied the anecdote in her own memoirs
That Hayek himself in the 1980s explicitly denied ever meeting Thatcher
context: The Margaret Thatcher Foundation records the anecdote as beloved-of-biographers but cautions it may be too perfect to be true; Ranelagh 1991 is the source, not a contemporaneous document. Neither Thatcher's memoirs nor Hayek's biography retracts the story -- the Foundation simply flags it as unverified testimony. Source: Margaret Thatcher Foundation Hayek archive (https://www.margaretthatcher.org/archive/Hayek).  (Legend.)

question: Delegates from the thirteen colonies voted on 22 June 1775 to issue two million dollars in paper money. Their Congress could not tax anyone, since only the states had that power, so nothing stood behind the bills but the promise of a future country. What was this Revolutionary War money called?
answer: Continental currency
choices: Continental currency
The greenback
The Spanish milled dollar
The Massachusetts note
context: The June 22 1775 resolution authorized $2 million in bills of credit -- soon known as 'Continentals' -- to fund the Revolutionary War effort. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: A barber of 1781 was said to be papering his shop walls with the money Congress had printed for the Revolutionary War. One paper dollar was worth about one cent in silver that summer and nothing by the end of the year. A saying about worthless things came out of the collapse and stayed in American English for a century. Which phrase?
answer: Not worth a Continental
choices: Not worth a Continental
Broke as a Yankee
Cheap as tobacco
Poor as a Whig
context: The phrase 'not worth a Continental' became the standard American idiom for anything valueless. Barbers reportedly papered their shops with unwanted Continentals as decoration. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: A farmer took Continentals for his grain during the Revolutionary War and grew poorer as Congress printed more and each bill bought less. When the paper finally fell to near-zero value, one group was hit hardest. Who suffered most?
answer: Soldiers' families and small savers who held the paper
choices: Soldiers' families and small savers who held the paper
Wealthy Philadelphia merchants who traded abroad
British creditors owed money by colonial planters
French officers serving under Rochambeau
context: Soldiers who earned in Continentals watched the paper their families held evaporate. Farmers who accepted Continentals for grain became poor; those who insisted on gold were denounced as gougers. This asymmetric destruction became a Founding-era grievance. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: A farmer could be punished in 1777 for asking more than the official price for his grain. Delegates in Congress and several state governments, watching the Continental lose value fast, had chosen to fix prices and wages rather than stop the printing. How did those controls fare?
answer: They were evaded within months and dropped inside a year
choices: They were evaded within months and dropped inside a year
They held prices steady until the war was over
They worked until British forgers flooded the states
They lasted until the new Constitution banned them
context: Congress and several state governments imposed wage and price controls in 1777-78, hoping to freeze the visible collapse. The controls were widely evaded and abandoned within about a year. Source: Grokipedia 'Continental currency' (2026-09-05).

question: A shopkeeper refused the collapsing Continental paper money during the Revolutionary War and found himself facing a legal penalty. His state legislature had gone further than price controls: it required him to accept the paper at its full printed face value in trade for real goods. What kind of law was that?
answer: Legal-tender laws
choices: Legal-tender laws
Coinage acts
Homestead exemptions
Sinking-fund provisions
context: Legal-tender laws penalize refusal of a specific currency at face value. In the Continental case they were widely evaded -- sellers demanded gold or fled the market rather than accept the paper. Source: Grokipedia 'Legal tender' (2026-09-05).

question: James Madison and the other framers, who had lived through the Continental's collapse, barred the states in 1787 from ever printing paper money again. Article I, Section 10 of the Constitution uses an exact eighteenth-century phrase for that kind of paper. What phrase does it use?
answer: Bills of credit
choices: Bills of credit
Circulating scrip
Continental notes
Public tickets
context: Article I Section 10 forbids any state to 'emit Bills of Credit'. Article I Section 8 confines federal monetary power to 'coin Money, regulate the Value thereof'. Both clauses were drafted with the Continental collapse in living memory. Source: US Constitution, Article I.

question: The framers of 1787 barred the individual states from printing paper money and put tight limits on even the federal government's power to coin money. That was a strong stand for hard money, money tied to gold or silver rather than paper decree. Where did the framers' conviction come from?
answer: An empirical lesson drawn from a catastrophe they had personally lived through
choices: An empirical lesson drawn from a catastrophe they had personally lived through
A theoretical preference borrowed from Adam Smith's 1776 book
A concession to British commercial interests
A late compromise proposed by Alexander Hamilton alone
context: Madison, Hamilton, and every other delegate had watched the Continental hyperinflate. Their hard-money bias was earned firsthand, not imported from any theorist. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: Frederic Bastiat taught his readers to look for two things whenever a government acts: what is Seen, the obvious effect, and what is Unseen, the effect nobody notices until later. A reader who turns those two columns on the American Revolution's Continental paper money gets which pairing?
answer: Seen: government paying soldiers; Unseen: soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed
choices: Seen: government paying soldiers; Unseen: soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed
Seen: prices climbing in the shops; Unseen: the extra goods the new money called forth
Seen: Congress printing bills; Unseen: the gold the states quietly paid out behind them
Seen: farmers paid for their grain; Unseen: the taxes the paper money spared them
context: Bastiat's frame: the visible act (payment) hides the invisible destruction (evaporation of the recipient's savings). The Continental is the earliest well-documented American case of the Cantillon-effect asymmetric damage every paper-money collapse produces. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: Silver men in the American West turned on the Coinage Act of 1873. Passed quietly and without much fanfare, it stopped the free coinage of silver into dollar coins and left the country on gold alone. Debtors and the silver states pinned a bitter nickname on it that stuck for decades. What was it?
answer: The Crime of '73
choices: The Crime of '73
The Panic of '73
The Deal of '73
The Gold Ring
context: Silver interests alleged the change was a conspiracy by Eastern bankers to enrich creditors. Most historians think the decision was not a conspiracy, but the political label stuck for a generation. Source: Grokipedia 'Coinage Act of 1873' (2026-09-05).

question: Lawmakers moved America onto a stronger dollar in 1873, and prices drifted down in the years that followed. Who did it hurt most?
answer: Farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks
choices: Farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks
New York bondholders owed fixed sums
Retired officials on fixed pensions
New England mill owners selling abroad
context: Farmers borrowed money in the plentiful greenback dollars of the 1860s and had to repay in the harder-to-earn gold-standard dollars of the 1870s and 1880s. Falling crop prices with fixed debts transferred wealth from debtors to creditors. Source: Grokipedia 'Crime of 1873' (2026-09-05).

question: William Jennings Bryan led the Democrats' silver wing in the 1890s against the party's gold men, and he wanted to mint silver freely, which would put a lot more money into the American economy. A Kansas farmer had a big mortgage, a fixed dollar debt to pay the bank every month. Which side would that farmer most likely support?
answer: The pro-silver side, because more money in the economy raises prices
choices: The pro-silver side, because more money in the economy raises prices
The gold-only side, because it keeps money valuable
Neither, because it does not affect farmers
The gold-only side, because it helps them repay loans faster
context: Bryan was 36 at the 1896 Democratic National Convention. His silver-currency populism galvanized rural voters and defined the Democratic Party for a generation. Source: Grokipedia 'William Jennings Bryan' (2026-09-05).

question: William Jennings Bryan, a 36-year-old Nebraskan, rose before the Democratic National Convention in Chicago on 9 July 1896 to speak for indebted farmers against eastern creditors. Which phrase did he end on?
answer: You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold
choices: You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold
Give me liberty or give me death
Malice toward none, charity for all
The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
context: Bryan's peroration -- 'you shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns; you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold' -- carried the hall, and he won the nomination the next day, on the fifth ballot. It became one of the most quoted political speeches in American history. Source: Grokipedia 'Cross of Gold speech' (2026-09-05).

question: William McKinley beat William Jennings Bryan in 1896, 271 electoral votes to 176, in the first American presidential race fought openly on the currency. Bryan had promised to put more money into circulation; McKinley had promised to keep the dollar as it stood. What was the central money question of that election?
answer: Whether to back the dollar with only gold or also with silver
choices: Whether to back the dollar with only gold or also with silver
Whether to raise tariffs on foreign goods
Whether to let banks print their own private paper money
Whether to abolish the income tax entirely
context: McKinley, backed by industrialist Marcus Hanna's fundraising machine, won 271 electoral votes to Bryan's 176 in the 1896 election. Source: Grokipedia '1896 United States presidential election' (2026-09-05).

question: William Jennings Bryan lost the 1896 election, and over the next decade his fight over the currency faded, though neither side had won the argument. An outside event added huge amounts of bullion to the world money supply, raising prices and easing farmers' debts without any legal change at all. What was that event?
answer: Major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado
choices: Major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado
The Federal Reserve began open-market operations
European nations shipped gold reserves to New York for safekeeping
A cyanide-leaching breakthrough doubled US silver output
context: The Klondike strike (1896), the Witwatersrand gold rush in South Africa (1886 onward, expanding through the 1890s), and Colorado mining organically expanded the gold money supply. Prices rose, debtors were relieved, and Congress passed the Gold Standard Act in 1900. Source: Grokipedia 'Klondike Gold Rush' (2026-09-05).

question: A Kansas farmer and the bank that held his mortgage stood on opposite sides of the American money fight, which ran from 1873 to 1896. The fight taught who gains when money is hard, its value holding or rising, and who gains when it is soft, its value falling. Which pairing best sums that up?
answer: Hard money benefits savers and creditors; inflation benefits debtors
choices: Hard money benefits savers and creditors; inflation benefits debtors
Hard money benefits urban workers; inflation benefits rural landowners
Hard money benefits banks only; inflation benefits governments only
Hard money benefits importers; inflation benefits exporters
context: The distributional effect is symmetric and unavoidable. Inflating the money supply erodes the real value of nominal debts, transferring wealth from lenders to borrowers. Both effects are real and both are political. Source: Rothbard, A History of Money and Banking in the United States (2002).

question: Murray Rothbard looked back on the American silver fight and refused both camps. His Austrian tradition rejected the silverites' plan to add money by law, and it rejected any permanent forced deflation too. It wanted something different from either. What did it actually favor?
answer: A money supply set by the market, which no lobby can vote into inflation
choices: A money supply set by the market, which no lobby can vote into inflation
A fixed legal ratio of silver to gold, set once and never changed
A paper dollar grown by a fixed rule of three percent a year
A single world central bank issuing one shared currency
context: The Austrian move: the problem with Free Silver was not that it would have inflated, but that it would have inflated by government decree at a legislated ratio. A market-selected commodity money removes both discretion and lobbying. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: William Jennings Bryan, the silverite Democrat, took on the gold-standard Republican William McKinley in 1896. It was the first American presidential contest fought openly on the currency question, and McKinley won. What does that contest show about the choice of monetary regime?
answer: Money policy is always distributional -- there is no neutral choice between hard and soft money
choices: Money policy is always distributional -- there is no neutral choice between hard and soft money
Politicians can always neutralize the effects of monetary policy with fiscal measures
Elections rarely turn on economic issues alone
The gold standard was universally supported across all US regions in 1896
context: Every monetary regime enriches one group and disadvantages another. The Cantillon effect makes this unavoidable. The Austrian argument is not that hard money is neutral but that market-determined money removes the political discretion that lobbies compete for. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: Mao Zedong launched a ten-year purge inside his own Communist Party in 1966 and called it the Cultural Revolution. Mao sent millions of teenage students in red armbands into the streets to punish teachers, officials and neighbors for being 'not revolutionary enough.' Millions of Chinese were beaten, jailed, sent to labor camps or killed. What danger does that decade reveal?
answer: One party with total power can turn on its own people
choices: One party with total power can turn on its own people
A revolution grows gentler once its enemies are gone
Young people make the most loyal guardians of a state
A strong leader keeps a party from splitting apart
context: The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution ran 1966-76, formally launched with the May 16, 1966 Notification declaring class enemies had infiltrated the party at every level. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution.

question: A teenage student in a red armband, one of millions called the Red Guards, heard Mao Zedong name his teachers and local officials as enemies of the revolution, and Mao let the students go after them. What often happens when young mobs get that kind of power over adults?
answer: Widespread violence and settling of personal grudges
choices: Widespread violence and settling of personal grudges
Strict discipline, since the young follow orders best
Fair hearings, since the students knew the accused well
A quick return to order once the first targets fall
context: The Red Guards were students mobilized in the millions from summer 1966. They attacked the 'Four Olds' (old ideas, culture, customs, habits) and denounced teachers and officials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards.

question: A Red Guard mob in China's Cultural Revolution dragged a teacher before a crowd of hundreds. He had to stand or kneel wearing a placard that listed his supposed crimes while the crowd shouted denunciations at him for hours. What was this public ritual called?
answer: A struggle session
choices: A struggle session
A show trial
A rectification meeting
A denunciation forum
context: Struggle sessions (pi dou hui) targeted teachers, doctors, engineers, party rivals, and Buddhist monks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_session.

question: Mao Zedong gave the Red Guards a list of targets to smash wherever they found them: the ideas, culture, customs and habits handed down from the past. Books were burned, temples were smashed and people were humiliated in the streets. What did his followers call the list?
answer: The Four Olds
choices: The Four Olds
The Four Modernizations
The Four Freedoms
The Four Reforms
context: The 'Four Olds' (Si Jiu) framed the destruction of historic buildings, temples, books, artworks, and traditional practices during the campaign's peak in 1966-67. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Olds.

question: Mao Zedong turned on a man he had once chosen as his heir. Liu Shaoqi, the sitting President of China, was arrested, paraded before crowds, beaten and branded the country's top 'capitalist roader,' and he died in a prison cell in 1969 without medicine or basic care. What does his fate show about power under Mao?
answer: Even top loyal officials could be destroyed if Mao wanted them gone
choices: Even top loyal officials could be destroyed if Mao wanted them gone
Officials were safe once they had stepped back from power
The Party punished only those who broke its written rules
Only officials tied to foreign powers were in real danger
context: Liu Shaoqi, state president of the PRC, had helped organize the retreat from the Great Leap famine. Denounced by Mao, he died in prison November 12, 1969 of untreated pneumonia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Shaoqi.

question: Police arrested a small group headed by Mao Zedong's widow in October 1976, a month after his death, and with that the Cultural Revolution formally ended. Its members went on trial in 1980 and 1981. What was the group called?
answer: The Gang of Four
choices: The Gang of Four
The Central Case Group
The Little Red Council
The Beijing Bloc
context: The Gang of Four -- Jiang Qing (Mao's widow), Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen -- were arrested one month after Mao's death on September 9, 1976. Their trial in 1980-81 blamed them for the excesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_of_Four.

question: Mao Zedong set the Cultural Revolution going in May 1966, and it ran until his death ten years later. Millions of people were locked up or exiled to the countryside in those years. Historians' estimates of the direct deaths span a wide range. What is the standard range?
answer: About 500,000 to 2 million
choices: About 500,000 to 2 million
About 50 million to 200 million
context: Direct Cultural Revolution death estimates range from ~500,000 to ~2 million. Millions more were imprisoned or sent down to the countryside for reeducation through manual labor. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: Communist Party officials set down a verdict on Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution in 1981, five years after his death, in their 'Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party Since the Founding of the People's Republic.' It was the Party's own formal judgment. What did the resolution say?
answer: It was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the PRC
choices: It was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the PRC
It was a necessary period of ideological cleansing
It was largely misled by foreign interference
It was a success in mobilizing the countryside
context: The 1981 Resolution formalized the party's judgment that the Cultural Revolution was catastrophic, though it did not indict Mao personally to the same degree. The judgment remains formal party doctrine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_on_Certain_Questions_in_the_History_of_Our_Party_since_the_Founding_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China.

question: Mao Zedong told China's students to 'smash' anything old, and millions of families, party officials' children among them, were pulled from the cities to work in the countryside. Which economics tradition warns loudest against this kind of top-down social remake?
answer: Austrian economics: no planner can know enough to run a society
choices: Austrian economics: no planner can know enough to run a society
Keynesian economics: a slump deepens unless the state steps in to spend
Marxian economics: capitalism breeds crises that ruin its own workers
Development economics: farms must free up workers for industry to grow
context: The Austrian case, from Mises and Hayek, is that the knowledge a society runs on is scattered among millions of people; a campaign that smashes teachers, engineers and shopkeepers destroys that knowledge with them. Source: Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945).

question: Satoshi Nakamoto published his Bitcoin paper in 2008, after twenty years of tries at money made of computer bits, DigiCash and b-money among them. Each attempt ran into one problem that gold never had, built into how digital files work. What was it?
answer: A digital file can be copied and spent twice
choices: A digital file can be copied and spent twice
Digital files are too heavy to move
Computers cannot count money
Nobody wants online money
context: David Chaum founded DigiCash in Amsterdam in 1989 to license his 1982 blind-signatures work as an anonymous digital cash system. PayPal (1998, Confinity) was e-mail money for eBay; Silk Road (2011) was a Tor darknet market; Coinbase (2012) is a modern Bitcoin exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DigiCash.

question: Eric Hughes posted a founding essay to the cypherpunks' mailing list in March 1993. Its first sentence is often quoted as the root of the whole line of thinking that ran from his circle to Bitcoin. Which sentence opens it?
answer: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.'
choices: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.'
'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'Cypherpunks write code.'
'The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it.'
context: Hughes opens 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' (March 9, 1993) with this line. The 'specter' opener is Tim May's 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto; 'Cypherpunks write code' appears later within Hughes's essay as the operative motto; the routing-around-censorship line is John Gilmore's aphorism. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html.

question: Eric Hughes and two friends met in Oakland in 1992 to put secret codes in ordinary people's hands. Why did they think it was urgent?
answer: A state that reads every message can control people
choices: A state that reads every message can control people
Criminals were reading most email
Banks would not go online without codes
Spies were stealing trade secrets
context: Their worry was power, not convenience: a state that can read what people say to their friends can decide which friends they keep. The group took its name from the hacker and writer Jude Milhon at one of the early meetings. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Jude Milhon, a hacker and writer, named the group that Eric Hughes, Timothy May and John Gilmore started in the autumn of 1992. They met first in a house in Oakland, then argued about codes and privacy on a mailing list. What name did she give them, the one that stuck?
answer: the cypherpunks
choices: the Free Software Foundation
the cypherpunks
the Electronic Frontier Foundation
the Chaos Computer Club
context: Jude Milhon, known as St. Jude, was a hacker and a writer for Mondo 2000; the name she coined at one of the early meetings joins 'cypher' to 'cyberpunk'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Timothy May spent part of the late 1970s hunting a strange fault: memory chips kept corrupting themselves at random. The culprit was alpha particles from tiny amounts of radioactive matter in the chips' casing. The stock options from that job let him retire in his thirties. Which company was it?
answer: Intel
choices: Intel
Motorola
Texas Instruments
IBM
context: Timothy May worked at Intel; he helped solve alpha-particle contamination in DRAM chips in the late 1970s. Motorola, TI, and IBM were competitors on other semiconductor problems. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: John Gilmore hosted the group's mailing list on his own server in the early 1990s, when Washington's export rules counted strong encryption as a weapon of war, close to illegal for private citizens to use. The list existed to defend one political claim. Which claim?
answer: Ordinary people should be able to use unbreakable codes without asking permission
choices: Ordinary people should be able to use unbreakable codes without asking permission
Code makers should leave a spare key with the courts for warrants
Strong codes should be licensed by the state to vetted citizens
Privacy should be won through new laws in Congress, not software
context: The claim was about permission: American export rules of the early 1990s counted strong encryption as a munition, and the cypherpunks wanted anyone free to use it. Many on the list fought the government's 1993 Clipper chip plan, which would have left a spare key with the authorities. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's white paper of 2008 credited earlier work by two regulars of the 1990s mailing list John Gilmore hosted: a proof-of-work stamp against email spam, and a sketch for a currency with no bank at all. Who wrote those two?
answer: Adam Back and Wei Dai
choices: Adam Back and Wei Dai
David Chaum and Stefan Brands
Phil Zimmermann and Bruce Schneier
Ralph Merkle and Whitfield Diffie
context: The white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money (1998) and Adam Back's Hashcash, a proof-of-work stamp against spam. Hal Finney (reusable proofs of work) and Nick Szabo (bit gold) were on the same list. Chaum's DigiCash needed a central mint; Zimmermann wrote PGP; Merkle and Diffie were public-key pioneers. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Someone using a pen name sent a message on 31 October 2008 to a cryptography mailing list descended from John Gilmore's old server, sixteen years after Eric Hughes's circle first met in an Oakland house. What did the message carry?
answer: A design for electronic cash passed peer to peer, with no bank in the middle
choices: A design for electronic cash passed peer to peer, with no bank in the middle
A plan for digital coins issued jointly by a group of banks
A scheme for anonymous e-cash issued through one central mint
A proposal for digital money backed by gold held in a vault
context: The message was Satoshi Nakamoto's white paper, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', whose abstract proposes cash sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Three Bay Area engineers made a bet in an Oakland living room in the autumn of 1992, and it took sixteen years to pay off. Their mailing list went on to draw in the coders who would later design a new money. What proposition did they stake it on?
answer: That mathematics and code could give ordinary people privacy the government could not take away
choices: That mathematics and code could give ordinary people privacy the government could not take away
That academic conferences alone could deliver privacy without any working software
That legislative advocacy was the only viable path for privacy technology
That corporate partnerships were the correct model for delivering cryptography
context: The cypherpunk founding bet: math + code could deliver ordinary-user privacy without state permission. Bitcoin's launch is the largest single realization of that bet. Academic-conference-only, legislative, and corporate-partnership paths are exactly what the community rejected. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypherpunk.

question: Richard Nixon put his name to the Endangered Species Act in December 1973. A farmer who spots a rare woodpecker or a desert tortoise on his land can be told he may no longer farm, log or build on that patch, and the government pays him nothing. What does rural folk wisdom tell him to do?
answer: Shoot, shovel, and shut up
choices: Shoot, shovel, and shut up
Fence it, feed it, and forget it
Sell up, ship out, and start over
Call it in and claim the reward
context: The Endangered Species Act of 1973 was signed by Nixon on December 28, 1973. Uncompensated use-restriction on private land is the structural feature that generates the perverse incentive. Source: fws.gov (ESA history).

question: Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael published a study in 2003 of North Carolina landowners who feared one rare bird. If it nested on a man's land, the US Endangered Species Act could lock up the property, and he could never build or log on it again. Which bird was the study about?
answer: The red-cockaded woodpecker
choices: The red-cockaded woodpecker
The spotted owl
The sage grouse
The whooping crane
context: Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael, 'Preemptive Habitat Destruction Under the Endangered Species Act' (Journal of Law and Economics, 2003), documented preemptive pine harvest near red-cockaded woodpecker colonies. Source: jstor.org (Lueck + Michael 2003).

question: A landowner near a rare bird's colony in the American South learned that the Endangered Species Act forbids disturbing land near active nests. Economists found that he and his neighbors moved quickly. What did the rule actually produce?
answer: Destruction of mature pines before the birds could arrive
choices: Destruction of mature pines before the birds could arrive
Widespread planting of new pine seedlings
Voluntary conservation easements on new tracts
Nesting-box installation programs by landowners
context: The rational landowner destroys suitable habitat BEFORE a listed species arrives, so the property does not become subject to ESA restrictions. The statute causes the habitat destruction it was designed to prevent. Source: Lueck + Michael, Journal of Law and Economics (2003).

question: A rancher finds a protected animal on his land and is told he can no longer plow, build or cut timber on much of it. Every American gets a small warm feeling from knowing the species is safer, while he and a handful of owners like him pay heavy real costs in lost income. In public choice, what is this pattern called?
answer: Concentrated costs combined with dispersed benefits
choices: Concentrated costs combined with dispersed benefits
Concentrated costs combined with concentrated benefits
Dispersed costs combined with dispersed benefits
Symmetric costs and benefits on all parties
context: The specific landowner who draws the unlucky species-discovery outcome bears a concentrated cost; species-preservation benefits are shared by everyone in dispersed form. Both this mirror and Olson's original pattern produce systematic political-economy failures. Source: Adler, 'Money or Nothing' (Boston College Law Review 2008).

question: Elinor Ostrom studied how groups of people protect the resources they share. For saving a rare bird on private land, what kind of setup does her work favor?
answer: Local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem
choices: Local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem
A federal agency that buys and runs every habitat itself
Strict private ownership, with the state staying out entirely
National parks that take the land out of private hands
context: Ostrom's design principles (Governing the Commons, 1990) favor control from close at hand: local user groups with clear boundaries, rules they write themselves and a shared stake. Anderson and Leal apply the same thinking to wildlife on private land. Source: Ostrom (1990); Anderson + Leal, Free Market Environmentalism (Palgrave 2001).

question: A Southern landowner quietly killed a rare woodpecker on his property and buried it, fearing the Endangered Species Act would lock up his land. Delhi's old cobra bounty and a ban on driving that sends families out for another car went wrong in the same way as that law. In political-economy language, what is this class of failure called?
answer: Perverse incentives
choices: Perverse incentives
Distributional coalitions
Regulatory capture
Rent-seeking
context: Perverse-incentive failures occur when a rule creates individual incentives whose aggregate effect defeats the rule's stated purpose. The Delhi Cobra Effect, Mexico City license-plate driving restrictions, and ethanol mandates on feedstocks are related cases. Source: Sowell, Applied Economics (Basic 2007).

question: Suppose you sit in a legislature and read about a law that forbids harming certain rare animals and lets the government freeze what an owner may do with land where one is found, with no payment. In real cases, owners quietly cleared their trees before a survey could find the animal. What public-choice lesson should you draw?
answer: A rule that loads its whole cost on one owner makes him dodge it before it hits
choices: A rule that loads its whole cost on one owner makes him dodge it before it hits
A rule works only if its fines outweigh what an owner gains by breaking it
A rule fails unless inspectors can survey land before owners hear of it
A rule loses public support once its benefits are spread thin over everyone
context: The Adler-Lueck synthesis: uncompensated concentrated-cost regulations attract preemptive destructive behavior, and clearing trees before a survey breaks no law, so larger fines would not touch it. Compensation aligns landowner incentives with the regulation's stated purpose. Source: Adler (2008); Lueck + Michael (2003).

question: An Iowa corn grower found a new buyer in 2005, when the Renewable Fuel Standard began requiring a set amount of ethanol, fuel alcohol made from corn, in American gasoline. Millions of acres of corn now go into car engines instead of onto dinner plates. What does this rule tend to do to the price of corn as food?
answer: It makes food-corn more expensive because so much corn is used as fuel
choices: It makes food-corn more expensive because so much corn is used as fuel
It makes food-corn cheaper because farmers plant much more corn
It leaves food-corn prices alone because the fuel corn is extra
It raises gasoline prices while food prices stay the same
context: The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) was set in 2005 and expanded in 2007. Its stated purposes were less dependence on imported oil and lower greenhouse-gas emissions; its chief beneficiaries were US corn growers and ethanol producers such as ADM and POET. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Renewable_Fuel_Standard_(United_States).

question: A housewife banged a pot through the streets of a Latin American capital in January 2007, one of tens of thousands of angry protesters marching with farmers and workers. The price of her country's most important staple food had roughly doubled in just a few months, and families could no longer afford it every day. What was the staple, and where did the protests happen?
answer: Maize tortillas, in Mexico City
choices: Maize tortillas, in Mexico City
Rice, in San Salvador
Wheat bread, in Buenos Aires
Cassava flour, in Caracas
context: The Mexican tortilla-price spike tracked the US corn-price spike almost exactly. Similar food-price protests broke out in Egypt, Haiti, and other importing countries through 2007-2008. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: A family in a poor country, already spending most of its income on food, started skipping meals as the world prices of wheat, rice and corn soared in 2007 and 2008. The World Bank later estimated how many people that rise pushed back into extreme poverty, then defined as living on under about $1.25 a day. Roughly how many?
answer: More than 100 million
choices: More than 100 million
About 500,000
About 2 million
About 1 billion
context: The World Bank's own calculations identified more than 100 million pushed below the extreme-poverty line, mostly in food-importing countries in Africa and Asia. The scale of the international spillover is why the ethanol mandate is a Bastiat case at planetary scale. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: Donald Mitchell, an economist at the World Bank, tried in a 2008 internal memo to explain why world food prices had roughly doubled between 2002 and 2008. Some observers blamed drought, some rising Chinese demand, some oil prices. Mitchell's own calculation pointed at a specific policy category as the biggest policy-driven cause. Which one?
answer: Biofuel mandates diverting food crops to fuel
choices: Biofuel mandates diverting food crops to fuel
Chinese state grain stockpiling
Cuts to European Union farm subsidies
Rich countries' cuts to food aid
context: Mitchell's memo (later leaked to the press) estimated biofuel demand accounted for a large share of the price rise. Drought and oil prices also mattered; but biofuel demand was the largest policy-driven contributor and could have been reversed by legislative action alone. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: A high-school student asks an economist in the tradition of Frederic Bastiat how a 2005 American law about gasoline could have set off food-price riots in another country's capital by 2007. The economist notes that American farmers moved huge fields out of food crops and into fuel corn. Which reasoning move does the economist press?
answer: Seen versus unseen: the farm boom is seen, the dearer food abroad is not
choices: Seen versus unseen: the farm boom is seen, the dearer food abroad is not
Moral hazard: insured farmers planted riskier crops than before
Crowding out: federal borrowing raised poor countries' interest rates
The Cantillon effect: new dollars reached Iowa before Mexico City
context: Applied Bastiat: seen is US energy-independence talking points and Iowa corn-farm prosperity; unseen is the Guatemalan or Mexican family whose staple food now costs twice as much because of a US law about motor fuel. The dispersed costs cross national borders. Source: grokipedia.com/page/2007%E2%80%932008_world_food_price_crisis.

question: A Boeing salesman watched an airline order Airbus's re-engined A320 in place of his 737 soon after December 2010. The European plane burned much less fuel per flight, and airlines around the world were switching to it. What is this kind of competitive pressure most likely to push Boeing to do?
answer: Redesign its own plane to be more fuel-efficient
choices: Redesign its own plane to be more fuel-efficient
Cut its prices until the airlines came back
Leave the market for small jets to Airbus
Ask Washington to block sales of the Airbus
context: The Airbus A320neo (New Engine Option) launched in December 2010, forcing Boeing to respond quickly with the 737 MAX derivative rather than a clean-sheet replacement. The MAX entered service in May 2017. Source: boeing.com; airbus.com.

question: A Lion Air crew took off from Jakarta, Indonesia, in a brand-new Boeing 737 Max in October 2018, and the plane went down in the Java Sea shortly afterward. Five months later a second Max flying out of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, crashed six minutes after takeoff. Both had the same flaw in an automatic system that kept pushing the nose down. How many people died in the two crashes combined?
context: Lion Air 610 killed 189; Ethiopian 302 killed 157. Combined toll 346. Both crashes involved MCAS activation from erroneous angle-of-attack readings, with pilots unable to recover the automatic nose-down trim. Source: NTSB, KNKT (Indonesia), and ECAA (Ethiopia) final reports.

question: A Boeing engineer signed off on a safety check for a Boeing plane, doing a job for the Federal Aviation Administration, which regulates civilian flight in the United States. For nearly 20 years before the two 737 Max crashes of 2018 and 2019, the agency had let the company's own employees handle many such checks. What is the deep problem with a company checking its own product for the regulator?
answer: The reviewer's paycheck depends on the product passing
choices: The reviewer's paycheck depends on the product passing
The reviewer will always end up much too strict
The regulator will always ignore the results anyway
The reviewer will not understand the product being tested
context: The Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program authorized manufacturer engineers to act as FAA designees for certain certification tasks. The critical MCAS single-sensor decision and manual-omission call were made under ODA authority without independent FAA review. Source: faa.gov (ODA program history).

question: House of Representatives investigators spent 18 months on Boeing's 737 Max after two of the new airliners crashed within five months in 2018 and 2019. They wanted to know how the plane's flight-control software had gotten past pilots, airlines and safety regulators. Their committee's 2020 final report used one phrase for Boeing's behavior. What phrase did it use?
answer: A culture of concealment
choices: A culture of concealment
A culture of carelessness
A culture of haste
A culture of arrogance
context: The House T&I Final Committee Report (September 16, 2020) documented what it called a 'grossly insufficient' certification process and 'a culture of concealment' at Boeing. Source: transportation.house.gov (Final 737 MAX Committee Report).

question: Federal investigators dug into how Boeing had gotten its 737 Max approved after two of the jets crashed within five months of each other in Indonesia and Ethiopia. In 2021 the company reached a settlement with the Justice Department, admitting it had misled safety officials about the plane's flight-control software. About how big was that settlement?
answer: About $2.5 billion
choices: About $2.5 billion
About $250 million
About $25 million
About $25 billion
context: Boeing agreed to a $2.5B deferred prosecution agreement with the DOJ in January 2021 for fraud on the FAA. It is one of the largest such settlements in aviation history and is treated as close to a legal admission of the regulatory-capture pattern. Source: justice.gov (Boeing DPA January 2021).

question: Alaska Airlines pilots were climbing over Portland, Oregon, on 5 January 2024 when a door plug blew off their Boeing 737 Max 9 at about 16,000 feet. The cabin depressurized in seconds, but they landed safely and nobody died. The scare renewed a specific worry about a company with two fatal Max crashes behind it. Which worry was that?
answer: That cost cutting had undermined factory quality control
choices: That cost cutting had undermined factory quality control
That its flight software could still push the nose down
That airlines were skipping required maintenance checks
That its new engines were shaking the airframe apart
context: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 lost a plug-door in flight on January 5, 2024. The NTSB investigation revealed missing bolts and highlighted Boeing quality-control problems distinct from but adjacent to the 737 MAX certification story. Source: ntsb.gov (Flight 1282 preliminary report 2024).

question: George Stigler predicted in 1971 that regulators would come to serve the firms they police. Public-choice writers call the 737 Max case, in which the US Federal Aviation Administration let Boeing itself sign off on the safety of its new plane, a 'structural' failure and not a bribery scandal. What does 'structural' mean here?
answer: The people who know enough to check the design work for the company being checked
choices: The people who know enough to check the design work for the company being checked
A few officials broke rules the system itself should have caught
Boeing's chief executive personally overturned FAA decisions
The 737's airframe was a 1960s design stretched past its limits
context: The Stigler capture prediction meets its structural limit case in aviation certification: the FAA regulates aircraft manufactured by very few US companies, and the depth of engineering knowledge required to certify a modern airliner exists overwhelmingly inside the manufacturer. ODA formalized this asymmetry. Source: Stigler, Bell Journal (1971); Levine + Forrence (1990).

question: Congressional investigators looked into how the Federal Aviation Administration had approved Boeing's 737 Max after the two crashes of 2018 and 2019. Lawmakers answered in December 2020 with the Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act. Which specific reform did that law require?
answer: Stronger independent FAA review of a manufacturer's own safety sign-offs
choices: Stronger independent FAA review of a manufacturer's own safety sign-offs
A ban on manufacturers' own engineers doing any certification work
A new independent agency to take over all aircraft certification
A rule that every new airliner be designed from a blank sheet
context: The Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (December 2020) reformed the ODA program, required additional whistleblower protections, and imposed new manufacturer-notification and FAA-oversight duties. Source: congress.gov (Public Law 116-260, Division V).

question: An Iowa farmer reads through the latest US Farm Bill, scored at roughly $1.5 trillion over ten years. Congress renews it about every five years, and it bundles money for farmers with money for feeding poor families. Which single part of that spending is by far the biggest?
answer: SNAP (formerly food stamps)
choices: SNAP (formerly food stamps)
Crop insurance
Direct commodity subsidies
Conservation reserves
context: SNAP consumed approximately 76% of 2018 Farm Bill projected ten-year spending. Farm commodity programs were ~7%; crop insurance ~9%; conservation ~7%. The vast majority of the 'Farm Bill' is nutrition assistance, not farm spending. Source: cbo.gov (2018 Farm Bill scoring).

question: A US senator from Ohio badly wants federal money for a new bridge, and a senator from Texas badly wants a new army base. Neither project would pass alone, since most other senators care about neither. So the two combine both in one larger bill and promise to vote for each other's. What is this old trick called?
answer: Logrolling
choices: Logrolling
Filibustering
Gerrymandering
Caucusing
context: Logrolling is the vote-trading mechanism Buchanan + Tullock analyzed as a defining feature of majority-rule legislative bodies. Each side votes for the other side's priorities to secure its own. Source: Buchanan + Tullock, Calculus of Consent (Michigan 1962), Chapter 10.
