question: Two US senators struck a deal in 1973 that welded food-stamp money for poor city families and subsidies for rural farmers into one huge bill. They were friends from opposite parties, a Republican from Kansas and a Democrat from South Dakota. Who were they?
answer: Bob Dole and George McGovern
choices: Bob Dole and George McGovern
Barry Goldwater and Hubert Humphrey
Charles Percy and Edmund Muskie
Robert Taft and Estes Kefauver
context: Robert Dole (R-KS) and George McGovern (D-SD) architected the ongoing bundling of nutrition assistance and farm programs beginning with the 1973 Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act. Every farm-bill reauthorization since has kept the bundle. Source: Grokipedia 'Farm bill'; Guenther, 'Robert Dole' (2018).

question: A mother pays for groceries with food-stamp money while a farmer cashes a price-support check, both thanks to one law, the US Farm Bill. Every few years Congress renews the whole bundle rather than split it up. Which team of lawmakers keeps the bundle glued together year after year?
answer: Urban Democrats plus rural Republicans
choices: Urban Democrats plus rural Republicans
Urban Republicans plus rural Democrats
Farm-state Democrats plus farm-state Republicans
Southern Democrats plus Northern Republicans
context: Urban and suburban Democrats have the votes for SNAP but not for farm subsidies; rural Republicans have the votes for farm subsidies but not for SNAP. Bundled in a single bill, each side votes for the other's priorities to secure its own. Source: Grokipedia 'Farm bill'; Sheingate, The Rise of the Agricultural Welfare State (Princeton 2001).

question: House members voted in 2013 to split food-stamp aid out of the farm bill and pass it as a separate law. Farm-state and big-city members of Congress had long voted together by keeping the two bundled. What happened to that split when the House and Senate wrote the final law?
answer: The split failed and the two programs were bundled back together
choices: The split failed and the two programs were bundled back together
The split became law right after the House vote
The president vetoed the split and Congress overrode him
The Senate approved the split by unanimous consent
context: The 2013 House vote to separate SNAP from the farm bill passed on party lines but failed in conference. The final 2014 Farm Bill reconstituted the historical bundle. The pattern held: separation destroys the bipartisan coalition each half needs. Source: congress.gov (2013 farm bill legislative history).

question: A shopper at a grocery checkout swipes a special debit card that only works on food. It comes from the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the old food-stamp program and one of the largest anti-poverty programs in the United States. As of 2023, about how many Americans were receiving this help every month?
answer: About 42 million
choices: About 42 million
About 4 million
About 200 million
About 420,000
context: SNAP covered approximately 42 million recipients as of 2023, mostly in urban and suburban households. The urban-suburban geographic base is what gives Democratic legislators the personal stake in preserving the bundle. Source: fns.usda.gov (SNAP data).

question: A US president used the new Line-Item Veto Act of 1996 to strike a health-care payment out of a bundled bill without having to veto the whole thing. The intended recipient sued to stop him. On 25 June 1998 the justices struck the entire law down as unconstitutional. What is that landmark case called?
answer: Clinton v. City of New York
choices: Clinton v. City of New York
INS v. Chadha
US v. Nixon
Bowsher v. Synar
context: Clinton v. City of New York, 524 US 417 (1998), struck down the 1996 Line-Item Veto Act as unconstitutional. Bundled bills therefore remain a device Congress can protect through the presentment clause. Source: supremecourt.gov (524 US 417).

question: A senator wants a small favor for his home state, a bridge or a research center, and he knows one bill will pass no matter what: the National Defense Authorization Act, the enormous yearly military funding law that no senator dares vote down. So he quietly attaches his favor to it, buried in hundreds of pages. What is that legislative trick called?
answer: A rider
choices: A rider
A veto
A filibuster
A caucus
context: The NDAA is 'must-pass' annual legislation, so unrelated riders often ride on it. The same logrolling mechanism operates: riders that could not pass alone secure passage attached to a bill neither party wants to be seen voting against. Source: crsreports.congress.gov (NDAA analysis).

question: A rural senator and a big-city senator vote yes together on the US Farm Bill. For decades it has bundled farm subsidies with food-stamp help for poor families in cities, under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. What is the general public-choice reason for this kind of odd bundling?
answer: Each half alone could not get a majority, so bundling them creates one
choices: Each half alone could not get a majority, so bundling them creates one
Both halves are run by one department, so one bill saves paperwork
Food prices and farm incomes move together, so one law can steady both
Courts have ruled that farm and food spending must share one statute
context: Buchanan-Tullock logrolling operating as designed. The diagnostic question: what happens to the voting coalition if the bill is unbundled? If it collapses, the bundle is the reason both halves pass. This is not corruption -- it is coalition mechanics. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962), Chapter 10.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock launched what came to be called public-choice economics with The Calculus of Consent in 1962. They studied the trick of bundling two unrelated laws so that lawmakers who each want only half will vote for the whole. Their theory makes a sharp prediction about any attempt to split such a bundle in two. What does it predict?
answer: The voting coalition collapses and neither half passes
choices: The voting coalition collapses and neither half passes
Both halves pass separately by even larger majorities
Only the more expensive half survives
Only the cheaper half survives
context: The unbundling test: if the bundle exists for coalition mechanics, separation removes the vote-trade that makes each half viable. This is why the 2013 House SNAP separation attempt failed in conference. Source: Buchanan + Tullock (1962); the 2013 farm bill legislative history.

question: An old man of eighty-nine, Friedrich Hayek, published a book in 1988 calling socialism a 'fatal conceit,' a deadly kind of pride. What did he say was so proud about central planners?
answer: They thought a small group could plan what millions of people need
choices: They thought a small group could plan what millions of people need
They thought history itself was bound to prove them right
They thought workers alone should own every factory
They thought their party could never lose a vote
context: The Fatal Conceit was Volume 1 of the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek. The multi-decade Chicago project is now edited by Bruce Caldwell. Source: University of Chicago Press catalog page (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/F/bo3643985.html).

question: Friedrich Hayek refused in his 1988 book to call the free market 'capitalism,' a word he thought made it sound like a system rich people had invented for themselves. He gave it his own long name instead, for a system that lets strangers trade goods across a whole continent using customs and rules that no committee ever wrote. What does Hayek call it?
answer: The extended order of human cooperation
choices: The extended order of human cooperation
The spontaneous market equilibrium
The great division of intellectual labor
The self-regulating price mechanism
context: Hayek: 'our civilization depends, not only for its origin but also for its preservation, on what can be precisely described only as the extended order of human cooperation, an order more commonly, if somewhat misleadingly, known as capitalism.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Extended order' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_order).

question: Friedrich Hayek opened his final book with a claim about morals: they are a third kind of guide for human action, separate from two others and not built out of either. Old traditions and moral rules, he argued, carry a wisdom neither of those two could invent. Between which two guides did he place them?
answer: Instinct and reason
choices: Instinct and reason
Faith and science
Law and conscience
Self-interest and duty
context: The opening chapter of The Fatal Conceit is 'Between Instinct and Reason.' Hayek: morals 'are not a creation of man's reason but a distinct second endowment conferred on him by cultural evolution.' Source: Reason magazine review 'The Moral Glue' (December 1988) (https://reason.com/1988/12/01/the-moral-glue1/).

question: Friedrich Hayek took aim in The Fatal Conceit at brilliant engineers who could design factories, airplanes and bridges and believed they could design a whole economy the same way, from the top, with one plan. What claim did he make to show why that mistake was fatal?
answer: That the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold
choices: That the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold
That workers under socialism systematically consume less than under a market economy
That central planning tends to produce insufficient consumer choice at the retail level
That the state's monopoly on currency causes long-run inflation on a predictable lag
context: Hayek: the extended order 'constitutes an information gathering process, able to call up, and put to use, widely dispersed information that no central planning agency, let alone any individual, could know as a whole.' The fatal conceit is imagining a designed replacement could hold that knowledge. Source: Wikipedia, 'Extended order.'

question: David Hume, a Scottish philosopher of the 1700s, wrote that 'the rules of morality are not the conclusions of our reason.' Friedrich Hayek opened his attack on socialism, The Fatal Conceit, with that line. Which broader claim does it support?
answer: Long-tested traditions can be wiser than any single clever planner
choices: Long-tested traditions can be wiser than any single clever planner
Morals are only feelings, so no moral rule is truly better than another
Morals come from instinct, so teaching can never change them
Morals rest on faith alone, so reason must stay out of ethics
context: Hayek opens with David Hume's line 'the rules of morality are not the conclusions of our reason,' anchoring the book in the Scottish Enlightenment view (Hume, Ferguson, Smith, Mandeville) that a working society uses evolved rules its members did not invent. Source: Andrew J. Oliet substack review (https://andrewjoliet.substack.com/p/navigating-dual-moralities).

question: Friedrich Hayek insisted that nobody designed the rules that let people cooperate at huge scale: private property, honest trade, keeping contracts, the family. They survived and spread over many generations. What does Hayek call this process?
answer: Cultural evolution
choices: Cultural evolution
Rational reconstruction
Institutional consent
Democratic revision
context: Hayek's mechanism: cultural evolution -- the extended order 'arose from unintentionally conforming to certain traditional and largely moral practices, which spread by means of an evolutionary selection.' Source: Reason Papers essay on Hayek's extended order (https://reasonpapers.com/pdf/23/rp_23_3.pdf).

question: Soviet planners drew Friedrich Hayek's fire in The Fatal Conceit, but he warned about a milder Western version too: even friendly Keynesian management, he said, shared the error. What single move ties his critique of Soviet planning to his critique of Western technocracy?
answer: Both treat the evolved order as though a rational designer could grasp and improve on the knowledge it embodies
choices: Both treat the evolved order as though a rational designer could grasp and improve on the knowledge it embodies
Both underestimate the aggregate demand generated by public investment in physical infrastructure
Both fail to enforce the sound-money discipline that only a gold standard can supply
Both misread Adam Smith as a laissez-faire absolutist rather than a moral philosopher
context: Hayek's target in The Fatal Conceit is not only Soviet planning (visibly collapsing as he wrote) but also Western Keynesian macroeconomic management as a milder form of the same category mistake -- the fatal conceit is that any planner can hold the dispersed knowledge the extended order embodies. Source: Wikipedia, The Fatal Conceit; Cato Regulation 'Against Tribal Instincts' (https://www.cato.org/regulation/spring-2018/fatal-conceit).

question: Bruce Caldwell, the editor now overseeing the Collected Works of F. A. Hayek, has argued from textual evidence that The Fatal Conceit was reworked more heavily than a normal editing pass would explain, though the core argument remains unmistakably Hayek's. Which reasoning move about textual sources does his caution press?
answer: That a heavily rewritten manuscript should be read as a joint editor-author work, with specific passages flagged as uncertain
choices: That a heavily rewritten manuscript should be read as a joint editor-author work, with specific passages flagged as uncertain
That the entire book should be treated as a posthumous forgery and removed from the Collected Works
That the book's central arguments are refuted by the manuscript-editing anomalies alone
That Hayek's earlier books should be re-read as similarly rewritten by unnamed editors
context: Bruce Caldwell has argued textual evidence points to 'a product more of [Bartley's] pen than of Hayek's' -- so scholars should treat specific passages as uncertain while acknowledging the core argument (extended order, cultural evolution, fatal conceit) is unmistakably Hayek's mature synthesis. The book remains Volume 1 of the Collected Works. Source: Wikipedia; Alan Ebenstein biography review (https://www.independent.org/tir/2001-fall/friedrich-hayek/).

question: Woodrow Wilson signed a law two days before Christmas in 1913 creating a new American central bank, the body that decides how much money exists and where interest rates go. What is that central bank called?
answer: The Federal Reserve
choices: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
The Mint
The Bank of America
context: Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, the day the Senate gave its final approval, 43 to 25; the House had approved the final version 298 to 60. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: Lawmakers who wrote the Federal Reserve Act in 1913 spread the new central bank across the country, answering an old fear that one city would control the nation's credit. Each district would get a Reserve Bank of its own, belonging to the member banks there. How many districts were drawn?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
Four
Fifty
Six
context: The Act allowed not fewer than eight nor more than twelve districts; the Reserve Bank Organization Committee drew twelve in April 1914: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas, San Francisco. Each Reserve Bank was owned by its member commercial banks. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: Woodrow Wilson signed a banking law in December 1913 that created a new kind of paper money, issued through the new central bank. Over the following decades it pushed the older kinds of paper dollar out of use, and it is the paper money Americans carry today. What are those bills formally called?
answer: Federal Reserve Notes
choices: Federal Reserve Notes
Treasury Notes
United States Notes
National Bank Notes
context: Every dollar bill printed today is a Federal Reserve Note; National Bank Notes ended in 1935 and United States Notes in 1971. The first Federal Reserve Notes carried a 40 percent gold reserve; today they rest on the assets the Fed holds. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Federal_Reserve_Act; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Note.

question: Charles Lindbergh Sr. warned the House in 1913 that the new bill would set up a trust more gigantic than any other on earth. What fear lay beneath his objection?
answer: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
choices: That control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes
That paper money would replace gold coins in daily use
That most private banks would go out of business quickly
That the federal government would soon take over all factories
context: Rep. Charles Lindbergh Sr. (R-MN) opposed the bill from the House floor in December 1913, warning it would create 'the most gigantic trust on earth'. His son the aviator was 11 years old at the time. Source: Congressional Record, House, December 22, 1913.

question: Two Democrats steered the Federal Reserve Act through Congress in 1913, an Oklahoma senator and a Virginia congressman who had spent years pressing for a paper currency elastic enough to grow and shrink with the needs of business. The Act is sometimes known by their names. What were their last names?
answer: Owen and Glass
choices: Owen and Glass
Aldrich and Vreeland
Sherman and McKinley
Bland and Allison
context: Senator Robert Owen (D-OK) chaired Senate Banking; Representative Carter Glass (D-VA) chaired House Banking. The Act is sometimes called the Owen-Glass Act. Glass later co-sponsored the 1933 Banking Act (Glass-Steagall). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act.

question: A trader at the Federal Reserve buys securities from banks one morning to add reserves and push interest rates down; another day he sells them back to drain reserves and push rates up. This open-market buying and selling is the central bank's day-to-day tool. Which single main type of security does it trade?
answer: Treasury securities
choices: Treasury securities
Corporate bonds
Mortgage-backed securities
Foreign-currency reserves
context: Open-market operations are the Fed's day-to-day tool: buying Treasuries adds reserves and pushes rates down; selling Treasuries drains reserves and pushes rates up. The NY Fed desk executes them. In 2008-09 the Fed extended purchases to mortgage-backed securities under emergency authority. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

question: Woodrow Wilson signed the bill creating the Fed in 1913, and years after he died in 1924 a quotation spread in which he supposedly confessed, on his deathbed, that by creating it he had inadvertently destroyed his country. Which statement best describes the quote's documentary status?
answer: Its confession has no verified source and is likely invented
choices: Its confession has no verified source and is likely invented
It is in Wilson's collected papers at Princeton
The New York Times printed it the week he died
It appears in Wilson's last annual message to Congress
context: Historians have found no source for the deathbed confession ('I am a most unhappy man. I have unwittingly ruined my country'). The fake grew around a genuine line in Wilson's 1913 book The New Freedom: 'A great industrial nation is controlled by its system of credit. Our system of credit is privately concentrated.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson.

question: Congress gave the Fed two goals in the late 1970s that can pull apart. Critics say that makes the bank hard to hold to account. Why?
answer: It can blame a miss on one goal on the other
choices: It can blame a miss on one goal on the other
Courts cannot enforce goals so vague
Congress shares blame for any miss
Its two lobbies cancel each other out
context: The pair is usually called the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices, first written into the Federal Reserve Act by the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977 and restated by the Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978. When the two pull apart, a miss on either can be defended as service to the other. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm; https://www.richmondfed.org/~/media/richmondfedorg/publications/research/economic_brief/2011/pdf/eb_11-12.pdf.

question: A Federal Reserve official opens the 1978 Humphrey-Hawkins Act and finds the goals of her job written into it, a pair usually stated together and a third that everyone treats as following from them. What are the two goals in the pair?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Maximum growth and low taxes
Trade balance and currency reserves
Balanced budget and low national debt
context: The Federal Reserve Act (as amended in 1978) directs the Fed to 'promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates'. The third goal is treated as derivative. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/section2a.htm.

question: European treaty writers set up the European Central Bank in 1998 to run the new euro, and they gave it a rulebook unlike the Federal Reserve's. A 1978 law had told America's central bank to chase two goals at once; theirs got one main goal only. What is that single goal?
answer: Keep prices steady
choices: Keep prices steady
Get everyone a job
Hold lots of gold
Grow the economy fast
context: Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union makes price stability the ECB's primary objective; other goals may be supported only 'without prejudice' to it. This single-mandate design was influenced by the German Bundesbank's inflation-fighting record. Source: ecb.europa.eu/mopo/intro/objective.

question: Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps showed in 1967-68 that any long-run trade-off between inflation and jobs would break down, because workers who learn to expect higher prices adjust. Then in 1978 lawmakers wrote the Federal Reserve's two goals into law. What was awkward about the timing?
answer: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
choices: The trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation
The economy was then enjoying its longest boom since the war
Inflation had just fallen to its lowest level in decades
The Phillips curve was a brand-new discovery
context: By 1978 stagflation (simultaneous high inflation and unemployment) had made the naive Phillips-curve trade-off untenable. The dual mandate embedded the trade-off in statute at the very moment academic economics was walking away from it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: Congress told the Federal Reserve in 1978 to chase two goals at once, one about jobs and one about the value of the dollar. Austrian-school economists in the line of Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises argued that such a bank will feel a steady political pull toward one side. Which side does the Austrian critique say tends to win in practice?
answer: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
choices: The employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not
The price side, because inflation directly hurts bond markets that lobby the Fed
Both sides equally, since the mandate is symmetric on paper
Neither side, since the Fed is technically independent of politics
context: The Austrian public-choice reading: unemployment produces immediate political pressure; a couple of extra points of inflation is diffuse and delayed. A Fed with both goals therefore leans easy over time, producing persistent low-grade inflation and asset-price booms. Source: mises.org/library/case-100-percent-gold-dollar.

question: A saver looks up the gauge behind the Federal Reserve's public aim of 2 percent yearly inflation. But 'inflation' can mean many things: housing prices, stock prices, the M2 money supply, or the price of what a family actually buys. The Fed has steered by one specific measure since 2012. Which measure does it track?
answer: The PCE price index
choices: The PCE price index
The Case-Shiller housing price index
The S&P 500 total return
The M2 money supply
context: Since January 2012 the Fed has stated its 2 percent goal in terms of the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE), a broad gauge of what households buy; officials also watch a 'core' version without food and energy. Austrian critics note that the target leaves house and share prices outside it. Source: federalreserve.gov/faqs/economy_14400.htm.

question: Jerome Powell, then chair of the Fed, repeatedly called the price rises of 2021 'transitory,' meaning they would soon pass on their own. Gasoline, groceries and rent kept climbing, and in 2022 the Fed reversed course and hiked interest rates sharply. Austrian critics of the law that tells the Fed to fight both inflation and unemployment saw a pattern in the miss. What pattern did they see?
answer: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
choices: The employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error
Supply shocks that no central bank could have foreseen
Federal spending that swamped whatever the Fed did
Big firms raising prices faster than their own costs
context: Fed leadership held rates near zero through most of 2021 while inflation ran above 5 percent, using the labor-market recovery as reason to delay. When the pivot came in March 2022, the Fed had to tighten unusually fast. Austrians treat this as the mandate's incentive structure playing out on schedule. Source: federalreserve.gov press releases 2021-22.

question: Milton Friedman wanted the Federal Reserve out of the business of sitting in a room picking interest rates by hand. He asked for a mechanical rule instead: one simple number, held steady year after year, that the Fed could not override on a whim. What was his proposed rule?
answer: A constant money-supply growth rate
choices: A constant money-supply growth rate
A constant unemployment target
A constant real wage index
A constant nominal exchange rate
context: Friedman's 'k-percent rule' would have set money-supply growth at a low, constant percentage annually, removing Fed discretion over the employment-inflation trade-off entirely. Rothbard argued Friedman's rule was still fiat and preferred a gold-anchored money. Source: Friedman, A Program for Monetary Stability (1960).

question: Congress gave one institution two jobs in a 1978 law named after a senator who died before it passed: hold prices still and keep as many people working as it can. Those two goals, Austrian critics argue, often clash directly. Which clash do they point to?
answer: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
choices: Printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable
Cutting rates to lift employment weakens the dollar abroad, which the same law forbids
Holding prices steady needs a balanced federal budget, which only Congress can deliver
Putting more people to work pushes wages down, which drags prices below the target
context: Hubert Humphrey (D-MN, former Vice President under Johnson and 1968 Democratic presidential nominee) died January 13, 1978. Augustus Hawkins (D-CA), the House co-sponsor, lived until 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey.

question: Thomas Sowell listened to people fight over one law after another, welfare rules, gun rules, tax rules, school rules, and he said they were not really arguing about the laws. Deep down, he said, both sides held two very different views of one thing. Different views of what?
answer: What human beings are capable of
choices: What human beings are capable of
Who ought to hold political power
How wealth ought to be divided up
Which rights the law must protect
context: Sowell's constrained vision treats human capacities as permanently limited by flaws, scarcity and incomplete knowledge, so every arrangement buys one thing by giving up another. The unconstrained vision treats those limits as artifacts of bad institutions that clear-sighted people could redesign away. Sowell's most quoted sentence belongs to the first: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: A newspaper columnist claims a new government program is working, and his whole proof is three heart-warming interviews with people who say it changed their lives. Readers of Thomas Sowell boil his method down to five hard questions to press on any policy claim. Which of the five does that column beg?
answer: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
choices: What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
context: Sowell's complaint in The Vision of the Anointed is that a claim gets accepted 'even though evidence is seldom asked or given'. Three people who feel helped reveal nothing about the people the programme missed, harmed, or would have helped anyway, and those are the ones no reporter interviews.

question: A mayor boasts that his city's new housing program built 4,000 apartments and moved 4,000 families in. Every proud number counts what the program made. Readers of Thomas Sowell carry five hard questions to press on any such claim. Which one was skipped?
answer: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
choices: At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: The money, the land, the timber and the builders' hours all had other employments, and those employments are now gone. Sowell's point is that a benefit figure standing alone is not analysis -- it is advertising. The cost is real whether or not anybody publishes it.

question: A writer lists real failures at a private insurer, claims denied and customers stranded, and says the state should take over. Thomas Sowell replies that the insurer is real, but the state in the writer's head is not. Which of the five questions is he pressing?
answer: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
choices: Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
context: This is the move at the heart of Knowledge and Decisions: markets and governments are both ways of deciding, and both are staffed by real people with limited knowledge. Comparing a real market with an ideal government is not a comparison at all. Sowell's question does not settle who wins -- it insists that both contestants show up.

question: A tenant in a rent-capped flat pays less in the first year, exactly as promised, and the cap is declared a success on that evidence. Landlords, builders and would-be tenants have not yet had time to do anything about it. Which of the five Sowell questions has been skipped?
answer: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
choices: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
context: Applied Economics carries the subtitle Thinking Beyond Stage One for exactly this reason. A landlord who cannot raise the rent can still stop maintaining, convert the building, or sell it; a builder can put his capital somewhere else entirely. None of that shows up in year one, and all of it lands on the tenants the cap was written for.

question: A candidate promises to end homelessness for good, with zero downside for anyone. Thomas Sowell would say no such plan can exist, and not because this one is flawed; the reason lies in what policy always is. Which of the five questions does he press?
answer: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
choices: What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss
What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data
At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before
And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one
context: 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.' -- A Conflict of Visions (1987). The trade-off question is not the same as the cost question: cost asks what the resources gave up, trade-offs asks which problems a society agrees to accept in exchange for the ones it is removing. A programme with no downside is not a bargain a human being can strike.

question: A politician and an economist weigh the same policy in Thomas Sowell's Applied Economics of 2003. Sowell's charge is not that politicians are stupid; it is that their analysis reliably halts at one particular point. Where does it halt?
answer: At the policy's first, immediate result
choices: At the policy's first, immediate result
At the point where the money runs out
At the next general election in the cycle
At the boundary of their own department
context: Hence the subtitle: Thinking Beyond Stage One. Sowell's chapters run housing, medical care, discrimination and national development through the later repercussions, which he says are often very different from the immediate effects and much longer lasting. Source: Wikipedia, 'Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One'.

question: Friedrich Hayek published a famous essay in 1945 showing how market prices carry scattered knowledge from stranger to stranger. Thomas Sowell agreed, then extended the idea with a further question about every institution he studied: markets, courts, firms, families, legislatures. What further question does he ask?
answer: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
choices: How each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken
How each one distributes the gains among the people taking part
How much each one costs the taxpayer to administer in a year
How quickly each one can be replaced when the public turns on it
context: This is Sowell's extension of Hayek and the reason 'compared to what?' is an institutional question rather than a debating trick. A firm that misjudges its customers loses money and has to change; an agency that misjudges its clients may get a larger budget. Both make mistakes. What separates them is what happens next. Source: Wikipedia, 'Knowledge and Decisions'.

question: A senator proposes to cancel all outstanding student debt. Thomas Sowell would grant that the first effect is exactly what its authors promise: today's borrowers stop owing. One of the five questions asks what follows. Which second-round effect does it put first?
answer: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
choices: Colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation
Banks tighten lending to every borrower who is not at a college
Graduates who repaid early petition Congress for equal treatment
States cut their own university funding by the amount forgiven
context: All four are second-round effects worth tracing; Sowell's question puts the incentive change first because it is the one that alters what people do from now on, rather than redistributing what has already happened. The question does not say the policy is wrong; it shows which column of the ledger the proposal has left blank.

question: Suppose you learn Thomas Sowell's five questions and run them on rent control, tariffs and the minimum wage, and you end up disagreeing with him about all three. The questions have still done their work. What is it that they actually deliver?
answer: An account of what a policy costs and causes, for each person to weigh
choices: An account of what a policy costs and causes, for each person to weigh
A ranking of policies from the most harmful down to the least harmful
A test that every sound policy passes and every unsound one fails
A method for predicting which policies a legislature will adopt
context: The five-question distillation -- trade-offs, at what cost, compared to what, what hard evidence, and then what happens -- is a reader's compression rather than a list Sowell packaged in one book; the questions appear across A Conflict of Visions, Knowledge and Decisions, The Vision of the Anointed, Applied Economics and dozens of columns. They yield a full account and no verdict. Two people can run all five honestly on the same policy and still weigh the answers differently, because what a society should trade for what is not an economic question.

question: A new regional Reserve Bank president finds that he votes at every rate-setting meeting, while the presidents of the other regional banks take turns. His bank's seat has been permanent since 1942. Which city is his bank in?
answer: New York
choices: New York
Chicago
San Francisco
Dallas
context: The New York Fed president is a permanent voter and vice chair of the FOMC; the other eleven regional presidents rotate through four voting seats. New York's de facto permanent vote under the 1935 structure was made official in 1942, and the New York bank carries out the committee's trades in the markets. Source: https://www.kansascityfed.org/ten/looking-back-the-federal-open-market-committee-and-its-voting-rotation/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Bank_of_New_York.

question: A new president finds that most of the seven governors on the Federal Reserve Board in Washington were picked by his predecessors and will stay for years. Lawmakers in 1935 built the Board that way to keep it out of party swings. What keeps the governors in their seats?
answer: Each serves a single fourteen-year term
choices: Each serves a single fourteen-year term
Each serves for life, like a Supreme Court justice
Each can be removed only by a two-thirds Senate vote
Each can be fired only by a vote of the other governors
context: Governors are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate for single fourteen-year terms, staggered so that one ends every two years: the longest fixed terms in the federal government outside the Supreme Court's life tenure. A president may remove a governor only for cause. Source: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/structure-federal-reserve-board.htm.

question: Alan Greenspan cut interest rates after the stock crash of 1987, and he did it again whenever stocks dropped hard in the years that followed. What do big investors do after years of a central banker cutting rates to save them?
answer: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
choices: They take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out
They pull their money out of stocks and into safe bonds
They hedge every bet more carefully than before
They demand higher interest rates on every loan
context: Greenspan chaired the Fed 1987-2006 across the Black Monday 1987 crash, the 1998 LTCM rescue, the 2000 dot-com bust and the 2004-06 rate cycle. His dominance of FOMC agenda-setting became a case study in chair-driven committee dynamics. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan.

question: A banker whose bank runs short of reserves one evening borrows from another bank for just a few hours. The Federal Reserve targets the rate on loans of that kind, and moving that one rate ripples out through every other rate in the economy. What is this key rate called?
answer: The federal funds rate
choices: The federal funds rate
The discount rate
The prime rate
The London interbank rate
context: The FOMC votes a target range for the federal funds rate -- the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other. The New York Desk then conducts open-market operations to keep the effective rate in that range. Source: federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm.

question: Friedrich Hayek argued in 1945 that no group, however smart, can gather up the scattered facts held by a country's borrowers, savers and firms. Austrian critics turn his point on central banks that set rates. What is this move usually called?
answer: The knowledge problem
choices: The knowledge problem
The free-rider problem
The principal-agent problem
The tragedy of the commons
context: Hayek argued that the price system distributes knowledge no central board could gather in time -- the 'knowledge problem'. Applied to the FOMC: twelve people cannot know the 'correct' interest rate for an economy of hundreds of millions. Source: Hayek, American Economic Review, September 1945.

question: A new president of a Federal Reserve district bank takes his place on the rate-setting committee, and public-choice critics see a governance gap in how he got there. Private commercial banks in his district help decide who gets the job. Which body actually chooses each district bank's president?
answer: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
choices: The Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank
All nine directors of that regional bank, bankers included
The Class A directors, the bankers on that regional board
The member banks of the district, voting directly
context: Each regional bank has nine directors in three classes. Since the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 only the Class B and C directors, the non-bankers, choose the president, and the Board of Governors approves the choice; the Class B directors are elected by the member banks. There is no Senate confirmation. Source: https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2022/feb/role-bankers-on-federal-reserves-boards-directors.

question: A Federal Reserve chair changes one word in the short statement after a rate-setting meeting, say from 'patient' to 'measured,' and billions of dollars in stocks and bonds move within seconds. A whole profession of reporters and analysts has grown up around this word-by-word reading. What are the people who do it called?
answer: Fed watchers
choices: Fed watchers
Reserve auditors
Rate scouts
Balance-sheet analysts
context: 'Fed watcher' names an entire subprofession -- economists at investment banks, journalists at Bloomberg and Reuters, and think-tank analysts whose full-time job is reading FOMC statements, minutes, and chair speeches for subtle shifts. Adjective changes ('appropriate', 'patient', 'accommodative') routinely move markets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fedspeak.

question: A New York shopkeeper is handed a note from a Georgia bank he has never heard of, one of hundreds of different bills moving through the country before the Civil War. He needs to know whether that faraway bank is still open and what its notes are really worth. Where does he look it up?
answer: Printed banknote reporters
choices: Printed banknote reporters
Federal exchange rates
Treasury bulletins
Chamber-of-commerce circulars
context: Banknote reporters were subscription publications listing every known bank and the current discount at which its notes traded. A note from a distant bank might sell at 90 cents on the dollar; from a failed bank at zero. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_banking.

question: Salmon Chase went looking for enormous sums at Abraham Lincoln's Treasury to pay for the Civil War. The National Banking Acts he designed in 1863 and 1864 let new federal banks issue paper notes backed by government war bonds. Beyond the war money, what problem did those laws solve?
answer: The country had no single trusted paper currency
choices: The country had no single trusted paper currency
Farmers could not borrow to buy new machinery
The Treasury had no way to collect income taxes
Southern banks held most of the nation's gold
context: The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 created federally-chartered national banks that could issue a uniform note backed by Treasury bonds held as reserves. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/national-banking-acts.

question: Lawmakers set out in 1865, in the last months of the Civil War, to kill off state-chartered banknotes and push every bank into the new national system. They never banned the state notes, yet within a couple of years the notes had all but vanished. How did Congress drive them out?
answer: It taxed the notes at 10 percent
choices: It taxed the notes at 10 percent
It made every state bank swap its notes for gold
It barred state notes from crossing state lines
It bought the notes up with greenbacks and burned them
context: The 10 percent tax on state-bank notes, passed in March 1865 and upheld by the Supreme Court in Veazie Bank v. Fenno (1869), made state note issue commercially pointless. State banks that survived shifted to deposit banking. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_bank; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veazie_Bank_v._Fenno.

question: Arthur Rolnick and Warren Weber, economists at the Minneapolis Federal Reserve, took a fresh look in 1983 at the actual bank failure records from the 1830s to the Civil War. Old American textbooks called those years, when no federal central bank oversaw the banks, pure chaos. What did the two find about bank failures in states with good free-banking rules?
answer: They were modest and comparable to later regulated eras
choices: They were modest and comparable to later regulated eras
They ran to five times later loss rates
They wiped out about half of all deposits nationally
They caused a permanent gold outflow
context: Rolnick and Weber studied bank failure rates and noteholder losses in the leading free-banking states (New York, Massachusetts) and found them modest. This is now standard revisionist scholarship. Source: minneapolisfed.org/research/qr/qr731.pdf.

question: King William III was fighting France when the Bank of England was created in 1694. The First Bank of the United States came in 1791 with the debts of the Revolutionary War behind it, and Salmon Chase built a national banking system in the middle of the Civil War. Why do wartime rulers push so hard for a central bank?
answer: To make it easier to borrow the huge sums a war costs
choices: To make it easier to borrow the huge sums a war costs
To stop enemy agents from forging the nation's money
To hold down food prices for soldiers' families at home
To keep gold from leaving the country for the enemy
context: Salmon Chase (Treasury 1861-64, later Chief Justice of the United States) designed the National Banking system to help finance the Union war effort by creating a captive market for Treasury bonds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase.

question: A Michigan noteholder set off into remote woods to swap a bank's paper money for gold or silver coins, which he could do only at its redemption office. Some banks in Michigan and Indiana hid those offices where hardly any human could reach them, and people joked that a certain forest creature was more common at the counter than customers. What was the term for these banks?
answer: Wildcat bank
choices: Wildcat bank
Fly-by-night bank
Ghost bank
Backwoods trust
context: 'Wildcat bank' comes from the 1830s-40s midwestern banks whose redemption offices were placed in wooded locations far from ordinary commerce, on the theory that wildcats outnumbered actual noteholders. The colorful term outlived the era. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildcat_banking.

question: J. P. Morgan organized the rescue of the 1907 bank panic himself, because the National Banking system built around the Civil War had deliberately left one crucial feature out. Critics had feared it would concentrate too much power in one spot. After panics in 1873, 1893 and 1907, the gap became the main political case for the Federal Reserve of 1913. What was missing?
answer: A lender of last resort
choices: A lender of last resort
A gold standard
Federal insurance of bank deposits
A single national clearinghouse
context: National banks could issue a uniform currency but no institution stood ready to supply emergency liquidity in a panic. Every major panic (1873, 1893, 1907) had to be handled by ad-hoc private rescues, culminating in Morgan's 1907 intervention. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/national-banking-acts.

question: A Union soldier in the American Civil War drew his pay in a brand-new kind of paper money. The Treasury, without enough gold on hand to pay him and buy weapons, had printed it with no metal behind it at all, just the federal government's promise. What nickname did people give those notes?
answer: Greenbacks
choices: Greenbacks
Federal Reserve Notes
Silver Certificates
Continental dollars
context: Greenbacks were the fiat US Notes issued by the Treasury under the Legal Tender Acts starting 1862. They circulated at a discount to gold during the war and returned to par when convertibility was restored in 1879. They are distinct from national-bank notes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenback_(money).

question: A merchant who was offered a note from a shaky state bank priced it at a steep discount, and a printed guide listed the going rate. Hundreds of state-chartered banks issued their own notes from roughly 1837 to 1863, and note-holders had to know which were sound. Friedrich Hayek would describe this kind of order in his 1945 essay on prices. What kind of solution was it?
answer: An emergent order, with prices carrying each bank's reputation
choices: An emergent order, with prices carrying each bank's reputation
A cartel, with the big-city banks fixing every discount
A licensed utility, with each state approving the guides
A futures market, with traders betting on bank failures
context: The Hayekian reading: the banknote-reporter system was a decentralized market for reputation and risk information; discount prices carried the signal. This is a small-scale example of the price-system-as-knowledge-aggregator that Hayek 1945 would later theorize. Source: minneapolisfed.org/research/qr/qr731.pdf.

question: Friedrich Hayek called thirty-nine economists and thinkers to a Swiss mountain hotel above the village of Mont Pelerin in April 1947. Central planning was rising fast, in Stalin's Soviet Union and in the growing welfare states of Western Europe, and most university professors backed it. What older intellectual tradition did he call them together to defend?
answer: Classical liberalism
choices: Classical liberalism
Utilitarianism
Tory conservatism
Mercantilism
context: Hayek convened the founding conference of the Mont Pelerin Society, April 1-10, 1947, at the Hotel du Parc in the village of Mont Pelerin near Vevey. Mises, Friedman and Robbins were all in the room; Hayek organised it and served as the society's first president, 1947-1961. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'; Grokipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: Frank Knight objected in 1947 when the scholars gathered at Mont Pelerin nearly named their new society after two 1800s liberal writers. They were 'two Catholic aristocrats,' he said, and Ludwig von Mises worried their old mistakes would stick to the group. So the society took the village's name. Which two writers had been proposed?
answer: Lord Acton and Alexis de Tocqueville
choices: Lord Acton and Alexis de Tocqueville
Adam Smith and David Ricardo
John Stuart Mill and Herbert Spencer
Edmund Burke and Benjamin Constant
context: The group was to have been the Acton-Tocqueville Society. Knight's objection and Mises's carried the day, and the name of a Swiss hillside above Lake Geneva went instead onto the most influential classical-liberal association of the century. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society', citing Alan Ebenstein, Friedrich Hayek: A Biography (2014), ch. 18.

question: Milton Friedman, thirty-four, was in the room when the Mont Pelerin scholars adopted their Statement of Aims in April 1947. It warned that in much of the world the conditions of human dignity and freedom had already gone, and that even 'that most precious possession of Western Man' was threatened. Which possession did it mean?
answer: Freedom of thought and expression
choices: Freedom of thought and expression
Private property and the free market
Freedom of worship and of conscience
The right to vote in free elections
context: The Statement opens: 'The central values of civilization are in danger.' It names freedom of thought and expression as 'that most precious possession of Western Man,' threatened by creeds that seek to suppress all views but their own, and goes on to blame theories that question the rule of law and a decline of belief in private property and the competitive market. Source: https://www.montpelerin.org/statement-of-aims/.

question: Friedrich Hayek's guests at Mont Pelerin ran up a bill of 18,062.08 Swiss francs over ten days in 1947, and 93 per cent of that bill was settled not by the scholars, nor by their universities, but by one institution alone. What kind of institution paid the overwhelming share?
answer: A Swiss commercial bank
choices: A Swiss commercial bank
An American charitable foundation
A British government department
A Vatican educational trust
context: The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, later Credit Suisse (taken over by UBS in 2023), paid 93 per cent of the conference costs. Smaller sums came from the William Volker Fund via Harold Luhnow, from the Bank of England via Alfred Suenson-Taylor, and from the Foundation for Economic Education. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society', citing Mirowski and Plehwe (2009), p. 15.

question: Milton Friedman argued in his 1953 essay 'The Methodology of Positive Economics' that a theory should be judged only by whether its predictions come true, even if its starting assumptions look completely fake or unrealistic. Friedrich Hayek refused to accept that test for economics. What was his main objection?
answer: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
choices: That treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish
That predictions in economics can never be made short-run enough
That an economist's assumptions matter more than any test can show
That economics should be studied as a branch of law and history
context: Hayek attacked what he called scientism in The Counter-Revolution of Science (1952) and returned to it in his 1974 Nobel lecture 'The Pretence of Knowledge': an economics that counts only what it can count will quietly drop the dispersed, local, tacit knowledge that makes markets work at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Milton Friedman wrote the introduction to the fiftieth-anniversary edition of Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom, and admired the man for half a century. On one piece of Hayek's economics he was blunt to the point of rudeness, and said so in print more than once. Which part of Hayek's work did Friedman call false?
answer: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
choices: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts
Hayek's account of how prices carry information
Hayek's account of how legal rules evolve
Hayek's account of how planning erodes liberty
context: 'The Hayek-Mises explanation of the business cycle is contradicted by the evidence. It is, I believe, false.' Friedman first pressed the objection in a 1964 NBER article and again in Economic Inquiry in 1993, examining U.S. cycles from 1879 to 1988 and finding no significant link between the length of an expansion and the severity of the contraction after it. Source: Mark Skousen, 'Economics on Trial', The Freeman (FEE), March 1, 1995.

question: Gunnar Myrdal, a Swedish social democrat who had spent his career arguing for planning, split the 1974 economics Nobel with Friedrich Hayek, who argued central planning could never work. What does that shared award show about the state of the field at that time?
answer: Serious economists still disagreed at the deepest level about whether planning was possible
choices: Serious economists still disagreed at the deepest level about whether planning was possible
Every top economist had come to agree that planning worked well
Every top economist had come to agree that planning could never work
The committee refused to pick a side because the two men were personal friends
context: The 1974 prize went jointly to Hayek and the Swedish social-democrat Gunnar Myrdal 'for their pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations and for their penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena.' Tinbergen won in 1969, Kuznets in 1971, Leontief in 1973. Eight Mont Pelerin members have taken the prize in all: Hayek, Friedman, Stigler, Allais, Buchanan, Coase, Becker and Vernon Smith. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Friedrich Hayek'; Wikipedia, 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto ran Bitcoin's software on his own computer on 3 January 2009 and mined the very first block of the chain, block number zero. What has that first block been called ever since?
answer: the genesis block
choices: the genesis block
the coinbase block
the halving block
the segwit block
context: The first block is 'the genesis block' or 'Block 0'; it was mined January 3, 2009. 'Coinbase' names the special transaction inside each block that mints new coins to the miner; the halving is a recurring reward-cut event; SegWit was a 2017 protocol upgrade. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: A programmer using the name Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's very first block in January 2009, and it paid a 50-coin reward to the address named in the software. A quirk in the first version of the code gave that reward a strange fate, unlike any reward mined since. What can never happen to it?
answer: it can never be spent or moved to another address
choices: it can never be spent or moved to another address
it can never be seen by other nodes
it can never be traced to the address it was paid to
it can never be read in the block's own data
context: By a quirk of the original code the genesis-block coinbase output is unspendable: the 50 BTC sits in the chain, visible to every node, but can never be moved, so it never circulates. The 21-million cap, which follows from the halving schedule, is unchanged. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto sealed a line of text into the coinbase transaction of Bitcoin's first block in January 2009, the entry that creates new coins. The line was a front-page headline, copied from a London newspaper printed that same morning. Which paper?
answer: The Times
choices: The Times
The Financial Times
The Guardian
The Daily Telegraph
context: The embedded text reads 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' -- the actual front-page headline of the London Times that day. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Bitcoin's anonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, mined his first block on 3 January 2009 and permanently embedded in it a real newspaper headline printed that same day. Many read it as his reason for building a currency no government could inflate. What did the headline talk about?
answer: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
choices: the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks
the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates
the European Central Bank launching the euro
the Bank of Japan announcing quantitative easing
context: The Times, January 3, 2009 front page: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' referred to Alistair Darling, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, preparing to rescue major British banks a second time following the 2008 financial crisis. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Times archive.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto made one newspaper headline do two jobs at once when he put it in Bitcoin's first block. The first was cryptographic: the dated text went into the block's hash. What was that first function called?
answer: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
choices: a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined
an encryption key preventing later modification
a mining-difficulty target for Block 1
a signature identifying Satoshi's private key
context: Including a January 3, 2009 headline proves the block could not have been mined earlier, the same trick as a hostage holding up that day's newspaper to prove a video is new. The Bitcoin protocol has separate difficulty and signature machinery. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's first block on 3 January 2009, and then he stopped. He did not mine block 1 right after, presumably to be sure his new software worked correctly on a live network before letting the chain grow. Roughly how long was the gap before block 1 appeared?
answer: about six days
choices: about six days
about six hours
about six weeks
about six minutes
context: Block 0 was mined January 3, 2009; Block 1 was mined January 9, 2009 -- a gap of about six days. From that point on, blocks arrived on roughly the ten-minute schedule that has held ever since. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block; Bitcoin block chain.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto embedded a line of news in Bitcoin's first block, and Austrian-school writers in the tradition of Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek read it as a signal. It says, they argue, that Bitcoin can do something no government-issued fiat money can. Which move does their argument make?
answer: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule and refuse to rescue failed banks
choices: That a monetary system can bind itself to a rule and refuse to rescue failed banks
That a monetary system can be democratically voted into and out of existence each cycle
That a monetary system's founder must remain publicly known to legitimize it
That a monetary system requires state backing to be trusted
context: The genesis-headline argument (Ammous, Song, Antonopoulos) is a rules-vs-discretion move: Bitcoin binds itself at issuance to a fixed schedule with no bailout discretion. Democratic overturning, publicly-known founder, and state backing are precisely what Bitcoin does NOT rely on. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Mao Zedong ordered every family farm in China into giant government-run collectives in 1958 and called the campaign the Great Leap Forward. Peasants were pulled away from planting rice and grain and told to melt down their own tools. The famine that followed was the deadliest in recorded history. What was its main cause?
answer: Farmers were forced off their own plots and had no reason to work hard
choices: Farmers were forced off their own plots and had no reason to work hard
Three years of drought and floods ruined the harvests
The Soviet Union cut off grain shipments after a quarrel
A plant disease spread through the rice fields
context: The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) was Mao's attempt to overtake Britain in steel output within 15 years through people's communes and backyard industrial furnaces. Beijing long blamed 'three years of natural disasters'; historians working in the archives put policy first. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chinese_Famine.

question: A Chinese peasant family lost its land to Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward and was pushed into a huge farming group of five thousand households or more, both an economic unit and a local government. What were the groups called?
answer: People's communes
choices: People's communes
Village councils
Farm brigades
Peasant soviets
context: People's communes of 5,000 households or more replaced smaller cooperatives in 1958. Private plots, tools, and cookware were absorbed. The commune was both economic unit and local government. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_commune.

question: Mao Zedong promised in 1958 to pass Britain in steel production within fifteen years, and the industrial side of his Great Leap Forward asked ordinary peasants to make the metal. They melted down their cookware, farm tools and door hinges in tiny village kilns to meet local quotas, and almost none of it came out usable. What were those village-scale kilns called?
answer: Backyard steel furnaces
choices: Backyard steel furnaces
Rural blast plants
Village steel mills
Communal foundries
context: Backyard furnaces (tulufeng) produced mostly unusable pig iron. The destruction of farm implements happened exactly as collectives needed them for the harvest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward.

question: Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet scientist, claimed that seeds crammed close together and soil plowed very deep would boost harvests to record levels. Mao Zedong trusted him and ordered Chinese farmers to plant and plow that way in the Great Leap Forward. Lysenko's ideas were pseudoscience, not real biology, and in Mao's China no one dared say so publicly. What happened to the harvest?
answer: It collapsed, and tens of millions starved
choices: It collapsed, and tens of millions starved
It fell slightly, and imported grain made up the gap
It held steady, because farmers quietly ignored the orders
It rose for a decade, though more slowly than promised
context: Lysenko's rejection of Mendelian genetics had been imposed on Soviet agriculture by Stalin. Chinese agriculture adopted Lysenkoist close-planting and deep-plowing techniques during the Great Leap, with disastrous results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysenkoism.

question: A commune leader in Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward, terrified of being punished for missing his harvest quota, reported far more grain than his fields had produced. Beijing believed the paper numbers. What did the Chinese state do with this pretend 'extra' grain that existed only in the reports?
answer: Exported it to earn foreign currency
choices: Exported it to earn foreign currency
Stored it in national reserves
Distributed it back to the communes
Fed it to livestock
context: Beijing exported grain based on the inflated commune reports, drawing on 'reserves' that did not exist. This continued as village granaries emptied and peasants starved. Source: Yang Jisheng, Tombstone (2008).

question: Peng Dehuai, one of Mao Zedong's own top generals, wrote him a private letter at the Lushan conference in July 1959. It criticized the Great Leap Forward: inflated harvest reports, labor wasted at the furnaces, hunger in the villages. What did Mao do with the letter?
answer: He had it handed round the meeting and had Peng denounced
choices: He had it handed round the meeting and had Peng denounced
He burned it unread and kept Peng in his post
He accepted it and slowed the campaign for a year
He answered privately and sent Peng to inspect the famine
context: Mao had Peng's letter circulated among the delegates on 17 July 1959, though Peng had tried to keep it private, then had him denounced and dismissed as defence minister. Jailed and beaten in the Cultural Revolution, Peng died in prison in 1974. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Dehuai.

question: Frank Dikötter argued in his 2010 book 'Mao's Great Famine' that deaths from Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward reached about 45 million people. Why do modern historians now say the toll was far higher than earlier Cold War guesses?
answer: Local Communist Party archives, once opened, showed the true numbers were hidden for decades
choices: Local Communist Party archives, once opened, showed the true numbers were hidden for decades
Beijing released an official famine death count in the 1990s
Declassified spy-satellite photos showed villages emptied
Western aid agencies counted the dead as the famine unfolded
context: Frank Dikotter's Mao's Great Famine (Bloomsbury, 2010) drew on party archives to argue for a 45-million total. It won the Samuel Johnson Prize for non-fiction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao%27s_Great_Famine.

question: Mao Zedong pushed China into the Great Leap Forward in 1958, and forced communes, grain requisitions and fake harvest reports brought on the deadliest famine in human history. Different demographic methods give different totals, but modern scholarly studies by Yang Jisheng, Frank Dikötter and others cluster in one broad range. What is the standard scholarly range for excess deaths?
answer: About 15 to 45 million
choices: About 15 to 45 million
About 1.5 to 4.5 million
About 150 to 450 million
context: Yang Jisheng estimates ~36 million; Dikotter ~45 million; Jasper Becker's Hungry Ghosts (1996) synthesized earlier work in a 15-30 million range. The lower bound is ~15M, the upper ~45M. Source: aggregation of Yang, Dikotter, Becker.

question: Ludwig von Mises published an essay in 1920 arguing that a socialist economy could not calculate rationally: without private property in the means of production there are no real market prices, so planners have no way to know which uses of steel or grain are wasteful. For his argument, Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward is the largest single vindication in history. What mechanism did it demonstrate?
answer: With nothing to check them against, false grain reports ran on until granaries emptied
choices: With nothing to check them against, false grain reports ran on until granaries emptied
With no private plots, peasants had no reason to work for the commune
With no free elections, no official could be voted out for failing
With no free press, word of the hunger could not reach Beijing
context: Mises's 1920 argument at the largest possible scale: no market prices meant no way to correct commune-level lies about production before the empty stomachs did the correcting. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation-socialist-commonwealth.

question: Party leaders formally shut down Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward in January 1961, after mass famine and collapse. Two more moderate men then ran a partial retreat from 1961 to 1965, letting peasants sell some crops and reopening small markets to feed the country. Mao would answer them five years later by unleashing the Cultural Revolution. Who were the two men?
answer: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping
choices: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping
Hua Guofeng and Wang Hongwen
Lin Biao and Kang Sheng
Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao
context: Liu Shaoqi (as state president) and Deng Xiaoping led the 1961-65 recovery, restoring some private plots and market allocation. Mao's answer was the 1966 Cultural Revolution, which purged both. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931976).

question: Stalin's police sent each regional office an order on 30 July 1937 saying how many people there to shoot and how many to send to the camps. What kind of order was that?
answer: A quota to fill, guilty or not
choices: A quota to fill, guilty or not
A budget for new prisons
A list of traitors caught in the act
A verdict from a court after trial
context: NKVD Order 00447 (July 30, 1937) established 'first category' (execution) and 'second category' (10-year camp) quotas by region. Local officers were rewarded for exceeding the quota. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NKVD_Order_No._00447.

question: Historians opened the Soviet archives after 1991 and got a firm count of the people Stalin's police shot from July 1937 to November 1938, the stretch Russians name after the police chief Nikolai Yezhov. Roughly how many were shot in that year and a half?
answer: About 700,000
choices: About 700,000
About 70,000
About 7 million
About 20,000
context: The NKVD's own records count 681,692 executions for 1937-38, more than a thousand a day, out of about one and a half million arrested; wider estimates of the purge's dead run from about 700,000 to 1.2 million. Western scholars who had dismissed the high estimates as Cold War inflation were answered by the archives. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge.

question: Nikolai Bukharin stood trial in March 1938, years after Lenin had called him the party's favourite, and Joseph Stalin had him shot. Mao Zedong turned on the men who had marched with him on the Long March, and Robespierre had sent fellow revolutionaries to the guillotine. Why does a new ruler turn on the very allies who helped him to power?
answer: They know his weaknesses and might replace him
choices: They know his weaknesses and might replace him
Foreign powers pay them to turn against the revolution
They demand a share of the wealth the revolution seized
They lose faith in the revolution once it has won
context: Bukharin was tried in the March 1938 Trial of the Twenty-One and shot. He had been Lenin's designated 'darling of the party'. Trotsky had already been exiled (1929) and was assassinated in Mexico in 1940. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_the_Twenty-One.

question: Joseph Stalin accused his senior Red Army officers of conspiring with Nazi Germany, and the killing tore through the army from marshals down to colonels, leaving it still rebuilding when Germany attacked in June 1941. At the start the army had five marshals, its highest rank. How many of those five did the purge kill?
answer: Three of five
choices: Three of five
One of five
All five
None
context: Tukhachevsky and Yegorov were shot; Blyukher died in custody under torture in November 1938. The purge also removed thirteen of fifteen army commanders and eight of nine fleet admirals, and some 35,000 officers in all, many of them executed. The Red Army was still recovering when Germany invaded in June 1941. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Blyukher.

question: A censor scratched Nikolai Yezhov's face out of an official photograph after Yezhov, the man who had run Stalin's terror, was seized in 1939 and executed in February 1940. Lavrentiy Beria, who replaced him, was arrested and shot in his turn in 1953. What does this pattern teach about a totalitarian regime?
answer: Even the enforcers get killed once their work is done, so no one is ever safe
choices: Even the enforcers get killed once their work is done, so no one is ever safe
Killing the enforcers proved the regime was reforming itself
Only men who had lost the dictator's favour were ever in danger
The secret police, not the dictator, held the real power
context: Beria replaced Yezhov in November 1938 and ran the NKVD (later MVD) through Stalin's death in 1953. Beria himself was arrested and shot in December 1953. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria.

question: A Soviet police squad arrested an ethnic Polish family in 1937 under an order of August that year aimed at Poles across the Soviet Union. Police shot about 111,000 people in that one operation, and orders like it followed for Germans, Koreans and Finns near the frontiers. What do these orders show about how far Stalin's terror could reach?
answer: It could target people just for who their grandparents were, not for anything they had done
choices: It could target people just for who their grandparents were, not for anything they had done
It could punish people only for crimes their relatives had committed
It could arrest foreigners, but Soviet-born citizens were safe
It could strike only in lands where the Red Army had fought
context: NKVD Order 00485 (August 11, 1937) targeted ethnic Poles across the USSR. About 111,000 were shot in the Polish Operation. Similar orders targeted Germans, Latvians, Greeks, and other border-nation communities. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Operation_of_the_NKVD.

question: The anonymous programmer who invented Bitcoin switched the network on for the first time on 3 January 2009, with a block called the genesis block. From then on, the code rewarded whoever added a new block with freshly minted bitcoins. How many did each block pay at the start?
answer: 50 BTC
choices: 50 BTC
25 BTC
6.25 BTC
1 BTC
context: The initial block reward was 50 BTC per block. 25 BTC was the reward after the first halving in 2012; 6.25 BTC applied 2020-24; 1 BTC has never been a block-reward value. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin's code counts down to each halving in blocks, not in calendar days. The mining reward is cut in half after a set number of blocks, which works out to roughly once every four years. How many blocks pass between halvings?
answer: 210,000 blocks
choices: 210,000 blocks
21,000 blocks
1,000,000 blocks
50,400 blocks
context: The halving happens every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years at ~10-minute block times). Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin miners saw their reward cut for the first time in November 2012, at the first halving. Since the network started in January 2009, every new block had paid the same reward. How many bitcoins did each block pay after the first halving?
answer: 25 bitcoins
choices: 25 bitcoins
10 bitcoins
5 bitcoins
Zero bitcoins
context: The first halving cut the reward from 50 BTC to 25 BTC in November 2012. The second (25 -> 12.5) came July 2016; the third (12.5 -> 6.25) May 2020; the fourth (6.25 -> 3.125) April 2024. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: Bitcoin's inventor gave miners a reward that halves about every four years and will one day reach zero, after which no new coins are ever made. What is the main point of a reward that keeps shrinking?
answer: To keep new supply scarce and predictable forever
choices: To keep new supply scarce and predictable forever
To lower the fees users pay as the network grows
To cut the electricity that mining burns over time
To slow the network so blocks arrive less often
context: The April 2024 halving cut the reward to 3.125 BTC per block. The 2028 halving is expected to cut it to 1.5625 BTC. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: A programmer adds up every mining reward written into Bitcoin's code, from the very first block onward. Because the reward halves again and again, the sum comes to one fixed total. What is Bitcoin's final cap?
answer: 21 million bitcoins
choices: 21 million bitcoins
100 million bitcoins
1 billion bitcoins
210 million bitcoins
context: The geometric halving series sums to 21 million BTC -- the fixed hard cap, expected to be effectively reached around 2140. After that miners earn only transaction fees, not new coins. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply.

question: A customer pays for one cup of coffee in bitcoin, handing over a sliver of a single coin. One bitcoin can be split into a hundred million tiny units, which lets a currency with a fixed cap price a single cup. What is each of those smallest units called?
answer: a satoshi
choices: a satoshi
a bit
a wei
a millibit
context: One satoshi = 0.00000001 BTC (10^-8 BTC), named for Satoshi Nakamoto. 'Bit' and 'millibit' are informal larger sub-units (1 bit = 100 satoshis); 'wei' is Ethereum's smallest unit, named for cypherpunk Wei Dai, not a Bitcoin unit. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Units.

question: Milton Friedman argued for decades that when money grows faster than goods, prices must rise. He wanted a central bank bound by a rule; Bitcoin's design goes a step beyond. What property of Bitcoin's cap sets it apart from every money system before it?
answer: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
choices: the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote
the cap doubles automatically whenever the block-time drifts
the cap adjusts based on global GDP growth
the cap is set by an annual vote of Bitcoin holders
