context: The 21M cap is enforced by every node's software; raising it would require every user to accept a protocol change that would fork Bitcoin. It cannot be adjusted for GDP, drift, or voter preference. Every fiat central bank has discretion to expand; Bitcoin has none. Source: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Controlled_supply; Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Paul Krugman and other Keynesian economists see Bitcoin's fixed cap as a serious flaw, not a strength. Their worry is not inflation but what a rigid money supply does in a slump, when spending is already falling. What is the main Keynesian complaint?
answer: That a fixed supply forces prices and wages down in a slump, making debts heavier
choices: That a fixed supply forces prices and wages down in a slump, making debts heavier
That a fixed supply automatically triggers hyperinflation whenever velocity falls
That a fixed supply cannot be divided into small enough units for retail commerce
That a fixed supply requires a central bank to enforce it
context: The standard Keynesian critique -- Krugman, DeLong, Summers -- is that a fixed-supply currency has no elastic response to demand shocks, so nominal prices and wages must fall (Fisher's debt-deflation). Hyperinflation is by definition monetary expansion, not fixed supply; Bitcoin divides to 10^-8; a fixed cap is what removes any need for a central issuer. Source: Ammous vs Krugman debates; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_deflation.

question: A young Austrian economist teaching in London wrote a long two-part review essay in the journal Economica in August 1931. It attacked the newest big book from Cambridge University's most famous living economist, and the pairing sparked one of the biggest arguments in twentieth-century economics. Who was the reviewer, and who was his target?
answer: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
choices: F. A. Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes
Ludwig von Mises reviewing Alfred Marshall
Murray Rothbard reviewing Paul Samuelson
Milton Friedman reviewing Joan Robinson
context: Hayek published Part I of his review of Keynes's A Treatise on Money (1930) in the August 1931 issue of Economica; Keynes replied and Hayek rejoined in November 1931; Hayek's Part II appeared in February 1932. Source: The Coolidge Review, 'Why the Keynes-Hayek Clash Endures' (https://www.coolidgereview.com/articles/keynes-hayek-debate-endures).

question: Friedrich Hayek, an Austrian, and John Maynard Keynes, an Englishman, argued in newspapers and journals in the early 1930s about how to save the economy. Their fight was over what a government should do in a slump, with businesses failing and workers losing their jobs by the millions. What was the core disagreement between them?
answer: Keynes said governments should spend more; Hayek said that would make things worse later
choices: Keynes said governments should spend more; Hayek said that would make things worse later
Hayek said governments should spend more; Keynes said that would make things worse later
Keynes said balance the budget at once; Hayek said borrow to build roads
Keynes said cut wages to restore profits; Hayek said wages must never fall
context: Economica was the LSE journal that ran the Hayek review, Keynes's reply, and Hayek's rejoinder across four issues from August 1931 to February 1932. Keynes's own Cambridge-based Economic Journal ran a separate front in the debate (Sraffa's 1932 review of Hayek). Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: Friedrich Hayek tore John Maynard Keynes's big new Treatise on Money apart page by page in a long two-part review, soon after moving from Vienna to teach in London in 1931. His main charge: Keynes had ignored an older European school of thought on interest rates and its underlying benchmark. Which school did Hayek say Keynes had skipped?
answer: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
choices: The Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate
The Marshall-Pigou tradition on partial equilibrium welfare economics
The Marx-Engels tradition on the falling rate of profit
The Walras-Pareto tradition on general equilibrium mathematics
context: Hayek's central technical charge against Keynes's Treatise was that Keynes had a monetary theory disconnected from capital theory and had ignored the continental (Knut Wicksell in Sweden, Ludwig von Mises in Vienna) tradition on the natural rate of interest -- the foundation Hayek's own business-cycle theory was built on. Source: Mises Institute, Hayek's 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J. M. Keynes.'

question: John Maynard Keynes mostly refused to answer the technical points when he replied to Friedrich Hayek's 1931 Economica review of his Treatise on Money. Instead he pivoted to attack Hayek's own 1931 book on business cycles, calling it 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read.' Which book of Hayek's was Keynes attacking?
answer: Prices and Production
choices: Prices and Production
The Pure Theory of Capital
The Road to Serfdom
Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle
context: Keynes wrote that Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) was 'one of the most frightful muddles I have ever read' and 'an extraordinary example of how, starting with a mistake, a remorseless logician can end up in Bedlam.' Keynes's move -- attack the OTHER book rather than defend his own -- became famous for its aggression. Source: The Coolidge Review.

question: John Maynard Keynes quietly arranged for a Cambridge colleague named Piero Sraffa to write a scathing takedown of Friedrich Hayek's 1931 book, which argued that easy money from central banks caused booms and busts. Sraffa's piece appeared in 1932, and professional opinion swung against Hayek's theory for a generation. What does the Sraffa episode reveal about an academic discipline's opinion?
answer: A well-placed critical review can shift a whole field's views
choices: A well-placed critical review can shift a whole field's views
A field changes its mind only when new evidence arrives
Opinion always follows the side that has more students
Personal attacks always backfire on whoever makes them
context: Piero Sraffa was an Italian-born Cambridge economist and a Keynes ally. His hostile 1932 review argued that without money there is a MULTIPLICITY of commodity own-rates and no unique natural rate of interest can be identified -- the concept of the 'own-rate of interest' was introduced (unnamed) in that review. Hayek replied in the Economic Journal in June 1932 with 'Money and Capital: A Reply to Mr. Sraffa.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Sraffa-Hayek debate' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sraffa%E2%80%93Hayek_debate).

question: John Maynard Keynes and his students argued at one university in the 1930s that governments should spend heavily to fight downturns. Friedrich Hayek and Lionel Robbins argued at another that markets and sound money worked best when governments stayed out. Their feud became the century's central economics debate. Which two schools were behind the fight?
answer: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
choices: Cambridge and the London School of Economics
Cambridge and Oxford
Oxford and the London School of Economics
Cambridge and Manchester
context: Keynes was at King's College, Cambridge; Hayek had arrived at the London School of Economics on Houghton Street in 1931. The 1930s Cambridge-vs-LSE feud framed the whole landscape of British economics until the war. Source: Adam Smith Institute review, 'Keynes Hayek: The Clash That Defined Modern Economics' (https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/thinkpieces/review-keynes-hayek-the-clash-that-defined-modern-economics).

question: John Maynard Keynes published his masterwork on macroeconomics in 1936, the book that would reshape twentieth-century thinking about employment, interest and money. Friedrich Hayek, his most technical Austrian critic, made a choice about that book that he later called one of the great professional regrets of his life. What did Hayek do?
answer: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
choices: He wrote no review of the General Theory at all
He wrote a hostile Economica review that Keynes never answered
He co-authored a rebuttal book with Ludwig von Mises
He challenged Keynes to a public debate at Cambridge
context: Hayek chose not to review the General Theory in 1936. He gave several reasons later, including that Keynes was notorious for changing his mind, so Hayek expected the position would soon be revised again; by the time it was clear Keynes was serious, the Keynesian revolution had swept the profession with no serious Austrian rebuttal in print for a generation. Source: Bruce Caldwell, 'Why Didn't Hayek Review Keynes's General Theory?' Duke University (https://public.econ.duke.edu/~bjc18/docs/Why%20Didn't%20Hayek%20Review%20General%20Theory.pdf).

question: Friedrich Hayek held his fire when John Maynard Keynes brought out 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' in 1936, and years later Hayek explained why. A long technical reply, he reasoned, would be wasted effort, because of something he knew about Keynes. What did Hayek cite?
answer: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
choices: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions
Keynes refused to engage in print with any Austrian economist
Keynes had privately told Hayek the General Theory was a joke
Keynes had already promised a full retraction in a coming article
context: Hayek said in interviews that Keynes had a well-known propensity to change his positions, so writing a long technical review of one Keynes book seemed likely to be answered by yet another Keynes book that revised everything -- as had partly happened with the Treatise on Money after Hayek's 1931 review. Source: Caldwell, Duke University essay.

question: The Second World War drove the London School of Economics out to Cambridge, and Friedrich Hayek arrived in the town of the man he had spent the 1930s attacking in print. What did John Maynard Keynes do when his old opponent arrived?
answer: He found Hayek rooms at King's College
choices: He found Hayek rooms at King's College
He had Hayek barred from lecturing in Cambridge
He refused to meet Hayek for the rest of the war
He challenged Hayek to a public debate at the Union
context: Keynes was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge. When the LSE was evacuated to Cambridge, where it stayed from 1939 to 1945, Keynes helped Hayek find rooms at King's and found Hayek's son Laurence a place at King's College School. The two men shared the night watch for fires from the college roofs, and Hayek later called the hospitality one of his pleasantest memories of the war, a striking coda to the 1931-1932 attack in Economica. Source: University of Cambridge Alumni magazine, 'City of refuge' (https://www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/magazine/issue-98/city-of-refuge).

question: A requisition brigade emptied a Ukrainian peasant family's storeroom in 1932, carrying out Joseph Stalin's grain quota, and the same happened in village after village. The families had nothing left to eat. What happened to the people of Ukraine that winter and into 1933?
answer: Millions starved to death
choices: Millions starved to death
They became the richest region of the Soviet Union
They received free bread from the government
The population grew quickly
context: Holodomor combines the Ukrainian holod (hunger) and mor (mortality, plague). It is used specifically for the 1932-33 famine as a policy-driven catastrophe distinct from natural crop failure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: Joseph Stalin set a grain quota for Ukraine in 1932 that no village could meet, and that was the point of it. His search crews went into peasant homes to enforce it. What did the crews take?
answer: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
choices: Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves
Only the marketable surplus
Only mid-quality grain
Only what was above household needs
context: Requisition brigades searched houses and took stored food, cured meat, and seed grain. Peasants with no reserves and no seed for next year starved by early 1933. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: Starving Ukrainian villagers headed for towns in Russia early in 1933, hoping to beg or buy bread, after Joseph Stalin signed an order on 22 January sealing Ukraine and the Kuban. Guards posted on every road and rail line checked travel papers. What happened to villagers who tried to leave?
answer: They were turned back or arrested
choices: They were turned back or arrested
They received travel permits and rations
They were resettled in Siberia with food
They were allowed passage but taxed heavily
context: The January 22, 1933 order sealed Ukraine and the Kuban internally, stopping the peasant escape that had helped during earlier famines. It converted a policy-caused shortage into a policy-caused mass death. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: Joseph Stalin's officials put a Ukrainian village on a state register in 1932 after it missed its grain quota. From then on all trade with it was cut off, the last food was taken from its shelves, nobody was allowed out, and a sign at its boundary marked what it had become. What were such villages called?
answer: Blacklisted villages
choices: Blacklisted villages
Suspended communes
Under-quota settlements
Restricted zones
context: 'Blacklisted villages' (chorna doshka villages) were targeted for full economic isolation and starvation. Signs marked the boundaries. The mechanism killed by community, not by household. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: Scholars began counting the dead of Stalin's Ukrainian famine in earnest after 1991, when the party and secret-police archives opened. The famine of 1932 and 1933 had hit some of the best farmland in Europe. What range of deaths do peer-reviewed studies give today?
answer: About 3.5 to 7.5 million
choices: About 3.5 to 7.5 million
About 35 to 75 million
context: Most peer-reviewed studies (Snyder's Bloodlands 2010, Ukrainian government 2008 study, Andriewsky, Graziosi) cluster at 3.5-5 million; the upper bound reaches ~7.5 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor.

question: Members of Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted on 28 November 2006 to give the famine of 1932 and 1933 a legal name. For decades the Soviet state had denied that its own policy caused the deaths. What did the Verkhovna Rada officially call the famine?
answer: A genocide
choices: A genocide
A humanitarian catastrophe
A policy failure
A wartime atrocity
context: The Verkhovna Rada's November 28, 2006 law recognized the Holodomor as a genocide of the Ukrainian people. The European Parliament followed with a similar resolution in December 2022 during Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holodomor_genocide_question.

question: Joseph Stalin sent armed squads into Ukrainian villages in the early 1930s to break peasant resistance to his collective farms. Millions starved in their own farmhouses while grain sat guarded in Soviet warehouses. Ukrainians do not call it simply a famine, a word that suggests bad weather. What do they call it?
answer: The Holodomor
choices: The Holodomor
The Great Leap
The Cultural Revolution
The Great Purge
context: Anne Applebaum's Red Famine: Stalin's War on Ukraine (Doubleday, 2017) is the standard modern reference. Serhii Plokhy's The Man with the Poison Gun and other work cover adjacent Ukrainian history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Famine.

question: Soviet officials confiscated the herds of Kazakhstan's nomads in 1932 and 1933 and made it a crime to kill an animal privately. About 1.5 million Kazakhs died in the famine that followed, the Asharshylyk. About what share of the whole Kazakh people was that?
answer: About 40 percent
choices: About 40 percent
About 4 percent
About 15 percent
About 80 percent
context: About 1.5 million Kazakhs died (roughly 40% of the ethnic Kazakh population). The famine transformed Kazakhstan's demographic balance for decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakh_famine_of_1930%E2%80%931933.

question: Joseph Stalin's government stripped Ukraine's countryside of food in 1932 and 1933, and millions died on some of the best farmland in Europe. Which combination turned a shortage into mass death?
answer: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
choices: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages
An early frost combined with a locust plague
A blockade by Western powers restricting food imports
A Ukrainian nationalist boycott of Soviet economic institutions
context: The three-step policy mechanism -- impossible quotas, sealed borders, blacklisting -- converted a policy-induced shortage into targeted mass death. This is what distinguishes the Holodomor from natural famine. Source: Applebaum, Red Famine (2017).

question: Members of the European Parliament voted in December 2022 to recognize Stalin's Ukrainian famine of 1932 and 1933, and lawmakers in Germany, Poland, Ireland and other countries have voted the same way. Why does such formal recognition matter?
answer: It records the deaths as a deliberate crime, not an accident of bad weather
choices: It records the deaths as a deliberate crime, not an accident of bad weather
It pays money to the surviving families of the victims
It reverses the Soviet Union's own censorship of the event
It criminally prosecutes surviving Soviet officials
context: The European Parliament passed a December 15, 2022 resolution recognizing the Holodomor as genocide. The timing during Russia's invasion of Ukraine added political weight to the recognition. Source: europarl.europa.eu (2022/2988 RSP).

question: Pol Pot announced Year Zero when he took Cambodia in April 1975: history would start fresh from his victory. Custom, Buddhist religion, family bonds and all schooling were to be cleared away and built again from nothing. What did clearing the slate mean in practice?
answer: Destroying the people and traditions that did not fit the plan
choices: Destroying the people and traditions that did not fit the plan
Rebuilding every city on a modern Soviet model
Asking foreign experts to redesign the farms
Letting the people vote on what to keep
context: Year Zero meant every trace of the previous urban-professional society was to be erased. Money was abolished, the central bank building blown up, private property abolished. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Zero_(political_notion).

question: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge guerrillas captured Phnom Penh in April 1975 and ended Cambodia's long civil war. The capital held roughly 2 million people. Within three days of taking it, they did something to those people that no modern regime had ever attempted against its own capital. What did they do?
answer: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
choices: Force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot
Executed all professional-class residents immediately
Confined them to reeducation blocks by street
Deported them by rail to Vietnam
context: Hospitals were emptied of patients, monasteries of monks, universities of professors -- all forced out on foot within days. This is the first act of the Year Zero policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Phnom_Penh.

question: Pol Pot took Cambodia in April 1975, and his Khmer Rouge hunted teachers, doctors, engineers and clerks, meaning to wipe out every city-educated person in the country. Wearing one everyday item was enough to mark a man for execution, because it suggested he could read. Which item?
answer: Glasses
choices: Glasses
A wristwatch
Leather shoes
A hat
context: Wearing glasses marked a Cambodian as educated. Speaking French, having soft hands, or having worked in a profession similarly marked people for execution or death by forced labor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_genocide.

question: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities in 1975 and sent citizens to work camps and to hundreds of rural execution sites now known as the Killing Fields. Roughly one Cambodian in every four or five died in only four years. What does mass killing on this scale usually require?
answer: A government with total power and no check on its rulers
choices: A government with total power and no check on its rulers
A short-term food shortage caused by bad weather
A small group of unhappy soldiers acting alone
A neighboring country secretly funding the killings
context: The Killing Fields at Choeung Ek is the most-visited memorial site. Hundreds of similar sites across Cambodia together hold the remains of roughly 1.5-2 million victims. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_Fields.

question: Ben Kiernan made careful studies of how many died under Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979, and Yale's Cambodian Genocide Program did the same. They set the dead against a population of about 7 to 8 million before 1975. Proportionally that killing was the worst genocide of the 20th century. What is the standard death-toll range?
answer: About 1.5 to 2 million
choices: About 1.5 to 2 million
About 15 million to 20 million
context: About 1.5-2 million Cambodians died -- roughly a fifth to a quarter of the entire population. Nazi Germany killed a smaller fraction of its own population than the Khmer Rouge killed of theirs. Source: The Black Book of Communism (1999).

question: Pol Pot studied in one European capital in the early 1950s on a scholarship and took up hardline Marxist ideas from the local left. Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan and Son Sen studied beside him, and the four came home dreaming of a purely agrarian utopia. All of them went on to lead the Khmer Rouge. Which capital shaped them?
answer: Paris
choices: Paris
London
Moscow
Rome
context: The Cercle Marxiste-Leniniste in Paris in the early 1950s included Saloth Sar (later Pol Pot), Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, and Son Sen. They returned home with the pure-agrarian-utopia idea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Pot.

question: Vietnamese soldiers crossed into Cambodia in December 1978 and toppled Pol Pot within weeks. No revolt at home ended his rule; an invasion did. What did that war show about shared communist ideology?
answer: Being communist did not prevent wars between them
choices: Being communist did not prevent wars between them
Communist states fought each other only when the West stirred them up
Shared ideology kept the war short and the occupation brief
The Soviet bloc expelled Vietnam for attacking a fellow regime
context: The Vietnamese invasion began December 25, 1978 and captured Phnom Penh on January 7, 1979. Vietnam installed the Kampuchean People's Republic and occupied the country until 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian%E2%80%93Vietnamese_War.

question: Judges sitting inside Cambodia convicted Kaing Guek Eav, known as 'Duch,' of crimes against humanity in 2010, more than three decades after Pol Pot's regime fell. He had commanded the S-21 torture prison in Phnom Penh, where roughly fifteen thousand Cambodians were killed. The judges' tribunal was a UN-backed hybrid. What was it called?
answer: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
choices: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia
The International Criminal Tribunal for Cambodia
The Phnom Penh War Crimes Court
The UN Cambodia Commission
context: The ECCC (Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia) convicted Duch (Kaing Guek Eav) in July 2010 and later convicted senior leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan. Pol Pot died under house arrest in 1998 without trial. Source: eccc.gov.kh.

question: Walter Wriston, chairman of the giant bank Citibank, repeated his famous line about lending to foreign governments in a column for the New York Times in September 1982. The debt crisis was breaking around him as Latin American borrowers stopped paying. What was the line?
answer: Countries don't go bankrupt
choices: Countries don't go bankrupt
Currencies always float
Dollars always come home
Banks never fail
context: Walter Wriston, Citibank chairman 1967-84, argued sovereigns could always repay because they could tax and print. His September 1982 op-ed in the New York Times crystallized the doctrine -- just as the crisis was breaking. Source: nytimes.com Wriston 'Banking Against Disaster', September 14 1982.

question: Paul Volcker, chairman of the Federal Reserve, pushed short-term interest rates above 19 percent in 1981 to break America's runaway inflation. Mexico, Brazil, Argentina and other poor countries had borrowed billions from big US banks at floating rates that shifted with US policy. What happened to those countries when his hikes hit?
answer: Their debt payments exploded and many countries went bust
choices: Their debt payments exploded and many countries went bust
They got a big grant from the World Bank to pay it off
The dollar collapsed, wiping out their debts
Nothing much, their loans were in local money
context: Volcker (Fed chair 1979-87) pushed the fed funds rate above 19 percent in 1981 to break US inflation. The rate spike also blew up dollar-denominated foreign loans across Latin America. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/anti-inflation-measures.

question: Officials at the International Monetary Fund and the Federal Reserve leaned on American banks after Mexico stopped paying in 1982. Letting the loans fail was ruled out: the banks kept them on the books, advanced fresh credit and stretched the payments over many years. What is the main effect of pretending a shaky debt is still healthy?
answer: The pain is spread out but the bad loan never really goes away
choices: The pain is spread out but the bad loan never really goes away
The bank's shareholders swallow the whole loss at once
The banks earn far more interest than they would have
Growth soon pays the loan off, as if nothing happened
context: 'Concerted lending' meant banks were pressured to keep extending fresh credit so that old loans could technically stay current. This bought time for bank balance sheets at the cost of years of Latin American recession. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: Nicholas Brady, the US Treasury Secretary, proposed a swap in 1989 for the enormous sums Mexico, Brazil and other poor countries owed US commercial banks and could not pay. The banks would give up their old loans and take new paper, partly backed by the US Treasury. What was the main economic idea behind this Brady Plan?
answer: Turn unsellable bad loans into bonds that can be sold, spreading the loss
choices: Turn unsellable bad loans into bonds that can be sold, spreading the loss
Cancel every debt and start over from zero
Force poor countries to hand over natural resources instead
Have the US taxpayer directly pay off every foreign loan
context: Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady's 1989 plan converted the old loans into new tradable bonds partially backed by zero-coupon US Treasuries as collateral. This finally let banks acknowledge and market-price losses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: A cautious investor wanted something rock-solid behind the new country paper of Nicholas Brady's 1989 plan. Brady gave him an instrument that pays no interest along the way and pays back its full face value at the end. What did Brady use as the backing?
answer: US Treasury zero-coupon bonds
choices: US Treasury zero-coupon bonds
Federal Reserve deposits
US gold reserves
SDRs from the IMF
context: Countries bought long-dated US Treasury zeros with a portion of new-loan proceeds; the zeros' face value at maturity guaranteed the principal on the Brady bonds. This gave holders a hard collateral floor while letting the coupon on the sovereign portion trade at deep discount. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Bonds.

question: Writers in the tradition of Ludwig von Mises read the Latin American debt workout of the 1980s as a classic case of privatized gains and socialized losses. The 1970s loans made Citibank and other US banks huge profits for years. Then Mexico stopped paying in 1982, and the workout protected one group and hurt another. Who paid the price, and who was let off the hook?
answer: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
choices: Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure
Latin American publics bore currency gains; US banks paid full losses
European banks bore the losses; US banks were untouched
The IMF absorbed the losses through direct grants
context: The Austrian reading: the workout socialized the costs of bad lending onto Latin American publics via the Lost Decade, while US bank creditors were rescued from the market discipline that would have failed several of them. This is the template that repeated in 1998, 2008, and 2010. Source: mises.org/library/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: Walter Wriston pushed Citibank into massive loans to Latin American governments in the 1970s, sure the lending was safe. When Mexico stopped paying in August 1982, the harm was extreme. Economists later flagged one feature of that lending as the root of the damage. Which lending practice made the damage so bad?
answer: Dollar-denominated loans to sovereign borrowers
choices: Dollar-denominated loans to sovereign borrowers
Local-currency loans with fixed exchange rates
Gold-backed loans with hard collateral
Loans indexed to consumer prices
context: The Latin American loans were mostly dollar-denominated. When US rates spiked under Volcker, sovereign borrowers owed more dollars in interest than their export earnings could cover, and had no domestic monetary tool to help. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

question: Frédéric Bastiat, dying of tuberculosis, sent a short pamphlet called The Law to press in June 1850. Its first pages say what law is for: to defend three things that belong to every person before any government exists. Which three did he name?
answer: Life, liberty, and property
choices: Life, liberty, and property
Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
Life, health, and safety
Speech, assembly, and conscience
context: 'The law is the collective organization of the individual right to lawful defense.' Bastiat's triad is nearly Lockean: he says life, liberty and property exist BEFORE any law and give the law its purpose, which is to protect them, not to redistribute them.

question: An English translator in 1859 had to find two words for a blunt French term of Frédéric Bastiat's: spoliation légale. Bastiat used it in The Law for law turned to seizing one man's earnings and passing them to another, until law itself becomes a tool for robbery. Which two English words have rendered it ever since?
answer: Legal plunder
choices: Legal plunder
Public spoilage
Common transfer
Social equalization
context: Bastiat's spoliation legale becomes 'legal plunder' in every standard English edition since Hodgson 1859; the term is Bastiat's own coinage for the phenomenon. Source: fee.org/resources/the-law.

question: Suppose you are handed a proposed law and want to put it to Frédéric Bastiat's test. His pamphlet The Law of 1850 offers a single question anyone can ask. According to Bastiat, you ask whether the law does what?
answer: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
choices: Takes from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong
Fails to secure a positive right to housing or employment for every citizen
Was passed by a majority smaller than two-thirds of the elected assembly
Diverges from the natural-law tradition articulated by medieval theologians
context: Bastiat's second test in the paragraph: 'See if the law benefits one citizen at the expense of another by doing what the citizen himself cannot do without committing a crime.' Source: mises.org/library/law.

question: A French shopper of 1850 paid extra for a coat because a tariff shielded its maker at home. In The Law, Frédéric Bastiat counted that tariff as plunder carried out by statute, and he set protectionism, socialism and communism side by side. Which image did he use to tie the three together?
answer: One plant at three stages of its growth
choices: One plant at three stages of its growth
One beast with three hungry heads
One river split into three channels
One road with three tollgates on it
context: Bastiat writes that 'protectionism, socialism, and communism are basically the same plant in three different stages of its growth'; legal plunder is plainest in communism, where it is complete, and in protectionism, where it is limited to particular groups and industries. Source: Bastiat, The Law (1850), tr. Dean Russell (FEE, 1950); https://americanliterature.com/author/frederic-bastiat/book/the-law/three-systems-of-plunder

question: An English reader went looking for Frederic Bastiat partway through the 1900s and found just three short works by the Frenchman: The Law, Economic Sophisms and Selected Essays on Political Economy. One small liberty-minded group in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York, published all three. Which group was it?
answer: The Foundation for Economic Education
choices: The Foundation for Economic Education
The Cato Institute
The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Mont Pelerin Society
context: FEE was founded 1946 by Leonard Read in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. Its editions were excellent for their day but covered only a fraction of Bastiat's actual output; most of his correspondence, journalism, and Assembly speeches had never been translated. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Pierre Goodrich, a lawyer and businessman, wanted old books by dead economists who defended free markets, thinkers like Frederic Bastiat and Adam Smith, reprinted and handed out. He meant students centuries later to be able to read them. What way of preserving a tradition does his project show?
answer: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
choices: Private funding keeping ideas alive across generations
A commercial publisher printing whatever sells best
A collector buying up rare first editions
A government grant for reprinting the classics
context: Liberty Fund's Collected Works of Frederic Bastiat is projected to run to six volumes. Goodrich, an Indiana lawyer and businessman, endowed the foundation specifically to sustain the classical-liberal scholarly tradition. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: Editors at the Liberty Fund brought out the third volume of Frederic Bastiat's collected works in 2017, part of a six-volume set in modern English. It holds the candlemakers' satire and also his most famous essay, from 1850, the one with the shopkeeper's broken window. What is that essay called?
answer: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
choices: 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen'
'Protectionism and Communism'
'Justice and Fraternity'
'Property and Plunder'
context: 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas' (1850). Volume 3 also contains the Economic Sophisms, Bastiat's satirical essays including the Petition of the Candlemakers demanding a law against the sun. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: David Hart, the English editor of Frederic Bastiat's collected works, also built a free online resource. It puts the whole of Bastiat, and hundreds of other classical-liberal texts, within reach of any reader with internet access, at zero cost. What is the resource called?
answer: The Online Library of Liberty
choices: The Online Library of Liberty
The Ludwig von Mises Institute online archive
The Cato Institute policy library
The Project Gutenberg library
context: The Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org), run by the Liberty Fund, puts Bastiat's writings and hundreds of other classical-liberal texts online at no cost. The tradition is being cultivated, not just preserved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Liberty_Fund.

question: The nonpartisan watchdogs at OpenSecrets added up what companies and interest groups paid in 2023 to shape federal laws, rules and regulations. They had tracked that lobbying bill every year since 1998, and the total had risen in most of those years. About how much did federal lobbying cost in 2023?
answer: About $4.2 billion
choices: About $4.2 billion
About $420 million
About $42 billion
About $42 million
context: Federal lobbying spending grew from about $1.4 billion in 1998 to a record of about $4.2 billion in 2023, by OpenSecrets' count (about $4.1 billion in 2022). Source: https://www.nbcnews.com/investigations/lobbyists-spent-record-42-billion-2023-federal-lawmakers-rcna135943.

question: A reader running down the OpenSecrets table for 2023 stops at the top line. One single industry laid out about $385 million that year pressing federal lawmakers and regulators for favorable rules, ahead of every other. Which industry led the list?
answer: Pharmaceuticals and health products
choices: Pharmaceuticals and health products
Defense contractors
Motion pictures and television
Iron and steel
context: Pharmaceuticals/health products led at ~$385M in 2023, followed by electronics manufacturing and equipment (~$228M) and insurance (~$164M). Source: opensecrets.org (Top Industries 2023).

question: An OpenSecrets researcher ranking the biggest single lobbying spenders of 2023 put one large business federation first, at close to $70 million. It has come out on top in most recent years, pressing federal officials for rules and spending that favor its members. Which group is it?
answer: The US Chamber of Commerce
choices: The US Chamber of Commerce
The National Rifle Association
The American Bar Association
The American Legion
context: The US Chamber of Commerce has been the largest single-organization federal lobbying spender in most recent years; it and the National Association of Realtors have been the two top spenders across the years OpenSecrets has tracked. Source: opensecrets.org (Top Organizations); https://www.rawstory.com/lobbyist-washington-dc/.

question: Marianne Bertrand, Matilde Bombardini and Francesco Trebbi dug through US lobbying records in 2014 to answer a sharp question. Does a lobbyist earn her big fees for her grasp of the policy issue, or for her friends among the politicians? Their working paper carried a memorable title. What was it?
answer: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
choices: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know?
The Price of Access
Do Lobbyists Matter?
Money and Influence
context: Bertrand + Bombardini + Trebbi, 'Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? An Empirical Assessment of the Lobbying Process' (American Economic Review, December 2014). Their finding: mostly whom. Source: aeaweb.org (Bertrand et al. 2014).

question: A lobbyist takes a lawmaker to dinner in Washington, one small piece of the money flowing into federal lobbying every year. Gordon Tullock argued in a 1967 paper on the welfare costs of tariffs, monopolies and theft that such spending is a real cost to a society. In Tullock's view, what does that spending actually buy?
answer: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
choices: Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions
Money is spent purely to educate legislators about general policy tradeoffs
Money is spent to win voters over to a party's whole program
Money is spent to keep lawmakers informed of what the public wants
context: Tullock's rent-seeking framework: $4B/year is not being spent to persuade Congress of general truths. It is being spent to capture concrete, industry-specific policy outcomes. The stated purpose (democratic participation) is not always false; the aggregate spending is not consistent with it either. Source: Tullock (1967); opensecrets.org.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock turned their public-choice reasoning on a kind of law that keeps appearing in Washington. It is long and complex, it targets one industry such as sugar, banking or defense, and armies of lobbyists have worked on it. When a new law like that lands, what should a careful policy watcher suspect by default?
answer: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
choices: The beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public
The statute fixes a problem the public has long complained about
The statute's costs fall mostly on the industry it targets
The statute is too technical for any lobbyist to have shaped
context: When a proposed statute is complex, industry-specific, and heavily lobbied, the Tullock-Olson default is that the concentrated organized interests are the primary beneficiaries. The First Amendment protects petition; the point is the aggregate incentive structure, not anybody's honesty. Source: Tullock (1967); Olson (1965).

question: Suppose you are dying of thirst in a desert. Someone offers you a glass of water and you would trade almost anything for it. After four glasses, a fifth hardly tempts you. Why is the fifth glass worth so little to you next to the first?
answer: Each extra glass meets a smaller need than the one before
choices: Each extra glass meets a smaller need than the one before
The seller charges more for the fifth glass
Water is cheap everywhere, so no glass is worth much
A thirsty body can absorb only four glasses
context: Menger's Grundsaetze der Volkswirtschaftslehre insisted that value is subjective, ranked by an individual chooser, and always applies to a specific additional unit rather than to a good as a class. That single move dissolved a hundred years of classical puzzles. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger and the Sesquicentennial Founding of the Austrian School'.

question: Two people find identical gold coins on the beach. One is a rich collector who already has thousands of them. The other is a broke schoolboy with no bus fare home. Who values that one coin more?
answer: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
choices: The poor kid, because he needs it more right now
The rich collector, because he understands gold
They value it equally because it is the same coin
Neither, because gold has no real value
context: Marginal utility puts the coin's value in the next use each finder has for it: the boy's fare home ranks far above one more coin in a full drawer. Value lives in the chooser's ranking, not in the gold itself. Source: Mises Institute, 'Carl Menger and the Sesquicentennial Founding of the Austrian School'.

question: Leon Walras dreamed up a model in the 1870s of a whole economy at once, with every price, every buyer and every seller tied together in one huge mathematical system. Modern computers can crank through it for hours. What is the biggest practical problem with Walras's dream?
answer: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
choices: Real people change their minds and new products appear every day
Mathematicians have proved the equations can have no solution
The model works only for an economy with a single currency
Real prices are set by law, so no equation can capture them
context: Walras held the chair of political economy at the Academie de Lausanne (later the University of Lausanne) from 1870; his book was printed there in 1874. The Lausanne School of general equilibrium takes its name from the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leon Walras'.

question: Carl Menger published his new idea about value in Vienna in 1871, not knowing that an economist in Manchester was landing on the same one that very year. Leon Walras followed in Lausanne by 1874. Who was the man in Manchester?
answer: William Stanley Jevons
choices: William Stanley Jevons
Alfred Marshall
John Stuart Mill
Francis Edgeworth
context: Jevons's The Theory of Political Economy appeared in 1871, the same year as Menger's Principles; he held the chair of political economy at Owens College, Manchester. Marshall would not publish his Principles until 1890, Edgeworth's Mathematical Psychics came in 1881, and Mill belonged to the earlier classical generation. Historians call the 1871-1874 cluster the marginal revolution. Source: Britannica, 'William Stanley Jevons'.

question: Carl Menger, whose book of 1871 had founded the Austrian school in Vienna, read Leon Walras's plan to model the whole economy as one giant mathematical system. He thought Walras was wrong at the deepest level, not just as a matter of technique. What was Menger's core objection?
answer: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
choices: Economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations
The mathematics of 1874 was not yet advanced enough for the task
General-equilibrium models understate the importance of labour-time in value
Walras had rejected marginal utility in favour of pure cost-of-production
context: Menger accepted the marginal-utility insight the three founders shared; his disagreement was about method. This methodological gap between the Austrian and Lausanne roads persists to the present day and underlies the Austrian critique of modern DSGE modelling. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: Hermann Heinrich Gossen, a German civil servant, laid out the falling value of each extra unit in an 1854 book that sank almost without trace. In 1878 a scholar in Manchester found a surviving copy and told the English economist who had published the same idea in 1871. What did that economist do?
answer: He credited Gossen in his own book's second edition
choices: He credited Gossen in his own book's second edition
He bought up every copy to bury the rival claim
He accused Gossen of stealing ideas from English writers
He said nothing, and never mentioned Gossen's book
context: Gossen's 1854 Entwickelung der Gesetze des menschlichen Verkehrs laid down what are still called Gossen's Laws of diminishing marginal utility and equimarginal allocation. Robert Adamson of Manchester found the surviving copy in 1878 and Jevons publicly acknowledged Gossen's priority in the second edition of his own book. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gossen's laws'.

question: Carl Menger argued in Vienna in the 1870s that what a good is worth hangs on the marginal unit, not the total, and two other economists, in England and in Switzerland, landed on the same insight on their own. Once that move was on the table, a whole class of older classical theories collapsed at one stroke. Which theory did it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
choices: The labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx
The quantity theory of money later revived by Milton Friedman
The theory of comparative advantage stated by David Ricardo
The Malthusian population principle
context: Every step of the labour-theory chain assumed value was a property of the good, fixed by its cost or labour input. The marginalist move denies the assumption: value is a ranking of the next unit by a specific chooser. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus were unaffected -- each addressed a different question. Source: cruel.org, 'Phases of the Marginalist Revolution'.

question: Three economists in three countries hit the same core insight within three years, then took it down three separate roads. The roads split sharply into the Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools, one writing prose, one drawing diagrams and one solving equations. What does that split suggest about economics?
answer: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
choices: Its identity is at least as much about method as about content
It is primarily an empirical laboratory science like chemistry
It is settled by mathematical proof once its axioms are stated
Its schools differ mainly in which countries they study
context: The Austrian, Cambridge and Lausanne schools agreed on the marginal-utility insight but disagreed sharply about whether economics should be prose-based praxeology, partial-equilibrium diagrams, or systems of simultaneous equations. Those methodological choices still divide the profession. Source: Springer, 'Austrian School of Economics'.

question: Carl Menger told the German Historical School in 1883 that collecting facts was not enough. Those economists held that the only way to know an economy was to gather piles of historical facts and numbers from one particular country. What did Menger say economics also needed?
answer: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
choices: Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country
The exact weight of every coin in circulation
A list of every farmer's birthday
A map of every road in the country
context: The book was Untersuchungen ueber die Methode der Socialwissenschaften (Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences, with Special Reference to Political Economics), 1883. Schmoller held the chair at the University of Berlin from 1882 and led what economists call the 'younger' German Historical School. Ricardo was 60 years dead; the physiocrats a century earlier; Veblen and the American institutionalists would come after 1899. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: A girl named Maya watches her older brother argue with their parents at dinner on twenty nights in a row. Each time he raises his voice, the argument gets louder and meaner. On the twentieth night she thinks, 'Raising your voice always makes arguments worse.' What kind of reasoning is she using?
answer: Inductive
choices: Inductive
Deductive
Circular
Random
context: Induction moves from cases to a general rule; deduction moves from general premises to specific conclusions (like geometry proving a theorem from axioms). The German Historical School was inductive-first; Menger's Austrians were deductive-first. This deductive-vs-inductive split is what a 'method-war' -- a Methodenstreit -- is FOUGHT OVER. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Gustav Schmoller in Berlin and Carl Menger in Vienna fell into a long, bitter argument in the 1880s. Schmoller reviewed Menger's book with open contempt, and Menger answered with an angry pamphlet. What was their fight really about?
answer: The right method for doing economics
choices: The right method for doing economics
How high tariffs on grain should be
Whether to abolish paper money
Whether workers should form unions
context: Methodenstreit literally means 'method-fight' or 'quarrel over method' -- Streit is the German for a dispute or fight. Kulturkampf was Bismarck's 1870s fight with the Catholic Church; Klassenkampf is Marx's class struggle; Vernunftstreit is not a standard historical term. The word Methodenstreit is now used by historians for any deep methodological quarrel, but by default it means THIS ONE. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Carl Menger published 'Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences' in 1883 and took geometry as his model. Economics, he argued, is a science of that same kind. From which base does a geometry-like science reason?
answer: From general first principles down to specific cases
choices: From general first principles down to specific cases
From specific cases up to tentative rules
From surveys of the general population
From statistical patterns in historical data
context: This is deduction: axioms first, theorems derived. Menger's atom was the individual acting to satisfy a want; from that atom he derived subjective value, marginal ranking, price formation. Ludwig von Mises would later name the method PRAXEOLOGY (Human Action, 1949). The Historical School's method -- from cases up to tentative rules -- is induction; surveys and statistical patterns are its tools. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Gustav Schmoller reviewed a book by Carl Menger with open contempt and pinned a sneering label on Menger's circle, taken from the place where its members worked. The insult stuck, and the group proudly kept it. By what name is this school of economic thought known today?
answer: The Austrian School
choices: The Austrian School
The Chicago School
The Cambridge School
The Berlin School
context: The very name 'Austrian School' was invented by an opponent as a put-down and adopted by the accused as a name of honor. The Manchester School was the free-trade movement around Cobden and Bright (1830s-60s); the Lausanne School was Walras and Pareto's mathematical-equilibrium tradition; the Cambridge School was Alfred Marshall's neoclassical mainstream. Schmoller's slur is now the name of a Nobel-decorated tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Carl Menger wrote a short, angry book in 1884 to answer a harsh review by Gustav Schmoller. It came as a set of open letters to a friend, under the title 'The Errors of Historicism in German Economics.' Which reasoning move did Menger press against Schmoller's Historical School?
answer: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
choices: That economic laws are universal and hold in every time and place, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them
That economic laws depend entirely on the historical period, so no universal science of economics is possible
That only mathematical models can settle economic questions
That government must collect national statistics before any economic argument is legitimate
context: Hayek later said Menger 'ruthlessly demolished Schmoller's position' in the 1884 pamphlet. The point is exact: a scarce means will still be economized in ancient Rome and in modern Vienna; a chooser will rank in every century. History is DATA, not the SOURCE. Menger did not reject historical study; he denied it could replace theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Gustav Schmoller spoke from the chair at Berlin, with the leading journal and the national economics association in his hands, when he publicly declared Vienna-school thinkers unfit for the German academy. What concrete consequence did that declaration have across Germany?
answer: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
choices: A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments
An immediate ban on Menger's Principles being sold in Germany
Menger's removal from his chair at the University of Vienna
The dissolution of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik
context: Schmoller controlled Prussian academic appointments through his Berlin chair, his editorship of the leading journal, and his chairmanship of the Verein fuer Socialpolitik. His public verdict effectively closed the German academic market to Austrians well into the 1900s -- a professional freeze, not a book ban. Menger kept his Vienna chair; the Verein continued and Schmoller kept chairing it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Two economists, one in Berlin and one in Vienna, began a personal fight in 1883, the Methodenstreit, over how economics should be done. Gustav Schmoller died in 1917 and the feud went with him, but the split stayed, and the argument still comes back in every generation. Which lasting divide in twentieth-century economics traces back to Berlin in 1883?
answer: Methodological individualism versus historical-institutional analysis
choices: Methodological individualism versus historical-institutional analysis
Free trade versus protectionism
Gold standard versus fiat currency
Micro versus macro economics
context: The Austrian line (Menger, Boehm-Bawerk, Wieser, Mises, Hayek) kept methodological individualism -- the individual choosing actor as the atom of analysis. The descendants of the German Historical School (Veblen, Commons, and later institutional, behavioural, and evolutionary economics) kept the historical-institutional focus on how rules, habits, and organizations shape choice. Both traditions still argue the 1883 quarrel every generation. Free trade vs protectionism, gold vs fiat, and micro vs macro are separate debates. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Ludwig von Mises published an essay in 1920, thirty-seven years after Carl Menger's method book, and it gave the Vienna school a pillar it had not had. Menger's quarrel with Gustav Schmoller over method had already supplied much of what the school stood on, but not this. Which pillar came from Mises's later work, not from the 1883 quarrel?
answer: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
choices: The socialist calculation critique of central planning
The rejection of the labor theory of value
The claim that value is subjective
The insistence on universal deductive laws
context: Ludwig von Mises's 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' -- the argument that without market prices no rational allocation is possible -- came in 1920, thirty-seven years after Menger's method book. Subjective value, the rejection of labor value, and universal deductive laws were all Menger 1871 and 1883 -- the founding moves. The calculation critique is the DAUGHTER of the founding method, not the mother. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodenstreit.

question: Friedrich Hayek joined other young Vienna scholars one evening in the 1920s for three hours of argument over economics, history and philosophy in a small office. The seminar had no fees, no exams and no degree, and Hayek credited its host with teaching him real economics. Whose seminar was it?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Carl Menger
Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk
Joseph Schumpeter
context: Mises (1881-1973) worked at the Handelskammer -- the Austrian Chamber of Commerce -- as an economic policy adviser from 1909 onwards, and used his office there as the meeting room. The seminar is remembered as the Mises-Kreis or the Privatseminar. Menger had retired in 1903 and died in 1921; Boehm-Bawerk died in 1914; Schumpeter had left Austria for Bonn and would soon leave for Harvard. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/ludwig-mises-and-the-vienna-private-archive/.

question: Ludwig von Mises told the young economists who gathered in his Vienna office that no group of officials in a capital, however brilliant or kind, could run a nation's economy well. What reason did he give?
answer: Millions of people have information the planners never see
choices: Millions of people have information the planners never see
Planners are too few to watch every factory at once
Officials always end up favouring their own friends
No plan can survive a change of government
context: Mises set out the case in his 1920 essay on economic calculation: without market prices for land, machines and materials, planners cannot tell waste from wise use, and those prices sum up what millions of people know. Hayek, a regular in the room, later stressed how scattered that knowledge is. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: One regular of Ludwig von Mises's Vienna seminar won a share of the 1974 Nobel Prize in economics, and another helped found game theory alongside the mathematician John von Neumann in 1944. Which pair from the seminar were they?
answer: Friedrich Hayek and Oskar Morgenstern
choices: Friedrich Hayek and Oskar Morgenstern
Joseph Schumpeter and Karl Polanyi
Richard Strigl and Paul Rosenstein-Rodan
Felix Kaufmann and Eric Voegelin
context: Hayek shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal, for work on money and economic fluctuations. Morgenstern co-authored Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with John von Neumann in 1944, the founding book of game theory. Both took part in Mises's seminar in the 1920s. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern.

question: Friedrich Hayek, a regular of Ludwig von Mises's Vienna seminar, moved to the London School of Economics in 1931 and carried the Austrian tradition into English. A colleague there who wanted an alternative to Cambridge economics had invited him. Who was it?
answer: Lionel Robbins
choices: Lionel Robbins
William Beveridge
Arnold Plant
Harold Laski
context: Lionel Robbins, head of economics at the LSE from 1929 and author of An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science (1932), invited Hayek, who joined the faculty in 1931; his LSE lectures became Prices and Production. Beveridge was the School's director, Plant a fellow economist, Laski its leading socialist political scientist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek.

question: One regular of Ludwig von Mises's Vienna seminar was no economist: a bank lawyer by day and a sociologist by vocation, he argued that economics rests on what people mean by their own actions. Philosophers and even art historians came too. Who was the sociologist?
answer: Alfred Schuetz
choices: Alfred Schuetz
Otto Neurath
Moritz Schlick
Rudolf Carnap
context: Schuetz (1899-1959) worked days as a bank lawyer and joined the Privatseminar in the 1920s; his book The Phenomenology of the Social World (1932) argued that economics rests on the meanings actors give their own actions, a fit with Mises's methodological individualism. He escaped to New York in 1939. Neurath, Schlick and Carnap belonged to the neighbouring Vienna Circle of logical positivists, not the Mises circle. Source: privatarchiv-mises.uni-graz.at/en/mises-private-archive/.

question: Kurt Gödel and John von Neumann debated at a Mathematical Colloquium in interwar Vienna, apart from Ludwig von Mises's seminar. Its host belonged to the Vienna Circle of philosophers, and his father had launched the Austrian school with Principles of Economics in 1871. Who was the host?
answer: Karl Menger the younger
choices: Karl Menger the younger
Rudolf Carnap
Hans Hahn
Philipp Frank
context: Karl Menger the younger (1902-1985), son of Carl Menger the economist, did dimension theory in mathematics, edited the proceedings of his Mathematical Colloquium (which included Goedel's incompleteness results and von Neumann's work), and sat in the Vienna Circle. The Menger name reaches into TWO of interwar Vienna's most consequential intellectual gatherings -- his father founded one tradition, and Karl the younger crossed into the other. Carnap, Hahn, and Frank were Vienna Circle members but not sons of the Austrian School's founder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: Ludwig von Mises left Vienna for a professorship abroad in the spring of 1934, and his seminar stopped. Within a few years most of its other members had gone too, and the city's whole circle of economists, mathematicians and philosophers broke apart. Why did they go?
answer: Its members were Jews or liberals who had to flee Central Europe as the Nazis rose
choices: Its members were Jews or liberals who had to flee Central Europe as the Nazis rose
The Rockefeller Foundation ordered them all to come to the United States
The Austrian government paid for their emigration
They were all fired from their Vienna university positions in 1934
context: The Anschluss of March 1938 made staying impossible for the Jewish and liberal members; Mises had left in 1934 and Hayek in 1931 -- both jumps early enough that they moved as scholars, not as refugees. Machlup was on Rockefeller in America when the Anschluss happened and stayed; Morgenstern was visiting Princeton and chose to stay; Haberler was already at Harvard by 1936. The Rockefeller Foundation funded some fellowships but did not order anyone; the Austrian government did not pay; most of them never held salaried Vienna chairs to be fired from. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Machlup; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Morgenstern; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: A politician running for office promises voters free college for everyone, free health care for everyone and better pay for all workers. He says the rich will pay every last dollar. But even taking everything they own would not cover the tab. Who ends up paying the rest of the bill?
answer: Middle-class and poor families, through higher taxes or inflation
choices: Middle-class and poor families, through higher taxes or inflation
Foreign lenders, who buy up the new government bonds
Nobody, since the spending pays for itself through growth
Big corporations, through a much higher profits tax
context: Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020, self-identifying as a democratic socialist. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders.

question: Bernie Sanders ran for president in 2016, and in the years after it one American group grew fast. It went from about 6,000 members in 2014 to around 92,000 by 2021, with chapters in cities across the country and elected members in Congress. What is the group called?
answer: Democratic Socialists of America
choices: Democratic Socialists of America
Progressive Democrats of America
The Justice Democrats
Our Revolution
context: DSA membership grew roughly 15x between 2014 and 2021. Prominent elected DSA-affiliated figures include Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib. Source: dsausa.org membership statistics.

question: Bernie Sanders campaigned for the presidency as a democratic socialist. American democratic socialists often push a package of policies together: a $15 federal minimum wage, rent control in big cities, drug prices set by government, and one tax-funded health plan covering everyone in place of private insurance. That last piece has a short name he made famous. What is it?
answer: Medicare for All
choices: Medicare for All
The Public Option
Universal Care Bill
The Health Charter
context: Medicare for All (M4A) proposes a single-payer national health-insurance program with government-negotiated provider prices. Sanders's Senate version and Rep. Pramila Jayapal's House version are the reference bills. Source: sanders.senate.gov/medicare-for-all.

question: A mayor signs a $30-an-hour minimum wage, well above what many small shops can afford to pay. His supporters point to the workers whose pay goes up. A critic answers with a move Frederic Bastiat made famous in 1850. Which reasoning move does the critic press?
answer: Seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost
choices: Seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost
The Cantillon effect -- the first recipients gain purchasing power
Moral hazard -- workers take on more risk
Rent-seeking -- lobbyists capture the state
context: Bastiat's method: the visible beneficiary is the worker whose wage rises; the invisible cost is the worker priced out of the labor market entirely. Milton Friedman pressed the same point against minimum-wage laws. Naming the move does not settle the verdict. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Milton Friedman and George Stigler published a famous pamphlet, Roofs or Ceilings?, in 1946, attacking rent control in postwar American cities. From that pamphlet down to today's Austrian writers, critics of rent control have pressed one argument above all the others. Which one is it?
answer: The supply response: capped rents mean fewer apartments over time
choices: The supply response: capped rents mean fewer apartments over time
The Cantillon effect: cheap credit reaches landlords first
Moral hazard: tenants take less care of cheaply rented flats
Regulatory capture: big landlords end up writing the caps
context: The critic's move: rent held below cost makes supplying rental housing less profitable; supply falls, and future tenants pay the hidden cost. Source: Friedman-Stigler, Roofs or Ceilings? (1946).

question: Ludwig von Mises published an essay called Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth in 1920. Earlier critics had attacked socialism on moral or political grounds, but Mises took a different route. He argued that the system could not work even if every planner were a saint. What kind of argument did he make?
answer: A mechanical argument about the informational role of prices
choices: A mechanical argument about the informational role of prices
A historical argument about how such states had fared
A psychological argument about workers' effort
A demographic argument about feeding a growing population
context: Mises 1920's move: prices carry information (about scarcity, urgency, tastes) that no committee can substitute for. This is a mechanical claim about how information is aggregated -- it does not depend on any political verdict. Source: mises.org/library/economic-calculation.

question: Bernie Sanders has run for president as a democratic socialist without proposing Soviet-style central planning of every factory and farm. A careful reader does not treat his program and the Soviet system as identical. What is the key difference between them?
answer: His plan sets prices in some sectors but leaves ownership private
choices: His plan sets prices in some sectors but leaves ownership private
His plan nationalizes industry but leaves prices to the market
His plan keeps one-party rule but allows private shops
His plan plans every sector, but through elected councils
context: The distinction matters for accuracy: 2020s democratic socialism as advocated in America does not propose Gosplan-style planning. It DOES propose replacing market prices with government-set ones in labor, housing, healthcare, education, energy. The reasoning moves against Gosplan apply less catastrophically in scale but by the same mechanism. Source: dsausa.org platform.

question: Medicare officials sit down with a drug company to negotiate the price of a medicine for America's seniors. A critic who has read Friedrich Hayek's 1945 essay says the government is really setting the price. Which classical Austrian reasoning move most directly applies to Medicare drug-price setting?
answer: The knowledge problem, applied to which new drugs get researched
choices: The knowledge problem, applied to which new drugs get researched
Moral hazard, applied to patients who overuse cheap medicine
Regulatory capture, applied to drug firms that write the rules
The Cantillon effect, applied to new money spent on health care
context: The critic's move: without price signals, planners cannot know which future drug lines are worth the research; negotiated prices below what the market would pay cut the reward for marginal innovation. Source: mises.org/library/pharma-pricing.

question: A reader picks up two pamphlets. One banner says 'socialism', the other 'consumer protection', and both call for a government-set price. She has followed the chain of reasoning Ludwig von Mises built about prices in 1920, and she means to test both. What rule about reasoning moves should she hold to?
answer: The reasoning moves apply the same way regardless of the label the advocate uses
choices: The reasoning moves apply the same way regardless of the label the advocate uses
The reasoning moves apply only to Soviet-style planning
The reasoning moves apply only if the policy is unpopular
The reasoning moves depend on the political party proposing them
context: Mises 1920 was a mechanical argument about prices, not a political attack. The reasoning moves apply to any policy that suppresses a price signal, regardless of whether the label is 'socialism', 'progressive reform', 'social democracy', or 'consumer protection'. Source: Mises, Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920).

question: A Bordeaux newspaper writer wanted a railway between two distant cities broken at his own, so local hands would unload every crate and every traveler would stop over. Frederic Bastiat answered with a joke. Who would really win from the break, and who would lose?
answer: The town's workers win; travelers and both big cities lose time and money
choices: The town's workers win; travelers and both big cities lose time and money
Everyone wins because more jobs are created
Only the government wins from new taxes
The train companies win by charging more for tickets
context: Bastiat's essay names Bordeaux, the port on the Garonne on the line between Paris and the Spanish border, and the writer, M. Simiot. Source: https://mises.org/online-book/bastiat-collection/17-negative-railway.

question: A Bordeaux newspaper writer, quoted by Frederic Bastiat, wanted the planned line broken at his city, so freight would come off the trains and travelers would stop over. The break, he said, would bring work to local trades. Which trades were among those he named?
answer: Boatmen, porters and hotel-keepers
choices: Boatmen, porters and hotel-keepers
Blacksmiths, farriers and wheelwrights
Bakers, butchers and vintners
Weavers, dyers and tailors
context: Bastiat quotes the list: boatmen (or bargemen), porters, commission agents, hotel-keepers and so on, every trade that lives off a break in the line; every other town on the route then has the same claim. Translations differ in the wording. Source: https://mises.org/online-book/bastiat-collection/17-negative-railway.

question: Frederic Bastiat mocked a Bordeaux newspaper writer in Economic Sophisms with a joke, the 'negative railway.' The writer wanted a planned line broken at his city; the line itself was real, a plan to link two European capitals. Which two?
answer: Paris and Madrid
choices: Paris and Madrid
Paris and Rome
Paris and Vienna
Paris and Berlin
context: Bastiat quotes the question M. Simiot put in a Bordeaux newspaper: should the proposed railway from Paris to Madrid have a break at Bordeaux? Source: https://mises.org/online-book/bastiat-collection/17-negative-railway.

question: Frederic Bastiat took a Bordeaux newspaper writer at his word, mocking protectionists who wanted deliberate inefficiencies to 'create jobs.' If breaking the line at Bordeaux would help the local trades, he asked, why not break it at every town along the route? What is left if the joke is followed all the way through?
answer: A series of unconnected roads that is not a railway at all
choices: A series of unconnected roads that is not a railway at all
A perfectly efficient distribution of freight-handling employment
A modest annual improvement in national industrial output
A revenue base large enough to fund the line's construction
context: This is Bastiat's whole point: if breaking the line creates jobs, then it must create MORE jobs at every station, and the make-work argument requires the very thing that makes the work possible to be destroyed. Source: mises.org/library/economic-sophisms.

question: A shopkeeper's son throws a stone, and the neighbors say the repair job will actually help the economy. Frederic Bastiat told that story to make the point of his 'negative railway' a second way, with pure destruction in place of forced train stops. Which twin story is it?
answer: The broken window
choices: The broken window
The candlemakers' petition
The Chinese and the English
The two moralities
context: The broken-window says destruction is not creation; the negative-railway says friction is not creation. Together they close both flanks of the 19th-century make-work argument. Source: fee.org/resources/economic-sophisms.

question: Frederic Bastiat told a story in his Economic Sophisms: someone argues that extra stops along a train line will boost the economy, because more towns will sell food and lodging to passing travelers. Bastiat called this the 'negative railway.' What is wrong with treating those stops as a benefit?
answer: Delays and extra costs make trade worse, not better
choices: Delays and extra costs make trade worse, not better
The towns would earn too little to make the stops worthwhile
Travelers would switch to coaches to avoid the stops
The stops would push the line's building costs too high
context: The Bordeaux writer's whole argument treats extra HANDLING (friction) as extra income; Bastiat's reductio is that if friction were income, the ideal railway would be no railway at all. Source: https://mises.org/online-book/bastiat-collection/17-negative-railway.

question: A new machine arrives, and someone makes the case Frederic Bastiat mocked in a Bordeaux newspaper writer. The seen loss is the work the machine now does; the unseen part is what the spare hours go on to make and the cheaper goods everyone can buy. The newest version runs almost word for word the same. Which modern scare is it?
answer: That artificial-intelligence tools destroy writing jobs
choices: That artificial-intelligence tools destroy writing jobs
That electric vehicles destroy petroleum jobs
That online retail destroys shipping jobs
That smartphone cameras destroy photography jobs
context: The negative-railway shape: the visible job that the machine 'takes' is the SEEN; the UNSEEN is the new work the released labor does and the lower-cost goods everyone else now enjoys. The 2020s AI-writing panic recycles the argument almost word for word. Source: cato.org/commentary/luddite-arguments-then-and-now.

question: Richard Nixon shut a door on live television in August 1971. Foreign countries had been able to send dollars to the US Treasury and get real gold back; after his speech, they could not. What did the change mean for the dollar from then on?
answer: The dollar was backed only by trust in the government, not by gold
choices: The dollar was backed only by trust in the government, not by gold
The dollar was tied to a basket of foreign currencies instead
The dollar was tied to silver in place of gold
The dollar could be swapped for gold only by Americans
context: Closing the gold window ended the Bretton Woods promise that foreign central banks could turn dollars into gold at $35 an ounce; from then on the dollar's value rested on the issuing government alone. Americans themselves had not been allowed to hold monetary gold since 1933. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: American viewers heard Richard Nixon announce three big economic moves at once on August 15, 1971. One cut foreign countries off from trading their dollars for US gold. Another struck at trade partners. The third was a first for peacetime in US history, a heavy-handed move on the home front against inflation. What was that home-front move?
answer: A 90-day wage-and-price freeze
choices: A 90-day wage-and-price freeze
A national sales tax
A one-year rent moratorium
A gasoline-rationing order
context: The 90-day freeze was extended in successive Phases through April 1974. It bought a temporary appearance of price stability into the 1972 election year, then unravelled into the 1973-75 inflation acceleration. Source: nixonlibrary.gov/economic-policy.

question: John Connally met worried European finance ministers in Rome in late 1971, right after Richard Nixon cut the dollar's link to gold. They complained of a flood of dollars they could no longer redeem. The US Treasury Secretary shrugged and said, 'The dollar is our currency, but it's your problem.' What does his quip point out about being the world's main reserve currency?
answer: The country that issues it can print more and let others feel the pain
choices: The country that issues it can print more and let others feel the pain
The issuer must defend its currency's value for the sake of others
Holders of the currency can force the issuer to redeem it
A reserve currency's value is set by the countries holding it
