context: Connally (Treasury 1971-72) delivered the line at a Group of Ten finance-ministers meeting in Rome, November 1971. He later switched parties to Republican and ran briefly for president in 1980. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Connally.

question: Richard Nixon accused Japan and West Germany on August 15, 1971, of keeping their currencies artificially cheap so their exports would beat American ones. His speech that night also shut off foreign access to US gold and fought inflation at home. Against those trade partners he took a third step. What was it?
answer: A surcharge on imports
choices: A surcharge on imports
A ban on gold exports
A quota on Japanese cars
A freeze on foreign investment
context: The 10 percent import surcharge was intended to force partners (chiefly West Germany and Japan) to revalue their currencies upward against the dollar. It was lifted that December after the Smithsonian Agreement adjusted parities. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/gold-convertibility-ends.

question: John Connally, Richard Nixon's Treasury Secretary, led the talk over one secret weekend at Camp David in August 1971. The small group around the president decided there to sever the last official link between the US dollar and gold. What is the main effect of removing a gold link from a currency?
answer: The government can print far more money without a hard limit
choices: The government can print far more money without a hard limit
The dollar's value is pegged to the price of oil instead
Foreign banks can no longer use dollars for trade
Prices fall, since money is no longer tied to scarce metal
context: The August 13-15, 1971 Camp David weekend brought Fed chair Arthur Burns, Connally, George Shultz, Paul Volcker (then Treasury undersecretary), and others together to plan the announcement. Safire's memoir 'Before the Fall' documents the weekend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock.

question: A Bitcoin fan shares a chart with two lines: what American workers produce in an hour, and what they are paid for it. For a quarter-century after World War II the two lines climbed side by side. Bitcoin fans call August 15, 1971, when Richard Nixon ended the dollar's last tie to gold, the birthday of the fiat-money problem. What happened to the lines after 1971?
answer: Output per hour kept rising, but pay almost stalled
choices: Output per hour kept rising, but pay almost stalled
Pay raced ahead, but output per hour almost stalled
Both lines fell together for the next twenty years
The two lines stayed locked together, just as before
context: This is the productivity-pay gap chart, built from Bureau of Labor Statistics data. From 1948 to the early 1970s, output per hour and typical pay rose almost in step; from then on output kept climbing while typical pay grew far more slowly. The Bitcoin community reads the break as the mark of the end of the gold link. Economists still argue over how to measure the gap and how much of it the money change caused, so the chart opens a question rather than settling one.

question: Delegates from 44 Allied nations gathered at a hotel in a small New Hampshire town in July 1944, as World War II was winding down. They designed a new world money system: every foreign currency pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar pegged to gold at $35 an ounce. Richard Nixon ordered the US Treasury to stop trading dollars for gold on August 15, 1971, killing that last gold link. Which 1944 system did his move destroy?
answer: Bretton Woods
choices: Bretton Woods
The Gold Standard
The Marshall Plan
The Basel Accords
context: The July 1944 conference met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Its system was a gold-exchange standard: foreign governments, not ordinary holders, could turn dollars into gold at $35 an ounce, unlike the classical gold standard, under which anyone could redeem notes for coin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system.

question: New York lawmakers passed the Haas Act in 1937 and capped the city's yellow cabs near 12,000, each needing a small metal license called a medallion. The number held for decades while more and more people needed rides. What happens to the price of a medallion under a cap like that?
answer: The price of a license rises very high because new ones cannot be made
choices: The price of a license rises very high because new ones cannot be made
The price of a license stays at the fee the city first charged for it
The price of a license falls as the cabs it covers grow old and worn
The price of a license follows the cost of a new cab, and nothing more
context: The Haas Act of 1937 created the New York City taxi-medallion system. The cap made each medallion an artificially scarce property right that would eventually trade for over a million dollars. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: A New Yorker bought his way into a yellow cab in 2014 with a government license called a medallion. The law allowed only about 13,400 of them. Roughly what did one medallion cost at the peak?
answer: $1.3 million
choices: $1.3 million
$13 million
context: The NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission auction records show medallion prices rising from $2,500 in 1947 to $200,000 in 1997 to about $1.3 million in 2013-14. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: A young San Francisco startup brought a phone-based ride app to New York City in 2011. To sidestep the city's cap on yellow taxis, it registered as a 'black car' service rather than as a taxi. A rider tapped a button on a smartphone, and a driver arrived in minutes. Which company was it?
answer: Uber
choices: Uber
Lyft
Curb
Via
context: Uber's NYC launch in 2011 categorized each driver as a for-hire vehicle (FHV) rather than a taxi, bypassing the yellow-cab medallion cap entirely and letting supply expand to meet demand. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Uber.

question: A buyer paid more for one New York taxi medallion in 2013 than most American houses cost. Then a phone-based ride service came in, and by 2019 the price had crashed about 92 percent. Roughly what price was left?
choices: $1 million
context: Medallion auction prices tracked the collapse: about $1.3M (2013) to about $700K (2016) to about $100K (2019). Many owners had borrowed against medallions as collateral. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: A New York medallion owner sells his metal disc for a fortune, and everyone can see what the cap on taxis has done for him. Frederic Bastiat taught a method for spotting the losers no one is talking about, which he called 'what is seen and what is unseen.' Using his method, who is the hidden loser here?
answer: The riders who cannot find a cab and walk, wait, or drive drunk
choices: The riders who cannot find a cab and walk, wait, or drive drunk
The bookkeepers who record the taxi companies' profits
The mechanics who service each yellow cab already on the road
The city clerks who publish the auction results each year
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): the visible medallion owners were rich; the invisible losers were the would-be riders denied service and the would-be drivers blocked by the cap. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_medallion.

question: Undercover testers sent out by Mayor Bloomberg's city hall hailed yellow cabs across New York, and the same neighborhoods kept getting passed by. The cabs lived on street hails, and drivers avoided long trips because empty return rides ate their pay. Which parts of New York were the best-known example?
answer: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
choices: The outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens
The Financial District and Midtown Manhattan
LaGuardia and JFK airport terminals
Times Square and Rockefeller Center
context: Yellow-cab economics depended on street hails, so drivers concentrated in Manhattan; the app-hail model let for-hire vehicles serve outer-borough demand that had gone unserved for decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taxi_and_Limousine_Commission_(New_York_City).

question: Brian Rosenthal published a Pulitzer-winning investigative series in May 2019, in the New York Times, on the crash of the city's yellow-taxi medallion market. For years medallion prices had stood above $1 million before they collapsed, and he tracked roughly 950 owner bankruptcies. What was the series's headline focus?
answer: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
choices: How reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers
How Uber built a monopoly in New York City
How the Haas Act created New York's first cab rules
How the NYC Taxi Commission was reformed in 2019
context: Brian Rosenthal's series showed that many owner-drivers had bought medallions at peak prices with loans they could not repay after the collapse. It won the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting. Source: pulitzer.org/winners/brian-m-rosenthal-new-york-times.

question: Frederic Bastiat taught that a policy's true cost includes every trade and every job that never happened because of it. New York's medallion prices crashed by 2019, after ride apps broke the cap on yellow cabs. Reading the collapse Bastiat's way, what was it actually revealing about the cap's long run?
answer: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting for 76 years
choices: The capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting for 76 years
A one-time market crash with no link to earlier medallion prices
Uber's illegal subsidies briefly undercutting an otherwise fair market
A currency-inflation effect running through all New York asset prices
context: Bastiat's move: the medallion price had capitalized the transfer FROM riders and blocked drivers TO cap-protected owners; the collapse reversed a transfer that had run one way since 1937. Painful for owners, but a reversal. Source: bastiat.org (That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, 1850).

question: Ludwig von Mises warned his Thursday-evening seminar at New York University that a government printing large amounts of new money drives prices up. A dollar buys less bread this year than last, but the loss does not fall evenly. Which group tends to be hurt the most by rising prices?
answer: People with savings and people on fixed incomes
choices: People with savings and people on fixed incomes
Borrowers paying back fixed-rate loans
Owners of land, gold and other real goods
The banks that receive the new money first
context: Mises's NYU seminar met on Thursday evenings from 1948 until 1969, in the Graduate School of Business Administration on Trinity Place and later on Washington Square. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises; mises.org/online-book/my-years-ludwig-von-mises/chapter-ix-lus-famous-seminar.

question: Ludwig von Mises faced his students at New York University in the 1940s as a visiting professor the university did not pay. He could not land a paid teaching job at any big US school, so a private group covered his salary. Why did it have to step in?
answer: Universities would not hire scholars whose ideas they disliked
choices: Universities would not hire scholars whose ideas they disliked
The government had barred refugees from paid university posts
The university had no money left after the Depression
He demanded a salary far above what any school would pay
context: The William Volker Fund of Kansas City funded much of the mid-century Austrian revival in America. Source: grokipedia.com/page/William_Volker_Fund.

question: Lawrence Fertig, who worked in advertising on Madison Avenue, paid out of his own pocket so that Ludwig von Mises could keep running his weekly seminar at New York University. Mises's free-market ideas were out of fashion, and for over twenty years a group of private admirers kept him teaching. What does that privately funded seminar reveal about ideas the mainstream refuses?
answer: Even unpopular ideas can survive if some people value them
choices: Even unpopular ideas can survive if some people value them
Only ideas the government approves can survive
Only ideas that make money in the short run survive
All ideas that survive must be true
context: Lawrence Fertig, a Madison Avenue advertising executive who admired Mises's work, personally supplemented Mises's NYU salary and endowed a lecture hall named after him. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Murray Rothbard published a giant treatise called Man, Economy, and State in 1962. Instead of opening with charts and equations, the book began with a single man alone on an island, Robinson Crusoe style. Rothbard then built up trade, prices and money one careful step at a time from that lone figure. Why start economics from just one person alone?
answer: To show that every trade and price begins with individual choices
choices: To show that every trade and price begins with individual choices
To prove that trading with others always leaves both sides poorer
To show that prices must be set by a planner before trade begins
To argue that money came first and trade grew out of it later
context: Rothbard attended the NYU seminar from 1949 and remained through the 1960s. His subsequent writing carried the seminar's tradition to a wider American audience. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Murray_Rothbard.

question: Israel Kirzner, a doctoral student of Ludwig von Mises, set out to explain what an entrepreneur does. Coffee sells for $3 at one shop and $8 across town. One person buys low, sells high and closes the gap, as if she had seen a wrong price on a shelf. According to Kirzner, what drives new firms and better prices?
answer: Alertness to opportunities other people have overlooked
choices: Alertness to opportunities other people have overlooked
A government official approving each new business idea
Random luck with no skill or noticing involved at all
Copying exactly what every other seller is already doing
context: Israel Kirzner's NYU PhD under Mises produced Competition and Entrepreneurship (Chicago, 1973), the foundational modern statement of Austrian entrepreneurship theory. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Israel_Kirzner.

question: Hans Sennholz took his doctorate under Ludwig von Mises as the first American to do so, and went to teach at Grove City College, a small liberal-arts school in Pennsylvania. He stayed for his entire career, teaching Austrian economics. What was the effect on Austrian economics in America?
answer: Austrian ideas kept a foothold in a few colleges even when mainstream departments ignored them
choices: Austrian ideas kept a foothold in a few colleges even when mainstream departments ignored them
Every US university started teaching Austrian economics by 1970
Austrian economics survived only in Europe and never reached the US
Mainstream US departments quickly adopted the Austrian view of banking
context: Hans Sennholz taught for decades at Grove City College, where he trained a generation of Austrian-friendly American economists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hans_Sennholz.

question: Ludwig von Mises gave his last seminar at New York University in December 1969, closing a long American teaching career. Like many top Austrian School economists he had fled Hitler's Europe. Friedrich Hayek had gone to the University of Chicago, Fritz Machlup to Princeton and Gottfried Haberler to Harvard, and several kept teaching well into the late 1960s. Why did these long American teaching careers matter so much for economics?
answer: They carried Austrian ideas into a whole new generation of English-speaking students
choices: They carried Austrian ideas into a whole new generation of English-speaking students
They turned the departments they joined into Austrian strongholds
They moved American economics toward central planning and price controls
They kept Austrian ideas inside a small circle of German-speaking emigres
context: Mises's last seminar was December 1969; he died in October 1973 at age 92. The seminar ended without a successor; the American Austrian tradition would not have another dedicated graduate program until Auburn (1982) and George Mason. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: Theodore Roosevelt faced a banking panic in October 1907 with no central bank of any kind. Depositors were running to withdraw their money, big New York firms were failing, and his government had no tools to stop it. Who ended up organizing the rescue that saved the New York banks?
answer: A group of wealthy private bankers, using their own money
choices: A group of wealthy private bankers, using their own money
Congress, by passing an emergency bill overnight
The state of New York, by taking over the failing banks
New York City, by guaranteeing every deposit in town
context: J.P. Morgan (70 years old in 1907) coordinated the private rescue, summoning bank and trust presidents to his personal library and pooling their capital. It was the last major US financial rescue conducted by a private individual acting as de facto central bank. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: A depositor hurried to the Knickerbocker on Fifth Avenue on October 22, 1907, the day it failed. It took deposits like a bank, but it faced looser reserve rules and could gamble more heavily on Wall Street. What kind of financial company was it?
answer: A trust company
choices: A trust company
A commercial bank
A stock exchange
An insurance company
context: The Knickerbocker Trust Company was the third-largest trust in New York. Trust companies held bank-like deposits but faced looser reserve rules than national banks. When Knickerbocker's president was linked to the Heinze copper-corner scheme, depositors fled. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knickerbocker_Trust_Company.

question: Two brothers tried to corner the shares of United Copper, a copper mining firm, in October 1907, backed by the president of the Knickerbocker. Their scheme failed, and terrified depositors ran on every bank tied to them, until the panic nearly collapsed the American financial system. Which brothers ran the failed corner?
answer: Otto and Augustus Heinze
choices: Otto and Augustus Heinze
Frederick and Charles Barney
James and John Stillman
Nelson and Winthrop Aldrich
context: The Heinze brothers tried to squeeze short-sellers of United Copper Company stock. When the squeeze collapsed on October 16, 1907, depositors at banks associated with the Heinzes started pulling funds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: J. P. Morgan summoned the heads of every rival bank to one room in New York during the panic of October 1907. According to his son-in-law, he locked the doors on them and refused to let them leave until every one had signed a check toward a rescue fund. Where did he keep them?
answer: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
choices: His personal library at 219 Madison Avenue
The floor of the New York Stock Exchange
The board room of the Bank of New York
The White House Cabinet Room
context: The building is now the Morgan Library and Museum. The 'locked in the library' detail comes from Morgan's son-in-law Herbert Satterlee's 1939 biography and is well-attested in period accounts. Source: themorgan.org/about.

question: J. P. Morgan told the head of the New York Stock Exchange during the Panic of 1907 that closing it 'would be too great a shock.' Then he called the city's bank presidents to his Madison Avenue mansion and demanded cash to prop up Wall Street. Roughly how much did he raise, and how fast?
answer: About $25 million in 15 minutes
choices: About $25 million in 15 minutes
About $250 million in an hour
About $1 billion in a day
About $2 million in 15 minutes
context: Morgan raised roughly $25 million from bank presidents assembled in his library in about 15 minutes to keep the NYSE open. Adjusted for the era, this was the operative moment of the private rescue. Source: Satterlee, J. Pierpont Morgan: An Intimate Portrait (1939).

question: Depositors ran on one more major New York firm after the Knickerbocker failed in the 1907 panic. J. P. Morgan, organizing the rescue of Wall Street from his Madison Avenue home, had judged the Knickerbocker too far gone and let it go. This one he concluded was solvent and worth saving with an emergency loan pool. Which firm did he save?
answer: Trust Company of America
choices: Trust Company of America
Bankers Trust
United States Trust
Manhattan Trust
context: Trust Company of America was hit by a run in the days after Knickerbocker's failure. Morgan judged it solvent, arranged a private syndicate to backstop its deposits, and it survived. This is the earliest well-documented case of a private banker distinguishing solvent from insolvent institutions in a panic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907.

question: Charles Kindleberger studied J. P. Morgan's rescue of Wall Street decades later and warned that it could never happen again: leaving future panics to one aging private banker was no long-term plan. Morgan had propped up the stock exchange and its firms from his New York mansion with his own credit and cash. What did Kindleberger say the rescue was 'the last time' any single person did?
answer: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
choices: Acted as a central bank in a major crisis
Owned a majority stake in a Wall Street trust
Held gold reserves for the US Treasury
Personally set discount rates for member banks
context: Kindleberger's Manias, Panics, and Crashes uses the Morgan 1907 episode as the pivot case -- the last time an individual performed the lender-of-last-resort function that permanent central banks now provide. Source: Kindleberger + Aliber, Manias, Panics, and Crashes.

question: Adam Smith opened a chapter of his 1776 book with a puzzle he could not solve. One common thing is very useful, he wrote, yet it buys almost nothing in trade; another is almost useless, yet it trades for a great deal. Which two things did he compare?
answer: Water and diamonds
choices: Water and diamonds
Bread and gold
Iron and silver
Salt and pearls
context: The passage runs 'Nothing is more useful than water: but it will purchase scarce any thing; scarce any thing can be had in exchange for it. A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' It is the founding statement of the paradox of value. Source: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations Book 1 Ch 4, via geolib.com.

question: Adam Smith dodged the puzzle he had posed in 1776: why one of the most useful things there is sells for almost nothing while a nearly useless one sells for a fortune. He split the word 'value' into two senses instead and moved on. Which two did he name?
answer: Value in use and value in exchange
choices: Value in use and value in exchange
Natural price and market price
Real value and nominal value
Absolute value and relative value
context: Real / nominal and natural / market are also genuine Smith distinctions but they belong to different chapters; the paradox-of-value passage explicitly opens with value-in-use and value-in-exchange as the two senses of the word. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paradox of value'.

question: Two writers after Adam Smith went looking for value inside production, in the work poured into making a thing, and pressed the idea harder than anyone. One set it out in a book of 1817, the other in a book of 1867. Who were the two?
answer: David Ricardo and Karl Marx
choices: David Ricardo and Karl Marx
Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill
Jean-Baptiste Say and Frederic Bastiat
Nassau Senior and John Elliott Cairnes
context: Ricardo's Principles of Political Economy and Taxation appeared in 1817; Marx's Capital appeared in German in 1867. Both took embodied labour to be the objective source of value -- Marx developed it into a theory of surplus value and exploitation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Labor theory of value'.

question: Carl Menger read the daily commodity reports in the prime minister's press office and saw prices that did not follow the labor spent on the goods. His Principles of 1871 went on to dissolve Adam Smith's puzzle of cheap water and costly diamonds. Where, on Menger's account, does a good's value live?
answer: In how one chooser ranks one more unit against its other uses
choices: In how one chooser ranks one more unit against its other uses
In the average number of labour-hours embodied in producing it
In the objective usefulness of the substance to human survival
In the cost of the land, labour and capital used to make it
context: Menger's move was that no chooser ever compares 'water as a class' with 'diamonds as a class'; a chooser always compares one more unit of a good, given current holdings, against the next-best alternative use of the same effort or money. Source: Wikipedia, 'Principles of Economics (Menger book)'.

question: A farmer in one of Carl Menger's stories keeps five sacks of grain: for his bread, his livestock, seed, beer and his pet parrots. A rat ruins one sack. Which use does he give up, and what does that choice set?
answer: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
choices: The parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
His own bread -- and the most-urgent use sets the value of any one sack
Every use loses equally -- so the value is the average of the five uses
The bread and the seed together -- because they are the productive uses
context: Menger's insight is that a rational chooser losing one unit will drop the least-urgent use first; therefore the value of any one interchangeable unit equals the importance of the marginal use, not the peak use. This is diminishing marginal utility stated at the level of a specific person's ranking. Source: Libertarianism.org, 'Menger's Principles of Economics: The Marginal Revolution'.

question: A family in a modern city turns on the tap and water runs as freely as it likes, while diamonds stay as rare as ever. Carl Menger's method asks not what water as a whole is worth but what one more glass is worth to that family right now. Why does that next glass rank so low, and the next diamond so high?
answer: Water is plentiful, so one more glass meets a trivial need; scarce diamonds meet top-ranked ones
choices: Water is plentiful, so one more glass meets a trivial need; scarce diamonds meet top-ranked ones
Water is a public good and diamonds a private good, so only the diamonds carry a market value
Diamonds embody far more labour-hours per unit than water, and labour is what sets value
The city sets the price of tap water below its true value, while diamond prices float freely
context: Once value is a ranking of the marginal unit, high total utility and high marginal utility come apart. Water's total utility is enormous but its marginal utility to a plumbed household is nearly zero; a first diamond's marginal utility to someone who has never owned one is large. Source: Study.com, 'Diamond-Water Paradox'.

question: A traveller trudges across the Sahara with one canteen of water and his pockets stuffed with diamonds. Reversing the scarcities like this is the best test of Carl Menger's answer to Adam Smith's old puzzle. On the marginal-unit view, what happens to the traveller's ranking of the next glass against the next stone?
answer: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
choices: The ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond
The ranking stays the same -- diamonds always outrank water because they always cost more to make
The ranking splits -- water wins in use, while the diamonds still win in exchange
The ranking evens out -- each good counts for exactly what it would sell for in town
context: That the ranking reverses on the reverse scarcities is the diagnostic test of the marginal-unit move: value was never a property of the good, it was a ranking that depended on how much of each the chooser already held. Source: Adam Smith Works, 'Three Ways of Looking at the Water-Diamond Paradox'.

question: Carl Menger answered Adam Smith's diamond puzzle in 1871, and his answer reached far beyond the puzzle itself. The answer overturned more than one older idea at once. Which did it most decisively dislodge?
answer: The labour theory of value, because it put value in the good, not in a chooser's ranking
choices: The labour theory of value, because it put value in the good, not in a chooser's ranking
The quantity theory of money, because it treated the money supply as exogenous
The theory of comparative advantage, because it depended on labour cost differences
The Malthusian theory of population, because it assumed diminishing returns in agriculture
context: Every step of the labour-theory chain -- Smith on embodied labour, Ricardo's refinement, Marx's socially necessary labour -- assumed value belonged to the good. Denying the assumption denies the whole chain. William Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Lausanne reached the same marginal answer in 1871-74, and with it the whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good, labour-hours or cost of production alike, lost its footing. Comparative advantage, the quantity theory and Malthus depend on other assumptions and are unaffected. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marginalism'.

question: Colonel Willoughby Verner wrote a letter to The Times of London in 1908. Tall hedges along English country roads had been trimmed low so that drivers of the new motor cars could see farther around the bends. He wrote in to describe what those clear sightlines had actually done. What did he report?
answer: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
choices: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common
Drivers took to the lanes, and horse traffic vanished
Drivers kept to main roads, and village trade collapsed
Drivers slowed at bends, and crashes became rarer
context: Grokipedia's Risk compensation article records Verner's 1908 letter to The Times as the earliest documented observation of the pattern: improving the road did not buy the safety the improvement promised, because drivers spent part of it on speed. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: Ralph Nader wrote a book in 1965 saying Detroit cared more about power and style than about surviving a crash. Senate hearings the next year showed what General Motors had done to him, and the news swung public opinion behind the first federal auto-safety law. What had General Motors done?
answer: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
choices: Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader
Quietly recalled the model Nader had singled out for attack
Bought his publisher and cancelled the second print run
Paid a rival engineer to write and publish a rebuttal book
context: President Lyndon Johnson signed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act on September 9, 1966, with Nader among roughly 200 people at the Rose Garden ceremony. The Act produced the first mandatory federal vehicle standards, effective with the 1968 model year. Sources: Wikipedia, 'National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act'; Wikipedia, 'Ralph Nader'.

question: American football teams swapped leather headgear for rigid plastic-shell helmets in the late 1940s. Skull fractures fell, as the designers expected. But cervical-spine injuries rose, and researchers traced the rise to a change in how players now hit each other. What did players start doing?
answer: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
choices: Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet
Gripping the facemask to swing an opponent down
Driving the helmet into the opponent's front knee
Locking both arms around the opponent's waist
context: The leather helmet made spearing too painful to attempt; the plastic shell made it survivable for the tackler, so the technique spread and the neck paid for it. The protection was real, and the behaviour moved to consume part of it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: Sam Peltzman studied the new American cars in a 1975 paper. From 1968 every one had to carry seat belts, padded dashboards and safer steering columns. Deaths per crash had dropped as the engineers promised, but total highway deaths had not fallen. What did his data show that closed the gap?
answer: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
choices: Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent
Rear-seat passenger deaths rose faster than front-seat deaths
Belts were fitted in the cars but almost no driver buckled them
New highway building pushed traffic onto narrow rural roads
context: Peltzman, 'The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation', Journal of Political Economy 83(4), 677-725, August 1975. The crash-test literature implied annual highway deaths would be about 20 percent greater without the mandated devices; Peltzman argued the offsets were close to complete, with lives saved inside the car paid for by deaths outside it and by more accidents overall. Source: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/260352

question: A councilwoman proposes that every cyclist must wear a helmet. To back the plan, she points the council to laboratory crash tests showing how much a helmet reduces head injuries in a hard fall. Sam Peltzman warns the council that the lab number is the wrong one to plan on. What is his objection?
answer: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
choices: That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain
That the council cannot know which streets its cyclists actually fear most
That the helmet makers will end up writing the standard the council adopts
That the cost falls on cyclists while the credit goes to the councillors
context: The three rejected choices are real reasoning moves aimed elsewhere: Hayek's knowledge problem, George Stigler's regulatory capture (1971), and Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits with dispersed costs (1965). The move being made here is incentive recognition -- the engineering estimate describes the device, not the person using it.

question: W. Kip Viscusi checked the poisoning data after the Food and Drug Administration ordered child-safe caps on aspirin and some other drug bottles in 1972. Aspirin poisonings had not dropped, and poisonings from other painkillers had gone up. What did Viscusi say parents were doing?
answer: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
choices: Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach
Buying larger bottles because the safe caps cost more per pack
Switching to painkillers the new rule did not yet cover
Storing several drugs together in one unmarked kitchen jar
context: Viscusi named it the 'lulling effect': a cap that is hard for an adult to open gets left loose, and a cap advertised as child proof invites a parent to relax the precaution the child actually depended on. W. Kip Viscusi, 'The Lulling Effect: The Impact of Child-Resistant Packaging on Aspirin and Analgesic Ingestions', American Economic Review 74(2), 324-327, May 1984.

question: A safety-minded driver buys airbags and antilock brakes through the market, with no law telling her to. Buyers like her come first, and that flatters the devices in the aggregate figures. Winston, Maheshri and Mannering tested detailed crash data on this in a 2006 study. What did they find the two devices had done to crashes and injuries?
answer: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
choices: Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed
Cut both sharply, because careful drivers used the devices carefully
Cut injuries but not collisions, matching the crash-test estimates
Raised both above the rates recorded for cars without the devices
context: Winston, Maheshri and Mannering, 'An exploration of the offset hypothesis using disaggregate data: The case of airbags and antilock brakes', Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 2006. Their disaggregate data mattered: the drivers who buy safety equipment are unusually careful to begin with, so aggregate comparisons flatter the devices. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11166-006-8288-7

question: A skier buckles on a helmet at the top of a real mountain. Sam Peltzman's reasoning says people who feel safer take bigger risks, as buckled-in drivers speed up. Researchers went looking for that offset in helmeted skiers and snowboarders, and they did not find it: no faster skiing, no harder crashes, and head injuries down 30 to 50 percent with no rise in reckless behavior. What does the ski result show?
answer: That the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law
choices: That the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law
That the offset appears under mandates but never with voluntary equipment
That the offset appears in road vehicles but never in sporting equipment
That the offset was refuted by the ski data and should now be abandoned
context: A systematic review of 23 studies of cycle-helmet use points the same way: only two found helmeted riders taking more risk, 18 found no such effect, and 10 linked helmets to more cautious riding (the categories overlap). The reasoning move tells you what to go and measure; it does not tell you the answer in advance. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: Leslie Robertson reworked Sam Peltzman's U.S. car data in 1977 and challenged his result. He said seat belts cut deaths among car riders, with no matching rise among people outside the cars. On what ground did he attack Peltzman's model?
answer: That it left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate
choices: That it left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate
That it used state records too coarse to separate rural from urban roads
That it began its series in 1947, before any of the devices had existed
That it counted serious injuries as deaths wherever hospital records failed
context: Later critics pressed the same line: Leonard Evans argued in a 1998 review that claimed evidence for full behavioural offset in transport came from aggregating dissimilar data and ignoring exposure. The dispute is about measurement, not about whether drivers respond to incentives at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: Gerald Wilde, a psychologist, advanced a claim in 1982 stronger than the economists had made. Where Sam Peltzman had said drivers spend part of a safety gain on speed, Wilde made a claim about how much danger someone will put up with in the first place. What did Wilde claim?
answer: That each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it
choices: That each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it
That risk tolerance climbs with age and drops away again after sixty
That drivers copy the risk level of whatever vehicles surround them
That risk tolerance is set by law and enforcement, not by the driver
context: Wilde set out risk homeostasis in 1982 and expanded it in Target Risk (1994). The theory predicts full cancellation: lower the objective risk and the person restores the felt risk by other means, so safety countermeasures are futile unless the appetite itself is addressed. That is a far stronger claim than Peltzman's, and much harder to defend -- which is why the two should not be treated as the same idea. Source: Grokipedia, 'Risk compensation' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_compensation).

question: David Henderson, writing at Econlib, took on the way the press routinely reports the offsetting-behaviour finding: 'safety rules do not save lives.' He argued that this states the claim far more strongly than the economics supports. Suppose a study finds that a seat-belt law did reduce deaths, and also finds that belted drivers drove faster. What should the analyst conclude?
answer: Both results stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain
choices: Both results stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain
The two results contradict each other, so one of the datasets must be wrong
The offset shows the law failed, whatever the death figures appear to say
The death figures settle the matter, so the speed result can be set aside
context: Henderson: the effect predicts offsetting behaviour, and says nothing about whether the offset is large enough to cancel the benefit entirely. That is an empirical question, answered study by study. The reasoning move earns its keep by telling you that the engineering number is an upper bound and that you must go and measure the human response -- not by handing you a verdict on the policy. Source: David Henderson, 'What the Peltzman Effect Is and Isn't', Econlib (https://www.econlib.org/what-the-peltzman-effect-is-and-isnt/).

question: Frédéric Bastiat published a mock petition in 1845 from France's candle-makers. With a straight face they asked the Chamber of Deputies for a law shutting every window and shutter in France by day, so people would burn candles at noon. What was the joke poking fun at?
answer: Businesses that beg the government to hurt competitors so they can charge more
choices: Businesses that beg the government to hurt competitors so they can charge more
Shoppers who buy cheap foreign goods instead of supporting French makers
Lawmakers who tax windows and doors to raise money for the state
Candle-makers who charge too much for wax because they face no rivals
context: The petition names 'all windows, dormers, skylights, inside and outside shutters, curtains, casements, bull's-eyes, deadlights, and blinds' -- every household aperture that lets in the free rival's product. Source: fee.org/resources/a-petition.

question: Bastiat wrote a mock petition in which France's candle-makers addressed the Chamber of Deputies with perfect gravity. A foreign rival, they wrote, was pouring cheap light into France and undercutting every French maker of lamps and candles on price. In their second paragraph they named it. Which rival did they name?
answer: The sun
choices: The sun
The whale
British gaslight
The tallow farmer
context: 'This rival is none other than the sun.' Bastiat's satire lets the petitioners say the quiet part loud: their real complaint is that free sunlight is more efficient than any French candle. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: Frédéric Bastiat had his candle-makers list everyone who would prosper once the windows of France were shut by day. Tallow farms would spread, with more cattle and pasture; whaling fleets would put to sea for oil; forests would fall to build the ships; carpenters would get work making shutters. Which real argument for tariffs did that chain of blessings parody?
answer: The multiplier argument for tariffs
choices: The multiplier argument for tariffs
The infant-industry argument for tariffs
The national-defense argument for tariffs
The reciprocity argument for tariffs
context: The petition ridicules the 19th-century multiplier claim ('every candlemaker's job creates jobs upstream in tallow, in oil, in wood, in shipping') by taking the exact same argument seriously and applying it to a tariff against the sun. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: Milton Friedman brought Bastiat's candle-makers back in 1980, in Free to Choose, a book and television series he and his wife made. He used the petition as a test for any trade argument, and writers still reach for it over robots, foreign labour, cheap imports and cheap solar panels. Which pair does the candle-makers' test look for?
answer: Abundance treated as a threat, scarcity treated as a benefit
choices: Abundance treated as a threat, scarcity treated as a benefit
Consumption treated as a threat, saving treated as a benefit
Imports treated as a threat, exports treated as a benefit
Immigration treated as a threat, emigration treated as a benefit
context: Friedman's Free to Choose (1980) uses Bastiat's petition to press the diagnostic question: does the policy treat MORE goods for less work as a bad thing? If so, it is the candlemakers' argument. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_to_Choose.

question: Frédéric Bastiat did not argue against tariffs head-on. He answered the protectionists, who wanted French makers shielded from cheaper goods from abroad, with a demand for a law closing every window in France by day. What reasoning move was that?
answer: Reductio ad absurdum -- pushing the other side's logic until it looks silly
choices: Reductio ad absurdum -- pushing the other side's logic until it looks silly
Straw man -- pretending opponents said something they never did
Ad hominem -- attacking the other side's character
Appeal to authority -- quoting a famous name instead of arguing
context: Swift's 1729 A Modest Proposal takes the exploitative-labor logic of 18th-century Irish policy seriously enough to propose eating Irish children; Bastiat's 1845 candlemakers takes protectionism seriously enough to tax the sun. Same technique, two masterpieces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Modest_Proposal.

question: A New Zealand-born economist at the London School of Economics published a paper in 1958 on nearly a century of British wage data, from 1861 to 1957. When unemployment was low, wages rose quickly; when it was high, wages barely moved. The rule was later named after him. What is it called?
answer: The Phillips curve
choices: The Phillips curve
The Kuznets curve
The Laffer curve
The Lorenz curve
context: A.W. Phillips's 1958 paper 'The Relation between Unemployment and the Rate of Change of Money Wage Rates' plotted a historical correlation. Later economists reinterpreted it as a policy trade-off. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_curve.

question: Milton Friedman told the American Economic Association in December 1967 that cutting unemployment by making some extra inflation works only once. As soon as workers see prices rising, he warned, they demand higher wages and the trick fails. What did he say about the long run?
answer: The trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes
choices: The trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes
Inflation permanently lowers unemployment
Unemployment permanently lowers inflation
Both must rise together forever
context: Friedman's presidential address 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (published in the American Economic Review, March 1968) is the foundational statement of the natural-rate critique. Friedman won the Nobel Prize in 1976. Source: aeaweb.org (AER 1968).

question: Milton Friedman addressed the American Economic Association in December 1967 and attacked the menu that seemed to trade rising prices for jobs. Another economist had reached the same result on his own that same year, and the Nobel Prize went to him in 2006. Who was he?
answer: Edmund Phelps
choices: Edmund Phelps
Robert Lucas
James Tobin
Robert Solow
context: Phelps's papers of 1967 and 1968 reached the natural-rate conclusion independently of Friedman, and the 2006 Nobel Prize honoured his analysis of trade-offs over time in economic policy. The result is often called the Friedman-Phelps critique. Lucas (1995), Tobin (1981) and Solow (1987) won the prize for other work; Solow had helped draw the menu itself. Source: nobelprize.org (Phelps 2006).

question: Richard Nixon leaned on Arthur Burns, chairman of the Federal Reserve, to keep money loose and interest rates low in the run-up to the 1972 election, so voters would feel prosperous on election day. Burns went along. Nixon carried forty-nine states, and the rest of the decade paid for it. What lesson does the story teach?
answer: A central bank that helps politicians in the short run creates bigger inflation later
choices: A central bank that helps politicians in the short run creates bigger inflation later
A central bank that eases before an election wins lasting growth for the country
A central bank that keeps money loose can hold unemployment down for good
A central bank that obeys a president keeps markets calm and prices steady
context: Arthur Burns chaired the Fed 1970-78 under Nixon, Ford, and Carter. His diaries and Nixon-tape transcripts document political pressure to keep money easy through Nixon's 1972 re-election. Miller succeeded Burns briefly (1978-79); Volcker followed. Source: federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-inflation.

question: Bill Phillips built a strange machine at the London School of Economics in 1949. Colored water ran through clear tanks and pipes to model the British economy, one tank for savings, one for taxes, one for imports. An operator turned a valve and watched one policy change ripple through the country. Why do most modern economists doubt a machine like this could ever predict an actual economy?
answer: Real economies are made of millions of people making choices, not smooth flows
choices: Real economies are made of millions of people making choices, not smooth flows
Real economies move faster than water can flow between glass tanks
Real economies need far more tanks and pipes than any room could hold
Real economies change their tax laws too often for fixed pipes to follow
context: The MONIAC (Monetary National Income Analogue Computer), built by Phillips at LSE in 1949, was a hydraulic analog computer that used flowing water to model Keynesian income-expenditure identities. Working units are preserved at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and Cambridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MONIAC.

question: Murray Rothbard read Milton Friedman's 1968 case against printing money to lower unemployment and agreed as far as it went. Friedman said workers catch on to rising prices and demand higher wages. Rothbard, following Ludwig von Mises, pressed a deeper point. What is that deeper Austrian point?
answer: Every attempt to fine-tune with new money ends in the same boom-and-bust cycle
choices: Every attempt to fine-tune with new money ends in the same boom-and-bust cycle
The natural rate of unemployment sits far closer to zero than Friedman claimed
Wages are stickier in money terms than Friedman's simple model assumed
The money-supply figures are too imprecise for any central bank to steer by
context: Rothbard's Austrian reading: Friedman correctly saw that expectations undo the trade-off, but the deeper point is that credit expansion distorts the whole capital structure, and the liquidation that follows is the very stagflation Friedman diagnosed. Source: mises.org/library/americas-great-depression.

question: Many traders got a surprise from Jerome Powell on September 18, 2024. His Federal Reserve had held its key rate at 5.25 to 5.50 percent for 14 months to fight post-COVID inflation, and now it cut for the first time in years. How big was that first cut?
answer: 50 basis points, an oversized cut
choices: 50 basis points, an oversized cut
25 basis points, a standard cut
75 basis points, an unusual cut
100 basis points, an emergency cut
context: The September 18 2024 pivot was a 50-basis-point cut, larger than the traditional 25bp starting move. It brought the funds rate to 4.75-5.00% and began a new cutting cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell announced a rate cut on September 18, 2024, though inflation had not yet come all the way down to the Fed's 2 percent goal. He explained the move by pointing to a different part of the economy, where the news had turned weaker. What did he point to?
answer: Labor-market cooling
choices: Labor-market cooling
Rising consumer confidence
A widening trade deficit
Falling residential construction
context: Powell framed the cut as a preemptive response to labor-market weakening. CPI had come down from the 9.1% peak to roughly 2.5% by August 2024, but core inflation remained sticky around 3.2% -- above target. Source: federalreserve.gov (Powell Jackson Hole speech August 23 2024).

question: Federal Reserve officials told the public and the markets that inflation could fall back to their 2 percent target without much rise in unemployment. Their chair, Jerome Powell, had raised interest rates to fight the worst American inflation since the early 1980s. What is this hopeful outcome usually called?
answer: The soft landing
choices: The soft landing
The dual mandate
The Taylor rule
The Greenspan put
context: A 'soft landing' means inflation falls to target without a recession. The Fed staked its 2023-24 messaging on that outcome; whether it held is still argued. The dual mandate is the Fed's pair of goals, the Taylor rule a formula for setting rates, and the Greenspan put the market's faith that the Fed will rescue falling stocks. Source: Grokipedia 'Soft landing (economics)' (2026-09-05).

question: Arthur Burns raised interest rates in the mid-1970s, when American prices had climbed painfully high, and inflation began to fall. As soon as the economy slowed, he cut rates back down to protect jobs. By the end of the decade prices were climbing faster than before. What lesson do many economists draw from that episode?
answer: Cutting rates too early can trigger a second, worse inflation wave
choices: Cutting rates too early can trigger a second, worse inflation wave
Cutting rates in a slowdown keeps jobs safe at little cost to prices
Price and wage controls work better than rate hikes against inflation
Raising rates once is enough to end inflation for good
context: Arthur Burns (Fed chair 1970-1978) eased too soon after the inflation wave of 1973-74, and the second wave of 1979-80 had to be crushed by Paul Volcker at rates near 20%. Economists across camps, Larry Summers among them, raised the parallel in the 2020s. Source: Grokipedia 'Arthur Burns' (2026-09-05).

question: Paul Volcker decided to stop American inflation no matter what, after a decade of stagflation had left prices still rising fast. He pushed short-term interest rates all the way up to about 20 percent. Loans for cars, houses and businesses became painful, a deep recession followed and unemployment jumped above 10 percent. But prices finally settled. What does his 20-percent squeeze reveal?
answer: Very high interest rates can crush inflation but hurt borrowers first
choices: Very high interest rates can crush inflation but hurt borrowers first
Only a recession, never interest rates, can bring prices back down
Inflation fades by itself once a decade of rising prices runs its course
Rate hikes work only when paired with wage and price controls
context: Volcker took the Fed chair in August 1979 and hiked the funds rate to a peak of about 20% in 1981 to crush the second wave of inflation that Arthur Burns's premature cuts had helped seed. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell lowered interest rates in September 2024, with inflation still above the Fed's 2 percent target. Austrian and monetarist critics saw the move as more than one man's error. What pattern did they say it showed in how central banks handle the political costs of tight money?
answer: Central banks cut too soon, since joblessness costs them now and inflation only later
choices: Central banks cut too soon, since joblessness costs them now and inflation only later
Central banks hold rates high too long, since inflation costs them more than joblessness
Central banks shrug off political costs and follow whatever their forecast models say
Central banks move only when markets force them, whatever the political cost of delay
context: The Burns parallel captures the pattern. The immediate visible cost of tight money (unemployment, low asset prices) is politically painful; the deferred cost of a second wave arrives after officials have moved on. The incentive structure inside central banking is tilted toward premature easing. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Followers of Milton Friedman and Ludwig von Mises watched the Fed cut rates in September 2024 with inflation still above the 2 percent target, and rival camps watched from the far side of a lasting dispute. The cut made a rare live test of it. Which dispute is it?
answer: Whether new money feeds consumer prices on a long lag or can be absorbed by supply
choices: Whether new money feeds consumer prices on a long lag or can be absorbed by supply
Whether the Federal Reserve is a private or a public institution at heart
Whether Bitcoin will replace gold as the main reserve asset of central banks
Whether commercial banks or central banks create most of the money in use
context: The 2020-25 policy cycle is the largest natural experiment on this question since the 1970s. The outcome will shape monetary economics for a generation. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: A shopper in early 2022 found each dollar buying less as prices across America climbed too fast. Jerome Powell's Federal Reserve, the central bank in charge of American money, reached for its main tool to cool things down. What does a central bank usually do at such a moment?
answer: Raise interest rates so borrowing money costs more
choices: Raise interest rates so borrowing money costs more
Lower interest rates so people can afford the higher prices
Print more money so wages can keep up with prices
Cap store prices so shoppers can afford the basics
context: The Fed's first rise of the cycle came on March 16, 2022: a quarter-point, and the first increase since December 2018. Ten more followed, carrying the federal funds rate to 5.25-5.50% by July 2023. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell answered the fastest inflation in 40 years with four back-to-back extra-large rate hikes in 2022. US consumer prices were rising more than 9 percent a year by the middle of that year, and his committee moved at its June, July, September and November meetings. Each of the four hikes was the same size, bigger than a standard hike. How big was each?
answer: 75 basis points each
choices: 75 basis points each
50 basis points each
100 basis points each
25 basis points each
context: The four consecutive 75-basis-point hikes in mid-2022 were the fastest tightening pace since Paul Volcker's 1979-82 inflation-crushing cycle. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell announced alongside his rate rises that the Fed would let old Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities on its balance sheet mature without buying new ones to replace them. At its peak the plan drained up to 95 billion dollars a month from the Fed's holdings. What is this shrinking of the balance sheet called?
answer: Quantitative tightening
choices: Quantitative tightening
Operation Twist
Yield-curve control
Sterilized intervention
context: Quantitative tightening (QT) is the mirror of QE: instead of buying bonds and creating reserves, the Fed lets bonds mature and destroys reserves. QT began June 2022 at $47.5B/month and rose to $95B/month by September 2022. Operation Twist (2011) swapped short bonds for long ones without shrinking the balance sheet. Source: Grokipedia 'Quantitative tightening' (2026-09-05).

question: A Fed watcher checked the price reports after each rate hike of 2022 and saw consumer prices still climbing month after month. Only in 2023 did inflation clearly start to slow. Economists say monetary policy works 'with long and variable lags.' What does this delay show about how rate changes work?
answer: Rate changes take many months to fully affect prices
choices: Rate changes take many months to fully affect prices
Rate changes matter less to prices than the supply of oil and food
Rate changes were too small to matter until they passed 5 percent
Rate changes reach prices only after Congress cuts its spending
context: Milton Friedman made the phrase 'long and variable lags' famous. The Fed's first 75-basis-point hike came on June 15, 2022; consumer prices peaked at 9.1 percent a year in the June figures, published on July 13, and slowed clearly only during 2023. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: Federal Reserve officials set aside two items that swing around a lot in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) in 2023 to see the underlying trend. That stripped-down measure stayed stubbornly above 4 percent through most of the year, even as the headline CPI fell. Which measure did the Fed watch most closely as evidence of ongoing persistence?
answer: Core CPI, excluding food and energy
choices: Core CPI, excluding food and energy
Headline CPI, including all items
The producer price index
Import price inflation
context: Core CPI strips out volatile food and energy prices to reveal underlying trend. Its stickiness in the 4-5% range through 2023 kept the Fed from cutting rates even as headline inflation fell to about 3%. Source: Grokipedia 'Consumer price index (United States)' (2026-09-05).

question: Austrian-school economists, heirs of Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, watched Jerome Powell raise interest rates in 2022 and 2023 faster than at any time since the early 1980s, to fight the worst inflation in forty years. They had warned for decades of the hidden fragility central-bank money creates, and they said the Fed had painted itself into a specific structural trap. What is the trap they identify?
answer: Hike enough to end inflation and banks break; stop short and inflation stays
choices: Hike enough to end inflation and banks break; stop short and inflation stays
Hike and the dollar soars, crushing exports; cut and the dollar sinks abroad
Shrink the balance sheet and bond yields spike; grow it and stocks bubble
Raise reserve rules and lending stops; drop them and deposits flee abroad
context: This is the classic Austrian business-cycle bust phase. The malinvestment built by artificially low rates must be liquidated. Attempting to prevent the liquidation prolongs the misallocation; permitting it produces the visible crisis. Source: Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Jerome Powell took the federal funds rate to a peak of 5.25 to 5.50 percent by July 2023, the highest in two decades. That peak is still often compared unfavorably with the Paul Volcker era. Volcker, Fed chair from 1979 to 1987, crushed 1970s stagflation by pushing the rate far higher than anything modern Fed chairs have set. What was the Volcker-era peak?
answer: About 20 percent
choices: About 20 percent
About 8 percent
About 12 percent
About 25 percent
context: Volcker's federal funds rate hit a peak of about 20% in 1981. Powell's 5.5% is roughly one-quarter of Volcker's. The reason: the US debt-to-GDP ratio is now roughly 120% versus 32% in 1981, so small rate rises now produce large debt-service costs. Source: Grokipedia 'Paul Volcker' (2026-09-05).

question: Paul Volcker crushed inflation in the early 1980s with US federal debt at only about 32 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). Jerome Powell fought inflation from 2022 with that debt at about 120 percent of GDP. Every extra percentage point on the Fed's policy rate now costs the Treasury tens of billions more each year in interest. What does the comparison show about high government debt and monetary policy?
answer: It lowers the ceiling on how high the Fed can safely raise rates
choices: It lowers the ceiling on how high the Fed can safely raise rates
It raises the ceiling, since a bigger debt gives the Fed more room to act
It changes nothing, since the Fed sets rates with no regard to the budget
It makes rate rises cheaper, since most of the debt is locked in at old rates
context: Fiscal dominance -- the situation in which monetary policy is constrained by the government's debt-service math -- explains why the modern Fed cannot go anywhere near Volcker-era rates. High debt shortens the fuse on which monetary tightening operates. Source: Ammous, The Fiat Standard (2021).

question: Mancur Olson argued in his 1982 book that special-interest groups pile up in long-peaceful, stable countries: labor unions, business cartels, farm lobbies, professional licensing guilds. Each one grabs a piece of the national pie, and in the end they choke off growth. What term did Olson use for these groups?
answer: Distributional coalitions
choices: Distributional coalitions
Encompassing organizations
Countervailing powers
Iron triangles
context: Distributional coalitions is Olson's term for organized groups that secure privileges for their members at the expense of the general economy. His contrasting case was the encompassing organization, a group so large that it bears much of the cost of its own demands. Countervailing powers (Galbraith) and iron triangles (political science) name other things. Source: Olson, The Rise and Decline of Nations (Yale 1982).

question: Mancur Olson set out to explain why a country wrecked by war or revolution often bounces back and outgrows its old, stable rival, starting from what piles up in a quiet country over the decades. Why do the shocks help?
answer: The shocks smash the built-up interest groups blocking growth
choices: The shocks smash the built-up interest groups blocking growth
The shocks make citizens more patriotic and hard-working
The shocks force everyone to adopt new technology
The shocks kill enough people to raise wages
context: Olson's structural claim: shocks that destroy old cartels, unions, and licensing guilds give the rebuilt economy a fresh start without encrusted privileges. Rebuilt economies get to skip decades of accumulated rent-seeking. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), Chapter 4.

question: Mancur Olson needed a test of his claim that a war, a revolution or an occupation can clear the way for fast growth. He found his best case in the years after World War II: two defeated nations whose recoveries of the 1950s and 1960s outran victorious Britain. Which two did he point to?
answer: West Germany and Japan
choices: West Germany and Japan
France and Italy
Austria and Belgium
Poland and Czechoslovakia
context: West Germany and Japan grew dramatically faster than the victorious US and Britain in the two decades after 1945. Olson credits the destruction of prewar cartels and guilds -- not merely the effects of Marshall aid or savings rates. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), Chapter 5.

question: A farm lobbyist in a country untouched by war or revolution for many decades wins one more special deal, as the unions, business lobbies and industry associations around him have done for years. Tax breaks and protective rules pile up quietly. In his 1982 book, what did Mancur Olson say usually happens to that country's growth?
answer: Growth slows because too many groups protect their own turf
choices: Growth slows because too many groups protect their own turf
Growth speeds up because each deal makes its industry stronger
Growth holds steady because the deals cancel one another out
Growth slows only once the country's savings start running out
context: Britain had accumulated distributional coalitions since the Industrial Revolution without a similarly disruptive shock. Olson used its relative decline to illustrate the structural mechanism. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), Chapter 5.

question: Mancur Olson said national decline was not fated. He argued that a determined government could dismantle entrenched interest groups deliberately, without a war, and restore growth. Later scholars often point to two reform programs of the 1980s as textbook cases of exactly that. Which two?
answer: Thatcher's Britain 1979-90 and Roger Douglas's New Zealand 1984-88
choices: Thatcher's Britain 1979-90 and Roger Douglas's New Zealand 1984-88
Reagan's America 1981-89 and Mulroney's Canada 1984-93
Kohl's Germany 1982-98 and Chirac's France 1986-88
Nakasone's Japan 1982-87 and Fraser's Australia 1975-83
context: Both programs deliberately took on entrenched unions, licensing guilds, and subsidy recipients; New Zealand's reforms under the Labour finance minister Roger Douglas were especially sharp. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rogernomics.

question: Mancur Olson took his argument about shocks and special-interest deals to American soil. He set one U.S. region, left in physical ruin by a war fought on its own ground, against an untouched rival that grew more slowly afterward. Which two regions did he pair?
answer: The postbellum US South versus the industrialized Northeast
choices: The postbellum US South versus the industrialized Northeast
The postwar Midwest versus the Pacific Northwest
The postwar Mountain West versus New England
The postbellum West Coast versus the Southeast
context: Olson noted that after the Civil War's massive destruction, the US South experienced periods of relatively rapid growth compared to the older industrial Northeast, which had accumulated denser interest-group structures. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), regional case chapters.

question: Mancur Olson published his book in 1982 with a riddle from the 1970s still unsolved, one that standard Keynesian theory said could not happen. He said his idea of interest-group sclerosis could explain the riddle. Which 1970s problem did he offer it for?
answer: The stagflation of the 1970s
choices: The stagflation of the 1970s
The oil-price shocks of 1973 and 1979
The collapse of the Bretton Woods system
The New York City fiscal crisis of 1975
context: Olson's subtitle -- Economic Growth, Stagflation, and Social Rigidities -- targets 1970s stagflation. His structural claim: accumulated coalitions increase costs, slow adjustment, and lock in inflationary pressures even without excess aggregate demand. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), Introduction.

question: A student reading Mancur Olson today worries that the whole theory sounds like a defense of war. His 1982 book showed defeated nations growing faster than the Allies who won, and some critics accused him of glorifying war. Olson himself repeatedly rejected that reading. Which best captures his own qualification of the argument?
answer: He explained a structural pattern; he never advocated destruction as policy
choices: He explained a structural pattern; he never advocated destruction as policy
He said the pattern held only for nations rebuilt with large foreign aid
He said the pattern was a quirk of timing that later data would undo
He said only a written constitution, never reform, could check the lobbies
context: Olson insisted his analysis identified a mechanism, not a prescription. His whole final chapter of Rise and Decline is devoted to peaceful reform paths -- because the shock path is monstrous. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), final chapter.

question: A reform minister in an old democracy sets out to cut one farm subsidy and finds the job far harder than it looks. Mancur Olson argued in his 1982 book that stable democracies grow thick over the decades with small, well-organized lobbies, farm groups, unions and trade associations, each guarding a special favor from the government. Using his group-action idea, which mismatch best explains why reform is so hard?
answer: Every coalition fights fiercely to keep its privilege; no cross-society force fights back
choices: Every coalition fights fiercely to keep its privilege; no cross-society force fights back
Every voter gains a little from the subsidy, so the majority votes to keep it
Every minister owes his seat to farmers, who outnumber the taxpayers who fund them
Every reform costs more to pass than the subsidy itself costs the taxpayer
context: The asymmetry is Olson's Logic writ large across national policy. Each subsidy recipient has enormous per-capita stake in defending its privilege; consumers and taxpayers have small per-capita stakes in the same issue and do not organize. Source: Olson, Rise and Decline (1982), Chapter 3.

question: Friedrich Hayek wrote a warning to Britain in 1944, with the bombs still falling on London. In The Road to Serfdom he said that keeping the country's heavy wartime rules on the economy after the peace would start Britain down a dangerous road. What kind of government did he warn against?
answer: A government that plans and controls almost every part of daily life
choices: A government that plans and controls almost every part of daily life
A government that leaves business to run itself with no rules at all
A government that hands power back to Britain's old landed families
A government that spends its peacetime budget on a standing army
context: F. A. Hayek's The Road to Serfdom was published in Britain by Routledge on March 10, 1944, with an initial print run of 2,000 copies that sold out in about a month. Source: University of Chicago Press, 'The Publication History of The Road to Serfdom' (https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/320553.html).

question: Friedrich Hayek, teaching at the London School of Economics, put an unusual line at the front of The Road to Serfdom in 1944. The short book warned against central planning, and the line named the very people he was warning. To whom did Hayek dedicate the book?
answer: To the socialists of all parties
choices: To the socialists of all parties
To the memory of Ludwig von Mises
To the young men of the free countries
To Lionel Robbins and the LSE colleagues
context: The book's dedication is 'To the socialists of all parties' -- Hayek's point being that comprehensive economic planning is dangerous whether it is proposed by parties calling themselves socialist or by nominally conservative parties that adopt the same tools. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Road to Serfdom' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Road_to_Serfdom).

question: Three American publishers turned down The Road to Serfdom before anyone took it. The Macmillan rejection said Friedrich Hayek was 'a little outside the stream of much present-day thought.' Which American press finally printed it, in September 1944?
answer: The University of Chicago Press
choices: The University of Chicago Press
Harvard University Press
Princeton University Press
Yale University Press
context: Macmillan, Little Brown, and Harper and Brothers all rejected Road to Serfdom before Chicago accepted it. The University of Chicago Press published the American edition on September 18, 1944, with an initial print run of 2,000 copies. Source: University of Chicago Press publication history.

question: Friedrich Hayek watched in person as one country drifted from big-government economic planning in the 1920s into full dictatorship by 1933. His 1944 book The Road to Serfdom warned Britain and America not to copy it. Which country was the warning about?
answer: Germany
choices: Germany
Russia
Italy
France
context: Hayek was born in Vienna in 1899 and had watched the German-speaking world walk this road in person. His thesis was that Britain and America, then flirting with wartime economic controls made permanent, were on the same road -- comprehensive planning would require ever more coercive power to override the countless individual choices it must direct. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Road to Serfdom.'

question: Editors at a major American picture magazine turned Friedrich Hayek's whole argument into a comic-strip layout, frame by frame, in February 1945. The Road to Serfdom had become a surprise hit in America. General Motors reprinted the picture version as a pamphlet and handed out millions of copies to workers. Which magazine ran it?
answer: Look
choices: Look
Reader's Digest
Life
Time
context: Look magazine published a picture-book version of Road to Serfdom in February 1945; General Motors reprinted the illustrated version as a pamphlet for mass distribution. This is one of the strangest crossovers of an academic economics book into 1940s American pop culture. Source: David Hart, 'Hayek's Illustrated The Road to Serfdom' (http://davidmhart.com/liberty/GermanClassicalLiberals/Hayek/IllustratedRoadSerfdom/index.html).

question: George Orwell reviewed Friedrich Hayek's warning about a government taking over the whole economy, in the Observer on April 9, 1944. Orwell granted that the danger Hayek feared was real. On Hayek's argument, what happens to citizens when one central plan replaces millions of private choices?
answer: They lose the freedom to choose their own work, prices, and daily lives
choices: They lose the freedom to choose their own work, prices, and daily lives
They keep their freedoms but grow poorer as the plan wastes resources
They lose their savings as planners print money to pay for the plan
They gain steady jobs for life in return for paying higher taxes
context: George Orwell reviewed Road to Serfdom in the Observer on April 9, 1944, summarizing Hayek's thesis as 'Socialism inevitably leads to despotism' and adding his own worry that the collectivist alternative Hayek warned against was itself a genuine danger -- Orwell's own subject in Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four. Source: Reason magazine, 'The Connection Between George Orwell and Friedrich Hayek' (https://reason.com/2011/12/21/george-orwell-and-friedrich-hayek/).

question: John Maynard Keynes wrote Friedrich Hayek a personal letter about The Road to Serfdom on June 28, 1944. Keynes, Hayek's professional opponent for thirteen years and the intellectual force behind the wartime controls Hayek warned against, called it 'a grand book' and told him, 'we all have the greatest reason to be grateful to you for saying so well what needs so much to be said.' What was Keynes's reservation?
answer: He disagreed with Hayek about where the line of state action should be drawn
choices: He disagreed with Hayek about where the line of state action should be drawn
He rejected Hayek's account of the 1920s Weimar Republic as historically wrong
He accused Hayek of stealing the argument from Ludwig von Mises without credit
He said the American edition would fail because Americans could not follow the argument
context: Keynes's June 28, 1944 letter was warm about the book's moral warning against comprehensive planning while disagreeing with Hayek about where exactly to draw the line between legitimate state action and the road to servitude. The letter shows the Hayek-Keynes personal relationship survived their 1930s public warfare -- and is one of the surprising documents of 20th-century economics. Source: Lionel Page on X (https://x.com/page_eco/status/1826581296686215338).

question: The new leader of the British Conservative party walked into a research-department meeting in 1975. By a story her own foundation warns may be too neat to be true, she drew Friedrich Hayek's longer book of 1960 out of her handbag, slammed it onto the table and told her staff, 'This is what we believe.' What does this moment show about how politics changes?
answer: A political party can be reshaped when a leader takes a set of ideas seriously
choices: A political party can be reshaped when a leader takes a set of ideas seriously
A political party changes course only when its voters demand it first
A political party is reshaped by economic crises, not by books
A political party follows its research staff, who set the leader's agenda
context: Margaret Thatcher, elected Leader of the Opposition in 1975, made this celebrated Conservative Research Department gesture that summer. She had first read The Road to Serfdom as a student at Oxford in the 1940s; The Constitution of Liberty (1960) was the longer, denser book, and her governments from 1979 drew on Hayek's ideas.
