Source: Sotheby's, 'This Is What We Believe: Margaret Thatcher and F. A. Hayek' (https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/this-is-what-we-believe-margaret-thatcher-and-f-a-hayek).

question: A thoughtful critic reopens Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom, wanting to state its argument fairly before he accepts or rejects it. He sets the book's reputation aside and looks for the single reasoning move inside it. Which move does the book actually press?
answer: That comprehensive planning needs ever more coercion to override the choices it directs
choices: That comprehensive planning needs ever more coercion to override the choices it directs
That any government intervention in a market economy is inherently immoral
That socialist parties are always more corrupt than conservative parties
That planned economies must eventually fall behind capitalist economies in GDP
context: The book's argument is NOT that 'socialism is evil' or that any planner is corrupt; it is that COMPREHENSIVE planning -- because it must override countless individual choices about jobs, prices, production, and consumption -- inescapably needs progressively more coercive power to enforce its plan. Hayek believed the Weimar-to-Nazi path illustrated the mechanism; the student can accept or reject the argument, but the book's actual move is the coercion-follows-planning claim, not a verdict on any single party. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Road to Serfdom.'

question: A soldier on the Rhine took his wages in one small silver coin, and a baker at Ostia made change with the same coin. Rome first struck it around 211 BC, during the Second Punic War, and it carried one name for more than four centuries. What was this coin called?
answer: The denarius
choices: The denarius
The sestertius
The aureus
The drachma
context: The denarius circulated from about 211 BC through the third century AD, roughly 98% silver under Augustus (27 BC - 14 AD). Source: Grokipedia 'Denarius' (2026-09-05).

question: One Roman emperor ordered the first big cut to the silver in Rome's trusted coin in 64 AD. He needed the money to rebuild the city after the Great Fire and to pay for his own lavish spending. Which emperor was it?
answer: Nero
choices: Nero
Augustus
Trajan
Marcus Aurelius
context: Nero's 64 AD debasement cut the silver content from about 98% to about 93% and slightly reduced coin weight. The recovered silver funded reconstruction and imperial expenses. Source: Grokipedia 'Roman currency' (2026-09-05).

question: The emperor Gallienus paid huge armies to hold the frontier in the 250s and 260s, in a coin that had been almost pure silver under Augustus. For two centuries the mints had quietly shaved silver out of it and mixed in cheap copper, until a thin silver wash covered the base metal. About what percent silver was left?
answer: About 5%
choices: About 5%
About 40%
About 75%
About 90%
context: By the reign of Gallienus (253-268 AD) the denarius was essentially a bronze coin with a thin silver wash that flaked off in circulation. The empire's currency had lost roughly 95% of its original silver content over two centuries. Source: Grokipedia 'Roman currency' (2026-09-05).

question: An emperor's court spent the fresh, thinner coins first, at their old full face value. By the time they reached a shopkeeper in a country town, prices had risen and each bought less bread or cloth than before. Austrian economists say this quietly moves wealth from ordinary savers to whoever spends the new money first. What kind of tax do they call it?
answer: A hidden tax on money holders
choices: A hidden tax on money holders
A progressive tax on income
A tariff on foreign goods
A wealth tax on land
context: Debasement transfers purchasing power from every existing coin holder to the sovereign who spends the new dilute coins first, without ever passing a visible tax. The mechanism is invisible to the population being taxed. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: Diocletian faced runaway prices around 301 AD, after generations of rulers had shrunk the silver in Rome's coins until each bought less bread, wine and cloth. Instead of fixing the money, he issued the Edict on Maximum Prices, threatening death for anyone who sold above a legal ceiling. What comes of a cap stacked on money already cheapened?
answer: Shortages and black markets, because the underlying debasement is untouched
choices: Shortages and black markets, because the underlying debasement is untouched
Immediate price convergence to the legal ceiling
A voluntary drop in real wages sufficient to clear markets
Increased legal-market production and reduced smuggling
context: Price controls treat a symptom (rising prices) while leaving the cause (money-supply expansion) in place. The visible outcome is shortages and informal exchange, not stability. Source: Rothbard, What Has Government Done to Our Money (1963).

question: Diocletian capped Roman prices by decree, after centuries of emperors had quietly shrunk the silver in their coins so they could spend more without raising taxes. Austrian economists say the same pattern, thin the money first and then cap prices, shows up again and again. Which modern American case do they call a textbook rerun of the Roman story?
answer: Nixon's 1971 wage and price freeze on top of dollar debasement
choices: Nixon's 1971 wage and price freeze on top of dollar debasement
The 1944 Bretton Woods dollar-gold peg
Britain's 1717 informal move to the gold standard
The 1980s Volcker disinflation
context: Richard Nixon on August 15 1971 closed the gold window and simultaneously imposed a 90-day wage and price freeze, layering price controls on top of monetary expansion in the exact Diocletian shape. Same debasement + same controls + same shortages. Source: Grokipedia 'Nixon shock' (2026-09-05).

question: A grocer in Caracas was prosecuted for charging more than the legal price of food, while the central bank printed money on an enormous scale from 2013. The shelves emptied and millions of people left the country. Austrian economists call it the old Roman pattern run almost step for step. Whose price ceilings were these?
answer: Nicolas Maduro's government
choices: Nicolas Maduro's government
Augusto Pinochet's junta
Getulio Vargas's Estado Novo
Juan Peron's second presidency
context: The Maduro government's price controls on food, medicine, and consumer goods -- alongside heavy Reserve Bank money printing -- produced empty supermarkets, wheelbarrows of cash, and mass emigration. The Diocletian pattern replayed in real time. Source: Grokipedia 'Economic policy of the Nicolas Maduro government' (2026-09-05).

question: Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises gave Austrian economists one way to read an old script: debase the money, then punish shopkeepers for the prices that follow. An emperor cheapened Rome's silver coin in the 60s AD, and a government ordered supermarket price controls in the 2010s while the bolivar collapsed. What single recognition move sits at the heart of that reading?
answer: Prices are signals, not the thing itself; suppressing the signal does not fix the cause
choices: Prices are signals, not the thing itself; suppressing the signal does not fix the cause
Governments always intervene to reduce prices when necessary
Currency debasement is always corrected by market discovery
Black markets naturally disappear when governments enforce controls
context: The Hayekian point extended: prices communicate what is scarce and what is abundant. Legal ceilings that suppress prices below market-clearing levels destroy the signal without removing the scarcity. The scarcity moves to black markets or empty shelves. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945).

question: A Dominican friar at Salamanca handed his students a puzzle: silver arriving from the Americas a shipload at a time, and prices climbing to match. He held the chair there until he died in 1546 and is counted the founder of the School of Salamanca. Who was he?
answer: Francisco de Vitoria
choices: Francisco de Vitoria
Thomas Aquinas
Duns Scotus
Bartolome de Las Casas
context: Francisco de Vitoria (1483-1546) led the Salamanca faculty during the crucial New-World-collision decades of the 1530s and 1540s. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Francisco_de_Vitoria.

question: A priest teaching at Salamanca was writing a handbook for confessors in 1556 when he set down a rule about money: goods run cheap where money is scarce and dear where it is plentiful. His students called him Doctor Navarrus. What was his real name?
answer: Martin de Azpilcueta
choices: Martin de Azpilcueta
Luis de Molina
Domingo de Soto
Tomas de Mercado
context: Martin de Azpilcueta (1491-1586), also called Doctor Navarrus, wrote Manual de Confesores y Penitentes (1556), which contains the earliest clean statement of the quantity theory of money. His 1556 Commentary on the Resolution of Money linked the arrival of American bullion to rising Spanish prices, roughly 220 years before Adam Smith. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: Silver poured into Spain in the 1500s from one great mountain of ore high in the Andes, and a theologian at Salamanca saw Spanish prices roughly double inside his own working life. Which mine did the silver come from?
answer: Potosi
choices: Potosi
Zacatecas
Cerro de Pasco
Guanajuato
context: The Cerro Rico mine at Potosi (in modern Bolivia) was the largest source of the Spanish silver that flooded Iberian markets after 1545. Azpilcueta traced the price rise directly to that inflow. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: Milton Friedman compressed a finding into one famous line in 1963. Austrians enjoy noting that a Salamanca priest's handbook for confessors had reached the same finding in 1556, after American silver doubled Spanish prices. Which line of Friedman's had the priest beaten by four centuries?
answer: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon
choices: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon
There is no such thing as a free lunch
Only government can create true monopoly
The natural rate of unemployment is exogenous
context: Friedman's famous dictum restated the same insight Azpilcueta had made four hundred years earlier while writing a confessor's manual. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Martin_de_Azpilcueta.

question: A Jesuit of the Salamanca school took up the question of what makes a price just, in six volumes that came out from 1593 to 1609. Not the work or expense that went into a thing, he argued, but whatever buyers and sellers freely agree on in an ordinary market. Who was he?
answer: Luis de Molina
choices: Luis de Molina
Francisco Suarez
Robert Bellarmine
Domingo Banez
context: Luis de Molina's De Iustitia et Iure (1593-1609) argued the just price is the price willing buyers and willing sellers would trade at in a normally functioning market, an early subjective-value move that anticipated Menger 1871. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Luis_de_Molina.

question: Murray Rothbard published a two-volume history of economic thought in 1995 to fix a story that starts with Adam Smith in 1776, as if no one before Smith had reasoned carefully about prices and money. Which group did his volumes put back into the story?
answer: Medieval scholars who studied prices and money in monasteries and universities
choices: Medieval scholars who studied prices and money in monasteries and universities
Ancient Egyptian tax officials who ran the pharaoh's grain stores
Chinese silk-road merchants who first invented paper receipts
British factory owners of the 1800s industrial towns
context: Rothbard's An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought (2 vols, Edward Elgar, 1995) argued that the classical story starting with Adam Smith in 1776 had overwritten the earlier Salamanca contributions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/An_Austrian_Perspective_on_the_History_of_Economic_Thought.

question: Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776, and the standard textbook starts the story of economics there. Spanish priests taught and wrote at Salamanca in the 1500s. What does their work show about that story?
answer: Market ideas were being worked out for centuries before they became famous in English
choices: Market ideas were being worked out for centuries before they became famous in English
Adam Smith invented every economic idea from scratch by himself
Nobody thought seriously about money at all before the year 1700
Spanish scholars in the 1500s had no interest in trade or prices
context: Rothbard's 1995 An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought traced pre-classical economics back to the Salamancans and the medieval scholastics, undoing the Smith-as-founder story. Grice-Hutchinson's The School of Salamanca: Readings in Spanish Monetary Theory 1544-1605 (Oxford, 1952) was the first major English-language scholarly recovery of the tradition, from which Rothbard and Chafuen later drew. Source: mises.org/library/austrian-perspective-history-economic-thought; grokipedia.com/page/Marjorie_Grice-Hutchinson.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock set out in the 1960s to study senators, agency staff and city clerks as economists study shopkeepers. A senator wants re-election money; an agency chief wants a bigger budget. What was the main idea of the public choice economics they built?
answer: People in government act on incentives like everyone else
choices: People in government act on incentives like everyone else
People in government always put the public first
Voters always pick the best leaders
Bigger government always means better results
context: MacLean's book, 'Democracy in Chains: The Deep History of the Radical Right's Stealth Plan for America,' was published by Viking. It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist that year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: Nancy MacLean argued in Democracy in Chains, in 2017, that the Nobel-winning economist James Buchanan had led a hidden right-wing project against American democracy. Many economists and historians disputed the claim on sourcing grounds. Even so, major book-industry institutions gave the book prominent recognition. Which of these did it earn?
answer: It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist
choices: It was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist
It received the Pulitzer Prize for History in 2018
It was awarded the National Humanities Medal in 2019
It was chosen as the Book of the Year by the Financial Times
context: The mainstream-media reception shaped Buchanan's public image in the months after publication. That reception drove the intensity of the scholarly rebuttal that followed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: Alain Marciano and Jean-Baptiste Fleury took Nancy MacLean's Democracy in Chains apart line by line in December 2018. Her book had argued that the work of James Buchanan, the Nobel-winning co-founder of public choice, was really a secret plot against democracy for wealthy donors. Their long rebuttal ran in one of the field's top journals. Which journal published it?
answer: The Journal of Economic Literature
choices: The Journal of Economic Literature
The American Economic Review
The Journal of Political Economy
The Quarterly Journal of Economics
context: The essay, 'The Sound of Silence: A Review Essay of Nancy MacLean's Democracy in Chains,' was written by Jean-Baptiste Fleury and Alain Marciano. It is often cited as the definitive scholarly response. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: Michael Munger read the footnotes of Nancy MacLean's 2017 book Democracy in Chains, which accused the Nobel economist James Buchanan of a secret plot for wealthy donors. Peter Boettke, Fleury and Marciano, and Bernstein and Adler pushed back on her method too, and all of them landed on one specific charge about how she had treated Buchanan's writings and letters. What was the charge?
answer: That MacLean quoted Buchanan and his correspondents systematically out of context
choices: That MacLean quoted Buchanan and his correspondents systematically out of context
That MacLean invented fictional interviews with living historians
That MacLean plagiarized substantial portions from a rival author's work
That MacLean failed to disclose funding from a partisan advocacy group
context: Several key quotations were shown to reverse the actual meaning of Buchanan's writing; the alleged Buchanan-segregationist connection was not supported by the archival record MacLean cited. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: A high-school student sets two bodies of work side by side. One is Nancy MacLean's Democracy in Chains of 2017, which won the praise of the press and reached the National Book Award finals, arguing that James Buchanan's public-choice work was a secret plot for wealthy donors. The other is the stack of long rebuttals that scholars across the ideological spectrum wrote in reply, all pointing at the same quotation problems. What broader lesson does the pair teach about intellectual-history writing?
answer: When a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across ideological lines, that pattern is itself diagnostic
choices: When a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across ideological lines, that pattern is itself diagnostic
Any book on a Nobel-winning economist should be treated as automatically true
Any book criticized by libertarians must be presumed to be correct
Any book that reaches the National Book Award finals cannot contain systematic errors
context: The MacLean case is not one of 'both sides disagree.' Non-libertarian scholars who knew the primary sources (Munger, Fleury, Marciano) documented consistent misrepresentation. The pattern of rebuttal from experts across ideological lines is the relevant epistemic signal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Democracy_in_Chains.

question: George H.W. Bush signed the Clean Air Act Amendments in November 1990, and with them a pioneering market in pollution rights. Power plants got a fixed number of allowances they could buy and sell. Which pollutant did those allowances cover?
answer: Sulfur dioxide
choices: Sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen oxides
Particulate matter
context: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments created a cap-and-trade market in sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions from coal-fired power plants. It was the first large national environmental market of its kind. Source: epa.gov (Acid Rain Program history).

question: Ronald Coase wrote in 1960 about smoke and neighbours, and his thinking led, decades later, to a new way to fight sulfur pollution. A regulator could order every coal plant to fit the same scrubber. Instead the 1990 law let plants buy and sell permits, so that cheap cleaners sold their spares to expensive cleaners. What did that trading put to work that regulators in an office could not gather?
answer: The dispersed knowledge utilities have about their own abatement costs
choices: The dispersed knowledge utilities have about their own abatement costs
The consumer preference rankings of household electricity buyers
The private lobbying strategies of trade associations
The confidential financial ratios of individual firms
context: Coase's insight: no central regulator can know every utility's marginal abatement cost. A market in emission rights routes reductions to whoever can achieve them cheapest -- using dispersed knowledge no bureaucrat can gather. Source: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics (October 1960). The Hayek-adjacent knowledge-problem insight: cheap abatement information is dispersed across thousands of plants and cannot be gathered centrally. A market in emissions permits routes the information into the allocation via prices. Source: Coase (1960); Hayek AER (1945) as background.

question: A clean-air planner opens the 1960 paper by Ronald Coase, who won the Nobel Prize in 1991, and weighs how to write her rule. Coase's readers tell her the real choice is not 'rules versus no rules,' since either way she is regulating. What is the actual choice?
answer: Command-and-control versus property-rights-plus-trading
choices: Command-and-control versus property-rights-plus-trading
Federal versus state jurisdiction
Public versus private ownership
Voluntary compliance versus criminal enforcement
context: Both are forms of regulation. Command-and-control tells firms which technology to use; property-rights + trading sets a cap on total emissions and creates a market in the right to emit. The second uses dispersed knowledge; the first assumes the regulator has it. Source: Coase (1960); Ellerman + Joskow (2000).

question: Henry Waxman of California and Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote a bill in 2009 for a national market in carbon dioxide permits, with most of the permits handed to companies instead of sold at auction. Lobbyists fought one another over who would receive them. The bill passed the House but died in the Senate. What weakness of such a market did the lobbyists' scramble show?
answer: Free-permit allocation attracts rent-seeking capture
choices: Free-permit allocation attracts rent-seeking capture
Permit prices swing too wildly for firms to plan ahead
Auctioned permits push heavy industry to move abroad
Permit trading cannot measure each plant's emissions
context: Who gets the free initial allowances (rather than buying at auction) is a rent-seeking prize in the Tullock 1967 sense. Waxman-Markey allocated most permits free to incumbents, and the fight over the allocation was fierce; the bill never came to a Senate vote. Source: Tullock (1967) applied; Congressional Research Service (Waxman-Markey history).

question: An Austrian economist sat down in Vienna in 1920 to answer the people saying socialism would soon replace the market. Where the government owns every farm and factory, he wrote, no one trades, so no real prices exist and no one can compare the cost of one plan against another. Who was he?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Rudolf Hilferding
Joseph Schumpeter
Werner Sombart
context: 'Die Wirtschaftsrechnung im sozialistischen Gemeinwesen' appeared in Archiv fuer Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik volume 47, 1920. Mises first delivered the argument at the Nationaloekonomische Gesellschaft in 1919. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Calculation_in_the_Socialist_Commonwealth.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that a planned economy could not compare costs without market prices, and other economists fired back. A forty-year argument followed, with the Austrians on his side and Oskar Lange and his allies on the other. What is this famous fight usually called?
answer: The socialist calculation debate
choices: The Cambridge capital controversy
The socialist calculation debate
The Methodenstreit
The Keynes-Hayek exchange
context: The phrase covers the entire arc from Mises 1920 through the 1930s Lange-Lerner reply, Hayek's 1935 volume and 1945 essay, Mises's 1949 Human Action restatement, and the empirical verdict in 1989. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: Oskar Lange, a Polish economist then at Chicago, took up a big charge in the 1930s: that socialism could not work with no real prices. His fix was a planning office that set prices by trial and error, raising them when shortages hit and lowering them when a surplus appeared. What was his big claim?
answer: Central planners can copy what markets do for prices
choices: Central planners can copy what markets do for prices
Central planning is impossible in principle
Central planners can do without prices altogether
Central planners can set every price by labour hours
context: Oskar Ryszard Lange (1904-1965) taught statistics and economics at Chicago from 1938 to 1945; after the war he returned to Poland to serve its Stalinist government and try to prove his ideas in practice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_R._Lange.

question: Friedrich Hayek answered Oskar Lange's guess-and-check planning board in a short essay of 1945. Lange had argued that such a board could guess prices and adjust them like a market, and Hayek granted that this could work on paper. But he said it missed something markets do that planners cannot copy at all. Which ability did Hayek give to markets alone?
answer: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
choices: Aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds
Enforcing binding property rights against politically-connected insiders
Predicting long-run structural shifts in industry composition
Maintaining stable purchasing power across the business cycle
context: The market process is not primarily a calculating device; it is a knowledge-discovery device. The 'knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- who has a spare truck, which mine seam thinned out, which customer is ready to try a substitute -- exists only in the heads of the people on the spot. Prices summarise it. Source: fee.org/articles/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/.

question: Ludwig von Mises restated his case in a thousand-page book in New York in 1949, and for decades mainstream economists still thought Oskar Lange's guess-and-check board had beaten him on paper. Austrian economists said no, but had to wait on history. What single event in November 1989 made even friendly mainstream economists reopen the question?
answer: The fall of the Berlin Wall
choices: The signing of the Maastricht Treaty
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The Plaza Accord devaluation of the dollar
The passage of the Single European Act
context: On November 9 1989 East German official Guenter Schabowski, at a press conference, mistakenly announced immediate opening of the border; the wall was breached that night. Within two years every planned economy in Eastern Europe had collapsed and begun a market transition. Source: www.archives.gov/news/topics/berlin-wall-anniversary.

question: Robert Heilbroner, a long-time socialist who had spent decades defending planning, wrote a magazine essay in 1990. He admitted that the free-market side of the 1920 planning debate had turned out to be right, though his own bestselling history of economics had once left Ludwig von Mises out altogether. What does this admission show?
answer: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
choices: Even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions
Even a winning argument needs a famous convert before the public will listen
Even a lost debate can be won back by rewriting the history books later
Even an expert's party loyalty decides how he reads the evidence in the end
context: The line was: 'It turns out, of course, that Mises was right.' Heilbroner (1919-2005) had held the Norman Thomas chair at the New School and had, in the 1953 first edition of 'The Worldly Philosophers', omitted Mises, Hayek and Friedman entirely. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right.

question: Don Lavoie set the two halves of the Austrian case side by side in 1985. Ludwig von Mises had argued that central planners could not calculate without real market prices. Friedrich Hayek had pushed further: hand planners every price, and they still could not gather what a miner or a lorry driver picks up on the spot. What one objection did Lavoie see in the two?
answer: The knowledge problem: no central office can gather the scattered facts behind daily choices
choices: The knowledge problem: no central office can gather the scattered facts behind daily choices
The incentive problem: planners and managers gain nothing by using resources well
The scale problem: no machine of the day could solve so many equations at once
The coercion problem: a plan can be carried out only by forcing people to obey
context: Don Lavoie (1951-2001) set out this reading in Rivalry and Central Planning and its companion National Economic Planning: What Is Left? (both 1985), arguing that the standard account had wrongly split Mises's argument from Hayek's. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: A Soviet clerk wrote an abbreviation on a prisoner's papers, the short form of the Russian name for the Main Camp Administration. The camps it ran held people arrested for a careless joke, cutting timber and mining ore in killing cold across Siberia. What was the abbreviation?
answer: Gulag
choices: Gulag
Kolkhoz
Duma
Politburo
context: Glavnoye Upravleniye Lagerei (Main Camp Administration) ran the Soviet camp system. At its peak it comprised over 400 camps and held several million prisoners at any given moment. Anne Applebaum's Gulag: A History (2003) drew on the newly opened Soviet archives.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, once a camp prisoner himself, kept his manuscript hidden from the secret police and had it smuggled west on tiny rolls of film. It came out in Paris from 1973, for Western readers who had heard the Soviet camps were a small stain. What did it chiefly reveal?
answer: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
choices: The vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings
That the camps all closed for good after Stalin's death
That the camps had been run without Moscow's knowledge
That most prisoners were spies caught in the war
context: The Gulag Archipelago combined Solzhenitsyn's own eight years in the camps (1945-53), after his arrest for a private letter mocking Stalin, with hundreds of survivor accounts he had collected. It was published in Paris in three volumes, 1973-75; the English translation appeared 1974-78.

question: Soviet leaders struck at Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn in February 1974. Two months earlier the first volume of his account of the camps had come out in Paris, from a manuscript smuggled out of the country. What did they do to him?
answer: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
choices: Stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt
Sentenced him to a new 15-year camp term
Placed him under indefinite house arrest in Moscow
Sent him to internal exile in Kazakhstan
context: Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the USSR on February 13, 1974. He lived in Vermont from 1976 to 1994 and returned to Russia in May 1994 after the USSR's fall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Solzhenitsyn.

question: Anne Applebaum worked through the Soviet archives opened after 1991 to write the first full history of the camps in English, published in 2003 and awarded the Pulitzer Prize. She totalled the prisoners sent into the camps between 1930 and Stalin's death in 1953. Roughly how many were there?
answer: About 18 million
choices: About 18 million
About 1.8 million
About 180,000
About 180 million
context: About 18 million prisoners passed through the Gulag between 1930 and 1953, with roughly 1.5-1.7 million documented camp deaths. Applebaum's Gulag: A History (Doubleday, 2003), drawn from the newly opened Soviet archives, won the 2004 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. Further mortality in the deportation-settlement system for kulaks and deported peoples adds to the associated total.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn collected the stories of more than two hundred former prisoners after his own eight years in the camps, which followed his 1945 arrest for mocking Stalin in a private letter. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970 and mapped the whole camp system, region by region, in three volumes. What is the work called?
answer: The Gulag Archipelago
choices: The Gulag Archipelago
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
Cancer Ward
The First Circle
context: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1970 cited 'the ethical force with which he has pursued the indispensable traditions of Russian literature'. Solzhenitsyn could not travel to accept in Stockholm and finally received the medal at the 1974 Nobel ceremony after his expulsion. Source: nobelprize.org (Solzhenitsyn 1970).

question: Bernard-Henri Levy and Andre Glucksmann, two Paris thinkers who had come up on the left, turned publicly against Marxism once they had read Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's three volumes on the Soviet camps. They and their circle began saying aloud that such regimes produce camps, not paradise. What did the French press call the group?
answer: The Nouveaux Philosophes
choices: The Nouveaux Philosophes
The New Left
The Frankfurt School
The Situationists
context: The Nouveaux Philosophes (New Philosophers) -- Andre Glucksmann, Bernard-Henri Levy, and others -- publicly renounced Marxism partly under the impact of Solzhenitsyn's book. The moment marked the French intellectual left's break with communist theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouveaux_philosophes.

question: Thomas Sowell went after a group he called the anointed in The Vision of the Anointed, in 1995: people in universities, newspapers and government who, he said, treat their own good intentions as proof of success. The book's subtitle named the habit outright. What was it?
answer: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
choices: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
Ideological Origins of Political Struggles
A Common Sense Guide to the Economy
The Decline, the Deception, the Dogmas
context: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (Basic Books, 1995). The three rejected subtitles are also Sowell's own: A Conflict of Visions (1987), Basic Economics, and Inside American Education. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thomas Sowell' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sowell).

question: Thomas Sowell opened his 2010 book on intellectuals by refusing the everyday meaning of the word. He did not mean a clever person, and he did not mean a person with degrees. His definition was narrower than that, and it turned on the job itself. Whom did he count as an intellectual?
answer: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
choices: Someone whose occupational output is ideas themselves
Someone who holds a university post in the humanities
Someone who advises governments on questions of policy
Someone whose writing reaches a large popular audience
context: Sowell's phrase is that 'an intellectual's work begins and ends with ideas, not the practical application of ideas to real world problems.' The narrowness is deliberate and load-bearing: it is what lets him make the accountability argument later in the book, and it is why a surgeon or an engineer, however brilliant, is not an intellectual while doing his own job. Intellectuals and Society (Basic Books, January 5, 2010); a Revised and Expanded Edition followed in 2011.

question: A politician proclaims a crisis and backs a remedy promising result A, while critics warn it will produce result Z, and result Z arrives. Thomas Sowell set out that pattern in The Vision of the Anointed, and he gave it a fourth stage. What did he say that stage looks like?
answer: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
choices: The remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause
The remedy is quietly repealed and its authors move on to a fresh crisis
Congress commissions an independent review that settles the disagreement
The critics are invited to draft the replacement legislation themselves
context: Sowell's line on stage four: 'No burden of proof whatever is put on those who had so confidently predicted improvement.' The champions may also argue that things would have been worse still without the remedy -- a claim that cannot be checked, and is not offered to be checked. Source: Mises Institute, 'How The Vision of the Anointed Explains Every Crisis in America' (https://mises.org/power-market/how-vision-anointed-explains-every-crisis-america).

question: Suppose a political campaign wants the government to pay back all groups for wrongs done to their ancestors, so that outcomes finally come out even. Thomas Sowell, in The Quest for Cosmic Justice of 1999, called the wish behind such a plan decent. Still, he objected. Which objection did he press hardest?
answer: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
choices: That nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice
That voters would never approve the taxes such a programme has to raise
That the agencies running the programme would capture most of the money
That courts, not legislatures, must settle questions of historical wrong
context: This is Hayek's knowledge problem carried into the moral realm: redressing disadvantage across ethnicities, generations and geographies would require knowing what every group's circumstances actually were and what each owes the others -- knowledge that is scattered, contested and in most cases gone. The rejected choices are real objections too (public choice, regulatory capture, constitutional), but they are not Sowell's move here.

question: A battle commander misjudges one moment and pays with his own life. Thomas Sowell set the intellectual beside that commander, and beside a surgeon and an engineer, and said an intellectual's work is judged by a very different test. Whose vote decides if an intellectual has done well?
answer: The peers who read the work and praise it
choices: The peers who read the work and praise it
The voters who elect politicians who adopt it
The publishers and editors who paid for it
The students who are taught it at university
context: Sowell's point is not that intellectuals are stupid or wicked; it is that the feedback loop that disciplines a surgeon or a bridge-builder is missing. Ideas are judged by whether they sound good to other people in the same trade. Whether they 'make life better or worse for others', Sowell writes, 'is another question entirely.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: A headline announces a crisis: urgent, unbearable, requiring immediate action. Thomas Sowell's complaint about that moment, in his 1995 book, was not about the suffering described. It was that one particular check almost never gets run before the crisis is declared. Which check?
answer: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
choices: Whether the trouble had already been getting better for years
Whether a foreign country has already tried the proposed remedy
Whether the people affected were ever asked what they wanted
Whether the money to pay for the remedy exists anywhere at all
context: Sowell's wording: such a situation is 'routinely characterized as a crisis, even though all human situations have negative aspects, and even though evidence is seldom asked or given to show how the situation at hand is either uniquely bad or threatening to get worse. Sometimes the situation described as a crisis has in fact already been getting better for years.' A remedy introduced onto an improving trend can then claim credit for the trend.

question: Thomas Sowell pressed one case hardest in his charge that intellectuals pay no price for being wrong. British intellectuals campaigned on a question of national defence in the 1930s, and in his telling the country paid for their position within the decade. Which way did they campaign?
answer: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
choices: Against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed
For handing the navy's budget to the new air force
For a defence union with France and the Low Countries
Against keeping a garrison east of the Suez Canal
context: Sowell's wider claim in Intellectuals and Society is that during the twentieth century intellectuals 'have on balance made the world a worse and more dangerous place', often lending support to dictators. The interwar British case is his cleanest illustration of the accountability gap: none of the writers who argued against rearming lost their standing when the war came. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intellectuals and Society'.

question: An engineer publishes brilliant papers on bridge design, and by Thomas Sowell's test he is still not working as an intellectual when he designs bridges. Sowell's 2010 book Intellectuals and Society gave the word an unusually narrow meaning, tied to what a person's work turns out at the end. Why does the engineer fall outside it?
answer: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
choices: Because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls
Because he is paid by a firm rather than by a university
Because bridge design rests on physics rather than argument
Because he publishes for other engineers, not for the public
context: The test is not the subject matter, the employer or the audience -- it is whether the work terminates in ideas or in something the world can break. This is why Sowell's definition matters for the argument: the same person can be an intellectual on Tuesday, writing on social policy, and not one on Wednesday, signing off a span.

question: A campaigner defends a proposal by saying that all the experts agree with it, so obviously the country should do what they say. Thomas Sowell's 2010 book Intellectuals and Society is about the feedback a job gives the people who do it, and it turns that appeal into a question the listener ought to ask back. What is the question?
answer: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
choices: Which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong?
Which experts, and who paid for the studies they are citing?
How many experts disagree, and where has their work appeared?
How long have the experts held this view, and what changed it?
context: The rejected questions are worth asking too -- funding, dissent, and the history of a consensus all bear on it. But Sowell's specific contribution is the accountability question, because it sorts experts by the one variable his definition isolates: whether being wrong costs them anything. An epidemiologist, an actuary and a bridge engineer answer it very differently.

question: Thomas Sowell described in 1995 what policy elites do, and in 2010 he asked why they could keep doing it, decade after decade, without the pattern ever breaking. His explanation was structural rather than a claim about anyone's character. What was it?
answer: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
choices: Nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false
Their credentials shield them from having to argue with outsiders
The press shares their politics and declines to report the failures
Voters forget quickly and rarely reopen an argument about old policy
context: This is the spine of the trilogy: The Vision of the Anointed (1995) records the pattern, The Quest for Cosmic Justice (1999) examines the standard that licenses it, and Intellectuals and Society (2010) supplies the mechanism. Note what the argument does not claim -- not that the anointed are dishonest, and not that their conclusions are always wrong. It claims that the occupation carries no cost for being wrong, so nothing in it corrects the error. A reader can accept the mechanism and still disagree with Sowell about any particular policy.

question: A Paris reader opened the Journal des Débats on September 25, 1848, while the new provisional government was promising programme after programme, and found inside the sentence Frédéric Bastiat is best remembered for. What does it say about where a government's handouts come from?
answer: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
choices: Every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else
Government can print free money for everyone
Government workers pay their own salaries
Government spending never requires taxes
context: The essay 'The State' (L'Etat) appeared in near-final form in the Journal des Debats on September 25, 1848 after a shorter draft had run in Bastiat's own revolutionary paper Jacques Bonhomme in June. It was reprinted as a booklet by Guillaumin later the same year. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: '... the great ______ by which everyone seeks to live at the expense of everyone else,' Frédéric Bastiat wrote of government in September 1848. It became the most quoted line he ever wrote. Which word fills the blank?
answer: fiction
choices: fiction
leviathan
machine
market
context: The French original reads 'L'Etat, c'est la grande fiction a travers laquelle tout le monde s'efforce de vivre aux depens de tout le monde.' The Dean Russell English translation renders 'grande fiction' as 'great fictitious entity,' but 'great fiction' is the version that circulates in almost every 20th-century classical-liberal citation. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/frederic-bastiat-on-the-state-as-the-great-fiction-by-which-everyone-seeks-to-live-at-the-expense-of-everyone-else-1848.

question: Frédéric Bastiat opened an essay of September 1848 with a mock reward of a million francs, crowns, crosses and ribbons thrown in, for whoever could define one word clearly and honestly. Then he sent in his own entry, a jab at living at everyone else's expense. Which word did the reward hang on?
answer: The word 'the State'
choices: The word 'the State'
The word 'liberty'
The word 'property'
The word 'the People'
context: The essay opens: 'I would like to see a prize founded, not of five hundred francs, but of a million, with crowns, crosses and ribbons, for the person who gives a good, simple and intelligible definition of this word: the State.' The mock contest was rhetorical -- Bastiat never had to pay out because, as he framed it, no non-mystical definition could avoid collapsing into the transfer-shape his own line named. Source: https://www.panarchy.org/bastiat/state.1848.html.

question: France's voters sent Frédéric Bastiat to the Constituent Assembly in April 1848, and that September he wrote that everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else. The line reaches the ballot box as well as the purse. What does it say about voting and public spending?
answer: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
choices: Voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors
Voters can lower taxes just by voting for more spending
Governments always spend money on exactly the right things
Every citizen already produces enough to fund all programs
context: Jacques Bonhomme was Bastiat's short-lived revolutionary paper founded during the 1848 Paris moment; a draft of 'The State' ran there in June 1848 before the fuller version appeared in the Journal des Debats on September 25. 'Jacques Bonhomme' is the traditional French nickname for the rural common man -- the audience Bastiat pitched the essay to. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: Frédéric Bastiat aimed his essay of September 1848 at one particular room. Paris had risen in revolution that year, and a provisional government was promising new programmes. He printed the essay in the Journal des Débats, one of the city's leading dailies, to reach one slice of French society. Which readership was that?
answer: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
choices: The liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership
The Bonapartist Catholic peasantry
The Marxist Parisian workers' clubs
The Legitimist rural nobility
context: The Journal des Debats was historically the paper of liberal-Orleanist bourgeois opinion under Louis-Philippe and remained an influential centrist daily under the Second Republic. Bastiat chose it deliberately -- his target reader was the propertied liberal, not the barricade fighter. Source: https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/bastiat-and-the-state.

question: Frédéric Bastiat took a seat on one committee of France's Constituent Assembly in 1848, the year he wrote his line about everyone living at the expense of everyone else, and he was re-elected its vice-chairman again and again. Which committee was it?
answer: The finance committee
choices: The finance committee
The judiciary committee
The military committee
The colonial committee
context: Bastiat served on the Constituent Assembly's finance committee through 1848-1849 -- the committee handling the tax and spending questions his 'great fiction' line directly framed. Tocqueville, elected the same April, served in the Assembly as well and would soon join the government as foreign minister. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Bastiat.

question: Carl Menger broke with Adam Smith and David Ricardo in Vienna in the early 1870s. They had held that a good is worth the work poured into it: ten hours of labor should sell for double five hours'. Where did Menger say a thing's value comes from?
answer: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
choices: From how much the person choosing it wants it right now
From how many hours the worker spent making it
From how much the raw materials cost
From the average price it usually sells for
context: Menger's move was to relocate value from the OBJECT to the SUBJECT: the same loaf of bread ranks high to a hungry man and low to a full one, so value is not a property of the loaf. The labor theory (Smith 1776, Ricardo 1817, Marx 1867) had made value inhere in the good; Menger, Jevons, and Walras all replaced it in 1871-1874 with subjective valuation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book); mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Carl Menger refused to count mountain air and seawater as economic goods, though both meet real human wants. Nobody is ever forced to weigh one breath of mountain air against the next. On Menger's account, what must be true of a good before a chooser has to rank it?
answer: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
choices: The good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy
The good must have taken labor to produce
The good must be legally recognized as property
The good must have a market price above zero
context: For Menger, an unlimited good has utility but no VALUE, because no chooser is ever forced to give up one use to serve another -- there is no ranking at the margin. Only when the good is scarce relative to the wants it could satisfy does a chooser have to rank the marginal unit, and only then does the subjective theory generate a price. Labor-cost, legal recognition, and positive market price are consequences of scarcity, not its cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Menger.

question: A tailor spends 10 hours making a badly-cut, badly-sewn suit that hangs poorly. A second tailor spends 5 hours making a well-cut, well-sewn suit that fits beautifully. On the labor theory of value the first suit should be worth about twice the second. On the subjective theory that Menger pressed against the classical tradition, which comparison actually holds?
answer: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth more, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
choices: The well-made 5-hour suit is worth more, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher
The two suits are worth the same, because labor is labor
The 10-hour suit is still worth more, because it embodies more work
Neither suit has any value until a market price is quoted
context: This is the sharp edge of Menger's move against the labor theory: labor-hours cannot GENERATE value if a chooser ranks the badly-made product lower. Value flows one way only, from the ranking down to the price; labor spent producing something no one ranks highly is labor wasted, not value created. If the labor theory cannot survive this simple case, then Marx's entire theory of surplus value and exploitation -- built on the labor theory -- has no floor to stand on. Source: mises.org/articles-interest/subjective-theory-value.

question: A writer in exile in London built a whole theory of exploitation on David Ricardo's claim that labor is the source of value. He held that the labor time society needs to make a good sets its worth, and that the gap between that worth and the worker's wage is surplus taken by the boss. Austrians say Carl Menger's subjective theory knocks out its foundation. Whose 1867 book carries the argument?
answer: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
choices: Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1
John Stuart Mill, in Principles of Political Economy
Thomas Malthus, in An Essay on the Principle of Population
Jean-Baptiste Say, in A Treatise on Political Economy
context: Marx's 1867 Das Kapital vol. 1 inherits Ricardo's labor theory and refines it as 'socially necessary labor time'; the entire theory of surplus value, exploitation, and the falling rate of profit depends on labor being the source of value. If Menger's subjective account is right, this foundation is gone: value comes from the chooser's ranking, not from labor-hours. Boehm-Bawerk drove the point home explicitly in Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896). Mill (1848), Malthus (1798), and Say (1803) all predate Marx and do not carry the exploitation theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_theory_of_value.

question: A central planning board sits down to set a rational price for a good. On Carl Menger's subjective theory, the fact it needs lives inside each buyer's head: how he ranks one more unit against uses only he knows, a fact written down nowhere. Which later Austrian argument does this feed straight into?
answer: Mises's socialist calculation argument
choices: Mises's socialist calculation argument
Ricardo's comparative advantage argument
Friedman's monetarist quantity theory
Coase's transaction-cost theorem
context: Ludwig von Mises's 1920 Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth runs directly out of subjective value: if value lives in individual choosers' rankings, then a central planning board without market prices has no way to know how to allocate scarce means -- the information it would need is dispersed across millions of heads and revealed only through the choices those choosers actually make. Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' extends the same point. Ricardo, Friedman, and Coase pressed unrelated arguments. Source: mises.org/online-book/introduction-austrian-economics/4-subjective-theory-value.

question: Friedrich Hayek worked out in London in 1931 an idea Ludwig von Mises had planted in 1912. When a central bank holds down the price of loans, businesses build lots of new factories and houses. A few years later many of those projects turn out to be losers and shut down. In their Austrian account, what is that rise and fall?
answer: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
choices: The boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit
The swing in demand as buyers lose their nerve
The cost spiral as unions push up wages
The glut when firms make more than buyers want
context: Hayek's LSE lectures 'Prices and Production' (1931) built the roundabout-production capital theory of Boehm-Bawerk together with Mises's monetary seed into the full ABCT: artificially low interest rates from bank credit expansion distort the structure of production, generating an unsustainable boom that must end in a bust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Theory_of_Money_and_Credit.

question: A silver coin buys bread today because it bought bread yesterday, and the day before. Ludwig von Mises traced that chain back in 1912. When did he say it stops?
answer: When silver had uses of its own
choices: When silver had uses of its own
When a king stamped his face on it
When a bank first printed notes
When a law made it legal tender
context: Mises's move: today's demand rests on yesterday's known purchasing power, and the chain can be traced back through time until it reaches a moment when the money-good had a non-monetary use (gold as jewelry, silver as ornament, cattle as food). The circularity dissolves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_theorem.

question: A few Austrian economists looked at Bitcoin, first mined in January 2009, and saw something only digital, with no state behind it, that had never traded as anything else. They said Ludwig von Mises had ruled it out. Which part of his 1912 argument did they use against it?
answer: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
choices: The regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use
The quantity theory's requirement of stable velocity of circulation
The state theory's requirement of tax-driven acceptance
The real-bills doctrine's requirement of short-term commercial backing
context: The debate raged in Austrian circles from about 2011. Critics argued Bitcoin was born as pure money and therefore was ruled out on Misesian grounds; defenders had to find the prior demand Mises's chain required. Source: mises.org/quarterly-journal-austrian-economics/bitcoin-regression-theorem-and-emergence-new-medium-exchange.

question: Konrad Graf answered an old Austrian objection to Bitcoin in 2013. Critics had said it failed Ludwig von Mises's 1912 test of money. Graf replied that the earliest users, cypherpunks and cryptography hobbyists, already valued Bitcoin for a real, direct use before anyone treated it as money. What use did he point to?
answer: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
choices: Its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network
Its use as a store of value with a predictably fixed twenty-one-million supply cap
Its use as a settlement layer for high-frequency exchange trading
Its use as programmable collateral for decentralised lending contracts
context: The first buyers wanted the tokens because the underlying protocol did something no other technology could -- move digital value across a network without a trusted third party. That utility, present before any market price, was the non-monetary demand the regression theorem required. Source: www.konradsgraf.com/blog1/2013/2/27/in-depth-bitcoins-the-regression-theorem-and-that-curious-bu.html.

question: Robert Murphy and Silas Barta split from Konrad Graf and Peter Surda over Bitcoin and Ludwig von Mises's regression theorem. They refused to hunt for a prior non-money use at all, and they said the 1912 argument answered a different question than Bitcoin poses. How did they read the reach of the theorem?
answer: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
choices: As a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money
As overturned by Milton Friedman's 1956 restatement of the quantity theory
As applying only to commodities Menger's 1892 essay classified as saleable
As already refuted by Georg Knapp's 1905 state theory of money
context: Murphy and Barta treated the theorem as a historical explanation of how commodity monies emerged, not a constraint on future ones. Konrad Graf, Peter Surda, and Jeffrey Tucker took the other route -- accept the theorem, find the prior non-monetary demand. Source: stephankinsella.com/2025/07/austrians-bitcoin-impossible/.

question: Timothy Geithner took a new job in March 2014 as president of a firm, after running the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the arm of the Fed closest to Wall Street, and then the Treasury, where he steered the bank rescues of the crisis. What kind of firm was it?
answer: A private-equity firm
choices: A private-equity firm
A hedge fund
An investment bank
A credit-rating agency
context: Geithner joined the private-equity firm Warburg Pincus as president in March 2014. His 2014 memoir Stress Test explicitly defends the 2008-09 bailouts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Geithner; warburgpincus.com.

question: Janet Yellen stepped down as head of the Federal Reserve, the central bank that sets American interest rates, in 2018. Over the next two years she gave paid speeches and collected about $7 million, before President Biden made her his Treasury Secretary in 2021. Who paid most of that speaking money?
answer: Wall Street banks and trading firms
choices: Wall Street banks and trading firms
Tech companies and their founders
Universities and policy institutes
Trade unions and labor federations
context: Yellen's financial disclosures documented approximately $7M in Wall Street speaking fees over the two-year interval. The pattern -- top financial-regulator role followed by high-fee industry advisory -- matches the earlier three Treasury secretaries. Source: US Office of Government Ethics disclosures 2020-21.

question: Luigi Zingales, an Italian-born champion of free markets who teaches at Chicago, argued in 2012 that American finance had slid away from competition into a system where the largest firms get ahead through political ties rather than better products. He wrote a book for American readers calling for pro-market reform. What did he title it?
answer: A Capitalism for the People
choices: A Capitalism for the People
The Wealth of Nations Revisited
The Bailout State
Free Markets Under Fire
context: Luigi Zingales, A Capitalism for the People: Recapturing the Lost Genius of American Prosperity (Basic Books, 2012). Zingales -- Italian-born, teaching at Chicago Booth -- became a mainstream-economics voice against financial-sector regulatory capture. Source: basicbooks.com (Zingales 2012).

question: Robert Rubin left Goldman Sachs to serve as Treasury Secretary from 1995 to 1999, then spent ten years on Citigroup's executive committee. What is the name for a career move like his?
answer: The revolving door
choices: The revolving door
Insider trading
A market corner
A public buyback
context: Rubin spent twenty-six years at Goldman Sachs before the Treasury and a decade on Citigroup's executive committee after it. The same move turns up beyond finance: Scott Gottlieb, FDA Commissioner 2017-19, joined Pfizer's board in June 2019. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rubin; pfizer.com (board announcement June 2019).

question: Public-choice economists point to four of the men who ran the Treasury in the twenty-five years from 1988, from Nicholas Brady to Timothy Geithner, each arriving from a Wall Street house or the New York Fed and each lawfully confirmed. What claim do they make?
answer: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
choices: The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character
The pattern is simple expertise: only Wall Street trains people for the job
The pattern is personal greed: each man took the post to enrich himself
The pattern is party politics: each president rewarded his largest donors
context: Each of the four served legally and by presidential appointment. The critique targets the STRUCTURAL pattern that produces the pattern: the pool of qualified candidates comes from and returns to the industry. Source: Zingales (2012); Johnson (2009); Stigler (1971).

question: Antoine Cournot built his economic arguments out of heavy mathematics that only trained scholars could follow. Frederic Bastiat, a French classical liberal of the same century, took the opposite path on purpose. What kind of writing did he choose?
answer: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
choices: Plain prose aimed at the general reader
Formal mathematical proofs
Latin scholastic disputation
Long-form academic treatises
context: Bastiat wrote so that a French farmer could follow the argument, deliberately unlike Cournot's 1838 Recherches that used calculus to model demand curves. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Antoine_Augustin_Cournot.

question: Frederic Bastiat almost always started an essay with something a reader could actually call to mind: a broken shop window, a new railway, a debate in the French chamber of deputies. Only then did he draw a lesson. What is this opening move called?
answer: Starting with a concrete scene
choices: Starting with a concrete scene
Starting with a mathematical equation
Starting with a historical statute
Starting with a syllogism
context: Part one of the Bastiat method: put a scene in front of the reader before you make the argument. Source: bastiat.org.

question: Frederic Bastiat took a bad economic argument apart in a set order. He described what people see and applaud, named what the other side was missing, and then made one last turn that surfaced what the policy actually costs. What does that last step trace?
answer: The unseen consequences
choices: The unseen consequences
The historical antecedents
The mathematical proof
The alternative equilibrium
context: Part three: trace the unseen -- the tailor whose sale was lost when the shopkeeper repaired his broken window, the worker priced out by the minimum wage, the consumer who paid more for domestic goods. Source: bastiat.org.

question: A student brings Frederic Bastiat's method of the seen and the unseen to a shelf of classical-liberal books. The method serves him well on part of the shelf, but it was not built for every topic there. Which topic does it not by itself give him the tools for?
answer: Questions of monetary theory and the business cycle
choices: Questions of monetary theory and the business cycle
Questions of tariffs and other trade barriers
Questions of make-work public schemes
Questions of subsidies to favoured industries
context: For monetary theory the tradition needs Menger, Mises, and Hayek; for capital theory Bohm-Bawerk; for public choice Buchanan and Tullock. Bastiat's method is the first tool, not the only one. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Frederic_Bastiat.

question: A kid buying candy and a soda in an American corner store pays extra for one ingredient in both. Congress has propped up its price since 1934, partly with cheap federal loans to the American farmers who grow it. Which food is it?
answer: Sugar
choices: Sugar
Coffee
Cocoa
Vanilla
context: The US Sugar Program, established by the Sugar Act 1934, still runs under each Farm Bill; typical US price in the 2010s was about 35 cents per pound against a world price of about 17 cents. Source: gao.gov/products/rced-00-126.

question: Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to ask first, of any law that raises a price, who pays for it. Washington has held American sugar near double the world price for decades. Who bears the cost?
answer: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
choices: American shoppers -- they pay more for candy, soda, and food
Grocery chains -- they absorb the higher price themselves
Federal taxpayers -- they mail the growers a yearly check
Sugar workers -- they take lower wages to cover it
context: The Sugar Act of 1934 first structured the quota, loan, and allotment system that still supports US sugar prices through the Farm Bills. Source: grokipedia.com/page/United_States_Sugar_Program.

question: Kraft closed its Life Savers factory in Holland, Michigan, in 2003 and sent the candy's production to Montreal, where sugar sold for about half the price. Sugar makes up most of every Life Saver. Why was American sugar so much dearer?
answer: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
choices: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more
American sugar is taxed at the register to pay for school lunches
US sugar must be refined twice to meet federal food-safety rules
US shipping rules make sugar from abroad slow and costly to unload
context: Kraft Foods moved Life Savers production from Holland, Michigan to Montreal in 2003 because Canadian sugar was about half the US price under the US Sugar Program. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Life_Savers.

question: Two Chicago-area candy makers moved a large share of their candy-making to Mexico in the 2000s, and both said plainly why: they could not afford American sugar at about double the world price. Which pair was it?
answer: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
choices: Ferrara Pan and Brach's
Hershey and Mars
Wrigley and Tootsie Roll
See's and Ghirardelli
context: Ferrara Pan Candy Company moved much of its Chicago-area production to Mexico in the 2000s; Brach's Confections closed its Chicago plant in 2003 and moved to Mexico. Both cited US sugar prices. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Ferrara_Candy_Company.

question: An American candy maker signs for a truckload of sugar at about double the world price. Frédéric Bastiat taught readers to look past the growers a law protects to the industries that buy the same crop as an ingredient. What does his method predict firms like this will do?
answer: They move production to where sugar is cheap
choices: They move production to where sugar is cheap
They keep US production and absorb the input cost
They buy their own sugar farms to escape the price
They merge with the growers to share in the gains
context: The predicted move played out in 2003 when Life Savers relocated from Michigan to Montreal, in the 2000s when Ferrara Pan and Brach's moved much production to Mexico. Higher US input costs pushed candy jobs across the border. Source: trade.gov/employment-changes-us-food-manufacturing-impact-sugar-prices.

question: A shopper takes a bag of Domino Sugar off the shelf of an American supermarket. The best-known winners of the federal sugar program are one Florida family of Cuban descent, which controls both Domino and Florida Crystals; a 1998 estimate put its gain at $60 million a year or more. What is the family's name?
answer: The Fanjul family
choices: The Fanjul family
The Hershey family
The Mars family
The Coca-Cola Candler family
context: The Fanjul brothers of Florida control Florida Crystals and, since 2001, Domino Sugar. A 1998 TIME analysis of General Accounting Office figures put their yearly gain from the program at $60 million or more, which makes them the best-known case of a small, politically organized beneficiary group. Source: content.time.com (TIME, 'Sweet Deal', 1998).

question: Friedrich Hayek argued that the knowledge an economy runs on is spread across millions of people. Nobody knows where every apple is, how many nails a factory needs, or what shoe size Aunt Judy prefers. What puts all of it to work without any boss having to know it?
answer: Prices in a free market
choices: Prices in a free market
A government planning committee
A national computer running the whole economy
A single wise king
context: F. A. Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4, September 1945, pages 519-530 -- eleven pages that became one of the most-cited economics papers of the 20th century. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Use_of_Knowledge_in_Society).

question: Friedrich Hayek published eleven pages in September 1945 in the flagship journal of the leading US economics society. The paper, The Use of Knowledge in Society, became the most-cited paper of the modern Austrian school. Which journal printed it?
answer: The American Economic Review
choices: The American Economic Review
The Journal of Political Economy
The Economic Journal
Econometrica
context: The essay appeared in the American Economic Review, Volume 35, Number 4 (September 1945), pages 519-530. Hayek was writing from wartime London (LSE had by then returned from its Cambridge evacuation). Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: Friedrich Hayek told the planners of the 1930s, in his 1945 essay, that they had been solving the wrong problem. They treated the economy as if the resources and the wants were already known, so that only the sharing out remained. Honesty and cleverness, he held, would not help a planner with the real one. What did Hayek say the real problem is?
answer: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
choices: How to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality
How to equalize the marginal productivity of capital across all industries
How to compute the aggregate demand curve for a whole national economy
How to eliminate the fluctuations of the business cycle through fiscal policy
context: Hayek's reframing was the essay's central move: the socialist-calculation debate was not about better arithmetic; it was about the unavailability of the underlying data to any single mind or committee. The knowledge that a market uses to allocate resources is scattered across millions of heads and cannot be gathered up to a central board in usable time. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago hosted PDF (https://home.uchicago.edu/~vlima/courses/econ200/spring01/hayek.pdf).

question: Friedrich Hayek split knowledge in two in his 1945 essay. One kind, the scientific sort found in textbooks, a planning office might gather. The other belongs to individual people and concerns the customers, stock rooms, ships and jobs each one deals with. What did Hayek call the second kind?
answer: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
choices: The knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
The general theory of aggregate demand and supply
The rational expectations of forward-looking agents
The universal grammar of market institutions
context: Hayek's phrase: the important knowledge in an economy is 'the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' -- that a certain ship is half-empty, that a warehouse has a surplus, that a foreman on the third shift has spotted a way to save two hours. This knowledge is inherently local and inherently dispersed. Source: Hayek 1945, Econlib version (https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html).

question: Friedrich Hayek kept coming back to one metal in his 1945 essay. Somewhere a new use for it appears, or a mine closes, and its price rises; every user of the metal then uses less of it, even those with no idea why the price changed. Which metal did Hayek use?
answer: Tin
choices: Tin
Copper
Iron
Silver
context: The tin example on page 526 of the American Economic Review version is the paragraph everyone quotes. Hayek's point: a single number -- the tin price -- carries the whole world's changing knowledge about tin (mine closures, new uses, war coming) to every user of tin, without any user needing to know the underlying cause. Source: Hayek 1945, University of Chicago PDF.

question: Friedrich Hayek reached for a mechanical image of the price system in his 1945 essay: a machinery for registering change, where a producer has only to watch a few pointers move, the way an engineer keeps an eye on some dials. To which modern technology did he compare it?
answer: A system of telecommunications
choices: A system of telecommunications
A national railway timetable
A wartime radar screen
A newspaper printing press
context: Hayek's phrase: the price system is 'a kind of machinery for registering change, or a system of telecommunications which enables individual producers to watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials.' Prices carry knowledge no single mind holds. Source: Western Sydney Pressbooks critical-analysis version (https://westernsydney.pressbooks.pub/criticalanalysis/chapter/the-use-of-knowledge-in-society/).

question: Friedrich Hayek ended his 1945 essay in astonishment. When one raw material runs short, tens of thousands of strangers start to use it more sparingly, though no order has been issued and hardly anyone knows the cause. What one word did Hayek use for that achievement?
answer: A marvel
choices: A marvel
A miracle
A machine
A market
context: Hayek writes: 'The marvel is that in a case like that of a scarcity of one raw material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of people knowing the cause, tens of thousands of people whose identity could not be ascertained by months of investigation, are made to use the material or its products more sparingly.' The word MARVEL carries the essay's astonishment -- that a system no one designed does what no committee could. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'

question: Lionel Robbins, rebuilding a department in London, brought Friedrich Hayek over from Vienna in late January 1931 to give four lectures. The talks went down so well that Hayek was offered a permanent post. Which institution offered it?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Cambridge
The University of Oxford
University College London
context: Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding LSE's economics department, brought Hayek over from 27 to 30 January 1931 to give the lectures published later that year as Prices and Production. The talks landed so well that LSE offered Hayek the Tooke Chair the following year. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Friedrich Hayek gave four lectures in London in 1931 and was offered a post; from 1932 he held one endowed chair there, named for a nineteenth-century English economist. Which chair was it?
answer: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
choices: The Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics
The Cassel Chair of Economics
The Drummond Chair of Political Economy
The Marshall Chair of Political Economy
context: Named for the 19th-century monetary theorist Thomas Tooke, the Tooke Chair was LSE's senior economics professorship. Hayek held it from 1932, became a British subject in 1938, and finally left in 1950 for a position in Chicago's Committee on Social Thought. Source: LSE History blog, 'Friedrich A. von Hayek at LSE'.

question: Fritz Machlup toured American universities on a Rockefeller grant in 1933, visiting Columbia, Harvard, Chicago and Stanford. In 1935 he settled into a chair that would last twelve years. Where was it?
answer: The University of Buffalo
choices: The University of Buffalo
The University of Chicago
Princeton University
Cornell University
context: Machlup held his Buffalo chair from 1935 to 1947, later moving to Johns Hopkins and then Princeton. He was one of the first of Mises's Vienna circle to make a fully American career. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fritz Machlup'.

question: Gottfried Haberler took a post in Geneva in 1934 as an economist for an international body. The job yielded his survey of trade-cycle theories, Prosperity and Depression, before Harvard made him a professor in the autumn of 1936. Which body employed him in Geneva?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The Bank for International Settlements
The International Chamber of Commerce
The International Labour Office
context: Haberler served in the economic administration of the League of Nations in Geneva from 1934 to 1936. In autumn 1936 he moved to a Harvard professorship that lasted until his 1971 retirement. Source: Britannica, 'Gottfried von Haberler'.

question: Oskar Morgenstern, who ran Vienna's research institute on the business cycle and sat in Ludwig von Mises's seminar, was away from Austria on 13 March 1938, the day German troops crossed into it. Where was he, and what did he do?
answer: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
choices: On a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment
In Zurich on sabbatical; he returned home the following month
In London consulting for the Bank of England; he moved on to Cambridge
In Stockholm at a conference; he stayed and took a Riksbank post
