context: Morgenstern was travelling in America as a Carnegie Visiting Professor when the Anschluss occurred. From six invitations he chose a three-year appointment as Class of 1913 Lecturer in Political Economy at Princeton, and simply did not return home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Oskar Morgenstern'.

question: Ludwig von Mises left Vienna in 1934 for a paid professorship, something his own city had never given him: Vienna had only ever let him lecture without pay. He held the post until the German army's advance forced him out in July 1940. Which institution was it?
answer: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
choices: The Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva
The London School of Economics
The Sorbonne in Paris
The University of Zurich
context: Vienna had recognised Mises with only an unpaid Privatdozent title. The Geneva institute (Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales) gave him his first paid professorship. He held the chair from 1934 until 1940. Source: Mises Institute, 'Ludwig von Mises: The Logician of Freedom'.

question: Margit and Ludwig von Mises fled the German advance in July 1940, crossing France. Spain turned them away three times before its consulate at Toulouse granted a visa; the couple took the train across to the coast and sailed for America from the neutral port where Europe's refugees gathered that year. Which port?
answer: Lisbon
choices: Lisbon
Bilbao
Barcelona
Vigo
context: Portugal's neutrality made Lisbon the great escape port for European refugees in 1940. Mises and Margit sailed from there and docked in New Jersey on 2 August 1940, where their Viennese friend Alfred Schutz met them on the pier. Source: Future of Freedom Foundation, 'Celebrating the Arrival of Ludwig von Mises in America'.

question: Ludwig von Mises stepped ashore in New Jersey on August 2, 1940, a refugee from the German advance across Europe and a man many economists ranked among the greatest minds of his time. How old was he then, and what academic post awaited him?
answer: Fifty-eight, and no American university ever gave him a paid chair
choices: Fifty-eight, and no American university ever gave him a paid chair
Forty-four, and a full Harvard professorship awaited him
Sixty-seven, and a Yale endowed chair had been arranged in advance
Fifty-two, and a Chicago professorship followed within the year
context: Mises was born on 29 September 1881. He turned 59 the month after his arrival. From 1945 to 1969 he taught at New York University as an unpaid Visiting Professor; the William Volker Fund paid his stipend until 1962, and a consortium including the businessman Lawrence Fertig, who sat on the NYU board, took over afterwards. Source: FEE, 'Ludwig von Mises: A Prophet Without Honor in His Own Land'.

question: Karl Menger, a mathematician and the son of the Austrian school's founder, read the politics correctly and left Vienna a full year before the Anschluss, reaching America in the autumn of 1937. He resigned his Vienna chair in March 1938 and stayed on at a Catholic university there. Which one?
answer: The University of Notre Dame
choices: The University of Notre Dame
Georgetown University
Fordham University
The Catholic University of America
context: Menger arrived in South Bend, Indiana in autumn 1937 and stayed until 1946. His father Carl Menger had founded the Austrian School with the 1871 Grundsaetze; the son carried the family name into American mathematics. Source: MacTutor, 'Karl Menger'.

question: Gunnar Myrdal, the Swedish social democrat, shared the 1974 economics Nobel with a free-market economist, an odd pairing that struck observers. His co-winner had been a member of Ludwig von Mises's Vienna seminar in the 1920s, the only one of its members ever to win the prize. Which Vienna emigre was he?
answer: Friedrich von Hayek
choices: Friedrich von Hayek
Fritz Machlup
Gottfried Haberler
Oskar Morgenstern
context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel citation named his work on money, credit and interdependence between economic, social and institutional phenomena. Machlup, Haberler and Morgenstern each made major contributions in America but Hayek alone of the Vienna diaspora was Nobel-honoured. Source: Britannica, 'F. A. Hayek'.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920s Vienna, with a group of Austrian economists around him, that no small committee, however smart, could plan a whole country's economy the way a family plans its weekly budget. Why not, according to his argument?
answer: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
choices: No committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth
No committee can be trusted to share the goods out fairly
No committee can make people work as hard as owners do
No committee could add up so many numbers by hand
context: Mises set out the case in his 1920 essay on economic calculation under socialism: without market prices for land, factories and machines, planners have no common measure for comparing one use of them against another. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: Rudolf Carnap, a leading philosopher of the Vienna Circle, left for the United States in 1935 as Nazi power rose across Europe. The Circle had argued that only claims testable by logic and observation had real meaning. The American university he joined then became a main home of logical positivism in North America. Which school did he join?
answer: The University of Chicago
choices: The University of Chicago
Harvard University
The University of California, Berkeley
Columbia University
context: Carnap emigrated from Prague to the United States in 1935, took up a chair at the University of Chicago in 1936 and taught there until 1952 before moving to UCLA. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rudolf_Carnap.

question: Kurt Godel fled Vienna in early 1940 by a strange, roundabout route: east across the Soviet Union on the Trans-Siberian Railway, then Japan, then the Pacific by ship. He reached the United States and stayed for the rest of his life at the place where Albert Einstein became his close friend. Where did he end up?
answer: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
choices: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton
The Society of Fellows at Harvard
The Courant Institute in New York
The RAND Corporation in Santa Monica
context: Godel fled via the Trans-Siberian Railway and Japan in 1940, arriving at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where he became a colleague of Einstein and von Neumann. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kurt_Godel.

question: Suppose you trade your apple for a friend's cookie at lunch. You both smile and walk back to the table happy with the swap; nobody forced you, and nobody tricked either of you. Why did that little trade make both of you better off at the same time?
answer: Each side valued what it got more than what it gave up
choices: Each side valued what it got more than what it gave up
The apple and the cookie were worth exactly the same
The apple and the cookie cost the same to make
The trade made more food than the two had before
context: Carl Menger, who founded the Austrian School in 1871, built his theory of exchange on this point: a trade happens only when each side values what it gets above what it gives, so a free swap leaves both better off. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Carl_Menger.

question: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk taught a famous seminar in early-1900s Vienna whose young economists later split apart on politics. Ludwig von Mises grew up to defend free markets; Otto Bauer grew up to lead the socialists. The two sides then argued for years over one big question about how an economy should be run. What was it?
answer: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
choices: Whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well
Whether a nation should tie its money to gold or to silver
Whether a nation should shelter its farms and factories with tariffs
Whether a nation should pay for its wars with taxes or with loans
context: The 1905-1914 Bohm-Bawerk seminar had the future greatest Austrian liberal (Mises), the future Austrian Social Democrat foreign minister (Otto Bauer), and the future Marxist finance minister of Weimar Germany (Hilferding) sitting together. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Eugen_von_Bohm-Bawerk.

question: A country ends all its private markets and lets a small state committee set every single price by rule: no bargaining, no bidding, no shopping around. Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek said one tool that guides what gets made, and how much, then vanishes overnight. No central office, Mises added, can invent it. What tool is lost?
answer: Prices that reveal what people really want
choices: Prices that reveal what people really want
Quotas that set each factory's output
Rations that share out the goods by need
Taxes that pay for the country's public works
context: Mises made the argument in 1920 and Hayek extended it in 1945: market prices carry knowledge of scarcities and wants that no planning office can gather or invent. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Economic_calculation_problem.

question: A baker in Weimar Germany charged a few hundred marks for a loaf early in 1923 and hundreds of billions of marks by that November. The central bank was printing new paper marks in huge amounts to pay government debts and war reparations, with the Marxist economist Rudolf Hilferding at the finance ministry. What rule about money does that loaf show?
answer: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
choices: Prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value
Prices shoot up because bakers hoard flour to get rich
Prices shoot up because the harvests of 1923 failed
Prices only rise on goods brought in from abroad
context: Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910) was a leading Marxist analysis of banking; he later served twice as Finance Minister of Weimar Germany. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rudolf_Hilferding.

question: Members of a small cryptography mailing list opened a paper from Satoshi Nakamoto on 31 October 2008. It described Bitcoin, a money passed between people with no bank in the middle, and for a proposal so full of arithmetic it is famously short. About how long is its main body?
answer: About nine pages
choices: About nine pages
About one page
About fifty pages
About two hundred pages
context: Nine pages of body text, organized into twelve numbered sections plus an abstract and references. That is the length of a typical computer-science conference paper of its era. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto set out his design for a money that needed no bank in a paper of 2008, and he opened it by naming the problem he meant to fix rather than the fix itself. Which sentence is its first line?
answer: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
choices: 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.'
'Money is a social construct that will be replaced by decentralized applications.'
'The Federal Reserve is the enemy of every honest saver.'
'This paper introduces a new consensus mechanism called proof-of-stake.'
context: The opening sentence identifies the trusted-third-party dependency as the problem to eliminate. The rest of the paper explains the peer-to-peer solution. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A reader who turns to the end of Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin paper of 2008 finds a short reference list. Four earlier designs for digital cash had pointed the way: Wei Dai's b-money, Nick Szabo's bit gold, David Chaum's DigiCash and Adam Back's Hashcash. Only two of them appear among his references. Which two?
answer: b-money and Hashcash
choices: DigiCash and bit gold
b-money and Hashcash
DigiCash and Hashcash
bit gold and b-money
context: Both Hashcash and b-money were cypherpunk-lineage proposals from the 1990s that Satoshi combined and extended. DigiCash and bit gold are historically related but are not cited in the paper's references. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto shows in section 7 of the Bitcoin paper how a computer on the network can delete old, already-spent records and still keep proof that the history is untouched. Every block stores a compact fingerprint of its transactions, arranged so that one record can be checked without keeping all the rest. What is the structure called?
answer: A Merkle tree
choices: A Merkle tree
A linked list
A hash table
A relational database
context: Named for Ralph Merkle, who patented the structure in 1979. Each block header commits to the Merkle root of its transactions, so nodes can discard old bodies and keep only proofs. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: A Bitcoin wallet built on a shortcut from Satoshi Nakamoto's paper of 2008 keeps only the little headers of each block, plus a brief proof that a certain payment lies in one of them, and leaves the full record of every transaction to others. What is the point of the shortcut?
answer: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
choices: A small device can verify payments without running a full node
It makes every bitcoin transaction completely private
It removes the need for any miners at all
It changes bitcoin's fixed supply cap
context: SPV enables phone-and-laptop wallets to check that a payment is in the longest chain by requesting Merkle proofs from full nodes. It is what made mobile Bitcoin wallets practical. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto posted 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' to a cryptography mailing list in October 2008. Its twelve numbered sections cover the network, mining, incentives and privacy, and the last one sums up the coin as a string of digital signatures and the premise that honest miners outmatch any attacker in computing power. What is that twelfth section titled, and how long is it?
answer: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
choices: Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs
Discussion, roughly two pages
Bibliography, roughly one page
Appendix A, roughly three pages
context: The paper is famously terse. Satoshi said what needed saying and stopped. The Conclusion recaps the peer-to-peer solution and the assumption that honest miners hold more hashing power than any attacker. Source: bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Thomas Sowell recalled in his memoir A Personal Odyssey a small wooden house in North Carolina with no electricity and no running water. He told of one ordinary thing he had never learned as a young boy in that isolated home. What was it?
answer: That blond was a hair color
choices: That blond was a hair color
That milk came from cows
That the ocean was salt water
That radios carried live music
context: Sowell wrote in A Personal Odyssey (Free Press, 2000) that his childhood encounters with white people were so limited that he did not know blond was a hair color. He recalled a small wooden house in North Carolina on an unpaved street with no electricity or running water. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell', citing A Personal Odyssey.

question: A seventeen-year-old named Thomas Sowell quit Stuyvesant, a top public high school in New York City, running short on money and living in a home that fought too often. He was the first person in his family to study past sixth grade. Which job did he take?
answer: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
choices: Delivering telegrams for Western Union
Sorting mail at the main post office
Loading freight on the Brooklyn docks
Running an elevator in a midtown tower
context: Sowell dropped out of Stuyvesant at 17 because of financial difficulties and family quarreling, then worked long hours in a machine shop and as a delivery man for Western Union. He also tried out for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1948. Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Young Thomas Sowell of 1940s Harlem rode the bus home from his downtown high school, past rich stores, past a concert hall, past comfortable blocks, then over a bridge to his own tenement neighborhood. The gulf between the two worlds puzzled him. In his twenties, which thinker did he first turn to for an answer?
answer: Karl Marx
choices: Karl Marx
Adam Smith
Frederick Douglass
Benjamin Franklin
context: Sowell has said he was a Marxist through his twenties. Of the bus ride he wrote: 'The contrast between that and what I'd been seeing most of the trip really baffled me. And Marx seemed to explain it.' He wrote a Harvard senior thesis on Marxian economics and a Columbia master's thesis on Marxian business cycle theory. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: George Stigler drew Thomas Sowell to the University of Chicago in the fall of 1959, when the young man came to study for a graduate degree. The Chicago school taught that one everyday tool guides an economy better than any state plan drawn up in a ministry. What tool did it mean?
answer: The price of goods and labor in a free market
choices: The price of goods and labor in a free market
The customs and habits handed down in a community
The votes citizens cast for one policy or another
The rulings of courts on disputed contracts
context: Sowell chose Columbia in order to study under George Stigler, later a Nobel laureate; on learning Stigler had moved to Chicago he followed him there in the fall of 1959 and took his PhD at Chicago in 1968, with a dissertation on Say's Law and the general glut controversy. Friedman, Knight and Becker were all Chicago economists. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell took a summer job at the U.S. Department of Labor in 1960, studying Puerto Rico's sugar industry, where Washington set the wage floor. He saw that as that floor rose, the sugar payrolls shrank. He brought the finding to the office he had joined. What would his colleagues not do?
answer: Test whether the law was helping the workers
choices: Test whether the law was helping the workers
Release the employment figures he had assembled
Compare Puerto Rico with mainland sugar growers
Let an intern brief the division chief directly
context: Sowell has said his colleagues were surprised by his questioning and that 'they certainly weren't going to engage in any scrutiny of the law' -- their job was to enforce it, not to check it. He called this 'the beginning of the erosion of my faith in government programs.' Sources: Wikipedia 'Thomas Sowell'; Britannica 'Thomas Sowell'; New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell reached Harvard by an unlikely road (dropout, Marine, night classes at Howard) and graduated magna cum laude in 1958. Asked long afterwards to name the best thing about having gone there, he gave an answer that had nothing to do with the teaching. What did he say?
answer: That a graduate is never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
choices: That a graduate is never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there
That nobody there ever asked where a student had gone to high school
That a graduate learns how fast a reputation starts doing his arguing for him
That it teaches a graduate to distrust every credential, beginning with his own
context: Sowell's line: 'One of the best things about going to Harvard is that, for the rest of your life, you are neither intimidated nor impressed by people who went to Harvard.' He finished high school by equivalency after the Marines, took a civil service job in Washington and studied nights at Howard University before transferring. Source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell was preparing a college course on the Soviet economy when Friedrich Hayek's famous 1945 essay finally clicked for him. He saw why Soviet central plans kept failing and put the whole thing in one sharp line about who held what. Which line did he use?
answer: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
choices: Those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power
Those who wrote the plans never had to live under the plans they wrote
Those who owned nothing were told every day that they owned everything
Those who waited longest in the queue were always served last
context: Sowell: 'There was a knowledge problem that was inherent in that system. In a nutshell, those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power.' Hayek's essay is 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: Thomas Sowell has said that his summer of 1960, spent on Puerto Rico's sugar wages at the Labor Department, began the erosion of his faith in government programs, not because the numbers alone convinced him but because of how the people around him received them. He compressed that summer into one sentence he has been applying to institutions ever since. Which sentence?
answer: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
choices: That agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do
That good intentions and good results are different things, and only results can be counted
That every program grows until it costs more than the problem it was built to solve
That the people a program is meant to help are the last whose interests anyone counts
context: Sowell's own words: 'It forced me to realize that government agencies have their own self-interest to look after, regardless of those for whom a program has been set up.' This is public-choice reasoning arrived at by observation, before Sowell had read the public-choice literature. The line about intentions and results is closer to Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions', a genuinely different move. Source: New Criterion, 'The Triumph of Thomas Sowell'.

question: A former Intel physicist made a bold guess in a short essay of 1988. If regular people ever got hold of strong math to scramble their messages, wrote Timothy May, no state would be able to spy on their letters or block their payments. What did May think would grow up as a result?
answer: Private communication and private trade between strangers
choices: Private communication and private trade between strangers
A single world police force to break the codes
New state-run banks to guard everyone's codes
A flood of junk mail that nobody could block
context: May's 1988 essay is 'The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto'. Eric Hughes's 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' was a separate essay of March 1993. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May stole the famous first line of an 1848 pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels to open an essay of his own in 1988, swapping the word 'communism' for the name of the movement he was founding. Which opening line did May write?
answer: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
choices: 'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.'
'A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of digital cash.'
'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of secret codes.'
'Workers of the world, encrypt: there is nothing to lose but the chains.'
context: May's opening deliberately echoes the 1848 Communist Manifesto's 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May quit his day job at Intel young and settled above Santa Cruz to write about what math and computers would do to politics. His 1988 Crypto Anarchist Manifesto turns on one forecast about what computers would soon let people do. Which line is his?
answer: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
choices: 'Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.'
'Computer networks will soon let every citizen read the secret files of his government, so that no official will be able to hide anything at all.'
'Within a decade every home will hold a computer able to talk to every other, and the old post office will close its doors for good.'
'Soon any person with a modem will be able to publish to the whole world, and no editor or censor will be able to stand in his way.'
context: The exact sentence from May's manifesto. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: Timothy May named several concrete tools in his 1988 manifesto that he believed the math of strong encryption would soon make possible. Hal Finney, Wei Dai and, eventually, Satoshi Nakamoto worked on tools of that kind over the following decades. Which set of tools did May sketch?
answer: anonymous networks, digital pseudonyms, electronic contracts, and digital money
choices: anonymous networks, digital pseudonyms, electronic contracts, and digital money
quantum computers, code-breaking machines, satellite links, and secure phones
encrypted voting, digital passports, online courts, and e-government records
smart cards, chip-and-PIN cards, password managers, and fingerprint locks
context: The manifesto describes encrypted messages re-routed beyond tracing, electronic contracts between people who never learn each other's true names, and markets beyond the state; May's signature lists digital money, anonymous networks and digital pseudonyms among its tools. Source: https://www.activism.net/cypherpunk/crypto-anarchy.html.

question: An author released a short nine-page technical document on Halloween, almost exactly twenty years after Timothy May's 1988 essay. May had named no specific project, because none existed; he had described the shape of it: money sent person-to-person, with no bank in the middle and no state able to see or stop the transfers. The document matched that sketch almost point for point. Which document was it?
answer: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper
choices: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper
Wei Dai's b-money proposal
Nick Szabo's bit gold proposal
David Chaum's eCash paper
context: Satoshi Nakamoto's white paper of October 31, 2008 realized in engineering form the digital money May had forecast in 1988. Wei Dai's b-money (1998) and Nick Szabo's bit gold were earlier sketches in the same line, and David Chaum's eCash ran through a central issuer. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Obituary writers in the crypto press sat down in 2018 to place Timothy May, dead at sixty-six, in the chain of ideas that eventually produced Bitcoin. He did not build the project, but he had helped shape the culture around it thirty years earlier. Which role did the crypto world settle on giving him?
answer: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
choices: one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within
the actual person behind the Satoshi pseudonym
the founder of the Bitcoin Foundation
the CEO of the first Bitcoin exchange
context: May's 2018 obituaries credited him as a co-founder of the cypherpunk movement from which Satoshi wrote. He never claimed the Satoshi identity, did not found the Bitcoin Foundation, and did not run an exchange. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_C._May.

question: A child offered one cookie today or two tomorrow grabs the one today. A lender offered $100 back today or $100 next year asks $105 for the wait. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk put this fact at the heart of his 1889 book. What is it called?
answer: Time preference
choices: Time preference
Marginal utility
Opportunity cost
The endowment effect
context: Boehm-Bawerk's time preference is the ranking every chooser puts on a present good above the SAME good in the future -- two apples today over two apples next year, dinner tonight over dinner tomorrow. Marginal utility (Menger 1871, Wieser 1884) is a different concept about the LAST unit; opportunity cost (Wieser again) is about the next-best forgone use; the endowment effect (Thaler 1980) is a modern behavioural finding about ownership. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: A hedge-fund analyst asks a plain question: why should anyone pay interest? A man who lends $100 for a year and gets exactly $100 back seems no worse off. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk said he is worse off, because being repaid after a wait is not being made whole. What has the lender given up that must be compensated?
answer: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
choices: A year of consuming the money now instead of later
The labor-hours he spent earning the money
The physical wear on the coins from being handled
The cost of writing up the loan contract
context: This is the pure time-preference theory of interest in its cleanest form: interest is the price of WAITING, not a payment for risk or wear or paperwork. The lender defers a year of spending; only a promise of MORE than the original sum next year compensates him for that deferral. Mises would call the pure-time-preference component 'originary interest' in Human Action (1949); Rothbard would build his entire interest theory on this alone in Man, Economy, and State (1962). Source: econlib.org/library/Enc/bios/BohmBawerk.html.

question: A grandmother forgoes a cruise to leave money for a grandchild who will spend it decades from now. A monk under vows may live indifferent to whether the meal comes today or next week, and a child grabs the cookie at once. What does the Austrian tradition say every chooser, however patient, still has?
answer: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
choices: Some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later
A fixed rate of patience set by his upbringing for life
A moral obligation to prefer later over sooner
A market-determined interest rate identical to everyone else's
context: Even the patient monk still prefers a good NOW to the same good in the infinite future -- a promise of an apple in a thousand years is worth zero today to anyone who will not be alive to eat it. Time preference is positive for every actor with a finite horizon; only the SIZE varies. The child has a very high time preference (cookie now); the grandmother has a very low one; both have some. Source: mises.org/library/brief-defense-misess-conception-time-preference-and-his-pure-time-preference-theory-interest.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in Human Action, in 1949, that preferring sooner over later is no quirk some people have and others lack: every human choice ranks the two. He gave a special name to the interest that comes from that ranking alone. Which name?
answer: Originary interest
choices: Originary interest
Nominal interest
Compound interest
Marginal interest
context: Mises separated three components in market interest: (1) originary interest, the pure time-preference core; (2) an entrepreneurial component covering business risk; (3) a price premium covering expected inflation. Only the originary interest is praxeological -- built into human action itself -- and would remain in Mises's evenly rotating economy where risk and inflation are removed by assumption. Nominal, compound, and marginal are unrelated finance terms. Source: mises.org/online-book/human-action/chapter-xix-rate-interest/1-phenomenon-interest.

question: A banker quotes the rate on a loan, and Ludwig von Mises split such a number into pieces in Human Action. Part of it covers business risk and part covers expected inflation. Take those away, and the pure base rate that remains comes from just one thing about human nature. What did Mises say sets that base rate?
answer: How much people prefer having money now over later
choices: How much people prefer having money now over later
How productive machines and factories currently are
How much new gold is dug out of the ground each year
How high wages get pushed by big labor unions
context: Rothbard's is a Pure Time-Preference Theory of interest (PTPT) -- the productivity-of-capital account (going back to Boehm-Bawerk's own THIRD reason for interest, and to Fisher) is rejected as confused; risk and inflation get modelled as separate premiums added on top. The market rate a borrower actually sees is time preferences plus those premiums. Frank Fetter's 1904 Principles gave the pure account first; Mises and Rothbard both credit him. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf.

question: Two societies start with the same people and resources. Society A saves hard and puts off spending for a generation. Society B spends every dollar right away and borrows to spend more. Which of them does Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk's theory say ends up with the more capital-heavy economy?
answer: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
choices: Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production
Society B -- higher spending drives more investment
Both equally -- time preferences do not affect capital structure
Society B -- consumption is what stimulates growth
context: Deferred consumption is what FREES real resources for long-term projects: workers and materials not consumed today can be used to build tools, factories, and infrastructure whose payoff comes years out. Society B's aggressive present consumption leaves nothing for the long projects. This is why Austrians (Boehm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek) argue that SAVING -- not spending -- is the engine of a capital-intensive economy, directly against the Keynesian priority given to aggregate demand. Source: mises.org/library/book/positive-theory-capital.

question: A central banker pushes short-term interest rates well below the rate that would balance actual saving against actual borrowing. Business owners see the low rate and start factories, subdivisions and mines, reading it as a sign that plenty of long-term saving is available. But consumers have not in fact put off any spending; the low rate was a policy choice. Which Austrian move names what the low rate has done?
answer: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
choices: It lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction
It efficiently reallocates resources to their highest-value use
It cures the shortage of aggregate demand
It permanently raises the economy's growth rate
context: This is the time-preference core of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (Mises 1912, Hayek 1929-1931): when the central-bank rate is held below the market-clearing rate, entrepreneurs get a false signal that consumers have saved more than they have. Long projects get started that cannot in fact be finished with the real resources available. The bust is the market discovering the truth -- capital gets written down, malinvested projects are liquidated, workers laid off, and the economy returns to a structure the real time preferences will support. The rival readings, that cheap credit reallocates efficiently, cures weak demand or lifts growth for good, come from Keynesian and neoclassical camps. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_business_cycle_theory.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe argued in Democracy: The God That Failed, in 2001, that elected leaders think only about the next election, not the next generation. They promise big spending now on pensions, subsidies and wars, he wrote, knowing the bills will fall on leaders and children not yet born. Over generations, what did he say the habit produces?
answer: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
choices: Rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking
A permanent rise in the standard of living
A stable long-run balance in the political system
A gradual return to hereditary monarchy
context: Hoppe's central thesis links rising time preference to decivilization: short-horizon political incentives crowd out long-horizon private planning, borrowing-against-the-future replaces saving, and the visible symptoms are rising crime, degenerating standards, and swelling public debt. The argument is Hoppe's own and much disputed. Time preference is his master variable, and the mechanism runs straight out of Boehm-Bawerk's 1889 framework. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy:_The_God_That_Failed.

question: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk gave three reasons for positive interest in his 1889 book: future goods will be more plentiful, people carelessly discount their tomorrow-wants, and goods in hand work better for starting production. Frank Fetter, Mises and Rothbard later said only one of these truly belongs to the pure interest rate. Which reason is the pure-time-preference core?
answer: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
choices: The undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones
The greater physical productivity of tools made today
The larger future supply of goods
The scarcity of gold-based money
context: The Fetter-Mises-Rothbard purification argues that Boehm-Bawerk's first reason (larger future supply) collapses back into the second (it works only via preferences), and the third (productivity of present goods) is a productivity effect, not a time-preference effect. What is left as the ROOT of interest is the pure ranking of present over future -- reason two, in Boehm-Bawerk's numbering. Source: personal.utdallas.edu/~plewin/ptpt.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_and_Interest.

question: Jerome Powell, who chaired America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, faced a country in 2021 where food, gas and rent were climbing fast. He and other officials kept saying the rise would fade on its own soon, and they picked one calming word for it. What single word did they use?
answer: Transitory
choices: Transitory
Contained
Moderate
Seasonal
context: Jerome Powell, Janet Yellen, and most Federal Open Market Committee members publicly called the 2021 inflation 'transitory' at press conferences and hearings from April through November. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell at the Federal Reserve and Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen told the country through most of 2021 that a rising wave of prices would fade on its own within months. Their case rested on three supports: pandemic base effects, tangled global supply chains, and one more point about American jobs. What was that third point?
answer: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
choices: Continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely
Higher productivity would offset any wage pressure
Immigration would keep wage growth low
Automation would eventually replace scarce workers
context: The 'transitory' case argued that with unemployment still elevated, workers lacked bargaining power for the wage gains that would sustain price inflation. Critics pointed out that a 25%+ expansion in the M2 money supply is not absorbed by labor-market slack. Source: Grokipedia 'Inflation in the United States (2021-2023)' (2026-09-05).

question: Larry Summers, Bill Clinton's former Treasury Secretary and a Democrat, wrote a newspaper column in February 2021 about the size of the $1.9 trillion Covid spending bill. Most of his own party ignored him. Within a year, food, gas and rent were rising at the fastest rate in about 40 years. What had Summers warned about?
answer: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
choices: Inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods
A slump from a package too small to restart hiring
A debt crisis as foreign buyers dumped US bonds
A stock bubble fed by the stimulus checks
context: Summers's February 4 2021 Washington Post op-ed argued that the size of the Biden fiscal package created substantial inflation risk. Fed officials publicly dismissed the warning. He was largely proven right within twelve months. Source: Washington Post (February 4 2021).

question: A shopper watched gas, groceries and rent climb all through 2021, while the Federal Reserve, led by Jerome Powell, went on saying the rise would fade on its own soon. The Fed then raised interest rates in a rush over the next two years. What lesson do many critics draw from that episode?
answer: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
choices: Officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it
Officials should raise rates at the first sign of any rise in prices
Officials can leave price spikes for supply chains to sort out alone
Officials do best when they say nothing in public about prices
context: Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on November 30 2021: 'I think it's probably a good time to retire that word.' CPI was already at 6.8% year-over-year that month. Source: Grokipedia 'Jerome Powell' (2026-09-05).

question: Jerome Powell repeated his calming story about prices through 2021, and it is now widely cited as the modern Fed's worst forecasting error: the peak reading came in at more than four times the Fed's own 2 percent target. What lesson does the Austrian tradition of Mises and Hayek draw about how central banks predict inflation?
answer: Central banks favour supply-shock stories that excuse them over money stories that blame them
choices: Central banks favour supply-shock stories that excuse them over money stories that blame them
Central banks always over-tighten in response to their own inflation forecasts
Central bank models predict inflation correctly within two years, give or take
Central bank forecasts are unbiased on average and only occasionally wrong
context: The transitory episode is a case study in institutional motivated reasoning: the Fed had run enormous QE and preferred an explanation that did not implicate its own actions. A recognition move about how central banks talk about inflation. Source: George Selgin, Cato Institute commentary (2022-23).

question: Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek asked a hard question of socialism between the wars: could a state committee price every good a country makes, from bread and steel to shoes and tractors, without any market of people buying and selling? What was their answer?
answer: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
choices: No -- without market prices, planners are flying blind
Yes -- committees always know best
Yes, if the committee has enough computers
Yes, as long as the leader is smart
context: Hoff (1895-1982) took his doctorate at the University of Oslo. Ohlin, Frisch, and Myrdal were other Nordic economists of the same generation but on different sides of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: M. A. Michael translated Trygve Hoff's 1938 Oslo dissertation into English in 1949, and William Hodge of London published it. Hoff had written on an old quarrel: whether central planners could set prices for a whole country with no real market to guide them. What was the English title?
answer: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
choices: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society
The Constitution of Liberty
The Road to Serfdom
Human Action
context: The Norwegian original was 'Okonomisk kalkulasjon i socialistiske samfund.' The 1949 English edition brought Hoff's argument to a wider audience just as Human Action was appearing. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff took up in 1938 an argument that had run since 1920: whether central planners could ever price goods as well as a market does. He defended Ludwig von Mises against Oskar Lange point by point. Which writings did he draw on?
answer: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
choices: German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together
The German Marxist literature alone
The Anglo-American Marshallian tradition alone
The French general-equilibrium school alone
context: Hoff defended Mises against Oskar Lange in careful detail, marshalling the German, English, and Soviet evidence. The book was in a real sense the definitive 1938 statement of the Austrian side of the debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Trygve Hoff wrote outspoken editorials in Farmand, the widely read free-market magazine he edited in Oslo, and they made him a marked man once Nazi Germany occupied Norway. He also ran a family business. What did his second career cost him during the war?
answer: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
choices: He was arrested by the Nazi occupation of Norway and spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp
He fled to neutral Sweden and taught at Stockholm University for the duration
He served as economic advisor to the Norwegian government-in-exile in London
He worked as a translator for the Allied forces in Iceland
context: Hoff edited the anti-Nazi magazine Farmand. Nazi occupation authorities arrested him for the editorship. He survived; after the war Farmand became a leading Nordic classical-liberal publication and Hoff a major figure in the small postwar European liberal revival. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Karl Brunner, a Swiss-born monetarist, wrote a fresh foreword for Trygve Hoff's 1938 book after it had gone out of print. An American institute devoted to the Austrian school of economics brought the book back into circulation. Which institute was it?
answer: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
choices: The Ludwig von Mises Institute
The Cato Institute
The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
The Bank for International Settlements
context: The foreword was written by Karl Brunner, the Swiss-born monetarist. The reprint made Hoff's careful pre-Hayek-1945 defense of Mises available to modern Austrian scholars for the first time in decades. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Trygve_Hoff.

question: Gordon Tullock placed a nine-page paper in the Western Economic Journal in 1967, after better-known journals had turned the paper down. He argued that the small shaded triangle every textbook drew for the cost of a monopoly was far too small. What title did he give the paper?
answer: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
choices: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft
The Political Economy of Redistribution
The Vote-Trading Machinery of Congress
The Calculus of Public Choice
context: Gordon Tullock, 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' (Western Economic Journal, June 1967, later renamed Economic Inquiry). It was initially rejected by more prestigious journals before finding a home. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Tullock 1967).

question: A firm stands to gain $100 million a year if Congress passes a steel tariff, in Gordon Tullock's 1967 example. It could pay lawyers, Washington representatives and campaign funds to make sure the vote goes its way. How much would it be willing to spend on them, by Tullock's reckoning?
answer: Up to $100 million per year
choices: Up to $100 million per year
About $1 million per year
About $10 million per year
Whatever the median firm spends
context: Tullock's insight: firms will burn real resources on the competition for privilege up to the full value of the privilege sought. If competing firms fight the tariff, they will burn resources on the other side. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: A burglar breaks into a house in one of Gordon Tullock's 1967 examples. What the thief carries off, Tullock argued, merely moves wealth between pockets, leaving the total unchanged. Where did he say society's real loss from theft lies?
answer: The resources spent on locks, alarms, guards and burglars' tools
choices: The resources spent on locks, alarms, guards and burglars' tools
The income the victim's insurer pays out on the claim
The fall in prices as stolen goods flood the market
The tax revenue lost when stolen goods are resold
context: Tullock's illustration: theft merely TRANSFERS wealth from victim to thief -- the total is unchanged. The real deadweight loss is the whole edifice of prevention and preparation on both sides. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967), section on theft.

question: Anne Krueger took Gordon Tullock's idea about wasted lobbying and measured it in 1974 in two developing countries, where firms spent almost the full value of an import licence trying to win one. Which was the larger of the two countries she studied?
answer: India
choices: India
Brazil
Mexico
Egypt
context: Krueger studied India's licence system, which allocated the right to import and to run many kinds of business, and Turkey's import licences; her estimates put the rents at a large share of national income in both. Source: Krueger, American Economic Review (1974).

question: Gordon Tullock put three unlike things under one roof in his 1967 paper: a firm handed a legal monopoly, a tariff on foreign steel passed by Congress, and an ordinary burglar breaking into a house. What shared feature makes all three cost society more than the textbook triangle shows?
answer: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
choices: Each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize
Each cuts output below what a free market would produce
Each simply shifts wealth from one owner to another
Each raises prices for buyers above the competitive level
context: Whenever there is a REDISTRIBUTIVE prize on offer -- a rent -- real economic inputs get burned competing for the prize rather than producing value. The productive economy loses those inputs. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967).

question: Gordon Tullock turned his eye in 1967 to skilled, well-paid people who spend whole days helping one group take money from another by working the rules of government. They produce no crops, no houses and no medicine, only paperwork and favors. Which job is the classic example?
answer: Lobbyists
choices: Lobbyists
Stockbrokers
Bankers
Insurance agents
context: Tullock argued that talented lawyers and lobbyists whose entire work was securing regulatory privilege were engaged in a socially wasteful zero-sum contest. The productive economy loses their talent. Source: Tullock, Western Economic Journal (1967); Baumol, Journal of Political Economy (1990) on productive vs unproductive entrepreneurship.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock argued in the 1960s that some policies invite far more lobbying for special favors than others, since a favor worth having draws real money and talent into the chase. Which policy design tends to cut that waste the most?
answer: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
choices: Broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens
Elaborate industry-specific carve-outs and case-by-case licenses
Discretionary agency waivers granted by senior political appointees
Rotating tax preferences renegotiated each Congress
context: Broad rules leave nothing worth lobbying over; carve-outs and discretion create rents. This is why constitutional political economy favors general rules and why Buchanan named 'generality' as a core principle. Source: Buchanan + Congleton, Politics by Principle, Not Interest (Cambridge 1998).

question: Milton Friedman proposed in 1962, in Capitalism and Freedom, to replace the tangle of American welfare programs with one clean idea. Everyone would file a normal tax return, and anyone below a set line would get a check from the Internal Revenue Service, the reverse of paying tax. What is that kind of tax called?
answer: A negative income tax
choices: A negative income tax
A luxury tax
A sales tax
A tariff
context: Friedman's motivation was administrative simplification and preservation of work incentives via a gradual known phase-out. It differed structurally from the modern UBI concept, which typically adds a universal payment on top of the existing safety net. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: Milton Friedman's critics warned that once checks started arriving under his plan, people would quit their jobs in droves. Four big American and Canadian trials put the idea to the test between 1968 and 1979, mailing cash to families below a set income line. What did the trials actually find about work hours?
answer: Modest cuts of roughly 5 to 13 percent for main earners
choices: Modest cuts of roughly 5 to 13 percent for main earners
Steep cuts of roughly half for main earners
No change at all for main earners
Gains of roughly 5 to 10 percent for main earners
context: The New Jersey/Pennsylvania (1968-72) and Seattle/Denver (1970-77) US experiments and the Manitoba MINCOME (1974-79) Canadian experiment all found modest work-hour declines with substantial administrative-cost savings over the multi-program comparison. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Negative_income_tax.

question: An Illinois resident began drawing $1,000 a month for three years in a trial funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch, one of 1,000 people paid that way there and in Texas. It was the largest recent US test of no-strings cash. When the results came out in August 2024, what did the study find about work hours?
answer: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
choices: Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
Recipients reduced work hours by roughly 13 to 14 hours per week
Recipients raised work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week
Recipients kept working exactly the hours they had before
context: The study also found modest health improvements and no clear positive employment outcomes despite proponent hopes. The findings largely echoed the 1970s NIT experiments' pattern of moderate labor-supply reductions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Milton Friedman, the Chicago economist, put forward a cash plan in the 1960s, and Andrew Yang put forward another in his 2020 campaign. Both would send money straight to people, and the likeness hides a difference in design that decides what each plan does to the state. What is the key difference?
answer: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
choices: The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them
The older plan pays in vouchers; the newer plan pays in cash
The older plan is run by the states; the newer plan by Washington
The older plan covers only workers; the newer plan covers retirees too
context: Friedman would have supported replacing programs with an NIT and opposed adding a UBI on top of them. The two proposals share a label but have opposite structural implications for the state's role and for the effective marginal tax rate facing the recipient as income rises. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Charles Murray, an American libertarian scholar, proposed in his 2006 book In Our Hands to send every adult American 10,000 dollars a year. Social Security, Medicare, food stamps, housing aid and unemployment insurance all figure in how he would pay for it. What makes his plan different from an add-on plan?
answer: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
choices: It replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment
It pays only adults who hold a job of some kind
It goes only to families raising young children
It is funded by a new national tax on every sale
context: The Murray design is a UBI in label but an NIT in structure -- a flat universal payment that eliminates the existing multi-program stack. Same-label proposals with different phase-out and replacement structures produce very different outcomes. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: A Republican governor of one American state won his voters over in 1976 to setting aside a big share of the state's oil-royalty money in a special investment account. From 1982 the account paid every resident, men, women and children, a yearly cash dividend, some years a few hundred dollars and some years over two thousand, the longest-running cash-dividend program in the country. Which state runs it?
answer: Alaska
choices: Alaska
Texas
Wyoming
Oklahoma
context: The Alaska Permanent Fund was created in 1976 and the Dividend program began payouts in 1982. Every Alaskan resident (regardless of income) receives the annual share. It is the closest real-world US analogue of a UBI. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Alaska_Permanent_Fund.

question: A student asks a public-choice economist whether a monthly government check to every adult is 'obviously a good idea.' The economist refuses to answer yes or no. He sets two proposals side by side, Charles Murray's and Andrew Yang's, which share one name and differ in what they do to the programs already running. Which reasoning move is he pressing?
answer: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
choices: Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results
Judge a plan by its aims, not its rules; plans with one name share one goal
Ask who backs a plan, not what it says; a plan is as good as its sponsors
Trust the trials, not the design; only an experiment can rank two plans
context: This is Sowell's 'there are no solutions, only tradeoffs' at the policy-design level. A UBI on top of existing programs has different effects from an NIT that replaces them, and the move is to look under the label at the actual mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Basic_income.

question: Congress passed the Agricultural Act in 1949, ordering the federal government to prop up the price of one favorite farm product by buying any surplus and storing it. That program has kept running for over 70 years, protecting one specific industry. Which farm product does the government prop up?
answer: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
choices: Milk (and derivative dairy products)
Wheat only
Corn only
Soybeans only
context: The federal purchases were made largely as butter and processed cheese, which stored better than fluid milk. The program has been renamed and modified many times but the above-market-support core has persisted for 75+ years. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: A Department of Agriculture official looking over the federal stocks in 1981 saw a mountain of one dairy product, aging in giant refrigerated caves and warehouses across Wisconsin, Missouri and Kansas. Decades of dairy price supports had bought up all the extra milk American farmers made. Which item did the government have, and roughly how much?
answer: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
choices: Over 500 million pounds of processed cheese
About 10,000 pounds of yogurt
About 5 million pounds of ice cream
About 100 million pounds of powdered milk only
context: The stockpile became a national embarrassment. Congressional hearings and press coverage forced action; the Reagan administration began a distribution program the same year. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: Ronald Reagan's administration began handing huge yellow blocks of surplus federal food to food banks in 1981, rather than throw them away. The dairy price-support program had bought so much extra milk that federal warehouses were overflowing. The blocks became so common in poor neighborhoods that a new phrase entered American speech. What was the phrase?
answer: 'Government cheese'
choices: 'Government cheese'
'Federal butter'
'Reagan powder'
'The white brick'
context: The loaves were shelf-stable pasteurized processed cheese food. The distribution continued through the 1990s and became a cultural touchstone in low-income neighborhoods (referenced in hip-hop and stand-up comedy). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Government_cheese.

question: Congress rewrote the dairy rules in the 2014 Farm Bill, after 65 years of buying up surplus milk under the 1949 Agricultural Act. Farmers stayed protected above market prices, but a new insurance-style scheme paid a farmer whenever the gap between his milk price and his feed bill dropped below a level he chose. What did the 2014 Farm Bill put in the old program's place?
answer: The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) system
choices: The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) system
A federal ban on all dairy subsidies
A privatized dairy futures exchange
A European-Union-style quota auction
context: DMC pays farmers when the margin between milk price and feed cost falls below a chosen threshold. The mechanism is different from bulk purchase but the underlying above-market income guarantee for dairy producers persists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Milk_price_support.

question: Hugo Chavez won power in Venezuela in 1999 on a promise of socialism for a new century, and his government fixed the prices of food and fuel. Shopkeepers had to sell at those prices or face jail, though they often failed to cover what the goods cost to make or import. What did shoppers run into?
answer: Widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine
choices: Widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine
Plentiful cheap flour, chicken, toilet paper and medicine
A flood of cheap food smuggled in from Colombia
Steady supplies at the legal price as shops obeyed
context: Chavez ruled Venezuela from 1999 to 2013 and built the model his successor Maduro inherited. Producers facing prices below their costs cut output, and shelves emptied. The government blamed a 'capitalist conspiracy' and sent soldiers to force shops to sell at controlled prices.

question: A grocer raised his prices again and again through 2018 as Nicolas Maduro's government kept printing bolivars. Venezuela's own central bank, silent for about three years, published its figure for 2018 in May 2019. About how fast did it say prices had climbed that year?
answer: About 130,000% per year
choices: About 130,000% per year
About 500% per year
About 25% per year
About 3,000,000% per year
context: Venezuela's central bank put 2018 inflation at 130,060% in May 2019; the International Monetary Fund's estimate for the year, about 1.37 million percent, was some ten times higher. By 2019 a wheelbarrow of banknotes was needed for basic groceries -- the Weimar image replayed a century later, in Latin America. Source: business-standard.com (May 29 2019); gulfnews.com (May 30 2019); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Venezuela.

question: A Venezuelan family packed what it could carry and set off on foot for Colombia, leaving a country that had once been middle-income. By 2024 the United Nations was tracking one of the largest peacetime exoduses in modern history. About what share of the country had left?
answer: About one quarter, some 7.7 million people
choices: About one quarter, some 7.7 million people
About one tenth, about 3 million people
About half, about 15 million people
About one twentieth, about 1.5 million people
context: The 7.7 million displaced Venezuelans make this the largest displacement crisis in modern Western Hemisphere history -- larger than any war-driven displacement in Latin American history. Neighbors like Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, and Chile have absorbed the majority. Source: Grokipedia 'Venezuelan refugee crisis' (2026-09-05).

question: A shopkeeper in Venezuela began quoting his prices in a foreign currency he trusted more than the bolivar, though no law told him to. Millions of other Venezuelans found their own ways around the wrecked national money. What did the country end up doing?
answer: Pricing goods in US dollars, paid with remittances sent by relatives abroad
choices: Pricing goods in US dollars, paid with remittances sent by relatives abroad
Pricing goods in the petro, the state's own oil-backed token
Pricing goods in Chinese yuan, earned through the state's oil deals
Pricing goods in euros, sent home by Venezuelans working in Spain
context: Bodegas quietly priced goods in US dollars, and many families lived on Zelle transfers and other remittances from relatives abroad. The Venezuelan economy dollarized from below, without any legal change; the state's petro token never caught on. Source: Grokipedia 'Economy of Venezuela' (2026-09-05).

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that a socialist economy cannot allocate resources rationally without market prices to signal scarcity, and for most of the next century his critics called the claim untestable. Mao's famines and the Soviet collapse took place behind closed borders, hard to see even for those inside. Venezuela's collapse was filmed on phones as it happened, a short flight from Miami. Which move did the Venezuelan case sharpen?
answer: The calculation problem is no abstract dispute; it is a current, observable fact
choices: The calculation problem is no abstract dispute; it is a current, observable fact
Price controls always eventually work if enforced hard enough
Central planning is a good idea in principle but hard to execute in practice
Modern digital tools solve the calculation problem central planners once faced
context: The Mises argument that seemed like a theoretical dispute in 1920 became a public fact playing out on smartphone video. Old newsreels of Soviet or Maoist collapse are historical footage; Venezuela is on YouTube in Spanish that Google Translate handles instantly, so a Western student can watch the calculation problem play out in real time.

question: A young Venezuelan set up a cryptocurrency mining rig at home during the country's collapse in the late 2010s. Prices for most goods rose thousands of percent a year, but one resource stayed extremely cheap, because the government kept its consumer price well beneath what it cost the state to produce. Which resource did he use to earn Bitcoin?
answer: Electricity
choices: Electricity
Gasoline
Bottled cooking gas
Tap water
context: By 2018 Venezuela had one of the largest per-capita Bitcoin-mining populations in Latin America. Cheap electricity plus hyperinflation made mining locally-generated sound money one of the most rational responses available to a Venezuelan saver. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: Nicolas Maduro's government cut Bitcoin mining off Venezuela's national power grid in May 2024, citing the strain on electricity supply. Bitcoin had long let Venezuelans store savings outside state control. What had his government done to the country's miners in the years before?
answer: Sent police to raid mining operations and seize rigs
choices: Sent police to raid mining operations and seize rigs
Legalized Bitcoin as a second national currency alongside the bolivar
Offered miners a tax holiday to keep their rigs running
Made owning Bitcoin a crime punishable by prison
context: Police raided mining operations and seized rigs through the late 2010s, and in May 2024 the electricity ministry began cutting mining farms off the national grid. Owning Bitcoin stayed legal. Source: cointelegraph.com/news/venezuela-bans-crypto-mining-to-protect-power-grid.

question: A Venezuelan family opened a box of rice, oil, cornmeal and canned fish in the late 2010s, after private stores could no longer stock food at the mandated prices. Nicolas Maduro's government handed out such subsidized boxes through neighborhood committees loyal to the ruling party, and the boxes took their name from those committees. What is the Spanish acronym?
answer: CLAP
choices: CLAP
PSUV
PDVAL
MERCAL
context: CLAP stands for Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion, 'Local Committees for Supply and Production.' The boxes typically contained rice, cornmeal, oil, sugar, and canned goods, and distribution was controlled by neighborhood collectives loyal to the ruling PSUV party. PDVAL and Mercal were earlier state food chains. When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something became political loyalty. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CLAP_(Venezuela).

question: Reuters and New York Times journalists reported on the subsidized grocery boxes Nicolas Maduro's government handed to poor families after Venezuela ran out of food under socialist central planning. Families whose block did not vote for Maduro's Socialist United Party, they found, quietly stopped receiving them. What political use of government-controlled food does the program reveal?
answer: It can be used as a tool to force people to support the ruling party
choices: It can be used as a tool to force people to support the ruling party
It always reaches families faster than private stores could
It costs the government less than letting people shop for themselves
It ends up giving every family the same amount of food
context: Opposition figures and reporters for Reuters and the New York Times documented the loyalty condition between 2016 and 2019. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Comit%C3%A9_Local_de_Abastecimiento_y_Producci%C3%B3n.

question: Two authors, a Venezuelan software engineer and an American economist, wrote 'The Venezuelan Cryptocurrency Boom' for the Human Rights Foundation in 2019. Their case study documented how ordinary Venezuelans, not speculators or day traders, used Bitcoin to escape hyperinflation, receive help from relatives abroad and hold savings the government could not seize or inflate away. Who wrote that report?
answer: Alejandro Machado and Jill Carlson
choices: Alejandro Machado and Jill Carlson
Michael Saylor and Cathie Wood
Vitalik Buterin and Charles Hoskinson
Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison
context: The report catalogued how Bitcoin (and Ethereum) let Venezuelans preserve savings, receive remittances, and transact outside the bolivar. It became one of the standard cited sources on the Venezuelan case in Bitcoin policy debate. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: Ludwig von Mises argued in 1920 that when a government destroys market prices, something else has to decide who gets what, since goods do not allocate themselves. Venezuela's split economy showed what that 'something else' looks like in practice. Which two things filled the gap that prices used to fill?
answer: The underground global market via Bitcoin, and political loyalty via CLAP
choices: The underground global market via Bitcoin, and political loyalty via CLAP
World Bank grants, and IMF-funded imports
A restored gold standard, and barter networks in coffee
Chinese state loans, and Colombian food aid
context: Two allocation mechanisms for a country whose market prices had ceased to function: hard-money exit for the technically skilled, party-loyalty allocation for everyone else. The Austrian-tradition prediction was that suppressed prices would reappear as SOMETHING; Venezuela made the something visible. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bitcoin_in_Venezuela.

question: A government tells every grocer in the country to sell milk for one dollar a gallon. But the farmer's feed, labor and refrigerated trucks already cost more than a dollar before the store shelves it. Every gallon sold is a loss, and store owners are not stupid. What happens to the milk supply on the shelves?
answer: There will be a shortage -- milk will disappear from shelves
choices: There will be a shortage -- milk will disappear from shelves
There will be a glut -- unsold milk will pile up on shelves
Supply holds steady -- farmers will cut their costs to match
Supply holds steady -- the law will make stores keep selling
context: Nicolas Maduro won the April 14, 2013 special election following Chavez's death on March 5, 2013. He extended and later expanded price controls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Maduro.

question: A news crew in Venezuela filmed a line that stretched around the block in 2013, all for one basic household product. Nicolas Maduro's government had tightened the price caps it inherited from Hugo Chavez, and in January 2014 it capped hundreds of everyday goods by law. The product became a global symbol of the crisis. What were Venezuelans queueing for?
answer: Toilet paper
choices: Toilet paper
Coffee
Sugar
Salt
context: The 2013 Venezuelan toilet-paper shortage became a symbol of the price-control-induced supply collapse. Flour, cooking oil, milk, rice, and soap also disappeared -- but toilet paper became the political news story. Source: reuters.com Venezuela shortage coverage 2013.

question: A shopper bought capped goods in a Venezuelan state store and sold them on outside at their true prices, on a black market Venezuelans called bachaqueo. Nicolas Maduro's government answered not by raising the caps but by installing a biometric machine at every state-store checkout, so that no one could draw the same quota twice. What kind of system did Venezuela install?
answer: A fingerprint-indexed rationing system
choices: A fingerprint-indexed rationing system
A retinal-scan purchase system
A voice-recognition allocation tool
A national ID card with QR codes
context: The Sistema Biometrico put fingerprint scanners at state supermarket checkouts to limit how often each shopper could buy the same price-capped goods. It was the government's answer to the bachaqueo resale market. Source: bbc.com Venezuela biometric rationing.

question: Hugo Chavez froze prices, and Nicolas Maduro went on to ration goods at state stores and then to hand out food boxes by loyalty to the ruling party. Every step replaced ordinary market pricing with a new state mechanism. Austrian economists read the chain through Ludwig von Mises's 1920 paper on socialist economies. What core point does it teach?
answer: When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something becomes political power
choices: When market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something becomes political power
When market prices are abolished, demand falls away -- and the shortages soon cure themselves
When market prices are abolished, producers cooperate -- and supply soon rises to meet need
When market prices are abolished, state revenue rises -- and it pays for the goods the shops lack
context: The chain: price controls -> supply withdrawal -> queues -> rationing -> political-loyalty allocation. When the price mechanism is suppressed, allocation becomes political, and the CLAP boxes made this literal. Source: mises.org/library/venezuela.

question: A historian of Venezuela's ruin refuses the story that price controls alone destroyed the country. The shortages, he grants, began before the sanctions and tracked the enforcement of the law. But he points to other blows that hit the country as well. What does the standard honest accounting count?
answer: Oil-price collapse 2014, sanctions from 2017, monetary chaos
choices: Oil-price collapse 2014, sanctions from 2017, monetary chaos
An IMF bailout in 2018, a coffee blight, a run on the peso
A 2014 earthquake, a locust plague, a border war with Guyana
A 2015 hurricane, a copper-price crash, an invasion from Colombia
context: The full picture includes the 2014 oil price collapse, US sanctions escalating from 2017, and monetary emission chaos. The Fair Price Law's supply-collapse effect began before major sanctions and tracked enforcement of the law itself. Source: piie.com Venezuela analysis.

question: A Russian shopkeeper lost the right to run his own store after the communist takeover of 1917. From then on the state alone decided what each shop would sell and at what price, and later communist countries copied the plan. What usually happens to food and other everyday goods on the shelves?
answer: Shelves get emptier and lines get longer
choices: Stores fill up with new products
Shelves get emptier and lines get longer
Prices drop for everyone
People get more choices at lower prices
context: The Fall of Saigon on April 30, 1975 ended the Vietnam War. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976 after reunification. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Saigon.

question: Vietnam's new rulers in Hanoi arrested former South Vietnamese officials, soldiers, teachers and Catholic priests after April 1975 and sent them to sites deep in the jungle. Some were held only a few weeks. Others endured more than 15 years of forced labor, hunger and political lectures. What did the government call these places?
answer: Re-education camps
choices: Re-education camps
Reeducation prisons
Labor communes
Retraining schools
context: Vietnamese hoc tap cai tao (re-education camps) held an estimated 1-2.5 million people between 1975 and the mid-1980s. Vietnam's own government has admitted over 165,000 deaths in the system. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-education_camp_(Vietnam).

question: An ethnic-Chinese merchant family of Saigon crowded at night into a tiny wooden fishing vessel, after Vietnam's new communist government had seized its shop. Hundreds of thousands of others fled the same way, across the South China Sea toward Thailand, Malaysia or Hong Kong. What common name did the world give these refugees?
answer: The Boat People
choices: The Boat People
The Sea Refugees
The Vietnam Diaspora
The Mekong Exiles
context: About 800,000 Vietnamese fled by sea in unseaworthy craft between 1975 and 1990, and the UN refugee agency puts the deaths at sea at 200,000 or more. The exodus was concentrated in 1978-79 following the state seizure of Chinese-Vietnamese commerce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_boat_people.

question: Hanoi's planners took every decision about the rice crop out of Vietnamese farmers' hands after the communist takeover of 1975. The country had grown rice for centuries, yet within a decade it was running short. In 1986 the government tried a big reform. What single change most likely ended the rice shortage?
answer: Letting farmers grow, sell, and price their own rice
choices: Letting farmers grow, sell, and price their own rice
Importing more fertilizer and tractors from the Soviet Union
Merging small collectives into larger state rice farms
Printing more money so families could afford to buy rice
context: Doi Moi (renovation) restored household farming, legalized private enterprise, permitted foreign investment, and deregulated prices. Vietnam became a rice exporter within three years and joined the WTO in 2007. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doi_Moi.

question: A rice farmer in the Mekong Delta left his collective farm after the Communist Party launched its package of reforms in 1986. Within a few years the country's place in the world rice trade had changed completely from the 1970s and early 80s. What happened by 1989 or 1990?
answer: It became a rice exporter
choices: It became a rice exporter
It doubled its rice imports
It banned all rice exports
It rationed rice more tightly
context: Vietnam went from chronic rice shortage in the mid-1980s to net rice exporter within three years of the 1986 reforms. By the 2000s it was among the world's top three rice exporters. Same land, same farmers, market prices restored. Source: worldbank.org Vietnam data.

question: The Communist Party in Hanoi watched prices rise more than fivefold in 1986, after a botched currency reform the year before, and it finally had to admit that its Soviet-style planning had failed to feed the country. That December it launched market reforms that let farmers keep and sell their own crops. What did the Party name these reforms?
answer: Doi Moi
choices: Doi Moi
Perestroika
The Great Leap
Shock Therapy
