context: Vietnam's inflation rose from about 92 percent in 1985 to several hundred percent in 1986 (estimates run from about 450 to 775 percent), after the reform of prices, wages and money of September 1985. The reforms brought inflation under 40 percent within three years. Source: World Bank Vietnam data; hkcer.hku.hk/Letters/v35/rriedel.htm.

question: Communist rulers pushed the whole of Vietnam into collective farming and food rationing after unifying the country in 1975. Rice output collapsed, and by the early 1980s Vietnam was importing rice to feed its own people. Then came the reforms of 1986, and before long the picture had reversed. In the socialist calculation debate, Mises and Hayek against the central planners, what does this Vietnamese story teach?
answer: The same farmers can go from famine to export within a few years once prices return
choices: The same farmers can go from famine to export within a few years once prices return
Only foreign aid can lift a country out of shortage
Central planning succeeds if run long enough
Market prices work only in industrial economies
context: Same land, same farmers, chronic shortage before 1986; rice-exporter within three years after. The Vietnamese case is the smaller-scale confirmation of the Chinese Reform-and-Opening pattern. Source: mises.org/library/vietnam-reforms.

question: A husband and wife opened a little workshop for research at Indiana University, in the town of Bloomington, in 1973. They studied how villages, cities and local governments actually solve shared problems, such as policing, water and forests, instead of assuming one central boss on top. Who was this husband-and-wife team?
answer: Vincent and Elinor Ostrom
choices: Vincent and Elinor Ostrom
Milton and Rose Friedman
James and Anne Buchanan
Friedrich and Helene Hayek
context: Vincent Ostrom (1919-2012) was a political scientist; Elinor Ostrom (1933-2012) was an economist who won the Nobel Prize in 2009 for her commons research. Both died in June 2012 within weeks of each other. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom studied city councils, school boards, water districts and courts, each with its own authority, instead of one boss on top telling everyone what to do. He co-founded the Bloomington School with his wife Elinor. What did he call these many-center systems?
answer: Polycentric political systems
choices: Polycentric political systems
Monocentric political systems
Corporatist political systems
Consociational political systems
context: The term captures Ostrom's core intuition: federalism, overlapping jurisdictions, and multiple service providers each performing part of a governance function. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: Three scholars wrote a paper in 1961 for the American Political Science Review that became a founding document for the modern study of local government. It argued that a patchwork of many little local governments in a metropolitan area could work better than one big consolidated one. One author was the political scientist Vincent Ostrom. Who were his two co-authors?
answer: Charles Tiebout and Robert Warren
choices: Charles Tiebout and Robert Warren
James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
Milton Friedman and George Stigler
Ronald Coase and Douglass North
context: The paper, 'The Organization of Government in Metropolitan Areas: A Theoretical Inquiry,' attacked the 1950s metropolitan-consolidation movement by showing that fragmented local governments often performed better than consolidated ones. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: American urban reformers of the mid-1900s pressed a plan for the big cities and their suburbs, and Vincent Ostrom and two co-authors took aim at it in 1961. Their paper stood up for the patchwork of small towns and special districts around those cities. Which movement was the paper fighting?
answer: The metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged
choices: The metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged
The federal-revenue-sharing movement, which held that Washington should send block grants to states
The zoning-relaxation movement, which held that local land-use rules should be repealed
The public-broadcasting movement, which held that municipal radio should replace commercial media
context: The consolidation view had held that thousands of cities, school districts, and water districts in American metropolitan areas were inefficient and should be merged. Ostrom's team showed empirically that fragmented systems often had more responsive service delivery, more experimentation, and more citizen exit-and-voice options. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polycentric_governance.

question: Vincent Ostrom turned his many-centers framework in 1971 on one landmark case in the history of politics. He argued that its makers had set out to arrange power so that no single ruler ever sat on top. Which case did the 1971 book focus on?
answer: The American founders' federal design for the United States
choices: The American founders' federal design for the United States
The Swiss founders' federal design for the cantons of Switzerland
The Dutch rebels' federal design for the United Provinces
The Allies' federal design for postwar West Germany
context: The Federalist Papers (Publius) were Ostrom's core primary sources. He argued the founders had deliberately chosen multiple layers of government with separately-derived authorities over the alternative of unified national government. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom spent his last books, in the 1990s, measuring American government against the design he had found in the Federalist Papers, with the New Deal and the Great Society long behind it. He ended with a warning about where the country was headed. What did he warn was happening?
answer: Centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders designed
choices: Centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders designed
Fragmentation was leaving the federal system too divided to govern a modern nation
Rival local governments were racing one another to the bottom on taxes and services
Direct democracy was displacing the representative republic the founders designed
context: Ostrom saw the New Deal, Great Society, and post-9/11 security-state expansions as a long-run drift away from the American founders' polycentric design. The 1997 book carried a Tocquevillean warning: democracies whose polycentric structure is dismantled become vulnerable to collapse. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Elinor Ostrom, Vincent's wife, showed that villages, fishing communities and irrigation groups around the world successfully manage shared pastures, forests and water without either state ownership or private property. She became, in 2009, the first woman ever to win a specific top prize in economics. Which prize did she win?
answer: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences
choices: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences
The John Bates Clark Medal in economics
The Frisch Medal of the Econometric Society
The Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics
context: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize is the economics prize given with the Nobels, and Elinor Ostrom was the first woman to win it. Her work on the commons demonstrated that community self-governance often solves resource-management problems that neither pure state ownership nor pure private ownership handles well. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Elinor_Ostrom.

question: Vincent Ostrom outlived one blow by just seventeen days. He had spent his career studying how ordinary communities govern their shared resources without top-down control, and he passed away on June 29, 2012. What had happened seventeen days before?
answer: His wife and fellow scholar, Elinor Ostrom, had died
choices: His wife and fellow scholar, Elinor Ostrom, had died
His research workshop at Indiana had been shut down
His colleague James Buchanan had died that same month
The Nobel committee had withdrawn Elinor's 2009 prize
context: The two co-founders of the Bloomington School died within weeks of each other -- unusual for a scholarly couple who had shared a research program for 40 years. The Ostrom Workshop at Indiana continues today under that name. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Vincent_Ostrom.

question: Joseph Stalin's officials stripped Ukrainian villages of grain in the early 1930s, and millions of peasants starved to death. Walter Duranty, the New York Times Moscow bureau chief, kept writing that no famine was happening, and readers around the world believed him. Whose interests did his false reporting help most?
answer: The government causing the famine
choices: The starving families in villages
Other reporters trying to tell the truth
The government causing the famine
Foreign shoppers buying that country's grain
context: Walter Duranty (1884-1957) was the New York Times Moscow correspondent 1922-36. His friendly coverage of Stalin's Five-Year Plan won the 1932 Pulitzer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty.

question: Walter Duranty told his American readers in March 1933 that reports of famine were made up, at the peak of Stalin's man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine. In place of the plain word 'famine', he used a soft, technical-sounding phrase for the mass starvation. What phrase did he use?
answer: Widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition
choices: Widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition
Regional agricultural disruption
Temporary supply reallocation
Isolated harvest shortfalls
context: Duranty's March 1933 New York Times phrasing -- 'there is no actual starvation or deaths from starvation, but there is widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition' -- became the emblematic euphemism-sentence of press cover-up. Source: New York Times, March 31, 1933.

question: A young Welsh journalist held a press conference in Berlin in March 1933. He had just walked on foot across Soviet Ukraine, without any state minder, and had seen village after village of peasants starving under Stalin's grain seizures, while Walter Duranty of the New York Times kept denying any famine. What was the Welshman's surname?
answer: Jones
choices: Jones
Muggeridge
Chamberlin
Lyons
context: Gareth Jones (1905-35), former private secretary to David Lloyd George, walked through Ukraine in March 1933 and published his account at a Berlin press conference on March 29, 1933. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist).

question: Walter Duranty of the New York Times fired back in print two days after a young Welsh journalist broke the news of the Ukrainian famine at a Berlin press conference in March 1933. Duranty had spent years telling American readers that Stalin's Soviet Union was working well. Now he had to answer a reporter who had walked through the starving villages himself. What did Duranty call the report?
answer: A big scare story
choices: A big scare story
A well-intentioned mistake
A partisan exaggeration
A regional oddity
context: Duranty's New York Times article of 31 March 1933, 'Russians Hungry, But Not Starving', dismissed the reports as part of 'a big scare story in the American press'. Jones answered in a letter to the editor pointing out he had walked the ground, unaccompanied. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty.

question: A young Welsh reporter walked into Soviet Ukraine on foot in March 1933 and found village after village starving. He told the story from Berlin the moment he crossed out, and the Soviet government banned him from ever entering the country again. Why does a government punish a reporter for telling the truth about a famine?
answer: The truth would show that the government's own policies caused the famine
choices: The truth would show that the government's own policies caused the famine
The truth would start a panic and a run on the state's grain stores
The truth would tempt foreign armies to strike while the country was weak
The truth would scare the remaining farmers into fleeing their land
context: The Soviet authorities banned Gareth Jones from returning after his Berlin press conference of 29 March 1933. Stalin's government denied that any famine existed, since admitting it meant admitting what its grain seizures had done. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Jones_(journalist).

question: Members of the Pulitzer Board sat down in 2003, after decades of protest by Ukrainian-American groups, to review a prize of 1932. Walter Duranty of The New York Times had won it for glowing reporting in 1931 on Stalin's five-year plan, and he went on to deny the Ukraine famine that killed millions of peasants. What did the Board decide?
answer: It found the work fell seriously short but declined to withdraw the prize
choices: It found the work fell seriously short but declined to withdraw the prize
It found the work deliberately deceptive and withdrew the prize at once
It found the work sound by the standards of 1931 and let the prize stand
It made no finding and left the decision to Columbia's trustees
context: The Board's statement of 21 November 2003 said that Duranty's 1931 work, measured by today's standards for foreign reporting, falls seriously short, but that there was not clear and convincing evidence of deliberate deception, the relevant standard in this case. The prize-winning articles predate the famine. Source: pulitzer.org/news/statement-walter-duranty.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin in 2009 on an idea that Wei Dai and other cypherpunks had circled for a decade. Their question was who, or what, decides how much of a money exists. What did their designs share with Bitcoin?
answer: The money's supply is fixed by math, not by a person deciding
choices: The money's supply is fixed by math, not by a person deciding
The money's supply is set by a vote of the network's users
The money's supply follows a store of gold held in trust
The money's supply grows with the number of people using it
context: Wei Dai wrote the Crypto++ library and posted b-money in November 1998. Back wrote Hashcash; Szabo drafted bit gold; Finney wrote RPOW. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei_Dai.

question: Wei Dai built a free library of strong ciphers long before Bitcoin existed, and he still keeps it up for other programmers to drop into their own applications. What is the library called?
answer: Crypto++
choices: Crypto++
OpenSSL
BouncyCastle
libsodium
context: Wei Dai's library is Crypto++. OpenSSL, BouncyCastle, and libsodium are separate popular crypto libraries with different authors. Source: https://www.cryptopp.com/.

question: Wei Dai posted a two-page plan to a cypherpunk mailing list in November 1998. It sketched a digital cash with no bank and no government in the middle. What did Dai name it?
answer: b-money
choices: b-money
bit gold
Hashcash
DigiCash
context: Wei Dai's b-money was posted in November 1998; the text is only about two pages long. Bit gold is Szabo's separate proposal; Hashcash is Back's 1997 anti-spam scheme; DigiCash is Chaum's 1989 company. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Wei Dai left the master ledger off every server when he designed b-money in 1998, breaking with earlier digital cash, which had depended on a trusted issuer. He gave each user a job instead. What was the job?
answer: Maintain a separate private copy of every user's balances
choices: Maintain a separate private copy of every user's balances
Keep only his own balance and trust the others to report theirs
Take a turn, one user a day, holding the single shared ledger
Approve each payment by a vote before it entered the record
context: In b-money every participant maintains a separate database of how much money belongs to each pseudonym and updates it from signed transactions broadcast to everyone. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Wei Dai admitted in an appendix to his b-money paper of 1998 that one part of the design worried him. Computer technology, he noted, advances fast and not always in public. Which part did he call one of the more problematic?
answer: Money creation, since every account keeper had to agree on a computation's cost
choices: Money creation, since every account keeper had to agree on a computation's cost
Privacy, since a payment could be traced back to the payer's real name
Contracts, since nothing could force a cheating party to pay his fine
Storage, since no single computer could hold the record of every account
context: The appendix reads: 'One of the more problematic parts in the b-money protocol is money creation.' Every account keeper had to agree on the cost of particular computations, and that cost shifts as computing advances. Bitcoin later fixed the issue of new coins on a schedule written into its code. Source: https://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto emailed a paper on Halloween 2008 to a cryptography mailing list, describing Bitcoin, an electronic money that needed no bank. Its reference list opens with an earlier cypherpunk proposal, cited ahead of everything else. Which proposal is Reference 1?
answer: Wei Dai's b-money
choices: Wei Dai's b-money
Adam Back's Hashcash
Nick Szabo's bit gold
Chaum's DigiCash
context: Reference 1 of the Bitcoin white paper is Wei Dai's b-money. Hashcash is Reference 6; bit gold and DigiCash are not cited. Source: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto wrote to Wei Dai in August 2008, months before the Bitcoin white paper went out, and the emails are now public. Ten years earlier Dai had posted b-money, a sketch of a digital cash with no bank behind it. What did Satoshi ask him?
answer: The year b-money was published, so that he could cite it
choices: The year b-money was published, so that he could cite it
Whether Dai would join him as the paper's co-author
Whether Dai would help pay for the network's first servers
Whether Dai would keep the coming paper a secret
context: Satoshi's email of 22 August 2008 says he needs the year of publication of the b-money page for the citation in his paper; Dai replied that b-money was announced on the cypherpunks list in 1998. Source: https://www.gwern.net/docs/bitcoin/2008-nakamoto.

question: Officials at the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank, kept printing paper marks after World War 1 to pay the country's huge reparations debts, instead of raising taxes. By 1923 the presses were running day and night. What happened to prices in German shops?
answer: Prices went up so fast that money became almost worthless
choices: Prices went up so fast that money became almost worthless
Prices rose a little, at about the pace wages rose each year
Prices fell, because shops had more cash with which to buy stock
Prices held steady, because the government fixed them by law
context: The Reichsbank was Germany's central bank from 1876 to 1948. Under Weimar-era pressure it printed paper marks -- Papiermark -- until the 1923 collapse. Source: Grokipedia 'Reichsbank' (2026-09-05).

question: German families fed bundles of paper marks into their kitchen stoves in the autumn of 1923. A dollar that had bought about 190 marks in January 1922 now bought about 25 billion. Why did they burn their money?
answer: The notes were cheaper to burn than the firewood they could buy
choices: The notes were cheaper to burn than the firewood they could buy
The government had ordered all old notes destroyed by the winter
The notes were forgeries, and holding them had become a crime
Burning the old notes earned each family a refund from the state
context: A dollar bought about 190 paper marks in January 1922 and about 25 billion by October 1923, and at the peak prices doubled every few days. A bundle of notes would buy less fuel than it gave off as heat. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: A worker in Weimar Germany drew the first of his two daily wages one morning in 1923 and hurried to the shops by midday to beat the afternoon price. Photographers caught one scene from those months of hyperinflation that became the classic picture of a money collapse. What did that photograph show?
answer: A wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread
choices: A wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread
A queue of savers outside a shut bank
A crowd of strikers at the Reichsbank
A row of cold, smokeless factory chimneys
context: Photographers documented Berliners pushing wheelbarrows of paper marks to bakeries. Children built block towers out of bundled 100,000-mark notes because paper had less use-value than firewood. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: A woman in Weimar Germany left her shopping basket on the sidewalk for a moment during the hyperinflation of 1923, as one famous anecdote has it. When she came back, one thing had been stolen and one had been left behind in disgust. What had happened to her basket and her money?
answer: The basket was stolen; the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk
choices: The basket was stolen; the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk
The money was stolen; the basket was left where it stood
The vegetables were stolen; the money was left in the basket
The basket was refilled; the money was replaced with newer notes
context: By late 1923 a woven basket was worth more than the paper banknotes it carried. The anecdote circulates in memoirs and later histories as a compressed image of what hyperinflation does to the use-value of a currency. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: Hjalmar Schacht, Germany's currency commissioner, brought out the Rentenmark in November 1923 to replace the almost worthless paper mark. Workers who had begged to be paid twice a day trusted the fresh money almost overnight. Why did they trust it?
answer: The new currency was tied to something real and could not just be printed at will
choices: The new currency was tied to something real and could not just be printed at will
The new currency was guaranteed by the Allies, who promised to redeem it in gold
The new currency came with a law that cancelled Germany's reparations debts
The new currency was printed in larger notes that were far harder to forge
context: Schacht became commissioner for national currency in November 1923 and later Reichsbank president. The Rentenmark was secured on German land and industry and issued in strictly limited amounts, at one Rentenmark to a trillion paper marks, and it ended the hyperinflation within weeks. Source: Grokipedia 'Hjalmar Schacht' (2026-09-05).

question: A German pensioner counted up what he had left as the hyperinflation of 1921 to 1923 finally ended. Germans in every walk of life had suffered, but one group was crushed almost completely. Its bank accounts, life-insurance policies and pensions, all counted in old paper marks, had become worthless. Which group was it?
answer: The middle class of professionals and small savers
choices: The middle class of professionals and small savers
The urban working class of factory hands and laborers
The rural peasantry of small farmers and their families
The industrial magnates of the Ruhr and their partners
context: A retired doctor with a lifetime of savings in mark-denominated bonds was destroyed. A day laborer paid weekly was less devastated because he could spend before prices rose again. Rural farmers with real assets did comparatively well. The destruction was asymmetric. Source: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' (2026-09-05).

question: A German with a heavy mortgage watched the hyperinflation of 1923 shrink his debt to almost nothing, while his neighbor's pension went the same way. People who held farmland often came out ahead too. Austrian economists press one specific point about so uneven a pattern. What point is it?
answer: It is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction, playing out in real time
choices: It is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction, playing out in real time
It is Say's law working through wage stickiness
It is Ricardian equivalence collapsing under debt
It is Kondratiev-wave secular disinflation
context: The Cantillon effect: newly created money reaches some holders before others; the last to receive lose the most. Weimar concentrated that loss on savers and rentiers -- exactly the middle-class base of any liberal political order. Source: Grokipedia 'Cantillon effect' (2026-09-05).

question: Frederic Bastiat taught that every economic act has two sides: 'what is seen', the immediate visible effect, and 'what is not seen', the hidden or delayed damage. Germans lived one surface reality from day to day through the hyperinflation of 1921 to 1923, while a deeper catastrophe unfolded underneath. Which pair best fits Bastiat's split?
answer: Seen: money still being paid; Unseen: a generation's savings evaporating
choices: Seen: money still being paid; Unseen: a generation's savings evaporating
Seen: full employment in the factories; Unseen: rising real wages
Seen: rising exports abroad; Unseen: cheaper imports at home
Seen: political calm in Berlin; Unseen: heavier taxes on the rich
context: The wages kept arriving in nominal terms -- workers still got paid on Friday. What was invisible: every existing mark of savings was being systematically destroyed at the same time. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: A single mother earning $30,000 a year gets a $2,000 raise. The raise lifts her above a cutoff, and all of her government help, about $10,000 a year in food stamps, Medicaid and a housing voucher, stops at once. How does she come out?
answer: She is worse off by about $8,000
choices: She is better off by exactly $2,000
She is worse off by about $8,000
She is better off by $12,000
She is better off by $10,000
context: Because lost benefits can exceed added wages, a raise that increases earned income can decrease total household resources. The effective marginal rate on the raise dollar can exceed 100%. Source: Atlanta Fed CLIFF documentation (2018-).

question: Thomas Sowell pointed to a family fact that, he said, the welfare debate forgets. In census after census before the Second World War, one figure was higher for black Americans than for white Americans. It fell steeply from the 1960s on, a fall Sowell linked to that decade's new welfare programs. Which figure was it?
answer: The share of women who were married
choices: The share of women who were married
The share of adults holding a college degree
The average family income relative to whites
The homeownership rate
context: The Census Bureau's 2012 study of American marriage since 1890 found that black women were more often married than white women before the Second World War. From the 1960s the black marriage rate fell steeply, and by the 1980s black women were much less likely to be married than white women. Sowell argues that welfare programs which penalised marriage helped drive the change; other scholars give more weight to the loss of factory jobs and other causes.

question: A low earner in America picks up more hours, and her Earned Income Tax Credit grows with them, up to a limit. The credit has been in place since 1975. It is a check that climbs with her hours, instead of one that vanishes at her first raise. What is the main goal of that design?
answer: To make working pay more than not working
choices: To make working pay more than not working
To replace food stamps with one yearly cash payment
To move aid money from Washington to the states
To cap welfare spending at a fixed sum each year
context: The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) was established in 1975 as a targeted refundable tax credit for low-income working families. It carries the Friedman NIT idea partially into US law, though its own phase-out kinks contribute to some cliffs. Source: irs.gov (EITC history).

question: A family's income rose past 400 percent of the Federal Poverty Level, and all of its federal help with health-insurance premiums vanished at once. That was one of the biggest welfare cliffs in modern American policy, and a federal law of 2010 created it. Which law was it?
answer: The Affordable Care Act
choices: The Affordable Care Act
The Bipartisan Budget Act
The FAMILY Act
The SECURE Act
context: The ACA (2010) originally cut off premium subsidies at 400% FPL, creating a large cliff. The American Rescue Plan (2021) and Inflation Reduction Act (2022) temporarily removed the cliff through 2025. Source: healthcare.gov (ACA subsidy schedules).

question: A working parent takes a small raise and loses more in food stamps, Medicaid, housing aid and child-care subsidies than the raise pays in wages. Austrian and public-choice economists insist that this welfare cliff comes from no cruelty or corruption among federal officials, and that it would happen no matter which political party ran the agencies. What do they say causes it?
answer: Stacking many means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-outs
choices: Stacking many means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-outs
Setting one income cutoff that every federal program must share
Letting each state cut benefits whenever its budget runs short
Paying benefits as tax credits that arrive months after a raise
context: Each program is often reasonable in isolation. The cliff emerges when several programs phase out in the same income range without coordinated schedules. Friedman's NIT proposal addresses this by design; the current stack does not. Source: Friedman (1962); Mulligan (2012); Atlanta Fed CLIFF documentation.

question: An American muckraker, famous for his 1904 book The Shame of the Cities, went to Soviet Russia two years after the Bolshevik revolution, in 1919. That April he wrote to a friend: 'I have seen the future, and it works.' Who wrote it?
answer: Lincoln Steffens
choices: Lincoln Steffens
Upton Sinclair
H. L. Mencken
Walter Lippmann
context: In his 1931 autobiography the line he gives Bernard Baruch reads 'I have been over into the future, and it works'; the famous shorter wording comes from a letter of April 1919 to Marie Howe. Source: https://www.quotecounterquote.com/2010/06/i-have-seen-future-and-it-works.html.

question: Sidney and Beatrice Webb visited the USSR in 1932 and praised Stalin's five-year plans in a glowing book of 1935. The two were Fabians, British socialists who pushed for slow reform rather than violent revolution. They had also helped to found a well-known British university. Which university was it?
answer: The London School of Economics
choices: The London School of Economics
The University of Oxford
The University of Manchester
The University of Edinburgh
context: The LSE was founded in 1895 by the Webbs and other Fabians. Their 1935 book 'Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation?' was published by Longmans in London and New York. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sidney_and_Beatrice_Webb.

question: Beatrice Webb and her husband Sidney brought out a two-volume defense of Stalin's Soviet Union in 1935, called 'Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation?' They reissued it in 1937, with Stalin's Great Terror at its height, and the second edition made one change that mattered. What did the second edition do?
answer: Dropped the question mark
choices: Dropped the question mark
Added a subtitle referring to Trotsky
Removed all references to Stalin by name
Cut the length in half
context: The dropping happened at the peak of Stalin's Great Terror (1937-38). The Webbs are now interred in Westminster Abbey; Prime Minister Clement Attlee arranged their reinterment there in 1947. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Sidney_and_Beatrice_Webb.

question: Walter Duranty, who filed from Moscow for the New York Times, won the Pulitzer in 1932. He denied the Ukrainian famine in 1933, while a Welsh reporter, Gareth Jones, was reporting it truthfully. What line of Duranty's about the famine is quoted most often?
answer: 'You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs'
choices: 'You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs'
'I have seen the future, and it works'
'Peace in our time'
'The end of history'
context: Duranty used the line in 'Russians Hungry, But Not Starving', his New York Times article of 31 March 1933, which also waved away the famine reports as a 'big scare story'. Duranty's Pulitzer has never been rescinded. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Duranty.

question: Friedrich Hayek puzzled over why so many Western professors, journalists and novelists kept excusing Soviet-style planned economies. He took up the question in his 1944 book The Road to Serfdom, a warning that even democratic Western countries could slide into tyranny by embracing central economic planning. What did he think drew these thinkers?
answer: The appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project
choices: The appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project
The money Moscow quietly paid to friendly Western writers and editors
The flattery of guided tours and banquets laid on for famous visitors
The fear that criticism would cost them their friends on the political left
context: Hayek's point was that intellectuals professionally trained in orderly rational administration mistook the visible order of a planning bureaucracy for actual competence, while dismissing the invisible market coordination they could not see. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: Writing during World War 2, Friedrich Hayek warned the West in The Road to Serfdom that central planning of the kind used in Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union ends in tyranny. Its tenth chapter carries a title that has become one of the most-quoted phrases in political theory. What is that title?
answer: 'Why the Worst Get on Top'
choices: 'Why the Worst Get on Top'
'The End of History'
'The Great Transformation'
'The Managerial Revolution'
context: The chapter argues that totalitarian regimes reward specifically the personality traits Western intellectuals were slowest to recognize, because those traits are the opposite of the professional-administrative virtues the intellectuals themselves prized. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: A student reads that the Soviet archives, open for a generation now, have confirmed Stalin's Ukrainian famine and the Gulag. Yet Walter Duranty still holds his 1932 Pulitzer, the Webbs' book praising Stalin sits uncensored in libraries, and a muckraker's claim to have been over into the future still appears in his 1931 autobiography. A historian in F. A. Hayek's tradition points to one pattern. Which is it?
answer: The Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its apologetics
choices: The Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its apologetics
Prize boards judge a work only by the standards of the years it was written
Western readers still know too little of the archives to press for change
The apologists were too few and too obscure to need confronting
context: Historians in Hayek's tradition read it as an institutional failure: individual figures have been criticized, but the prestige structures around them (the Pulitzer, the LSE, Westminster Abbey, where the Webbs lie) have largely remained intact. Source: grokipedia.com/page/The_Road_to_Serfdom.

question: A merchant in the year 1300 takes a bag of gold coins from a stranger in payment. Before he hands over his cloth, he bites one coin and weighs the bag on his balance. Which property of good money is he relying on?
answer: Recognizability
choices: Recognizability
Divisibility
Portability
Durability
context: Recognizability -- verifiability by inspection, weight, and simple test -- is why traders learned the bite test for gold and the density check that distinguishes gold from pyrite. The six properties are a diagnostic checklist for any candidate money. Source: Grokipedia 'Money' (2026-09-05).

question: A trader holds a diamond in one hand and a gold coin in the other. For thousands of years gold has served as money and diamonds have not. Economists list the tests good money must pass. Which of them does the diamond fail?
answer: Divisibility -- diamonds cannot be split without loss of value
choices: Divisibility -- diamonds cannot be split without loss of value
Durability -- diamonds crack and wear away in everyday handling
Portability -- diamonds are too costly to carry safely on the road
Scarcity -- diamonds are dug up faster than traders can use them
context: A one-carat diamond is worth more than two half-carat diamonds. Splitting a diamond destroys value. Gold splits without loss because a gold coin has the same value per gram whether whole or halved. Source: Grokipedia 'Divisibility' (2026-09-05).

question: A European trader landed a cargo of cheap Indian Ocean shells in West Africa, one of the shipments that left the local money worthless. Cowries, seashells and clay tokens served as money in one place or another, and all of them seemed to work at first. Which property of good money did they fail on?
answer: Scarcity -- they can be gathered or fired at will
choices: Scarcity -- they can be gathered or fired at will
Durability -- they rot or rust rapidly
Divisibility -- they cannot be split cleanly
Recognizability -- traders cannot identify them on sight
context: The cowrie shell was money in West Africa for centuries; European traders eventually undermined the system by shipping cheap shells from the Indian Ocean. Any money that can be produced cheaply loses its ability to store value. Source: Grokipedia 'Cowrie shell money' (2026-09-05).

question: Saifedean Ammous compared gold, silver and bitcoin in his 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard using one simple test: divide how much of the total supply already exists by how much new supply gets added each year. Economists call the result stock-to-flow. What does this test measure about a form of money?
answer: How hard it is to make more of it, which protects its value over time
choices: How hard it is to make more of it, which protects its value over time
How widely it is used, which decides how easily it can be spent
How fast its price swings, which decides how risky it is to hold
How much it costs to store, which decides how much a saver keeps
context: Ammous's The Bitcoin Standard (2018) argues from stock-to-flow that bitcoin is the successor to gold as hard money. Source: Grokipedia 'Saifedean Ammous' (2026-09-05).

question: A student checks the stock-to-flow scale, which compares what already exists with each year's fresh supply, and finds gold near sixty, silver near twenty-two and farm goods far lower. Gold's lead rests on a single physical fact about the metal. What is that physical fact?
answer: Gold does not rust or rot, so nearly all of it ever mined is still around
choices: Gold does not rust or rot, so nearly all of it ever mined is still around
Gold is too soft for tools, so none of it is used up by industry
Gold lies so deep that mines can reach only a fixed amount each year
Gold is too heavy to ship far, so little of it ever leaves the vaults
context: Gold does not corrode or oxidize. A gold coin buried in 500 BC comes out shiny. The world's above-ground stock is roughly 200,000 tonnes; annual mining adds about 3,000 tonnes -- 1.5% of the total. Source: World Gold Council (goldhub.com).

question: A student reads across separate civilizations, Egyptian, Roman, Chinese, Indian and West African, and finds gold chosen as money again and again. Austrian and Bitcoin-standard writers draw from that pattern a test for any money that hopes to replace gold. What do they conclude?
answer: Gold won on physical properties, so a successor must beat it on one without losing others
choices: Gold won on physical properties, so a successor must beat it on one without losing others
Gold won on beauty alone, so a successor must look as fine in jewellery and coin
Gold won by royal decree, so a successor needs only a strong state to back it
Gold won along the trade routes, so a successor must first win over the big traders
context: The argument from convergence sets an engineering test for any candidate money: it must beat gold on at least one property (portability, divisibility, verifiability) without giving up any of the six. Source: Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018).

question: Bitcoin's builders set out in 2009 to pass the same six-part test of sound money that gold passes. They matched the metal on durability and on sameness from unit to unit. On three other counts, the argument runs, they went past anything gold can match. Which three improvements does Bitcoin offer?
answer: Finer divisibility, instant portability by wire, and verification by code
choices: Finer divisibility, instant portability by wire, and verification by code
Physical backing, government issuance, and legal-tender protection
Industrial uses, a physical form, and a supply that grows with demand
Lower fees, central-bank oversight, and a supply set by a miners' vote
context: Bitcoin matches gold's durability and fungibility, and the argument says it beats it on three counts: it splits to eight decimal places, travels at the speed of a wire transfer, and can be checked by anyone running the code, all under a fixed 21-million cap. Source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008).

question: Robert Heilbroner, a socialist all his life, wrote plainly in a 1990 magazine essay that Ludwig von Mises had been right. He gave a name to the results of Soviet pricing: mills turning out steel nobody bought, warehouses full of unsold shoes, shelves empty of anything people wanted. What phrase did he use?
answer: Grotesque misallocations of effort
choices: Grotesque misallocations of effort
Chronic underconsumption of finished goods
Unresolved contradictions between owner and worker
Persistent overaccumulation of surplus capital
context: Heilbroner conceded that the Soviet pricing methods had produced 'grotesque misallocations of effort' -- steel factories with no buyers, warehouses of unsalable shoes, chronic shortages of what people actually wanted -- exactly the pathology Mises had predicted seventy years earlier. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right.

question: China's leaders began letting farmers sell any crop above the state quota after December 1978, and harvests jumped within two seasons. Why did they jump?
answer: Farmers worked harder to keep more
choices: Farmers worked harder to keep more
The state paid for new tractors
Communes pooled land into big fields
Good weather followed bad harvests
context: The December 1978 Third Plenum is treated as the birth of the reform-and-opening-up era. The household responsibility system, which let a family keep what it grew beyond the quota, spread across China's farms by the early 1980s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up.

question: Don Lavoie argued in Rivalry and Central Planning, in 1985, that economists had met Mises's point about prices but never faced Hayek's point about knowledge. Later Austrians, Peter Boettke, Joseph Salerno and Guido Huelsmann among them, described a pattern in how the profession took the collapse of 1989. What pattern did they describe?
answer: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
choices: The profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict
The profession quietly withdrew all remaining market-socialist proposals by 1995
The profession credited the Austrians in its textbooks by the mid-1990s
The profession took up Hayek's point on knowledge and rebuilt its models on it
context: Lavoie, Salerno, Boettke, and Huelsmann observed the same pattern Thomas Kuhn described in 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' -- a discipline can accept the outside facts while continuing to teach the old textbook framing. That, they argued, is why market-socialist proposals keep reappearing in every generation. Source: www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning.

question: Ludwig von Mises warned in 1920 that a fully planned economy would end in shortages, gluts and waste. Robert Heilbroner, the socialist author of The Worldly Philosophers, conceded in 1990 that the long Soviet experiment had settled the matter. The Black Book of Communism counts about a hundred million dead under communist regimes worldwide. What question had the planned economies answered?
answer: Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
choices: Whether Marx's labour theory of value could be salvaged with better mathematics
Whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point
Whether socialist countries could avoid dependence on world trade
Whether workers' councils could substitute for private firms as legal owners
context: The 1920 essay had said no -- not because central planners lacked good intentions, but because the information needed to compare production plans exists only in the dispersed heads of the people doing the producing and consuming. The 20th-century death toll of Communism, put by the Black Book of Communism at roughly 100 million, was the price of running the experiment. Source: mises.org/mises-wire/socialist-robert-heilbroners-confession-1990-mises-was-right; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Book_of_Communism.

question: An English-speaking economist picked up a new volume in 1935 and met, for the first time, Ludwig von Mises's 1920 essay on whether planners can calculate. Friedrich Hayek had edited and introduced the collection. What effect did that translation and editing have?
answer: It set the terms of the whole planning-versus-markets debate for decades
choices: It set the terms of the whole planning-versus-markets debate for decades
It ended the debate at once, since the planners had no reply to offer
It went unread until the 1970s, when stagflation revived interest in it
It turned most English economists against planning before the war began
context: 'Collectivist Economic Planning: Critical Studies on the Possibilities of Socialism', edited by F.A. Hayek (Routledge, London, 1935). Hayek's own introductory essay 'The Nature and History of the Problem' framed the debate for a whole generation. Source: mises.org/library/book/collectivist-economic-planning.

question: A government department head sits down to fill out next year's funding request. His department's funding rises every year no matter how well its workers do, each rise brings him a bigger office and staff, and he never has to compete for customers. What is he most likely to ask for?
answer: An even bigger budget
choices: A smaller budget
An even bigger budget
The same budget again
A budget tied to results
context: William Niskanen (1933-2011) was a Chicago-trained economist who served in Nixon's OMB, sat on Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers from 1981 to 1985, at the end as acting chairman, and chaired the Cato Institute's board from 1985 to 2008. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Niskanen.

question: Instead of assuming that bureaucrats work for the public good or their agency's mission, William Niskanen asked what they actually gain over a career. Salary, prestige, staff and promotions, he found, all rise with one thing. Which thing did he say they really maximize?
answer: The size of their agency's budget
choices: The size of their agency's budget
The public's trust in their agency
The number of rules their agency writes
The length of their own time in office
context: Niskanen's model: salary, staff, prestige, perquisites, agency power, and promotion prospects are all positively correlated with agency budget. A bureaucrat rationally advancing his or her career therefore fights for a bigger budget. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 4.

question: William Niskanen studied why federal agencies keep growing year after year, whichever party holds the White House and whoever sits at the top of each one. What was his real claim about the growth?
answer: The career incentive structure rewards budget-expanding behavior
choices: The career incentive structure rewards budget-expanding behavior
Bureaucrats are captured by lobbyists for the industries they oversee
Bureaucrats grow agencies because voters keep demanding more services
Bureaucrats are less honest than people who work in private business
context: Niskanen models an INCENTIVE STRUCTURE, not a moral failing. Whatever an agency's official mission, the structure that rewards its staff systematically favors expansion. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface.

question: An agency director reads the good news: the disease his federal office was fighting has been pushed back and the program is complete. William Niskanen's model predicts that he will almost never announce that the mission is finished. He will find new priorities and new problems to grow into instead. What reason does the model give?
answer: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
choices: Announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts
New problems really do keep arising for every agency to tackle
Congress passes laws to keep agencies alive regardless of mission
Admitting the job is done would cost the agency the public's trust
context: A completed-mission announcement is against every staff member's career interest. The predictable behavior is instead mission creep -- redefining the mission as new problems the agency must address. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 5.

question: Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981, and his administration promised to shrink the federal government. His team fought for budget cuts, agency reorganizations and hiring freezes, and he attacked government bloat in dozens of speeches. Over his two full terms, what actually happened to the total number of federal civilian jobs?
answer: It barely moved from where it started
choices: It barely moved from where it started
It fell by roughly forty percent
It rose by roughly a hundred percent
It fell back to Depression-era levels
context: Federal civilian employment stayed essentially flat under Reagan (1981-89) despite aggressive rhetoric. Individual agency budgets fluctuated modestly; the total was very sticky. Niskanen predicts exactly this stickiness. Source: OPM historical federal civilian employment data (bea.gov, opm.gov).

question: Anthony Downs sorted the people inside every bureau into personality types for his 1967 book Inside Bureaucracy: climbers chasing promotion, conservers protecting their safe posts, zealots devoted to one cause, plus advocates and statesmen. From these patterns he drew one big teaching about a large bureaucracy. What is it?
answer: People inside government act on their own goals, just like people outside it
choices: People inside government act on their own goals, just like people outside it
People inside government put the public first once they are well trained
People inside government follow the rules, whatever their own goals may be
People inside government work hardest when their agency is smallest
context: Anthony Downs, Inside Bureaucracy (Little Brown, 1967). Downs classifies bureaucrats by mix of self-interest and mission-interest; Niskanen models the aggregate effect. The two frameworks fit together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Downs.

question: William Niskanen built a model in 1971 that treats agency chiefs as people looking after their own careers, not as selfless servants of the public. It predicts patterns no one would expect if agencies just served the public good. Which pattern is not one of his predictions?
answer: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
choices: Agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest
Agencies rarely announce that their mission is complete
Agencies with unclear performance metrics tend to grow fastest
Agencies grow during friendly administrations and shrink little under opposition
context: Niskanen predicts the OPPOSITE: agencies with UNCLEAR performance metrics grow fastest, because failure cannot be measured. Where failure IS measurable, budget increases become harder to justify. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), Chapter 6.

question: William Niskanen built his 1971 model around a bureau chief as self-interested as any businessman. The old assumption was that agencies simply serve the public. Niskanen's whole argument comes down to one sentence about what economics adds when applied to public employees. Which sentence is it?
answer: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions
choices: Assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions
Assuming bureaucratic competence leads to systematically wasteful budgets
Measuring agencies by their spending leads to systematically worse service
Paying officials market wages leads to systematically smaller agencies
context: Niskanen's contribution: give up the benevolent-planner assumption and predictions about bureau behavior become far more accurate. This is the symmetric application of standard economic reasoning to political actors. Source: Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (1971), preface and Chapter 12.

question: Europe's great powers mobilised for war at the turn of July and August 1914. Within days of one another they all did the same thing to their money, and the classical gold standard died in little more than a week. What did each do?
answer: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
choices: Suspended the redemption of paper money for gold
Devalued its currency by 50%
Nationalized its central bank
Adopted a fixed foreign-exchange peg
context: Russia's State Bank suspended gold payments on 27 July 1914, Germany's Reichsbank on 4 August and the Bank of France on 5 August, and the other belligerents followed within days. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_crisis_of_1914.

question: Europe's governments went to war in August 1914 with guns, shells and soldiers to pay for. While the promise to swap paper notes for gold still held, there were only two honest ways to raise the money. What were they?
answer: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
choices: Taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders
Requisitioning goods or seizing enemy property
Selling colonies or licensing trade monopolies
Devaluing the currency or issuing new coins
context: Under gold, states could raise money only by taxing (unpopular, slow) or borrowing (limited by lender willingness). Once off gold, they could print paper and defer the reckoning until after victory. Source: Grokipedia 'World War I reparations' (2026-09-05).

question: An Austrian economist in Vienna published a book called Nation, State, and Economy in 1919, just after the First World War. He argued that the printing press had hidden the war's cost: paid for honestly, it would have hurt sooner, and war-weariness would have set in much earlier. Who was he?
answer: Ludwig von Mises
choices: Ludwig von Mises
Friedrich Hayek
Joseph Schumpeter
John Maynard Keynes
context: Mises wrote that by the issue of paper money not one cannon or grenade more was produced than could have been made without the printing press; what inflation did was hide the war's real cost from the people paying it. Source: https://mises.org/online-book/nation-state-and-economy/war-and-economy/4-economys-war-costs-and-inflation.

question: Winston Churchill, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, put Britain back on gold in 1925, so that paper pounds could again be traded for gold on demand. He fixed the pound at a rate that left it too strong on world markets and pushed deflation, wage cuts, and unemployment on British coal miners and factory workers. At what rate did he fix it?
answer: The prewar 1914 parity
choices: The prewar 1914 parity
The market rate of early 1925
Ten percent below the 1914 parity
A rate agreed at Genoa in 1922
context: On advice from Bank of England officials, Churchill returned sterling at the 1914 rate of $4.86, even though the pound's real value had fallen. British exports became uncompetitive; unemployment stayed high through the late 1920s. Source: Grokipedia 'Return to gold' (2026-09-05).

question: John Maynard Keynes went after Winston Churchill in print in 1925, after the Chancellor of the Exchequer put the pound back on gold at a rate many economists thought too high. Keynes's weapon was a short pamphlet. What was it called?
answer: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
choices: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
The Return to Gold: A Warning
The End of Sterling
The Twenty-Fifth of April
context: Keynes's 1925 pamphlet echoed the title of his 1919 attack on the Versailles Treaty, 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'. Keynes and the Austrians agreed about the 1925 decision (both thought it wrong) though for different theoretical reasons. Source: Grokipedia 'John Maynard Keynes' (2026-09-05).

question: Europe's warring powers all did the same thing to their money within days of one another in the summer of 1914, as their armies marched. Austrian economists draw from that move a thesis about money, war and the power of the state. What is it?
answer: Sound money limits state power, and war-making states always want to escape that limit
choices: Sound money limits state power, and war-making states always want to escape that limit
Sound money is just a technical rule with no effect on politics or wars
Sound money encourages military spending by making wars cheaper to fund
Sound money is preferred by governments and only opposed by private banks
context: A state bound to pay gold must tax or borrow openly to fight; once off gold it can print. Mises argued in 1919 that inflation hid the war's real cost from the people paying it, and Austrian writers read the later escapes from gold the same way. Source: Mises, Nation, State, and Economy (1919).

question: Armies across Europe mobilised in August 1914. Writers in the Austrian school refuse to file the 20th century's industrial wars under politics and its monetary breakdowns under money. They read the two as bound together at the deepest level. Which statement best captures that link?
answer: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
choices: The industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event
The wars caused monetary collapse and the collapse then caused more wars
The monetary breakdowns came first and made the great wars likely to start
The wars and the monetary breakdowns shared a cause in falling world trade
context: Austrian writers build the counterfactual on Mises's argument of 1919 that inflation hid the war's cost: without the printing press, war-weariness would have come much sooner. On this reading the century's political and monetary catastrophes share one root. Source: Mises, Nation, State, and Economy (1919).

question: Mao Zedong forced peasant farmers off their family plots and onto giant collective farms called people's communes in his Great Leap Forward. Village grain was hauled off to feed the cities and to sell abroad for machinery. Yang Jisheng, a schoolboy in Hubei, believed the party's denial and understood only later. What was the main result out in the countryside?
answer: The worst famine in history -- tens of millions starved
choices: The worst famine in history -- tens of millions starved
A record harvest -- the communes doubled the grain crop
A slow decline -- harvests slipped a little each year
A shift to cities -- most peasants left the land for good
context: Yang was born 1940 in Hubei province. Dikotter, Banister, and Ashton are Western scholars of the same famine; Yang was the insider-journalist who counted from within. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: Yang Jisheng, a journalist at China's state news agency, published a massive book called Tombstone on the famine of 1958 to 1962, when Mao Zedong's forced collectivization starved tens of millions of peasants. His entire life project was triggered by a specific personal event during the famine. What was it?
answer: His own father starved to death in the family's village
choices: His own father starved to death in the family's village
His own village was burned in a Red Guard raid
His own mother was denounced as a class enemy
His own house was seized by the local commune
context: The party had denied there was a famine; the young Yang, then at boarding school and a Communist Youth League member, believed it. The man he called his father was in truth the uncle who raised him; Yang brought him rice, but he was too weak to eat and died three days later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Jisheng_(journalist).

question: Yang Jisheng spent seven years secretly digging through provincial Communist Party archives, adding up county death records the Party never wanted foreigners to see. He was counting the peasants who starved in the Great Leap Forward, Mao Zedong's forced collectivization drive, after their grain was seized to feed cities and export markets. He published in Hong Kong in 2008. Roughly what figure did he arrive at?
answer: About 36 million
choices: About 36 million
About 3 million
About 300,000
About 300 million
context: Prior Western estimates (Judith Banister 1987, Basil Ashton 1984, both around 30 million) had been top-down demographic estimates from national census gaps. Yang's was the first bottom-up count from actual provincial records. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Great_Chinese_Famine.

question: Judith Banister and Basil Ashton had already estimated in the 1980s that tens of millions died in the Great Leap Forward famine that Mao Zedong's forced collectivization had caused, subtracting expected births from later census counts. Then in 2008 Yang Jisheng published Tombstone, and he did something they could not. What was his methodological breakthrough?
answer: He drew on internal party archives that no outsider could see
choices: He drew on internal party archives that no outsider could see
He counted from letters that survivors smuggled out to relatives abroad
He counted from grave markers surveyed by hand in every county
He counted from aerial photographs of abandoned villages
context: Yang's Xinhua credentials and personal connections gave him access to provincial archives that had never been available to Western scholars. The bottom-up method vindicated the older top-down estimates and added specificity province by province. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Tombstone_(book).

question: Harvard's Nieman Fellows chose Yang Jisheng for their 2016 Lyons Award, an honour for conscience and integrity in journalism, for his archive-based history of the Great Leap Forward famine. Officials from Xinhua, the state news agency he had served for decades, then met with him. What did they tell him?
answer: That he was forbidden to travel to the United States to accept it
choices: That he was forbidden to travel to the United States to accept it
That he could go to Harvard only if a state minder went with him
That he would be charged with revealing state secrets to foreigners
That he could accept it in person but must not speak to the press
context: Yang had flown to New York in 2013 to accept the Manhattan Institute's Hayek Prize for Tombstone. In 2016 Xinhua officials told him he was forbidden to travel, and no public reason was given; PEN America condemned the ban. Tombstone remains banned on the mainland. Source: https://pen.org/press-release/pen-america-condemns-travel-ban-on-chinese-author-yang-jisheng/.

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz sat in the audience in Chicago in November 2002 as Ben Bernanke, a Federal Reserve governor, spoke at Friedman's ninetieth-birthday conference. He took up the charge their book of 1963 had made about the Depression. What was that charge?
answer: The Fed caused the Great Depression by failing to lend to banks in the crisis
choices: Import tariffs caused the Great Depression by strangling international trade
The Fed caused the Great Depression by failing to lend to banks in the crisis
The Fed caused the Great Depression by feeding a credit boom in the 1920s
Rigid wage rules under President Hoover caused the Great Depression
context: The Friedman-Schwartz thesis is now standard even inside the Fed. The remaining dispute is not whether the Fed failed but what the correct alternative response would have been -- which is where Austrian critics part ways with the monetarist prescription. Source: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History (1963); Rothbard, America's Great Depression (1963).

question: Ben Bernanke warned his Chicago audience in November 2002 that he was about to misuse his standing as a spokesman for the Federal Reserve. He closed his talk by turning to Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz in the audience at Friedman's ninetieth-birthday conference. What did he tell them?
answer: You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
choices: You were partly right. We made errors, and we have learned from them
You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again
You may be right. But the evidence is not yet decisive, and we will study it
We agree in part. But the fiscal side mattered just as much as we did
context: Bernanke abused (his word) his official status as a Fed representative to deliver the extraordinary concession directly to the 90-year-old Friedman. The full text is on federalreserve.gov. Source: Grokipedia 'Ben Bernanke' (2026-09-05).

question: Ben Bernanke, chairman of the Federal Reserve by 2008, met the housing bust six years after his speech at Milton Friedman's ninetieth birthday, as banks that had lent against houses teetered. Austrian-school economists attacked the way he met the crisis. What did he do that they attacked?
answer: Launched massive quantitative easing and held interest rates near zero
choices: Launched massive quantitative easing and held interest rates near zero
Let failing banks close one after another, as the Fed had in 1931
Raised interest rates sharply into the recession to defend the dollar
Sold off the Fed's bonds to shrink the money supply in the panic
context: The Austrian critique: in avoiding the 1930s error, Bernanke made an opposite one, keeping rates artificially low for years, mispricing capital across the economy and, the critics argue, laying the ground for later inflation. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012, updated 2014).

question: Anna Schwartz, Milton Friedman's co-author, gave the Wall Street Journal an interview in October 2008, at ninety-two, about Ben Bernanke's handling of the collapse; Friedman, dead since 2006, missed the crisis. What was her assessment?
answer: That he was fighting the last war, with tools meant for the 1930s
choices: That he was fighting the last war, with tools meant for the 1930s
That his rate cuts would restore price stability within a year
That he had moved too slowly and should have lent far more
That he should hand the crisis over to Congress and the Treasury
context: In 'Bernanke Is Fighting the Last War', Brian Carney's interview in the Wall Street Journal of 18 October 2008, Schwartz argued that the crisis was no replay of the 1930s: lending froze because lenders doubted borrowers' balance sheets, not for want of liquidity. Source: Wall Street Journal, 18 October 2008, reprinted at the-masterblog.blogspot.com/2008/10/weekend-interview-wsjcom.html.

question: Ben Bernanke had given twenty years at Princeton to studying how the Federal Reserve let banks and money collapse in the 1930s. As its chairman in 2008 he let no such cascade of failures run, yet Austrian critics charged that he had flunked another test. What recognition about how central banks learn does his story press?
answer: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next
choices: The lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next
Every crisis is unique, so no lesson from the last one applies to the next
Critics will charge any chairman with failure, whatever he does in a crisis
Central banks learn only from crises abroad, never from their own past
context: Austrian critics argue that by avoiding the 1930s mistake Bernanke made a different one, holding rates near zero for years. On their reading the doctrine forged in one crisis becomes the blind spot of the next. Source: Peter Schiff, The Real Crash (2012).

question: Robert Mugabe's government began seizing farms in 2000 from the experienced commercial farmers who had run them for decades. It handed the land to political supporters, many of whom had never grown a crop. What was the likely result for the country's food supply?
answer: The country went from feeding itself to needing food aid
choices: The country went from feeding itself to needing food aid
Food grew cheaper as the new owners competed to sell
Harvests rose as more families farmed land of their own
Grain exports climbed to their highest level in decades
context: Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017. The fast-track land reform of 2000 onward wrecked commercial farming, and with it much of the country's export earnings and tax base. Source: Grokipedia 'Land reform in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: A shopper in Zimbabwe handed over one brand-new banknote in January 2009, worth around 30 US dollars on its first day in circulation. President Robert Mugabe's Reserve Bank had just printed it, after years of nonstop money-printing, and it has been photographed in economics textbooks ever since. What was its face value?
answer: 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
choices: 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
1 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
10 billion Zimbabwe dollars
1 quintillion Zimbabwe dollars
context: The 100,000,000,000,000-Zimbabwe-dollar note is one of the largest denominations ever issued; only Hungary's last pengo notes of 1946 carried bigger numbers. The BBC put its worth at around US$30 on its first day. In 2009 the country suspended its own currency and let the US dollar and others take over. Cato senior fellow Steve Hanke had tracked the hyperinflation in real time. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwean_one_hundred_trillion_dollar_note; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_pengő.

question: A farmer in Zimbabwe refused to sell his food for Zimbabwean dollars in 2008, because by evening the paper would be worthless. Prices were doubling every day under President Robert Mugabe's printing spree. Ordinary Zimbabweans dropped the local money and switched to foreign currencies. Which foreign currencies did they pick up?
answer: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
choices: The US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula
The British pound and the euro only
The Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan
The Kenyan shilling and the Egyptian pound
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans used whichever foreign currency they could get. The government formally accepted the dollarization; the Zimbabwe dollar was demonetized in June 2015. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: A Zimbabwean shopkeeper was using US dollars for everyday trade when the Reserve Bank formally killed the old currency in 2015, yet the giant banknotes of the hyperinflation did not disappear. They remain the most famous surviving artifact of a money gone wild. What is the new role of these banknotes today?
answer: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
choices: Souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets
Legal tender in Zimbabwe's tourist markets at a fixed rate
Scrap paper pulped and recycled into new banknotes
Exhibits held only in museums and central-bank vaults
context: A Zimbabwean 100-trillion-dollar note now sells for roughly $2 to $15 USD on collector sites -- a physical, cheap, permanent reminder of what fiat-currency collapse looks like. Source: collector-market listings on eBay and specialist numismatic sites (2020-2025).

question: Robert Mugabe seized productive farms, and in June 2007 he ordered every shopkeeper to cut prices in half or go to jail. That order aimed at a symptom, rising prices, and ignored what was driving them. Austrian economists tell a simple story of how a hyperinflation is born, and Zimbabwe followed it exactly. Which two things combined to cause Zimbabwe's money crash?
answer: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
choices: A fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it
A trade deficit from failed exports plus a currency pegged to gold
A shortage of workers plus wage rises that unions forced on employers
A political crisis plus a Western embargo that cut off imports
context: The land-seizure program destroyed the productive tax base. The Reserve Bank was ordered to fund the state anyway. Money-printing without a growing real economy produces the Cantillon-effect destruction of savers, then hyperinflation, then abandonment. The classic Friedman monetary diagnosis: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. The price ceiling attacked the symptom (visible prices) while the disease (money creation) continued and accelerated. Sources: Grokipedia 'Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05); grokipedia.com/page/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe.

question: President Robert Mugabe printed the Zimbabwe dollar to death in the late 2000s, until prices were doubling about once a day. The way its story ended shows what money really is at bottom. What actually happened to Zimbabwe's money system at the end?
answer: Ordinary people switched to foreign money before the government allowed it
choices: Ordinary people switched to foreign money before the government allowed it
The government re-anchored the Zimbabwe dollar to gold, and it recovered
The IMF imposed a new central-bank currency on the country by treaty
A Southern African currency union absorbed the Zimbabwe dollar
context: By 2009 Zimbabweans were already pricing goods in USD, rand, and pula in the informal economy. The government then formalized what citizens had already done. Money is what people accept; the government simply catches up. Source: Grokipedia 'Dollarization of Zimbabwe' (2026-09-05).

question: Frederic Bastiat taught readers to compare what is seen from a government policy with what quietly stays unseen. President Robert Mugabe's Reserve Bank printed money at a runaway pace in 2008, and inflation ran out of control. Which pairing best captures the split Bastiat would draw for Zimbabwe?
answer: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
choices: Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed
Seen: land handed to landless families; Unseen: thousands of new jobs in the cities
Seen: shops full of imported goods; Unseen: a slow decline in the country's exports
Seen: farmers paid record prices for grain; Unseen: a quiet rise in foreign reserves
context: The visible policy achievement (paying the army and civil service) hid the invisible destruction (every existing bank balance and cash holding in the country evaporating). The Cantillon effect on a national scale. Source: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen (1850).

question: A shopkeeper watches bread prices climb week after week, because the government prints money nonstop to pay its bills. The president blames the shops and orders every one to halve its prices, or its owner goes to jail. What happens in the stores?
answer: Shelves empty because selling below cost bankrupts stores
choices: Prices stay low because shops trim their staff and costs
Shelves empty because selling below cost bankrupts stores
Shelves fill because the low prices draw in new suppliers
Prices stay low because the new money covers the loss
context: The scene is Zimbabwe in June 2007, when Robert Mugabe's government ordered prices cut by about half. Police and army units enforced the order in Harare and Bulawayo supermarkets, arresting shopkeepers who did not comply. Source: mg.co.za/article/2007-07-03-shelves-empty-in-zim-amid-govt-crackdown/.

question: Shoppers in Harare and Bulawayo stripped the supermarket shelves bare after Robert Mugabe ordered prices cut roughly in half on June 26, 2007, to fight Zimbabwe's runaway inflation. But the empty shelves were only the start, and a bigger effect soon followed. What happened next, within weeks?
answer: Food factories began to shut, unable to produce at the mandated prices
choices: Food factories began to shut, unable to produce at the mandated prices
The central bank raised interest rates sharply to defend the currency
The IMF signed an emergency lending program with the government
Neighboring Botswana closed its border to stop the smuggling
context: The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries had warned that forced cuts would deepen manufacturers' troubles, with industry already working at about a third of capacity; the biggest bakeries said they would stop baking, since no firm can make a loaf at a mandated price below the cost of the flour and fuel. Source: https://www.thezimbabwean.co/2007/07/bakeries-close-down/ ; mg.co.za/article/2007-06-26-zim-retailers-defy-govt-orders-to-cut-prices.

question: A high-school student asks a follower of Friedrich Hayek, who studied how price signals coordinate an economy, what makes Zimbabwe so useful for teaching how price controls fail. Robert Mugabe had ordered every shop there to cut prices in half in June 2007 or face jail, and the shelves emptied. The economist points to one specific property of the case. Which property?
answer: The whole chain from decree to empty shelves ran in days, not years
choices: The whole chain from decree to empty shelves ran in days, not years
The order covered a single product, so its effect was easy to isolate
The government kept careful records that let economists measure each loss
No other cause was at work, since the money supply stayed steady
context: Most price-control failures unfold over years and can be argued about. Zimbabwe's shelves were bare within days of the order of 26 June 2007, and the closures followed within weeks: decree, the low legal price on the label, the goods vanishing, the queues, the shut factories. Source: mg.co.za/article/2007-07-03-shelves-empty-in-zim-amid-govt-crackdown/.

question: Neighbors in Houston, Texas, gather to keep a smelly chemical plant from moving in next to a school. Most big American cities would settle it with zoning, lines on a map that separate homes, stores and factories, but most of Houston has none. What might a no-zoning neighborhood use instead?
answer: Private agreements written into each home's deed
choices: A citywide vote on each new factory or store
Private agreements written into each home's deed
Fees the county charges for building near homes
A state agency that draws the city's land map
context: Houston, Texas is the largest US city without a conventional zoning code. Land-use control there is done through private deed restrictions, not city ordinance. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Zoning_in_Houston.

question: Two economists sat down in 2002 to write a paper on why apartments in New York and Boston cost so much more to buy than to build. They set the brick-and-mortar cost beside the sale price. The gap, sometimes 50 percent or more, showed what strict zoning laws cost city renters, they argued. Which pair of economists wrote that paper?
answer: Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko
choices: Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz
Paul Krugman and Enrico Moretti
Raj Chetty and John Friedman
context: Glaeser (Harvard) and Gyourko (Wharton) published 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' as NBER working paper 8835 in 2002 and in the FRBNY Economic Policy Review in 2003. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: A homeowner argues that the rule allowing only single-family houses on her street protects the neighborhood's character. Frederic Bastiat, the French economist of the 1800s, had a famous method for claims like hers. He always asked what cost a rule carries that nobody actually sees. Applied to zoning, which unseen cost does his method point to?
answer: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
choices: The apartments and houses the code prevented from being built
The published municipal permit fees
The construction jobs on the buildings that were built
The listed prices of the homes that already exist
context: Bastiat's move from That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen (1850): existing homes and their prices are visible; the never-built housing, the families priced out of the metro area, and the 2-hour commuters are the invisible casualties. Source: bastiat.org.

question: A worker in a cheaper town gives up on moving to a growing American city, where strict zoning codes keep housing scarce and expensive. Economists point out that workers like him are hurt the most, and still the codes stay tight for decades. What pattern of local politics best explains why, in city after city?
answer: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
choices: Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot
Builders fund local campaigns to keep rival builders out of the market
Renters outnumber owners and vote for strict codes to hold rents down
State legislators write local codes and rarely visit the cities they rule
context: Concentrated benefit + dispersed cost with a franchise twist: existing owners benefit from constrained supply and vote for it; the priced-out do not live in the city yet, so their preferences carry no votes. Source: nber.org/papers/w8835.

question: A Californian with a single-family lot won the right in 2021 to split it and build up to four homes, when Senate Bill 9 overrode city codes that had banned anything but one house per lot. By the ordinary logic of supply and demand, what should this law do to housing prices in those cities?
answer: Push prices down over time by allowing more homes to be built where demand is highest
choices: Push prices down over time by allowing more homes to be built where demand is highest
Push prices up because each new unit adds demand for land
Have no effect on prices, since zoning rules do not affect the market
Push prices down only in rural areas where lots are already large
context: California SB 9 (signed September 2021, effective January 2022) plus SB 10 gave the YIMBY movement a big statewide preemption win. Source: grokipedia.com/page/California_Senate_Bill_9.
